title_r: The contribution of stimulus frequency and spatial attention to the N2 and P3 in Go/Nogo: A multilab replication and new analyses
abstract_r: EEG studies show that stimuli requiring withholding a response (Nogo) elicit larger frontal N2 and frontocentral P3 event-related potentials (ERPs) than stimuli requiring a response (Go). However, the functional significance of these components remains debated due to overlapping neural processes and potential confounds in Go/Nogo tasks. One concern is that Nogo trials are typically less frequent than Go trials to induce a stronger response tendency. Since N2 and P3 are modulated by stimulus frequency, some argue that Nogo effects may reflect a response mismatch signal from infrequent Nogo trials. To test this, Eimer (1993) manipulated Go/Nogo trial frequency, using a 75/25 ratio in Experiment 1 and a 50/50 ratio in Experiment 2. While the N2 and P3 effects were numerically larger in Experiment 1, they remained robust in Experiment 2, with both components showing greater amplitudes for Nogo trials. These findings contradict the response mismatch hypothesis and emphasize the importance of equating trial frequency in Go/Nogo studies. Eimer (1993) also manipulated spatial attention to determine whether the N2 effect reflects an automatic (i.e., attention-independent) process. Results showed that N2 effects were modulated by attentional cues, ruling out a purely automatic process and highlighting the role of processes that affect initial stimulus detection and discrimination in these tasks. The present study replicates Eimer’s Experiment 2 from and assess the robustness of the results across analysis pipelines. Moreover, it will extend the original analyses by determining whether 50/50 Go/Nogo paradigms reliably induce prepotent response tendencies. As part of the #EEGManyLabs project, 5 labs will independently replicate the original study, ensuring high statistical power. Results will be integrated via meta-analysis, offering insights into the replicability of classic EEG findings and N2/P3 sensitivity to stimulus frequency and spatial attention in Go/Nogo tasks. The large dataset will serve as a valuable resource for future meta-analyses.

title_r: Using EEG to test if spoken image labels propel subliminal images into consciousness
abstract_r: This preregistered study will investigate whether linguistic information is able to influence low-level visual perception. We claim that many pre-existing studies supporting this view have significant shortcomings: in brief, these studies confuse measures of objective performance with that of subjective experience, and cannot exclude the possibility that their observed effects might have been mediated by post-sensory processes instead (e.g., semantics, memory). Our proposed paradigm combines elements from two published studies by Sekar et al. (2011) and Lupyan and Ward (2013). Participants (N = 18) will observe and rate visual targets of fixed intensity corresponding to their 50% identification threshold; visual targets are preceded by matching and mismatched spoken verbal cues. For every target presented, participants carry out an identification task and rate their subjective experience (“didn’t see”, “couldn’t identify”, “unsure”, and “sure”). If verbal cues can influence subliminal visual information, we ought to observe improved identification of targets that were rated with “didn’t see”. In addition, we will record encephalographic (EEG) signals to target stimuli. We aim to replicate the consciousness related evoked potential identified by Sekar et al. (2011), which was originally observed in MEG and enhanced in trials associated with full/partial awareness (“couldn’t identify”, “unsure”, and “sure”). We will also test if matching verbal cues increase the amplitude of this potential in the same manner as conscious perception.

title_r: Error processing and religious conviction: A multi-lab replication
abstract_r: One function of religion might be to reduce cognitive conflict and anxiety. In a highlycited paper, Inzlicht and colleagues’ Study 1 (2009) assessed the association between selfreported religious zeal and conflict monitoring. Conflict monitoring was measured using the error-related negativity (ERN), an event-related potential that is sensitive to the conflict between an erroneous behavioral response and cognitive representation/knowledge of the correct response. Results showed that individuals with higher levels of self-reported religious zeal had smaller ERNs on a color-word Stroop task, suggesting less cognitive conflict when faced with opposing response tendencies leading to errors. In addition, individuals higher in religious zeal were slower and more accurate on incongruent trials, suggesting deliberate responding in which they sacrificed speed for accuracy. Work that has examined closely related concepts (e.g., religious fundamentalism) has failed to corroborate Inzlicht and colleagues’ (2009) findings, though other work has provided broad support for the original results. No direct replication of Inzlicht and colleagues (2009) has been attempted. As part of the #EEGManyLabs initiative (Pavlov et al., 2021), we will perform an international, multi-site replication of Study 1 from Inzlicht and colleagues (2009).

title_r: Dementia mindset of caregivers providing residential care for older persons: study protocol for a replication study on the validation of the Dementia Mindset Scale
abstract_r: INTRODUCTION: Professional caregivers' perspectives on dementia and on people living with dementia (PlwD) can influence their feelings, judgements and behaviours in work situations, for example, how they think about symptoms, disease progression and the impact on a person's quality of life. Their individual dementia mindset, which can be investigated with the 12-item Dementia Mindset Scale (DMS), might influence job satisfaction, work-related well-being and person-centred care. The aim of the proposed replication study is to confirm the results of the original study of the DMS and to test whether a malleable mindset is correlated with higher levels of caregiver education, dementia-specific professional experience/competence and dementia knowledge. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: Professional caregivers in residential care facilities for older persons who work directly with PlwD will be asked to answer an anonymous web-based online survey. The survey encompasses five standardised questionnaires: the DMS, the Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale, the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory, the Job-related Affective Well-being Scale and the Sense of Competence in Dementia Care Staff Scale. In addition, job satisfaction, the educational background, professional experience and work situation are surveyed. For replication, the analyses will re-evaluate the psychometric properties (structural validity, model fit, internal consistency and predictive validity) by applying descriptive statistics, regression analysis, confirmatory factor analysis and correlation analysis. The additional analyses will use descriptive statistics, regression analysis and correlation analysis. Rasch analysis will be used to rank the difficulty of the items. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This study was approved by the ethics committee of the German Society of Nursing Science (ID number 23-004). No personal information will be gathered. The results of the study will be distributed nationally and internationally through peer-reviewed academic journals, conferences, institutional websites and journals for nursing care practice.

title_r: Computational Study Protocol: Leveraging Synthetic Data to Validate a Benchmark Study for Differential Abundance Tests for 16S Microbiome Sequencing Data
abstract_r: <ns4:p>Background The utility of synthetic data in benchmark studies depends on its ability to closely mimic real-world conditions and to reproduce results obtained from experimental data. Here, we evaluate the performance of differential abundance tests for 16S metagenomic data. Building on the benchmark study by Nearing et al. (1), who assessed 14 differential abundance tests using 38 experimental datasets in a case-control design, we validate their findings by generating synthetic datasets that mimics the experimental data. We will employ statistical tests to rigorously assess the similarity between synthetic and experimental data and to validate the conclusions on the performance of these tests drawn by Nearing et al. (1). This protocol adheres to the SPIRIT guidelines and is, to our knowledge, the first of its kind in computational benchmark studies. Methods We replicate Nearing et al.’s (1) methodology, incorporating synthetic data simulated using two distinct tools, mirroring each of the 38 experimental datasets. Equivalence tests will be conducted on 43 data characteristics comparing synthetic and experimental data, complemented by principal component analysis for overall similarity assessment. The 14 differential abundance tests will be applied to both synthetic and experimental datasets, evaluating the consistency of significant feature identification and the number of significant features per tool. Correlation analysis and multiple regression will explore how differences between synthetic and experimental data characteristics may affect the results. Conclusions Synthetic data enables the validation of findings through controlled experiments. We assess how well synthetic data replicates experimental data, validate previous findings and delineate the strengths and limitations of synthetic data in benchmark studies. Moreover, to our knowledge this is the first computational benchmark study to systematically incorporate synthetic data for validating differential abundance methods while strictly adhering to a pre-specified study protocol following SPIRIT guidelines, contributing significantly to transparency, reproducibility, and unbiased research.</ns4:p>

title_r: Replication of “Nano-Flares: Probes for Transfection and mRNA Detection in Living Cells”
abstract_r: In hundreds of articles published over the past two decades, nanoparticles have been described as probes for sensing and imaging of a variety of intracellular cytosolic targets. However, nanoparticles generally enter cells by endocytosis with only a small fraction reaching the cytosol. Most of those articles do not describe the mechanisms of nanoparticles entry into the cell and therefore the paradox of sensing a target in the cytosol when most particles do not access that compartment remains. To address this paradox, we are initiating a replication project of some of the most influential articles in this field with the aim of confirming their ability to detect their targets and getting additional insights into their intracellular localisation. This article is a pre-registered report for the second replication of this project, namely the replication of Seferos et al ‘Nano-Flares: Probes for Transfection and mRNA Detection in Living Cells’. To achieve our aim, we will carry out both a direct replication of the experiments in the original article, with the addition of some experiments and controls (in particular optical and electron microscopy). We hope that this study will contribute to a better understanding of the intracellular fate of nanoparticles and, with the help of the scientific community, help set standards in the design and reporting of studies in this field.

title_r: The connection between articulatory skill and higher-level executive function in monolinguals and bilinguals
abstract_r: While the existence of a bilingual advantage in higher-level executive function remains controversial, recent studies showed bilinguals consistently outperform monolinguals in learning new patterns of pronunciation (in both natural or artificially constructed novel dialects). Since audition and articulatory control are involved in this type of learning, the question arises to what extent these lower-level functions are enhanced in people with superior performance on phonetic learning tasks. Dugaillard & Spinu (2019) found that sequential bilinguals outperformed monolinguals and simultaneous bilinguals on a tongue-twister task (Goldrick & Blumstein 2006, McMillan&Corley 2010), suggesting an advantage in articulatory skill. In the current study, we aim to replicate the original findings with a new group of bilinguals and further explore the connection of articulatory skill with one aspect of executive function (i.e. interference/conflict resolution). The experimental tasks include (1) reading artificially constructed tongue-twisters such as “kifkivkivkif” three times in succession, matching a 150 bps rhythm on a metronome, and (2) a classic Simon task asking participants to react or inhibit their response to congruent and incongruent stimuli. We expect the findings to shed more light on the bilingual advantage phenomenon and the connection between lower- and higher-level cognitive functions in both populations.

title_r: Effects of Spatial Attention on Visuocortical Processing: A Multi-Laboratory Replication of Clark & Hillyard (1996)
abstract_r: Whether selective attention alters initial sensory processing or instead only operates at higher cortical stages (often referred to as early vs. late selection) is a foundational question in cognitive neuroscience. Investigating the influence of covert visual selective attention, Clark and Hillyard (1996) found that directed attention modulated the amplitude of several early components (P1 and N1) of the visual event-related potential (ERP) derived from the ongoing electroencephalogram (EEG). However, attended and non-attended visual stimuli did not produce statistically different amplitudes in the C1 or P2 components. Dipole source estimation of the neural locus of these ERPs indicated that the C1 originated in primary (striate) visual cortex (V1), while the later components primarily arose from extrastriate visuocortical areas. Together, these results led to the conclusion that sustained spatial attention enhances the sensory gain of early visual processing in V1 via feedback projections from the extrastriate visual cortex where the P1 and N1 are generated. Despite the influential nature of this original work in EEG and cognitive neuroscience more broadly, recent research has reignited the debate on which stage of the visual processing hierarchy is influenced by attention. As part of the #EEGManyLabs project (Pavlov et al., 2021), we will be revisiting this issue by conducting a multi-site, high-powered direct replication of Clark and Hillyard (1996).

title_r: Reversal or no reversal, that is the question – A conceptual replication of cross-cultural spatial-numerical associations
abstract_r: Reading direction is a central determinant of spatial–numerical associations, yet evidence from right-to-left (RL) readers remains inconsistent, ranging from weakened to reversed spatial-numerical associations (SNAs). Shaki et al. (2009) provided the only systematic cross-cultural comparison controlling for reading direction of both words and digits. They reported canonical SNAs in Canadian left-to-right (LR) readers, no SNAs in Hebrew readers with mixed habits (RL words, LR digits), and a reversed SNAs in Palestinian adults with consistent RL reading. Subsequent studies produced mixed results for populations with similar reading profiles, potentially reflecting uncontrolled bilingualism, differing directional habits, and culturally shaped spatial routines, such as object counting and finger counting. Given the theoretical importance of a reverse SNAs and the absence of a successful replication of this finding in standard parity tasks, the present study replicates Shaki et al. (2009), using the refined go/no-go methodology while additionally documenting participants’ object- and finger-counting preferences. We will test German LR readers, Israeli mixed-direction readers, and Palestinian RL readers with adequately powered samples (n = 39 per subgroup). This replication will clarify whether and how culturally transmitted directional habits contribute to spatial–numerical mappings.

title_r: Closing the attentional window - exp 2
abstract_r: Our first experiment was a conceptual replication of Sana and Carpenter (2023) experiment one. They found that when material at the end of the lesson was tested there was larger benefit to non-pretested material and less of a benefit to pretested material, in comparison to when pretested questions were at the beginning. This was close to replicating, however the interaction was not significant. Exploratory analyses suggested that the main influencing factor was the passage participants read. They proposed that when participants are pretested this opens a attentional window that increases attention on all material until the answers are found. When the pretested material is at the beginning there is no, or reduced, benefit to non-pretested information. In contrast, when it is at the end of the lesson the material before the pretested information is attended to more closely which in turn benefits memory after a short delay. Participants will study one long expository text about Yellowstone national park. This text was used previously in Sana and Carpenter (2023). Participants will will: 1) Answer 10 short questions before reading the text (No feedback) 2) Read the text (8 minutes) 3) Answer 5 short questions as a distractor task (5 minutes, no feedback) For example, “Names as many breeds of dog as you can” for one minute 4) Answer 20 multiple-choice questions (10 pretested, 10 non-pretested, no feedback) We suspect that the entire experiment will take 30 minutes, to complete this process. We use very similar material and questions and aimed to follow their procedure as closely as possible. If we are able to successfully replicate the main effect of pretesting and interaction then we plan to follow up with a subsequent experiment in order to test the boundaries of the attentional window hypothesis.

title_r: The influence of face race and face sex on the recognition of faces morphed to vary in emotional intensity from angry to happy
abstract_r: The main goal is to understand how social category information (e.g., race and gender) influences the recognition of facial expressions that vary in emotional intensity. More specifically, I examine, using a neutral baseline, whether emotion recognition is facilitated for faces that belong to social categories that are stereo-typically associated with specific emotions. So, for example, the study permits a test of whether people are more likely to categorize male vs female neutral expressions as angry. This study will extend my pre-registered secondary analyses of data that was originally collected Korb, S., & Massaccesi, C. (2020, December 29; https://osf.io/29mn7/).The study by Korb and Massaccesi was also a pre-registered replication of an earlier study by Harris et al (2016). The study by Harris et al was designed to examine the effects of face sex on forced choice angry and happy decisions for faces morphed to vary in emotional intensity from angry to happy. The research by Harris et al was novel because the authors calculated indices of psychophysical performance (e.g., Point of Subjective Equality). In this specific study, I will 1. establish the generality of the effects across face race - the initial studies examining morph intensity have used only the faces of white individuals. I will establish if similar effects hold for the faces of black individuals. One hypothesis is that people are prejudiced towards black individuals making them more likely to respond "angry" than happy when the faces are of black individuals with a neutral expression. 2. establish whether the same effects are found for a new different stimulus set Further objectives are: 1. Bayesian Modelling. I will model choice decisions in a Bayesian Hierarchical Logistic Regression Model and RTs in a Bayesian Hierarchical ex-Gaussian Regression Model. Finally, a Bayesian Hierarchical Drift Diffusion Model in which choice decision and reaction times (RT) are modeled as a joint outcome, will also be estimated.

title_r: Future Relevance and Sleep-Associated Consolidation
abstract_r: Background: In their seminal study, Wilhelm et al. (2011) found that the memory benefits of sleep were enhanced when participants expected a test, suggesting that sleep selectively strengthens memories expected to be of future relevance. We failed to replicate this finding in recent work, with our data showing that memories were strengthened over sleep (vs wake) irrespective of whether participants expected a test or not (see Experiment 1). A potential explanation of this failed replication is that baseline performance levels were too high to allow a benefit of test-expectancy to emerge after sleep. To address this possibility in the current study, we will repeat Experiment 1, but increase the difficulty of our memory task to reduce baseline performance. Procedure: Learning takes place in the morning (Wake group) or evening (Sleep group). Participants encode 100 related word pairs (e.g. horizon-sun), with each pair appearing for 5 s (200 ms inter-stimulus interval). A cued recall task is used to assess baseline memory performance immediately after learning. On each trial, the first word of the pair (e.g. horizon) is presented and participants are asked to type the associated target word (e.g. sun) within 10 s. Feedback on the correct pairing is displayed irrespective of the participant’s response. The cued recall task is repeated if participants do not reach a performance criterion of 40% correct. Participants are excluded if they do not meet this criterion after two testing rounds. After the baseline test, participants are either informed that they will be re-tested in the next session (Expected condition) or are told that they will perform a different set of tasks (Not Expected condition). Twelve hours later, participants return to complete a final round of cued recall without feedback.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Saks & Wozniak (2011), from the Journal of Labor Economics
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Saks & Wozniak (2011) is that migration is procyclical, even after accounting for relative variation in local economic conditions over the cycle. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Combining evidence from a number of data sets spanning the entire postwar era, we find that internal migration within the United States is procyclical." Evidence for the finding is presented in column 2 of Table 1, where the authors regress the aggregate CPS [Current Population Survey] migration rates on each of the three measures of the national business cycle and control for the standard deviation of state analogs of these measures. The measure of the national business cycle selected for the SCORE program is the employment gap, which the authors define as the logarithm of aggregate employment relative to its trend, where this trend is estimated from a Hodrick-Prescott (HP) filter. To be consistent with the timing of the migration data, the authors define the annual employment gap as the average monthly gap from April of the previous year to March of the current year. The dependent variable is the detrended migration rate for the population age 14 and up [see the top panel of Table 1, column 2 and the table caption for additional details about the model selected as evidence for the SCORE program]. Dispersion in local conditions is not significantly related to migration, and controlling for dispersion does not qualitatively alter the correlation of migration with the national business cycle (coefficient on national employment gap term = .0010 (.0003), significant at the 5% level).

title_r: To Think or to Feel? Distinguishing Affective and Semantic Valence of Words in Bilinguals
abstract_r: This research is a conceptual replication of Ferré et al. (2022), who found that native English speakers gave more extreme valence ratings to a list of English words than L2 English speakers and that the difference of the ratings between L1 and L2 speakers were larger when participants focused on their feelings. This shows that valence type distinction (affective vs. semantic valence) can also be found when using words as stimuli and should be considered in research of affective language processing in bilinguals. The goals of this present research are to find out whether the rating differences of words can also be found in Indonesian–English bilinguals when tested in either one of their two languages and when given different instructions to manipulate the rated valence type.

title_r: How (im)plausibility in active/passive primes modulates structural priming?
abstract_r: Christianson, Luke, and Ferreira (2010) showed that plausibility modulates structural priming. They had participants listened to active/passive sentences that were plausible (The angler caught the fish or The fish was caught by the angler) or implausible (The fish caught the anger or The anger was caught by the fish) and then described a transitive event. Christianson et al. showed standard structural priming following plausible primes, but reversed structural priming following implausible primes (i.e., more active picture descriptions following an implausible passive prime than following an implausible active prime). In addition, a previous preregistered experiment (https://osf.io/wnyja) showed reduced instead of reversed structural priming. Thus, we preregister a conceptual replication of Christianson et al. (2010) to further investigate how (im)plausibility in active/passive primes modulates structural priming. Following Christianson et al. (2010), we will add a variable (comprehension question type: agent question vs. patient question) to the design of our previous experiment. In our previous experiment, we used 2 (plausibility: plausible vs. implausible sentence) * 2 (structure: Active vs. Passive) *2 (Question position: comprehension question before picture description vs. comprehension question after picture description; in blocks) to test how people use structural reanalysis when they encounter an implausible sentence (pre-registration can be found here: https://osf.io/wnyja). In this study, we will still explore how people analyse an implausible transitive sentence in a structural priming paradigm and whether comprehension question type has effects on interpretation and structural priming.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Linkenauger et al, 2009, in Psychological Science
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Linkenauger et al. (2009) is that in Experiment 1, right-handed people perceive their left and right arms to be different lengths (specifically right arms to be longer than the left arms), but in contrast, because left-handed people have nearly equal-sized cortical representations for their left and right arms, they perceive the lengths of their right and left arms as similar. This is based on the following sentence from the paper’s abstract: “When looking at each arm and hand individually, right-handed participants perceived their right arms and right hands to be longer than their left arms and left hands, whereas left-handed participants perceived both arms accurately”. The claim is tested by converting participants’ arm-length estimates to a ratio between perceived arm length and actual arm length, and conducting a repeated measures ANOVA with arm specified as a within-participants factor and right- and left-handedness as a between-subjects factor. This yielded a significant interaction between arm measured and participant handedness, F(1, 28) = 4.74, p_rep = .90, partial eta squared = .15.

title_r: The "Go, No-Go" paradigm to assess spatial numerical associations
abstract_r: This study will use the "Go/No-go" paradigm to investigate spatial numerical associations (SNAs) within UK adult participants. Eccher et al. (2025) used a computerised Go/No-go task to investigate SNA in a sample of Himba adults, Italian adults and Italian preschoolers. In each trial, participants were presented with a central fixation cross, followed by the first dot array (henceforth the “reference stimulus”) made up of 4, 12 or 36 dots. After a brief blank screen, participants then saw a second dot array (henceforth the “test stimulus”) displayed to either the left or right of the screen. In the increasing condition, participants were told to press the space bar when the test stimulus contained MORE dots than the reference stimulus. For example, when the reference stimulus contained 4 dots, the participant’s response would be recorded as correct only if the test stimulus contained 12 or 36 dots. If the reference stimulus was 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the test stimulus contained 36 dots. In the decreasing condition, participants were then instructed to only press the space bar when the test stimulus contained fewer dots than the reference stimulus. When the reference stimulus contained 36 dots, a participant's response would be recorded as correct when the test stimulus contained 12 or 4 dots. If the reference stimulus contained 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the target stimulus contained 4 dots. Both the increase and the decrease tasks started with 12 trials to familiarize the participants with the task (“training trials”), followed by 48 “experimental trials”, 30 of which were targets (i.e. trials that required a response) and 18 were distractors (i.e. trials that did not require a response). 50% of all trials were considered “SNA congruent”, whereby stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from left-to-right. The other 50% of trials were considered “SNA incongruent”, as the stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from right-to-left. For example, if a participant was completing the “increasing” condition and the test target stimulus contained 4 dots and the test stimulus contained 12 dots and presented on the right, this would be considered SNA congruent, as the target stimulus is always presented in the centre, and so the presentation of stimuli moves from left-to-right in order of magnitude. Conversely, in the “decreasing” condition, an SNA congruent trial may be one in which the target stimulus contains 36 dots, and the test stimulus contains 4 dots which is presented on the left. For further details of SNA congruent/incongruent conditions, see “Manipulated Variables"). We aim to replicate the original study’s findings, which demonstrated the potential presence of a spatial-numerical association. That is, participants will be faster and more accurate when responding to numerosities presented in a left-to-right direction, increasing in terms of magnitude, while participants’ responses will be slower and less accurate when those same numerosities are presented in a right-to-left order in terms of magnitude. Crucially, in our replication, we will conduct the experiment online rather than in person; we will recruit adult participants in the UK; make a slight modification to the timing of the no-go trials, reducing the duration from three seconds (as in the original study) to 1.5 seconds; and we will double the number of trials. We analysed the reaction time of the Italian adult group and found that the mean reaction time (excluding all incorrect responses) ranged from 0.43 seconds in the increasing congruent condition to 0.48 seconds in the decreasing incongruent condition. The maximum recorded response time was 0.84 seconds. Based on these findings, we reduced the target stimulus duration from three seconds (as used in Eccher et al., 2025) to 1.5 seconds. Finally, we decided to duplicate the number of trials to obtain more robust data for each participant. In the original study, the spatial-numerical association was observed only in the decreasing condition, where the target numbers were either 4 or 12. We want to determine whether this spatial-numerical association changes depending on whether the target is 4 or 12. Specifically, the spatial-numerical association may be driven by the number 4, as people can easily subitize small sets, quickly recognising that the set contains four dots. This may lead to a stronger association with a verbal label, which could explain why the number 4 is processed faster when presented on the left compared to the right. We expect participants to respond more quickly when 4 is on the left rather than the right. However, this effect may not be present for 12 dots, as larger sets cannot be subitized.

abstract_r: This fork is part of the Direct+Plus CREP replication (https://osf.io/px0sw/) of a study by Diener et al. (2010). Every student manages a fork of the official replication OSF page as a part of a seminar at the Department of Occupational, Economic and Social Psychology, led by Andre Julian Hartmann and Martin Müller (both graduate students) at the University of Vienna (Austria). As stated above the project is a direct replication of the Diener et al. (2010) study and is conducted in the context of a master seminar class in economic psychology at the University of Vienna. It is part of the CREP project. Additionally a direct+ replication was added. Therefore several interesting hypotheses regarding the relationship between income and happiness were presented in the context of the seminar class and finally the most interesting research question (about spending behavior and prosocial spending) was chosen and included in the study. Furthermore two additional questions were added for a Direct+ Plus replication in order to validate a measure for experienced wealth of students.

title_r: Keep your distance please! Examining the effects of social anxiety on appraisals of displays of compassion from others
abstract_r: Studies have found that socially anxious individuals are especially fearful of receiving compassion from others (Gilbert et al., 2011; Merritt & Purdon, 2020). Fear of receiving compassion from others might stem from erroneous beliefs in which compassion is appraised as threatening and likely to activate maladaptive social schemas (Eisner et al., 2009; Gilbert et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2021; Kelly & Dupasquier, 2016; see also Merritt & Purdon, 2020). Ultimately, fear of receiving compassion contributes to the increased utilization of safety behaviours (Ho et al., 2021), and decreased support seeking (Dupasquier et al., 2018) and self-compassion (Gilbert et al., 2011). Given such negative implications, we are investigating how individuals with social anxiety respond to affiliative emotions, such as compassion and care from others. Prior studies have shown that individuals with high trait social anxiety and those with social anxiety disorder tend to appraise both real and imagined social blunders as being more socially costly, embarrassing, humiliating, and likely to elicit negative responses from others than those with low trait social anxiety and those with anxiety disorders other than social anxiety disorder (Moscovitch et al., 2012, 2015). Hence, through this study, we expect to replicate past findings. Further, based on literature on positivity deficits and negative responses to positive social stimuli in social anxiety (Cohen & Huppert, 2018; Eisner et al., 2009; Kashdan & Steger, 2006; Kashdan, 2007; Kashdan, Weeks & Savostyanova, 2011; Roemer et al., 2005; Turk et al., 2005; Weeks & Howell, 2012), we aim to determine whether individuals with high vs. low social anxiety differ in their evaluation of self and others upon receiving a positive interpersonal response to their social blunder. We also aim to determine whether compassionate responses will be appraised as especially threatening for individuals with high levels of social anxiety, given that (a) compassionate responses inadvertently make the social blunder salient for the participants by explicitly mentioning the social blunder to better empathize and provide support around it; and (b) concern from others is generally perceived as a confirmation of having exposed self-perceived flaws among individuals with social anxiety (Moscovitch, 2009). Finally, given the finding that concerns about revealing self-flaws, especially appearing socially incompetent, account for unique variance in socially anxious participants’ inflated cost estimates of social blunders, over and above symptoms of social anxiety and depression (Moscovitch et al., 2015), we aim to determine that the relationship between social anxiety and negative appraisals of self and others when emotional distress about the blunder is high, especially for compassionate responses. The findings from this project could have important implications for understanding how socially anxious individuals may respond to offers of compassionate social support from others and to compassion-based approaches to treatment in clinical settings. This project is affiliated with the University of Waterloo and has received ethics clearance through a University of Waterloo Research Ethics Board.

title_r: Study 1: Understanding lexical development through eye tracking using the looking-while-listening paradigm
abstract_r: Study 1 will be a conceptual replication and extension of a previous study (Sander-Montant et al., 2022) (Pre-print available at 10.31234/osf.io/zd3m8). Using data from monolinguals and bilinguals, the previous study compared four models of lexical development that placed either maturation (age), language experience (proportion of exposure to testing language in a 0.1-1 continuum), or their combination, as the main drivers of lexical development in infants and children. The results of the previous study suggested that maturation and experience play independent, additive roles in lexical development. However, the models in the previous study were constructed using archival data from 5 studies collected between 2012 and 2019. Thus, in Study 1 we will attempt to fit the same statistical models to newly collected looking-while-listening data collected specifically to test our research questions, in order to see if we find a similar pattern of results to Sander-Montant et al. (2022).

title_r: Materials
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate De Neys original study of participant’s substitution bias through two math questions in varying order, and then asking the participants to rate their confidence in their answers. The problems we will add to the replication study as our own were used in Sacha Bourgeois-Gironde, Jean-Baptiste Van Der Henst (2009), in which the authors attempted to get access to automatic responding by presenting more information that could assist the participant. The problems are presented to participants after the De Ney’s et al. protocol, and are counterbalanced (half participants will receive two item question first then one item, and the other half will receive one item then two item). Each condition will be comprised of 25 students, so approximately 100 students in the study total. These problems are presented with a rating of confidence question. The survey will be given online via Qualtrics for easier access as well as face-to-face in classrooms. We hypothesize students will rate their confidence higher when the substitution is absent when compared to the substitution being present. We also hypothesize with multiple choice options, the accuracy in answers will be improved and confidence will be highest.

title_r: CREP #23-30 Replication of Stellar, Gordon, Anderson, Piff, McNeil, & Keltner (2018; Study 3) at Avila University
abstract_r: We are a group of researchers from Avila University's PY 262: Psychological Statistics & Methods II course, Spring 2023. Jordan Wagge is the professor, Eleanor Dick is the graduate assistant, and all other contributors are undergraduate students. The purpose of the study is to determine whether the effect found in Study 3 of Stellar et al. (2018) replicates across settings and time. In this study, participants watched EITHER a two-minute video of an instructional video for building a retaining wall, OR a two-minute video about the size of the solar system. Participants then completed a timed task (2 minutes) discussing their strengths and weaknesses; participants who watched the solar system video provided fewer strengths but the same number of weaknesses compared to participants in the wall-building video, indicating the solar system video produced more humility (through the experience of "awe") than the retaining-wall video. In our replication, we are adding a third condition, which will be the same video of the solar system but without sound. Because we are adding this third condition, our N will be 150 (100 to replicate the original study conditions and an additional 50 for our new condition). We predict that these participants will fall somewhere in between the space sound video and the retaining-wall video on the number of strengths reported. We are also adding a brief 10-question Big-5 inventory (Rammstedt & John, 2007) to examine the relationship between personality traits and cultivated humility. Specifically, we think that the Big 5 will be related to humility in he following ways: H1. Openness to experience: People who are more open to experience will be more affected by the awe video than people who are less open to experience. H2. Conscientiousness: Participants who are high on conscientiousness will demonstrate a larger effect than participants low on conscientiousness. H3. Extraversion/Introversion: No predictions H4. Agreeableness: No predictions H5. Neuroticism: More weaknesses overall All participants will be provided a link to an online survey (see materials). This research will not be completed in the lab. In the survey, they will read the consent form watch 1 of 3 2-minute-ish videos respond to questions about how they feel respond to questions about the study respond to a brief big-5 personality inventory Participants will be Avila University students enrolled in PY 101 and participating through the participant pool, or other courses for credit (with equitable alternatives offered). They will also be personal contacts of the students in the course (see attached recruiting blurb in "materials"). All participants must be at least 18 years old.

title_r: Replicating the connection between hindsight bias and seeding effects in the domain of sugar content
abstract_r: Hindsight bias is the phenomenon that when people estimate the quantities of objects and then learn the correct answers, they have difficulties recalling their original, naïve estimates. Specifically, their recalled estimates are often biased towards the newly learned correct answers (Blank et al., 2007). Traditionally, hindsight bias has been viewed as a cognitive error. Alternatively, hindsight bias might reflect adaptive knowledge updating processes (Hoffrage et al., 2000). In our prior work, we proposed a framework that conceptualizes hindsight bias as resulting from knowledge updating (Groß et al., under review). Based on this framework, we predicted that it should be possible to elicit hindsight bias not only by providing direct feedback for previously estimated objects (as in typical hindsight-bias studies), but by providing any information that leads to knowledge updating. We tested this prediction by providing relevant domain information (e.g., actual values for other objects from the domain). Our hypothesis was supported – the provision of domain information not only led to knowledge updating in the form of transfer learning (improved estimates for new objects) but also to hindsight bias. Additionally, we tested the prediction that providing irrelevant numerical information that cannot be used to update domain knowledge (because it refers to a different domain) should not trigger transfer learning and consequentially should not trigger hindsight bias. This hypothesis was supported as well. Together these findings highlight that hindsight bias might be a by-product of adaptive knowledge updating (Hoffrage et al., 2000). This project is a conceptual replication of the finding that hindsight bias and knowledge updating are closely linked (Groß et al., under review). In our prior experiment, we used country populations as the knowledge domain, a domain that had been thoroughly studied in the context of knowledge updating (Brown, 2002). In the current project, we aim to replicate this finding in a different real-world knowledge domain, the sugar content of food items.

title_r: With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility... Does it? - A study about the formation of false memories, source credibility and trust in news
abstract_r: Many studies have shown that memories can be changed when differing post-event information is received (e.g., Loftus & Palmer, 1974; Loftus & Zanni, 1975). It is even possible that people can remember details or whole events that never have happened (e.g., Loftus & Pickrell, 1995). That is also called the misinformation effect or the formation of false memories. In a former study we have found that source credibility has a significant influence on the decision of whether the news are false or true and that a greater number of false memories is generated when false information is given by a source with rather high perceived credibility compared to a source with low credibility (Utecht et al., 2022). In our present study, we want to replicate and extend these findings by using a very similar design as Utecht et al. (2022). Specifically, we will investigate false memories after repeated misinformation by the same source, when the first misinformation is followed by an erratum notice provided by the respective source. Based on previous findings (e.g., Utecht et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2010), it is likely that effects differ depending on the initially perceived credibility of the source. Main goal of our planned study is to analyze whether the development of false memories is affected by retractions from high- and low- credibility sources. Specifically, we assume that less false memories are created after an erratum notice of the news source. Besides, we expect a larger reduction of false memories if the news source is perceived as highly credible. In addition, we expect a decrease of perceived trustworthiness after false information for initially less credible and credible sources, with larger effects for the later ones. We plan to test this by i) asking directly for trustworthiness ratings before and after providing the erratum notice and ii) by also analyzing the amount of correctly remembered information. Here we expect a decline as a consequence of a reduction of perceived source credibility. A recent study by Kalogeropoulos et al. (2019) examined how different types of news consumption are correlated with trust in news overall. It showed that using primarily social media as a source of news is negatively correlated with confidence in news overall. We want to address this point in our study as well, because we think these findings could have severe consequences regarding the formation of false memories. To sum up, the goals of our study are to replicate and extend our previous finding that more false memories are formed when a rather credible compared to a less credible source gives false information about an event. Furthermore, we want to investigate whether the number of created false memories changes when the same source informs participants that they received false information and then again reports wrong information about a similar event. Moreover, we want to analyze whether the amount of remembered correct information also declines in such a scenario. Additionally, we want to examine whether the level of trust in media is associated with the preferred type of sources (traditional vs. social media) for news, and whether this correlates with the generation of false memories. abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Tsay et al (2014) is: We selected the claim that musical novices are able to quickly identify the winning groups of top international ensemble competitions through visual cues (Statement 2). title_r: Can Imagined Contact Really Be Delivered Through the Web? Preregistered Tests of Web-Delivered Imagined Contact (Study 3)
abstract_r: The purpose of this research is to test whether the positive effects of imagined contact remain when the contact scenario is delivered through the web. Previous research has determined that direct intergroup contact (real-life contact) significantly reduces prejudice towards a variety of outgroups (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006). A meta-analysis by Pettigrew and Tropp (2006) presents empirical evidence suggesting that direct intergroup contact, when structured according to pre-established conditions set forth by Allport (1954), can significantly reduce prejudice for a vast array of groups. The positive effects of imagined contact scenarios have been documented by Husnu and Crisp (2010). However, the imagined contact study conducted by Husnu and Crisp was done in a controlled laboratory setting (2010). The present study will test the effect of web-delivered imagined contact. In order to do this, the current research will compare the effectiveness of 2 different imagined contact scenarios. The first scenario will be an elaborated control and will be an exact replication of the scenario used in experiment 4 of West et al., 2011. The second scenario will be an elaborated treatment and is also an exact replication of the experimental condition scenario used in study 4 of West et al., 2011. Both conditions will be recorded and played for participants in an audio clip format. As in the West et al. (2011) study, the current research will examine the effects of imagined contact on schizophrenic individuals using attitudes and intergroup anxiety measures. Two previous studies conducted by Dr. Nicol and OCdt Bordeleau showed that elaborated imagined contact delivered through the web did not reduce intergroup anxiety towards American-Muslims. The second study, which removed any pictures that were included in the first study and was comparable to that delivered by West et al. (2011), focussing on an interaction with someone diagnosed with schizophrenia, did not find significant results between the control and experimental conditions. The present study will limit the comparability problem associated with the previous study by replicating quasi-exactly study 4 of West et al. (2011) by including an audio description of the contact experiences. By doing so, the results of the current study will be more easily comparable to the results obtained by West et al. (2011). The present study will be able to highlight whether or not the method of delivery (web) leads to significant improvement in attitudes and/or a reduction in intergroup anxiety. Furthermore, the present research will enhance the imagined scenario by having it read to the participants in the format of an audio capsule. For the present study, it is hypothesized that web-delivered imagined contact in the format of an audio capsule will significantly improve participants’ attitudes and decrease intergroup anxiety towards Schizophrenic individuals.

title_r: Disentangling effects of prior inescapable stress experience on behavioural control
abstract_r: Rationale: Mental health disorders such as depression and anxiety have been proposed to be characterized by maladaptive behavioural strategies resulting from altered beliefs about environmental controllability. One such phenomenon, learned helplessness, occurs when individuals fail to adapt their behaviour due to a belief that their actions cannot influence outcomes (Huys & Dayan, 2009). Despite the importance of learned helplessness, the mechanisms and computations contributing to learned helplessness remain unclear. While researchers have proposed that changes in behavioural control reflect biased estimation of outcome controllability, most existing behavioural control learning studies have failed to disentangle controllability from reward probability: Reward probability is often higher in controllable than uncontrollable phases of these tasks (Dorfman & Gershman, 2019; Csifcsak et al., 2020). Accordingly, increases in behavioural control might reflect increases in controllability or reward probability. In this study, we aim to use an (in)escapable shock exposure procedure to induce beliefs of environmental uncontrollability before subjects perform tasks isolating effects of outcome controllability versus probability on behavioural control. Based on prior evidence, we hypothesize that exposure to inescapable vs escapable stress impairs instrumental learning. Specifically, we predict that this impairment surfaces as deficient action value updating, deficient win-stay/lose-switch tendency (reduced impact of previous wins (vs losses) for particular cues on the probability of repeating the same choice for those cues), and concomitant deficient suppression of Pavlovian bias, as indexed by greater probability of Go for win-reward than avoid-loss cues. Critically, the procedure will allow us to disentangle effects of inescapable vs escapable stress exposure on cognitive control, as indexed by reliance on an instrumental win-stay/lose-switch tendency, increased action value learning rate, and reduced Pavlovian bias from separable effects on (i) behavioural activation, which would surface as an increase in a nonspecific No-Go bias, irrespective of the valence of the cues (across both win-reward and avoid-loss cues), and (ii) the anticipation of positive outcomes in general, which would surface as an impairment in state (rather than action) value learning rate. Critically, in previous work with this task, we have shown that participants' degree of behavioural control and their degree of self-reported sense of control correlate with controllability and positive outcome probability respectively. Accordingly, exposure to inescapable stress might impair control behaviour due to reducing reliance on an instrumental action learning strategy, while also separately attenuating control perception due to reducing reliance on a state value learning strategy (Dorfman and Gershman, 2019; Csifcsák et al., 2020; Gershman et al., 2021; Csifcsák et al., 2021; Sedlinská et al., 2023; Mahajan et al., 2024). In addition, we aim to replicate previously reported effects of inescapable versus escapable stress on the inference of controllability, as measured with the explore-predict task (Ligneul et al., 2022). By investigating how prior inescapable stress affects instrumental learning, controllability inference, Pavlovian biases, control perception, and controllability estimation, we seek to clarify the learning processes and computational mechanisms of learned helplessness. Consequently, this research will provide new insights into the computational mechanisms of learned helplessness and contribute to the development of behavioural experiments for disentangling cognitive control from behavioural activation and negative outcome anticipation. Objective: Our primary objective is to investigate the impact of prior (in)escapable stress exposure on (mal)adaptive behavioural strategy selection and controllability estimation. Study design: Single-visit, single-blind, between-subjects design. Two groups of subjects will be exposed to either escapable or inescapable stress, prior to completing a motivational Go/No-Go learning task and a controllability inference task. Study population: 62 healthy human volunteers aged 18 to 40. Intervention (if applicable): Exposure to either escapable or inescapable mild electroshocks for inducing learned helplessness. Main study parameters/outcomes: The primary outcomes are behavioural measures collected during our adapted Go/No-Go learning task and the explore-predict task (Ligneul et al., 2022). For the adapted Go/No-Go learning task, primary outcomes are (1) behavioural win-stay/lose-switch tendency, 2) instrumental action value learning rate, 3) Pavlovian bias, 4) state value learning rate, 5) nonspecific Go bias, 6) self-reported control ratings. For the explore-predict task, primary outcomes are model-agnostic estimates of subjective controllability (accuracy on state-transition predictions) and transfer entropy-model-derived parameter estimates of controllability learning rate and arbitration threshold.

title_r: ON THE VERGE OF PLAUSIBLE: UNDERSTANDING CONTRIBUTIONS OF PARAFOVEAL & FOVEAL PLAUSIBILITY EFFECTS DURING READING
abstract_r: Current controversy exists within the field of psycholinguistics regarding exactly when high-level semantic information (e.g., the plausibility of upcoming words) first becomes available to the reader. Eye tracking studies have revealed that readers rapidly extract information not only from fixated words in central foveal vision (i.e., the central 2° of visual angle where visual acuity is highest), but also from upcoming words in parafoveal vision (i.e., the central 2 -5° of visual angle) prior to fixation (Rayner, 1975; Schotter, et al., 2012). In fact, a plausibility preview benefit (e.g. shorter reading times for plausible, relative to implausible parafoveal previews) has also been shown to be irrespective of the relationship between the preview and foveal target. These findings suggest that plausible previews can be processed to a high enough level prior to fixation. However prior experiments on plausibility violations have not yet systematically examined the influence of parafoveal processing on plausibility violations. To address a current gap in the literature, the proposed study will use a gaze-contingent boundary paradigm (GCB) and orthogonally cross the (im)plausibility of the parafoveal preview and target word (i.e., similar to the frequency manipulation used in Schotter et al., 2016) as readers self-pace through sentences. We expect to replicate prior plausibility effects and to directly observe the direction of the novel interaction between parafoveal preview validity (e.g. valid identical preview versus invalid change condition) and foveal plausibility (e.g. target is plausible or implausible). In addition to addressing questions surrounding conflicts in theoretical accounts of the plausibility preview effect, our design will allow us to separate out parafoveal and foveal contributions to plausibility processing in reading.

title_r: ON THE VERGE OF PLAUSIBLE: UNDERSTANDING CONTRIBUTIONS OF PARAFOVEAL & FOVEAL PLAUSIBILITY EFFECTS DURING READING
abstract_r: Current controversy exists within the field of psycholinguistics regarding exactly when high-level semantic information (e.g., the plausibility of upcoming words) first becomes available to the reader. Eye tracking studies have revealed that readers rapidly extract information not only from fixated words in central foveal vision (i.e., the central 2° of visual angle where visual acuity is highest), but also from upcoming words in parafoveal vision (i.e., the central 2 -5° of visual angle) prior to fixation (Rayner, 1975; Schotter, et al., 2012). In fact, a plausibility preview benefit (e.g. shorter reading times for plausible, relative to implausible parafoveal previews) has also been shown to be irrespective of the relationship between the preview and foveal target. These findings suggest that plausible previews can be processed to a high enough level prior to fixation. However prior experiments on plausibility violations have not yet systematically examined the influence of parafoveal processing on plausibility violations. To address a current gap in the literature, the proposed study will use a gaze-contingent boundary paradigm (GCB) and orthogonally cross the (im)plausibility of the parafoveal preview and target word (i.e., similar to the frequency manipulation used in Schotter et al., 2016) as readers self-pace through sentences. We expect to replicate prior plausibility effects and to directly observe the direction of the novel interaction between parafoveal preview validity (e.g. valid identical preview versus invalid change condition) and foveal plausibility (e.g. target is plausible or implausible). In addition to addressing questions surrounding conflicts in theoretical accounts of the plausibility preview effect, our design will allow us to separate out parafoveal and foveal contributions to plausibility processing in reading.

title_r: WT: The Impact of Interest in Controlling and Feedback-Oriented Gamification: Revisiting Gamification Studies with a new Approach.
abstract_r: A conceptual replication of the study conducted in "Do Points, Levels and Leaderboards Harm Intrinsic Motivation? An Empirical Analysis of Common Gamification Elements" by Elisa D. Mekler, Florian Bruhlmann, Klaus Opwis, Alexandre N. Tuch (2013). In the study of Mekler et al. (2013) a 2x2 experiment was conducted where they examined the influence of gamification elements on intrinsic motivation and its components as well as performance. The participants had to tag a set of 18 abstract paintings in the platform Tagem. Gamification elements where implemented after a short trial phase of 3 pictures. The gamification conditions were: points, points and levels as well as points and leaderboard. The gamified conditions led to significantly higher performance, and to the authors surprise, participants intrinsic motivation was not influenced by the different conditions. Participants reported similar interest and task enjoyment across all conditions, and there was no effect on autonomy or competence need to be found. Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 1985), which is the most prevalent theory used for explaining gamficiation effects, would assume that gamification elements, being external rewards, would impair intrinsic motivation making the results by Mekler et al. (2013) surprising and contradicting the theory. The aim of this thesis is to revisit the study with intent to improve the intrinsic motivation of the participants by implementing a different, more interesting set of pictures into the Tagem platform. In the study by Mekler et al. (2013) a set of rather unappealing abstract paintings is used. In a pre-study, these were compared to journalistic photographs which yielded much higher interest in a group of students. It is possible that the original paintings were not interesting enough and could thus not produce enough intrinsic motivation in the participants for the expected negative effects of gamification to show. Hypothetically, working with the "Interesting" set of pictures will bring forth a higher base intrinsic motivation and thus the effects of gamification will differ from the original findings. Additionally, the sample in this study is aimed to be much higher than in the original experiment, which might also enable further insights. In a third condition group “Interesting-Gamified-Controlling” we deliberately implement a controlling element, being a expected monetary reward contingent to performance. This element makes it more comparable to a classic experiment done by Deci (1971) where a negative effect of rewards on intrinsic motivation could be documented. This is therefore expected to further impair intrinsic motivation and simultaineously elevate the quantity of generated tags. RQ1: Does the effect of gamification elements on intrinsic motivation differ in comaprison to the effects reported in Mekler et al. (2013). If so, in what way? RQ2: How does gamification influence the quantity of generated Tags in each of the conditions? RQ3: What influence does the expected monetary reward have on intrinsic motivation in the "Interesting-Gamification-Controlling” condition?

title_r: Seeing Black and White in school: Students’ skin color and teachers’ attitudes and recommendations
abstract_r: Students from Portuguese Speaking African Countries are twice more likely to be in professional education in Portugal. Previous research has showed that teachers tend to have lower expectations towards Black students, namely a study by Meeus and colaborators found that, in Chile, teachers were more likely to have lower expectations that Black students would attend college. In a study in Switzerland by Batruch et al. (2019), where there is a gap in the access to higher school tracks of students with a lower socioeconomic status (SES), it was found that teachers were more likely to recommend low-SES students to lower tracks. We want to replicate both previous findings, in a sample of Portuguese teachers and regarding skin color and not socio-economic background.

title_r: Stage 1 registered report for replication of Experiment 1 and 2 of “Axe the tax: Taxes are disliked more than equivalent costs” (Sussman & Olivola, 2011)
abstract_r: Stage 1: Sussman and Olivola (2011) reported that people in the US show a stronger preference to avoid tax-related costs than to avoid tax-unrelated monetary costs of the same size and coined the term Tax Aversion to describe the phenomenon. The original Experiment 1 and 2 results indicated that people are willing to incur increased timely costs to receive a discount when it refers to taxes (e.g., “axe-the-tax discount”) than when it just refers to a regular discount (e.g., “customer rewards”). Their paper has received considerable attention and is often cited in tax behavior research when referring to citizens’ general aversion to taxes. We propose close replications of Experiments 1 and 2 in two high-powered studies in the US (N = 600 and N = 700, respectively). Because the original study was conducted in a country that relies on a sales tax system, where consumption taxes are very salient, we additionally propose conducting both replication studies in the UK to test whether the effect also applies to a value added tax system (again N = 600 and N = 700, respectively). The replication studies will test whether Tax Aversion is a stable phenomenon in the US and whether the effect extends to a consumption tax system where payments do not represent an out-of-pocket cost.

title_r: This is a replication of experiment 1 of Maayan et al.’s Publication of “Feelings of Culpability: Just Following Orders Versus Making the Decision Oneself”
abstract_r: Culpability is the amount of responsibility warranted for a crime or wrongdoing. It is a continually conversed topic especially in the court. The amount of culpability an individual feels they deserve varies from person to person. For example, if a person were to steal from a grocery store and is charged with stealing. Generally this behavior is frowned upon in society but the individual might feel his actions to be justified. In the study “Feelings of Culpability: Just Following Orders Versus Making the Decision Oneself,” Malayan and her colleagues wanted to explore the relationship between the amount of agency individuals have in the decision making process and the amount of culpability they feel as a result. The original study was conducted by randomly placing participants into two groups: high agency and low agency. They were given imaginary roles of engineers who were working on designing an autonomous car and programming it to react in a potential accident. There were two approaches: the first was to design the car to prioritize the driver’s safety above others (deontological); the second option was to prioritize the safety of as many people as possible even at the expense of the driver’s safety (utilitarian). In the high agency group, they were given the opportunity to choose which one they felt was best. For the low agency group they were assigned one of the two options by a supervisor. After five years, a tragic accident occurs where the car behaves based on what the individuals chose (deontological or utilitarian). In both imagined scenarios the car functions properly but innocent people are killed as a result of the car’s programming. Participants were then asked how they felt about the programming followed by how responsible they felt for the result of the accident (their “moral culpability”). The original study’s hypothesis was that those who were in the high-agency condition would feel more culpable for their decision than those in the low-agency condition. In contrast with the researchers’ hypothesis, the results showed individuals who had high agency felt “less guilt” than those who were given low agency. For our study, we plan to conduct an exact replication to see if the results of the original study are accurate based on if we are able to obtain similar findings.

title_r: The effect of unimodal and multimodal information in a low-level detection task in younger and older adults (face-to-face - lab experiment)
abstract_r: Previous research has shown an age by multimodal interaction in low-level detection tasks such that older adults benefit more from multisensory information than young adults (Laurienti et al., 2006; Hugenschmidt et al., 2009). In contrast, our lab (OSF Registries | The effect of unimodal and multimodal information on lexical decision and free recall in younger and older adults) found a multimodal benefit over unimodal information for both age groups for lexical decision accuracy and memory recall. The different findings may have been due to our study using a multimodal condition that did not use a sufficiently redundant multimodal condition. In our study, both the auditory and visual targets were the same language-based word stimuli, likely processed by language parts of the brain for both modalities. This is different to the work from Laurienti’s lab as they used the actual colour red or blue alongside the auditory word for their multimodal condition (Laurienti et al., 2006; Hugenschmidt et al., 2009). Our lab attempted to replicate Laurienti’s paradigm which is based on the response to the colour of a disk that is red or blue (visual colour), the words red or blue (auditory speech), or both of the above (multimodal: colour-speech) (|The effect of unimodal and multimodal information in a low-level detection task in younger and older adults). We included additional conditions in which the red and blue disks are replaced with the words ‘red’ and ‘blue’, either alone (visual word) or in combination with the spoken words (multimodal: word-speech). We hypothesised that young and older adults would benefit equally from the multimodal stimuli when both contain language information, but that older adults will benefit more than young adults when the multimodal stimuli contribute language information that is not present in the visual stimulus. The results showed no interaction effects between age group (young, old) and modality (auditory speech, visual colour, visual words, audiovisual colour-speech, audiovisual word-speech) for accuracy or response time. However, a multimodal benefit was found over comparable unimodal information for both age groups for response time. Therefore, we did not replicate the multisensory information boost for older adults compared to young adults (Laurienti et al., 2006). The lack of congruency between our findings and Laurienti et al.’s (2006) prompted our lab to contact the corresponding author. After helpful discussions with the author, our lab aimed to directly replicate Lauirenti et al. (2006) by including task-irrelevant green stimuli (OSF Registries | The effect of unimodal and multimodal information in a low-level detection task in younger and older adults (Experiment 3)). Task-irrelevant green stimuli were to be ignored by the participant when presented unimodally (visual colour or auditory speech). In contrast, during a multimodal (colour-speech) presentation, the green stimulus was only ever presented along with a blue or red stimulus (i.e., there were no congruent green multisensory trials) and in this instance, participants were instructed to respond to the red or blue stimulus and ignore the green. Therefore, Laurienti’s paradigm required participants to always respond to the colour of a disk that is red or blue (visual colour), the words red or blue (auditory speech), or whenever red or blue is presented in at least one of the modalities (visual, auditory) in the multimodal (visual colour - auditory speech) presentation. We hypothesised that older adults would disproportionally benefit from the integration of multisensory information in comparison to young adults. However, similar to our labs previous findings, the results did not mirror those of Laurienti et al. (2006), rather a multimodal benefit was found over the visual condition for both age groups for response time. The key difference between our lab’s replication of Laurienti et al. (2006) is that our study was conducted online, whereas Laurienti et al.’s study was laboratory based. Therefore, the discrepancy between the findings could be due to the two testing formats. The current study will replicate Laurienti et al.’s (2006) two-alternative forced-choice discrimination task by conducting in-lab testing. In line with the findings of Laurienti et al. (2006), we hypothesise that older adults will disproportionally benefit from the integration of multisensory information in comparison to young adults.

title_r: Biofeedback as a short-intervention to improve cardiac interoception
abstract_r: The processing of internal bodily signals - interoception - is a multifaceted construct, including the accurate detection of body sensations (interoceptive accuracy), the interpretation and integration of these (Khalsa et al., 2018). An altered perception of interoceptive stimuli is a relevant etiological factor with regards to chronification of somatic symptoms (Barsky, 1992). According to the predictive coding framework for medically unexplained symptoms, the perception of symptoms might be decoupled from actual somatosensory input and be more dependent on central nervous predictions of the occurrence of symptoms. Decoupling of perception from somatosensory input can be assessed with signal detection tasks. Here, the sensitivity for a certain (bodily) signal is separated from a response bias ranging from conservative to liberal. A liberal “better safe than sorry” strategy corresponds to decoupled, illusory perceptions (Van den Bergh, Brosschot, Critchley, Thayer, & Ottaviani, 2021; Van den Bergh, Witthoft, Petersen, & Brown, 2017). Empirical evidence supports the notion of a more liberal perception of interoceptive stimuli given high levels of somatic distress (Pohl et al., 2021; Wolters, Gerlach, & Pohl, 2021). Hence, biofeedback might not only address deviant interoceptive accuracy, but also biased processing in situations with uncertainty. Cardiovascular biofeedback was reported to be an effective intervention to reduce somatic symptoms (Schaefer, Egloff, Gerlach, & Witthoft, 2014) and improve interoceptive accuracy (Meyerholz, Irzinger, Witthoft, Gerlach, & Pohl, 2019). Nonetheless, the methodology used when measuring interoception as well as the use of biofeedback in the field of cardiovascular interoception are debated (Brener & Ring, 2016; Rominger, Grassmann, Weber, & Schwerdtfeger, 2021; Zamariola, Maurage, Luminet, & Corneille, 2018). Recently, we examined a novel cardiovascular signal detection task for the assessment of cardiac interoceptive perception (Pohl et al., 2021). In this study, we aim to replicate our previous findings that cardiac biofeedback improves cardiac accuracy in a mental tracking task (Meyerholz et al., 2019) and examine the raised concerns regarding the biofeedback training and the interoception assessment. title_r: Follow-up: Influence of label on categorization
abstract_r: The study is a follow-up study of the bachelor thesis (Influences of non-informative language on object categorisation, Werner (2021)). It is a conceptual replication of the study by Lupyan et al. (2007). Using pictures of fish, the category affiliations of two kinds of fish has to be learned. The participants are divided into two groups, a label group and a no-label group. The category affiliation is learned through auditory feedback. The label group also got a written label per category. All participants first go through a training phase (4 blocks) and then directly through a test phase (4 blocks) without feedback and label. On the following day, the participants complete the test phase again.
