title_r: Psychometric evaluation of the Metacognitions Quesitonnaire-30 in anxiety and depressive disorders
abstract_r: Metacognitive theory refers to individuals’ awareness and regulation of their own thinking process (Wells, 1995). This framework underpins the Self-Regulatory Executive Function (S-REF) model developed by Wells and Matthews (1994; 1996), which proposes that psychological disorders are maintained by cognitive-attention syndrome (CAS). The CAS comprises worry, rumination, threat monitoring, and maladaptive coping behaviours, all of which are driven by underlying metacognitive beliefs. The beliefs --- particularly positive beliefs about the usefulness of worry and rumination, and negative beliefs about their uncontrollability and potential harm --- are central to metacognitive therapy (Wells, 2009). In generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), individuals tend to hold both positive and negative metacognitive beliefs about worry. According to Wells (1995), positive beliefs promote the use of worry as a coping strategy (Type I worry), while negative beliefs give rise to meta-worry (Type II worry), resulting in heightened distress and perceived uncontrollability. Empirical evidence consistently highlights the primacy of negative metacognitive beliefs in GAD symptomatology, with such beliefs showing strong associations with diagnosis, symptom severity, and treatment outcomes (White et al., 2024; McEvoy et al., 2015b). In social anxiety disorder (SAD), metacognitions are implicated in both anticipatory anxiety and post-event rumination (Gkika et al., 2017). Although some studies have identified links between SAD and positive beliefs about worry or the need to control thoughts (Fisak & Hammond, 2013; McEvoy & Perini, 2009), findings have been mixed. More recent research suggests that general metacognitive beliefs, such as low cognitive confidence and heightened self-consciousness, may indirectly contribute to SAD through the CAS (Bakali et al., 2024). In contrast, the metacognitive model of depression highlights the role of rumination. Positive beliefs about rumination may contribute to the development of depressive symptoms (e.g., “Thinking about my problems will help me understand them”), while negative beliefs about the uncontrollability and harm of rumination are implicated in the maintenance of depressive episodes (Papageorgiou & Wells, 2001, 2003). These negative metacognitions amplify hopelessness and inhibit effective problem solving. Longitudinal research has demonstrated that both positive and negative metacognitive beliefs contribute to the development and maintenance of depression. Specifically, positive metacognitive beliefs about rumination have shown to predict the severity of rumination and depressive symptoms over time (Weber & Exner, 2013), while negative metacognitive beliefs about uncontrollability and danger of rumination predict depressive status after six months, even after controlling for baseline depression and stressful life events (Yilmaz et al., 2011). Cartwright-Hatton and Wells (1997) developed the 65-item Metacognitions Questionnaire to measure aspects of metacognition hypothesised to be relevant to the psychopathology of emotional disorders. The instrument was subsequently shortened to a 30-item version (MCQ-30; Wells & Cartright-Hatton, 2004). The MCQ-30 comprises five subscales that purportedly measure (i) positive beliefs about worry [POS], (ii) negative beliefs about uncontrollability and danger [NEG], (ii) cognitive confidence [CC], (iv) negative beliefs about the consequences of not controlling thoughts [NC], and (v) cognitive self-consciousness [CSC]. A total score is also calculated. The MCQ-30 is a widely used instrument --- according to Google Scholar, as of mid-2025 Wells and Cartright-Hatton’s (2004) scale development paper has been cited 2175 times. A systematic review (White, 2022) of metacognition measures found that the MCQ-30 has reasonable psychometric properties, but that research has been limited to samples of University students, the general community, and people with medical problems such as cancer and epilepsy. No studies evaluating the psychometrics of the MCQ-30 among patients diagnosed with mental disorders were identified— even though the questionnaire is primarily designed to measure metacognitive beliefs in that population. White et al. (2024) conducted the first psychometric evaluation of the (English) MCQ-30 in a clinical sample, comprising 139 patients diagnosed with GAD. They found that the NEG subscale was more strongly correlated with measures of worry, GAD symptoms, fear of anxiety, and impairment than the other subscales or total score. White et al suggested that the NEG subscale “could be a more accurate and parsimonious measure of the metacognitive beliefs relevant to GAD than the full MCQ-30” and recommended that in clinical practice the negative beliefs subscale be used instead of the full scale to guide case formulation and treatment. Another key finding was that the POS and NEG subscale scores were uncorrelated (r = -.02), contrary to Wells’ metacognitive theory of emotional disorders, which suggests that positive and negative metacognitive beliefs should be associated. Baptista et al. (2020) evaluated the psychometric properties of a French translation of the MCQ-30 among depressed inpatients (N = 73) and a community sample (N = 467), and found evidence of questionable reliability and validity in the depressed sample. Only the MCQ-30 total score and CC subscale had Cronbach’s alpha reliability coefficients above the minimally acceptable level of .80 recommended for applied research (Clark & Watson, 2019; Lance et al., 2006). Reliabilities for the NEG (α = .69) and CC (α = .65) subscales were very low. The POS and CSC subscales were not correlated with depressive symptoms, indicating a lack of convergent validity. Structural validity problems were also evident – several items had item-subscale correlations that were lower on the subscale to which they are assigned than other subscales. For example, the item “My worrying could make me go mad” is part of the NEG subscale, but that item corelated more strongly with NC (r =.46) than NEG (r = .26). Important limitations of the Baptista et al.’s study are the modest sample size, the inpatient sample – meaning that the results may not generalise to outpatient settings – and fact that a French translation, rather than the original English instrument, was used. An important issue to evaluate in future psychometric evaluations of the MCQ-30 is the possibility of floor effects. McEvoy et al. (2015a) utilised the POS and NEG subscales in a study evaluating a metacognitive therapy (MCT) protocol for repetitive negative thinking (RNT). Scores on the POS and NEG subscales can range from 6 to 24 – meaning there are 19 possible unique values. However, following MCT 38% of patients had the minimum possible score of 6 on the POS subscale, and 28% on the NEG subscale. Average POS and NEG subscale scores in community samples also tend to be highly skewed and very close the floor (e.g., M = 8.34 and M = 8.18; White et al., 2024). Those findings suggest that the MCQ-30 may struggle to differentiate individuals who endorse relatively low levels of metacognitive beliefs. In summary, there is a pressing need to evaluate the distributional characteristics, reliability, validity, and sensitivity to change of MCQ-30 scores among people diagnosed with emotional disorders. Researchers and clinicians need guidance as to whether only the NEG subscale or the MCQ-30 total score should be utilised. White et al., (2024) recommended using the NEG subscale only, but that recommendation may be premature given it was based on an analysis of a single GAD sample. Whether their finding that the NEG subscale is more valid and sensitive to change than the other subscales generalises to other GAD samples, and beyond GAD to other mental disorders, is unknown. Another consideration is that MCT protocols typically target both positive and negative metacognitions (e.g., McEvoy, 2015b). Assessing positive metacognitions in addition to negative metacognitions would therefore seem important to ensure that both targets of treatment are measured, even if the POS subscale has inferior psychometric properties to the NEG subscale. Consequently, further evaluation of the POS subscale in addition to the NEG subscale is warranted. The overarching aim of the current research project is to substantially advance knowledge about the psychometric properties of the MCQ-30 among adults diagnosed with emotional disorders to guide future research and clinical practice. The project will comprise two substudies that will draw on data routinely collected at an Australian clinical psychology outpatient clinic that specialises in the treatment of depressive and anxiety disorders. The first study will involve a sample of approximately 100 individuals diagnosed with GAD who were treated with MCT for RNT, and completed the MCQ-30 before and after treatment. Aims of study 1 are to evaluate the (i) distributional properties (e.g., skew; floor effects), (ii) reliability, (iii) validity, and (iv) sensitivity to change of MCQ-30 total and subscale scores. Study 1 is effectively a conceptual replication of White’s (2024) evaluation of the MCQ-30’s psychometrics, and will enable us to determine whether their key finding --- that the MCQ-30 NEG is more valid and sensitive to change than the other subscales and total score --- can be replicated in an independent sample of GAD patients recruited from a different outpatient clinic. Study 2 will expand upon Study 1 by examining the psychometric properties of the NEG and POS subscales in a very large (N~1150) sample of individuals diagnosed with a broader range of depressive and anxiety disorders. The extent to which MCQ-30 POS and NEG subscale scores vary by diagnosis, and their sensitivity to change in different types of psychotherapy, will be examined in the second study.

title_r: Force Modulation: A Behavioural Marker of Mind-Wandering
abstract_r: The Metronome Response Task (MRT) is a well-known experimental measure of mind-wandering. Replications of the MRT have been successful, all demonstrating that the task can differentiate mind-wandering episodes from non-mind-wandering ones. However, there’s been a lack of consensus regarding the MRT’s ability to differentiate between spontaneous and deliberate forms of mind-wandering (e.g., Seli et al., 2013 vs Anderson et al., 2021). We will propose a more cognitively demanding, novel laboratory task (named the In Sync Task; IST) that will, hopefully, be able to separate instances of spontaneous mind-wandering from deliberate mind-wandering. Importantly, the IST has been tested (and compared to the MRT) in an unpublished pilot study (Go, 2017), in which it managed to differentiate spontaneous and deliberate mind-wandering with its behavioural measures. Our primary objective will be to replicate the findings of the unpublished pilot study and add evidence regarding the IST’s efficacy. Unlike the MRT, the IST involves having participants respond to audio tones that are presented in triplets, each of which comprises tones that vary in loudness (soft, moderate, loud). All triplets start with the softest tone, and end with the loudest tone. Here, participants will not only have to respond synchronously to the tones’ onset (by pressing a modified mouse equipped with a force transducer), but they will also have to modulate the force with which they use to respond to the tones. Specifically, participants will be asked to press the softest to the soft tone, press moderately to the moderate tone, and press the hardest to the loud tone. Because of this, we will measure rhythm response time (RRT; a typical measure of the MRT) variance in both tasks, but in the IST, we will also measure the slope of force presses over tone intensity (measured in decibels). Here, the idea is that if the participants’ thoughts are imputed to be on-task (i.e., the 9 trials prior to an “on-task” answer to a thought probe), the slope of force over tone intensity will be steeper than for the 9 trials before reports of mind-wandering. In the proposed study we will test participants on the MRT and on the IST using a between-subjects design. In addition to the above behavioural measurements, we will assess the time orientation of participants’ mind-wandering during both tasks in hopes of replicating earlier findings showing that spontaneous mind-wandering is associated with past thoughts, whereas deliberate mind-wandering tends to involve more future-oriented thoughts (e.g., Seli et al., 2017). This is done so that we can showcase the IST (like the MRT) can assess additional dimensions of mind-wandering (e.g., time orientation). Citations: Anderson, T., Petranker, R., Lin, H., & Farb, N. title_r: Force Modulation: A Behavioural Marker of Mind-Wandering
abstract_r: The Metronome Response Task (MRT) is a well-known experimental measure of mind-wandering. Replications of the MRT have been successful, all demonstrating that the task can differentiate mind-wandering episodes from non-mind-wandering ones. However, there’s been a lack of consensus regarding the MRT’s ability to differentiate between spontaneous and deliberate forms of mind-wandering (e.g., Seli et al., 2013 vs Anderson et al., 2021). We will propose a more cognitively demanding, novel laboratory task (named the In Sync Task; IST) that will, hopefully, be able to separate instances of spontaneous mind-wandering from deliberate mind-wandering. Importantly, the IST has been tested (and compared to the MRT) in an unpublished pilot study (Go, 2017), in which it managed to differentiate spontaneous and deliberate mind-wandering with its behavioural measures. Our primary objective will be to replicate the findings of the unpublished pilot study and add evidence regarding the IST’s efficacy. Unlike the MRT, the IST involves having participants respond to audio tones that are presented in triplets, each of which comprises tones that vary in loudness (soft, moderate, loud). All triplets start with the softest tone, and end with the loudest tone. Here, participants will not only have to respond synchronously to the tones’ onset (by pressing a modified mouse equipped with a force transducer), but they will also have to modulate the force with which they use to respond to the tones. Specifically, participants will be asked to press the softest to the soft tone, press moderately to the moderate tone, and press the hardest to the loud tone. Because of this, we will measure rhythm response time (RRT; a typical measure of the MRT) variance in both tasks, but in the IST, we will also measure the slope of force presses over tone intensity (measured in decibels). Here, the idea is that if the participants’ thoughts are imputed to be on-task (i.e., the 9 trials prior to an “on-task” answer to a thought probe), the slope of force over tone intensity will be steeper than for the 9 trials before reports of mind-wandering. In the proposed study we will test participants on the MRT and on the IST using a between-subjects design. In addition to the above behavioural measurements, we will assess the time orientation of participants’ mind-wandering during both tasks in hopes of replicating earlier findings showing that spontaneous mind-wandering is associated with past thoughts, whereas deliberate mind-wandering tends to involve more future-oriented thoughts (e.g., Seli et al., 2017). This is done so that we can showcase the IST (like the MRT) can assess additional dimensions of mind-wandering (e.g., time orientation). Citations: Anderson, T., Petranker, R., Lin, H., & Farb, N. title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Ma-Kellams et al. (2011), from Psychological Science
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Ma-Kellams & Blascovich, 2011 is that after priming of mortality salience (vs. a control prime for dental pain), European Americans become derogating of dissimilar others (i.e. expressing negative attitudes toward prostitution after reading about a prostitution defendant). In contrast, East Asian participants’ approval of prostitution increased after priming of mortality salience (compared to control prime). The explanation is that, in the control condition, Asian Americans tend to be relatively socially conservative, but under mortality-salience conditions, they magnify the general East Asian tendency toward collectivism and interdependence to the point of embracing non-normative individuals. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “Given fundamental East-West differences in self-construal (i.e., the independent vs. interdependent self), we predicted that members of Eastern cultural groups would affirm other people, rather than defend and affirm the self, after encountering conditions of mortality salience.” The main analysis was a 2 (condition: mortality salience vs. control priming task) × 2 (ethnicity: European American vs. Asian American) univariate ANOVAs on the dependent variable of the Prostitution Attitudes Scale scores, which yielded a significant interactive effect on PAS (Prostitution Attitudes Scale) score, F(1, 38) = 10.263, p = .003

title_r: The Relationship between Exposure to Childhood Trauma and Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: Examining a General Mixed Group
abstract_r: Exposure to childhood trauma (CT), which is very common, is related to a wide range of problems and psychopathology, including posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). CT as a general construct is often divided into five subtypes, namely sexual abuse (SA), physical abuse (PA), emotional abuse (EA), physical neglect (PN), and emotional neglect (EN) (World Health Organization, 2022a, 2022b). According to the A-criterion of PTSD, not all five trauma types are sufficient to lead to a PTSD diagnosis (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). While SA and PA meet this criterion, EA and neglect do not. However, several studies have shown that in particular, EA (but in some cases also EN) is predictive of the severity of PTSD and psychopathology in general. Previous studies that examined the relationship between the five CT types and PTSD severity are often focused on children and adolescents. These studies found support for EA being the only predictor of PTSD severity and the strongest predictor of three PTSD symptom clusters (i.e., intrusions, avoidance, and arousal) (Cecil et al., 2017; Hoeboer et al., 2021; Nöthling et al., 2019; Sullivan et al., 2006). In addition, in one of our earlier studies, we examined the relationship between the five CT types and the severity of PTSD symptoms in adults who received a primary PTSD diagnosis according to trauma in childhood (before the age of 16) (Rameckers et al., 2021). According to our findings, we found that only EA was predictive of the severity of PTSD in a multiple regression model. A model selection procedure also indicated that EA was indeed the only important predictor of PTSD. Moreover, we also found that EA was the strongest and most important predictor of three PTSD symptom clusters: intrusions, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and arousal. No association between any of the CT types and avoidance was found. In another recent study, EA and EN were combined into one overall concept of psychological maltreatment in childhood, and this was the only CT predictor of a worse sense of self in a group of students. For all students who were exposed to psychological maltreatment in childhood, a sense of self was also related to a higher PTSD severity (Watts et al., 2023). To examine if we can replicate these findings and to explore if these findings generalize to a broader clinical and non-clinical group of adults, we will study a similar research question in the present study. More specifically, we will study the relationship between exposure to the five CT types (SA, PA, EA, EN, and PN) and the severity of self-reported PTSD symptoms in a broad and general group of participants. In addition, we will test the same research question for the separate PTSD clusters.

title_r: Response dynamics of ongoing-task performance during prospective memory tasks
abstract_r: Maintaining an intention to perform a specific action in the future, known as prospective remembering, under certain conditions is associated with performance costs in ongoing activities that are performed while maintaining the intention. While such costs in prospective memory (PM) tasks have been documented extensively (Cottini & Meier, 2020) it is currently debated, whether they represent effects of a resource-demanding monitoring for PM cues or a strategic delay of ongoing-task responses (e.g., Heathcote et al., 2015; Strickland et al., 2017). Anderson et al. (2018) assessed effects of different performance-strategy instructions on ongoing-task costs and associated parameter configurations in an accumulator model of ongoing-task performance in order to more closely map changes associated with PM monitoring and a strategic delay of ongoing-task responses. There key findings were that strategic delay instructions produced distinct and different behavioural effects and model parameter configurations than monitoring instructions, and that processes elicited by standard PM instructions more closely resembled effects of PM cue monitoring. By contrast, in a recent study, Kurtz et al. (2022) used mouse-movement tracking in a PM task in order to assess sub-process underlying ongoing-task costs during active PM tasks and aftereffects of completed intentions. Here the authors found evidence for a strategic delay of ongoing-task responses in terms of a mouse movement that was more in the middle between response options for the ongoing task and the PM task during the first half of the mouse movement. However, since this was also accompanied by response slowing during the first half, it is unclear to what extent PM monitoring may have contributed to ongoing task costs. While this discrepancy between findings may in parts be due to differences in task design and the characteristics of the measures that were employed in each study, it is unclear how specific monitoring or delay strategy instructions would affect response dynamics during PM tasks. Therefore, in the present study, we will combine these approaches and conduct a conceptual replication of the Anderson et al. (2018) study with a mouse-movement tracking paradigm that is based on the Kurtz et al. (2022) study. Specifically, we will assess response dynamics of ongoing-task and PM performance in a mouse-tracking paradigm when giving participants task either a standard PM instruction or instructions that are designed to foster either or a monitoring-based or a delay-based performance strategy. With this, we aim to a) characterize response dynamics of different strategies to perform an ongoing task during a PM task and b) assess whether response dynamics during standard PM instructions differ substantially from delay strategies or PM monitoring strategies. Additionally, we will investigate effects of such performance strategies on the processing of irrelevant distractor stimuli during a PM task and assess effects on aftereffects of responding to prospective memory cues (Meier & Cottini, 2022).

title_r: Forming Differentiating Impressions of Individuals
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that stereotypes are formed for attributes that have large intergroup differences (Ford & Stangor, 1992) and that there may be an attention shifting mechanism that accounts for learning about the traits of social groups (Sherman et al., 2009). The present study is a conceptual replication of Ford and Stangor (1992) and examines if perceivers use attributes with greater mean differences to distinguish between individual targets. This study is one of three that examines if the methodology used to examine learning of group attributes can describe the learning of individual people.

title_r: How useful are homogeneous and heterogeneous representations in propositional items for children?
abstract_r: Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education in particular, uses different types of external representations, such as text, graphics, formula, visualizations, and more, for describing and explaining complicated topics and models (Rau, 2020). When different types of representation are combined with each other in the learning materials, this enables learning with multiple representations (MERs; Schüler, 2020). Theoretical approaches, such as the Cognitve Theory of Multimedia Learning (Mayer, 2014) and the Integrated Model of Text and Picture Comprehension (Schnotz & Bannert, 2003) suggest that MERs foster different learning processes and also problem solving. These assumptions are supported by empirical evidence (e.g., Eitel et al. 2013; Hu et al. 2021; Lee et al. 2006). Most empirical studies on the effect of MERs address heterogeneous combinations of representations (Lindner et al., 2016; Schüler et al., 2015) including analog (pictures, illustrations) and symbolic (text, formula) representations which form heterogeneous MERs (Malone et al., 2020). Less is known on the effect and processing of homogeneous MERs, which combine multiple analogous or multiple symbolic representations. In our previous research, we compared similarities and differences in university students' information processing between heterogeneous and homogeneous MERs in propositional logic tasks (Ott, Brünken, Vogel, & Malone, 2018), with the result that performance was better when homogeneous-symbolic MERs (text + formula) were used instead of single representations (text or formula). Moreover, homogeneous-symbolic MERs were as useful as functionally equivalent heterogeneous MERs (e.g., text + graphics). Eye-tracking analyses also showed that different types of MERs triggered different processing of information. In a subsequent study, we were able to replicate these results for the domain of solving linear systems of equations (Malone et al. 2020). The aim of the present study is a conceptual replication of the study by Ott et al. (2018), in which we will examine the extent to which these results are also evident for school children in grades 5 to 6. While university students are rarely but occasionally confronted with logical expressions and notation during their education, it can be assumed that these are completely unknown to the target group. We have therefore developed an age-appropriate computer-based multimedia learning program to teach basic propositional logic symbols and concepts. In addition, we developed an item set analogous to the items in Ott et al. (2018), which contains less complex logical expressions than the original tasks. Both were piloted in a preliminary study with 30 students.

title_r: Replication of Gino, Wilmuth, and Brooks (2015)'s research on gender differences in attainability and desirability of professional advancement.
abstract_r: This research will investigate whether previous findings by Gino, Wilmuth, and Brook (2015) on gender differences in perceived attainability and desirability of career advancement replicate among the general U.S. population. According to Gino and colleagues (2015), women's under-representations in high-level positions in professional settings might be attributed to gender differences in life goals, particularly power-related goals. In other words, since professional women tend to value power-related goals less than do men, they are less likely to seek opportunities to advance their position than men, even though they see the opportunities as equally attainable. Consistent with this argument, their Study 3 indicated that professional men reported higher ratings of their ideal position (i.e., desirability) than professional women, whereas they did not significantly differ in ratings of their highest possible position (i.e., attainability). We will replicate this study but with hypotheses that the directions of gender effects on attainability and desirability perceptions of professional advancement would be different from the original findings.

title_r: A systematic replication of the worst performance rule
abstract_r: The worst performance rule (WPR) states that when reaction times are ranked from fastest to slowest and then correlated with intelligence test scores, the slowest reaction times predict participants' intelligence better than the mean or best reaction times. Previous research suggests that the size of the WPR effect may be moderated by the difficulty or g-loading of RT tasks. Because there is substantial variation in sample size, sample characteristics and trial numbers across the different studies, we aim to replicate the WPR in a large, heterogenous sample using a variety of RT task. Our main aim is to replicate that the size of the WPR effect varies systematically with the difficulty or g-loading of tasks.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Wissmath et al. (2020), from medRxiv
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Wissmath et al. (2020) is that agreement with containment measures is likely to decrease stress. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “In particular, individuals who did not agree with the containment measures, as well as those who saw nothing positive in the crisis, experienced even higher levels of stress.” The claim was tested by multiple comparisons (ANOVA) of different subgroups, specifically comparing those that agree with containment measures versus those with “no agreement” and “no agreement at all” on stress. This analysis revealed that the majority of respondents (66%) agreed with the measures of the Swiss authorities. These individuals scored lower on stress than individuals who felt that the measures were either not sufficient or too extreme (F = 48.8, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.036).

title_r: Sparkman & Walton (2017) at King's College London
abstract_r: The direct replication of Sparkman and Walton's study 1 aims to replicate the effect of the type of descriptive norm on the intention to consume meat, whereby reading a message presenting a dynamic norm leads to a higher interest in reducing meat consumption than reading a message presenting a static norm. Therefore, we will be testing Hypothesis 1: participants will report higher interest in eating less meat after reading a dynamic norm than after reading a static norm. We also will be exploring three extensions and their related variables. 1. Two conditions were added to also manipulate the framing of the behaviour, contrasting the original negative (cut of a behaviour) framing with a positive one (increase in a partially equivalent behaviour). Thus, instead of the norm describing people eating less meat, it describes people eating more plant-based food. Here we are interested in the exploratory hypothesis of a difference in interest in eating less meat, between the positive and the negative framing, as well as in the exploratory hypothesis of an interaction between type of norm and framing.It should be noted that these two additional conditions were not shown to participants who completed the two next extensions. This will be tested through a 2x2 between ANOVA (framing: positive, negative; norm: dynamic, static). 2. An individual differences measure was added, namely the 11-item sense of agency scale (Tapal et al., 2017). Here again, the hypotheses are exploratory, with an hypothesis of sense of agency predicting interest in eating less meat, and interacting with the type of norm to predict this interest. As mentioned, participants who completed this extension did not see the two additional conditions manipulating the framing of the message, and therefore there was no hypothesis of interaction between framing and sense of agency. This will be tested through a regression analysis, with type of norm and sense of agency as predictors, and interest in eating less meat as outcome. 3. An individual differences measure was added, namely the 11-item conformity scale (Mehrabian & Stefl, 1995). Here again, the hypotheses are exploratory, with an hypothesis of conformity predicting interest in eating less meat, and interacting with the type of norm to predict this interest. As for sense of agency, participants who completed this extension did not see the two additional conditions manipulating the framing of the message, and therefore there was no hypothesis of interaction between framing and conformity. This will be tested through a regression analysis, with type of norm and conformity as predictors, and interest in eating less meat as outcome. After the students have submitted their lab report, interested students will be invited to join the CREP aspect of the project: a more appropriate (fuller) exploratory analysis will be conducted then, namely a regression with type of norm, sense of agency and conformity as predictors, and interest in eating less meat as outcome. Due to the flow of the survey, there will be no participants under the positive framing conditions with sense of agency and conformity data, therefore the framing will not be used in this fuller analysis.

title_r: A Replication Study of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation-Induced Heart-Brain Coupling
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is a prominent stimulation target for the treatment of Major Depressive disorder (MDD) with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). The therapeutic effect of DLPFC stimulation likely stems from the DLPFC–subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) connectivity. A recent study suggested that there is an overlap of the hubs in the depression network, including the DLPFC, sgACC, and vagus nerve (VN), with the heart-brain axis, and that stimulation of these hubs consequently leads to heart rate (HR) decelerations. A specific 10 Hz Dash rTMS protocol (‘neuro-cardiac guided rTMS version 2.0’, NGC-2.0 rTMS) has been proposed to induce coupling of TMS and HR changes (heart-brain coupling; HBC).  This research encompasses two studies aimed at exploring the effects of NGC-TMS targeting the DLPFC. In the Study-1, we will replicate and corroborate previous findings with a larger cohort of twenty healthy young participants. These participants will undergo NGC-TMS sessions targeting the DLPFC, supplemented by sham TMS, across three sessions. Following these findings, the Study-2 will examine the robustness of HBC by assessing various stimulation intensities by targeting the most effective target identified in the Study-1.

title_r: The impact of face ethnicity on sensitivity to pain facial expression
abstract_r: Quality pain care is a fundamental human right. Nonetheless, differences exist between racial minorities relative to racial majorities in their ability to fully experience this right (Kissi et al., 2022). Although there are plenty of factors that could possibly explain such an unequal treatment (e.g., attentional processing disparities, false beliefs about biological differences, biased mental representation based on stereotypes and prejudices, etc.), current research has highlighted a wealth of evidences suggesting that race influences face perception (Mende-Siedlecki et al., 2019). More properly speaking, because of perceptual alteration in face processing when evaluating Black faces, White perceivers may display a more lenient threshold for pain on White faces and more stringent threshold for Black faces (Mende-Siedlecki et al., 2019). For instance, Peter Mende-Siedlecki’s conceptual replication studies – Perceptual Contributions to Racial Bias in Pain Perception (Mende-Siedlecki et al., 2019); Cues to racial prototypicality exacerbate bias in pain perception (Drain et al., 2020); What factors fuel racial bias in pain perception and treatment?: A meta-analysis across 40 experimental studies (Lin et al., 2020); Seeing No Pain: Assessing the Generalizability of Racial Bias in Pain Perception (Mende-Siedlecki et al., 2021); Assessing the speed and spontaneity of racial bias in pain perception (Mende-Siedlecki et al., 2022) – come across the same results implying that differences in detection of pain for the other-race emerge from a perceptual bias. However, the systematic use of a yes-no task which is sensitive to one’s decisional bias leaves a margin of error in pain detection that could be influencing the gaps in thresholds for pain that were observed in those previous studies. That’s said, the aim of the present research is to check whether the disparities in thresholds for pain still remain when we use a task controlling for decisional biases. Thus, we will conduct two experiments. In experiment 1, we will use a yes/no task like the one used in the aforementioned studies, to verify if we replicate the finding of a more lenient threshold for pain on White faces and more stringent threshold for Black faces. In experiment 2, we will use the same stimuli, but in a 2-IFC task. In the 2-IFC task, two faces will be presented one after the other, and the participant will be asked to indicate which of the two faces displays the most intense pain expression. One of the face will be neutral, and the other one will display a pain facial expression ranging from a very low intensity (5%) to a very high intensity (100%). In contrast with the yes/no task, the 2-IFC task therefore involves an objectively correct answer. Such experimental task designs have been proposed as being mostly criterion-free (Kingdom & Prins, 2010; Lu & Dosher, 2013); they reduce the likelihood of decisional biases in the results.

title_r: Do cultural traits have an influence on level of obedience? A replication of Milgram’s Behavioral study of Obedience in Australia, Italy, and South-Africa
abstract_r: Original study The study that we are replicating is Milgram’s study on obedience (Milgram, 1963). In this study, Milgram wanted to find out how far people would go by inflicting pain on other people when they were told to do so. Participants had to administer shocks to their ‘learners’ when the experimenter would tell them to do so. The shocks that were given were increasingly stronger, up to the point where a shock would be lethal to the one receiving it. Unbeknownst to the participant, no actual shocks were given. Instead, a tape recorder was played with pre-recorded sounds of a person in pain and agony for each shock level. 65% of the participants (26 out of 40) gave the highest voltage shock (450 Volts) when instructed to do so. Every participant gave a shock of at least 300 Volts. Participants were uncomfortable doing so as every one of them paused the experiment at least once to ask if everything was okay. After being reassured by the experimenter, they continued the experiment. This study shows that ordinary people can become extremely violent and would even go as far as killing another human being when instructed to do so. The conscious (knowing that what they do is wrong) and auditorial clues (hearing the other person scream) were not strong enough to resist the commands of the person of authority. Importance of replication There are several reasons for replicating this study. As shocking as the results are, Milgram’s experiment was not without its flaws. The way the experiment was conducted would not be allowed today because of ethical reasons. Therefore, this replication will not allow shocks to be administered over 150 Volts. The reason for this is because in Milgram’s original study over 80% of participants went over 150 Volts. Of those people, another 80% continued to 450 Volts. This was later replicated by Burger. In his study that went only to 150 Volts, 70% of the participants had to be stopped at that point (American Psychological Association, 2008). 150 Volts seems to be a ‘point of no return’ and can therefore be used instead of the 450 Volts maximum. Because of the very persistent attitude of the researcher, it could have been that participants were bullied into completing the experiment. This is also a form of experimenter bias where the researcher has a negative effect on the research data. Therefore, this replication will have a control group with a very strict professor, just as in Milgram’s study, and an experimental group with a more relaxed professor who does not push the participants as far. Also, the reward in terms of money could have biased the participants into completing the experiment. Another set of interesting questions comes to mind when reviewing the results of this study which was conducted with only Americans. How would this phenomenon work across cultures? Would people living in collectivistic cultures be as obedient as people living in individualistic cultures? Another question that can be asked is if people today would be as obedient as in the time the original study took place in 1961, over 60 years ago. Predictions Earlier replications, among others by Burger, have shown that the percentage of obedience does not change over time (Bierbrauer, 2014). Therefore, we predict the same percentages of obedience in our replication study. However, these percentages may differ between cultures and that is what we are interested in. We expect individualistic cultures to be less obedient than in the original study, be it slightly. We also expect collectivistic cultures to be more obedient than the original study.

title_r: Stage 1 registered report for replication of Experiment 1 and 2 of “Axe the tax: Taxes are disliked more than equivalent costs” (Sussman & Olivola, 2011)
abstract_r: Stage 1: Sussman and Olivola (2011) reported that people in the US show a stronger preference to avoid tax-related costs than to avoid tax-unrelated monetary costs of the same size and coined the term Tax Aversion to describe the phenomenon. The original Experiment 1 and 2 results indicated that people are willing to incur increased timely costs to receive a discount when it refers to taxes (e.g., “axe-the-tax discount”) than when it just refers to a regular discount (e.g., “customer rewards”). Their paper has received considerable attention and is often cited in tax behavior research when referring to citizens’ general aversion to taxes. We propose close replications of Experiments 1 and 2 in two high-powered studies in the US (N = 600 and N = 700, respectively). Because the original study was conducted in a country that relies on a sales tax system, where consumption taxes are very salient, we additionally propose conducting both replication studies in the UK to test whether the effect also applies to a value added tax system (again N = 600 and N = 700, respectively). The replication studies will test whether Tax Aversion is a stable phenomenon in the US and whether the effect extends to a consumption tax system where payments do not represent an out-of-pocket cost.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Tertytchnaya et al. (2018), from American Political Science Review
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Tertytchnaya et al. (2018) is that, when remittance inflows increase, incumbent approval will also increase, but when these payments decline, recipients will punish incumbents. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Relying on a unique four-wave panel study of Kyrgyz citizens between 2010–2013 and a cross-sectional sample of 28 countries in Central Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia, we show that when people experience a decrease (increase) in remittances, they become less (more) satisfied about their household economic situation and misattribute responsibility to the incumbent at home." The claim is tested with panel survey data from the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 waves of the LiKsurvey, which tracks the same 3,000 households in all seven Kyrgyz oblasts (regions) and the two cities of Bishkek and Osh. The dependent variable is the difference in levels of trust in the President across survey waves. In the model chosen as evidence for the SCORE program (Model 1 of Table 2), the main independent variable is changes in the amount of remitted income. The regression analysis is based on a panel data model that accounts for repeated observations of individuals and includes both household and survey wave fixed effects, as well as additional controls listed in Table 2. The results show that an increase in remittances coincides with an increase in trust in the president, while a decrease in remittances decreases trust in the president (coefficient on Change in Amount of Remittances term = 0.048, SE = 0.019, p ≤ 0.05).

abstract_r: General Information This fork is part of the Direct+Plus CREP replication (https://osf.io/px0sw/) of a study by Diener et al. (2010). Every student manages a fork of the official replication OSF page as a part of a seminar at the Department of Occupational, Economic and Social Psychology, led by Andre Julian Hartmann and Martin Müller (both graduate students) at the University of Vienna (Austria). Materials All materials are developed together with the students during the seminar and will be added to the project before starting data collection. In addition to the items of the original study, items for further research questions will be added as a direct+ replication. We also participate in the Direct+Plus project by Jordan Wagge containing two questions that deal with financial security. Procedure All students are using the same survey, advertising materials, and OSF page since this is an online study. Every student will sample N = 10 (total targeted sample: N = 270) students living in Vienna within their social circle. Original Abstract The Gallup World Poll, the first representative sample of planet Earth, was used to explore the reasons why happiness is associated with higher income, including the meeting of basic needs, fulfillment of psychological needs, increasing satisfaction with one's standard of living, and public goods. Across the globe, the association of log income with subjective well-being was linear but convex with raw income, indicating the declining marginal effects of income on subjective well-being. Income was a moderately strong predictor of life evaluation but a much weaker predictor of positive and negative feelings. Possessing luxury conveniences and satisfaction with standard of living were also strong predictors of life evaluation. Although the meeting of basic and psychological needs mediated the effects of income on life evaluation to some degree, the strongest mediation was provided by standard of living and ownership of conveniences. In contrast, feelings were most associated with the fulfillment of psychological needs: learning, autonomy, using one's skills, respect, and the ability to count on others in an emergency. Thus, two separate types of prosperity—economic and social psychological—best predict different types of well-being. Student Researchers Winkler Matthias

title_r: The emotional body and time perception: A replication of Sylvie Droit-Volet (2015)
abstract_r: The purpose of the experiment is two-fold. We are both partially replicating and modifying the experimental design from Droit-Volet & Gil (2016) who examined the effects of emotional bodily expressions, without facial cues, on perception of time using a temporal bisection task. There will be two conditions to which a participant can be randomly assigned: one with the original images, and one with reduced outlines where the salient emotional expression has been removed. In the first condition design, if the originally recorded effect is reliable, we expect that the durations will be perceived as longer for the fearful stimulus and that the magnitude of the lengthening effect of fearful vs sad postures will increase with the duration range. Since the paper focused on fearful responses being the salient arousing emotion that was able to impact time perception relative to the low-arousal bodily presentation of sadness, this will be the only comparison that we test. The happy/sad condition will be removed since no effect was found and we want to have the highest statistical power for looking for the main effect. This is why the first condition in the study that we are conducting is only a partial replication. In the second condition design, we perform the same tests but with the reduced images. We hypothesize that we will get similar effects for the high-arousal vs low-arousal images since this difference in image complexity is preserved and we find the original paper’s neuroscientific explanation to be an unlikely cause with insufficient verification. We are also working under the assumption that the arousal of the original image, on average, correlates with the complexity of the blob image. This is because the fearful bodily expressions frequently showed more animation, resulting in greater image complexity, while sad images looked more linear. We are neglecting to include two other components from the Droit-Volet & Gil (2016): their Experiment 2 and the survey at the end of the image processing. The reason for not including their Experiment 2, showing that the effect increases with the duration, is that this component depends on the foundation of there being a reliable effect in the first place, which is the main focus of our experiment. Including it is therefore unnecessary to our primary goal, and although it might be interesting, would ultimately increase the duration of the experiment and limit the number of participants that we could pay and therefore the statistical power for the main effect. Our reasoning for not including the survey is that when using the blob-images for our second experimental condition, the goal is to prevent there from being a singular salient emotion that is perceivable in the bodily expression. By asking them about the emotion present in each image we worry that we will both increase the duration of the experiment and also weaken our own manipulation. We are therefore also removing the survey from our partial replication test of the fearful/sadness effect since we will not have a comparison. This is not a concern for us because in Droit-Volet & Gil (2016) their survey demonstrated the robustness of emotional salience resulting from their stimuli selection process, and we followed guidelines that we believe are comparable if not stricter. We also conducted a separate survey to validate the production of our blob images with 20 participants that confirmed that the process had successfully destroyed any universal emotional salience in the body expression. The repository used for our experiment code can be found at: https://github.com/wolstad/droit-volet-time-perception-study-replication- .

abstract_r: Terror Management Theory (TMT) is a central concept within many psychological disciplines; Kasser and Sheldon's (2000) work provides a major contribution to TMT through the finding that mortality salience was associated with an inclination towards materialism. title_r: Experiment 1: Replicating the instruction-based congruency effect (IBCE)
abstract_r: Associated project: https://osf.io/tvkgp/ In this experiment, we seek to replication the diagnostic-inducer task created by Liefooghe et al. (2012, 2013). We will adjust the experiment slightly with inspiration from Abrahamse et al. (2022). Changes from Liefooghe et al., 2012: - Diagnostic lengths are randomly sampled between the 4 and 16 (less predictable lengths). - Stimuli consists of three-letter non-words that rarely (if ever) occur in the English language. They are sampled from Subtlex-UK and tested for distinctness with Levenshtein distance. - Feedback provided after each wrong/slow trial. - A practice round of the diagnostic (16 trials) & inducer (6 trials) is presented. Task description: In this experiment, participants are to execute two separate tasks sequentially. The first task is called the diagnostic task and the instructions are "if italic press left / if upright press right" (where left/right is randomized between participants). The instructions specified that the participants must categorize a three letter stimulus (e.g., abc) as either appearing in italic or upright using a left or right response. When the target appears in a certain colour (e.g., red), participants must respond to the stimulus according to the second task. The second task is called the inducer task and the instructions are "if xxx press left / if yyy press right". Where the words are randomly sampled from a predefined word list, and is only executed once during each block and is never repeated. Before a new block, new instructions appear indicating two new stimuli related to the responses (left/right). As an example, if the stimulus abc appears in italic and the diagnostic task (task 1) requires a left response to an italic stimulus, and the inducer task (task 2) requires a left response to abc, the trial is congruent. If, on the other hand, abc is upright, the trial would be incongruent, since the inducer task would require a left response, but the diagnostic task would require a right response.

title_r: Contributions of dopamine-related neurophysiology to incentive-boosted cognitive control brain function and abilities.
abstract_r: Tissue iron estimates, have been identified as a novel, noninvasive, indirect magnetic resonance (MR) measure of dopamine (DA)-related neurophysiology that can be used to probe the integrity of the basal ganglia in developmental populations. Specifically, MR measures of tissue iron in regions of the basal ganglia have been associated with positron emission tomography (PET) measures of presynaptic vesicular DA storage [1], cognitive functioning [2], incentivized inhibitory control [3], and frontostriatal circuit development during normative adolescence. Further tissue iron is significantly decreased among individuals with conditions characterized by low DA [4,5]. Tissue iron co-localizes with DA vesicles and is necessary for DA synthesis and tissue iron concentrations have shown to support D2 receptor and DA transporter densities [1,6] and the function of DA neurons [7,8]. Interestingly there is some, albeit limited preclinical and human evidence of developmental shifts in DA synthesis, availability, and signaling from childhood to adulthood [9,10] as well as shifts in the cognitive and behavioral implications. However, such developmental shifts are still not fully understood. Additionally, prior studies have shown that while inhibitory control continues to develop during adolescence, if rewards are given for correct performance, adolescent inhibitory control can approximate that of adults (Geier et al., 2010; Geier and Luna, 2012). Furthermore, this ‘boosting’ effect of rewards is supported by enhanced activation within reward-related regions including the ventral striatum, and cognitive control regions, including the frontal eye fields, suggesting that rewards can drive neural activation within circuits required for correct inhibitory control performance (Paulsen et al., 2015; Padmanabhan et al., 2011). Critically, Parr et al. (2022), recently showed that basal ganglia tissue iron estimates, obtained by time-averaged and normalized T2* weighted imaging (nT2*w), are associated with individual differences in the magnitude of incentive-boosted inhibitory control [3]. Specifically, the effect of incentives on inhibitory control performance was strongest in those with high levels of tissue iron, predominantly in adolescence. However, this indirect measure of dopaminergic physiology has not yet been linked to the enhancing effect of rewards on brain activation during adolescent inhibitory control, and further, has not yet been leveraged to understand the development of risk-taking and substance use behavior. Using a different incentive-boosted inhibitory control task in adolescents, we aimed to replicate and extend Parr et al.’s (2022) finding by not only examining basal ganglia tissue iron associations to incentive-boosted inhibitory control behavioral performance, but also examining individual differences in underlying task-based brain function. Further we will relate individual differences in tissue iron, incentivized inhibitory control performance, and task-activation to task-based risky decision-making trajectories across adolescence as well as real world risk-taking behaviors such as substance use. Further, we will probe age by tissue iron interactive effects on risk-taking outcome measures of interest to assess a previously posited theory of developmental shifts in DA links to behavior. Specifically, neuroscientists have posited a developmental theory suggesting that because DA availability and signaling may peak during adolescence [11], and because DA regulates performance in an inverted U-shape function [9,10], the optimal dopaminergic tone in terms of cognitive and behavioral outcomes (e.g., cognitive control, risk-taking, substance use) may shift across development. Specifically, those individuals with higher a dopaminergic tone may be closer to optimal DA levels during childhood and adulthood but, in contrast, may have excessive DA levels during adolescence and are thus more at risk for negative outcomes during that period. Whereas those individuals with a lower dopaminergic tone may be closer to optimal DA levels during adolescence but have insufficient DA levels in childhood and adulthood. As examining dopaminergic tone in human adolescents is difficult, empirical evidence assessing this theory is limited. As such we hope to probe age by tissue iron interactions on risk-taking and substance use outcomes, to assess whether cognitive behavioral implications DA-related neurophysiology estimates change across age.

title_r: Does Blatantly Contradictory Information Eliminate the Misinformation Effect? A Replication of Loftus (1979)
abstract_r: In 1979, Elizabeth Loftus published “Reactions to Blatantly Contradictory Information”. Loftus demonstrated that participants who received a piece of blatantly contradictory information almost uniformly rejected that misinformation (we term this the blatant misinformation effect). In addition, the participants who had received the blatant misinformation were also more likely to reject the more subtle pieces of misinformation, compared to the participants who did not receive the blatant misinformation (we term this the inoculation effect). Although this study is influential, the inoculation effect has never been replicated (Google Scholar, 2020). In the current study, we will attempt to replicate Experiment 1 from Loftus (1979) using new materials (created to be as similar as possible to the original materials but appropriate for current times). In addition, we will perform a conceptual replication of Experiment 1, with some changes made to the materials and procedure that are intended to improve the experimental design. We will also examine whether the presence/absence of initial testing would influence the inoculation effect.

title_r: Influence of rhythmic contexts on perceived event duration: evidence from behavior and pupillometry
abstract_r: Abstract Rhythmic contexts are ubiquitous in our lives, influencing our behavior significantly. Music, dance, speech, and even natural events such as sea waves have an inherent temporal structure, understood as rhythms. The Dynamic Attending Theory (DAT) states that attention can be entrained to external rhythms, enhancing our behavior in terms of preparation (e.g.., faster responses) and/or perception (e.g., better discrimination). Notwithstanding the great influence of the DAT, several studies actually failed to observe entrainment effects in tasks measuring either accuracy or response speed. The present study aims to further explore this issue by trying to replicate a seminal work by McAuley and Fromboluti (2014), which confirmed the predictions of the DAT using an oddball auditory paradigm. Extending this original study, we will also incorporate eye-tracking measures of attention as well as measures of musical skills and spontaneous motor tempo to assess the role of individual differences in the supposed entrainment effects. Overall, we expect to replicate the original study by McAuley and Fromboluti (2014) and to provide complementary evidence about rhythmic entrainment that takes into account interindividual differences. Keywords Dynamic Attending Theory, rhythm, oscillation cycles, foreperiod effect, timing, eye-tracker, pupillometry

title_r: Directly replicating Shen et al.'s (2019) "Fake images" study
abstract_r: This study aims to directly replicate Shen et al.'s study: "Fake Images: The effects of source, intermediary, and digital media literacy on contextual assessment of image credibility online" from 2019 (DOI: 10.1177/1461444818799526). Therefore, this study's research questions, hypotheses, and stimuli are based on the original study by Shen et al. The only changes were made regarding the data collection (sample source and amount of compensation) as well as naming of a platform (updated name of the social media platform Twitter to X since 2023). Since the publication of the original study, research on the data quality of platforms such as MTurk, CloudResearch, and Prolific has shown a decrease in those platforms' quality. Peer et al. (2021) found that MTurk shows significantly lower data quality than the other platforms measured by attention, comprehension, reliability, and dishonesty. Webb and Tangney's (2022) paper has shown that the majority of collected data from MTurk participants can be removed after data cleaning since they didn't pass basic qualifying criteria for a study and thus negatively affect the research. Knowing these factors we plan to increase the quality of the data by conducting the data collection with the service provider CloudResearch. In contrast to Shen et al. (2019), who gathered their participants directly from MTurk, CloudResearch claims to regularly screen a pool of MTurk participant to identify and remove bad actors and technical tools such as bots that complete the surveys (Hartmann et al., 2023). This preserves data quality and minimizes the impact of tools, which have become more prevalent since the publication of the original study. For the recruitment of US students, we use the platform Prolific, which gives us access to this specific target group by selecting qualification criteria accordingly and also increases data quality. For ethical reasons, we have decided to pay the participants in our replication study at a rate applicable to today's higher wage structure. Our compensation is based on the minimum wage in the US state of California, which, in 2023, is $15 per hour. This payment was scaled down to a processing time of 5 minutes, resulting in a payment of $1.25. Due to our limited budget, we will be working with a total of 669 participants. Although this is less than the Shen et al. (2019) study, a power analysis indicates this number of participants to be more than sufficient. The distribution of MTurk and student participants will be in the same proportion as in Shen et al.'s research to ensure a comparable sample. Lastly, we decided to change the platform description within the questionnaire from “Twitter” to “Twitter / X”, since the social media platform changed it's name in july 2023. title_r: Registered Report: The transcriptional network for mesenchymal transformation of brain tumours
abstract_r: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of 50 papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012. This Registered Report describes the proposed replication plan of key experiments from “The transcriptional network for mesenchymal transformation of brain tumours” by Carro et al. (2010), published in Nature in 2010. The key experiments included in this replication focus on testing the contribution of two “master regulator” transcription factors (C/EBPβ and STAT3) toward synergistically initiating the mesenchymal transformation of gliomas. During this replication attempt, CEBPB and STAT3 expression will be ablated in a human glioma cell line with the resulting changes in mesenchymal markers measured, as shown in Figure S8A. Tumor cells treated with shRNAs targeting both CEBPB and STAT3 will be injected into immunocompromised mice, and the resulting effects in tumor severity and mesenchymal signature will be assessed, as shown in Figures 5A and 5B. The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is a collaboration between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange and the results of the replications will be published in eLife.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Travers & Krezmien (2018) in Exceptional Children.
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication in Travers & Krezmien (2018) is that, compared to California, the odds ratio of autism identification was lower in the state of Ohio. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Between-state analyses revealed White students and minority students in most states were underidentified compared to White students with autism in California." The claim was tested by regressing autism identification (i.e., 0 = no autism, 1 = autism) in a logistic regression (logit link) model, with states (49 states and Washington, D.C.) entered as categorical predictors (see Figure 2.) The focal test is the comparison between California and Ohio, using the 95% confidence intervals around odds ratios to evaluate under-representation compared to California. Ohio was significantly less likely to identify students with autism than was California, as indicated by an odds ratio of autism identification whose 95% confidence interval lay entirely below 1.0.

title_r: The effect of individual differences in Episodic Future Thought on sketching true and false intentions
abstract_r: This is the second study in a series of studies exploring whether differences in Episodic Future Thought ability (EFT; i.e., the ability to mentally visualise future events) affects the ability to lie about intentions. In study 1, we used 4 EFT tasks to examine which EFT measure best correlated with lying ability. The correlation between the 4 tasks was lower than we would have expected if the tasks were all measuring EFT. We therefore speculated that the 4 measures might be measuring some other aspect of the EFT tasks (e.g. talkativeness), rather than EFT itself. To test this, we intend to replicate our previous study, but ask participants to report the EFT via sketches as well as verbally. That way, if the verbal EFT task is predictive of lying in sketches, we will then know the task is measuring more than talkativeness. This study consists of 3 parts. Part A of the study consists of 2 tasks: a lying about intentions task and an episodic details task. Participants will then take part in the same lying about intentions experiment as study 1, which is largely based on Granhag and Knieps (2011). Participants will be asked to plan a mock criminal event (placing a memory stick containing illegal material on a specific shelf in the physics section of the university library) and plan a cover story to tell the interviewer in case they are intercepted. Participants will also be asked to plan one of five randomly selected innocent tasks, such as buying two gifts for a friend from a local shop. Just before the participant leaves the building, they will be intercepted by an interviewer and taken to a nearby room for questioning. The interviewer will be blind to which tasks are actually part of the study and the participant’s task is to deceive the interviewer successfully. The interviewer will first ask the participant about their intentions, followed by questions about any mental image that was activated during the planning of their task. Finally, participants will be asked to sketch a picture of their most dominant mental image of what it will be like when they complete their task. Participants will then return to the original room and complete a detailed post-interview questionnaire beginning with questions directly related to EFT, followed by questions adapted from the Memory Characteristics Questionnaire (MCQ, Johnson, Foley, Suengas & Raye, 1988) relating to the phenomenological characteristics of their most dominant mental image including perceptual details. To assess participant’s EFT ability, participants will complete an episodic details task adapted from D’Argembeau, Ortoleva, Jumentier and Van der Linden’s (2010) study. The episodic details task requires participants to imagine a possible situation that they may encounter in the future (‘imagine something you will do on your next holiday’). Participants will be told to describe the specific event as if they were physically present in the situation including as many details as possible. Participants will then respond to a series of questions adapted from the MCQ (Johnson et al, 1988) indicating their phenomenological experience of the task. In the previous study (study 1), this EFT task was the most predictive measure of the amount of details and number of words participants used, when describing their true and deceptive intention. Participants will also complete the revised Hexaco Personality Inventory (Ashton & Lee, 2009) in which they will rate 60 statements about themselves from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). This questionnaire measures six broad personality factors: Honesty-humility, emotionality, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness to experience. Participants will then take part in the same ‘intent to deceive’ experiment as study 1, which is largely based on Granhag and Knieps (2011). Participants will be asked to plan a mock criminal event (placing a memory stick containing illegal material on a specific shelf in the physics section of the university library) and plan a cover story in case they are intercepted. Participants will also be asked to plan one of five randomly selected innocent tasks, such as buying two gifts for a friend from a local shop. Just before the participant leaves the building, they will be intercepted by an interviewer and taken to a nearby room for questioning. The interviewer will first ask the participant about their intentions, followed by questions about any mental image that was activated during the planning of their task. Finally, participants will be asked to sketch an image of their most dominant mental image of what it will be like when they complete their task. Participants will then return to the original room and complete a detailed post-interview questionnaire beginning with questions directly related to EFT, followed by questions relating to the phenomenological characteristics of EFT. In part B of this study, we will ask a separate group of participants to rate the veracity of the verbal descriptions of the truthful and deceptive tasks provided in part A. Participants will also rate their confidence in their veracity judgements as well as the plausibility of the story. In part C of this study, we will ask participants to rate the veracity of the sketches collected part A. We will also ask them to rate the abstractness of the sketches. This task is a replication of Calderon, Giolla, Ask and Granhag, (2018). Calderon et al. found that participants judged drawings of false intentions as more abstract than true intentions drawings.

title_r: Referencing Context in Sentence Processing: A Bayesian Replication of the Interactive Mental Models Hypotheses
abstract_r: The role of contextual influences on sentence processing remains underdeveloped and is often assumed to play some vaguely defined role in sentence processing. In 2005, Grodner, Gibson, and Watson (GGW) used self-paced reading to test the extent to which preceding discourse structure and complexity influence the interpretation of restrictive relative clauses. Their findings suggest that discourse can influence unambiguous syntactic selection processes and does so rapidly, such that discourse can project syntactic structures onto subsequent text during reading. Although being moderately cited since its publication, there has been no replication attempt to this date, all the while the field has developed more sophisticated methods for crossed designs and has highlighted the need for robust replication attempts to mitigate an ever-growing replication crisis. The proposed study seeks to provide a direct replication of GGW’s Experiment 2 in the hopes of reinforcing evidence for the Strong Interactive Mental Models Hypothesis to lay the groundwork for future research in the development of discourse models of structural ambiguity resolution.
