title_r: Replicating Lee et al. (2014): The Impact of Avatar Gender on Performance in Mathematical Tasks.
abstract_r: Stereotypes can have a real impact on performance, particularly in academic contexts, where individuals may underperform due to the fear of confirming negative societal expectations (Steele & Aronson, 1995). One way to mitigate these effects is by examining how virtual representations, such as avatars, influence individuals' behaviors and attitudes. In this context, Lee et al. (2014) explored the potential for avatars to reduce stereotype threat, particularly for women in mathematics. The current study seeks to replicate their work to further understand the impact of avatar utilization on performance in mathematics. Stereotype threat Stereotype threat is a phenomenon occurring when individuals, aware of a stereotype about their social group in a domain, fear confirming that stereotype, leading to an impaired performance in this domain (Steele & Aronson, 1995). In their pioneering study, Steele and Aronson (1995) demonstrated that the intellectual performance of Black students declined when a test was presented as an assessment of intelligence, compared to when no stereotype was activated. This effect has been replicated in diverse populations and contexts. For instance, Chateignier et al. (2011) observed similar outcomes among Franco-Arab students. In older adults, stereotype threat related to cognitive decline was detected as well, impairing memory performance when the stereotype was made salient (Levy, 1996). Of our interest, much research has focused on the impact of stereotype threat on women’s performance in mathematics. Spencer et al. (1999) showed that women’s performance on complex mathematical tests declined significantly when the stereotype that women are less competent in math than men was made salient. When the stereotype was deactivated (i.e., by stating that there were no gender differences in mathematical ability) women performed at the same level as men. In the same vein, Beilock et al. (2007) demonstrated that stereotype threat affects not only standardized tests but also modular arithmetic, relying on working memory. Furthermore, stereotype threat can influence young girls in elementary school. Galdi et al. (2013) showed that even subtle activation of a sexist stereotype significantly impaired girls’ math performance, highlighting that these effects can manifest early in life. Meta-analyses have further documented the impact of stereotype threat on women’s math performance. For example, Nguyen and Ryan (2008), and Doyle and Voyer (2016) reviewed over a hundred studies and found small-to-moderate but significant effects of stereotype threat on math performance. These meta-analyses also identified conditions under which stereotype threat is most likely to occur, such as difficult tasks, a higher identification with mathematics, and a high salience of the stereotype. Stereotype lift Stereotype lift is a concept introduced by Walton and Cohen (2003) in a meta-analysis conducted on 43 studies on stereotype threat. Their goal was to explore whether stereotype activation could enhance the performance of non-stereotyped individuals, instead of impairing the performance of stereotyped individuals. Their findings confirmed this hypothesis, leading to the introduction of the concept of stereotype lift. Stereotype lift occurs when individuals are exposed to negative stereotypes about another social group. This awareness can boost the performance of non-stereotyped individuals. However, this effect is not found when the negative stereotype about the outgroup is refuted (Walton & Cohen, 2003). In the domain of mathematics, Mendoza-Denton et al. (2008) found that men's math performance improved when the positive stereotype about their abilities in math was confirmed. Also, women perceived math tests as more challenging when the stereotype was confirmed, while men found them less difficult. The improvement of men’s performance might be explained by the process of downward comparison, where individuals boost their self-esteem by comparing themselves favorably to negatively stereotyped members of an outgroup (Fein & Spencer, 1997). Such comparisons could enhance confidence and involvement in the task, leading to better performance (Chalabaev et al., 2008). Proteus effect The rise of virtual environments allowed new ways of exploring how digital representations influence human behavior. A pioneering study on the topic was conducted by Yee and Bailenson (2007). They demonstrated that the visual characteristics of avatars significantly affect individuals’ behavior in virtual settings. In fact, participants with attractive avatars interacted more closely with others and spoke more about themselves, while those with taller avatars displayed greater confidence. From these observations, Yee and Bailenson (2007) introduced the Proteus effect, which posits that the appearance and behavior of an avatar can impact the attitudes and actions of the individual controlling it. The Proteus effect is anchored in self-perception theory (Bem, 1974), which suggests that individuals infer their internal states and attitudes by observing their own actions and representations. When applied to the Proteus effect, this theory implies that the visual characteristics of an avatar influence how individuals perceive themselves, which in turn shapes their behavior. Notably, the Proteus effect operates independently of others' perceptions (Yee & Bailenson, 2007), emphasizing that behavioral changes come from self-perception rather than external expectations. For example, an individual embodying a confident avatar (e.g., tall stature, dominant posture) may internalize this representation as a reflection of their own confidence, which in turn influences their actions. In addition, the SIDE model (Social Identity model of Deindividuation Effects) proposed by Reicher et al. (1995) is another theory used to explain the Proteus effect. Contrary to the idea that anonymity in online settings leads to a loss of self (i.e., deindividuation theory), the SIDE model proposes that it enhances the salience of social identity and promotes conformity to social norms. This model underlines that behavior in anonymous or virtual contexts is not impulsive but instead, is shaped by the social norms activated in these situations (Perfumi, 2020). Since its initial discovery, several studies have explored the Proteus effect and tried to extend its application to various avatar characteristics. For example, Fox et al. (2013) demonstrated that sexualized avatars could lead to increased self-objectification and heightened acceptance of rape myths. Other research has examined the Proteus effect in relation to different avatar traits, such as gender (Lee et al., 2014; Sherrick et al., 2014), race (Ash, 2015), weight (Peña & Kim, 2014), or creativity (Guegan et al., 2016). However, not all studies have successfully reproduced the findings of Yee and Bailenson (2007). Some investigations failed to bring out any Proteus effect (Ash, 2015), while others reported contradictory results. For instance, Sherrick et al. (2014) found that participants with male avatars displayed more feminine behaviors, and those with female avatars displayed more masculine ones, contrary to what was expected. In line with these mixed findings, it appears that the effect size for the Proteus effect is relatively small. Indeed, a meta-analysis of 46 studies found a small-to-medium effect size (Ratan et al., 2019), but this effect size was considered overestimated in a subsequent meta-analysis by Clark (2020). Current study Building on the Proteus effect, Lee et al. (2014) explored ways to mitigate stereotype threat effects on performance, particularly for women in mathematics, in a study we aim to replicate. In their study, participants were represented by either male or female avatars in a virtual environment, and their performance on a math task was assessed. The task required solving 20 arithmetic problems within 10 minutes, with co-actors represented by avatars as well. Participants either competed or cooperated with their co-actors. The study tested the hypothesis that individuals with male avatars would perform better than those with female avatars on quantitative tasks regardless of their actual gender, due to stereotype lift. Additionally, Lee et al. (2014) hypothesized that motivation would mediate this virtual stereotype lift effect. Their research demonstrated that individuals represented by male avatars outperformed those with female avatars on competitive mathematical tasks, independently of participants’ actual gender. This study provided evidence that avatar characteristics can reinforce or mitigate the influence of educational stereotypes on performance. However, replication is essential to ensure the reliability and generalizability of these findings; to our knowledge, no replication of Lee et al. (2014) has been realized to date. Therefore, the goal of the current study is to replicate the original study by Lee et al. (2014) as faithfully as possible, keeping the same hypotheses, materials, and procedure. This means using the same avatars, competitive math tasks, and a motivation questionnaire as Lee et al. (2014), with the objective to confirm and extend their findings on the impact of avatar representation on performance in virtual environments.

title_r: Fork of Sparkman & Walton (2017)
abstract_r: We are 3 undergraduate students of Psychology at the UGA (Grenoble Alpes University). By working on our Study and Research Assignment and under the supervision of Amélie Gourdon-Kanhukamwe we participated in the CREP (Collaborative Replications and Education Project). We choose to replicate the first experiment of Sparkman and Walton described in their 2017 paper “Dynamic Norms Promote Sustainable Behavior, Even if It Is Counternormative''. STUDENT RESEARCHERS Elsa BETTEGA Lou DE RANGO Nadia GRZYBOWSKA PROJECT SUPERVISION Amélie GOURDON-KANHUKAMWE Summary This article studies the influence of dynamic norm compared to static norm on individual behavior. A dynamic norm focuses on the change of a norm over time, whereas the static norm focuses on the current state of a norm. The hypothesis of Sparkman and Walton is that by presenting a message carrying a dynamic norm, compared to one carrying a static norm, participants will be more interested in changing their normative behavior. In the first experiment this unsuitable normative behavior is the one of meat consumption. During the experiment, participants answered an online survey. They were separated in two groups, each were shown a fact about the american meat consumption. In one group this fact was presented with the form of a static-norm and the other in the form of a dynamic-norm. Next every participant answered a question about their interest in reducing their meat consumption on a scale of 1 to 7 (1=not at all, 4=somewhat, 7= extremely). They were then asked the percentage of people making an effort to limit their meat consumption as well as the number of meatless meals eaten each week by the one who limited their meat consumption. They finished by reporting : their gender, political ideology (on a scale of 1 to 7, 1=very liberal, 7= very conservative) and whether they were vegetarian or vegan. The only IV (Independent Variable) in the experiment is the kind of norm induced in the message presented. This IV is provoked, inter-participant and of two modalities : dynamic-norm and static-norm. The DV (Dependant Variable) of the experiment is the answer of the first question about meat consumption, all the others are CV (Controlled Variable). The results were on the 122 participants, 4 were put aside (by being vegan or vegetarian they could hardly reduce their meat consumption). The results follow the hypothesis of Sparkman and Walton, participants showed more interest in following a counternormative behavior, reducing their meat consumption habit, when in the dynamic-norm condition. An effect of gender and political ideologies were also present and with these effects controlled, there was still a significant effect of the dynamic norm. Our Replication We intend on doing a replication experiment, we will then explore the same hypothesis as Sparkman & Walton about the impact of the dynamic-norm on the same counternormative yet sustainable behaviour. In addition, we will verify if the same effect of gender and political orientation is to be found in France. We planned on doing an online survey using Qualtrics. Unlike the original experiment the participants will not be remunerated. On the last online survey we led we ended up having approximately 200 participants. We then hope to have as much on this survey. By using G*Power we know that, if we manage to have between 150 or 260 participants the statistic power of the study would be between 0.80 and 0.95. ORIGINAL OSF PAGE : This page contains all the collected study materials and instructions from authors that we have compiled. We also include any comments from other contributors or follow up instructions that we have learned since the beginning of the project. Click "read more" below or choose the "Wiki" option above for further information. For technical problems, please contact OSF help desk (support@osf.io). For questions or information about the studies contact either either Kiersten Baughman (kierstenbaughman7@gmail.com) or Becka Plitt (becka.plitt@gmail.com) so that the materials can be made available on this website. Abstract It is well known that people conform to normative information about other people’s current attitudes and behaviors. Do they also conform to dynamic norms—information about how other people’s behavior is changing over time? We investigated this question in three online and two field experiments. Experiments 1 through 4 examined high levels of meat consumption, a normative and salient behavior that is decreasing in the United States. Dynamic norms motivated change despite prevailing static norms, increasing interest in eating less meat (Experiments 1–3) and doubling meatless orders at a café (Experiment 4). Mediators included the anticipation of less meat eating in the future (preconformity) and the inference that reducing meat consumption mattered to other people (Experiments 2 and 3). In Experiment 5, we took advantage of a natural comparison to provide evidence that dynamic norms can also strengthen social-norm interventions when the static norm is positive; a positive dynamic norm resulted in reduced laundry loads and water use over 3 weeks during a drought. Materials The original paper is here. This project will only be replicating the first study as described in the paper. The original materials for Experiment 1 are here. Sample To obtain a CREP completion certificate the minimum N for this project is 100. Notes from Original Author Perhaps most importantly, a successful replication of Experiment 1 would depend upon a successful manipulation of the salience/knowledge of static and dynamic norm information (the primary IV). This may or may not be as easy as it appeared in our research, where we had people simply read a statement providing static or dynamic norm information. It is easy to manipulate what people read, but it is not necessarily easy to manipulate what is salient in the reader's mind as a consequence of reading it. Specifically, people may read a static norm statement and then it may remind them of the trend in people eating less meat overtime (i.e. the dynamic norm). If this were the case, one should not predict the results we saw in our research, but instead a null result (see the general discussion of the paper). Further, there is good reason to believe this may be the case in this context. We ran the meat consumption studies starting in 2012. Since then, discussion of the decline in meat consumption in the US has been thoroughly highlighted by almost every major media outlet (see the New York Times, Guardian, the Atlantic, Washington Post, MSNBC, NY Post, Mashable, EVEN FOX NEWS, as well as online channels). Hence, it may be highly salient to participants, even if they're in the static norm condition. This may make it difficult to manipulate the IV successfully, as those in the static norm condition may already essentially be in the treatment condition. Perhaps worse, in the last few years there was actually a slight increase in meat consumption, and, even though there was a prior decade of decline, many media outlets are quick to jump to the conclusion that the trend has reversed, and now more and more people are eating meat (see USA today, VOX, among other outlets like blogs and such). This may easily lead participants to not trust the dynamic norm information provided in the original study. That said, I have a few thoughts on how to mitigate the above: After study 1, we began to include a free response with the IV that asked P's to answer why they thought the norm info we gave them was the case (see materials for studies 2, 3, and 4, e.g. "Why do you think this is?"). This is helpful for two reason: first, it ensures that participants on a platform like mturk actually read the information they're provided and respond to it; and second, it gives you a window into what they're thinking about. Thus, you have at least a rough way to assess if you've manipulated the salience of static or dynamic norms successfully. You can use this to see if anyone doesn't provide a coherent response (if they leave it blank, or write gibberish, they failed to complete the IV portion of the study and could be dropped). And, to the salience-related point above, it allows you to code what percent of participants in the static norm mention any attitude or behavior change overtime (i.e. if they say "People are becoming more health conscious." or "I think eating meat has declined because... " this indicates they are thinking about the dynamic norm, even though they're in the static norm condition, which would be a failure of to manipulate the IV). In our work, I believe we saw about 5-10% of people imply something had changed in the static norm group. We felt this was relatively low, so we weren't worried about it. But, if for instance you saw 20% or more of people mention that related attitudes, concerns, or behavior of others has shifted or changed in some way, that would suggest a greater portion of people are now thinking about the dynamic norm in the static norm condition. Indeed, these would only be the people who explicitly mentioned it, and as such is a conservative estimate of the true number of people who were thinking about the dynamic norm. That said, you could use this metric as a moderator: i.e. those who mention something changing in the static norm should not show differences between the statis norm, while the subset who mention no social change should be more likely to show differences compared to the dynamic norm condition. You might consider piloting materials to check for some of the concerns I mentioned above. You could ask participants for an assessment of believability. And you can ask participants "Did you already know this information?" after being given the dynamic norm. This would help you determine if the facts we shared are now simply common knowledge in the dynamic norm condition. This could also be a potential moderator

title_r: Investigating Fast-mapping in healthy adults using an implicit measure: looking at referent typicality
abstract_r: Fast Mapping (FM) has been proposed as a cortical-based learning process that allows for rapid memory formation, independent of the typical, hippocampally-dependent episodic memory system. This incidental learning procedure was originally proposed in adults and involves presenting a familiar reference picture alongside an unfamiliar object and its label. The known referent is thought to be mechanistically important in supporting the integration of new information into pre-existing semantic knowledge, especially in patients suffering from Hippocampal amnesia (Sharon et al., 2011). Coutanche and Thompson-Schill (2014) found that FM learning in healthy young adults showed an advantage for implicit memory tests but not for explicit memory tests. More specifically, they demonstrated that participants show better same-day lexical learning under the FM condition compared to the explicit encoding (EE) condition. However, our previous methodologic replication attempt of their study with over 80% statistical power and a sample of 56 young adults did not reproduce their same-day lexical competition finding. Instead, in a post-hoc analysis we found a facilitatory semantic priming effect instead of inhibitory lexical competition, which we attempted to replicate in a subsequent study but found no effects, i.e., neither semantic priming nor lexical competition. Nonetheless, Coutanche and Koch (2017) suggested that the typicality of the known referent might play a crucial role in FM learning. Their findings suggest that when a known referent is more typical, there is less same-day lexical learning. If our referents were too typical for our sample (despite using very similar stimuli to Coutanche and Koch, 2017), this could explain our failure to replicate their lexical competition effect. Therefore, in the experiment proposed here, we will explicitly manipulate the typicality of the referent item, and investigate whether this affects the degree of lexical competition (or semantic priming), e.g, only being found for less typical referents.

title_r: Investigating Fast-mapping in healthy adults using an implicit measure: looking at referent typicality
abstract_r: Fast Mapping (FM) has been proposed as a cortical-based learning process that allows for rapid memory formation, independent of the typical, hippocampally-dependent episodic memory system. This incidental learning procedure was originally proposed in adults and involves presenting a familiar reference picture alongside an unfamiliar object and its label. The known referent is thought to be mechanistically important in supporting the integration of new information into pre-existing semantic knowledge, especially in patients suffering from Hippocampal amnesia (Sharon et al., 2011). Coutanche and Thompson-Schill (2014) found that FM learning in healthy young adults showed an advantage for implicit memory tests but not for explicit memory tests. More specifically, they demonstrated that participants show better same-day lexical learning under the FM condition compared to the explicit encoding (EE) condition. However, our previous methodologic replication attempt of their study with over 80% statistical power and a sample of 56 young adults did not reproduce their same-day lexical competition finding. Instead, in a post-hoc analysis we found a facilitatory semantic priming effect instead of inhibitory lexical competition, which we attempted to replicate in a subsequent study but found no effects, i.e., neither semantic priming nor lexical competition. Nonetheless, Coutanche and Koch (2017) suggested that the typicality of the known referent might play a crucial role in FM learning. Their findings suggest that when a known referent is more typical, there is less same-day lexical learning. If our referents were too typical for our sample (despite using very similar stimuli to Coutanche and Koch, 2017), this could explain our failure to replicate their lexical competition effect. Therefore, in the experiment proposed here, we will explicitly manipulate the typicality of the referent item, and investigate whether this affects the degree of lexical competition (or semantic priming), e.g, only being found for less typical referents.

title_r: Economic Inequality and the Perceived Economic Value of Education
abstract_r: In order to participating in the validation of a scale measuring the perceived value of education (i.e, the descriptive perception that succeeding at school is important to obtain a higher economic status later). This research aims to test experimentally replicate the effects from Study 2 as well as results from the literature (Sommet et al., 2021). More precisely, we aim to experimentally replicate that higher economic inequality is related to higher perceived economic value of education and the higher the support for competition at school (results from Study 2). title_r: The predictive value of E/I for electrical brain stimulation efficacy: using data from the SHARP program
abstract_r: The present project uses data from the multi-site Strengthening Human Adaptive Reasoning and Problem-Solving (SHARP) program. This program was focused on enhancing adaptive reasoning and problem solving in healthy humans by means of electrical brain stimulation (tDCS, tRNS, and tACS) and computer-based cognitive training. This training is referred to as the Flexible, Adaptive, Synergistic training (FAST) and combines training of different executive functions in a computer game designed to engage. This game consists of a Robot Factory game which was developed by SimCoach games. Participants played the game for 9 or 11 consecutive days while receiving either tDCS, tRNS, tACS or a control condition of tDCS or tRNS (sham) over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). The main aim of this program was to target the neural networks associated with the executive functions assessed in the Robot factory game by increasing neural plasticity, and therefore enhancing adaptive reasoning and problem solving. SHARP was designed and implemented by experts in different fields from Honeywell, the University of Oxford, Harvard Medical School, and Northeastern University. The analyses mentioned in the preregistration will focus on phases 1B and 2B of the SHARP program and their results related to resting-state (rs) theta power. Phase 1B was focused on validating the intervention and phase 2B tried to demonstrate the effectiveness of individualization based on rs-theta power, which was unsuccessful. Therefore, the present project will replicate the analyses presented in phase 1B and 2B using the aperiodic exponent to see whether the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance in the brain, which may have been confounded with the periodic activity in the original analysis, underlies stimulation efficacy as opposed to rs-theta power. Additionally, this will be a large-scale conceptual replication comparing the findings with the results presented by van Bueren and colleagues (2023) in terms of stimulation efficacy markers, especially the aperiodic exponent (E/I).

title_r: Influence of emotional valence and arousal on voluntary task switching.
abstract_r: Previous research has found that inducing positive emotion leads to smaller switch costs, while inducing negative emotions leads to larger switch costs in a cued task switching paradigm. This has been interpreted as showing that positive emotion leads to a more flexible cognitive control state, while negative emotions promote more stable control. To test this interpretation, Demanet et al. (2011) sought to investigate whether participants would also be more likely to choose to switch tasks in a voluntary task switching paradigm when shown positive pictures (and less likely when shown negative pictures). They found that inducing positive emotion had no effect on switch costs, although high arousal pictures had higher switch costs compared to neutral pictures. Importantly, they found no difference in task choice. The current experiment is a conceptual replication of Demanet et al. (2011), using a dual-registration procedure, a larger number of participants, and a focus on levels of picture arousal in the self-assessment mannikin (SAM). We are interested in exploring whether a difference in task choice can be found following these adjustments to the Demanet et al. (2011) paradigm.

title_r: Dissociating sensory, decisional, and metacognitive noise in perceptual decision making
abstract_r: Perceptual decisions are influenced by sensory, decisional, and metacognitive noise. In two previous experiments, we isolated these noise types using an external noise paradigm, where the same stimulus value could be associated with two categories. Notably, we found that metacognitive noise exceeded decisional noise, and it increased for confidence criteria further from the decision criterion. This indicates that noise in confidence ratings may largely stem from the decisional noise of the initial perceptual judgment and that it is signal-dependent, increasing with more extreme evidence values (Shekhar & Rahnev, 2021). In the current preregistered experiment, we aim to replicate and extend these findings using conventional perceptual decision-making paradigms. The experiment includes a discrimination task and a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) task. In the discrimination task, subjects will judge whether the orientation of a Gabor patch is greater or less than 45 degrees to the right of vertical and rate their decision confidence. In the 2AFC task, In the 2AFC task, subjects will be presented with two tilted Gabor patches: one exactly 45 degrees from vertical and the other slightly deviating from 45 degrees. They need to identify which of two Gabor patches is tilted clockwise from the other. We will use a computational model from the previous experiments to estimate sensory noise in the 2AFC task. After determining the sensory noise, we will apply another model from the earlier experiments to assess decisional and metacognitive noise in the discrimination task.

title_r: Font-size effects on Studying decisions 3
abstract_r: This study is a conceptual replication of https://osf.io/4hc6y We previously found evidence that people choose to study small font word pairs over large font word pairs, but only if better cues (covert retrieval success) are not available. This suggested that the effect of font size on judgments of learning (JOLs) have potential application beyond the lab--the overconfidence in memory for large font items affects self-regulated learning decisions. However, we did not replicate they typical font size effects on JOLs (but found an effect on study decisions). We suspect that people have additional cues to use when judging word pairs (e.g., word relatedness) that minimize the effect of font size on JOLs and study decisions. Thus we expect to find larger effects when using individual words as stimuli.

title_r: REPLICATION OF: Automatic and Controlled Processes in Stereotype Priming
abstract_r: This project aims to replicate the experimental procedure and findings of the article titled “Automatic and Controlled Processes in Stereotype Priming” (Blair & Banaji, 1996). The original study included four experiments examining the activation of stereotypes and the effects of intentional strategies in moderating stereotypical responses. Our replication will focus on the Experiment 3, where a four-way interaction (SOA x intentional strategies x prime gender x target gender) is investigated. We expect to replicate their findings that controlled processes can override automatic stereotypic processes to a considerable degree, and cognitive constraints (manipulated by SOAs) play an important role in moderating the process. Our experimental procedure mostly follows the original study. Blair, I. V., & Banaji, M. R. (1996). Automatic and controlled processes in stereotype priming. title_r: The Effect of Time Pressure on Automation Reliance in a Face Matching Task
abstract_r: Participants can significantly improve their own face matching performance when assisted by a highly accurate simulated Automated Facial Recognition System (AFRS; Carragher & Hancock, 2023). However, the performance of these human-AFRS teams was suboptimal, such that the AFRS achieved higher accuracy alone. This result points toward issues around operator misuse and/or disuse of the AFRS (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997). The aim of the current study is to investigate the operational factors that might influence reliance on the AFRS decision aid. One factor known to increase reliance on automated decision aids is task difficulty (Schwark et al., 2010). In the context of face matching tasks, time pressure (the amount of time that the stimulus is visible) is known to have a significant effect on accuracy. Fysh and Bindemann (2017) reported that performance on a face matching task was highest when participants were given 10 seconds to view each face pair, and lowest when the presentation time was decreased to 2 seconds. Alenezi et al. (2015) reported that the average time taken to respond in a face matching experiment without time pressure was around 5 seconds. Here we investigate whether time pressure influences reliance on decisions from an AFRS in a one-to-one forensic face matching task. Pilot data collected in a student project (see https://osf.io/t8cfr) indicated a pattern of gradual decrease in initial accuracy as time pressure increased, replicating Fysh and Bindemann (2017). However, the accuracy of final decisions made with AFRS assistance remained relatively consistent among all time pressure conditions. This pattern of results indicated that participants increased their reliance on AFRS decisions in higher time pressures, consistent with the idea that automation use is more likely on harder tasks. Although these results were consistent with our predictions, the pilot data suffered a limitation – the higher than expected unassisted accuracy of participants. The high unassisted accuracy meant that there was little room for improvement with the assistance of the AFRS, which may have contributed to key results failing to reach significance, even though the pattern of results matched our predictions. We wish to replicate the method of the previous experiment using a harder face matching task to explore whether time pressure affects operator reliance on a simulated AFRS. As such, the current pre-registration is closely modelled on that for the student project described above (https://osf.io/t8cfr).

title_r: Word-Repetition Rate and Cognitive Defusion: A Replication of Differential Effects on Believability and Discomfort.
abstract_r: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a third-wave psychotherapy with comparable efficacy to Cognitive Behavioural Therapy in treating a variety of mental health conditions (Gloster et al., 2020; Öst, 2014). A core tenet of ACT is cognitive defusion, the ability to detach from your thoughts (Harris, 2019), which can be facilitated through strategies such as the word repetition technique. This technique is designed to fundamentally change a thought’s initial functioning context and subsequently reduce its familiarity and associated meaning (Titchener, 2010; Hayes et al.,1999). While existing research supports the efficacy of the word repetition technique (Masuda et al., 2004; Masuda et al., 2009; Pilecki & McKay, 2012), the parameters under which it is most effective are not specified (Tyndall et al., 2017; Lavelle et al., 2021). As such, a recent study by Tyndall et al. (2017), examined rate of word repetition to identify whether this component differentially affected participant self-reported believability and discomfort produced by negative self-evaluative words. Specifically, participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: 0.5s; 1s; and 2s where they repeated their self-selected negative self-evaluative word at the specified rate. Results suggested participants in the 0.5s and 1s groups had significantly lower scores of believability and discomfort recorded immediately post-intervention, with the 1s condition maintaining the lowest scores at 1-month follow-up. Despite yielding statistically significant findings with moderate to large effect sizes, Tyndall et al. (2017) acknowledged several important limitations. The study was arguably underpowered, potentially increasing the risk of Type II errors. Additionally, offering participation incentives may have introduced bias, particularly given the reliance on self-report measures. The sample comprised exclusively undergraduate psychology students, limiting generalizability to broader populations. These limitations highlight the need for a well-powered replication study that addresses these methodological concerns A critical limitation was the absence of a control condition, which would have enabled meaningful comparisons between word repetition conditions and no intervention. This omission is particularly significant given conflicting findings in the literature. Previous evaluations (De Young et al., 2010; Lopez de Uralde-Selva & Valero-Aguayo, 2021) suggest that word repetition techniques may not differ significantly from control conditions in producing cognitive defusion. Taken together, the proposed study is a conceptual replication of Tyndall et al. (2017) with the following changes: The analyses are sufficiently powered, and participant recruitments is informed by an apriori power analysis. Participant recruitment will span beyond university student samples and be conducted using an online platform (Microsoft Teams). Participants will not be provided with incentives for taking part (e.g., research time for completing modules). The 2s rate condition from Tyndall et al. (2017) which was the least effective condition will be replaced by a control condition whereby participants will receive no word repetition intervention and instead complete a brief reading comprehension task from the Gorilla repository.

title_r: Dishonesty and Creativity
abstract_r: In their seminal work, Gino and Wiltermuth (2014) posited a captivating notion: dishonesty enhances creativity. However, in light of the retraction of their work due to data falsification, as well as recent meta-analytic results that cast doubt upon the link between these constructs, the question of whether dishonesty leads to greater creativity remains an unanswered, empirical question. As the veracity of this claim holds immense value to psychology and the world at large, we conducted two high-powered, pre-registered replication studies (experiments 3 and 4 from the retracted research) to examine whether the presence of a causal link is scientifically warranted. Results reveal dishonesty had < a small | a medium | no > effect on creativity, a finding that < was | was not > qualified by experimental design (i.e., incentivizing dishonest behavior in different ways). In sum, our results < confirm | disconfirm > the original claims made by Gino and Wiltermuth, highlighting < the potential advantages of rule-breaking behaviors on creativity | the necessity for additional research to explore alternative means of inducing creativity >. NOTE: Given the exploratory nature of this replication attempt, statements that will be conditionally selected based upon results are indicated above with "< | >".

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Raver & Nishii (2010), from The Journal of Applied Psychology
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Raver & Nishii (2010) is that racial minority group members report experiencing significantly higher levels of Ethnic Harassment (EH), reflected in the paper’s abstract (“Racial group differences in EH (Ethnic Harassment) emerged”). Poisson regression analysis was used to test for differences in the frequency of EH reported by responders who were racial or ethnic minorities vs. Caucasian, yielding that Caucasian participants were reported significantly lower EH than those in minority groups (Beta = -0.17, p < 0.05).

title_r: 124_Switching between external and internal attention from a declarative working memory perspective: Degrading the external stimuli
abstract_r: Currently, there is no unitary understanding of the relation between internal attention (used in the domain of memory) and external attention (used in the domain of perception). Some researchers define them as different processes, while others propose that they are highly overlapping. A recent study of Verschooren et al. (2020, DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/xhp0000758) investigated the behavioral cost of switching between external stimuli and internal representations and observed an asymmetric switch cost. Participants switched on a trial-by-trial basis between external stimuli and internal representations (retrieved from memory) in a probe-to-target matching task. The researchers found a larger switch cost when switching towards the internal representations compared to the external stimuli. The aim of this project is to investigate whether this asymmetrical switch cost might be due to an asymmetry in strength between the external stimuli (i.e. present on screen) and the internal representations (i.e. retrieved from memory). In particular, we aim to examine whether the switch cost pattern becomes less asymmetrical when the asymmetry in strength is reduced. To do so, we will do a conceptual replication of the original study (Experiment 1; Verschooren et al., 2020) using degraded external stimuli. We expect the external stimuli to be reduced in strength and thus, more similar in strength to the internal representations. This study follows up on our preregistered direct replication (https://osf.io/75t4m) of the original study (Experiment 1; Verschooren et al., 2020).

title_r: Replication of Novel Groups Study at BYUI Spring 2025
abstract_r: The current study will replicate the original study by Woitzel and Alves (2024). This replication attempt specifically focuses on Experiment 4b, which examined the difference in impressions of individuals toward different types of traits that were presented by the members of ingroups and outgroups, from the original study. The samples in this replication were recruited from the students enrolled in PSYCH 111 courses at Brigham Young University-Idaho during the Spring 2025 semester with a total size of (-). The survey was created based on the survey that was used in the original study, which was obtained through the Open Science Framework (OSF), and distributed to the participants online. The theory of the original study states that negative attitudes towards out-groups, minorities, and novel groups are formed, not only from a desire to boost one’s own outlook of themselves, but also from how we learn about different groups. To be more specific, the order in which we gain information about different groups and their different attributes leads to negative attitudes being formed about out-groups, minorities, and novel groups. The purpose of this study is to examine if individuals, when evaluating sequential groups independently of their in-group or out-group status, will evaluate the second-encountered group mainly on distinct attributes, meaning positive or negative, more than the first encountered group.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Abouk & Heydari (2020), from medRxiv
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Abouk & Heydari (2020) is that the tendency to remain at home is driven strongly by the statewide stay-home order. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “They show that while strong policies such as statewide stay home mandate and non-essential business closure have strong causal impact on reducing social interactions, most of the expected impact of more lenient policies (such as large gathering ban and school closure mandates) are already reaped from non-policy mechanisms such as voluntary actions and public awareness.” The claim was tested by estimating a difference-in-differences regression, where, for each policy, there is defined a binary variable, set to one if a given state adopts that policy after a certain day during the sample period, and otherwise zero. This analysis indicated that statewide stay-home orders significantly increase the measure associated with presence at home by about six fold (relative to states without such a policy; from Table 2: estimate of “statewide stay-home order” on “presence at home” = 2.058, p < 0.01).

title_r: The revival of Bobo the doll
abstract_r: We are replicating Alfred Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross’ study on transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models (1961). The study emphasizes the importance of observational learning on aggression in children, in an immediate social influence setting. The subjects were children between the ages of 37 to 69 months (36 boys and 36 girls) who were enrolled in the Stanford University Nursery School. There were two models (one male and one female) and one female who conducted the study for all 72 participants. The children would, in the experimental part of this study, first be placed in a room with an activity of high interest to them. In the same room, a model would exhibit either aggressive or non-aggressive behaviors (towards a tinker toy set, a mallet, and the 5-foot bobo doll). After this, the children were moved to another room with different toys. Some of the toys present were “aggressive”, like the bobo doll, a mallet, darth guns and so on. The other toys were non-aggressive. Some children did not observe a model and were only placed in the latter room (playing with toys without exposure to a model's behavior). These subjects worked as a control group. Through observing subjects exposed to these different behaving models, and further observing what kind of behavior they exhibited (towards the toys) after being exposed to the models, Bandura et. al. found that children imitate behavior from observation, especially if the models were exhibiting aggressive behavior and/or were male (Bandura, D. Ross & A. Ross, 1960, p. 578). Replicating this study is scientifically important because a replication might indicate whether or not the results/conclusions of Bandura et. als. study are applicable today. And since this study was conducted in 1961 (61 years ago), we might expect social behavior, like imitation from observational learning (of aggression in this case), to change through the years. E.g.; we believe and predict that socio-economic development has influenced children's observational and imitational abilities through e.g. watching TV, using cell phones, and having tablets as “nannies”. Further, we believe that this lack of physical interaction with models, starting early in childhood, will lead children to pay less attention to models later on in different circumstances, i.e. they might imitate less. The rise of individualism, especially in western countries, might also affect children’s observational and imitational abilities. The focus on the individual might make people want to act more independently, and i.e. not imitate behavior as much. Because of socio-economic development and individualism, we predict (in H1) that participants from the experimental group will imitate less behavior (especially aggression) than the participants in the original study. Feminism might also have play in the eventual results of this replication because women’s place in society has changed a lot the last 61 years - women are more equal to men today than earlier years. Therefore, we predict that (H2) participants will exhibit an equal amount of imitation, regardless of the model’s gender. If we find (huge) differences in the results of the original study and our replication, our understanding of human history and development is in for discussion. Alternatively, a replication with results that differ from the original study could indicate poor validity and/or reliability of the original study. If that turns out to be true, we might have to dismiss Bandura et. als. findings on observational learning in aggression. Therefore, we will conduct a direct replication experiment.

title_r: AI Voice Perception - Crime Nudges
abstract_r: In previous research, we demonstrated that listeners displayed a Human Categorisation Bias when tasked with identifying Human and AI-enhanced voices. This bias was stronger in regional dialects, for those with greater familiarity with them. One explanation is because participants had prior beliefs about technology's ability to accurately represent these underrepresented varieties. Another study we replicated this paradigm, but with the inclusion of additional information. One condition contained a positive nudge, indicating that AI technology has become advanced enough to replicate Scottish accents and dialects. A negative nudge condition indicated that this technology still struggles with Scottish accents and dialects. A control condition did not provide any information about this technology. The results demonstrate no differences in between the Negative and Control condition, but both differed from the Positive nudge condition, in which the magnitude of the Human Categorisation Bias was halved. In this follow up, we want to investigate which other nudge information might also affect this bias. We will include nudge information that states: 1) "Recent advancements in AI voice technology mean that it is now possible to authentically replicate Scottish accents and dialects" (Positive Nudge, same as previous study) 2) "AI voices are increasingly used in scams, fraud, and deception. Mistaking an AI voice as a real Human can have serious real world consequences" (Crime Nudge) 3) Recent advancements in AI voice technology mean that it is now possible to authentically replicate Scottish accents and dialects. AI voices are increasingly used in scams, fraud, and deception. Mistaking an AI voice as a real Human can have serious real world consequences." (Combined Nudge)

title_r: Does intrinsic voice memorability affect memory for spoken content?
abstract_r: Intrinsic stimulus memorability, which has thus far largely been characterized for visual stimuli (Bainbridge et al., 2013; Isola et al., 2014) was recently explored for the first time in the auditory domain by our research team (Revsine et al., 2024). Speakers were found to be consistently memorable or forgettable to participants, across two different utterances. This result begs the question of whether this intrinsic voice memorability affects memory for speech content, when the content is varied across speakers. We recently ran an experiment testing this question, using speakers with high and low average d’ from our previous study, but now each speaking a unique sentence. Participants listened to and then verbally recalled each sentence following a distractor task. Unexpectedly, we found that speaker d’ had no effect on the recall of the sentences. However, we found that the hit rate (HR) of the stimuli from a prior experiment in which participants heard multiple utterances (Revsine et al., 2024; Experiment 3) did negatively correlate with recall error rate. We suspect that due to the nature of the recall experiment, which does not involve false alarms, HR as a memorability metric may be more predictive of memory for content than d’. Therefore, we are running an experiment to see whether we can replicate this effect, using HR instead of d’ to select highly memorable and forgettable stimuli. To investigate the relationship between memorability and listening effort, we will also record pupillometry data while participants perform the task, as pupil size is known to be a proxy for listening effort (Pichora-Fuller et al., 2016). In sum, this study will provide novel insight into the behavioral and cognitive mechanisms underlying memory for speech.

title_r: An adapted storage-retrieval MPT analysis of the wakeful resting effect
abstract_r: In a previous study (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/ZRJ94), we used a storage-retrieval multinomial processing tree (MPT) model to disentangle storage and retrieval contributions to the wakeful resting effect in episodic memory. In line with both consolidation accounts and more traditional retroactive interference (RI) accounts, wakeful resting after learning had positive effects on storage and retrieval probabilities for previously studied vocabulary compared to a condition where participants studied further vocabulary. However, we failed to replicate positive effects of wakeful resting compared to a social media condition found by Martini et al. (2020). In the present study, we will adapt the order of memory tests which might have counteracted the social media effect in our previous study. Additionally, we will investigate the relationship of participants’ sensory processing sensitivity (SPS; see Marhenke et al., 2023) with both their recall and recognition performances, and their storage and retrieval MPT parameter estimates.

title_r: Working Memory and Eyewitness Metamemory as Reflectors of Identification Accuracy when Memory Strength Varies
abstract_r: We will investigate individual differences in working memory capacity and eyewitness metamemory as potential reflectors of eyewitness identification accuracy when eyewitnesses vary in memory strength, as well as explore the confidence-accuracy relationship across levels of these variables. Working Memory Capacity Working memory, a limited-capacity system for managing and manipulating information (Baddeley, 1986), is related to eyewitness recall performance (Chae & Ceci, 2005; Jaschinski & Wentura, 2002). Andersen et al. (2014) found that higher working memory capacity predicted more accurate identifications in target-present simultaneous lineups and fewer filler identifications in target-absent lineups, though results varied by lineup type. Further research is needed to clarify this relationship. Metamemory Metamemory involves awareness of one’s memory abilities (Dunlosky & Bjork, 2008). Saraiva et al. (2019, 2020) found that metamemory judgements were related to lineup performance; that is, Contentment and Strategies factors of a recently developed metamemory scale EMS (Saraiva et al., 2019) predicted better while Discontentment factor predicted lower accuracy. We aim to replicate and extend these findings, using discriminability measures and administering the EMS after lineup decisions to reflect practical scenarios (cf. before as done in the original study). Memory Strength and Confidence-Accuracy Relationship We will manipulate memory strength to a) generalize individual differences as reflector variables findings across varying levels of memory for a crime, b) explore interactions of memory strength with individual differences, and c) test competing models of the confidence-accuracy relationship: the optimality hypothesis (Deffenbacher, 1980) and the constant likelihood ratio model (Semmler et al., 2018). Prior studies suggest that awareness of memory quality influences confidence and the confidence-accuracy relationship (Pezdek et al., 2020; Grabman et al., 2019). We predict that the confidence-accuracy relationship will remain consistent across memory strength conditions (as per the constant likelihood ratio model), assuming participants are aware of their memory quality for the crime. However, if participants lack awareness of their working memory capacity, we expect the optimality hypothesis to hold, with higher-capacity individuals showing stronger confidence-accuracy links. To test this, we will assess participants’ beliefs about their memory quality, general memory ability, and the influence of factors like delay and face recognition ability.

title_r: Working Memory and Eyewitness Metamemory as Reflectors of Identification Accuracy when Memory Strength Varies
abstract_r: We will investigate individual differences in working memory capacity and eyewitness metamemory as potential reflectors of eyewitness identification accuracy when eyewitnesses vary in memory strength, as well as explore the confidence-accuracy relationship across levels of these variables. Working Memory Capacity Working memory, a limited-capacity system for managing and manipulating information (Baddeley, 1986), is related to eyewitness recall performance (Chae & Ceci, 2005; Jaschinski & Wentura, 2002). Andersen et al. (2014) found that higher working memory capacity predicted more accurate identifications in target-present simultaneous lineups and fewer filler identifications in target-absent lineups, though results varied by lineup type. Further research is needed to clarify this relationship. Metamemory Metamemory involves awareness of one’s memory abilities (Dunlosky & Bjork, 2008). Saraiva et al. (2019, 2020) found that metamemory judgements were related to lineup performance; that is, Contentment and Strategies factors of a recently developed metamemory scale EMS (Saraiva et al., 2019) predicted better while Discontentment factor predicted lower accuracy. We aim to replicate and extend these findings, using discriminability measures and administering the EMS after lineup decisions to reflect practical scenarios (cf. before as done in the original study). Memory Strength and Confidence-Accuracy Relationship We will manipulate memory strength to a) generalize individual differences as reflector variables findings across varying levels of memory for a crime, b) explore interactions of memory strength with individual differences, and c) test competing models of the confidence-accuracy relationship: the optimality hypothesis (Deffenbacher, 1980) and the constant likelihood ratio model (Semmler et al., 2018). Prior studies suggest that awareness of memory quality influences confidence and the confidence-accuracy relationship (Pezdek et al., 2020; Grabman et al., 2019). We predict that the confidence-accuracy relationship will remain consistent across memory strength conditions (as per the constant likelihood ratio model), assuming participants are aware of their memory quality for the crime. However, if participants lack awareness of their working memory capacity, we expect the optimality hypothesis to hold, with higher-capacity individuals showing stronger confidence-accuracy links. To test this, we will assess participants’ beliefs about their memory quality, general memory ability, and the influence of factors like delay and face recognition ability.

Dr. Anthony Krafnick will be the faculty mentor throughout this project from the IRB process through data analysis. Our project number for the larger CREP project is AC1803. See the parent OSF page for the larger Accelerated Crep project with additional details including Turri et al. (2015)'s original abstract: https://osf.io/x978m/ Our Replication We will complete a direct replication of Experiment 1 from Turri et al. (2015) in an attend to estimate the Gettier intuition effect size. Each subject will complete the experiment using SoSciSurvey software, organized across the Accelerated Crep project sites. Each subject will be randomly assigned (via SoSciSurvey) to one of the three knowledge conditions (knowledge, Gettier case, ignorance), for each of the three vignette types (Gerald, Emma, Darrel) with counterbalancing employed. See the Materials page for a PDF of screenshots from the Dominican University collection site. Participants will be recruited through Dominican University's subject recruitment pool and will complete the study with a link to the SoSciSurvey page for our site specific link. Data analysis will be completed using the direct replication statistics support provided by Accelerated Crep and linked with the main page for this collection site.

title_r: Partner Preferences in Members of a High-IQ Society
abstract_r: To date, only few studies have examined partner preferences of highly gifted individuals. As stated by the similarity-attraction hypothesis, the more similar two people are, the greater the attraction between them (Byrne, 1971). Accordingly, highly intelligent individuals should be drawn to similarly intelligent partners. However, for the general population, studies consistently found traits other than intelligence to be more important in mate selection (Walter et al., 2020). Whether highly intelligent individuals’ partner preferences differ from the general population’s remains to be investigated. Walter et al. (2020) reexamined mate preferences across 45 countries in a large-scale replication study. In this study, “kind” was the highest-rated trait in a potential partner, though the rating difference was not tested for significance. The authors also found that across cultures, women, on average, had a higher preference for a partner with good financial prospects than men (b = −0.30, SE = 0.03, p < .001), whereas men preferred physically attractive partners more than women did (b = 0.27, SE = 0.03, p < .001). In this study, men also reported having a partner younger than themselves whereas women reported having partners older than themselves on average (b = −0.96, SE = 0.05, p < .001), indicating that women prefer older men and men prefer younger women, and confirming previous studies. Gignac et al. (2018) examined the construct of sapiosexuality indicating an attraction to the intellectual or mental qualities of a person. Their results showed a curvilinear relationship between attractiveness and intelligence, with a threshold at the 90th percentile beyond which the level of attractiveness decreased. Based on the similarity attraction hypothesis, one might argue that this threshold is higher for highly intelligent individuals. In addition, Gignac et al. (2018) developed the Sapiosexuality Questionnaire (SapioQ) to measure sapiosexuality. They found that women scored higher on the SapioQ with a moderate effect size (d = -0.34). Jonason et al. (2019) found that women’s self-rated mate value is associated with greater attraction to men who are more intelligent than themselves, whereas men’s mate value is unrelated to the desirability of women as a function of their intelligence. Dijkstra et al. (2012), examining a sample of highly intelligent individuals, showed that relationship status affects partner preferences, with single individuals assigning particular importance to the (potential) partner’s intelligence.

Gignac et al. (2018) examined the construct of sapiosexuality indicating an attraction to the intellectual or mental qualities of a person. Their results showed a curvilinear relationship between attractiveness and intelligence, with a threshold at the 90th percentile beyond which the level of attractiveness decreased. Based on the similarity attraction hypothesis, one might argue that this threshold is higher for highly intelligent individuals. In addition, Gignac et al. (2018) developed the Sapiosexuality Questionnaire (SapioQ) to measure sapiosexuality. They found that women scored higher on the SapioQ with a moderate effect size (d = -0.34). Jonason et al. (2019) found that women’s self-rated mate value is associated with greater attraction to men who are more intelligent than themselves, whereas men’s mate value is unrelated to the desirability of women as a function of their intelligence. Dijkstra et al. (2012), examining a sample of highly intelligent individuals, showed that relationship status affects partner preferences, with single individuals assigning particular importance to the (potential) partner’s intelligence.

title_r: Why are stoics unhappy? An idionomic analysis of the relationship between valued action and affect. [working title]
abstract_r: An existing body of research suggests that engaging in values-consistent behaviour is associated with greater lower symptomology of depression, anxiety, and stress, more satisfaction with life, more positive emotions, lower distress, and greater hedonic wellbeing (Gloster et al., 2017; Gregoire et al., 2021; Tunc et al., 2023; Villate et al., 2016; Sahdra et al., 2024). Interventions that are intended to increase engagement in values-consistent behaviour have therefore been posited as an effective way to decrease suffering in individuals (Gloster et al., 2017). Based on the nomothetic results, it is unsurprising that clinicians have come to this conclusion. However, a burgeoning area of research is beginning to show that applying such nomothetic results to individuals in clinical practice may be premature. Specifically, Hayes and Colleagues have started to demonstrate that nomothetic research methodologies are masking significant levels of individual difference (Ciarrochi et al., 2023, pre-print; Gloster et al., 2024; Hayes et al., 2022; Sahdra et al., 2024). As such, they have embarked on a novel research project, which they term “idionomic” research. The current study aims to examine the links between values-consistent behaviour and affect in a clinical in- and out-patient population, as a conceptual replication of Sahdra et al., (2024). We intend to utilise de-identified archival data from Gloster et al., (2022). The original study examined the efficacy of individualised Acceptance and Commitment therapy in a transdiagnostic, treatment-resistant population. To examine psychological flexibility, treatment parameters, and contextual variables in real time, the original study collected ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data at baseline, one-week post-treatment, and 12 months follow-up. For the current study, an idionomic analysis of baseline EMA data will be performed to explicate the individual relationships between values-consistent behaviour and affect, and the heterogeneity of these relationships, largely following the procedure outlined in Sahdra et al., (2024). By investigating this EMA data, we hope to build support for the findings of Sahdra et al., (2024) and build on these findings to increase clinical utility.

title_r: The Own-Race Bias for Face Recognition in a Multiracial Society: Replication
abstract_r: Own-Race Bias (ORB) is a phenomenon in cognitive science describing the tendency of individuals to recognize own-race faces easier than other-race faces (Meissner and Brigham, 2001). Wong, Hoo Keat et al. (2020) found that there is better recognition performance in own-race faces opposed to other-race faces in Asian, Indian, Malaysian, and Caucasian participants when only internal features were included. However, participants performed equally well at recognizing own-race and other-race faces by the inclusion of external features. Furthermore, responses from a social contact questionnaire measured social contact within participant groups, which evidenced strong interactions and greater quantity and quality of contact between own-race participants as opposed to other-race participants. In the current experiment, we want to examine the Own-Race Bias phenomenon by running a high-powered online conceptual replication of Wong et al. (2020; Experiment 1). Wong et al. examined facial recognition performance by providing the following options: (1) yes, and (2) no, one for 5 seconds each. 16 of these faces were from the learning phase while the other 16 were distractors not seen before.

title_r: Replication of Sparkman & Walton (2017) at Dickinson College
abstract_r: We are students and a professor at Dickinson College leading this replication study as a class project towards fulfilling the requirements of our statistics course for Spring, 2023. Only the teaching assistants are currently listed as collaborators, but the intention is to offer to interested students to join the project after the semester. In addition to a direct replication of static vs. dynamic norm on meat consumption, we will extend the original study in two ways (see below). The research design will be 2(norm: static or dynamic) X 2(attribution: involuntary behavior or not). Students in this class will collaborate on this study and recruit adult participants from their social networks. The target sample size is 300, which means approximately 75 participants for each of the four conditions. The extensions address two concerns raised by the original author. The original author suggested probing participants’ understanding of the norm statement they are assigned to. Specifically, we will add two questions (“Why do you think this is?” “Did you already know this information?”) after each norm statement. Asking these questions will allow us to examine if the effect will be moderated by what the participants think of the information presented. For example, participants reading the static norm may infer change over time, which would indicate failure to manipulate static norm. Or if participants reading the dynamic norm think the change is common knowledge, they may not be affected. We will also manipulate attribution of the information about meat consumption. This addresses the possibility that change in meat consumption due to external limitations is not as motivating as change chosen voluntarily. Thus, we will add two conditions: static norm plus a description that it is largely due to supply shortages and rising prices and dynamic norm plus the same description. As the description emphasizes the change is not driven by perceived importance or deliberate choice, participants may be less inclined to change themselves.

title_r: Replication of Sherif´s Norm Formation Study
abstract_r: Sherif´s Norm Formation study was conducted in 1935. The experimenter put people in a dark room watching a light ray. By projecting the light on a screen, it appears to move although it doesn't. The instruction was: “When the room is completely dark, I shall give the signal READY, and then show you a point of light. After a short time, the light will start to move. A few seconds later the light will disappear”. The participants were then asked to guess how far the light moved through the room, first individually and then in the group. The group consisted of three participants, two of which had very similar individual guesses and one who guessed very differently. When the individuals of the group had to say their guess out loud, the third one, who’s speculation was different, changed their answer and conformed to the answer of the other two. The group came to an agreement although the individual answers were different from each other (Holt, 2019, p. 245, 246). It is important to replicate this study to be able to generalize the results to other situations. Applying the method to a different scenario and getting the same outcome, could show that the theory of conformity is applicable to many different situations. In other words, replication helps verify that the presence of a specific behavior at one point in time is not just due to chance. Often, there are a huge number of variables that can result in biases and wrongful conclusions in every psychological study, so with each replication the conclusion becomes more valid and trustworthy (Woodell, 2020). The report that the Open Science Collaboration (2015) put forth, showed that journals were more likely to publish innovative studies over replication studies (Woodell, 2020). A reason could be that many researchers are opposed to conducting a replication study, because it means admitting that the original research could have variables and biases affecting the results. The original study was based on research of male students from Colombia University. When replicating this study, we will make the subject pool more diverse. This is important because it will make the results more fit to be generalized. To do this, we will implement different genders, as well as different age groups. In contrast to the original study, this will likely give the results more depth, as the subject pool is less strict and unvarying. We predict we will find that teenagers from 13-16 years old are more likely to conform. Generally, they are often more self-conscious, lack experience and knowledge, and are usually known for caring a lot about what their peers think of them. In addition, we would not state that there will be a gender difference across age groups. There could be aesthetic judgements that the group members make of each other that could influence their answers. However, we believe that the adults from 35-38 years old would also conform to some extent. We predict that they would take longer than the teenagers to come to an agreement in the group. Our replication will contain a total of 200 people. They would be divided into six different groups based on their age, gender, and role in the study. The adults are from 35-38 years old, and the teenagers are from 13-16 years old. In summary, we would make a conceptual replication of the Sherif's Norm Formation study, in which we would conduct similar tests in our study by asking participants to guess an unknown length, having the same number of people in each group and procedure as in the chosen study of Sherif.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from McLaren (2012), from World Politics
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from McLaren (2012) is that individuals expressing most concern about the impact of immigration on the national community will be most distrusting of politicians and political institutions (Proposition 1). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "The findings indicate that even after controlling for other predictors of trust in the political system, concerns about the effect of immigration on the national community have an impact on trust in politics." The claim is tested with multivariate analyses conducted using HLM on four rounds of the ESS [European Social Survey]. The author uses multilevel modeling with a three-level model with the individual at level 1, variables that are measured at the country level and that vary across the four rounds of the ESS (country-round) at level 2, and variables measured at the country level that do not vary across the four rounds at level 3. The dependent variable, political distrust, measures how much the respondent trusts each of three institutions: the country’s parliament, the legal system, and politicians; for the SCORE program, the parliament measure is used [the author finds support using each measure]. The independent variable of interest is concern about immigration (see the Parliament columns in Table 3 for details on the model selected for the SCORE program). The results indicate that after controlling for fairly powerful predictors of distrust in politics, concern about immigration has a statistically significant effect on distrust in politics, with maximum effects of 1.7 on the 11-point measure of distrust in parliament (coefficient [b] on concern about immigration term = 0.17, SE = 0.00, p = 0.000). Concern about immigration ranges between 0 and 10, and moving from 0 to one would be associated with a 1.7 unit change on distrust in the parliament, which also is measured on a scale from 0 to 10.

title_r: Don’t listen to yourself! A preregistered auditory distraction study about ignoring one's own voice and that of others
abstract_r: Our own voice is a very special stimulus. Of all the sounds we hear in our everyday lives, it belongs to those that we encounter most often. It is an important part of our representation in the world and a key communication tool. Other self-relevant stimuli such as our own name are known for their particularly high attention-grabbing potential, albeit it is unclear whether this is in fact due to their self-relevance or the strong call for action that is associated with hearing our own name. In this preregistered conceptual replication study, we will compare the disruptive effect of one's own voice to that of another person's voice to investigate whether a self-relevant stimulus without a strong call for action still has the capacity to capture our attention. We will use a classic serial recall paradigm with three auditory conditions: (1) A quiet control condition, (2) an own voice condition, in which participants listen to an artificially generated clone of their own voice, and (3) an other voice condition, where participants listen to the voice of their yoked-control partner. If we observe an own voice effect, we will also explore whether it habituates and is modulated by recognition or resemblance.
