summary: Study Information
Trying to be happier really can work: Happiness and paintings
Conceptual Replication of Ferguson, Yuna & Sheldon, Kennon. (2013). Trying to be happier really can work: Two experimental studies. The Journal of Positive Psychology. 8. 23-33. 10.1080/17439760.2012.747000. 

Authorship
Brianna Chmielewski, Kamila Plaza, Meagan Rosario, Tyra Watkins
Research Questions

1.	Does the manipulation of mood encouragement have an impact on how individuals feel about an image? 
2.	Does the manipulation of the type of image have an impact on how individuals feel about an image?
3.	Is there an interaction between mood encouragement and type of image on mood? 

Hypotheses
•	Does the manipulation of mood encouragement have an impact on how individuals feel about an image? 
More specifically, do emotionally encouraged versus not encouraged groups feel more or less happy when analyzing an “ambiguous” and “happy” painting?
Our hypothesis is that the manipulation will be very effective. In the original study by Ferguson and Sheldon (2013), those who were part of the encouraged-to-improve-mood group felt a greater boost in mood when they listened to the positive classical song (p= 0.001, d= 0.76) and felt less of a positive mood when they listened to the ambiguous classical song (p= 0.72, d= 0.08). There was no difference in reported mood for the ambiguous song based on the group they were in (p= 0.82, d= 0.05).
•	Does the manipulation of the type of image have an impact on how individuals feel about an image?
	
Our hypothesis is that those viewing the positive image will report higher levels of mood compared to those viewing the ambiguous image. In the original study, Ferguson and Sheldon (2013) found that there was a significant effect of type of music on positive mood (p = .002). Since this is a conceptual replication, we expect to see similar results as this study. 

•	Is there an interaction between mood encouragement and type of image on mood? 

We expect to see those in the encouraged condition will be more impacted if in the positive condition rather than the ambiguous condition. We expect to see this because similar results were found in Ferguson and Sheldon’s study (2013). 

Sampling Plan
Data collection procedures

We plan to collect our data by using convenience sampling on students at Dominican University. Participants will be recruited by letting friends know about the study and asking our professors to send information to other classes to maximize our recruitment. There will be no compensation for this study other than credit that will be awarded to those currently enrolled in PSYC 101 and/or NEUR 105. Participants will be excluded from the initial pool if they fail the manipulation check or if they do not complete a substantial portion of the survey.
Sample size
Sample goal is at least 100 participants.
Sample size rationale
Based on the Dominican University population, we predicted that a sample size of at least 100 participants will satisfy our study to get an acceptable amount of results. 
Stopping rule
Sample size will not be limited to a certain amount; the more participants, the better. 

Variables
Manipulated variables
•	Type of images (ambiguous or happy) 
•	Encouraged to boost mood vs not encouraged to boost mood
Measured variables
•	How participants felt after viewing their assigned image. 
 2 measures:  
→ Rate their agreement (1= not at all, 15= extremely) on six different mood descriptors: happy, joyful, enjoyment/fun, pleased, content, and satisfied. Ratings were averaged.
→  Continuous line asked participants to indicate how positive they felt (line extended from “very negative” to “very positive”) relative to their negative feelings. Distance between positive and negative marks was measured using a ruler and converted into a proportion of entire line. 
 
Design Plan
Blind
Both the researchers and the participants are blind to the image manipulation. Computers will not be assigned to specific images, therefore we will not know who is in what group, and the participants will not be aware of the ambiguous and happy images until debriefing. 
Study design
2 x 2 factorial between-subject design .
Participants are randomly assigned within the online survey. 
Analysis Plan
Statistical models
TWO-WAY ANOVA

•	2x2 factorial ANOVA 
•	Analyze main effects and interactions between the two groups

Data exclusion

•	Participants who do not finish the survey.
•	Participants under the age of 18
•	Participants who do not pass the manipulation check.
•	Any participant who voices suspicion about the nature of the study
Missing data
Excluding participants entirely (except if missed demographic questions).

title_r: Cognitive Dissonance in University Students in Lillehammer
abstract_r: People are influenced by various ideas around them and they adopt a set of beliefs and attitudes that are unique to them. Behaviors are also shaped by attitudes. However, there may be times when people's behaviors and attitudes are inconsistent. The feeling of being mentally disturbed when there is conflict between people's cognitive processes, put forward by Festinger, is called "Cognitive Contradiction". Festinger first proposed the cognitive dissonance theory, which focuses on how they try to achieve internal coherence. He suggested that people need an internal consistency to ensure that their beliefs and attitudes are consistent. Inconsistent and conflicting beliefs, he thought, led to the dissonance that people were trying to avoid. This replication is based on the central thesis of cognitive dissonance theory and the experiment “Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance” done by Festinger & Carlsmith (1957). The experiment was based on the forced-compliance paradigm in which the participant performed a series of repetitive and boring menial tasks and then was asked to lie to the “next subject”, who was actually an experimental accomplice and say that the tasks were interesting and fun. The original study found out that when two beliefs are inconsistent, individuals experience negatively arousing cognitive conflict (dissonance). Due to this dissonance being aversive, individuals try to reduce it by changing one or the other beliefs. Festinger used money as a reward for the participants to lie. He correctly predicted that the subjects who were paid $1 for lying later evaluated the tasks as more enjoyable than those who were paid $20. As predicted, the subjects who were given $20 would not experience dissonance, whereas the $1 group would experience dissonance. The reason for this was that the $20 dollar group were well rewarded and had a good justification for lying, in contrast to the $1 group who had little justification for lying. Furthermore, we are doing a conceptual replication instead of a direct replication to minimize the risk of replicating the same mistakes in the original study and prove that this theory can generalize to a variety of tasks. Even though this classical study has been replicated multiple times it is still important in replicating a study in a vast majority of ways to ensure validity. Then, if we are able to replicate and achieve the same or similar results as the original study, it would give the study greater validity to the findings, in addition to that it is more likely that those results can be generalized to the larger population. Since we are doing a replication, we expect to predict the same results as in the original study. That is, the high reward group will think the task is more boring than the low reward group. Thus the low reward group has a higher level of cognitive dissonance than the high reward group. Because the participants are holding two conflicting beliefs they will experience a psychological discomfort, known as cognitive dissonance. We predict that participants will reevaluate the boring tasks as interesting and enjoyable to reduce the dissonance. This will not be the case for the control group.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Fox (2009) in Journal of Labor Economics.
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Fox (2009) is that firm-size wage gaps increase with job responsibility. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "I present the fact that wage gaps due to firm size increase with job responsibility." Firm-size wage gaps by job responsibility are estimated in the U.S. using the U.S. SIPP data. The author uses the three-digit occupation codes to formulate four examples of firm-size wage gaps between occupations, in which titles suggest one group of occupations may be supervising another group – the focal example used as evidence for the SCORE program is white-collar versus blue-collar workers. The author estimates a series of regressions that compare workers at large firms to workers at small firms within the same industry, where size in measured in three intervals for both firm size and establishment size: 1-24, 25-100, or more than 100. Each model regresses the log of hourly wages on indicators for the interactions of size intervals and job responsibility, an indicator for coverage by a collective bargaining agreement, an indicator for location in a metropolitan area, and industry indicators. Standard errors are corrected for heteroskedasticity across worker panels and an AR(1) term in worker-specific disturbances. The base estimation sample is all male, full-time employees in the private sector. The regression selected as evidence for the SCORE program compares the blue-collar wage gap between firms sized 1-24 and firms sized 100+ with the white-collage wage gap across the same two firm sizes. For firm size, a formal statistical test that the 100+ versus 1–24 size wage gaps are the same for blue- (wage gap = .181, SE = .007) and white-collar workers (wage gap = .236, SE = .008) is rejected with a p-value less than .001.

title_r: Predicting fluid and crystallized Intelligence from resting-state EEG
abstract_r: The current project aims to investigate the predictability of fluid and crystallized intelligence from resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) patterns using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA). We adopt the same analysis plan as in our previous preregistration (https://osf.io/sehd8) but aim to predict fluid and crystallized intelligence scores instead of Big Five personality trait scores in both a male and female subsample of the CoScience data set. We will use support vector regressions (SVR) for the prediction across EEG frequency spectra ranging from 0.5–30 Hz. By examining four different conditions (resting states with eyes open and eyes closed before and after unrelated tasks), we will estimate the stability of potential effects. In addition, we will extend previous work by controlling for potential confounds of sleepiness. In a second step, we aim to replicate potential meaningful results between resting-state EEG power and fluid intelligence in an independent data set from Ociepka et al. (2022).

title_r: Multiple cross-format discriminations across nonsymbolic ratios and symbolic fractions
abstract_r: Previous studies have demonstrated that humans can represent fractional magnitudes abstractly and amodally (e.g., Balci &amp; Gallistel, 2006; Bonn &amp; Cantlon, 2017; Jacob et al., 2012). One line of studies has supported this by showing that humans can compare across fractions and nonsymbolic ratios accurately and rapidly (e.g., Matthews &amp; Chesney, 2015; Kalra et al., 2020). In these cross-format comparisons, individuals have sometimes shown whereby they overestimate the sizes of nonsymbolic ratios relative to symbolic ones. We aim to replicate and expand these previous findings by conducting a series of cross-format comparison tasks comparing across different nonsymbolic ratios, across nonsymbolic and symbolic fractions and across nonsymbolic ratio and decimals. The nonsymbolic ratios will be instantiated by lines, circles, blobs and dots (Park et al., 2020). 1. Do the findings the adults can successfully compare across different nonsymbolic ratios and across nonsymbolic and symbolic fractions replicate? 2. Will all comparisons (between and within format) show distance effects? 4. In the cross-format comparisons between nonsymbolic ratio and symbolic fractions, is the bias toward overestimating nonsymbolic ratios similar across formats? 5. In the cross-format comparisons between nonsymbolic ratio and decimals, is there also a bias toward overestimation in nonsymbolic format? Experiment 1 will conduct a series of nonsymbolic ratio cross-format comparisons with various formats. Experiment 2 will test a series of cross-format comparisons across various nonsymbolic ratios and symbolic fractions. Lastly, Experiment 3 will test a series of cross-format comparisons cross various nonsymbolic ratios and symbolic decimals.

title_r: Social consensus effect in the illusory truth effect
abstract_r: The illusory truth effect refers to the phenomenon where repeated exposure to information makes it seem true, even if it is false. Pillai and Fazio (2024) examined whether the manifestation of the illusory truth effect varies depending on whether the repeated information is presented verbatim or as a paraphrase, and whether it originates from a single source or multiple sources. Their results indicated that neither the number of sources nor the mode of repetition—verbatim or paraphrased—significantly influenced the illusory truth effect. Instead, the findings suggest that the mere repetition of information, regardless of its source or expression, enhances perceived truthfulness. This implies that the fluency of information, heightened by repeated presentations of the same or similar content, is a key factor driving the illusory truth effect. In contrast, Eastern cultures—compared to Western ones—place greater emphasis on social harmony and group conformity, often defining the self in relation to others. Consequently, in Eastern cultural contexts, social consensus cues, such as agreement among multiple sources, may serve as group norms. This could potentially amplify the illusory truth effect, making it stronger than what is typically observed in Western cultures. Building on these insights, the present study will conduct a pre-registered replication of Experiment 1 from Pillai and Fazio (2024). The aim is to investigate whether the illusory truth effect differs when information is repeatedly presented from a single source versus multiple sources, each using different expressions.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Thomas et al. (2014), from the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
abstract_r: We selected the claim that in coordination environments, people strategically differentiate between shared knowledge and common knowledge, working together more frequently when they have common knowledge of the pay-offs than when they have shared or private knowledge (Statement 2). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Results showed that more participants attempted risky coordination when they and their prospective partner had common knowledge of the payoffs (broadcast over a loudspeaker) than when they had only shared knowledge (conveyed to both by a messenger) or private knowledge (revealed to each partner separately)" (Statement 1). The claim is tested by using chi squared tests to calculate if the observed frequency of participants deciding to work with a partner differed significantly from the expected frequency under the null hypothesis across the predictor levels of shared knowledge (Statement 3), which resulted in results consistent with the common knowledge recognition hypothesis: Participants were more likely to try to work together with common knowledge than with any other state of knowledge. From Table 1: chi squared = 63.70, n = 276, phi = .48, p < 0.001 (Statement 4).

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Mosimann & Pontusson (2017), in World Politics
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Mosimann & Pontusson (2017) is that the effect of union membership on support for redistribution is positive for high-wage workers who belong to unions that are responsive to the interests of low-wage workers; the specific test selected for the SCORE program compares union to nonunion members, for individuals with household incomes in the 9th decile for the sample of low-wage unionism (countries-year where unions primarily encompass low-wage workers). The claim is tested with individual-level data from the first seven rounds of the ESS [European Social Survey], covering the period 2002–14. The dependent variable is based on an ESS question asking respondents whether or not they agree with the proposition, “the government should take measures to reduce differences in income levels.” Evidence for the claim is found in Table 4, which reports predicted probabilities of support for redistribution in different union movement contexts, based on two-level linear probability models estimated with separate samples, and time-varying macro control variables (the models are reported in Appendix Table A2). The specific test selected for the SCORE program uses a t-test of equality to compare union and nonunion members, for individuals with household incomes in the 9th decile when the sample consists of low-wage unionism (country-years with union density below 45 percent and inclusiveness above 1.00). For high-income respondents, the largest union effect appears (descriptively speaking) in the sample that corresponds to low-wage unionism (union members in 9th income decile for low-wage unionism sample = .608 (SE = .041), nonunion members in 9th income decile for low-wage unionism sample = .511 (SE = .040), difference = .097 [9.7 percentage points], significant at .01%).

title_r: Illuminating for safety
abstract_r: This study is a replication study of the study titled: “Illuminating for Safety: Investigating the role of lighting appraisals on the perception of safety in the urban environment.”. written by L. van Rijswijk and A. Haans which was published in environment and behavior in 2017. The study is altered and expanded to fit with our time constraints and interests. In our study we research the effects of lighting, prospect, concealment and entrapment on how people judge environmental safety. This is done by having participants fill in a survey about photos of different nocturnal urban scenes. There are no other beings visible in the picture which means it is only the scene that people respond to. In the original study the was split up into 3 conditions but for our studies all the questions are asked to all the participants. A gender question was added to look into the differences that gender makes on the perceived safety.

title_r: Implicit and explicit reactions to faces wearing medical masks
abstract_r: In a previous study (Olivera-La Rosa, Chuquichambi, & Ingram, 2020) we found evidence that in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, people were more likely to evaluate faces wearing medical-style masks as trustworthy and say that they would be willing to be socially close to them (compared to control faces without a mask), but also more likely to say that the person wearing the mask was likely to be sick. Participants in that study, which was run in Spanish, were mainly university students from a variety of Spanish-speaking countries (principally Colombia, Spain, and Peru). In the current study, we aim to replicate these findings in English with US- and UK-based participants on Prolific. As well as replicating the previous study, we will extend the methods by adding an approach/avoid task to test implicit reactions, as well as the replicated explicit reactions, to masked and unmasked faces.

title_r: Disrupting Somatosensory Aversive Memory Consolidation via Targeted Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
abstract_r: Background Storing information is a fundamental propensity of neural systems across many species including humans. Memory allows organisms to learn from past experience, adapt behaviour, and survive in ever-changing environments. However, stored memories must update with new experiences to stay relevant (Lee, 2009). Rigid memories that fail to respond to new information can become maladaptive in psychiatric conditions such as addiction or trauma-related disorders (Yehuda et al., 2015). Either of these debilitating conditions affect around 5% of the UK population at any point in time (Adult Morbidity Survey, 2014), and both are risk factors for other common mental health problems. This underlines the quest for a better biological understanding of neural and behavioural mechanisms that confer memory flexibility in humans. One key mechanism for memory updating is reconsolidation, whereby a previously acquired memory, once reactivated, undergoes a transient period of instability before restabilizing (Nader et al., 2000; Lee, 2009). This process allows memories to incorporate new information and can be experimentally disrupted using pharmacological interventions (Nader et al., 2000) or by targeting neural signalling pathways in humans and non-humans (Elsey et al., 2018). Leveraging this vulnerability window has been proposed as a strategy for therapeutic memory modification (Kindt, 2018; Phelps & Hofmann, 2019). Despite significant progress at the molecular level, the systems-level mechanisms underlying reconsolidation remain largely unknown. Specifically, whether all nodes of a memory network are required for both consolidation and reconsolidation is a fundamental question in systems neuroscience. While aversive memory storage is traditionally associated with the amygdala, recent evidence underscores the role of primary sensory cortices (Banerjee et al., 2017; Letzkus et al., 2011; Staib et al., 2020; Weinberger, 2007). A pivotal study by Ojala et al. (2022) demonstrated that disrupting the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) using continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) before acquisition selectively impairs memory consolidation, but not learning itself, in a human fear conditioning paradigm. This finding suggests that S1 serves as a crucial node in aversive memory storage, but whether it is also necessary for reconsolidation remains an open question. The Present Study Building upon Ojala et al. (2022), we aim to replicate and extend these findings by determining whether S1 is required not only for consolidation but also for reconsolidation of aversive memories. In Experiment 1, we will investigate S1 involvement in consolidation by replicating the original study while introducing both positive and negative control conditions to strengthen interpretability. In Experiment 2, we will assess whether the same cortical region is necessary for memory reconsolidation. If cTBS disrupts reconsolidation in the same manner as consolidation, this would suggest a shared neural substrate for both processes. Furthermore, Ojala et al. (2022) inferred that S1 disruption affects consolidation rather than initial learning, but this conclusion was based on indirect evidence. To validate this claim, we will introduce an additional post-acquisition cTBS condition, allowing for a more direct test of whether the previously observed effects stem from disrupted consolidation rather than impaired learning. If S1 disruption impairs reconsolidation in the same way as consolidation, this would provide compelling evidence that sensory cortex activity is required for aversive memory updating, challenging traditional models that prioritize subcortical structures such as the amygdala. Moreover, if these findings generalize across sensory domains, they could inform non-invasive neuromodulation strategies aimed at selectively weakening maladaptive memories in clinical populations. By leveraging cTBS as a tool for memory modification, this study may provide a proof-of-principle for future therapeutic interventions targeting sensory representations of aversive memories in PTSD and anxiety disorders.

title_r: Metacognition in human intelligence, awareness, and mental health: I - Replicating a foundational study
abstract_r: Metacognition is not limited to visual perception but also applies to decisions involving other sensory modalities, and to cognition in general. Humans vary considerably in their metacognitive ability. A prior study (Fleming et al., 2010, Science) showed an intimate link between these differences and the anterior prefrontal cortex, and this study has become highly influential. title_r: The influence of facial race and facial sex on the recognition of faces morphed to vary in emotional intensity from angry to happy
abstract_r: The main goal is to understand how social category information (e.g., race and gender) influences the recognition of facial expressions that vary in emotional intensity. More specifically, I examine, using a neutral baseline, whether emotion recognition is facilitated for faces that belong to social categories that are stereo-typically associated with specific emotions. So, for example, the study permits a test of whether people are more likely to categorize male vs female neutral expressions as angry. This study will extend my pre-registered secondary analyses of data that was originally collected Korb, S., & Massaccesi, C. (2020, December 29; https://osf.io/29mn7/). The study by Korb and Massaccesi was also a pre-registered replication of an earlier study by Harris et al (2016). The study by Harris et al was designed to examine the effects of face sex on forced-choice angry and happy decisions for faces morphed to vary in emotional intensity from angry to happy. The research by Harris et al was novel because the authors calculated indices of psychophysical performance (e.g., Point of Subjective Equality). In this specific study, I will 1. establish the generality of the effects across face race - the initial studies examining morph intensity have used only the faces of white individuals. I will establish if similar effects hold for the faces of black individuals. One hypothesis is that people are prejudiced towards black individuals making them more likely to respond "angry" than happy when the faces are of black individuals with a neutral expression. 2. establish whether the same effects are found for a new different stimulus set Further objectives are: 1. Bayesian Modelling. I will model choice decisions in a Bayesian Hierarchical Logistic Regression Model and RTs in a Bayesian Hierarchical ex-Gaussian Regression Model. Finally, a Bayesian Hierarchical Drift Diffusion Model in which choice decision and reaction times (RT) are modeled as a joint outcome, will also be estimated.

title_r: Recognizing Words in the Item-Method Directed Forgetting Paradigm: Replication and Manipulating ISI
abstract_r: In item method directed forgetting, words designated as to be forgotten (F) are not remembered as well as words designated as to be remembered (R). For decades, the idea that only R items are rehearsed, with F items left to decay, has been captured by the single-process selective rehearsal account. In the current investigation, we propose a new version of the single-process account, arguing that a retrieval check—retrieval of the just-presented item—occurs upon presentation of an R cue but does not occur upon presentation of an F cue, and that this retrieval check underlies the directed forgetting effect. In two experiments, we report evidence consistent with this account, as well as evidence that questions the additional process of a resource-demanding withdrawal of attention from F items.

title_r: The first-mover disadvantage in negotiations: Clarifying its boundary conditions
abstract_r: Across a variety of contexts, past research finds that moving first in a negotiation generally yields better outcomes for oneself (Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001; Gunia, Swaab, Sivanathan, & Galinsky, 2013). Loschelder, Swaab, Troetschel, and Galinsky (2014), however, showed that as soon as the first offer addressed a compatible issue (i.e., an issue where both parties prefer exactly the same outcome) senders of this first offer, instead, faced a disadvantage. In their study, participants negotiated the sale of a pharmaceutical plant, where the sale price constituted a distributive issue while the transfer date was compatible (Loschelder et al., 2014). In their second experiment, the information included in the first offer was manipulated: first movers addressed either the distributive issue only, the compatible issue only or both issues. As the authors argue, revealing compatible preferences in their first move potentially weakens the senders’ bargaining position, as recipients can use this information as leverage to extract concessions. They might do so by pretending to reluctantly give in to the senders’ demands on the compatible issue in exchange for a concession regarding the distributive issue. In a first replication of Loschelder et al.’s (2014) second experiment, we found effects that were similar to the original study. Specifically, senders claimed less value in the two conditions where their first offers contained information regarding the compatible issue, which corresponds to a first-mover disadvantage (distributive issue only: M = 63.35%, compatible issue only: M = 41.42%, both issues: M = 43.88%, F(2, 129) = 3.24, p = .042, η² = .05). In a second replication, however, these effects were much weaker, to the extent that no effects of the experimental condition factor could be detected, in spite of a test power of about 70%. Interestingly, while we exactly followed the original experimental procedure in our first replication, we made a minor change in our second replication. In their original experiments, Loschelder et al. (2014) presented a questionnaire after the first offer but before the actual negotiation. The authors kindly provided this questionnaire to us for our replication, even though they did not report it in their original publication. This questionnaire contained items that encouraged participants to reflect on the first offer. For instance, participants were asked to indicate for each issue how much they believed to have similar or different preferences to their counterpart. Furthermore, participants indicated to what extent they would try to use the given information to their advantage. Drawing their attention to the preferences and to the use of information in their favor might have created a demand effect, thereby potentially enhancing (or even creating) the differences between experimental conditions. Based on these considerations, we did not apply the aforementioned questionnaire in our second replication. We were interested in finding out whether the original results could be reproduced under conditions in which the salience of the first offer and its potential implications were not boosted by a questionnaire – in other words, whether the original effects would replicate in a more “natural” negotiation setting. As became apparent, the effects obtained from our second replication were not comparable in strength. To be specific, we have not come to conclusive results in favor of any hypothesis so far, even though we have already surpassed the sample size that the original work was based on. Thus, it is possible that the salience of the initial offer–in combination with drawing participants’ attention to the potential leverage it entails–moderates the first-mover (dis)advantage. Providing thought-provoking questions related to the first offer constitutes a situation in which this first offer is highly salient. In contrast, omitting these questions, and thereby relating better to real life negotiations, makes the implications of said first offer less obvious. Since we consider the findings regarding a possible first-mover disadvantage highly relevant when deriving practical recommendations, in this study we will manipulate whether or not participants receive the questionnaire described above. We are especially interested in the effects the questionnaire has on the first-mover disadvantage (rather than the first-mover advantage). Therefore, of the three conditions of the original Loschelder et al. (2014, Exp. 2) study, we will only examine the condition in which participants solely address the compatible issue in their first offer. In line with previous work (Loschelder et al., 2014), we consider it possible that second-movers’ social value orientation (SVO) moderates the first-mover disadvantage: Since proself recipients are believed to leverage the information the first offer entails to a greater extent, the first-mover disadvantage is expected to be more severe. Compared to that, the disadvantage is potentially less extreme when first-movers are faced with a prosocial counterpart. Extending the original theory and following our reasoning in both replications, we propose that first-movers’ social value orientation influences the extent of the disadvantage as well. Proself first-movers are expected to propose more self-serving initial offers than prosocials because they tend to soley focus on their own profit (Steinel & De Dreu, 2004). As a result, they might make themselves more vulnerable to exploitation when communicating compatible preferences in their first offer. Hence, and correspondent to the original experiment as well as our two replications of said experiment, we hypothesize that the first mover disadvantage will be stronger when senders have a proself orientation as compared to a prosocial orientation. It should be noted that in neither of our two replications have we found these proposed effects. In our first replication, this could have been explained by a lack of power and by the psychometric quality of the applied SVO measurement. In our second replication, however, there was an imbalance in the distribution of SVO, with a larger proportion of participants having a prosocial orientation. We might find the effects in a new sample that is potentially more diverse since we will broaden our inclusion criteria as well as use a variety of platforms to recruit participants. Furthermore, we will present participants with the SVO Slider measure (Murphy, Ackermann, & Handgraaf, 2011) instead of the Triple Dominance Measure (Van Lange et al., 1997) which was used in the original work (Loschelder et al., 2014) because the former is more reliable and valid. Due to the current COVID-19 pandemic, it is not feasible to conduct face-to-face negotiations, as was the case in the original study. Hence, we will conduct the experiment online. This online setting will be designed to mimic the original face-to-face procedure as closely as possible. For that reason, participants will be able to chat and propose offers in an unrestricted way. All materials and questionnaires from the original procedure will be fully adopted.

title_r: Sample sizes in psychological research over time
abstract_r: Many studies in the psychological literature have small sample sizes and are underpowered (Bakker, van Dijk, & Wicherts, 2012; Cohen, 1990; Maxwell, 2004; Stanley, Carter, & Doucouliagos, 2018), which affects generalizability, estimation of effect sizes, and accurate planning of future studies. The most effective way to increase statistical power is to increase sample size. Nevertheless, sample size is not often directly investigated. One of the studies examining sample size in psychological research over time is the study by Marszalek, Barber, Kohlhart, and Holmes (2011). In this study, data from Holmes (1979, 1983) was used. Holmes examined sample sizes in four APA journals in 1955 and 1977. These journals were Journal of Abnormal Psychology (JAbP), Journal of Applied Psychology (JApP), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance (JEP), and Developmental Psychology (DP). According to Holmes (1979), “these journals were selected because they represent a broad coverage of psychological research” (p. 284). Marszalek et al. examined and added the sample size data from papers published in the same journals in 1995 and 2006. These years were chosen to investigate whether sample sizes increased as a result of the recommendations by Wilkinson and the Task Force on Statistical Inference (Wilkinson, 1999). They found that the sample sizes in psychology remained small and that the recommendations for increasing sample size had not been integrated in core psychological research. Around the time that the study by Marszalek et al. (2011) was published, the field of psychology went into a replicability crisis. Many studies failed to replicate, and the use of questionable research practices seemed to be widespread (Doyen, Klein, Pichon, & Cleeremans, 2012; John, Loewenstein, & Prelec, 2012; Open Science Collaboration, 2015). As a consequence, different initiatives were launched to improve psychological science. These initiatives include the introduction of preregistration and registered reports (Chambers, 2013; Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven, & Mellor, 2018), the awarding of open science badges to studies that share data, materials, and/or are preregistered (Eich, 2014; Kidwell et al., 2016), and an increased focus on direct replication studies and studies with null results (Baxter & Burwell, 2017; Simons, Holcombe, & Spellman, 2014). The crisis has also increased attention to the problems of small sample sizes and underpowered studies and resulted in several calls to increase psychological studies' statistical power (Bakker, Hartgerink, Wicherts, & van der Maas, 2016; Button et al., 2013; Szucs & Ioannidis, 2017). In the current study, we want to update the study by Marszalek et al. to investigate whether psychological studies' sample sizes have increased, specifically in response to the replicability crisis and the resulting focus on open science. We will add studies published in 2019 from the same journals. Because journals differ in how actively they adopted the open science practices, we will include two additional journals (Psychological Science (PS) and Journal of Experimental Social Psychology (JESP)) that have adopted open science practices more actively. Our research questions are: 1. Have sample sizes increased over time? 2. Have sample sizes in psychological research increased as a reaction to the replicability crisis? 3. Does the amount of increase in sample sizes depend on Journal level policies (open science)? 4. Does the amount of increase in sample size depend on study level characteristics (open science)? 5. Additionally, we want to investigate how well automatic procedures can select the sample size compared to selecting sample sizes by hand.

title_r: Investigating disjunctive syllogism with monkeys: A computerized task
abstract_r: Disjunctive syllogism is a rule of inference that uses propositional logic: given that only A or B is true, but not both, and we learn that A is not true, then we can infer that B is true. Recently, Ferrigno and colleagues (2021) illustrated that baboons could use disjunctive syllogism to make inferences about where to find a food reward in a manual task. The study proposed here is a conceptual replication of the Ferrigno and colleagues (2021) experiment. However, the present study includes two major differences: first, this experiment will be recreated as a computer program; monkeys will be tested on a virtual version of the task instead of a physical one. Second, this study will include tufted capuchins and rhesus macaques as subjects.

title_r: Crump & Milliken (2009) Replication Experiment
abstract_r: Individuals can reactively adjust their attention based on implicitly learned associations between external cues and the likelihood of conflict. To form these associations, individuals may engage in three primary learning processes. First, context-based learning may occur when individuals implicitly learn associations between salient contextual features (e.g., spatial location) of a stimulus and its proportion congruency. Second, conjunctive-based learning may occur when individuals implicitly learn context-item conjunctions and their proportion congruencies. Third, item-based learning may occur when individuals implicitly learn associations between stimulus features and their proportion congruencies, regardless of the context in which the stimuli appear. In the present study, we wish to replicate Experiment 2 from Crump & Milliken (2009), with four critical differences. First, in the Stroop paradigm participants will respond manually rather than vocally as in Crump & Milliken (2009). Second, the timing of events will be as follows: (1) a fixation cross (duration: 250 ms), (2) a color-word prime in the center of the screen (duration: 400 ms), (3) a color-patch probe in either the upper or lower location (duration: until response), and (4) a blank interstimulus interval (duration: 250 ms). Third, the stimulus frequencies for inducer and diagnostic items will be much larger than in Crump & Milliken (2009), with a minimum of 30 trials per condition (see Study Design for further details). Thus, they should provide more statistical stability and power than prior studies of the CSPC. Fourth, the overall proportion congruency (PC) will be more biased than in Crump & Milliken (2009), with an increase in the overall location-PC in the high PC location and a decrease in the overall location-PC in the low PC location. We reasoned that these manipulations in overall location-PC should further bias participants towards learning location-PC associations.

title_r: Too complex for Simon? The influence of stimulus complexity on the Simon effect: A replication of Hommel(1994)
abstract_r: This study investigates the influence of stimulus complexity onto the Simon effect. The Simon effect describes the correspondence between irrelevant stimulus location and response location (e.g. Hommel (1993)), meaning a spatially compatible response to a stimulus is faster than a spatially incompatible response even if stimulus position is irrelevant. According to Hommel (1993) the Simon effect is reduced when relevant and irrelevant stimulus features are temporally separated. This is called the temporal overlap account. Hommel(1993) demonstrated this effect across various experimental manipulations, including stimulus onset delay, stimulus eccentricity, and stimulus quality. In a subsequent study, Hommel (1994) extended this line of research by focussing on the role of stimulus complexity. There are two conditions differing in complexity. The simple condition involves the discrimination of colour stimuli (blue vs. yellow) within a reference frame. The moderately complex condition requires participants to distinguish between shape stimuli, specifically a square and a rectangle, also within a reference frame. According to Hommel (1994), the Simon effect decreases as task complexity increases. To further investigate this claim, we introduce a third, more complex form condition, in which participants respond to a five-pointed star and a six-pointed star. In contrary to Hommel (1994) we investigate not only the global Simon effect, but also the local Simon effect. Hommel (1994) and Umiltà and Liotti (1987) only mention „the Simon effect“, while we suggest that there are two different types of Simon effects as shown by Baess and Bermeitinger (2025). The global Simon effect arises when the spatial compatibility is determined by the absolute position of the stimulus on the screen (e.g., left vs. right side of a monitor). The local Simon effect emerges when spatial compatibility is defined within a localized frame of reference. The Stimuli appear either on the left or right of the monitor and always either within the left or right frame. Umiltà and Liotti (1987) observed only a local Simon effect in their delay condition, which led to the emergence of the debate between the Attentional Zooming Theory and the Temporal Overlap Theory. The Attentional Zooming Theory postulates that attention can shift between spatial locations, affecting response times in the Simon effect, based on target congruence. Hommel (1994) adopted the experimental layout used by Umiltà and Liotti (1987), but manipulated the difficulty of the relevant feature (color vs. shape). The aim of our study is to replicate the results of Hommel (1994). In line with Hommel (1994) we investigate the following hypothesis: We expect to find a global Simon effect in the colour condition and no global Simon effect in the form condition. Additionally, we expect to find no global Simon effect in the complex form condition. Reference: Hommel, B. (1994). Effects of irrelevant spatial S-R compatibility depend on stimulus complexity. title_r: Fans22
abstract_r: Following Halberstadt and Levine (1999; Effects of Reasons Analysis on the Accuracy of Predicting Basketball Games; Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 29, 517-530), we are conducting a series of replication studies in which sports fans forecast the outcome of upcoming sports games (e.g., baseball, football). In several studies conducted in Fall 2021 involving major league baseball, college football, and NFL football games we randomly assigned participants to read instructions to either rely on their intuition or reasoning when making their forecasts. In line with Halberstadt and Levine (1999), we predicted that participants who were asked to rely upon their intuition (gut reactions) would make more accurate forecasts about upcoming games than will those who are asked to provide and rely upon their reasons. We observed no difference in forecast accuracy for people asked to rely on their intuition and people who were asked to use reasoning. This registration covers the next three studies we have planned to continue this line of research. First, it is possible that the type of forecasts participants made in the first round of studies caused them to use reasoning even when asked to rely on their intuition. For the college football and NFL study we asked participants to forecast the winning team and the score for each team. It is possible that this task was outside what people are capable of doing using only their intuition. In Study 1a, we will only ask participants to forecast the winning team and how many points they will win by in order to simplify the forecast. After making their predictions, we will also ask how confident participants are about each of their predictions. Prior research has shown that people are more confident about their choice when selecting an intuitive as opposed to a non-intuitive alternative. Second, we will replicate Study 1a with decision strategy (intuition, reasoning) as a within-subjects factor in Study 1b. Third, Halberstadt and Levine (1999) found that reasoners made forecasts further from sports bookmakers' line scores than people who relied on intuition. Our previous studies have not supported this finding. However, in Study 2 we will again test this idea directly. We will provide participants with the line score and ask them to forecast who will exceed bookmakers' expectations. That is, will the "favorite" win by more points than what is expected, or will the underdog lose by fewer than the number of points predicted or win the game outright. Note that the three studies were not run in this order. Data collection occurred in the following order, Study 1a, Study 2, Study 1b.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Savani et al. (2010), from the Journal of Psychological Science
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Savani et al. (2010) is the study 3 claim that American participants tend to construe more of another actor’s actions as choices than do Indian participants; Americans therefore identify more instances in a video as times when the actor made a choice. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “[W]e found that people in U.S. American contexts, where the disjoint model of agency is prevalent, are more likely than those in Indian contexts to construe … other individuals’ behaviors as choices” This claim was tested in Study 3 by recording the number of button presses made by participants in either a control condition (pressing a button every time the actor touches an object with his hands) or the construal-of-choice condition (pressing a button whenever the actor made a choice) to a 2 (culture) × 2 (condition) ANOVA. This analysis yielded an interaction between culture (Indian, American) and condition (construal-of-choice vs. control task) in how often participants pressed the response button, F(1, 120) = 5.69, p < .02, p_rep = .96, such that American participants reported significantly more actions as choices than Indian participants.

title_r: Replication of Empathy Bias Study 2 by Fowler et al. 2020 at BYUI Fall 2021
abstract_r: Throughout history, the central cornerstone to living a moral life is dictated by the presence of empathy. However, in more recent times, evidence against empathy has presented that individual empathy is often biased (i.e. more strongly felt toward) to others that are closer in relationship. These findings have ensued a debate questioning whether empathy is inherently morally flawed and should therefore be abandoned in efforts to strive for equity. Furthermore, the debate focuses on whether empathy limits the levels of morality. However, little focus has been provided to whether moral belief may also limit the levels of empathy. In a study that was conducted on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (N=304), the researchers investigated the moral judgments of biased and equitable emotion of empathy. The method of this study focuses on using vignettes to examine the proximity of 100 relationships of a particular participant on a scale of 1 to 100. Scenarios are used to measure the level of empathy felt for each relationship, along with evaluation of participant explanations of chosen levels of empathy. Observing moral preferences for empathy across more socially close of distant persons, the most moral and socially valued approach is where equitable empathy is felt for all. The findings of this study provide newly founded theoretical insight into the relationship between empathy and morality, as well as implicating a more egalitarian future. Replication of this study will commence at Brigham Young University – Idaho. Participants include students in PSYCH 101 courses, the desired number of participants at 100. The original study was performed on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk, whereas the replication will be performed on Qualtrics. The original study had a wider variety of participants, including a higher number of participants. The replication will be done within a smaller population pool and consist of only psychology students of a particular age range. The fact the replication follows a smaller and more precise population pool causes some concern for the level of data received. There will be no additions to the study, as the contributors desire close replication.

title_r: Proactive control processes in rapid instructed task learning: An on-line replication of Cole et al., 2018
abstract_r: Cole et al., 2018 recently demonstrated that proactive cognitive control processes may play a significant role in the learning of novel tasks. In self-paced conditions, participants indicated on each trial when they had finished processing a set of 3 task rules, and were ready to apply these rules in responding to an upcoming target. Three key findings were observed with regard to preparation times, which were consistent with the hypothesis that preparation time serves as an index of proactive control. First, preparation times were longer for novel tasks than for highly practiced tasks. This difference provided evidence of increased cognitive demands when subjects prepared to execute novel task instructions. Second, a between-subjects correlation was observed: participants who had increased preparation times also had higher accuracy on novel tasks, and this relationship was reliably stronger on novel relative to practiced tasks. This correlation suggests individual differences in the extent to which proactive control was engaged. Third, a trial-by-trial correlation was also observed: trials with longer preparation times were more likely to be accurate, but again this relationship was selective to novel trials. This finding suggests that engagement of proactive control, though beneficial, may also be subject to factors that cause it to fluctuate across trials. We aim to replicate these effects in a larger, online sample collected from Amazon Mechanical Turk. By using the same study design and analyses in a new population, we hope to test the robustness and generalizability of the results reported by Cole et al. (2018), and provide a basis for further investigations of proactive control and the influence of additional factors such as motivational state and relevant individual differences dimensions (e.g. impulsivity, Need for Cognition).

title_r: Direct replication of Staw (1976)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Escalation of commitment refers to the decision error in which people stick to their original decision despite negative feedback (Sleesman, Conlon, McNamara & Miles, 2012; Staw, 1976; Staw & Fox, 1977). In 1976, Staw initiated experimental research on escalating commitment. In his study Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy: A Study of Escalating Commitment to a Chosen Course of Action, he showed that escalation was particularly pronounced when people were personally responsible for negative decision consequences. The interaction between responsibility and consequence was significant (p = <.019). Since then, there have been numerous studies investigating the escalation of commitment and the underlying effects. The findings are ambivalent, as the results often do not match or even contradict those of Staw (1976). There are many studies that used Staw's (1976) stimulus material, the A&S Financial Decision Case, or were based on his approach (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Armstrong, Coviello & Safranek, 1993; Bialek, Węgrzyn, & Meyers, 2021; Conlon & Parks, 1987; McCain, 1986; Morgan & Hansen, 2006; Pfeiffer, Schönborn, Mojzisch & Schulz-Hardt, 2007; Schoorman & Holahan, 1996; Schoorman, Mayer, Douglas & Hetrick, 1994; Singer, 1990; Singer & Singer, 1986). However, these studies did not test the interaction effect responsibility x consequence (Armstrong et al., 1993) and altered or excluded relevant aspects of the paradigm. For example, a different scenario and other variables were examined (Negrini, Riedl & Wibral, 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007) or the methodological approach was changed (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Bialek et al., 2021; Singer & Singer, 1986). For this reason, the planned study in the form of a direct replication should provide information on how robust and reliable Staw's (1976) results are if there are as few deviations as possible from the original study. Of particular interest is the replicability of the interaction effect personal responsibility x decision consequences. In addition, the reasons for the investment decisions are evaluated using content analysis. Armstrong et al. (1993) asked the participants to justify their decision, but did not analyze this. Other studies did not even include the justification in their design (Bialek et al., 2021; Negrini et al., 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007; Singer & Singer, 1986). The planned study therefore extends the existing literature with a replication of the study by Staw (1976), which not only records the participants' reasons for their decisions, but also evaluates them using content analysis.

title_r: Investigating Fast Mapping (FM) in healthy adults using an implicit memory measure: A replication
abstract_r: Fast Mapping (FM) is an incidental learning process that is hypothesised to allow rapid, cortical-based memory formation, independent of the normal, hippocampally-dependent episodic memory system. Recently, Coutanche and Thompson-Schill (2014) reported evidence for a learning advantage under an FM condition over a more conventional explicit learning condition (EE) in healthy young people using an implicit measure of learning, namely same-day lexical integration using a category (man-made/natural) decision task. They reported that under FM there were significantly slower RTs to hermit words, i.e., “galaxy”, whose made-up neighbors, i.e., “ganaxy” has been incidentally learned as unfamiliar animal name during the study phase; there was no slowing in the EE condition. They concluded that this offered evidence of same-day lexical integration learning that was present following FM, but not EE. When we ran a methodological replication with power of over 80% and N=56 young adults, but found no evidence of same-day lexical competition (i.e., slowing) following either FM or EE. However, a post-hoc analysis produced an interesting significant result. In all learning conditions ‘names’ (i.e, made-up neighbours, e.g., “ganaxy”, “naskin”) had been incidentally learned as unfamiliar animal names; we found facilitation (i.e., speeding) for natural words, e.g.,“galaxy”, but slowing for man-made words, e.g., “napkin” under the FM condition, suggesting a facilitatory semantic priming effect, instead of a inhibitory lexical competition effect. We now wish to attempt to replicate this significant semantic priming effect, which would further inform the mechanisms of FM learning. Our experiment will have four between-participant conditions: 1 FM and 1 EE condition where the ‘names’ are for unfamiliar animals, and 1 FM and 1 EE condition where ‘names’ are unfamiliar man-made objects. We predict that when studied neighbours (e.g., “ganaxy”, “naskin”) are names for (1) unfamiliar animal pictures, natural words (galaxy) will be speeded and man-made words (napkin) will be slowed, but for (2) unfamiliar man-made objects, natural words (galaxy) will be slowed and man-made words (napkin) will be speeded.

title_r: Post Hoc (Pilot Experiment 1)
abstract_r: This conceptual replication and extension of Redelmeier and Shafir (2024) aims to estimate the effect size of the post hoc effect in preparation for a larger replication using continuous dependent measures. In the original experiment, the authors manipulated whether the outcome improved or remained unchanged, and they asked participants whether they recommend that the agents continue the action (potential cause). Here, we will use the same kind of manipulation, but we will ask both for participants' recommendations and for their causal judgments. We will use continuous measures rather than the categorical measure that the original study used. We expect to conceptually replicate the original findings using a novel vignette and different measures.

title_r: Representation of dynamic and static materials in the human brain
abstract_r: We encounter a variety of different materials in our environment: rigid objects, deformable objects, as well as liquid and granular ‘stuff’. Yet, fMRI research has largely focused only on rigid objects. Several studies have investigated the role of the lateral occipital complex (LOC) in extracting the 3D shape of rigid objects (e.g., Kourtzi & Kanwisher, 2000) or the role of the ‘physics network’ in judging the physical properties and relations of rigid things (Fischer, Mikhael, Tenenbaum, & Kanwisher, 2016; Schwettmann, Tenenbaum, & Kanwisher, 2019; Pramod, Cohen, Tenenbaum, & Kanwisher, 2022). In a previous experiment (in the following referred to as Experiment 1; preregistered under: Paulun, V. C. (2023, January 17). Representation of dynamic materials in the human brain. Retrieved from osf.io/36bva) we found that both LOC and the physics system respond to dynamic materials more than scrambled or intact control conditions albeit the physics system responds more strongly to ‘Stuff’ than ‘Things’, whereas LOC responds at least as strongly (or more strongly) to deformable materials than to rigid things. We further found evidence for two bilateral regions, one ventral and one dorsal, that respond more strongly to ‘Stuff” > ‘Things’. The purpose of the current experiment (in the following referred to as Experiment 2) is threefold: 1) We want to replicate our previous findings while controlling for eye movements, i.e., subjects have to maintain fixation throughout the experiment. 2) We want to test whether the results depend on the dynamic nature of the stimuli or whether we will find the same pattern of results if we present static snapshots of the movies used in Experiment 1. 3) In case that we replicate the finding of a ventral region that responds more strongly to ‘Stuff’>’Things’, we want to better characterize the function of that region and relate it to previous work by adding additional functional localizers for color- and food-selective regions in the ventral stream.

title_r: Behavioural Detection of Emotional, High-Stakes Deception: Replication in a Registered Report
abstract_r: In this study, we propose a pre-registered replication of the research conducted by ten Brinke & Porter (2012). Their study identified four behavioural cues to deception that could distinguish deceptive murderers from genuinely distressed relatives, pleading for the safe return of a missing person, with a high degree of accuracy. By replicating this research using a new sample, we aim to assess the generalizability of these findings and provide further insights into the reliability of behavioral cues in distinguishing between deceptive and genuine pleaders.

title_r: Do different types of conflict interact?: An evaluation of Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) - Experiment 3
abstract_r: In distractor-interference tasks (e.g., Stroop, Simon, flanker), participants are slower and more error-prone in incongruent trials – where a distractor cues a different response than the target – than in congruent trials – where a distractor cues the same response as the target. This difference in performance, known as the congruency effect, arguably reflects greater response conflict in incongruent trials – which cue two opposing responses – than in congruent trials – which cue only one response. Although all distractor-interference tasks involve response conflict, the literature distinguishes between different types - or sources - of conflict that can occur in different tasks (Kornblum, 1990). Tasks such as flanker and Stroop involve stimulus-stimulus type conflict wherein the distractor and target convey semantically incongruent information. For example, in a color-based flanker task, the color of a central target square may be red, while the color of flanking distractor squares is green. On the other hand, the Simon task involves stimulus-response type conflict wherein the stimulus location is incongruent with the location of the correct response. For example, a Simon stimulus may appear on the left side of the screen but require a response with the right hand. Here, the distractor (stimulus location) is incongruent with the response (right-hand keypress) not with the identity of another stimulus. The distinction between different types of conflict suggests that people may process one type of conflict (e.g., stimulus-stimulus conflict) independently of another type of conflict (e.g., stimulus-response conflict). This is a core premise of conflict-specific accounts of cognitive control (Kornblum, 1990; Egner, 2008), which argue that control processes adapt to different forms of conflict independently of each other. In order to assess whether two distractors engender different types of conflict (e.g., stimulus-stimulus conflict and stimulus-response conflict), Egner (2008) proposed using hybrid distractor-interference tasks. For example, one could combine the Stroop and Simon tasks into a hybrid Stroop-Simon task. Here, on every trial, one would make a left or right response to identify the ink color of a Stroop color word stimulus presented on the left or right side of the screen. Egner (2008) argued that if Stroop and Simon distractors engender different types of conflict (i.e., stimulus-stimulus and stimulus-response conflict, respectively), which the brain processes independently, then the Stroop and Simon effects should sum additively. On the other hand, if Stroop and Simon distractors engender the same type of conflict, which the brain processes in a dependent fashion, then the Stroop and Simon effects should interact. However, two findings complicate the logic of Egner’s (2008) approach to identifying different domains of conflict, making it difficult to assess evidence for the conflict-specific account of cognitive control. First, within-trial interactions between the congruency of one distractor (e.g., Stroop) and the congruency of another distractor (e.g., Simon) may depend on the presence of a large congruency effect (Rey-Mermet, 2020). Second, a reactivation aversion effect (RAE) – in which one must execute a previously abandoned response – can produce interactions between two congruency effects regardless of whether the associated distractors engender the same or different types of conflict (Schlaghecken and Maylor, 2020). We elaborate on each of these findings below. First, Rey-Mermet (2020) found that within-trial interactions between the congruency effects of two distractors depend on the presence of a large congruency effect. In particular, Rey Mermet (2020) found – in a hybrid Stroop-flanker task – that interactions between Stroop and Flanker congruency are largest when the Stroop effect is large. Rey-Mermet (2020), therefore, concluded that observing a large congruency effect is a necessary condition for observing within-trial interactions of the sort that Egner (2008) describes. Weissman et al. (2020) observed similar results in a hybrid Stroop-Simon task. Here, the interaction between the Stroop and Simon effects was also greater when the Stroop effect was relatively large vs relatively small. With this in mind, it is unclear whether within-trial interactions between different congruency effects index dependent forms of conflict, or merely the presence of large congruency effects. Second, and crucial for the present study, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) found that a RAE – in which one must execute a previously abandoned response – can produce within-trial interactions between congruency effects in a hybrid prime-Simon task. In each trial of this task, participants first saw a prime arrow stimulus at the center of the screen. Next, they saw a probe arrow Simon stimulus. Participants were required to identify the direction of the probe arrow. The direction of the prime arrow could point in either the same (prime-compatible trials) or different (prime-incompatible trials) direction as the probe arrow, producing a prime compatibility effect. In addition, the location of the probe arrow could be the same (probe-congruent trials) or different (probe-incongruent trials) as the required response location, producing a Simon congruency effect. Critically, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) note that a RAE is possible only in prime-compatible, probe-incongruent trials. This is because the prime first cues one response (e.g., left), the probe location then cues the opposite response (e.g., right) and finally, the probe direction requires making the response originally cued by the prime (e.g, left). Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) argue that this response switching (e.g., left, then right, then left) creates confusion at a metacognitive level that lengthens response time selectively in prime-compatible, probe-incongruent trials. This possibility is problematic for Egner’s (2008) method because a RAE will produce an interaction between prime-compatibility and probe-congruency by increasing RT in prime-compatible, probe-incongruent trials. Consistent with this possibility, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) found an interaction suggesting a RAE in their prime-Simon task. Therefore, it appears a RAE can explain interactions between two distractor types without any recourse to dependence between two forms of conflict. Nonetheless, a modified version of Egner’s (2008) method may still be viable. In particular, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) suggest that one can avoid the influence of the RAE in their task by evaluating how the Simon effect differs between prime-neutral and prime-incompatible trials (rather than between prime-compatible and prime-incompatible trials). Indeed, since the RAE only influences RT in trials with congruent primes, the RAE cannot influence the Simon effect in prime-neutral or prime-incompatible trials. Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020), therefore, suggest that Egner’s (2008) logic can be reapplied to interactions between prime compatibility and probe congruency when one restricts the former factor to neutral and incompatible primes. Interestingly, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) found evidence (Experiment 1, horizontal trials) that the Simon effect did not differ between prime-neutral and prime-incompatible trials (i.e., they did not find an interaction). This finding is consistent with the notion that people process prime conflict (i.e., stimulus-stimulus conflict) independent of Simon conflict (i.e., stimulus-response conflict) (Kornblum, 1990). Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) also reported domain-specific congruency sequence effects: the prime-compatibility effect was reduced after prime-incompatible (vs prime-compatible) trials but not after Simon-incongruent (vs Simon-congruent) trials while the opposite was true for the Simon effect. These findings are consistent with the view that distinct control processes resolve different types of conflict (i.e., stimulus-stimulus and stimulus-response) (Egner, 2008). However, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) did not test the reverse intuition: the congruency effects associated with two distractors that engender the same type of conflict should depend on each other (i.e., interact). To investigate this hypothesis, in two prior experiments we employed a hybrid prime-flanker task that was similar to Schlaghecken and Maylor’s (2020) prime-Simon task. In Experiment 1, the prime stimulus was a single word and the probe stimulus was a horizontal flanker array composed of colored squares. Participants identified the color of the central square in the probe flanker array. Analogous to Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020), the prime word was compatible, neutral, or incompatible with the color of the central square in the flanker array. Moreover, the color of the flanking squares was congruent or incongruent with the color of the central square. The findings of Experiment 1 were mixed. On the one hand, we conceptually replicated two of Schlaghecken and Maylor’s (2020) findings. First, we observed a smaller flanker effect in prime-incompatible trials than in prime-compatible trials (p < 0.001), which is the traditional measure of whether two congruency effects interact (Egner, 2008). Second, we observed a larger flanker effect in prime-compatible trials than in prime-neutral trials (i.e., a RAE). On the other hand, we did not observe a smaller flanker effect in prime-incompatible trials than in prime-neutral trials (p = 0.076), which is Schlaghecken and Maylor’s alternative method for determining whether two conflicts are the same or different. Thus, the findings of Experiment 1 did not provide strong evidence that Schlaghecken and Maylor’s (2020) alternative method is sensitive to the presence of two distractors that engender the same type of conflict. title_r: Use of tweets in political news coverage in and outside election campaigns
abstract_r: Using tweets in political news has become a noticeable journalistic practice. This project examines the use of tweets in political news coverage in depths in and outside election campaigns. The use of tweets in news articles can be regarded as an expression of an accelerating media change towards a hybrid media system (Chadwick, 2017) in both journalism and politics, in which legacy media are adapting to new media technologies. Journalists use Twitter primarily as a legitimate and authoritative source of information for their news articles. At the same, politicians use Twitter primarily to reach out to citizens either directly or by placing their positions prominently on the news media agenda. This project examines the use of Twitter in political news coverage with a focus on journalists' perspective (study 1) and on polititicians' perspective (study 2). Study 1 is a conceptual replication and extension on the "Twitter in the News" study of Oschatz, Stier and Maier (2021) published in Digital Journalism (https://doi.org/10.1080/21670811.2021.1912624). We add to the understanding of the use and widespread of the journalistic practice in Germany by extending the media sample and comparing the use of tweets in and outside election campaigns. Study 2 is based on a theoretical agenda building approach. We explore to what extent and based on which characteristics and campaign strategies politicians and political parties are successful in getting their tweets featured in news coverage.

abstract_r: Eunsun Kyoug, Wenwen Cao, and Nammun Tsegmid are participating in a replication project of Segijn et al.’s study, "How Related Multiscreening Could Positively Affect Advertising Outcomes" (Journal of Advertising, 2017), as part of the JOUR 8502 course at the University of Minnesota. The purpose of this replication is purely educational—our goal is to learn how to design and conduct experiments rigorously. We want to emphasize that our intent is not to challenge or disprove findings of original study but rather to understand and apply experimental methodologies in a structured and reproducible manner. While we may conduct some exploratory analyses, our confirmatory analysis will focus on replicating one key effect reported in the original study. The original study comprises two separate studies; however, our replication effort will focus solely on Study 1.

title_r: ONE-SIDED COMMENTS ON OPINIONS AND INTENTIONS ON YOUTUBE: A REPLICATORY APPROACH
abstract_r: There has been evidence that one-sided social media comments influence people's opinion and intentions (Witteman et al., 2016). However, these findings have not been analyzed in the context of YouTube-videos. This study aims to replicate Witteman et al.'s (2016) findings on influence of one-sided social media comments in the context of a news article on home birth in this new context. Furthermore, research provides evidence on Attitude Importance (AI) to influence people's behavior on elaborating topics more thoroughly and deeply (Howe & Krosnick, 2017, p. 6.12). Additionally, Need for Cognition (NFC) is well-established in literature to moderate Opinion Change. Lower NFC-scores for instance is followed by significant changes of opinion when reading comemnts on news articles while higher NFC-scores remain without changes of opinion (Lee & Jang, 2010, p. 839). Therefore AI and NFC will be assessed as moderating constructs additionally in this study.

title_r: Semantic Structure and the (Reverse) Animacy Effect
abstract_r: Researchers have found that performance on free recall and recognition tends to be better for animal stimuli (e.g., words and pictures) than object stimuli (Leding, 2020; VanArsdall et al., 2013). This so-called “animacy effect” has been explained in terms of evolutionary psychology—we may be better at remembering things that have more survival relevance (e.g., animals) (Nairne et al., 2007). However, recent research has found that animacy may not always benefit memory-test performance —many studies have reported better performance on animals than objects on free recall, but Popp and Serra (2016) recently reported better performance on objects versus animals on paired-associate cued recall, We recently replicated this effect in a preregistered direct replication (Mah et al., in preparation). This “reverse animacy effect” has implications for theories of memory, but is not well understood. Therefore, the objective of this research is to investigate the causes of the reverse animacy effect in paired-associate cued recall. We speculate that the animacy and reverse animacy effects may be the result of the animal words being more interrelated than the object words. Greater within-category similarity could benefit free recall (via greater activation of more animal words during recall) but hurt cued recall (via more interference as a result of more non-target animal words being activated). Popp and Serra (2016) discussed this possibility, and there is some theoretical precedence for similarity-based interference effects in models such as the Search of Associative Memory (Raaijmakers & Shiffron, 1980; 1981)., This study will test this explanation by manipulating within-category similarity of animal and object words across free and cued recall. We will use a mixed design, with two factors (Memory type: Free, Cued; Animacy: Animals, Objects) manipulated within-subjects and a third factor (Within-category similarity: Animals-more-similar, Equal) manipulated between-subjects. Each subject will complete two FR study/list blocks and two CR study/list blocks; half of the subjects will do CR before FR, whereas the remainder will do FR before CR. We previously drafted a plan for a study testing this same hypothesis (see https://docs.google.com/document/d/18oKBq7jxl-4Pz7zZ6iQBIVeflmaU83QU7oXk0UzGi1s/edit) and tested 153 subjects but then discovered that a programming error produced varying numbers of animals versus objects in the first versus second lists of each type of test. Those data did not support the hypothesis that greater semantic relatedness for animals than objects gave rise to the reverse animacy effect, but arguably the programming error might have vitiated an effect of semantic relatedness. The current study corrects the programming error.

title_r: Im Schein der Fairness: Spielt die Erinnerung eine Rolle für den Einfluss der prozeduralen Fairness auf die Diskriminierungswahrnehmung?
abstract_r: With the planned experiment we would like to contribute to research on the perception of gender discrimination. It is important to know what factors influence the perception of discrimination in order to be able to judge more objectively whether or not women are being discriminated against and to find ways to reduce discrimination. There has already been a lot of research on this topic. One research field is the influence of diversity promotion programs on the perception of discrimination in organisations. Kaiser et al. (2013) already did a lot of research in that field. In a previous experiment (osf.io/e4ajm) we tried to replicate Kaiser et al.'s (2013) findings, that the presence of diversity structures decreased the perception of discrimination in organisations. They proposed that diversity structures increased perception of procedural fairness, which decreased perception of discrimination. In the planned study we want to focus on the direct effect of procedural fairness on perception of discrimination and answer the question: Is there an influence of procedural fairness on perception of discrimination? Furthermore we want to investigate the cognitive process of this effect more and answer the question: What role does memory play in this effect?
