title_r: The role of childhood trauma in a population segment with large economic burden
abstract_r: From a prevention standpoint, it is crucial to investigate which segment of the population develops problematic outcomes in different life domains in adulthood as these persons are the ones in need of societal resources. Moreover, to prevent the need for extensive societal resources, we need to examine predictors originating early in life. This knowledge can inform prevention approaches. A previous study in New Zealand by Caspi and colleagues (2016) found that a segment of 20% of their study population predicted a disproportionate high amount of negative economic and physical health outcomes. Up to date, studies in Netherlands have not yet examined specific population segments which could be targeted for prevention and early intervention approaches as well as which aspects would need to be targeted by prevention strategies. Besides, even in the New Zealand study, mental health was not studied as a negative economic outcome. The current study has two main goals: First, we will replicate the New Zealand study in a larger, well-powered Dutch population-cohort study. Second, we will expand the investigation by focusing on two outcome domains: 1) work & finances, and 2) mental health.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Lindqvist & Östling (2010) in American Political Science Review
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Lindqvist & Östling (2010) is that the correlation between polarization and government size is significantly stronger among democratic countries; the association between polarization and government size in strong democracies is the specific part of the finding selected for the SCORE program. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Political polarization is strongly associated with smaller government in democratic countries, but there is no relationship between polarization and the size of government in undemocratic countries." The analysis relies on a regression of government size (general government consumption as a fraction of total consumption, averaged from 2003-2005) on the standard deviation of four World Values Survey items measuring various economic aspects of left and right on a 1-10 scale, in four separate models. The authors estimate a regression for each of these measures in the paper; the SCORE program has selected the 1-10 scale where 1 means complete agreement that “Private ownership of business should be increased” and 10 means complete agreement that “Government ownership of business and industry should be increased.” In the ‘long’ specification chosen for the SCORE program, the authors control for the mean value of responses, along with geographic and colonial controls, and an additional set of potentially endogenous control variables. The authors split their sample such that countries with a Polity IV democracy score of 9 to 10 are strong democracies, while countries with scores 0 to 8 are weak democracies. The evidence selected for the SCORE program is the regression estimated on the strong democratic sample using the measure of polarization specified above (results are significant using three of the four measures in the paper with this specification). When the sample is restricted to strong democracies, the estimated effect of polarization on government consumption is statistically significant (coefficient in the ‘long’ specification for the “Private” measure of polarization = -18.73, heteroscedasticity robust SE = 4.79, p = .01).

title_r: The "Go/No-Go" paradigm to assess spatial numerical associations - Experiment 2
abstract_r: This study will use the "Go/No-go" paradigm to investigate spatial-numerical associations (SNAs) within UK adult participants. Eccher et al. (2025) used a computerised Go/No-go task to investigate SNA in a sample of Himba adults, Italian adults and Italian preschoolers. In each trial, participants were presented with a central fixation cross, followed by the first dot array (henceforth the “reference stimulus”) made up of 4, 12 or 36 dots. After a brief blank screen, participants then saw a second dot array (henceforth the “test stimulus”) displayed to either the left or right of the screen. In the increasing condition, participants were told to press the space bar when the test stimulus contained MORE dots than the reference stimulus. For example, when the reference stimulus contained 4 dots, the participant’s response would be recorded as correct only if the test stimulus contained 12 or 36 dots. If the reference stimulus was 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the test stimulus contained 36 dots. In the decreasing condition, participants were then instructed to only press the space bar when the test stimulus contained fewer dots than the reference stimulus. When the reference stimulus contained 36 dots, a participant's response would be recorded as correct when the test stimulus contained 12 or 4 dots. If the reference stimulus contained 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the target stimulus contained 4 dots. Both the increase and the decrease tasks started with 12 trials to familiarize the participants with the task (“training trials”), followed by 48 “experimental trials”, 30 of which were targets (i.e. trials that required a response) and 18 were distractors (i.e. trials that did not require a response). 50% of all trials were considered “SNA congruent”, whereby stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from left-to-right. The other 50% of trials were considered “SNA incongruent”, as the stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from right-to-left. For example, if a participant was completing the “increasing” condition and the test target stimulus contained 4 dots and the test stimulus contained 12 dots and presented on the right, this would be considered SNA congruent, as the target stimulus is always presented in the centre, and so the presentation of stimuli moves from left-to-right in order of magnitude. Conversely, in the “decreasing” condition, an SNA congruent trial may be one in which the target stimulus contains 36 dots, and the test stimulus contains 4 dots which is presented on the left. For further details of SNA congruent/incongruent conditions, see “Manipulated Variables"). We aim to replicate the original study’s findings, which demonstrated the potential presence of a spatial-numerical association. That is, participants will be faster and more accurate when responding to numerosities presented in a left-to-right direction, increasing in terms of magnitude, while participants’ responses will be slower and less accurate when those same numerosities are presented in a right-to-left order in terms of magnitude. In our replication, we will conduct the experiment online rather than in person; we will recruit adult participants in the UK; make a slight modification to the timing of the no-go trials, reducing the duration from three seconds (as in the original study) to 1.5 seconds; and we will double the number of trials. In the original study, there was a one-to-one correspondence between the total area taken up by the dot array stimuli and their numerical magnitude. That is, the 4-dot array will take up much less visual area than the 36-dot array. It may be that participants are making judgements based off total area of stimuli rather than extracting magnitude information. Therefore, in Experiment 2, we have produced two novel types of dot array stimuli: “controlled” and “correlated” stimuli. The correlated stimuli are those which have a one-to-one correspondence between total area and numerosity. The controlled stimuli all share the same total area of dots, regardless of numerosity. We have also created five stimulus variations for each type of dot array to further prevent participants from relying on pattern recognition, thus creating a total of 30 stimuli. Crucially, trials are always matched in terms of controlled or correlated stimuli; for example, if a participant sees a controlled reference stimulus, then the test stimulus will also be controlled. Further information can be found in the “Manipulated Variables” section.

title_r: Unknown vocabulary density and reading comprehension: Replicating Hu & Nation 2000
abstract_r: Hu and Nation’s (2000) study, which stipulated that second language (L2) readers need to be familiar with 98% of lexical items for adequate text comprehension, has become highly influential in L2 vocabulary research and pedagogy. This research has since been the foundation for numerous lexical coverage studies (e.g. Nation, 2006; Schmitt, 2010). However, the 98% critical threshold figure is based on findings from a research project in which a regression analysis was conducted with 66 university students in New Zealand. The present study replicates Hu and Nation’s research in a context different from a typical Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) context with a sample of 105 Sri Lankan adult L2 learners in a non-academic context. They will each take two different Vocabulary Levels Tests and read one of five versions of two reading texts at different levels of density of unknown words, before answering comprehension questions.

title_r: Support and Sexism in Relationships
abstract_r: This study is a conceptual replication and extension of Vollmann et al. (2011) investigating Social Support as a mediator of the relationship between stress and optimism. Based on the statistics reported in this study, although optimistic individuals perceived receiving higher social support; and individuals who perceived receiving higher social support reported less stress; perceived social support did not significantly mediate this relationship. "Finally, the indirect effect of optimism on perceived stress through social support from the recipients’ perspective was marginally significant, (p = .08, 95% CI (-0.08, 0.01)" (pp.149). There was also no significant mediating effect of perceived provided social support (p= .14). In this study, we looked to replicate Vollmann et al.'s (2011) study but extend it in two ways. First, we separately measured emotional and practical received and perceived support, rather than using a global 'social support' measure. Secondly we added a measure of ambivalent sexism.

title_r: Large online (conceptual) replication of LDW-Triggered overestimation effect.
abstract_r: "Losses disguised as wins" are a machine gambling event in which the user wins back less than the amount wagered (i.e. a net loss) and yet the machine celebrates the event as though it were a genuine win. Previous lab experiments have reported that participants tend to overestimate the frequency at which they won more than they wagered following a session of simulated slot machine gambling if losses disguised as wins (LDWs) were present during the session (see Graydon et al, 2017; Templeton et al, 2015; Jensen et al. 2011). Previous studies have reported effect sizes between approximately (Cohen's) d = 0.5 and d = 1.0, in samples usually less than 100 participants. We aim to perform a conceptual replication of the LDW triggered win overestimation in a large online sample using a video of online slot gambling. We hypothesize that respondents in the LDW condition will over-estimate the number of times a win occurred that was more than the amount bet.

title_r: Empathy among psychology and nursing students in Norway
abstract_r: For health professional, empathy is necessary in order to both understand those they are working with, and what they are possibly suffering from. As such empathy can actually be thought of as a skill that health professionals in all institutional settings (i.e. schools, hospitals, prisons etc) must make use of in order to perform their duties. In the current study we are interested in comparing two groups of students, psychology and nursing, that will soon begin their working careers. The aim is to see if their higher education studies has had an influence on their view of empathy, more precisely; if there is a difference in how these two groups rank the items used in our replication study from 2022. There will also be an open-ended question about the participants definition of empathy.

title_r: Student Project: Replication of Haesevoets, Van Hiel, Pandelaere, Bostyn, & De Cremer (2017, JDM, Study 4)
abstract_r: This project is an independent replication of Haesevoets, Van Hiel, Pandelaere, Bostyn, & De Cremer (2017, JDM, Study 4) conducted as part of the Hagen Cumulative Science Project I. A central finding of Haesevoets et al. (2017) is that, when customers are offered different levels of overcompensation, customer loyalty follows a quadratic trend. They found that mild overcompensation for a damaged product has on average a positive effect on customer loyalty up to a compensation level of about 150%, but that beyond this level the effectiveness of overcompensation, i.e. customer loyalty decreases again. However, within this inverted U-shaped function there were individual differences. The study found two classes of customers: A majority reacted positively to any forms of overcompensation: their loyalty increased, but flattened out into the higher ranges. But there was also a small number of people who reacted negatively to all forms of overcompensation. Thus the authors recommend that companies not use overcompensation above 150% as there is no increase in customer loyalty beyond that level in any of the two categories of respondents. In our replication, we mainly hope to identify this quadratic trend between compensation size and customer loyalty and find evidence that customers show an increasing positive reaction to overcompensation until around an overcompensation level of 130% and a maximum overcompensation level of around 150%.

title_r: Effects of Infant Behavioral Inhibition on Social Processing and Risk for Social Anxiety during Adulthood
abstract_r: Behavioral Inhibition (BI) is a temperament characterized by fearful, shy, timid, or withdrawn behavior in unfamiliar situations early in life (DiLalla et al., 1994; Fox et al., 2001). High infant BI puts children at risk for social difficulties, such as problems during peer interactions and social withdrawal (Clauss & Blackford, 2012; Sandstrom et al., 2020). Approximately 40% of children with BI develop anxiety disorders (Clauss & Blackford, 2012; Fox et al., 2001; Sandstrom et al., 2020), and the empirical literature has consistently identified relations between infant BI and social issues during childhood and adolescence (Chronis-Tuscano et al., 2009; McDermott et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2020). However, only a few studies have addressed the potential consequences of infant BI on socioemotional development in adulthood (Asendorpf et al., 2008; Caspi, 1996; Caspi et al., 2003). These studies assessed BI retrospectively and using self-reported symptoms. Recently, a prospective study by Tang et al. (2020) described the impact of infant BI, as measured with behavioral observations, on adult mental health and personality. Specifically, infants who scored high on BI at 14 and 24 months of age had poorer social and cognitive functioning and higher rates of introversion in adulthood. In the current study, we extend the study of Tang et al. (2020), by focusing on associations between infant BI, social processing, and social anxiety in early adulthood. This study is part of a larger longitudinal project investigating the influence of infant temperament on socioemotional development (Chronis-Tuscano et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2020). Since BI has been identified as a robust predictor of later social anxiety (McDermott et al., 2009; Chronis-Tuscano et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2020), we want to determine whether infant BI and concurrent social anxiety symptoms predict differential processing of social experiences during adulthood. With this aim, we can examine infant BI's predictive ability into adulthood and improve our understanding of complex processes that underlie social interactions, which is crucial for participants with elevated social anxiety. To do this, we use a cognitive task with social manipulation (the social flanker task; Barker et al., 2015; Buzzell et al., 2017, described below) to study the processing of social situations with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). A previous study by Smith et al. (Smith et al., 2019), applying a similar social flanker task in children, showed activation of the supramarginal gyrus, cingulate gyrus, inferior parietal lobe, medial frontal gyrus, insula, posterior cingulate gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus and precuneus during error processing compared to correct responses. Most importantly, in children with and without anxiety an increased activation of the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC) was found when making errors while the participants believed they were observed by peers, compared to when they were not observed by peers (Smith et al., 2019). This was related to the social anxiety scores, where more anxiety scores were related to more activation in the pgACC. This result suggests that the pgACC plays a crucial role in processing social interactions during performance monitoring, specifically in participants with clinical anxiety. On a mechanistic level, increased performance monitoring in a social context among participants with behavioral inhibition might reflect a rigid response pattern that hinders social interactions across development and is associated with adult psychopathology (Buzzell et al., 2017; Henderson et al., 2015). We intend to replicate this finding in adults, where we hypothesize (see section 4) that the pgACC will be more engaged when making errors while being observed during task performance compared to not being observed. To test this hypothesis, we re-invited participants (see section 12 and 13) from the longitudinal study on the impact of infant temperament on socioemotional development, who are now around 29 years of age, to assess brain responses with fMRI while performing a social flanker task (adopted from Smith et al., 2019). The social flanker task is a modified version of the Eriksen Flanker task (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974), measuring performance monitoring with two conditions: social and non-social (for trial-specific information, see section 12). In the social condition, participants believe they are observed and receive feedback on their performance from a peer. In the non-social condition, the participant is not observed and receives feedback generated by a computer. Also, in this ongoing visit, we will assess psychopathology (through clinical interviews and questionnaires), including the current social anxiety problems of the participant. Thus, the present study will examine the role of infant BI and current social anxiety symptoms on neural and behavioral responses to the social flanker task. This report is a pre-registration for the analyses applied in this study.

title_r: Does MRI scanner background noise from a novel silent fMRI sequence affect Prepulse Inhibition (PPI) in healthy adults?
abstract_r: This is a behavioural study to follow up our findings from an MRI study (not pre-registered) to investigate the neural correlates of Prepulse Inhibition (PPI) in a mixed sex sample of healthy adults. The MRI study: We implemented a novel silent fMRI sequence called Looping Star. Instead of rapidly switching gradients in conventional fMRI sequences, like echo-planar imaging (EPI), Looping Star makes small, incremental changes in the direction of frequency encoding gradients. This is approximately 5dBA louder than ambient noise and 27dBA quieter than GRE-EPI sequences (Damenstani et al., 2021). We ran an auditory task to investigate the neural correlates of Prepulse Inhibition (PPI), a modulatory effect of the startle reflex response which reflects sensorimotor gating. Acoustic prepulse paradigms (where loud noises are used to elicit the startle response) are commonly used in animal studies and behavioural research in humans. Therefore, we used an acoustic prepulse paradigm with Looping Star fMRI, thus removing the confound of loud scanner background noise from GRE-EPI sequences and a sparse sampling technique to allow presentation of the auditory stimuli. Our findings showed that PPI appeared to be a lot lower than previously studied (Naysmith et al., 2022). Naysmith et al. (2022) showed a decrease in startle response of ~44% when participants were comfortably seated in a quiet room. The auditory playlist was presented over a white noise background. However, in our MRI study, where participants were lying in the MRI scanner and the auditory playlist was presented over the Looping Star background noise, participants showed a decrease in startle response of ~13%. Follow-up behavioural study: We therefore wish to follow-up on our MRI study results to establish whether the Looping Star background noise affected PPI. We will replicate all conditions, with participants lying in the mock fMRI scanner and listening to the auditory playlist whilst startle response is measured with Electromyography (EMG). We will play the same playlist twice to the participants, whereby one playlist is presented over a recording of the Looping Star noise, and one playlist is presented over white noise (70dBA). These playlists will be counterbalanced to remove any order effects. PPI will be compared on both tasks to establish whether background noise affects PPI. We will also compare PPI between the groups we recruited in the original MRI study ((a)males, (b)females not on hormonal contraception, and (c)females on hormonal contraception). Whether there is an interaction between these two factors will also be investigated.

title_r: Understanding the visual constraints on lexical processing: New empirical and simulation results
abstract_r: It is well known that visual acuity is not uniform across the visual field. Acuity instead decreases precipitously from the center of vision. The region of maximum acuity, called the fovea, is comprised of the central 2º of the visual field, with a region of rapidly decreasing acuity called the parafovea extending an additional 5º of visual angle to either side of this. Although the photoreceptors required for perceiving fine detail are largely limited to these two regions of the visual field, it remains unclear precisely how the rapid drop off in visual acuity that results from the distribution of these photoreceptors affects our capacity to rapidly and accurately identify printed words. This project aims to investigate the physical constraints imposed by our visual system on reading by conducting a conceptual replication of a highly cited study by Rayner and Morrison (1981). The original study compared lexical-decision and naming performance at central fixation (0 degrees), or between 1 and 5 degrees to the left or right of central fixation. Participants were either instructed to maintain central fixation (no eye-movement condition) or move their eyes to the location of the stimulus (eye-movement condition). The proposed study improves on several features of the original study by (i) testing a much larger sample of participants; (ii) using a larger number of more highly controlled items that are not repeated during the experiment and that vary in both word length and frequency; (iii) ensuring participants maintain central fixation by tracking eye movements and terminating trials on which the participant moves their eyes.

title_r: Harnessing Simulated Experience to Help People Make Better Investment Decisions
abstract_r: In order to make satisfactory investment decisions, investors must know and understand the risks that they face. An investor's comprehension of risk can differ considerably depending on how that risk is learned or communicated. Finance professionals typically communicate risks using descriptions, for instance, in the form of financial reports, mutual fund brochures, insurance brochures, investor education programs, and market research. These documents report risks using summary of historical returns and their respective probabilities. However, investors could also acquire knowledge about financial risks in other ways, that is, by observing the development of stock prices or through their own investment experience. For instance, day-traders decide to purchase a stock by simply observing prior stock movements, or, individual investors increase their subscription to IPO auctions subsequent to previous successful experience (e.g., Kaustia & Knupfer, 2008). The literature documents that the manner in which knowledge about risks is acquired or communicated, has a dramatic influence on investor's understanding of risk and their willingness to accept it. For example, our previous work shows experimentally that people who learn about a stock market crash from experience are more likely to stay out of the market than people who learn from descriptions (i.e., the "depression babies" effect), even when wealth effects are kept equivalent (Lejarraga, Woike, & Hertwig, 2016). Recent studies have shown that, in general, people not only seem to be persuaded more by their experience than from described sources of information, but also may arrive at more accurate subjective assessments of a given risk, even if experience is simulated. For example, Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013) and Bradbury, Hens and Zeisberger (2014) show that simulations of the stock market, which are closer to the notion of witnessing than experiencing through action, help investors understand risk accurately, and lead them to invest more in the stock market than investors that learn from described sources. On the other hand, Lejarraga and Gonzalez (2011) show that exhaustive descriptive information is often neglected when the subjects have the chance to also experience the information by sampling. That is, people who have experience and descriptions, make choices as if descriptions were omitted. Consistent with this observation, Barron, Leider, and Stack (2007) show that people are more likely to ignore a described warning if they have already experienced a series of safe outcomes, but they are more likely to be persuaded by the warning if they have no previous experience. These studies converge in that people tend to overweight the information they gain from experience over that which is provided in a descriptive form, which can lead to more accurate risk assessments, as long as the experiences made are representative of the environment. Our studies attempt to extend previous research in two ways. First, we seek to conduct a conceptual replication of the study of Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013). This involves exposing participants in an investment task to four different risk communication interventions and observing how the interventions affect participants’ risk taking behaviour, factual knowledge about the encountered decision environmnet, and subjective assessments of confidence and satisfaction. Second, we will extend the study of Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013) by manipulating whether or not people have had prior experiences with the decision environment, when exposed to the risk communication intervention. Specifically, one group of people will build up experience with the decision environment by making a series of decisions with feedback prior to being exposed to the risk communication intervention, while the other group, akin to Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013), will be given the risk communication intervention straight away. Using this setup, we will be able to provide a better estimate of how effective the four risk interventions are in informing people about financial risks in situations involving no prior experiences and explore how and whether prior experiences impact the effectiveness of the four interventions.

title_r: Mapping neurobiological patterns of childhood adversity in psychiatry using normative modeling
abstract_r: Childhood adversity can have long-lasting effects on the development of the brain and represents a well-known risk factor for the emergence of mental health problems. However, previous efforts to identify the neural underpinnings of childhood adversity and their implications for mental health have been limited by a reliance on case-control comparisons and group summary statistics, which are based on the assumption that the investigated subgroups are inherently homogenous. These comparisons are inadequate to address the vast heterogeneity and comorbidity in psychiatric populations on the one hand, and co-occurring adversities on the other hand. Normative modeling represents an innovative alternative to these traditional approaches. This method enables the mapping of relationships between behavioral and biological measures of interest and provides statistical inference at the level of the individual, relative to a reference population (Marquand et al., 2016; Marquand et al., 2019). Previous studies have demonstrated that normative modeling is well-suited to characterize clinical heterogeneity (Wolfers et al., 2019; Zabihi et al., 2019), which is crucial to obtain a more nuanced understanding of the link between adversity-induced brain alterations and mental health. The normative modeling framework has recently been employed by Holz and colleagues (2023), who identified a stable and replicable neural signature of adversity in an at-risk cohort for mental health disorders. Noticeably, individual cortical volume contractions were shown to be predictive of later anxiety, emphasizing the value of subject-level brain alterations as predictors for clinical outcome measures. However, since only a few subjects progressed to meet the criteria for a formal psychiatric diagnosis, insights into the relationship between structural brain alterations and psychopathology remain limited. To address this, the current study will extend the findings by Holz et al. (2023) to a heterogeneous and multimorbid psychiatric patient sample as well as to different dimensions of trauma (emotional abuse, emotional neglect, physical abuse, sexual abuse). We will combine data from different cohort studies, including clinical samples from the ‘Measuring Integrated Novel Dimensions in Neurodevelopmental and Stress-related Mental Disorders’ (MIND-Set) study (van Eijndhoven et al., 2022) and ‘The Biological Classification of Mental Disorders’ (BeCOME) study (https://www.psych.mpg.de/2398388/become; Brückl et al., 2020). We will include additional healthy control samples from the ‘Healthy Brain Study’ (HBS; https://www.healthybrainstudy.nl), the IMAGEN cohort (https://imagen-project.org), and the ‘Mannheim Study of Children at Risk’ (MARS; https://www.zi-mannheim.de/en/research/departments-research-groups-institutes/child-adolescent-psychiatry-psychotherapy-e/research-groups-child-adolescent-psychiatry-psychotherapy-e/dev-neurosci.html). First, we will test whether we can replicate the identified pattern of adversity-induced volumetric changes from Holz et al. (2023) in a naturalistic and transdiagnostic clinical sample containing patients with mood disorders and neurodevelopmental disorders. Moreover, we aim to extend this pattern along multiple axes, namely to: (i) across a greater lifespan range, (ii) greater population diversity and (iii) accommodating multiple different clinical instruments. To achieve these objectives, we will build normative reference models capturing variation in cortical and subcortical brain volume, as predicted by early life adversities. Then, we will investigate whether, and if so how, individual volumetric deviations from the reference model are associated with clinical measures in terms of diagnostic information and symptomatology along cross-diagnostic symptom domains (as previously identified by Mulders et al., 2022).

title_r: European farmers’ risk attitudes – A cross-country replication of Bocquého et al. (2014)
abstract_r: Background: Risk and uncertainty are at the core of many questions in agricultural economics, and agricultural economists have been interested in estimating farmers’ risk attitudes for several decades (e.g., Binswanger, 1980; Iyver et al., 2020). In particular, risk attitudes are an important modeling input, and they are of broad interest to policy makers and insurance companies. There is a large diversity of approaches to study farmers’ risk attitudes, and this literature is scattered, with few studies systematically investigating differences across countries and farming systems (Iyer et al., 2020). One popular method to study risk attitudes are incentivized gambles and lotteries based on multiple price lists (e.g., Holt and Laury, 2002). These lotteries have been widely applied to investigate farmers’ risk attitudes (see Iyer et al., 2020 for a recent overview of studies). One of the most widely cited studies in this area is that of Bocquého et al. (2014). This study uses the multiple price lists developed by Tanaka et al. (2010) to investigate whether Expected Utility Theory (EUT) or Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) better describes farmers’ attitudes towards risk and uncertainty in a sample of French farmers. The authors use structural models to estimate EUT and CPT parameters. They also estimate models that adjust for socio-demographic heterogeneity. They find that farmers are risk-averse in the gain domain under EUT and exhibit loss aversion and overweighting of small probabilities under CPT. This replication proposal focuses on exploring the robustness and boundaries of the estimates of Bocquého et al. (2014). The replication will entail two exercises. First, we have obtained the original data and code from the authors and we will replicate the analysis. This allows us to establish a coherent econometric benchmark to compare the original model results with those obtained by us. Second, we will apply a similar protocol in several European countries and for different farming systems (see list below). Our replication focuses on the same question as the original study: Are farmers’ risk attitudes better described by EUT or by CPT? We also strive to showcase best practices for cross-country data collection in future replication efforts in experimental agricultural economics by embracing open science practices (i.e., follow a pre-registration with power calculations, open data, and open methods). Method: Our replication will reproduce the same experimental design (focused on the risk task, while the original study also had a longer survey including also an ambiguity and time tasks) but will deviate in some aspects. These deviations are needed, partly for feasibility considerations, but also because we strive to test a simpler protocol capable of yielding results of equivalent quality and robustness. First, the original study investigated 107 farmers from 64 towns in the French Bourgogne region in a 2-hour face-to-face interview. Our data collection will take place online or face-to-face, depending on feasibility in each of the case studies (see details below). In the online surveys, we implement a 2 minutes video explaining the task, as a compensation for a lack of personal interaction. Second, the sample will be more diverse, both in terms of origin and farm type. While French farmers will also be interviewed in the replication (from both South and North West of France), we will also rely on a mix of convenience and random samples of farmers from other European regions across a wide range of farming systems. We want to achieve a comparable statistical power as the original study (assuming the same effect sizes) at country level, i.e., there should be 107 farmers or more for most countries. In total, we expect a substantially larger pooled sample. We will discuss deviations from the original estimates (if any) against the background of amendments in the protocol and the cultural/economic contexts. Third, while every farmer received a payment in the original study, we will incentivize a certain proportion of farmers with a cash payment or a close equivalent (e.g., vouchers for a popular online shopping outlet in the respective country). Fourth, the exchange rate in the experiment will be known to our participants a priori, because the original procedure with an envelope that contains the exchange rate – only revealed after the lotteries – is difficult to mimic online. The analysis will report the results of the same structural models as the original study (without covariates) and to explore the impact of (other) covariates. Due to the different contexts, we will define a set of covariates that overlap for our various cases in the original study. Similar to the original study, we will employ a series of robustness tests to understand how other reference points than zero might drive results for CPT estimates. The authors have developed a joint survey instrument in Qualtrics in English. For each case study there is an individual survey in English and the local language. References: Binswanger, H. P. title_r: Will They Get Along? Infants’ Expectations about Third Party Social Relationships Based on Language: An online replication of Liberman et al. 2017
abstract_r: While research has shed light on infants’ ability to recognize and even prefer their native language at a remarkably young age, little research has studied whether infants use language as an indicator of social groups.The present study will be replicating a 2017 study “Preverbal Infants Infer Third-Party Social Relationships Based on Language” by Liberman, Woodward, and Kinzler. While the 2017 study was conducted in-person in a laboratory setting with video stimuli projected on a large screen, this study will be conducted online on the Lookit website (lookit.mit.edu). Another noteworthy difference is that the 2017 study involved infant-controlled test trials, while this study will not (i.e., test trials will be presented the same length regardless infant looking). This study will test whether the same patterns and findings from the 2017 study will be replicated in an online paradigm despite these differences.

title_r: How does presenting stimuli in and out of synchrony with a rhythm affect recognition memory? An EEG study.
abstract_r: Presenting items in a temporally structured manner during encoding leads to greater subsequent memory compared with when items are presented in an unstructured temporal framework (e.g., Jones & Ward, 2019; Thavabalasingam, O’Neil, Zeng, & Lee, 2016). Jones and Ward (2019) observed that presenting to-be-remembered objects in a rhythmic manner during encoding produced greater recognition compared with when objects were presented with arrhythmic onset timings, and memory-specific ERP components were differentially affected by rhythmic encoding – the FN400 old/new effect was unaffected by rhythmic encoding, while the late positive component (LPC) old/new effect was observed only for rhythmically encoded items. The Dynamic Attending Theory (DAT; Large & Jones, 1999) proposes that rhythms automatically entrain peaks of heightened attention that modulate the gain of sensory input, which provides a benefit to processing (encoding) stimuli presented in phase with the rhythm. This is in line with evidence that intrinsic brain oscillations entrain to external rhythms, aligning the neuronal firing such that stimuli presented in phase are at a processing advantage compared with those presented out of phase (Arnal & Giraud, 2012; Calderone, Lakatos, Butler, & Castellanos, 2014; Henry & Herrmann, 2014; Lakatos, Karmos, Mehta, Ulbert, & Schroeder, 2008). Given this, one would expect that presenting items out of synchrony with an entrained rhythm will be particularly detrimental to memory formation. This aim of this project is to test this hypothesis. A handful of recent studies have examined memory for items that were presented in and out of synchrony with rhythms, however, in all cases rhythm has been an irrelevant background feature. For example, Johndro, Jacobs, Patel, and Race, (2019) reported greater recognition of face stimuli that were presented in synchrony with a rhythmic auditory background beat during encoding, and Hickey, Merseal, Patel, and Race (2020) showed that enhanced neural tracking was associated with greater recognition of objects that appeared in-synchrony with an auditory background beat, compared to those that appeared out-of-synchrony. Here, we outline an experimental paradigm that allows us to explore how changes in the temporal structure of information presented during encoding effects subsequent recognition memory. Specifically, we aim to replicate previous findings showing that rhythmic presentation of stimuli enhances recognition. Second, we aim to test whether items presented out of synchrony with an ongoing rhythm during encoding effects subsequent recognition. Importantly, our paradigm allows us to also consider the underlying neural processes involved at encoding and recognition.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Stanley et al. (2020), from PsyArXiv
abstract_r: For replication, we selected the claim that those individuals who perform worse on the CRT (cognitive reflection test) were less likely to have engaged in helpful behaviours (related to the covid-19 pandemic) over the prior week. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “Our results indicate that individuals less willing to engage in effortful, deliberative, and reflective cognitive processes were more likely to believe the pandemic was a hoax, and less likely to have recently engaged in social-distancing and hand-washing.” The claim was tested by computing bivariate correlations between average CRT performance and measures of helping behaviours (social-distancing being one of 3 tested). title_r: Confirming pupil dilation as physiological marker of Bayesian inference in dynamic auditory localization
abstract_r: Bayesian theory has been applied successfully to explain human perception in noisy and volatile environments. Previous studies used explicit predictive-inference tasks to show that responses of the pupil-linked arousal system correlate with the weighting of prior knowledge during high-level perceptual decision making (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017, Nassar et al., 2012, Meyniel, 2020, Filipowicz et al., 2020). In the current study, we use a sound location estimation- rather than prediction task to investigate whether the pupil-linked arousal system also reflects implicit low-level weighting of perceptual priors. Participants are asked to localise the last sound in spatially dynamic sequences. Our experimental design features two conditions that are alternated on successive trials: (1) An audio-visual (AV) condition in which we present visual-spatial representations of the sound sources along with each sound except for the last. This condition will participants to maintain a stable spatial mapping between the sound sources of and their abstract visual representations that are required for behavioural responses. It further acts as a close replication of the study by Krishnamurthy et al. (2017). (2) An auditory-only (A) condition, which allows us to test whether spatial priors can be formed for purely auditory stimuli or whether visual representations of their source are required. Moreover, by lack of visual stimulation, the A-only condition is ideally suited to test the hypothesized relationship between the arousal system, assessed through pupillometry, and implicit low-level prior weighting in auditory spatial perception (even during ongoing sound sequence presentation, i.e., not contaminated by response preparation - see Exploratory analysis section).

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Chen & van Ours (2018), from Demography
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Chen & van Ours (2018) is that marriage makes couples happier than does cohabitation. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Well-being gains of marriage are larger than those of cohabitation." The authors analyze Dutch panel data to investigate whether partnership has a causal effect on subjective well-being. Subjective well-being is measured on an ordinal scale from 0 to 10. To account for time-invariant unobserved personal characteristics, the authors use a linear fixed-effects model. The specification of the model allows the authors to compare the effects of marriage and cohabitation to that of being single. The focal test result concerns the location of the difference in estimate coefficients on the married and cohabiting dummy variables (single is the reference category). The selected test result comes from the parameter estimated obtained for the women sample. The results are reported in Table 3, Panel d - under the heading “Female.” The estimated coefficients for “Marriage” and “Cohabitation” are .39 (SE = .08) and .21 (SE = .07) respectively. The difference is statistically significant, p = .004.

title_r: Replication of Experiment 1 from “The Impact of Partial Source Dependence on Belief and Reliability Revision” (2020)
abstract_r: This study is a direct replication of Experiment 1 from the paper “The Impact of Partial Source Dependence on Belief and Reliability Revision” (Madsen et al., 2020). The original study tested how people update their belief in a claim and the reliability of sources when they learn that those sources are not independent but instead share a background (e.g., same institution). It used a Bayesian framework to predict changes in belief and perceived reliability across multiple expert testimonies, manipulating both the prior likelihood of the claim (high vs. low) and the quality of the shared source (high vs. low). This replication adopts the same mixed-design structure with a within-subject factor for likelihood (salmon population growth vs. economy crash) and a between-subject factor for shared source quality (high vs. low). The purpose is to assess whether the original findings—particularly the effect of shared source dependence on belief revision and reliability judgments—can be reproduced in a new sample using an online platform. Expected outcomes include replicating the Bayesian updating patterns and the interaction effects tied to shared reliability. The study is preregistered to ensure transparency and methodological alignment with the original experiment.

title_r: Investigating the relationship between language laterality and hemispheric differences in orthographic neighbourhood size effects: Study 2
abstract_r: In the first part of this project (Mills et al., Study 1), we aimed to replicate and extend the findings of Parker et al. (2021). Parker et al. showed that, in a group of right handed participants, there was a facilitatory effect of orthographic neighbourhood size (N size) in the left visual field (LVF) and an inhibitory effect of N size in the right visual field (RVF). In Study 1 we failed to replicate Parker’s result in a group of left handed participants who were typically (left) lateralised on a dichotic listening task: there was no significant effect of N size in either the LVF or the RVF. In the second part of this project (Study 2) we are seeking to understand why we failed to replicate this result. There are a number of possible explanations for why we did not replicate Parker’s results. We have ruled out the possibility that Parker’s result was a false positive - the facilitatory effect of N size in the LVF is robust, and Parker’s study itself was a replication and was backed up by a meta-analysis of similar findings in the literature. Hence, it is surprising that this well-established result in the LVF was not replicated in Study 1. We believe it is more likely that our failure to replicate Parker’s findings was due to methodological differences between the studies in terms of the participant group, the task design or the stimuli, which are summarised in Table 1 (see additional materials) and discussed in detail below. 3.1. Participants Parker et al.’s study used right handed participants, whereas Mills et al. Study 1 used left handed participants: this difference may have caused our failure to replicate Parker’s results. It is known that left handers are more variable in their strength and direction of lateralisation than right handers (Bruckert et al., 2021; Woodhead et al., 2020); however, we controlled for this by testing the left handers’ lateralisation using a dichotic listening task, and selecting a sub-group of participants with typical (left) lateralisation as well as a sub-group with atypical (right or bilateral) lateralisation. We did not replicate Parker’s result in either group. It remains possible that there are unanticipated differences between right and left handed participants that drove the differences that we saw between Parker’s results and Study 1’s results. We will test this possibility in Study 2 by recruiting a new group of right handed participants, and use the same version of the task with them that we used in the left handed group from Study 1. This will allow a direct comparison of left and right handed participants with the same task. 3.2. Task Design A second possibility is that the task design used in Study 1 eliminated the N size effects. Parker’s study used an online lexical decision task with unilateral presentation. In this unilateral version of the task, one written stimulus was presented to either the LVF or RVF in each trial, and participants were required to respond by button press to indicate whether the stimulus was a word or a non-word. Mills et al., Study 1 used a modified version of this task with bilateral presentation. In the bilateral version of the task, two written stimuli were presented simultaneously in each trial, one in the LVF and one in the RVF. A centrally presented arrow indicated the stimulus that the participant was required to respond to. This bilateral version was chosen as it has been recommended by other researchers as being optimal in terms of balancing visual stimulation in the two visual fields and preventing automatic saccades or attentional bias towards the target stimulus (Hunter & Brysbaert, 2008). However, it may have had unanticipated consequences for the N size effect. We will test this possibility in Study 2 by comparing unilateral and bilateral versions of the task within the same participants. Parker’s task and Mills’ Study 1 differed in two further ways. Firstly, Parker’s task had LVF, RVF and central visual field (CVF) conditions, whereas the replication task only had LVF and RVF conditions. In Study 2 we will omit the CVF condition in the unilateral task. We will be able to compare the results of this task with Parker’s original results to see if this change is influential. Secondly, Study 1 employed backward masking after the written stimuli (e.g., +++++ presented to the LVF and RVF) to control the duration of visual stimulation, but Parker’s task did not. In Study 2 we will not change this aspect of the unilateral and bilateral versions of the task, so this possible effect of masking on the N size effect will remain unexplored. 3.3 Stimuli A final difference between Parker et al.’s study and the replication was the choice of written stimuli. Parker et al.’s controlled for lexical frequency only, whereas Mills et al. controlled for bigram frequency and age of acquisition in addition to lexical frequency. Overall, the stimuli had a lower lexical frequency. Furthermore, Mills et al. presented participants with 240 word targets, whereas Parker et al. presented 120 targets. In Study 2 we will use the same stimuli (and number of word targets) for both unilateral and bilateral versions of the task. 3.4 Aims Study 2 will test whether the facilitatory effect of N size in the LVF and the inhibitory effect of N size in the RVF observed by Parker et al are also observed under different conditions: It will test whether Parker’s results can be replicated in right handed participants, using the same unilateral task, but different stimuli (the stimuli from Mills’ Study 1). It will test whether Parker’s results can be replicated in right handed participants, using a bilateral task and stimuli from Mills’ Study 1.

title_r: Replication of the Tipping Point Index (TPI) Study in an Independent Sample.
abstract_r: The current study seeks to replicate Brewin et al., (2021) Tipping Point Index (TPI) study in an independent sample. The results of the original study showed that by answering two simple yes/no questions, the TPI can provide simple and immediate guidance to assist with decisions about whether to seek further assessment or treatment. Simple and valid measures which can highlight when someone may benefit from intervention may help individuals and systems respond to the needs of healthcare workers. By replicating Brewin et al., (2021), this study seeks to establish whether the TPI is a good screener in this new sample and if the same two items are the strongest predictors of depression and anxiety. This study will contribute to the existing findings by Brewin et al., (2021) and enhance the external validity and generalisability of the original findings.

title_r: Victim Blaming Study
abstract_r: In the case of domestic violence and sexual abuse, previous studies have linked victim-blaming with victim's feelings of shame, which increases the risk of developing symptoms of depression or PTSD (Bhuptani et al., 2011; Kennedy & Prock, 2016). Other studies have also shown that the more an individual believes in a just world (that the world is fair and that people get what they deserve), the more likely they are to blame victims of domestic or sexual violence instead of the perpetrator (Valor-Segura, Exposito, & Moya, 2011). Our study is a replication of a study completed in Spain in 2011. Valor-Segura, Exposito, & Moya (2011) investigated the influence of beliefs in sexism and beliefs in a just world on judgments of four different situations of domestic violence. Particularly, the study measured how these beliefs across different situations of domestic violence (situations with different causes) may influence the participant to blame the victim instead of the perpetrator. Our replication of Valor-Segura, Exposito, & Moya’s (2011) study follows a similar method. The participants will read a transcript of a call to a help-line where a woman recounts her recent experience of domestic violence. The participants will then be asked a short number of questions to measure whether or not they blame the victim or the perpetrator. Lastly, we will be measuring individuals' belief in a just-world as well as their level of hostile and benevolent sexism through another set of short questionnaires. The main difference in our replication will be that instead of presenting four different scenarios of domestic violence, we will only be presenting one, therefore we will not be looking at how the cause of the domestic violence situation affects victim-blaming. Additionally, our study will be using a sample of adult participants from Canada. We predict that participants holding greater just world-beliefs and hostile sexist beliefs will present a greater degree of victim blaming. We also predict that male participants will blame the victim more than participants who are female (or identify as another gender). Both predictions are informed by Valor-Segura, Exposito, and Moya’s (2011) results. In short, we predict that the original study will be generalizable to a Canadian population. Overall, our study seeks to gain a better understanding of the ideologies associated with victim-blaming. Additionally, it aims to increase the reliability of the original study’s results and see if the original study’s results can be generalizable to a Canadian population and to 2021.

title_r: Evaluation of the cardiovascular signal detection task (cvSDT): The influence of aroused bodily state and non-interoceptive strategies on sensitivity and response bias
abstract_r: The perception, integration and interpretation of signals from the body takes place on conscious and unconscious levels and is referred to as interoception (Khalsa et al., 2015). Interoceptive accuracy (‘interoceptive sensitivity’) is a dimension of body perception that is measured via objective methods such as heartbeat perception tasks (Garfinkel & Critchley, 2013). In the widely used heartbeat discrimination task, participants are asked to judge whether exteroceptive stimuli are synchronous with their heartbeats or not (Whitehead et al., 1977). According to signal detection theory, sensitivity and response tendency can be calculated. In this task, the measure of response bias represents the general tendency to agree, independent of an under- or overestimation of body sensations. However, the assessment of response bias (liberal to conservative) in the sense of an overestimation of physiological events (e.g., to perceive the heartbeat as faster as it actually is) is relevant for psychopathological investigations. Liberal response biases in that sense appear to be associated with somatic stress disorders and illness anxiety disorder (Wolters et al., 2022). In the novel cardiovascular signal detection task (cvSDT), participants count their heartbeats in trials of 5-13 heartbeats and then decide whether the number of beats counted is within a predetermined range (e.g., 6-8) or not (Pohl et al., 2021). The depicted range is either correct (e.g., 7 heartbeats measured) or false (less heartbeats were measured e.g., 5 or more heartbeats were measured, e.g., 9). In case of less measured heartbeats wrongly agreeing to the interval presents an overestimation of heartbeats, in case of more heartbeats measured erroneously deciding for the interval represents an underestimation of heartbeats. One main goal of this task is to measure the response tendency in terms of an over-/underestimation of heartbeats. Initial studies in our laboratory indicate that the induction of physiological arousal (via arithmetic tasks) leads to an overestimation of heartbeats and that this can be measured with the response bias c in the cvSDT. At rest, however, the cvSDT appears to capture the general tendency to agree (i.e., choose the answer “right [the interval is correct]”). However, empirical evidence for this assumption is still lacking. The primary aim of this research project is to evaluate methodological validity of the cvSDT. We are interested in gaining more insight into the cvSDT response bias via a comparison with the Whitehead task response bias using different conditions (rest/arousal). Additionally, we aim to replicate previous results on the relationship between sensitivity and bias of the cvSDT and the heartbeat perception score of the Heartbeat Counting Task (Schandry, 1981). We plan to examine, whether non-interoceptive strategies (time estimation, knowledge about HR, self-reported attention) are confounded with cvSDT indices. By simulating 'perfect perception', we want to generate norms (i.e., cut-off values) to separate perceivers from non-perceivers. For this, participants are asked to actively measure their pulse during a second cvSDT performance.

title_r: Fork of Wealth and Happiness: Replication of Diener, E., Ng, W., Harter, J., & Arora, R. (2010) at University of Vienna.
abstract_r: General Information: This fork is part of the Direct+Plus CREP replication (https://osf.io/px0sw/) of a study by Diener et al. (2010). Every student manages a fork of the official replication OSF page as a part of a seminar at the Department of Occupational, Economic and Social Psychology, led by Andre Julian Hartmann and Martin Müller (both graduate students) at the University of Vienna (Austria). Materials: All materials are developed together with the students during the seminar and will be added to the project before starting data collection. In addition to the items of the original study, items for further research questions will be added as a direct+ replication. We also participate in the Direct+Plus project by Jordan Wagge containing two questions that deal with financial security. Procedure: All students are using the same survey, advertising materials, and OSF page since this is an online study. Every student will sample N = 10 (total targeted sample: N = 270) students living in Vienna within their social circle. Original Abstract: The Gallup World Poll, the first representative sample of planet Earth, was used to explore the reasons why happiness is associated with higher income, including the meeting of basic needs, fulfillment of psychological needs, increasing satisfaction with one's standard of living, and public goods. Across the globe, the association of log income with subjective well-being was linear but convex with raw income, indicating the declining marginal effects of income on subjective well-being. Income was a moderately strong predictor of life evaluation but a much weaker predictor of positive and negative feelings. Possessing luxury conveniences and satisfaction with standard of living were also strong predictors of life evaluation. Although the meeting of basic and psychological needs mediated the effects of income on life evaluation to some degree, the strongest mediation was provided by standard of living and ownership of conveniences. In contrast, feelings were most associated with the fulfillment of psychological needs: learning, autonomy, using one's skills, respect, and the ability to count on others in an emergency. Thus, two separate types of prosperity—economic and social psychological—best predict different types of well-being.

title_r: Social Distance and Preference for Visual and Verbal Mediums in Interpersonal Communication: A Conceptual Replication of Amit et al. (2013, Experiment 2)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The present study aims to conduct a conceptual replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope’s (2013, Experiment 2) study, which explored the effect of social (psychological) distance on peoples’ medium preferences for interpersonal communication. The results showed that participants preferred mediums dominated by pictures for socially ‘close’ targets and mediums dominated by words for socially ‘distant’ targets. These findings support construal level theory (Trope & Liberman, 2010) which propose that people use more abstract representations when mentalizing targets that are more psychologically distant. The current study will conduct a conceptual replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope (2013, Experiment 2) to assess the robustness of the original conclusions by using a set of new pretested experimental materials.

title_r: Investigating the influence of joint attention on maintenance in working memory: a virtual reality EEG research project.
abstract_r: A joint focus of attention between two individuals can influence the way that observers attend, encode and value items. We have previously found that this joint attention can affect working memory for looked at objects both using 2D face stimuli (pictures) and virtual humans in immersive VR. In VR we also found a similar effect with a non-social stick cue that made a similar movement to the avatar’s head movement. We also previously found that the neurological effects, investigated by looking at alpha and theta power, differ between the social and non social cues, despite similar behavioural effects. In our previous studies we looked at the effect of the cues during encoding of working memory representations (pre-cuing). In the current project we will investigate the effect of cues during the maintenance interval meaning that the cue moves after the objects have left the scene and before memory is being probed (retro-cuing). Previous research (Nie, Ding, Chen, & Conci, 2018) has revealed an advantage in memory performance for items that have been validly socially cued during memory maintenance compared to invalidly cued items (the retro-cueing effect). Here we aim to replicate this effect using a realistic immersive VR setup to test the ecological validity of this effect. Participants will be required to remember 4 objects, 2 presented on the left and 2 on the right. The objects appear while the person looks at/ non-social cue points at the participant. Then, the objects disappear and the cue signals towards either the left or right location. This is followed by a blank maintenance interval, after which a probe object is shown. The probe could either be 1. an object that was previously present in the looked at/ pointed at location (valid), 2. an object that was previously presented in the looked/ pointed away from (invalidly cued) location, 3. an object that was absent from the array. During presentation EEG is recorded in order to investigate the influence of social and non-social cues on decreases and increases in alpha and theta during engagement (eye contact/ pointing), encoding, memory maintenance and memory retrieval.

title_r: Revisiting the Moral Forecasting Error
abstract_r: Predictions about the future are often inaccurate, but the direction of prediction errors may vary. Contrary to research on the intention-behavior gap, where people fail to live up to their future ambitions, a study on “moral forecasting” found that people behaved more honestly than they predicted. Since this interesting prediction error has only been identified in a few studies and its direction may seem surprising, psychological science could benefit from a high-powered replication. In Experiment 1, we will conduct a close replication using the original cheating task and a general population sample from the same country as the original study (Canada). By extension, we will also include the “mind-game paradigm” as an established deception-free cheating task to assess task generalizability. If the primary hypothesis is supported, then we propose a second extension in Experiment 2, by examining whether a cognitive debiasing intervention can reduce the moral forecasting error in a general population sample from the US. As a final extension we will also examine the social dimension of lay beliefs, by assessing whether moral forecasts for other people exhibit the same prediction error as moral forecasts for oneself. In the current experiments, the planned sample size will provide 90% power to detect ¼ of the observed effect size from the original study.

title_r: Investigating the inverse relationship between hippocampal and caudate nucleus volume across the lifespan and cognitive health spectrum and extending the investigation to relevant brain regions involved in navigation
abstract_r: Research in the past has highlighted an inverse association between hippocampal and caudate volumes in younger and older adults (Bohbot et al., 2007; Sodums & Bohbot, 2020) with some additional evidence in Alzheimer’s disease (Persson et al., 2018). These observations were interpreted as indicative of competitive interactions between two spatial navigation/memory systems supported by these structures, with the hippocampus underlying place-learning and allocentric navigation (using world-referenced coordinates to navigate) and the caudate nucleus underlying response-learning which is similar to egocentric navigation (using self-reference coordinates to navigate; Ekstrom et al., 2014; Ekstrom et al., 2017; Packard & Mcgaugh, 1996). However, the previous studies analyzing such relationships were based on relatively small sample sizes, had limited investigation of the possibility of this competitive relationship existing with other brain regions, and did not incorporate longitudinal analyses. In addition, one study (Persson et al., 2018) suggested that there may be an initial increase in caudate volume in aging, as a compensatory mechanism for hippocampal atrophy, followed by caudate atrophy during the progression of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Thus, our primary research goals are to a) determine whether we can replicate the inverse association between hippocampal and caudate volume in multiple samples across the lifespan and the AD spectrum; and b) determine whether the inverse association extends to other brain regions in the networks supporting the two navigation/memory systems again across the healthy lifespan and the AD spectrum; and c) examine longitudinal trajectories of the caudate nucleus, hippocampus and their ratio in older adults and across AD spectrum. Full details can be found in the attached preregistration document.

title_r: Category-specific and retrospective memory enhancement effects due to reward: Replication experiment
abstract_r: We initially aimed to investigate category-specific and retrospective memory enhancement due to reward not only for images but also for words and word-image pairs in a previously unexplored associative learning paradigm. However, our efforts to find reward-induced memory enhancement effects in these new paradigms were inconclusive, leading us to doubt the robustness of the reward-conditioning paradigm and overall findings of the [Patil et al. 2017] study. In our follow-up Experiment 2a (currently unpublished and preregistered on https://osf.io/fyt76), we aimed to closely replicate the effect of high-reward on category-specific and retrospective memory enhancement using the same design and stimuli as Experiment 1 in Patil et al. [2017] which tested recognition memory 24-hours after encoding. However, our experiment did not provide reliable evidence for this effect. In a further attempt to shed light on the underlying effect, and corroborate our failed replication attempt, we will now conduct another experiment with the same design as our previous Experiment 2a with higher statistical power. Again, in contrast to laboratory-based experiments in Patil et al. [2017], we will run our study online on Prolific.co. Our results so far call into question the reliability and generalisability of claims that memory can be selectively and retrospectively enhanced due to reward. We believe that our replication efforts including this planned experiment will be important for those studying adaptive episodic memory and the generalisability of behavioural tagging.

title_r: A syntactically controlled sentence corpus for the assessment of computational models of reading
abstract_r: Decades of research have led to many computationally implemented models of eye movement control in reading, which have been critical for the simulation of mental processes underlying reading and the generation of predictions for future research. To this end, various sentence corpora have been developed to evaluate and refine these models. However, extant corpora have all been deficient in their reporting of eye-tracking measures and the variability and difficulty of their grammatical structures. Thus, the present study aims to develop a large corpus of sentences with theoretically important linguistic features. Participants’ eye movements will be recorded while they read these sentences, and they will be tested on the verbal working memory (VWM) capacity and the quality of their lexical representations (lexical quality, LQ) to elucidate how individual differences on these measures influence eye movements. We expect to replicate the findings of previous studies, and that lexical representation quality will generally facilitate the reading of difficult sentences. However, readers with larger verbal working memory may read difficult sentences slower if they require the simultaneous maintenance of multiple possible parses before a correct parse is settled upon. The findings will be beneficial for the future development of computational models of reading that comprehensively simulate all aspects of human reading.

title_r: Differences in the age-varying association of school belonging with socioemotional flourishing among minority and non-minority university students
abstract_r: Purpose: The purpose of the study is to investigate the difference in the age-varying association of school belonging and socioemotional flourishing between minority and non-minority university students. Hypothesis: In line with Parr (2020) it is predicted that sexual and gender minority students along with racial and ethnic minority students will indicate lower levels of school belonging and flourishing. We also predict that younger (18-22 years of age) will show a higher association between school belonging and flourishing, while those aged 22-26 years will have a weakened association with school belonging and flourishing. Justification: The replication crisis, which is especially prevalent in psychology, is an issue where many published studies had not been replicated, and when they were the results did not match the original study. This called into question the scientific practices of these researchers and/or if the study’s results are generalizable beyond the initial sample population used. This study has yet to be replicated, and our replication of this study will either provide support for the conclusions of the study by Parr (2020) or demonstrate alternative explanations for the initial relationship found between socioemotional flourishing and school belonging. This study will help us better understand the difference in the age-varying relationship between socioemotional flourishing and school belonging between minority and non-minority university students, and, therefore, how to best make students of different ages and demographics feel like they belong at their school. Collecting information on participants' ethnicity, gender identity, and sexual orientation is necessary for this study as we are conducting an analysis on the differences in the relationship between flourishing and school belonging between minority and non-minority students, the information on ethnicity is required to determine whether the participant is part of a racial-ethnic minority, the information on gender and sexual orientation are required to determine whether the participant is part of a sexual-gender minority. We will also do further analysis to determine if there are any differences in the relationship between flourishing and school belonging for any specific minority group, which is why we have not asked participants to simply state whether they are part of a minority or non-minority group and are instead asking for specific information on their ethnicity, gender identity, and sexual orientation. By collecting demographic information on sexual orientation and ethnicity/race we are helping universities be able to assess how inclusive the communities within their universities are, and whether current supports in place to support minority groups help them succeed and feel included at the University. Objectives: Obtaining a better understanding of the difference in the age-varying relationship between socioemotional flourishing and school belonging between minority and non-minority university students, and, therefore, how to best make students of different ages and demographics feel like they belong at their school. We also hope to provide support for the generalizability of the Parr 2020 study and partake in good scientific practices through replication. Research Method/Procedures: This study population will be drawn from the general population of undergraduate students at Alberta Universities, restricted to those aged 18-26 years old currently enrolled in a program for the 2020-2021 school year. Comparisson groups will be constructed based on participants' responses to questions surrounding their gender identity, sexual orientation, and racial/ethnic identity. The demographics questions are sourced from the “Healthy Minds Study” from Eisenberg and Lipson (2017-2018). The classification for ethnic-racial classification has been edited to better reflect Canadian demographics, using the classifications exactly as Statistics Canada, Census of Population, 2016. Inclusion criteria for the sexual-gender minority group are those who indicate a sexual orientation of lesbian, gay, bisexual, queer, questioning, or self-identity, as well as those who indicate a gender identity of transgender male/transgender man or transgender female/transgender woman; or discordantly endorse sex at birth and gender identity (e.g., male sex at birth and female gender identity). Participants who endorsed a transgender gender identity and a heterosexual sexual orientation were included in this group. The second subsample will consist of cisgender heterosexual participants and will be composed of those endorsing a heterosexual sexual orientation and endorsing the same sex at birth and gender identity. Participants who identified as transgender and heterosexual were excluded from this group. This subsample will be examined as the non-minority group. The ethnic/racial group comparison also consists of two sub-samples. The first subsample will be composed of those indicating a minority racial/ethnic identity (African American/black; Asian Canadian/Asian, Hispanic/Latino/a; Middle Eastern, Arab, or Arab American; or other). Participants in this group can select more than one race/ethnicity, so this subsample included persons of mixed race/ethnicity (mixed minority races/ethnicities or individuals of mixed minority–white race/ethnicities). The non-Hispanic white subsample will be composed of participants endorsing only a white race/ethnicity and not endorsing any other race/ethnicity. Our analytic comparison groups (ex. racial/ethnic minority and non-Hispanic white) will be independent, while non-comparison groups will have overlapping respondents. For the assessment of school belonging and flourishing, we will be employing the same measures as the Parr 2020 study, as described below. To assess perceived school belonging, four items (“I see myself as a part of the campus community” (Perceived Cohesion Scale)“I fit in well at my school” “Other people understand more than I do about what is going on at my school” (Walton et al. study) “I feel isolated from campus life” (Healthy Minds Study)) will be used, and responses will be one a six-level Likert-type response format. As per the Parr study, items will be coded such that responses sum to a greater endorsement of perceived belonging. Flourishing will be identified using an eight-item Flourishing Scale developed by Deiner et al. in 2010. Responses on the seven-level Likert-type response will be summed to an overall flourishing score, and similar to the school belonging, a higher score is indicative of greater flourishing. The current year of university will also be asked, and respondents will indicate their age, in years, on the survey. Data Analysis Plan: We plan on using the same data analysis technique as Parr (2020). The mgcv package for R Version 3.6.0 will be used. Varying coefficient models (VCMs) will be used to analyze the age-varying relations of interest. Association between school belonging and flourishing will be analyzed using the model, and the variations across august will be able to be examined through this. In alignment with Parr’s (2020) analytic framework, we will use 95% confidence regions to determine statistical significance.
