title_r: Replication of a research claim from Gelfand et al. (2020), from PsyArXiv
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Gelfand et al. is that cultural tightness and government efficiency should combine to predict the infection rate associated with COVID-19, such that the nations that fare the best may have both culturally tight norms and efficient governments. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “Nations with efficient governments and tight cultures have been most effective at limiting COVID-19’s infection rate and mortality likelihood.” The authors predicted that cultural tightness and government efficiency would predict slower growth rates of COVID-19 and lower mortality likelihoods, and that nations with high cultural tightness and high government efficiency would show especially slow growth rate and mortality likelihood. The authors captured infection rate by fitting regression equations for each nation, log-transforming the outcome variable (cases per million people) and the predictor variable (days) to account for the exponential growth rate of the virus. Log-transformation converts exponential growth rates into linear growth rates, which can be predicted in a general linear model. This model found a significant interaction between tightness and efficiency, b = -.17, SE = .07, t(41) = -2.23, p = .031.

title_r: The relation between primacy bias in loudness discrimination and autistic traits
abstract_r: This study aims to investigate whether there is a relation between autistic traits and the primacy effect in the loudness discrimination paradigm (Oberfeld et al., 2018) in a population of typically developed participants. First, we expect to replicate the primacy bias findings of Oberfeld and others in the loudness discrimination paradigm (for an overview of previous studies, see Oberfeld et al., 2018). In this paradigm, participants listen to sounds consisting of equal-duration temporal segments which vary in sound level, and are asked to indicate whether this sound as a whole was loud or soft compared to previous trials ("global loudness judgment"). Previous studies showed that participants are on average more strongly influenced by the sound level of the earlier temporal segments in their loudness estimation than by segments occurring later within the sound (Oberfeld et al., 2018; Oberfeld & Plank, 2011; Ponsot et al., 2016). In other words, the first few temporal segments receive a higher perceptual weight in comparison to later temporal segments when judging the overall loudness of the sound, which can be described as a bias towards using information from the first segments, or a primacy effect. Second, we want to investigate whether there is a relation between the strength of this primacy effect and autistic traits in the typically developed population. It has been suggested that new information is more strongly weighted in autism compared to the typical population (Lawson et al., 2014; Palmer et al., 2017; Van de Cruys et al., 2014), and there is some evidence supporting that individuals with autism are less influenced by initial acoustic environments in an auditory paradigm (Goris et al., 2022). However, other studies have also found that individuals with autism weight recent stimuli less heavily in an auditory pitch discrimination task (Lieder et al., 2019).

title_r: Examination project: Replication of the Deese-Roediger-McDermott Paradigm and False Memory Effect
abstract_r: This study replicates the well-documented Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM) paradigm, examining the false memory effect, which is the tendency to remember non-presented but semantically related words. This phenomenon has broad implications for understanding memory reliability in real-world contexts, such as eyewitness testimony, therapeutic settings, and educational environments (Roediger & McDermott, 1995). Building on findings from prior research, the primary objective is to assess whether a contemporary sample will falsely recognise non-presented words, known as lures, after exposure to semantically related word lists. This is a confirmatory study, as the false memory effect has been well-documented in prior research. By employing the DRM paradigm, this study seeks to contribute to the ongoing discourse on memory's reconstructive nature and the prevalence of false memories across different settings (Loftus & Klemfuss, 2020). Research Question: Will a contemporary sample falsely recognise non-presented words (lures) after being shown semantically related word lists as outlined in the DRM paradigm?

title_r: Multiple Simon effects in horizontal and vertical stimulus arrangements: A replication of Rubichi et al (2004)
abstract_r: Since the seminal paper by Umilta and Liotti (1987), it has been longstanding question whether multiple Simon effects indicative of different reference frames can indeed be observed. Roswarski and Proctor (1996, Exp 3) reported indeed two different Simon effects, one based on the screen position (i.e. global Simon effect) and one based on the relative position within each side of the screen center (i.e. local Simon effect) when stimulus color was task-relevant. Therefore, three vertical lines were shown on the screen in order to subdivide the space on the screen. Rubichi and colleagues (2004, Exp 4) extended this horizontal stimulus setup and presented both, horizontal and vertical lines in order to test whether the simultaneous Simon effects can also be found for horizontal and vertical stimulus arrangements. They found that global and local Simon effects were indeed only evident for the horizontal stimulus arrangements, but not when the different stimulus positions were marked from top to bottom. Importantly, the critical comparison of horizontal and vertical stimulus arrangements involved two different groups of participants. The present study is a conceptual replication of the fourth experiment in the paper of Rubichi and colleagues (2004). Within the same group of participants, both stimulus arrangements involving the three (vertical or horizontal) lines.

title_r: Emotion-Enhanced Source Memory: What Are the Effects of Age and Experimental Setting?
abstract_r: There is robust evidence that our memory is more accurate for emotional compared to neutral stimuli. This so-called emotion-enhanced memory effect (Talmi, 2013) is well established in item memory, that is, memory for central information. For example, when participants are presented with a sequence of emotional versus neutral pictures or words, their recall of the emotional (versus neutral) items is better (Kang et al., 2014; Kensinger & Schacter, 2006). Some studies have established similar effects in source memory, that is, memory for contextual information (Johnson et al., 1993), when using emotional sources (Bell & Buchner, 2010; Smith et al., 2005; Ventura-Bort et al., 2016), but the findings are generally less consistent (see Arnold et al., 2021; Symeonidou & Kuhlmann, 2022 for null results). For example, over a series of experiments, Bell and Buchner (2010) have shown that participants remember socially threatening source information better compared to neutral sources (see Bell & Buchner, 2012 for an overview). Pairing neutral faces with descriptions of cheating (i.e., socially threatening), trustworthy or neutral behavior, the authors repeatedly established that source memory is better for the cheating source descriptions. In an attempt to extend these findings to negative sources more generally, I have conducted an experiment within the scope of a seminar on research methods (“ExPra”) at the University of Mannheim (in the year 2021). Following the basic procedure of Bell and Buchner, we similarly showed neutral faces along with emotional sources to our participants. Different from Bell and Buchner, however, we used inherently (instead of conceptually) emotional sources. More specifically, we paired the neutral faces (=items) with (non-verbal) affective bursts (=sources; e.g., crying or laughter, drawn from the normed database “International Affective Digitized Sounds” [IADS], Bradley & Lang, 2007). Replicating the results of Bell and Buchner, we found better source memory for the negative compared to the positive and neutral sound sources, suggesting a negativity bias in source memory. Building upon this research, the following project aims at investigating whether such emotionality effects in source memory extend to older adults. Furthermore, I plan to examine this research question in an online versus laboratory experimental setting to identify potential differences in effects (of source emotionality and age) across these environments. More details on the planned experiments and the rationale behind them are outlined next. Planned Experiments I am planning to conduct two experiments, which follow a similar procedure as the aforementioned ExPra study. Both planned experiments will focus on whether older adults show similar enhancement effects in source memory. This question is particularly intriguing because older adults have pronounced difficulties in remembering (neutral) sources (Old & Naveh-Benjamin, 2008) but, at the same time, have a stronger preference for emotional (and especially positive) over neutral stimuli compared to younger adults (Carstensen, 2006). Can we reduce older adults’ source memory deficit by using emotional (rather than neutral) sources? Some studies suggest that such a reduction is possible (May et al., 2005; Rahhal et al., 2002), while others (including my own) draw a less optimistic picture (Symeonidou et al., 2022). Different from May et al., however, we have used non-social material and/or item-source-pairs that were not inherently related (e.g., words as items, unrelated scenery pictures as sources) in our studies. Consequently, whether an item was presented in a positive or negative context did not necessarily inform about its socio-emotional relevance. It is thus worthwhile to re-investigate this question with socially relevant and more naturalistic material to better approximate a natural item-source situation. More specifically, in the planned study, participants will see neutral face pictures (=items) paired with positive, negative, or neutral scenery pictures (=source/context). title_r: Visual Transposed word parallel processing
abstract_r: Evidence has supported the idea that readers lexically process words serially (one at a time), but evidence by Mirault et al. (2018) has demonstrated a transposed word effect. This effect is where readers have difficulty deciding that sentences such as “do love you me? “are ungrammatical, in which the transposition of two adjacent words (i.e., love you) would form a grammatical sentence, compared to sentences in which the transposition of two words does not result in grammaticality (e.g. the cat white was slowly). This has been taken as evidence for the parallel lexical processing of multiple words simultaneously. Evidence has also shown that the transposed word effect can be attributed to a combination of noisy bottom-up word position coding and top-down syntactic constraints. This effect can be interpreted within serial, as opposed to parallel, reading models. The present study will examine the transposed word effect by varying type of processing for which each of the two transposed words will be presented. We aim to replicate the previous findings by presenting words presented one word following the previous word in a sentence, as opposed to on word being presented at a time. In this experiment, we manipulate sequence type. Thus, we expected that the transposed word effect in visual parallel paradigm to be replicated such that transposed words are responded to more slowly and are more error prone than control words. However, the main focus is on accuracy. In addition, we aim to compare the results of visual transposed word parallel processing with that of visual transposed word serial processing. This is to assess whether the transposed word effect occurs as a result of the integration of word n+1 may begin before the integration of word n is complete, which may allow the transposed word effect to occur (Huang & Staub, 2021) . As a result, the findings we observed may be more likely to ensue, as there is a higher likelihood that word n would not complete when the integration of word n+1 began when all words are presented in a parallel, as opposed to serial manner. If this is the case, then the transposed word effect should be numerically larger in parallel than serial.

title_r: Distinguishing between retrieval, reactivation and new learning in a memory reconsolidation paradigm.
abstract_r: This study will be a replication of a study by Sevenster et al. (2014). In the original study, it was found that a single prediction error (PE) is necessary to destabilize memories in a memory reconsolidation paradigm. When there is no PE or multiple PE during the reactivation session, the memory does not undergo reconsolidation. In the current study, we aim to replicate these findings. We expect propranolol to be effective at neutralizing the fear response on day 3 only a group of participants whose reactivation session consisted of a single PE. The reinforcement schedule during acquisition, reactivation, extinction and reinstatement will be an exact replication of the previous study. However, in the current study we will make use of different conditioned stimuli. Where Sevenster used fear-relevant spider stimuli, we will use more neutral fractal images since fear of spiders is highly prevalent and excluding participants with a fear of spiders will make the study less feasible. Already a low level of fear could unintentionally affect the physiological responding to the conditioned stimuli (CS). Furthermore, we will analyze the data using Bayesian statistics because it allows us to make use of sequential updating, and it allows us to quantify evidence for the null hypothesis, as the main hypothesis of the study concerns a lack of differential responding between the threat stimulus and the safe stimulus.

title_r: The role of nature versus nurture in the development and plasticity of the somatosensory processing stream
abstract_r: Non-human primate studies have shown that after a major loss of sensory inputs, S1 reorganises such that the deprived area of the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) becomes responsive to touch on intact body parts (Halder et al., 2018; Kambi et al., 2014; Merzenich et al., 1983). This phenomenon of cortical reorganisation has been suggested to have major clinical implications in humans (Jutzeler et al., 2015; Zörner et al., 2014). However, an understanding of the plasticity that underlies S1 reorganisation in humans, which could potentially be exploited to promote adaptive reorganisation and discourage maladaptive reorganisation, is missing. Non-human primate research suggests that cortical reorganisation is driven by brainstem plasticity (Kambi et al., 2014). However, plasticity at the thalamic and brainstem levels of the somatosensory processing stream has not previously been considered in humans, as it is notoriously difficult to investigate brainstem nuclei in vivo and non-invasively In this project, we aim to use recent methodological (f)MRI advancements to address this fundamental gap in knowledge using human congenital amputees as an experimental model. Congenital amputees are individuals born without an arm and/or hand, and therefore, their brains have never been exposed to the sensorimotor experience of the missing hand. Congenital amputees consequently exhibit extensive S1 reorganisation such that their S1 missing hand area is responsive to the stimulation of the residual limb, lips, and/or feet (Hahamy et al., 2017; Root et al., 2021; Stoeckel et al., 2009). As such, they provide a unique model to study 1) the neural mechanisms underlying S1 reorganisation and 2) the importance of early sensory experiences in the development of neural somatosensory processing. Here, we will comprehensively address functional and structural reorganisation in congenital one-handers along the entire human somatosensory processing stream, including the brainstem, a suggested key hub for reorganisation. First, we aim to replicate previous work showing functional cortical reorganisation in the S1 area corresponding to the absent hand. We will further explore whether there is evidence of subcortical reorganisation within the brainstem and thalamus of congenital one-handers and, if so, whether this correlates with the somatotopic mapping observed within S1. Second, utilising quantitative MRI, we will explore whether the amount of ‘remapped’ activity correlates with the local myelin content in the hand nuclei across the somatosensory stream, providing insight into whether sensorimotor experiences are necessary to prevent neural atrophy. Finally, as the remapping of body parts is possibly driven by adaptive behaviours, whereby the body part most used to compensate for the missing limb is remapped into the somatotopic hand area, we will assess compensatory behaviours through video analysis. Here, we hypothesise that the overuse of the intact limbs in amputees will predict cortical remapping in S1. Thereby, this project seeks to provide insight into the role of behaviour in shaping somatosensory processing. More broadly, this work will help define the mechanisms and limits of somatosensory plasticity following sensory deprivation and may inform future therapeutic strategies aimed at enhancing recovery and preventing maladaptive outcomes.

title_r: Mindfulness reduces habitual responding based on implicit knowledge: a replication of Whitmarsh et al. (2013)
abstract_r: Artificial grammar learning, a paradigm of study that examines one’s ability to learn a made-up grammar, is commonly used to investigate implicit learning - the capacity to develop knowledge of regularities without explicit awareness of the regularities. A single study has previously examined the relationship between artificial grammar learning and trait mindfulness - one’s dispositional capacity to nonjudgmentally pay and maintain attention toward the present moment (Brown & Ryan, 2003). Whitmarsh et al. (2013) reported that trait mindfulness, as measured by the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ), was associated with differences in several learning outcomes about the artificial grammar. Subjects underwent five days of testing where they were repeatedly exposed to strings of seemingly random letters (e.g., “MXSSSVR”) that, unbeknownst to them, could conform to a set of rules (i.e., come from an artificial grammar) and that they had to reproduce in a working memory task. At several time points, subjects were also asked to rate whether they liked the strings and only after training were they informed that some of the strings came from an artificial grammar. Because subjects gave ratings prior to being informed that the strings sometimes conformed to a set of rules, these judgments provided a measure of their implicit preference about the artificial grammar. Typically, subjects display a preference (greater liking) for grammatically correct strings. After they had been informed, subjects were then probed on their explicit awareness of the grammar, to determine whether they had knowledge of the rules underlying the grammar. These two measures—one implicit and one explicit—could then be used to assess implicit and explicit learning of the artificial grammar. If subjects showed an implicit preference (a higher number of ‘like’ ratings) for strings that were grammatical, this would suggest they had implicitly learned the artificial grammar. Whitmarsh et al. expected and found a negative correlation between trait mindfulness and implicit preference—subjects higher in trait mindfulness were less likely to develop an implicit ‘liking’ for strings that were grammatical compared with those that were not grammatical, even though trait mindfulness did not correlate with performance on the working memory task itself. Such a finding may seem surprising since it suggests a decreased ability for implicit learning in those with higher trait mindfulness, a construct that is traditionally associated with an increase in general cognitive functions such as attention, learning, and memory (Keng et al., 2011; Mesmer-Magnus et al., 2017). Yet, it may also denote a reduced tendency to automatically judge internal representations (in the case of the grammatical structure), which is thought to be a key component of mindfulness (Brown & Ryan, 2003; Bishop et al., 2004). Indeed, the negative correlation of mindfulness with preference judgements was found to be most strong for the “non-judging of inner experience” subscale of the FFMQ. These findings therefore suggest that, by reducing judgments about experiences, trait mindfulness may reduce preference development. However, a key limitation of the original work is its small sample size (N = 18), which raises the question of whether this result may simply be an artifact of an underpowered study. We will therefore seek to conceptually replicate Whitmarsh et al. (2013) with a larger sample size to assess whether this general set of findings (that is, a negative association between trait mindfulness and implicit/explicit learning in an artificial grammar learning task) holds with greater statistical power. To achieve a larger sample size, the study will be conducted online.

title_r: replication of Sartorius et al., 2016
abstract_r: In this study we aim to replicate one of the key findings from the paper by Sartorius et al. (2016, http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.euroneuro.2015.12.036). This replication is part of the overarching project “Replication of Findings in Neuroimaging – MDD” (ReFiNe-MDD, https://osf.io/n86q9/) using data from various cohorts. The project aims to a) estimate the percentage of replicable findings in the area of brain structural gray matter correlates related to variables relevant for depression, b) identify study characteristics associated with replicability of neuroimaging findings, and c) deduct methodological guidelines to foster replicability of findings in this area of research. Therefore, a minimum of 60 single replications will be conducted. In this individual replication, we will focus on the association of gray matter volume (GMV) changes following electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). ECT, a treatment option for severe and treatment-resistant depression, involves the application of an electrical current through scalp electrodes to induce a controlled seizure. Despite ECT’s clinical efficacy, the underlying neurobiological mechanisms driving its therapeutic effects remain incompletely understood (Oltedal et al., 2018). Neuroimaging studies consistently report ECT-induced increases in GMV, particularly within the medial temporal regions (Kritzer et al., 2023). Sartorius et al. (2016), whose study serves as the foundation for this replication, observed significant volume increases from pre- to post-ECT using voxel-based morphometry (VBM). These volumetric changes were evident both at the whole-brain level and within specific regions of interest, including the hippocampus, amygdala, and, to a lesser extent, the habenula. These findings are in line with the neurogenic theory of depression which suggests that depression impairs neurogenesis, a process potentially restored by ECT. However, the effects of ECT are not confined to the temporal lobe. Clinical studies have identified ECT-associated GMV changes in regions beyond the medial temporal lobe, including the basal ganglia, temporal pole, insula, and anterior cingulate cortex. Furthermore, animal models of electroconvulsive seizures demonstrate that the treatment can also stimulate gliogenesis, angiogenesis, and synaptogenesis in various brain regions (Ousdal et al., 2020). This variability in findings across ECT studies could partly be attributed to differences in data acquisition, image processing methods, and patient characteristics, including clinical and demographic factors (Ousdal et al., 2020). This highlights the importance of replication studies, which enhance the reliability of scientific findings by applying consistent methodologies. Accordingly, the primary objective of this thesis is to replicate the results reported by Sartorius et al. (2016), specifically examining the association between ECT and GMV changes. By adhering closely to the original study’s methods, this replication aims to clarify the robustness of the reported findings and contribute to a more nuanced understanding of ECT’s neurobiological effects.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Liu et al. (2016), from Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Making
abstract_r: We selected the claim that, controlling for creative self-efficacy and prosocial motivation, intrinsic motivation makes a unique contribution to creativity. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “Results from a meta-analysis of 191 independent samples (N = 51,659) documented in the relevant literature revealed that intrinsic motivation, creative self-efficacy, and prosocial motivation each had unique explanatory power in predicting creativity, and that the three motivational mechanisms functioned differently as mediators between contextual and personal factors and creativity.” The claim was tested by meta-analytic structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the unique influence of intrinsic motivation, creative self-efficacy, and prosocial motivation on creativity as well as their mediating effects. This analysis yielded that intrinsic motivation (B = .16, SE = .03, p < .01) was positively related to creativity.

title_r: The Influence of Others' Actions on Perspective Taking (Verbal Responses)
abstract_r: The present experiment is a follow-up study of our previous experiment that investigated how observation of others’ actions affects perspective taking (the link to the preregistration of the previous experiment is https://osf.io/qyf94). The current experiment will use a different method for registering participants’ responses. We will measure the reaction times and accuracy rates of participants’ verbal responses. In the previous study, participants responded by pressing keys on the keyboard presented in two different layouts. The response time analyses showed significant spatial key compatibility effects that made it harder to analyze the effects of action observation in perspective taking. Therefore, we aim to investigate this effect without the variance in the data that comes from using key responses that have spatial mapping. In addition, some researchers note that the pattern of increased reaction times with the increased angular disparity between the participant and the model in perspective taking tasks could be resulting from different spatial key compatibility effects (May & Wendt, 2013). Therefore, it is important to see if this pattern in the data could be also reliably found when not using a response method that has any spatial compatibility with stimuli. Kessler and Rutherford (2010) have shown that the increase of reaction times with angular disparity is persistent when using verbal responses. We aim to replicate these findings.

title_r: The trajectory of object feature forgetting
abstract_r: The long-term memory representations of objects and their features such as the exemplar, state, and colour are thought to fragment as a function of forgetting (Brady, Konkle, Alvarez, & Oliva, 2013; Utochkin, & Brady, 2020). For example, the state and colour of an object tend to be forgotten at different rates, and the successful retrieval of one feature (e.g., exemplar) no longer predicts the retrieval of another (e.g., state) after a delay (Brady et al., 2013; but see Balaban, Assaf, Arad Meir, & Luria, 2019). Additionally, the precision with which the spatial context and colour of objects are retrieved varies; the retrieval of the gist of one feature is dependent on another but the resolution with which each feature is retrieved is somewhat independent (Cooper, & Ritchey, 2019). Taken together, these findings suggest that different features tend to be forgotten independently over time and precise perceptual features objects may not be bound within the same representation. The behavioural findings described above can be explained if we consider that the neocortical representations supporting the memory of objects and their perceptual features (i.e., shape and colour) are overlapping and distributed in nature. Therefore, a memory of an object may be susceptible to feature-specific interference by encountering new objects sharing that feature (e.g., Sun et al., 2017). In addition, the replay of recent memories during consolidation (whilst awake and during sleep) may consistently favour those features closest to the semantic meaning of the object (i.e., the category), whilst neglecting to reactivate more specific or idiosyncratic perceptual details (Yassa & Reagh, 2013; Lifanov et al., 2020). Based on a representational view where object memories are supported by the perirhinal cortex and perceptual features are supported by visual cortical areas, with interference and reactivation affecting these memories, it could indeed be expected that different perceptual features may follow an independent course of forgetting (Andermane, Joensen, & Horner, 2021). In three recent experiments, we set out to confirm whether object memories (encoded as part of an episodic event) tend to fragment or remain holistic. Participants encoded episodic events by studying images of objects, famous people and locations, and were instructed to use mental imagery to create associations between the elements. We later tested participants’ memories on the features (i.e., state and colour) of the objects they learned. Using this method, in Experiment 1 we replicated the pattern of feature fragmentation seen for object memories (Brady et al., 2013), where retrieval dependency decreased from an immediate test to a 3-day delay. However, in Experiment 2, we found that retrieval dependency did not decrease from 1 hour after encoding to a 2-day delay. Together these findings suggest that the extent to which the representations fragment depends on the time points used to test object memory. Our results suggest that object feature representations may fragment rapidly (in the first few hours). However, object representations that are retained after this initial period of fragmentation may remain holistic. Thus, assessing retrieval dependency immediately after encoding and after a long delay (2 days) should reveal the full extent of object fragmentation (as observed in Experiment 1). Assessing retrieval dependency immediately after encoding and after a few hours (e.g., 5 hours) should reveal the rapid fragmentation of object representations. The present experiment will use a within-samples design; all participants will encode events consisting of an object, location, and person, and will be tested on their object memory immediately after encoding (T1), 5h later (T2), and 2 days later (T3). Different objects will be tested at each time point and we will assess memory for two object features; state (e.g., a jar that is open or closed) and colour (e.g., a blue or a pink jar). We chose T2 to be 5hs based on data from a pilot study in which we observed substantial object feature fragmentation 5h after encoding. Additionally, T3 was selected because we found testing object memory after 2 days resulted in mostly above-chance performance with fewer participant exclusions due to below-chance performance, relative to a 3-day delay. We predict that when encoding objects as part of an event, there will be an overall fragmentation of object features (as indexed by a decrease in dependency from T1 to T3). If fragmentation occurs rapidly, then we should also see a decrease in dependency from T1 to T2, with little difference between T2 and T3. We will also administer the self-report Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) (Marks, 1973) and the Object-Spatial Imagery Questionnaire (OSIQ) (Blajenkova, Kozhevnikov, & Motes, 2006), to further explore how individual differences in mental imagery relate to object memory. We previously found that for objects specifically (but not events) retrieval confidence at delay and the loss of confidence with forgetting was predicted by participants’ vividness of mental imagery (measured by VVIQ). Previous research has shown that object (but not spatial) memory and its level of detail is related to self-reported visual imagery (Bainbridge et al., 2019). Additionally, Bainbridge et al. found the VVIQ correlated with the object imagery component from OSIQ, but not spatial imagery. Thus, it is possible that the subjective experience of visual imagery probed by VVIQ (i.e., imagining friends and familiar places) is primarily supported by the accessibility of object representations and metacognitive insight about this accessibility. Therefore, in line with our previous findings, we expect a positive correlation between the reported vividness of imagery (VVIQ and object OSIQ subscale) and object retrieval confidence at T3, and a negative correlation between imagery and confidence loss (T1-T3).

title_r: The Effect of Context Reinstatement on the Deese/Roediger-McDermott (DRM) False Memory Task after Explicit Pre-test Warning
abstract_r: To study context effects on memory, Doss et al. (2018) superimposed a number of objects (e.g., ping-pong paddle, hammer, shovel) on various photos that served as background context. A context reinstatement effect in memory was found, such that reinstatement of the background scenes at test significantly increased correct recognition of objects (targets). However, the reinstated context also increased false recognition (false alarms) of objects that were not actually studied during the encoding phase but only resembled the targets (lures). Subsequent study replicated these findings (Doss et al., 2020). In a recent unpublished experiment, we extended the context reinstatement illusion reported by Doss to the Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM) task. Based on Doss et al., we hypothesized that the context illusion is driven by the retrieval of conceptual associations between objects and the contexts, which causes an illusory sense of memory when the object is similar to a studied object (e.g., making the lure feel more familiar or fluent, and/or triggering recollections of associations that would suggest the lure was earlier studied). If this hypothesis is true, then the illusion should generalize to conceptually related word lists such as those used in DRM. The DRM paradigm has been extensively used in cognitive psychology to study recalls and recognitions of items (e.g., sweet) that are semantically related to the studied items (e.g., sour, candy, sugar, bitter) but are not actually present during the encoding (i.e., false recall, false recognition) (Stadler et al., 1999). Consistent with our predictions, we found a context reinstatement effect on both true recognition of list items (targets) and false recognition of lures strongly associated with the list items (i.e., critical lures), as well as lures more weakly associated with list items (weak lures). These results were predicted by the conceptual associations hypothesis, and they cannot be explained by perceptual similarity. We also collected "remember/know" ("familiar/recollect") data and analyzed it using the Remember/Know procedure (IRK) that allows to account for potential underestimation of "familiar" judgments (Scimeca et al., 2011; for IRK procedure for remember/know judgments, see Yonelinas & Jacoby, 1995). We reasoned that it was likely that participants would spontaneously retrieve conceptual associations between items and background scenes (Aminoff et al., 2008). As such, we predicted that context reinstatement would be accompanied by increased "recollect" judgments for targets and lures, and it was. We were unsure if context reinstatement would also boost familiarity estimates, but it did, which is consistent with the idea that retrieving associations can make things feel familiar and also that context reinstatement might increase processing fluency in a more implicit sense. We will not include this judgment in the current study, because our goal is to further encourage participants to only endorse a test item when they are confident that they recollect it (and not use familiarity-based guessing). While this initial experiment was not pre-registered, the goal of the current pre-registered study is to replicate the previous experiment under conditions that should further encourage participants to more carefully monitoring of memory accuracy. If we were to replicate our initial results under these conditions, it would bolster the conclusion that the context reinstatement effect on the DRM task is driven by a context-biasing of memory that is difficult to avoid. Experiment 2 aspires to expand the outcomes of Experiment 1 with two major modifications, each designed to increase memory monitoring accuracy. The first alteration serves to make the encoding task more item-specific. In Experiment 1 participants were instructed to fit DRM lists into the scene which could induce list-level processing of the studied lists. In Experiment 2 participants are invited to link each presented DRM item with the scene encouraging item-level processing. A stronger pre-test warning is the second modification incorporated in Experiment 2, in which participants are explicitly instructed about the distortion memory effects of DRM list items. In summation, the current experiment strives to replicate the context reinstatement effect on target items and critical lures under encoding and retrieval conditions that more strongly encourage memory monitoring.

title_r: Is UWLS Really Better? A Replication and Pre-Registered Robustness Check of Stanley et al., Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (2023)”
abstract_r: In a recent paper, Stanley et al. (2023) collected 67,308 meta-analyses from the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR). They used these datasets to estimate three models: fixed effect (FE), random effects (RE), and a third estimator that is a variant of FE they call UWLS, for unrestricted weighted least squares. Their primary interest lay in comparing UWLS with RE. Using both BIC and AIC values, they found that UWLS was favored over RE in the great majority of cases. They obtained similar results comparing UWLS to FE. They concluded that UWLS "represents medical research better" than RE and FE. This study makes two changes to Stanley et al. (2023)'s analysis to determine if their conclusion is robust. First, it adds another estimator to the choice set. To Stanley et al. (2023)'s three estimators -- FE, RE, and UWLS -- we add a RE version of UWLS. Second, it simulates representative data sets from Stanley et al. (2023)’s meta-analysis sample and compares estimator performance on the basis of Bias, Mean Squared Error (MSE), and Coverage Rates (CR). The objective of our study is to determine if the UWLS estimator continues to outperform other estimators after making these two changes.

title_r: The influence of multi-face emotion variability on social evaluation
abstract_r: A previous study found that people made more positive evaluations for the faces on several social dimensions (e.g., authenticity, happiness, and trust) when the faces showed higher emotional variability (i.e., larger range or larger number of emotion types) relative to lower emotional variability (i.e., smaller range or smaller number of emotion types), because they perceived more authenticity in high emotional variability (Slepian & Carr, 2019). Our pilot experiment, on the other hand, showed that faces with low emotional variability were given more positive ratings compared to high emotional variability, contrary to Slepian & Carr (2019). However, there were extreme emotions in the high-variability condition in the pilot. Therefore, in this current study, in order to further clarify the effect of emotional variability on social ratings for faces, we plan to replicate our previous experiment while controlling for the presence of extreme emotions in both low- and high-variability conditions.

title_r: The effect of prompts on the sharing of news headlines in social media: a pre-registered replication study of Capraro and Celadin (2023).
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Misinformation, such as fake news and conspiracy theories, is contaminated among information on the internet. Specifically, research has found that 40% of information in the medical domain from the internet has been found to be misinformation (Waszak et al., 2018).
Today, various studies are being conducted to help prevent the spread of such misinformation. For example, increasing the sharing of accurate information by having people assess the accuracy of another article before a sharing task (Pennycook et al., 2020) or giving simple online literacy tips can reduce the sharing of misinformation (Epstein et al., 2021). Such methods of manipulating sharing on SNSs have been demonstrated.
However, while misinformation can be reduced, it is challenging to encourage the sharing of correct information. Capraro and Celadin (2023) found that adding a short sentence (prompt) to the 'share' option presented in the sharing task increased the sharing of correct information and reduced the sharing of misinformation. However, the participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk, resulting in a biased sample. Therefore, to confirm the generalizability of Capraro and Celadin’s (2023) findings, the present study will conduct a replication study using a different sample to examine the viability of a method that promotes sharing of correct information and reduces the sharing of misinformation.

title_r: Replication of De Vries et al. (2015) - Perceptions of greenwashing
abstract_r: The project aims to conduct a close replication of Experiment 2 in de Vries et al. (2015): “Sustainability or profitability? How communicated motives for environmental policy affect public perceptions of corporate greenwashing”, published in Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management. The original study investigated perceived greenwashing when an oil and gas company invested in an environmental measure. The study showed that when the company communicated that the investment was made for environmental reasons, people perceived more greenwashing than when a profit motive was communicated. In this study, we will replicate the original study (i.e., compare greenwashing perceptions when environmental and profit motives are communicated), and will also include several extensions: (1) a mixed-motive condition where the company communicates both environmental and profit motives; (2) an alternative scenario where the company investing in an environmental measure is a construction company rather than an oil company; (3) individual difference measures of attitudes to corporate social responsibility and beliefs about climate change.

title_r: Intervening on RBC Storage Time using Real-World Data from the REDS-III Cohort
abstract_r: This is an observational quasi-experimental study using a target trials emulations approach to estimate the comparative effectiveness of transfusion patients with exclusively fresher red blood cell units (RBCs) vs exclusively older RBCs. We recently published the study “Intervening on the storage time of RBC units and its effect on adverse recipient outcomes using real-world data”. Here, we used a causal inference methodology to emulate several randomized controlled trials determining the adverse effects of the storage time of RBC units in a Danish population. Our findings suggest that transfusing exclusively older RBC units stored for more than 1 or 2 weeks increases the 28-day recipient mortality. Here, we replicate a similar analyses in the REDS-III cohort to determine if the adverse effects of storage can also be observed in an American cohort.

title_r: The effect of the older siblings and postnatal maternal stress on language development
abstract_r: It has previously been shown that having an older sibling may influence language skills, with children who do not have an older sibling showing greater language scores compared to children with one older sibling (Havron et al., 2019). Closer looks at the characteristics of older siblings such as age gap and sex demonstrated an effect of older sibling’s sex. Specifically, children who had an older sister had better language scores than children who had an older brother with their language score not differing from language scores of children with no older sibling (Havron et al., 2019). In our replication study (Study 1, https://osf.io/d73yv/?view_only=a4c8f42625a84d38a23664bb8cb9e0c1) with the GUSTO cohort of children from Singapore, we replicated the finding from the EDEN cohort study (Havron et al., 2019), thus demonstrating better language skills in children with no older sibling compared to children with one older sibling. Unlike in the EDEN study, we have not replicated the effect of older sibling’s sex on children language skills. In this study, we are conducting a follow-up of our replication study by assessing the effects of other factors that may influence the language skills in our GUSTO cohort. One of the reasons proposed by Havron et al (2019) for the effect of sibling sex is maternal stress. The logic behind this claim is that maternal stress is related to poorer language scores (King & Laplante, 2005; Laplante, Brunet, Schmitz, Ciampi, & King, 2008; Laplante et al., 2004) and it has been found that raising a female baby is related to less maternal stress in comparison to raising a male baby (e.g., Scher & Sharabany, 2010). In order to investigate this possibility, as a first step in our follow-up study, we will assess the effect of maternal stress and the presence of an older sibling on language skills. Next, we will examine the effect of maternal stress and the older sibling’s sex on language skills. We explore the effects of maternal stress and older siblings on language skills in the above-mentioned GUSTO cohort. In this cohort, language measures were administered in four different languages (English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay, and Tamil) depending on the participants’ native language.

title_r: The Mere Urgency Effect: A study of decision process
abstract_r: In the modern world, people are frequently confronted with decisions about how to allocate their limited time and attention between tasks that vary in their degree of urgency and importance. In recent years, research has shown that people display a mere urgency effect (MUE) (original paper by Zhu et al., 2018). That is, they often choose to pursue urgent tasks irrespective of their material benefits. Zhu et al. (2018) suggest that the MUE operates through an attention-based psychological mechanism. Specifically, when individuals perceive a task as urgent, their attention shifts from the magnitude of potential payoffs to the time frames, which can lead to suboptimal decision-making behaviour. In both Zhu et al. (2018) and our replication efforts (forthcoming), attention was assessed via participants' self-reported attentional focus on two experimental questions concerning bonus amounts and expiration times (on a scale from 1 to 8). A potential concern with these measures is their reliance on participants' subjective perceptions of their attentional recall. A process measure of attention, such as mouse-tracking, could offer a more convincing demonstration of the attention-based psychological-account as the mechanism underpinning behaviour. Consequently, in this supplementary replication, we intend to incorporate a mouse-tracking experiment (akin to MouselabWEB, initially designed by Willemsen & Johnson (2011)) into Qualtrics through HTML editors, devised to examine the information acquisition behaviour underpinning decision-making. In the experiment, participants reveal information about their attention on bonus amounts and availability through time spent examining each attribute. This data will subsequently be analysed to understand how individuals allocate attention to various facets of the decision problem, the sequence in which they process information, and the overall strategies they employ during decision-making. The primary advantage of this method is its capacity to provide real-time, objective measures of attention allocation and information processing, affording us insight into the cognitive processes that underlie decision-making with respect to the MUE.

title_r: Learning to rapidly disengage from fear-conditioned stimuli.
abstract_r: Previous research has indicated that threat-related stimuli can capture attention automatically, suggesting attentional bias to the threat (Mulckhuyse & Dalmaijer, 2016). However, recent studies demonstrated that this bias can be reduced through statistical learning (e.g., Kim & Anderson, 2021; Theeuwes et al., 2025). For example, in Theeuwes et al. (2025), participants learned the high frequent distractor location, where one of the distractor colors was associated with shock threat. Their findings revealed both threat attentional bias effect and as a result of implicit learning a spatial suppression effect: The threat-related distractor not only captured more attention but was also suppressed when it appeared at the high frequent distractor location (Theeuwes et al., 2025). As the learning of high frequent distractor location has been suggested to reflect a pro-active suppression process (Huang et al., 2023), it is possible that suppressing the threat stimuli occurs proactively. Note that threat attentional bias has been suggested to include fast engagement and slow disengagement. Previous studies have mostly focused on the fast engagement component of attention (Kim & Anderson, 2021; Theeuwes et al., 2025) and less on delayed disengagement. Our previous experiments suggested another type of statistical learning, where the target and distractor are spatially associated. In our experiments, if the distractor is presented at a specific location in trials n, the target in trial n+1 will always be presented at another specific location (associated trials). Our behavioral experiment first demonstrated this learning effect, evidenced by faster reaction time on associated trials compared to non-associated trials. Furthermore, our follow up eye-tracking experiment indicated that this facilitation effect reflected a target location enhancement, evidenced by less capture trials between associated and non-associated conditions, while dwell time on the distractor was shorter in associated trials. Our findings suggest that participants were able to rapidly disengage from the distractor and re-direct their attention and gaze to its associated target location. In the current study, we will investigate whether this reactive attentional facilitation can be alearned for threat-related stimuli. Two eye-tracking experiments will be conducted. For the first experiment, the spatial association between target and distractor will be same for both threat and safe distractors; while for the second experiment, the spatial association will be different for threat and safe distractors. We expect to replicate previous research (e.g., Kim & Anderson, 2021; Theeuwes et al., 2025), suggesting that participants can also rapidly disengage from threat stimuli. To conclude this, we expect to observe both threat attentional bias effect and a learning effect, while no interaction between them.

In our experiments, if the distractor is presented at a specific location in trials n, the target in trial n+1 will always be presented at another specific location (associated trials). Our behavioral experiment first demonstrated this learning effect, evidenced by faster reaction time on associated trials compared to non-associated trials. Furthermore, our follow up eye-tracking experiment indicated that this facilitation effect reflected a target location enhancement, evidenced by less capture trials between associated and non-associated conditions, while dwell time on the distractor was shorter in associated trials. Our findings suggest that participants were able to rapidly disengage from the distractor and re-direct their attention and gaze to its associated target location. In the current study, we will investigate whether this reactive attentional facilitation can be alearned for threat-related stimuli. Two eye-tracking experiments will be conducted. For the first experiment, the spatial association between target and distractor will be same for both threat and safe distractors; while for the second experiment, the spatial association will be different for threat and safe distractors. We expect to replicate previous research (e.g., Kim & Anderson, 2021; Theeuwes et al., 2025), suggesting that participants can also rapidly disengage from threat stimuli. To conclude this, we expect to observe both threat attentional bias effect and a learning effect, while no interaction between them.

title_r: Climate feelings, climate action and well-being
abstract_r: The aim of the planned survey is a conceptual replication and extension of the study "From anger to action: Differential impacts of eco-anxiety, eco-depression, and eco-anger on climate action and wellbeing" by Stanley et al. (2021). Stanley et al. looked at the effects of the climate crisis on mental health, climate feelings and individual and collective action of the participants. They also investigated the effects of those climate feelings on the other two areas. In the context of this survey, climate anger was the only one of the three feelings surveyed that proved to be adaptive in the broader sense: in contrast to climate anxiety and climate depression, climate anger led to more action and better mental health. The planned replication study has several objectives. Firstly, the study aims to show whether a survey in Germany would produce similar results to the original study in Australia. Furthermore, the data collected in 2020 will be replicated in 2024. In addition, some items will be added to the survey in this study to enable a more differentiated survey, as recommended also by the first author of the study, Dr. Samantha Stanley. In addition, this study aims to expand the consideration of the relationships between eco-feelings, mental health and action: Thus, the correlation between eco-feelings and action will also be considered, taking mental health into account, in order to control for this influence. In addition, the connection between action and subjective well-being will also be examined. As in the original study, the survey will be conducted using a questionnaire that is completed online. The items of the questionnaire are centrally based on those of the original study, but, as already mentioned, are partially supplemented. The survey of climate emotions was not based on a specific query of the individual feelings on a scale as in the original, but instead three scales from the Inventory of Climate Emotions (Marczak et al., 2023) were used. The items for recording personal and collective action were also adapted to enable a more differentiated survey of these constructs.

title_r: Examining the age-related hyper-binding effect using a word 1-back task.
abstract_r: Inhibitory control decline is a marked feature of ageing. Older adults exhibit an increased susceptibility to binding target information with irrelevant distractors that spatially co-occur (Campbell et al., 2012), an effect known as hyper-binding. Increased distractibility has shown to both hinder and facilitate memory performance (Campbell et al., 2010). This suggests that memory decline in ageing cannot be captured simply by a deficit in binding separate memory units into a cohesive memory episode (Naveh-Benjamin, 2000). Previous studies have demonstrated hyper-binding between target pictures and distracting words, whereas here we aim to replicate the effect when distractors are pictures of famous faces and places, in anticipation of a future fMRI study where picture category can be used to examine neural representations of distractors. We also introduce a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) test to assess whether the costs and benefits of hyper-binding are observed when one only has to remember the category of the distractor (in which case, this simpler task can be used with fMRI).

title_r: Visual perception of color and its representation in language comprehension.
abstract_r: Theories on embodied cognition claim that mentally representing a particular property of an object activates its corresponding neural subsystem (Barsalou, 1999). Researchers applied the embodied representations of concepts to visual properties such as object’s orientation and shape in a sentence-picture verification task. The results have shown that when the pictures matched the orientation and shape implied by the sentence, the responses given by participants were faster than in the mismatch condition(Stanfield & Zwaan, 2001; Zwaan et al., 2002). The outcome of these studies suggests that all examined objects’ properties are represented in the same way. However, according to Connell (2007), colour is represented differently to shape and orientation as shown by the mismatch advantage in the sentence-picture verification task. Connell claims, that mismatch facilitation is the result of stable versus unstable embodied representations. These results are contrary to those obtained by Zwaan and Pecher (2012) in a series of replication studies in which the match facilitation was shown. The current study aims to resolve the discrepancy in the literature by replicating the original study (study by Connell, 2007). The experimental task will remain the same but the stimuli have been changed. We used the real-life pictures in our stimuli set and aimed to decrease the variability among the pictures and sentences.

title_r: Is the '1-in-X' bias affected by outcome severity? Follow-Up Study
abstract_r: There are two known cognitive biases that impact the perception of medical likelihood. The first is the ‘1-in-X’ bias whereby a person will consider the likelihood expressed by a ‘1-in-X’ ratio (e.g., 1 in 7) to be more probable than a likelihood expressed by a ‘N-in-X*N’ ratio (e.g., 10 in 70; Sirota & Juanchich, 2019), despite their probabilities being identical (Pighin et al., 2011). The second is the severity bias, whereby severe medical outcomes will be judged as more likely to happen compared to non-severe outcomes (e.g., possible insomnia vs. possible deafness; Bonnefon & Villejoubert, 2006). We recently ran an experiment to understand if the two biases interact. The study presented participants with a hypothetical scenario asking them to imagine that they are planning a trip abroad. Their doctor tells them about the possibility of contracting a disease whilst on this trip. The scenario was manipulated in two ways. The ratio format presented the possibility as a ‘1-in-X’ ratio or a ‘N-in-X*N’ ratio. The severity of the disease was also manipulated, as participants faced the possibility of contracting a low severity disease (Lyme Disease) or a high severity disease (Ebola). Participants were asked to estimate their chances of contracting the disease, and then indicated (Yes or No) whether they would accept a safe vaccine against the disease. We successfully replicated both biases and their effects on the perception of medical likelihood. However, the findings for our vaccine choice measure were not as expected. A severe disease was associated with a higher uptake of vaccine, but surprisingly, there was no association between ratio format (1-in-X vs. N-in-X*N) and vaccine uptake. We think that the lack of finding for vaccine choice can be explained by our methodology. That is, the vaccine is considered to be ‘safe’, and was therefore accepted by an overwhelming majority of participants (93%). We believe this has eliminated the relevance of the ratio format, because if, for example, you are under a 1-in-6 chance of catching a disease, you are no longer under that same risk if you have been vaccinated. In this study we will collect follow-up data, and we will use a new scenario that addresses the above limitation. Adapting a vignette used by Sirota and Juanchich (2019), participants will imagine that they have recently developed reactive arthritis and are unable to take ibuprofen to manage the pain. They are offered a steroid treatment (prednisolone) which comes with risk of a side effect. As in our original experiment, we will manipulate severity and ratio format. The potential side effect will be either low or high in severity (mild vs. severe acne), and the chance of getting the side effect will be expressed as either a ‘1-in-X’ or a ‘N-in-X*N’ ratio (1 in 6 vs. 7 in 42). Participants will then be asked if they would accept the treatment considering their chances of developing the side effect (Yes/No).

title_r: Visual Transposed word crossmodal parallel processing
abstract_r: Evidence has supported the idea that readers lexically process words serially (one at a time), but evidence by Mirault et al. (2018) has demonstrated a transposed word effect. This effect is where readers have difficulty deciding that sentences such as “do love you me? “are ungrammatical, in which the transposition of two adjacent words (i.e., love you) would form a grammatical sentence, compared to sentences in which the transposition of two words does not result in grammaticality (e.g. the cat white was slowly). This has been taken as evidence for the parallel lexical processing of multiple words simultaneously. Evidence has also shown that the transposed word effect can be attributed to a combination of noisy bottom-up word position coding and top-down syntactic constraints. This effect can be interpreted within serial, as opposed to parallel, reading models. The present study will examine the transposed word effect by varying modality input and type of processing for which each of the two transposed words will be presented. However, we aim to replicate the previous findings in students and assess this with different input modalities (auditory and crossmodal) and different processing strategies (visual transposed word parallel, crossmodal transposed word serial and crossmodal transposed word parallel). In this experiment, we manipulate sequence type and experiment. Thus, we expected that the transposed word effect in the crossmodal transposed word parallel processing should be replicated (such that transposed words are responded to more slowly and are more error prone than control words). The main focus is on accuracy. Huang and Staub (2021) argued that the integration of word n+1 may begin before the integration of word n is complete, which may allow the transposed word effect to occur. As a result, the findings we observed may be more likely to ensue, as there is a higher likelihood that word n would be completed when the integration of word n+1 began when all words were presented and heard, the transposed word effect should be smaller or not present in crossmodal serial relative to visual transposed word serial and parallel processing and auditory transposed word tasks.

title_r: Identity & Moral Expansiveness
abstract_r: This study aims to develop a new scale for measuring key aspects of identity. Existing measures of identity do not include a wide range of entities that are considered together in relation to a person's sense of self. Our study’s chief aim is to (1) test the reliability and validity of the sense of self scale (2) map the normative patterns of how entities are considered in relation to people’s sense of self (3) explore how identity expansiveness varies as a function of demographic characteristics (age, gender, socioeconomic status, and political conservatism) (4) compare identity expansiveness with moral expansiveness. A person’s sense of self, their identity, is affected by the environments in which they live (Dixon & Durrheim, 2000), and the people (Ellemers et al., 1999; Tajfel & Turner, 1979; Tajfel, 1981), animals (Amiot et al., 2019; Dhont et al., 2019), and objects (Belk, 2016; Belk, 1988; Miller, 2010) that they interact with in them. Seeing some things rather than others as forming part of a person’s identity may be important for understanding how people relate to others in terms of moral concern and helping behaviours. Research on how social identity affects helping behaviours provides some support for this view (Levine et al., 2005; Levine & Crowther, 2008). A person’s moral circle describes the breadth of their moral concern for others. Those included in it are considered worthy targets of moral concern compared with those outside, who are not (Singer, 1981). The ‘moral expansiveness scale’ (MES) was developed to map the content and structure of people’s moral circles (Crimston et al., 2016). This measure captures breadth i.e., the range of targets e.g. people, animals and environments, and depth i.e. the varying degrees of concern people have for these targets. Reliably measuring a person’s identity in relation to not only other people but also animals, places, and objects may be an important contribution for understanding how people relate to their environments and what relationship this has to moral concern and helping behaviour. In a similar exercise to the moral expansiveness scale (MES; Crimston et al., 2016) we will map people’s sense of self in relation to a range of people, animals, objects and environments. Modifying the MES, we include additional entities and change the focus of the task to map aspects of a person’s identity. We will also replicate the original MES to compare results of our scale with the original work, and to demonstrate whether our scale has the required reliability and validity. This study’s chief aim is scale development. As such it includes both confirmatory i.e. concerning scale reliability and validity, and exploratory hypotheses. We will compare the results of the sense of self task with the moral expansiveness task to see if there are any correlations between what people include in their identity, and what they have moral concern for.

title_r: Réplication de Troy, Ford, McRae, Zarolia, & Mauss (2017) à l'Université Grenoble Alpes
abstract_r: This study talks about emotion regulation capacity in human race. Previous studies suggest that being able to regulate emotions would be benefical but, an existing constraint could moderate that regulation. Here, we’re talking about the socioeconomic status (SES). Indeed, a higher socioeconomic status would allow a higher control on environnement, and so, turn the environnement in a more stable one. This position would be a restraint to control our emotions because in this condition, the person would not be able to do a cognitive reappraisal. Conversely, a poor SES would allow less control on our environnement and so, a strong self-regulatory power. Each study, with an analyse for those 3 studies showed that capacity reappraisal was linked to less depression for the people with a low SES but not the ones with higher SES. Based on this, authors tried to dismantle that link through their studies by testing the link between cognitive reappraisal ability (CRA) and depression. We will only replicate the first study, so we’ll only focus on that one. In total there was 429 participants, 301 from 19 to 74 years old, have contributed to study 1, 52% of them were men. We’ll seek to test if SES moderates the link between CRA and depression, by taking care to exclude stress of everyday life and his effects. In our reproduction, we will more particulary try to find the connection between CRA and mental health. Participants were recruited through « Mechanical Turk », a web site where they had to fill questionnaires in. They last about 15 minutes and are about socio-economic status, CRA, everyday’ stress and depression. 333 individuals accessed the questionnaire, but only 301 completed it and could, therefore be included in the analyzes. The study is divided in two parts. The first one is online (the questionnaire), and the second one is on laboratory in order to have more accurate and specific answers but also to avoid relying only on self reported data. Therefore, the sampling approach was convenient. We asked participants to answer a questionnaire via a website. So, assuming that a link exist between CRA and mental health, the hypothesis is, the more a person has a high SES, the less he would voluntarily regulate his emotional abilities. So there would be a link between SES and CRA, and also with depression according to the socioeconomic status (depending if it’s high or low). Thus, we can observe main effects of everyday’ stress and CRA. So, a significant interaction is observable between SES and CRA. A higher CRA is associated to less depressive symptoms for a low SES person but, on contrary, it would not be associated with depressive symptoms for a high SES. In each model, we can observe an interaction between the socioeconomic status and CRA (which is still significative)

title_r: Replication of Berman (2020) Moral Choice When Harming is Unavoidable -BYU-Idaho Winter 2021
abstract_r: The members of the research team are Abygail Wolff, Mary Lange, Spencer Norconk, and Loren Riddle, under supervision of Brady Wiggins, at BYU-Idaho. The original study, Moral Choice When Harming is Unavoidable, was done by Jonathan Z. Berman and Daniella Kupor in 2020: The specific study that is being replicated is study 1, "Pulling Life support from the terminally ill." This particular study was exploring the idea that most people avoid inflicting harm when there is an option to do no harm, and that individuals may be more willing to do greater harm for a greater benefit when harming is an unavoidable choice. They used the chi square test for their experiment. They found that the results of the study confirmed their hypothesis, and that participants were more likely to do greater harm where greater benefit was also a factor in unavoidable harm situations. We are conducting a replication of this study at Brigham Young University - Idaho, with our participants being students from the General Psychology Class. In our replication of the study we have added in one more hypothesis, We want to see if Gender may affect the individuals moral reasoning, this hypothesis won't affect the method as we are already gathering information on the participants gender. An individuals gender may have an impact on their personality and we want to see if that impact may affect their moral reasoning.

title_r: Forgetting Episodic Events and Their Perceptual Detail
abstract_r: When we remember events from our past, for example, a dinner we had with our friend, we tend to bring to mind an image involving the central elements of the situation – the location, the person we were with, and the food we had. Across multiple studies, Horner and colleagues (Horner & Burgess, 2013; Horner & Burgess, 2014; Horner, Bisby, Bush, Lin, & Burgess, 2015; Joensen, Gaskell, & Horner, 2019) have demonstrated that complex episodic events built via encoding word associations (kitchen-Barack Obama-hammer) are retrieved and forgotten in an all-or-none manner. Once one element of the event is cued, people are likely to recall the other elements involved in this event. These findings suggest that all elements of an episodic event are bound within an episodic representation, which upon retrieval is re-activated in full based on a partial cue (i.e., via the process of pattern completion, Horner et al., 2015). Whilst the identities of episodic event elements are retrieved in a holistic (all-or-none) manner, this may not hold true for lower-level perceptual aspects of long-term memory (LTM). For example, object features such as an object’s exemplar, state, and colour have been found to fragment as a function of forgetting (Brady, Konkle, Alvarez, & Oliva, 2013; Utochkin, & Brady, 2020). In particular, the state and colour of an object are forgotten at different rates, and the successful retrieval of one object feature (e.g., exemplar) no longer predicts the retrieval of another feature (e.g., state) after a delay (Brady et al., 2013; but see Balaban, Assaf, Arad Meir, & Luria, 2019). This also seems to be the case with regards to the precision with which the spatial context and colour of objects are retrieved; the retrieval of the gist of these aspects is dependent but the resolution with which each feature is retrieved is somewhat independent (Cooper, & Ritchey, 2019). Taken together, these findings seem to suggest that precise perceptual features of objects are not bound within the same episodic representation and that different features tend to be forgotten independently over time. We recently proposed that the findings described above can be reconciled if we consider the hierarchical nature of episodic memory and make a distinction between event-based and item-based neural representations (Andermane, Joensen, & Horner, 2020). Specifically, hippocampus-based representations of associations between elements from the same spatiotemporal context may remain relatively coherent over time and may be retrieved in full via the process of hippocampal pattern completion. In contrast, perirhinal object-based representations involving perceptual features (i.e., shape and colour) may fragment with time, given the overlapping and distributed nature of these representations, and their susceptibility to interference by individual low-level features. In two recent experiments, we asked participants to encode episodic events by studying images of objects, famous people and locations, and to use their mental imagery to create associations between the elements. We later tested participants’ memories of the associations between the elements of each event, as well as the association between object features. Using this method, we replicated the pattern of holistic forgetting previously observed for episodic event associations encoded via word pairs (Joensen et al., 2019) and the fragmentation seen for object features (Brady et al., 2013). In the present study, we will combine our two previous experiments (Experiment 1 for events, and Experiment 2 of objects) in a fully within-samples design. This will enable us to investigate how the same individuals forget different aspects of episodic events (i.e., the associations between elements versus their perceptual features). Importantly, we will rectify some of the minor issues in our previous two experiments, which may have led to inconclusive results. First, we will determine whether the dissociation between event and object memories holds when encoding circumstances are equivalent and favourable for encoding the events well (relative to the short encoding times in our Experiment 1). Second, we will make sure initial performance is not at ceiling in the first testing session (T1) and not at floor in the final session (T2) for either events or objects by introducing more favourable testing time points (T1 an hour after encoding rather than immediately after, T2 after 2 rather than 3 days). Third, we will also be able to compare the relative change in dependency for the two memory types across the two testing sessions in a fully within samples design. Finally, because of new testing stopping rules introduced in this pre-registration (i.e., a conclusive Bayes factor of above 6 for the T1-T2 dependency comparison or a maximum sample of 128 participants based on power analyses), we will be able to replicate the dissociation with confidence. As in Experiments 1 and 2, we will also administer the self-report Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) (Marks, 1973), to explore whether individual differences in mental imagery predict retrieval confidence. We previously found (in both experiments combined) that retrieval confidence at delay and the loss of confidence with forgetting predicted self-reported vividness of mental imagery. We aim to replicate this correlation in a confirmatory way and investigate if it is indeed specific to objects or events in an exploratory way. Mental imagery and episodic memory share similar phenomenal characteristics (Moscovitch, Cabeza, Winocur, & Nadel, 2016) and there are stable individual differences in self-reported vividness of imagery that are correlated with neural activation patterns during imagery (Cui, Jeter, Yang, Montague, & Eagleman, 2007). We will test the hypothesis that individual differences in imagery may represent accessibility of episodic memory traces and the strength of their reinstatement in neocortex. We expect a positive confirmatory correlation between the reported vividness of imagery and confidence at delay, and a negative correlation between VVIQ and confidence loss (for both memory types combined). Exploratory correlations between VVIQ and event/object memory confidence will assess whether the association is specific to objects or events (or both).

title_r: Illusion of control when gambling: An extension of Langer & Roth (Investigating post-loss speeding)
abstract_r: This project is based on our earlier direct replication of Langer & Roth (1975, see https://osf.io/uk6t3 and https://osf.io/xpr6m). The aim of this third extension is to rule out an alternative explanation for the bigger post-loss speeding effect in the descending group compared to the other two groups. Our first studies indicate that the effect of control manipulation and outcome of the previous trial might be confounded with a general effect of trial course (unrelated to the illusion of control). Specifically, participants generally speed up over the course of the experiment. But as there are more losses at the end of the experiment in the descending group compared to the ascending group, this complicates the interpretation of the latency data. For this, we will insert another 24 trials with wins and losses equally and randomly distributed. We will use the first 12 trials to calculate the post-loss speeding effect as a function of the illusion of control manipulation. We will use the last 12 trials to determine whether the illusion of control wears off (as suggested by the answers to the “practice” question in our previous experiments)
