title_r: A preregistered direct replication of the linguistic frame effect on perceived blame and financial liability
abstract_r: Fausey and Boroditsky (2010) demonstrated that agentive descriptions of accidents can increase perceived blame and financial liability. Here we propose a direct replication of their studies 1 and 2, both in the language originally used (English) and in Croatian. Participants in the first experiment will read either an agentive or a nonagentive description of an incident in a restaurant that resulted in a fire and will rate the level of blame and financial liability of the main character in the story. The second experiment will examine the direct influence of language on financial liability assessments while manipulating the blame level. Participants will be presented with the same story as in the first experiment (either agentive or nonagentive) with the added sentence about the blame level (low, middle or high) attributed to the main character by an independent panel. We plan to use the materials from the original studies and replicate the studies using a large sample of native English-speaking residents of the United States of America, as well as Croatian students in a total of four experiments.

title_r: Feedback on Failure
abstract_r: The study aims to replicate and extend a previous study by Eskreis-Winkler and Fishbach (2019)* which investigated the effect of feedback on learning. The previous study showed that people learnt less from failure feedback than success feedback even though they were equally informative. We plan to replicate experiment 2a of the previous study which consists of a training and post-test phase. For the training phase, participants are randomly assigned to receive success or failure feedback on the same questions. Specifically, the training phase consists of multiple-choice questions and feedback. The participants are asked to guess which of two researcher-invented symbols had a specific meaning. Then, they are given either success feedback (“You answered this question correct”) or failure feedback (“You answered this question incorrect”). An immediate posttest measures participants’ learning. As an extension, we add two additional conditions to introduce a new variable, which is "feedback type". Feedback type consists of two levels: Personal wording (the two conditions from the previous study) and impersonal wording (the two new conditions we introduce). title_r: Starting Big with Unfamiliar Objects
abstract_r: This study investigates the effect of “Starting big”—relying on multiword units by exposure first to unsegmented input—on second language (L2) learning outcomes. Prior work has shown that adults’ prior knowledge leads them to rely less on multiword units, hindering the learning of certain grammatical relations between words. Exposing adults to unsegmented input first leads them to rely more on multiword units, facilitating better grammatical learning in an artificial language (Arnon & Ramscar, 2012; Siegelman & Arnon; 2015). In the current study, we ask whether the facilitative effect of starting with multiword units will be stronger when the objects are unfamiliar. In this case, the initial association between the new object, the label and the article may be stronger than in the case of familiar objects (where there is an existing label in the L1). Learning from multiword units may be especially beneficial when learning simultaneously meaning, segmentation, and grammar, like infants do in the real world. We test this prediction in two artificial language learning studies focusing on grammatical gender with adult learners by comparing the effect of learning from multiword units in two conditions: with familiar objects and unfamiliar ones. In the first study, we aim to replicate the results from Siegelman and Arnon (2015) with an online study. We look at learning article-noun agreement in an artificial language, in which familiar objects (e.g., table, spoon) are given novel labels. We compare learning in two conditions: unsegmented-first: learners are first exposed to unsegmented input (no pauses between the words), and then to segmented input, and segmented-first: learners are exposed first to segmented input and then unsegmented input. We hypothesize that learning from unsegmented input first will lead learners to rely more on multiword units and through that to better learning of the article-noun pairings, as was found in the original study and in an additional replication (Abu-Zhaya & Arnon, 2024). In the second study, we use unfamiliar objects in the learning process so that both the language and the objects are novel to the learners. This better simulates infants’ learning processes, as they learn language alongside new concepts in the world. We compare learning in the two same conditions: unsegmented-first and segmented-first. We hypothesize that the same effect will be observed as with familiar objects, where grammatical relations will be learned better in the unsegmented first condition. Additionally, we predict the effect to be stronger than in the first study, such that learners will benefit more from the unsegmented input when learning about novel objects. The findings aim to provide evidence for the advantage of learning grammar from multiword units and offer an experience-based explanation for L1–L2 differences that relates building blocks to learning outcomes. Furthermore, the study will highlight the role of object unfamiliarity, exploring the claim that learners benefit more from unsegmented input when dealing with novel objects.

title_r: Understanding belief in political statements using a model-driven experimental approach [Stage 1 - Registered Report]
abstract_r: This manuscript has received in-principle acceptance (IPA) as a Registered Report (Stage 1). Abstract: Misinformation interferes with citizens' beliefs and behaviour posing a harm to society. Although frequently associated with false or misleading news, misinformation is also present in political discourse. In this study, we will experimentally investigate how partisanship and cognitive reflection are associated with belief in false statements made by Argentinian politicians. Participants will classify fact-checked political statements as either true or false, complete a cognitive reflection test, and report their voting preference. Drawing on Signal Detection Theory and hierarchical Bayesian statistical modelling, we will infer the effect that partisanship and cognitive reflection have on truth discernment and response bias. Based on existing literature, we make four predictions, each mapping onto a single model coefficient. Results will further explain how belief in political statements comes about and it will also serve as a conceptual replication of previous studies.

title_r: Assessing the Effect of Analytic Priming on Religious Beliefs using The Debiasing Training Task
abstract_r: Abstract: Experimental studies of the relationship between analytic thinking and religious belief have produced mixed results, with the seminal studies showing a decrease in religious belief following analytic priming, whereas other studies showed an increase in religiosity or no effect at all. To address these inconsistencies, we propose to conduct a high-powered conceptual replication of Gervais and Norenzayan’s (2012) experiments, using a priming technique pre-tested in our target population for its effectiveness in activating analytical thinking: the Debiasing Training Task. In case we obtain null results, we plan to conduct an equivalence test to determine if we can conclude with some confidence that the original phenomenon does not exist. To the contrary, we will also investigate the moderating effects of several factors that may work as boundary conditions for the detection of the original effect or even its reversion. Such moderators will include the perceived compatibility between science and religion, the self-relevance of reflection, and the metacognitive ambiguity of religious beliefs. This study seeks to deepen our understanding of the cognitive mechanisms underlying religious belief, contributing theoretically to the cognitive science of religion and practically to the development of strategies to address societal issues related to belief, science and public policy.

title_r: Source-goal asymmetry in non-linguistic events
abstract_r: Thematic roles play a significant role in linguistic theories and cognitive science. These roles are universally encoded across languages, often through morphology or syntax, with certain roles being prioritized over others. The emergence of these universal distinctions may stem from cognitive biases existing prior to the acquisition of external language, or from historical communicative pressures. In the former case, such distinctions would not be exclusive to language but rather reflect how events and actions are perceptually and cognitively encoded. In the latter case, privileged thematic roles would only hold significance within the realm of language. Research has focused mostly on an asymmetry between Sources and Goals. Papafragou (2010) initiated an investigation into this question using a change detection paradigm to explore the differential encoding of the goal and the source of movement. Participants were presented with a series of videos depicting various instances of movement (e.g., a beetle moving from a closet to a window). After viewing the entire series, participants were shown the series again, but this time with within-category substitutions of the source or the goal objects (e.g., changing the type of window or the type of closet). The study revealed that such changes were more likely to be missed if they pertained to the source of movement rather than the goal, aligning with how these two arguments are encoded in language. In a previous study (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MRWT8) we aimed to replicate and expand upon these findings by investigating additional anticipated asymmetries based on how thematic roles are encoded in language. Building on Papafragou (2010)'s task, the study explored not only the source-goal asymmetry but also potential asymmetries involving agent-patient, donor-recipient, or theme-instrument relationships. In that study we failed to find any effect for any of the roles, and we failed to replicate the source-goal asymmetry. In the present study, we try to replicate the original Papagragou (2010) task, with the methods and a population that is as close to the original as we can get.

title_r: Subjective prediction and word learning - 4
abstract_r: In a previous OSF prereg (https://osf.io/8wtsn), we replicated the study by De Loof et al (2018) that reported a linear increase in declarative memory with greater signed reward prediction error (SRPE) from negative to positive. However, we have since shown that the data from this paradigm can equally be explained by a simple memory model that does not appeal to any form of prediction error. This is a consequence of the particular variable choice paradigm introduced by De Loof et al. We plan to revert to a single-choice paradigm in which participants simply indicate their confidence (prediction strength) in one of 4 Swahili translations of an English word (using the same stimuli as in our previous experiments). A correct prediction will result in a small financial reward (incorrect predictions results in no reward), where "correct" is determined randomly to ensure correct/incorrect trial numbers around 50% (chance being 25%), to give impression that predictions can work. We predict that memory will be a function of prediction error, as defined by the difference between the presence/absence (1/0) of reward and prediction strength (scaled to 0-1). We will test both signed and unsigned versions of this prediction error.

title_r: Self-Informant Agreement on Dominance and Affiliation: A Replication of Ringwald et al. (2022)
abstract_r: Interpersonal interactions are influenced by dispositional traits as well as perceptions of self, the other, and other aspects of the situation (Moskowitz, 1994; Moskowitz et al., 1994; Pincus et al., 2014). The broad array of possible interpersonal behaviors expressed and perceived during interactions can be organised into two fundamental domains of dominance and affiliation (Bakan, 1966; Kiesler, 1996; Leary, 1957; Wiggins, 1979). These dimensions closely correspond to the Big Five constructs extraversion and agreeableness, respectively (McCrae & Costa, 1989; Wiggins & Pincus, 1994). These variables can also be used to link within-person, interaction-level processes to between-person differences in interpersonal functioning (Wright et al., in press). Thus, dominance and affiliation represent a map with which to understand how person, perceptual, and situational factors influence behaviors in interpersonal situations. Ringwald et al. (2022) recently estimated self-informant agreement on averages of and variability in dominance and affiliation (between-person level) and on situational shifts in behavior (within-person level); as well as the convergence between self- and informant reported behavior measured by both Ambulatory Assessment (AA) and cross-sectional methods. This study aims to replicate Ringwald’s et al. (2022) findings on self-informant agreement on perceptions of dominance and affiliation in interpersonal interactions.

title_r: Goal Setting With Struggling Students: Replication
abstract_r: A series of field experiments involving a goal setting intervention have shown promising results in recently by increasing academic performance and retention rates and reducing perceived anxiety among struggling students. Unfortunately, these studies are plagued by methodological insufficiencies, most notably the lack of an adequate control group, hindering their ability to inform science and policy because they cannot disentangle the apparent treatment effect from any demand effect. In this field experiment, using an adapted version of the intervention, we will rigorously replicate these studies using a treatment, placebo-treatment, and no-treatment group, to disentangle the treatment and demand effects and bring solid evidence to what could be an extremely low cost, yet highly effective treatment for struggling students.

title_r: Goal Setting With Struggling Students: Replication
abstract_r: A series of field experiments involving a goal setting intervention have shown promising results in recently by increasing academic performance and retention rates and reducing perceived anxiety among struggling students. Unfortunately, these studies are plagued by methodological insufficiencies, most notably the lack of an adequate control group, hindering their ability to inform science and policy because they cannot disentangle the apparent treatment effect from any demand effect. In this field experiment, using an adapted version of the intervention, we will rigorously replicate these studies using a treatment, placebo-treatment, and no-treatment group, to disentangle the treatment and demand effects and bring solid evidence to what could be an extremely low cost, yet highly effective treatment for struggling students.

title_r: Testing the Replicability of the Theory of Planned Behavior: A Large-Scale Multi-Sample Registered Replication Study
abstract_r: Identifying the determinants of social behavior, and the specific processes by which the determinants relate to behavior, are important in the development of theory to predict social behavior. Predicting behavior also has utility for organizations and stakeholders interested in developing effective interventions and strategies to promote behavior change. The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991) is a prominent social psychological theory developed to predict social behavior. The theory derives its assumptions from theories of attitude and social cognition (Albarracín & Johnson, 2019; Eagly & Chaiken, 1993; Fishbein, 1967), and focuses on predicting intentional behavior from sets of beliefs about future behavioral engagement. The theory has been tested in over 2000 studies, and over 30 meta-analytic syntheses. Cumulative findings indicate its efficacy in accounting for variance in behaviors across multiple domains. However, considerable unresolved heterogeneity in effects has been observed, which could be attributable to methodological artifacts or genuine variability across contexts, behaviors, and populations. In addition, some theory predictions, particularly interactions among constructs, have not been tested and replicated consistently. The current project will conduct a large-scale replication of the theory in general population and student samples adopting an identical protocol and measures. The result of the study will be a series of data sets testing theory predictions analyzed by meta-analytic structural equation modeling.

title_r: Replication attempt for Noah, Schul & Mayo : "Facial feedback and awareness of camera presence"
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Pre-Registration: Facial feedback and awareness of camera presence

Since Darwin (1872) suggested that an emotion that is freely expressed by the outward appearance will be enforced, whereas an emotion whose expression is suppressed will be shortened many Psychologists from all over the world have worked to get a better understanding of the so called Facial Feedback Hypothesis.
The Facial Feedback Hypothesis suggests that people´s affective responses can be influenced by their facial expressions, even when it is not directly connected to their emotional experiences. This suggestion was investigated by Strack, Martin, and Stepper (1988) and their results have shown that participants of their experiment rated cartoons as being funnier when they held a pen with their teeth (inducing a „smile“) as when they held the pen with their lips (inducing a „pout“).
Similar findings where shown by Laird (1974). According to this view, people deduce themselves to be sad when they are frowning, whereas people are seen as probably happy, if they are smiling
Recently Wagenmakers, Beek, Dijkhoff, & Gronau (2016) published a registered replication report of the previously mentioned study by Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988). The study featured 17 laboratories with a total of 1,894 female and male participants. There were four Variations in Wagenmakers et al.´s paradigm compared to Strack et al.´s original paradigm. (1) new cartoons were presented to the participants; (2) The experimenter did not explain the instructions anymore, they were now provided on the computer monitor. (3) To ensure that the participants perform the tasks correctly, a video camera was placed next to the computer. (4) the funniness ratings were gathered by using the phrasing from Strack, Martin, and Stepper´s Study 2 rather then Study 1.
Surprisingly the results of the replication experiments did not show any evidence for the facial feedback effect.
A possible explanation for this result can be given by recent findings from Noah, Schul & Mayo (under review). According to their study, feeling observed could have great influence on judgement dynamics. So it is possible that placing a video camera in front of the participants shortens or even eliminates the facial feedback effect.
Noah, Schul & Mayo suggest, that people adopt the perspective of the external observer (third person) when they feel observed. This effect might as well lower the subjects emotional expressions. 
To test this hypotheses we will conduct the experiment in two conditions, with and without a video camera placed in front of the participant.

Design:
The planned experiment hast two between-subjects factors (Facial activity: lips/teeth and Camera presence: yes/no). The DV is the average of the amusement rating of the four cartoons.

Participants:
We plan to recruit two hundred participants, if they are Psychology students only students from the 1st to 3rd term are allowed(to make sure they are not familiar with the facial feedback hypothesis). We aim to reach 50 participants in each of the four conditions, in return students will get course credit for participation. Non-students will receive no compensation.

Procedure:
The procedure will be mostly based on Wagenmakers et al.´s protocol. One big difference will be the absence of a video camera in one of the conditions.
Two persons will conduct the experiment, one of which for all cases with camera, the other for all cases without, each person will recruit 100 participants in accordance with Schul & Mayo. Each participant will be randomly assigned to the “smile”- or “pount”-condition, and will carry out the experiment alone in an isolated room. In the room the participants will find a desk with a computer, the task booklet, a pen, a box of paper tissues and an alcohol swab. Only in the camera condition a video camera will be connected to the computer and faced at the participant.

Before the experiment starts, the participant will be greeted by the experimenter and asked to turn off their cellphone for the whole time during the experiment. The experimenter will give the participant the information brochure and ask them to read it carefully and sign the informed consent form. The participant will be informed to notify the experimenter if any questions arise or when the informed consent form has been read and signed. The experimenter will leave the room and close the door behind them. After the participant has finished reading, asked any questions and signed the consent form, the experimenter will collect the information brochure and consent form. Then, the experimenter will launch the instructions on the computer, request the participant to read the instructions from the screen, and leave the room again. The instructions will explain and demonstrate the right and wrong ways of holding the pen according to the experimental condition. After the participant has read the instructions, the experimenter will return to the room and ask the participant whether the instructions were clear. Next, the experimenter will give the participant the task booklet. The booklet is a German translation of the booklet used by Wagenmakers et al. (2016) and contains four cartoons based on the findings of a pretest on 30 persons, two of which also previously used by Noah, Schul and Mayo,.

The booklet begins with a practice task, which requires drawing a straight line between two points while holding the pen in the requested position. The practice task will be completed in the presence of the instructor. After the practice task is completed the experimenter will inform the participant that now the actual experiment begins. The participant will be asked to hold the pen according to the instructions during all of the tasks (but will also mention that if the participant needs to swallow, it is allowed to shortly remove the pen). The experimenter will then leave the room and close the door behind them. In the camera condition we duplicate the procedure of the replication project of Wagenmakers et al. (2016) the experimenter will explain to the participant that the experiment will be videotaped to make sure the participant is holding the pen correctly throughout the task. She/he will then turn on the camera and leave the room. This procedure will be used to induce the feeling of being observed. The sessions will not be recorded or observed  in this or any other way.
The non-practice task presented first in the booklet will involve connecting 10 digits printed on a sheet of paper by a line in a numerical order using the pen between their teeth. Participants will be asked to rate the difficulty of this task on a 10-point scale which will be printed on the bottom of the page. For the next task there will be eight consonants and nine vowels printed on a page.  The participants task is to underline only the vowels. After finishing this task participants will again be asked to rate the difficulty of the task on a 10-point scale. The next task will be the task actually of interest. This task will show the four cartoons and the participants will be told that, as usual, some of them are funnier than others. The participants will then be asked to rate the emotion they have while looking at each of the cartoons. Again they will find a 10-point scale ranging from I felt not at all amused (0) to I felt very much amused (9). The participants shall read and rate each of the cartoons with the pen held in the original position. (lips/ teeth). 
After participants complete the previously described tasks they will be asked to remove the pen from their mouths and to answer 3 questions. (a) „How successful were you in holding the pen in the correct position during the entire experimental session?“ (0-9 scale); (b) „Did you understand the cartoons?“ (yes/no for each of the cartoons); and (c) „What do you think the purpose of this experiment is?“ (open-ended).
For the last step, participants will be asked to fill out a form about their age, gender, status as a student (yes/no), and occupation or field of study. After finishing all the tasks the experimenter will collect the booklet and ask the participants what expression they had during the experiment, if they succeded in holding the pen in the right position and whether they are familiar with the facial feedback hypothesis. Finally the experimenter will thank the participant and ask them not to tell anyone about the experiment until data-collection is finished.






Exclusion criteria:
The following criteria will exclude participants from the analysis after data-collection:
-	Participants who reportedly did not hold the pen as requested during the experiment.
-	Participants who reach an average cartoon rating exceeding 2.5 standard deviations above/below the mean rating of all participants.
-	Participants who will report that they didn’t understand more than two cartoons.
-	Participants who will correctly guess the goal of the study in the debriefing.

Analysis plan:
We will conduct a between groups two way ANOVA. The condotions  to be tested will be Camera presence (yes/ no) and Facial activity (lips for “pout”/ teeth for “smile”) with the average rating of the four cartoons as dependent variable. We will exclude cartoons that participants report they did not understand. Same as Strack et al., 1988 we suppose that in the no-camera condition, the cartoons will on average be rated funnier in the teeth condition compared to the lips condition. We also predict that this effect will be lower or non-existent in the camera condition. The level of significance will be set to 5%.

Materials:
A document showing cartoons, results of cartoon-pretests and the presented scale is available on the osf under this project.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from O’Brien & Noy (2015), from American Sociological Review
abstract_r: The claim selected from O’Brien & Noy (2015) is that, although the post-secular perspective entails high levels of science knowledge as well as favorable views of science and religion, when scientific and religious perspectives conflict (e.g. evolution), the post-secular latent class almost unanimously aligned their views with particular religious accounts. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Overall, most individuals favor either scientific or religious ways of understanding, but many scientifically inclined individuals prefer certain religious accounts." Participants’ responses to the General Social Survey (GSS) were submitted to a latent class analysis that resulted in a three-class solution characterized as representing traditional, modern, and post-secular perspectives on science and religion. Following this assignment, two-tailed t-tests were used to compare responses between the three groups; for the purposes of the SCORE project, the focal test is the comparison between the Traditional and Post-Secular groups on the question concerning evolution (‘Human beings developed from earlier species of animals’, yes or no). Members of the post-secular category were significantly less likely than members of the traditional group to respond that humans evolved from other animals (3 percent, significant at p < 0.05 on a two-tailed test, see Table 2, rightmost column).

title_r: Prereglog exmaple project
abstract_r: Study Information Title Registered replication of Weissman et al. (2014): "Determinants of Congruency Sequence Effects Without Learning and Memory Confounds" Research Questions We aim to replicate the key findings of Experiments 1 and 2 reported in Weissman, D. H., Jiang, J., & Egner, T. (2014). Determinants of congruency sequence effects without learning and memory confounds. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 40(5), 2022-2037. The main research question is: is the congruency sequence effect (i.e., the interaction of previous trial congruency with current trial congruency in conflict tasks) present once feature integration and contingency confounds are removed from 4 different conflict tasks? What is the size of the effect in these different paradigms? Hypotheses The specific findings we aim to replicate are: 1) the CSE is present in a prime-probe conflict task without learning and memory confounds, in an online sample. 2) even though the original study only detected the CSE in the online variant of the confound-free Simon task, and not the Stroop and the flanker, we expect to find the effect in the latter two tasks as well because power will be increased in our replication (by increasing sample size). We however expect that the asymmetry in the original study (CSE only in the prime-probe and Simon tasks, not in the other two) will be reflected in a difference in effect sizes across paradigms, i.e., the prime-probe and the Simon tasks will produce the largest effects, with the Stroop and the flanker leading to smaller CSEs. Sampling Plan Existing Data Registration prior to creation of data Explanation of existing data Data has not been collected yet. Data collection procedures Data will be collected online (i.e., participants will complete the task in their own homes, at their own convenience). Participants will be Hungarian undergraduate students from different departments (not just Psychology) who will receive course credit for participation. The only inclusion criterion will be that subjects be over the age of 18. Exclusion criteria will include color blindness and non-native status. As data collection will happen online, we expect to reach our target sample size fairly quickly, such as over the course of a week. We are also proposing this replication as a potential multi-lab study. If other labs were to join, they would be encouraged to run at least 50 participants per condition. No files selected Sample size Planned target sample size for each experiment and condition is at least 2.5 times the original target N reported by Weissman et al. For each experiment and each between-subject condition this was 50 in the original study, therefore we aim to collect data from 125 participants per condition. This means total N for Exp. 1 is 125, and total N for Exp. 2 is 375 (3 x 125). Total target N for the whole study is therefore 500. As mentioned above, this replication study is proposed as a potential multi-lab effort - other labs will be encouraged to set a target N of at least 50 per paradigm, matching the Ns of the original study. Sample size rationale Simonsohn (2015) suggests the "original N x 2.5" formula to calculate adequate sample sizes for replication projects. (Simonsohn, U. (2015). Small telescopes: Detectability and the evaluation of replication results. Psychological Science, 26(5), 559-569.) Stopping rule Data collection will be terminated when target N is reached. Variables Manipulated variables Current trial congruency: congruency of a given trial (Trial N) in the conflict tasks (prime-probe in Exp. 1, Stroop, flanker, Simon in Exp. 2). Levels: congruent (no conflict) and incongruent (conflicting). Previous trial congruency: congruency of the previous trial (Trial N-1) in the conflict tasks. Levels: congruent and incongruent. Task (between-subject): the conflict task participants complete. Levels: prime-probe, Stroop, flanker, or Simon. No files selected Measured variables Reaction time and accuracy will be measured in all of the tasks. No files selected Indices For each task, means will be calculated for four conditions (Previous Congruency x Current Congruency): congruent trials that were preceded by congruent trials (cC), incongruent trials that were preceded by congruent trials (cI), congruent trials preceded by incongruent trials (iC), and incongruent trials preceded by incongruent trials (iI). For mean RTs only trials that are correct and are preceded by an other correct trial will be used. For accuracy analyses, all trials (that remain after screening, see below) will be used. Two indices will also be calculated: a measure of the size of the congruency effect in RT by subtracting mean congruent trial RT from mean incongruent trial RT; and a measure of the size of the CSE in RT. This will be calculated the following way: (cI - cC) - (iI-iC), where the four components are mean RTs of the four different conditions described above. No files selected Design Plan Study type Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials. Blinding For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned. Study design Exp. 1: within-subject design with Previous Congruency and Current Congruency as factors. Participants will complete a single task with different conditions. Exp. 2: a mixed-design with Previous Congruency and Current Congruency as within-subject factors and task (with three levels: Flanker, Simon, Stroop) as a between-subject factor. (The two experiments, however, will be carried out simultaneously, thus our design can be thought of as a mixed design with the above mentioned within-subject factors and a between-subject factor with 4 levels: Prime-Probe, Flanker, Simon, Stroop). No files selected Randomization The trial sequence of the tasks will be randomized across participants. Analysis Plan Statistical models For both Exp. 1 and Exp. 2: two 2x2 repeated-measures ANOVAs will be run per task, one with the mean RT and one with mean accuracy as the dependent variables. In both cases, the two factors of the ANOVA will be Previous Congruency (congruent, incongruent) and Current Congruency (congruent, incongruent). The following cross-task analysis will also be conducted: a one-way between-subject ANOVA with task (levels: Prime-Probe, Flanker, Stroop, Simon) as the single factor, and the CSE index as the dependent variable will be run to examine if the size of the effect differs across tasks. If the Levene test indicates the violation of the assumption of homogeneity of variances, a Kruskal-Wallis H test will be run. To investigate whether the size of the CSE changes as a function of the magnitude of interference, correlations between the CSE and the congruency effect will be calculated, within each task. No files selected Transformations Previous and Current Congruency will be coded as follows: 0 = congruent, 1 = incongruent. Accuracy will be coded as follows: 0 = incorrect response, 1 = correct response. Follow-up analyses Following significant interactions, simple effects tests will be used to explore the pattern of the interactions. In the cross-task analyses, if the one-way ANOVA yields a significant result, Tukey's post-hoc test will be used to investigate pairwise differences. If instead of the one-way ANOVA a Kruskal-Wallis test is run, Dunn's test will be run to investigate pairwise comparisons. Inference criteria Bayes factors (BF) will be used to make inferences about the data. To ease interpretation of the results, we will use cut-offs suggested by Jeffreys (1961): a BF higher than 3 or lower than 1/3 will be taken to indicate support for the alternative or the null models, respectively. P-values will also be reported, but whenever the Bayesian and the frequentist analyses lead to different conclusions, BFs will be used to make decision. Priors for the different analyses will be determined the following way: 1) in within-task CSE analyses, a half-normal distribution will be used with a mean of 0 and a SD equal to the half of the congruency effect (in ms) for a particular task in the original data set by Weissman et al. (2014). To test the congruency main effect, the SD will be set to the congruency effect reported by Weissman et al. (2014) for that particular task. 2) for pairwise comparisons contrasting the magnitude of the CSE between tasks, a half-normal distribution will be used with a mean of 0 and SD equal to half of the greater congruency effect of the two in any given pair as reported by Weissman et al. (2014). 3) for the correlation between the CSE and the congruency effect, analyses will be conducted on the Fisher Z transformed r values, and a two-tailed normal distribution will be used as a prior, with a mean of 0 and a SD of 0.549 (corresponding to an r of 0.5). Data exclusion First, participants whose overall mean accuracy is below 70% or whose overall mean RT is more than 2.5 SDs away from the group mean will be excluded. Then, for each participant, trials more than 2.5 SDs away from the participants conditional means will be excluded as outliers. Trials immediately following outliers will also be excluded. (As mentioned above, for RT analyses, error trials and trials immediately following errors will also be removed.) Missing data Participants who do not complete the task will not be included in the analyses. Exploratory analysis NA

summary: The purpose of this project is to replicate and critically analyse the study presented in the Scott et al. (2023) CHI conference paper "Do You Mind? User Perceptions of Machine Consciousness". Furthermore, it will explore and extract relevant features of Perceptions of Machine Consciousness (PMC), methodological limitations, authors conclusions, and recommended research directions. This report will be used for prospective theory and empirical research on PMC.

Firstly, direct replication of the quantitative analysis will be performed and cross checked with the reported results. These analyses will be provided in a full report of the replication.pdf and the corresponding code within replication.RMD. 

Secondly, replication of the results from the studies qualitative analyses will be sought and explored using a method of Thematic Analysis outlined by Braun and Clarke (2006). Notably, the authors cited "Affinity Diagramming" (Blandfor et al) as the tool used for qualitative analysis of the data. The analysis, coding and defined themes will be reported within Qualitative_Analysis.xlsx. Both sentence completion and free form text responses will be analysed.

Lastly, limitations and experimental comparisons will be identified for further research and reported in the replication.pdf.

title_r: This is a replication of experiment 1 of Maayan et al.’s Publication of “Feelings of Culpability: Just Following Orders Versus Making the Decision Oneself”
abstract_r: Culpability is the amount of responsibility warranted for a crime or wrongdoing. It is a continually conversed topic especially in the court. The amount of culpability an individual feels they deserve varies from person to person. For example, if a person were to steal from a grocery store and is charged with stealing. Generally this behavior is frowned upon in society but the individual might feel his actions to be justified. In the study “Feelings of Culpability: Just Following Orders Versus Making the Decision Oneself,” Malayan and her colleagues wanted to explore the relationship between the amount of agency individuals have in the decision making process and the amount of culpability they feel as a result. The original study was conducted by randomly placing participants into two groups: high agency and low agency. They were given imaginary roles of engineers who were working on designing an autonomous car and programming it to react in a potential accident. There were two approaches: the first was to design the car to prioritize the driver’s safety above others (deontological); the second option was to prioritize the safety of as many people as possible even at the expense of the driver’s safety (utilitarian). In the high agency group, they were given the opportunity to choose which one they felt was best. For the low agency group they were assigned one of the two options by a supervisor. After five years, a tragic accident occurs where the car behaves based on what the individuals chose (deontological or utilitarian). In both imagined scenarios the car functions properly but innocent people are killed as a result of the car’s programming. Participants were then asked how they felt about the programming followed by how responsible they felt for the result of the accident (their “moral culpability”). The original study’s hypothesis was that those who were in the high-agency condition would feel more culpable for their decision than those in the low-agency condition. In contrast with the researchers’ hypothesis, the results showed individuals who had high agency felt “less guilt” than those who were given low agency. For our study, we plan to conduct an exact replication to see if the results of the original study are accurate based on if we are able to obtain similar findings. License: Add a license

title_r: Latin Square
abstract_r: This study aims at investigating the accuracy of verbal reports about the effects of stimuli on associations. It is a conceptual replication conducted as an online experiment of “Experiment 1: Erroneous Reports About Stimuli Influencing Associate Behaviour” published in “The Accuracy of Verbal Reports About the Effects of Stimuli on Evaluations and Behavior“ by Nisbett and Wilson in 1978. The authors explore the concept of simultaneous associations, such as two people humming the same song at the same time. Nisbett and Wilson assume that these occur as a result of a common external stimulus that both subjects were influenced by. They further assume that people cannot identify the external stimulus as a source of their association because of a poor ability to introspect about the causal effects on higher-order cognitive processes. (Nisbett & Wilson, 1978, p.119) Three questions are explored in “Experiment 1”: The first question is whether a cueing with word pairs that are memorised and/or picture stimuli that are evaluated by subjects renders a predetermined target response/association more accessible compared to subjects who are not cued for the respective target response. Furthermore, it is investigated whether subjects report the cueing stimuli as a cause for their response less frequently, i.e. only in four or less percent of cases, than other causes if asked in an open ended inquiry. The subsequent question examines whether, if the cueing stimuli are directly pointed out as a possible source of their responses, subjects cite them as the cause of their response independent of the actual cueing. Nisbett and Wilson report a significant effect of word pair cues on target response availability, as opposed to no significant effect of picture cues. The authors observe that picture and word cues come in last, i.e. only four percent in total, in a list of reasons given for subjects’ associations. They additionally conclude that subjects’ reports about the effects of cueing stimuli on target responses rather indicate a lack of awareness of their influence than actual introspection. (Nisbett & Wilson, 1978, p. 121-123). With the aim of a replication study in mind, we hypothesise that the same or similar effects should be found in this study.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Seaton et al. (2010), from the American Educational Research Journal
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Seaton et al. (2010) is that larger BFLPE (big-fish-little-pond) effects were associated with students who used memorization to a greater extent. Students in high-ability schools who used the memorization technique to a greater extent suffered a larger decline in mathematics self-concept than those who used the technique to a lesser extent. Although all students who used memorization had lower mathematics self-concepts if they attended high-ability schools than students of similar memorization usage who attended average- or low-ability schools, the drop in mathematics self-concept was more pronounced for students who used memorization to a greater extent. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Statistically significant moderating effects emerged in both areas; however, in relation to the large sample (N = 265,180), many were considered small." The claim was tested by regressing mathematical self-concept on predictor variables were individual mathematics ability (linear and quadratic), school-average mathematics ability, the moderator of interest - use of memorization studying, and the interaction of school-average mathematics ability with memorization. Due to the large number of tests of statistical significance being conducted, the significance level was set at p < .001. Effect size for the group-level construct of BFLPE was calculated using the equation shown on p. 406; effect sizes that approached 0.10 or greater were considered of interest. Use of memorization moderated the effect of school-average ability on mathematical self-concept (-.089, p < 0.001; see Table 3), with an effect size of -0.157 (see Table 4).

title_r: The "Go/No-Go" paradigm to assess spatial numerical associations - Experiment 2b
abstract_r: This study will use the "Go/No-go" paradigm to investigate spatial-numerical associations (SNAs) within UK adult participants. Eccher et al. (2025) used a computerised Go/No-go task to investigate SNA in a sample of Himba adults, Italian adults and Italian preschoolers. In each trial, participants were presented with a central fixation cross, followed by the first dot array (henceforth the “reference stimulus”) made up of 4, 12 or 36 dots. After a brief blank screen, participants then saw a second dot array (henceforth the “test stimulus”) displayed to either the left or right of the screen. In the increasing condition, participants were told to press the space bar when the test stimulus contained MORE dots than the reference stimulus. For example, when the reference stimulus contained 4 dots, the participant’s response would be recorded as correct only if the test stimulus contained 12 or 36 dots. If the reference stimulus was 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the test stimulus contained 36 dots. In the decreasing condition, participants were then instructed to only press the space bar when the test stimulus contained fewer dots than the reference stimulus. When the reference stimulus contained 36 dots, a participant's response would be recorded as correct when the test stimulus contained 12 or 4 dots. If the reference stimulus contained 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the target stimulus contained 4 dots. Both the increase and the decrease tasks started with 12 trials to familiarize the participants with the task (“training trials”), followed by 48 “experimental trials”, 30 of which were targets (i.e. trials that required a response) and 18 were distractors (i.e. trials that did not require a response). 50% of all trials were considered “SNA congruent”, whereby stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from left-to-right. The other 50% of trials were considered “SNA incongruent”, as the stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from right-to-left. For example, if a participant was completing the “increasing” condition and the test target stimulus contained 4 dots and the test stimulus contained 12 dots and presented on the right, this would be considered SNA congruent, as the target stimulus is always presented in the centre, and so the presentation of stimuli moves from left-to-right in order of magnitude. Conversely, in the “decreasing” condition, an SNA congruent trial may be one in which the target stimulus contains 36 dots, and the test stimulus contains 4 dots which is presented on the left. For further details of SNA congruent/incongruent conditions, see “Manipulated Variables"). We aim to replicate the original study’s findings, which demonstrated the potential presence of a spatial-numerical association. That is, participants will be faster and more accurate when responding to numerosities presented in a left-to-right direction, increasing in terms of magnitude, while participants’ responses will be slower and less accurate when those same numerosities are presented in a right-to-left order in terms of magnitude. In our replication, we will conduct the experiment online rather than in person; we will recruit adult participants in the UK; make a slight modification to the timing of the no-go trials, reducing the duration from three seconds (as in the original study) to 1.5 seconds; and we will double the number of trials. In the original study, there was a one-to-one correspondence between the total area taken up by the dot array stimuli and their numerical magnitude. That is, the 4-dot array will take up much less visual area than the 36-dot array. It may be that participants are making judgements based off total area of stimuli rather than extracting magnitude information. Therefore, in Experiment 2, we produced two novel types of dot array stimuli: “controlled” and “correlated” stimuli. The correlated stimuli are those which have a one-to-one correspondence between total area and numerosity. The controlled stimuli all share the same total area of dots, regardless of numerosity. We have also created five stimulus variations for each type of dot array to further prevent participants from relying on pattern recognition, thus creating a total of 30 stimuli. Crucially, trials are always matched in terms of controlled or correlated stimuli; for example, if a participant sees a controlled reference stimulus, then the test stimulus will also be controlled. Further information can be found in the “Manipulated Variables” section. For Experiment 2b, we wanted to further extend these findings to include an additional set of numerosities. In Eccher et al.’s (2025) original study, there were three numerosities used (4, 12, 36) which have a ratio of 3. As well as these stimuli, we created stimuli of 8, 16 and 32, this time with a ratio of 2, to investigate whether previously observed effects still hold for a new set of numerosities. As with stimulus type, the numerosity set will be consistent within trials, but the order of trials will be intermixed.

abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Gerhold (2020) is that women are more concerned about COVID-19 than men. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Women are more concerned about COVID-19 than men." abstract_r: Wieland, Sundali, Kemmelmeier and Sarin (2014) conducted three studies to explore contexts and mechanisms that might account for the gender effect in risk aversion. They found evidence to suggest that gender effects in risk aversion may be affected by elicitation method (willingness to pay, WTP vs. willingness to accept, WTA) and by decision domain (gambling framed vs. non-gambling framed decisions). Women offered significantly less money than men in WTP conditions but the same amounts as men in WTA conditions, suggesting a gender difference in the endowment effect. title_r: Replicating the intergroup empathy bias
abstract_r: People are social beings. This means that they organize themselves in social groups (Kondo, 2017). Individuals feel that they belong most strongly to the group with which they identify themselves (Kondo, 2017). Previous study results show that individuals are more likely to develop empathy for other people if they classify them as their in-group compared to people who do not belong to the in-group, i.e. members of the out-group (Vanman, 2016). This effect is most evident when the in-group and out-group are in a competitive environment (Vanman, 2016). Although empathy is considered a basic human trait, people often find it difficult to empathize with others, especially when it comes to people belonging to other cultural or ethnic groups (Cikara et al., 2014). Understanding what influences empathy could help predict behavior in contexts such as political conflicts. Therefore, Cikara and colleagues (2014) tested whether people develop less empathy when it comes to members of other groups compared to members of their own group, even if the group membership is trivial. On this theoretical basis, Cikara and colleagues (2014) developed four experiments. Here we will consider the first experiment for our replication. In this experiment, participants will be randomly assigned to two groups and will then be asked to judge how negatively they rate eight scenarios, four of which concern members of their own group, more precisely their in-group and four of which concern members of the other group, their out-group. Participants will be randomly allocated to two setting; cooperative and competitive. The participants will also see and rate eight positive scenarios from in- and out-group members to prevent some participants from guessing what the study is about.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Torelli et al. (2010), from the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
abstract_r: We selected the claim that horizontal collectivist cultural context (HC) is associated with a socialized power concept (Statement 2; Study 2 of manuscript). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Cultural variables are shown to predict beliefs about appropriate uses of power, episodic memories about power, attitudes in the service of power goals, and the contexts and ways in which power is used and defended" (Statement 1). The claim is tested by estimating a compositional multilevel model (for the situation recalling experiences in which one helped others), in which participants (Level 1) are nested within five (or seven) different cultural groups (Level 2). Vividness of recall associated with an exercise of socialized power was the dependent variable and the participant's cultural orientation (HC) was the focal predictor (decomposed into a within-level and a between-level component by using the cultural group means, HCj, as predictors in the Level 2 intercept equations). title_r: The Evaluation-Behavior Link Revisited: It All Depends On The Question You Have in Mind
abstract_r: According to theorists, a main function of emotions is to prepare individuals to react to changes in their environment (e.g., Arnold, 1960; Frijda, 1988; Plutchik, 1980; Zeelenberg et al., 2008; Zajonc, 1980). Consistent with this assumption, individuals approach faster stimuli evaluated as positive than negative and avoid faster stimuli evaluated as negative than positive (e.g., Chen & Bargh, 1999; Krieglmeyer & Deutsch, 2010; Rougier et al., 2018). This Approach-Avoidance (AA) compatibility effect on action tendencies has been replicated in many studies, even when stimuli were highly degraded (e.g., Alexopoulos & Ric, 2007; Pillaud & Ric, 2022; Rougier et al., 2018). In a series of two studies, Pillaud and Ric (2022) observed that the impact of masked affective stimuli on the AA compatibility effect was moderated by instructions. To account for these results, the authors proposed that affect could be used as a signal to prepare an adapted response to the current context (see Huntsinger et al., 2014; Schwarz & Clore, 2007). In other words, in a context in which participants are asked to detect whether a specific target is present vs. not, they can rely on the information provided by affective stimuli to anticipate its presence/absence. In such conditions, it is indeed hypothesized that participants would simplify the task by asking themselves whether the target is present or not. The presence of a positive stimulus would lead to a positive answer to this question (yes, it is) and to the preparation of the required response (approach or avoidance, depending on the condition). In contrast, a negative stimulus would provide a negative answer to the question (no, it is not present), which would lead to the preparation of the response associated with the absence of the target, whatever the movement executed to respond (i.e., approach or avoidance). The results of the two studies were in line with this explanation and at odds with the most commonly invoked explanations of the AA compatibility effect (Chen & Bargh, 1999; Eder & Rothermund, 2008; Krieglmeyer & Deutsch, 2010). However, it is possible that these effects occur in these studies because the affective stimuli were degraded and presented before the occurrence of the target on which the movement was required. In such conditions the influence of the affective stimulus is incidental whereas in classical studies on the AA compatibility effect, participants are asked to answer by approach/ avoidance on the basis of their evaluation of the stimulus to which the action is directed. Therefore, the theoretical explanation offered by Pillaud and Ric could be limited to such conditions implying the presentation of degraded stimuli prior to the target. Instead, Pillaud and Ric proposed that this explanation can also apply to usual conditions in which the AA compatibility effect is observed. They suggest that in such task, individuals simplify the task by asking themselves whether they should approach, as approach would be considered the default response option. This would be because approaching is associated with more potential benefits and risks than avoidance. Then, confronted with an object, participants would be more likely to ask themselves whether they should approach than whether they should avoid. We propose to further test these hypotheses in another series of studies. In a first study, we replicated these findings with visible affective stimuli (thus not degraded) in an incidental task. In this study participants had to move toward or away geometrical shapes (squares vs. diamonds) by either an approach or an avoidance movement. The presentation of each geometrical shape was preceded by a positive vs. a negative word for 150 ms and thus clearly visible. The main manipulation was the question participants were instructed to ask themselves while performing the task. For half of the participants, they were instructed to ask themselves whether they should approach the geometrical shape (i.e., what was assumed to be the default option). In such conditions, a positive stimulus would provide a positive answer to the question, and thus facilitate approach movement if required, while a negative one would lead to a negative answer and thus interfere with the execution of an approach movement. In other words, an AA compatibility effect was expected in these conditions. For the other half, participants were instructed to ask themselves whether they should avoid the geometrical shape. In this condition, we expected to observe a reverse AA compatibility effect. The results were consistent with our hypothesis and thus support our theoretical explanation of the AA compatibility effect. However, in this experiment, the affective stimuli (i.e., words) and the target to approach (vs. avoid) were still presented sequentially. So, we conducted a second experiment where the affective stimulus appeared on the same location and at the same time as the target (i.e., the affective stimulus and the target were the same object). To do so, we asked participants to respond by approach/avoidance to affective words on the basis of the color of the font in which they are written. Again, we manipulated instructions so that half of the participants were instructed to ask themselves whether they should approach the word, whereas the other half were instructed to ask themselves whether they should avoid the word. The results were again consistent with our hypothesis and thus support our theoretical explanation of the AA compatibility effect. However, the two previous experiments can be considered as not typical of the "classical" procedures that are usually used to measure the AA compatibility effect. Indeed, in the classical paradigm, participants are typically instructed to approach or avoid words according to their valence (i.e., positive vs. negative; e.g., Chen & Bargh, 1999; Rougier et al., 2018). Therefore, we propose to replicate our initial findings in conditions in which participants will have to approach (avoid) affective stimuli (i.e., words) as a function of their valence. Again, we will manipulate instructions so that half of the participants will be instructed to ask themselves whether they should approach the word, whereas the other half will be instructed to ask themselves whether they should avoid the word. We hypothesize to replicate the AA compatibility effect when participants will be instructed to complete the task while asking themselves whether they should approach and that the effect will be reversed when instructed to ask themselves whether they should avoid.

title_r: Do non-binary pronouns affect reading comprehension in English and French?
abstract_r: Language is an essential tool for expressing identity and communicating with others, and it has evolved hand in hand with society and cultural norms. As society progresses towards greater recognition and acceptance of gender diversity, language has adapted to accommodate these changes. One crucial aspect of this adaptation is recognizing and using non-binary pronouns in languages like English and French, each with its own specificity. In English, for example, Bandeen et al. (2020) say that "they/them" pronouns have become the standard for referring to non-binary individuals. Meanwhile, in French, due to its gendered nature, the development of "iel" and "ille'' was necessary to identify non-binary and gender-diverse individuals (Benjamin, 2017). However, how the use of these non-binary pronouns affects reading comprehension is still uncertain due to the lack of studies about it. Some institutions, such as l'Académie française, also state that non-binary pronouns make reading tricky (2021). I propose an experiment to analyze whether the cognitive load to process content with non-binary pronouns is heavier than gendered pronouns in English and French. Research conducted on "they" pronouns in English by Foertsch and Gernsbacher (1997) contrasted the use of the singular "they" and the generic "he" when gender-neutral pronouns started becoming popular in the 1990s. They found that people took longer to read passages when "they" was used instead of pronouns that matched gender expectations. For example, when the noun was stereotypically masculine, such as "that truck driver," participants would take longer to read the sentence when the pronoun was "they" than "he." Foertsch & Gernsbacher (1997) also investigated the effect of using non-binary pronouns in relation to both nonreferential nouns (i.e., the writer mentioned a generic person, such as "a truck driver") and referential nouns (i.e., the writer mentioned a specific person, like "that truck driver"), and found that readers were more used to seeing "they" referring to a particular individual than to a generic one. In French, since the new non-binary pronouns such as "iel" and "ille" are still not officially recognized by any government agency, there have been no published studies to determine their effect on cognition. However, in Sweden, Vergoossen et al. (2020) conducted an experiment on reading comprehension with "hen," a pronoun developed for non-binary people that aligns with the French "iel" and diverges from the English practice of using the plural "they" in singular contexts. They found that people showed no differences in understanding when reading a sentence with gendered pronouns and the new neutral one. Based on the literature reviewed, the present study proposes a conceptual replication of Foertsch and Gernsbacher's experiment in both English and French. It aims to analyze whether reading sentences with neutral pronouns is more cognitively demanding than reading gendered pronouns in both languages. It will be an online experiment with different referential noun phrases and pronouns as independent variables and reading speed as the dependent variable. In addition, it will use a measure of genderism as an exploratory moderator of the potential effects of pronoun use. Académie française. (2021, May 7). title_r: Do non-binary pronouns affect reading comprehension in English and French?
abstract_r: Language is an essential tool for expressing identity and communicating with others, and it has evolved hand in hand with society and cultural norms. As society progresses towards greater recognition and acceptance of gender diversity, language has adapted to accommodate these changes. One crucial aspect of this adaptation is recognizing and using non-binary pronouns in languages like English and French, each with its own specificity. In English, for example, Bandeen et al. (2020) say that "they/them" pronouns have become the standard for referring to non-binary individuals. Meanwhile, in French, due to its gendered nature, the development of "iel" and "ille'' was necessary to identify non-binary and gender-diverse individuals (Benjamin, 2017). However, how the use of these non-binary pronouns affects reading comprehension is still uncertain due to the lack of studies about it. Some institutions, such as l'Académie française, also state that non-binary pronouns make reading tricky (2021). I propose an experiment to analyze whether the cognitive load to process content with non-binary pronouns is heavier than gendered pronouns in English and French. Research conducted on "they" pronouns in English by Foertsch and Gernsbacher (1997) contrasted the use of the singular "they" and the generic "he" when gender-neutral pronouns started becoming popular in the 1990s. They found that people took longer to read passages when "they" was used instead of pronouns that matched gender expectations. For example, when the noun was stereotypically masculine, such as "that truck driver," participants would take longer to read the sentence when the pronoun was "they" than "he." Foertsch & Gernsbacher (1997) also investigated the effect of using non-binary pronouns in relation to both nonreferential nouns (i.e., the writer mentioned a generic person, such as "a truck driver") and referential nouns (i.e., the writer mentioned a specific person, like "that truck driver"), and found that readers were more used to seeing "they" referring to a particular individual than to a generic one. In French, since the new non-binary pronouns such as "iel" and "ille" are still not officially recognized by any government agency, there have been no published studies to determine their effect on cognition. However, in Sweden, Vergoossen et al. (2020) conducted an experiment on reading comprehension with "hen," a pronoun developed for non-binary people that aligns with the French "iel" and diverges from the English practice of using the plural "they" in singular contexts. They found that people showed no differences in understanding when reading a sentence with gendered pronouns and the new neutral one. Based on the literature reviewed, the present study proposes a conceptual replication of Foertsch and Gernsbacher's experiment in both English and French. It aims to analyze whether reading sentences with neutral pronouns is more cognitively demanding than reading gendered pronouns in both languages. It will be an online experiment with different referential noun phrases and pronouns as independent variables and reading speed as the dependent variable. In addition, it will use a measure of genderism as an exploratory moderator of the potential effects of pronoun use. Académie française. (2021, May 7). title_r: A Cross-linguistic Study on the Role of Generic Language in Social Categorization
abstract_r: Generic language (e.g., “Bears hibernate in the winter”, “Dogs bark”) makes broad statements about category properties that need not be true for all category members, although they are often interpreted as so. This form of language has important implications for conceptualizing social categories (e.g., Gelman, Ware, & Kleinberg, 2010; Rhodes, Leslie, & Tworek, 2012; Rhodes, Leslie, Bianchi, & Chalik, 2018; Noyes & Keil, 2019). For example, hearing generic statements highlights features as central to the category (Cimpian & Markman, 2009; Hollander, Gelman, & Raman, 2009), inducing essentialist assumptions about categories as richly structured and inductive (Rhodes, Leslie, & Tworek, 2012; but also see Noyes & Keil, 2019). Additionally--and most relevant for the present study--generic language facilitates toddlers’ learning about novel social groups in cases where other forms of language have not been enough (Rhodes et al., 2018). However, most previous studies were conducted with English-speaking participants, leaving the question open whether the effect of generics on social categorization generalize broadly to other linguistic contexts. To address this issue, we will test the role of generic language on social categorization in Chinese-speaking children. The Chinese language provides a theoretically interesting comparison with the English language due to their different linguistic formats of generics. In English, generics are often expressed in bare plural noun phrases (e.g., “Bunnies eat carrots”) or indefinite singular noun phrases (e.g., “A bunny eats carrots”). However, some linguistic features of the Chinese language, such as the lack of plurality and definite/indefinite articles, make the linguistic distinctions between generics and non-generic noun phrases much more ambiguous (Tardif et al., 2012). This linguistic ambiguity may delay the development of sensitivity to generic languages in Chinese-speaking children (Tardif et al., 2012). The current study aims to investigate the role of generics on social category learning in Chinese-speaking toddlers. First, we will replicate results from Rhodes and colleagues (2018) by testing an online sample of American children aged between 28 to 36 months to validate the online testing method. Additionally, we will recruit a sample of native Chinese-speaking children aged between 28 to 36 months to compare with the English-speaking sample.

title_r: Can multi-echo denoising remove motion-related noise? A replication & extension of Power et al. (2018)
abstract_r: Multi-echo denoising is a processing technique that leverages the manner in which fMRI signal decays over time in order to separate blood oxygenation-level dependent (BOLD) signals from non-BOLD noise. While this method is quite useful for improving fMRI signal-to-noise with limited spatial and temporal resolution costs, there are forms of noise that exhibit the same signal decay characteristics as neuronal signal. A recent publication by Power et al. (2018) [1] found that multi-echo denoising is unable to identify BOLD-based, spatially-diffuse noise caused by respiration-related motion, and further proposed global signal regression as a useful method for removing this kind of noise. In this manuscript, we replicate and extend the findings of Power et al. (2018) across a range of open-access multi-echo fMRI datasets in order to reproduce the original paper’s results, as well as to determine if global signal regression is an appropriate technique for dealing with the forms of noise that multi-echo denoising cannot.

abstract_r: ***A minor edit has been made to this pre-registration in the exclusion criteria section only. The remainder is copied over from the original "Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication" (osf.io/nqsw5) pre-registration.*** This pre-registration should be considered alongside the pre-registration entitled “Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication and Extension” (Kredlow, M. A. (2021, March 5). Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication and Extension. Retrieved from osf.io/4b2ea) as the groups in this study comprise 4 of the 12 groups in that larger study. In this experiment, we will attempt to replicate findings from Hupbach et al. 2007 (Experiment 1) by conducting an online version of their study. The current study will occur online and involve 3 sessions spaced ~48 hours apart (Monday, Wednesday, Friday). At Session 1, participants will learn 18 objects. At Session 2, following memory reactivation (or without reactivation) participants will learn 18 new objects. At Session 3, participants will be asked to recall the objects they learned at Session 1. A detailed description of the experiment is provided below: Session 1: Participants watch a video of the experimenter providing instructions for the experiment. Participants are asked to learn a list of 18 objects. To facilitate learning, they name the objects one by one, as each object emerges from a virtual blue basket. After participants name all 18 objects individually, there is a 30 second delay during which they solve a series of basic arithmetic questions. Then, participants are asked to recall the objects that they learned. They complete this process 4 more times. Session 2: Approximately 48 hours after Session 1, participants complete Session 2. Participants assigned to memory reactivation are shown an image of the blue basket from Session 1 and are asked whether they remember it. They are also asked a multiple choice question about the task that they completed at Session 1. They also see an instructional video of the same experimenter from Session 1 and the online study formatting (background color, layout, text font) is the same as Session 1. Participants who do not receive reactivation are given instructions by a different experimenter and the online study formatting (background color, layout, text font) is different than it was at Session 1. All participants are then asked to learn a new list of objects (different from the list they learned at Session 1). All 18 new objects are presented on one page. Participants are given up to 3 minutes to name the objects followed by 30 seconds to study the objects and try to remember them. After naming and studying the 18 objects, there is a 30 second delay during which participants solve a series of basic arithmetic questions. Then, participants are asked to recall the objects that they learned. They complete this process 4 more times. Session 3: Approximately 48 hours after Session 2, participants complete Session 3. Participants watch an instructional video given by the experimenter from Session 1. The online study formatting (background color, layout, text font) is the same as in Session 1. Then, participants are asked to recall as many objects as possible from Session 1 and are given unlimited time to do so. Once participants have recalled as many objects as possible, there is a 30 second delay during which participants solve a series of basic arithmetic questions. This process is repeated 4 more times. title_r: Understanding Face Familiarity through Naturally Varying Pictures of Chinese Faces: An ERP Study
abstract_r: Recognition and recollection of a face that you have seen previously is an important ability in social contexts. Failure to accurately recognise and recall a familiar face can be detrimental for effective socialisation, with often embarrassing consequences. Arguably, a familiar face can be defined as a face previously seen and encoded with semantic information, such as one’s name, job description, or even a specific memory that associates with the face. Therefore, familiar face recognition involves not only perceptual recognition of the face (i.e., “I have seen that face before”), but also accurate retrieval of related semantic information (e.g., “and I know her name is Jane”). Familiar face recognition likely relies upon robust identity mental representations, enabling recognition of a familiar person even amongst varying factors (e.g., changing hair styles, expressions, viewing angles, lighting; see Burton et al., 2011). To gain a better understanding of how these identity mental representations develop, previous studies investigated the specific neural activations (ERPs) likely associated with these mental face representations, namely the N250 (early and late) and a more sustained later N250 effect coined the Sustained Familiarity Effect (SFE; see Andrews et al., 2017; Wiese et al., 2019). Previous research investigating the N250 time windows and the development of familiar faces has focused on Caucasian participants viewing Caucasian faces (e.g., Weise et al., 2019; Andrews et al., 2017), furthermore, their experimental learning paradigm has focused on a small number of identities (e.g., remember the faces of two people). In many social settings, people often need to learn and remember multiple faces. In this study, we aim to replicate previous findings using East Asian faces. In addition, we employ a larger experimental learning paradigm of 10 identities using naturalistic photographs. Finally, we will gain a better understanding of the decision-making processing of determining if a face is familiar by using Drift Diffusion Modelling.
