title_r: Understanding Face Familiarity through Naturally Varying Pictures of Chinese Faces: An ERP Study
abstract_r: Recognition and recollection of a face that you have seen previously is an important ability in social contexts. Failure to accurately recognise and recall a familiar face can be detrimental for effective socialisation, with often embarrassing consequences. Arguably, a familiar face can be defined as a face previously seen and encoded with semantic information, such as one’s name, job description, or even a specific memory that associates with the face. Therefore, familiar face recognition involves not only perceptual recognition of the face (i.e., “I have seen that face before”), but also accurate retrieval of related semantic information (e.g., “and I know her name is Jane”). Familiar face recognition likely relies upon robust identity mental representations, enabling recognition of a familiar person even amongst varying factors (e.g., changing hair styles, expressions, viewing angles, lighting; see Burton et al., 2011). To gain a better understanding of how these identity mental representations develop, previous studies investigated the specific neural activations (ERPs) likely associated with these mental face representations, namely the N250 (early and late) and a more sustained later N250 effect coined the Sustained Familiarity Effect (SFE; see Andrews et al., 2017; Wiese et al., 2019). Previous research investigating the N250 time windows and the development of familiar faces has focused on Caucasian participants viewing Caucasian faces (e.g., Weise et al., 2019; Andrews et al., 2017), furthermore, their experimental learning paradigm has focused on a small number of identities (e.g., remember the faces of two people). In many social settings, people often need to learn and remember multiple faces. In this study, we aim to replicate previous findings using East Asian faces. In addition, we employ a larger experimental learning paradigm of 10 identities using naturalistic photographs. Finally, we will gain a better understanding of the decision-making processing of determining if a face is familiar by using Drift Diffusion Modelling.

title_r: Global/local modulations of effort allocation
abstract_r: Current theories on mental effort, such as the Expected Values of Control theory (EVC), suggest that task engagement is driven by a cost/benefit analysis, in which prospective benefits of exerting effort (e.g., rewards) are weighed against its costs (e.g., difficulty) and the net value of such comparison ultimately drives effort allocation (Shenhav et al., 2017). Accordingly, previous studies have shown that preparatory cues predicting the level of trial difficulty and reward influence task performance (Krebs et al., 2012; Schevernels et al., 2014). Participants specifically improved performance on hard trials when a high reward was prospected as compared to a low reward during performance of a gap discrimination task. In a series of online experiments, we attempted to replicate these findings with a Random Dot Kinematogram (RDK) task, in which each trial was preceded by a symbolic bidimensional cue (as in Vassena et al., 2019) anticipating the level of difficulty (easy or hard) and the level of reward (small or large). However, we did not observe a consistent modulation of performance based on cue attendance. Even though we simplified the cues in a follow up experiment (https://osf.io/u6da5/), we still employed symbolic and bidimensional cues. We consider that the complexity of the cues might have had an impact on participants’ compliance to use the cues to improve performance. Indeed, recent evidence suggests that it is possible to observe reward effects on RDK performance in a blocked design (Ritz et al., 2021), in which reward/non reward blocks were simply anticipated by a set of instructions. Moreover, Frober & Dreisbach (2016) reported increased reward effects on proactive control allocation in experiments employing reward vs. non reward miniblocks as compared to reward vs. non reward trial manipulations. They also observed a performance benefit on non reward blocks embedded in the reward manipulation context (i.e., when alternating with reward miniblocks) as compared to a preliminary baseline phase (i.e., before reward manipulation). Altogether, the authors suggested that engaging in proactive control is in itself effortful, so a complete disengagement from proactive control in non reward trials (vs. reward trials) or non reward blocks (vs reward blocks) might not be worth the effort of re-engagement in reward trials or reward blocks, respectively. Based on these outcomes, we could speculate that in our previous experiments, participants did not find it particularly beneficial to adapt effort allocation on a trial by trial basis, especially when the cues themselves required effortful processing (in an online setting). It should be noted, however, that Frober & Dreisbach (2016) compared the effect of trial by trial (reward) cues vs block (reward) cues between experiments, thus it is not clear whether the same outcome (i.e., larger effect of block cues) would be observed when both trial by trial cues and block cues are presented within the same experiment. Moreover, the EVC posits a tradeoff between benefits and costs in the decision to allocate effort, but it is not clear how global (i.e., block) benefits interact with local (i.e., trial) costs and viceversa. For example, the theory predicts increased effort allocation for large rewards and hard trials, but it’s not clear whether allocation should be greater in a global benefit context (with local costs) or in a global cost context (with local benefits). The purpose of the current study is to address both the complexity of the cues and the differential effect of global and local reward/difficulty cues on the modulation of effort allocation.

title_r: Replication of Sparkman & Walton (2017) at Université Grenoble Alpes
abstract_r: We are third-year psychology students, we carry out a replication of the study of Sparkman and Walton (2017) as part of an introduction to research and data analysis The study we chose to replicate (Sparkman & Walton, 2017) investigates whether dynamic norms have a greater impact on behavior change than static norms. Dynamic norms refer to how the behavior of others changes over time, whereas static norms are characterized as the current state of the norm. Thus, they seek to show that there will be more compliance with a dynamic norm than with a static norm. This study reports five experiments, the one we will replicate is the first one that focuses on compliance with static and dynamic norms in relation to meat consumption. For example, a static norm would be that a majority of people have reduced their meat consumption while a dynamic norm would be that an increasing majority are reducing their consumption, so this norm is evolving: here the proportion of people reducing their meat consumption will be even greater in subsequent years, so this norm is dynamic. We found it interesting to replicate this effect because, first, in this experiment, it was a small sample size (122 adults), and we thought it relevant to replicate the experiment with a larger number of participants, to see if the observed results were similar. In addition, since this experiment was conducted in 2017, and given the evolution of thinking, meat consumption, and norms, we felt it was important to compare these results to results obtained 4-5 years later to see if they were still significant. Moreover, since the set of participants was chosen through the "Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk)", the sample is not very representative, it is mainly disadvantaged students. More generally, replicating this experiment would allow us to learn more about the changes in individuals' behaviors and how they are implemented. Knowing more about this topic would be particularly useful when applied to climate change or discrimination. The original experiment was conducted with an online questionnaire, in exchange for a fee of $0.25. In this one, the presentation of the material was randomized. The participants in this experiment were part of a convenience sample, their participation in the experiment was voluntary, and the experiment was conducted in a between-subject design with two conditions : dynamic norm or static norm (participants were randomly assigned to one condition or the other). In addition, of the 122 participants, 99 participated in a pilot, between-subject study that involved obtaining participants' estimates of American meat consumption. These estimates were then used to conduct the experiment that we replicate. In the "static norm" condition, participants were presented with a finding about the meat consumption of a percentage of Americans, and in the "dynamic norm" condition, the finding was the same but made over the past 5 years. The percentage presented was the one obtained in the pilot experiment. The null hypothesis of the original study was that there was no effect of dynamic and static norms on intended consumption. The alternative hypothesis was then that there was a difference in intended consumption between the dynamic and the static norm. In the end, the null hypothesis was rejected. This project will be carried out in French and will only replicate the first study described in the article. It is a strict replication, without extension, with the only deviation being the use of convenience sampling, unlike the original study which used the MTurk platform. For this project, we will work with a French sample of 250 participants, who will be randomly allocated to either the dynamic or the static norm. The sample size of 250 was chosen to try to balance the original authors' recommendations to recruit more participants (350) with feasibility concerns (in particular regarding time to complete the data collection).

title_r: Replication of the Hindsight Bias and extension on the role of depressive symptoms
abstract_r: Replicability and reproducibility are essential for scientific credibility, promoted through open science practices. Mental health research often deals with variable and time-changing characteristics, making it challenging to implement these practices, especially in studies of social behavior and cognition. These studies must be investigated through replication-extension models to promote theoretical expansion and generalization. The seminal research by Fischhoff (1975) on hindsight bias is highly relevant, whereas evidence suggests interactions with depressive symptoms. However, few studies have explored such interaction, and no replications exist with the Brazilian population. This project aims to replicate Experiment 2 of the Fischhoff study (1975) in hindsight bias in a Brazilian sample, including an extension to the original research to broaden its scope of clinical relevance in depressive symptoms.

title_r: Dynamic processes in mother-infant interaction underlying attachment quality: A time-series approach.
abstract_r: Although the key role of infant-parent attachment in child development is well recognized, questions remain about the origins of early attachment relationships. In particular, there is a lack in understanding of how individual differences in attachment quality develop. Research has mainly focused on the role of the parent in the development of attachment relationships, whereas the role of the infant itself, as well as bidirectional processes between parent and infant are heavily understudied. Attachment theory suggests that individual differences in attachment quality develop as a result of repeated interactive processes between infant and caregiver that give rise to so called “internal working models”, i.e. expectations the infant develops about the behavior of the caregiver in reaction to the infant’s signals. Sensitivity, i.e. the ability of the caregiver to pick up the infant’s signals, interpret them correctly, and respond timely and appropriately, is the single most robust predictor of individual differences in attachment quality that has been identified so far (de Wolff & van IJzendoorn, 1997; Zeegers et al. 2017). Much less is known about the dynamic, bidirectional interactive processes between the infant and the caregiver that may shape how the infant’s expectations with regard to caregiver behavior develop in the course of the first year. It has been argued that a more fine-grained and precise investigation of interactive processes might help to elucidate the process of attachment development (Peck 2003; Beebe et al., 2010). A previous study (Beebe et al., 2010) conducted in 84 mother-infant dyads suggests that self- and interactive contingency in mother-infant interactions in different communication modalities (i.e. gaze, vocalizations, facial affect, etc.) might be mechanisms of attachment formation. Replication and extension of these findings are needed. We will replicate the findings from Beebe et al. (2010) by using state-of-the-art multilevel time series analyses, using dynamic structural equation modeling in Mplus and openly publishing the scripts used. We will use a sample similar in size (N= 90) as compared with Beebe et al. (2010), but with a more common distribution of attachment classification, enabling us to also examine insecure-avoidant attachment classifications specifically, something that Beebe et al. was not able to do because the group was too small (n=4). In addition, our sample consists of a group of nonclinical as well as depressed mothers, presumably leading to larger variation in interactive patterns, as compared to Beebe et al. who included only low-risk dyads.

title_r: The effect of augmented reality on global coherence formation processes during STEM laboratory work in elementary school children
abstract_r: Being a key feature of scientific work, hands-on experiments are a common part of scientific education. Whereas in a traditional experimental environment, learning information like measures or graphs must be presented spatially separated on an external display or sheet, Augmented Reality (AR) allows for integrating virtual learning information into the real-world experimental set-up and has shown to support learning processes (Garzón & Acevedo, 2019). As a conceptual replication of Altmeyer et al. (2020), the present study uses AR to enrich an experimental set-up on serial and parallel electrical circuits with real-time measurement data presented above the physical circuit components. The integration of external symbolic representations of measured values into the physical experimental setting creates a multimedia learning environment (Santos et al., 2014). Following the cognitive load theory (Sweller et al., 1998) and cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer, 2005, 2009), the AR condition displaying measured values in spatial proximity to the circuit components when looking through a tablet camera is assumed to support the formation of global coherence (Seufert & Brünken, 2004; 2006) between the representation of measured values and the physical components. The non-AR condition, in contrast, displaying measured values grouped together on an external tablet might hamper global coherence formation. The promotion of local coherence formation (Seufert & Brünken, 2004; 2006), however, does not differ between conditions, as they both allow for capturing all measured values at one glance. In line with Altmeyer et al. (2020), the main objective of the current study is to compare the effect of an AR-supported and a non-AR tablet-based presentation format of measured values provided during laboratory work on extraneous cognitive load (ECL) and different learning outcomes. Whereas Altmeyer at al. (2020) used a sample composed of university students, the current study will investigate the generalizability of previous effects on elementary school children. In order to obtain deeper insights in coherence formation processes during laboratory work, children’s gaze behavior will be recorded. Posttests covering different aspects of acquired local and global coherence are used to evaluate differences in learning outcomes due to the presentation format. Besides the shift to the sample of children, some further adaptions of Altmeyer et al.’s (2020) study will be realized. The laboratory work will be simplified according to the target-group: Whereas the laboratory work of Altmeyer et al. (2020) contained experiments on current and voltage, the present study will only consider current. A further adaption consists in the usage of two bulbs instead of three different resistors. On the one hand, this is due to children’s familiarity with light bulbs and on the other hand, referential connections between current and brightness of a bulb cover an additional aspect of global coherence formation. A further simplification is the possibility to observe and compare parallel and serial circuits simultaneously instead of consecutively. The simultaneous presentation is assumed to facilitate the derivation of Kirchhoff’s laws. Moreover, while Altmeyer et al.’s (2020) subjects were free to hold the tablet in their hands or place it on the table during lab work, subjects of the current study will be provided with fixed tablets. Fixed tablets ensure free hands and that all measured values are always visible at one glance, consistent for both conditions. Whereas Altmeyer et al. (2020) concluded that the low level of tasks difficulty during laboratory work might have concealed differences in ECL between conditions, the laboratory work of the present study is expected to be of adequate complexity for children as they lack prior knowledge. Additionally to the adapted posttests used by Altmeyer et al. (2020), further posttests expected to give further insights in the formation of global coherence formation in dependence on the presentation format will be conducted.

title_r: Is the Sunny Side Up? Replication of Meier and Robinson (2004)
abstract_r: We are replicating Study 1 from Meier and Robinson’s (2004) paper examining the relationship between affective evaluations and spatial location. This study was a high impact study with over 800 citations and, as best as we can tell, no close replications. The effect we are trying to replicate was their finding that participants evaluated the valence of words (positive or negative) faster when the word’s spatial position was congruent with metaphors linking “up” to positive valence and “down” to negative valence. More specifically, they found a valence X position interaction where participants were faster to categorize positive words presented at the top of the screen than the bottom of the screen and faster to categorize negative words presented at the bottom of the screen than the top of the screen.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Malik et al. (2020), from medRxiv
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Malik et al. (2020) is that social distancing measures introduced by governments reduce the mobility in the concerned cities. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Social distancing measures decreased the mobility by an additional 23% (95%CI: 20%, 27%)". A city was classified to have instituted social distancing measures if non-essential businesses were closed; these measures were further classified as moderate or intense based on the intensity of closure. The effect of time and social distancing measures was estimated using a multilevel mixed-effects linear regression model. Social distancing measures decreased the mobility by an additional 23% (95%CI: 20%, 27%). ---- Malik et al. claim that “There was no difference in mobility reduction based on whether the measures were moderate or intense”, but we do not plan to replicate this claim, i.e. the intensity of the closures will not be used in the replication as a variable.

abstract_r: General Information This fork is part of the Direct+Plus CREP replication (https://osf.io/px0sw/) of a study by Diener et al. (2010). Every student manages a fork of the official replication OSF page as a part of a seminar at the Department of Occupational, Economic and Social Psychology, led by Andre Julian Hartmann and Martin Müller (both graduate students) at the University of Vienna (Austria). Materials All materials are developed together with the students during the seminar and will be added to the project before starting data collection. In addition to the items of the original study, items for further research questions will be added as a direct+ replication. We also participate in the Direct+Plus project by Jordan Wagge containing two questions that deal with financial security. Procedure All students are using the same survey, advertising materials, and OSF page since this is an online study. Every student will sample N = 10 (total targeted sample: N = 270) students living in Vienna within their social circle. Original Abstract The Gallup World Poll, the first representative sample of planet Earth, was used to explore the reasons why happiness is associated with higher income, including the meeting of basic needs, fulfillment of psychological needs, increasing satisfaction with one's standard of living, and public goods. Across the globe, the association of log income with subjective well-being was linear but convex with raw income, indicating the declining marginal effects of income on subjective well-being. Income was a moderately strong predictor of life evaluation but a much weaker predictor of positive and negative feelings. Possessing luxury conveniences and satisfaction with standard of living were also strong predictors of life evaluation. Although the meeting of basic and psychological needs mediated the effects of income on life evaluation to some degree, the strongest mediation was provided by standard of living and ownership of conveniences. In contrast, feelings were most associated with the fulfillment of psychological needs: learning, autonomy, using one's skills, respect, and the ability to count on others in an emergency. Thus, two separate types of prosperity—economic and social psychological—best predict different types of well-being. Student Researchers Armbruster Gregor

abstract_r: This study follows upon a previous study we conducted that was a replication of Casey, J. P., Vanman, E. J., & Barlow, F. K. (2023). Empathic Conservatives and Moralizing Liberals: Political Intergroup Empathy Varies by Political Ideology and Is Explained by Moral Judgment. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 0(0). https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672231198001 We successfully replicated the article's main findings: 1. empathic concern for outgroup members was less than empathic concern for ingroup members; 2. "conservatives consistently showed more empathy to liberals than liberals showed to conservatives"; 3. "this asymmetry was partly explained by liberals' harsher moral judgments of outgroup members (Studies 1-4) and the fact that liberals saw conservatives as more harmful than conservatives saw liberals (Studies 3 and 4)." This study extends upon these findings to ask the following questions: Might conservatives' greater empathy for liberals (as compared to liberals for conservatives) indicate that we have mistakenly assumed symmetry between the political parties/ideologies, when the fact that liberals view conservatives as more harmful than conservatives view liberals implies a fundamental asymmetry between these two groups? Perhaps the perceived harm posed by other types of outgroups in conjunction with the perceived harmfulness of political cross-party members is an important missing element to properly understand who feels empathy for (or harmed by) whom? In the original study, the extension of empathy to cross-party targets was tested using targets who, from their names, were implied to be White. This study explicitly includes race/ethnicity (White vs. Hispanic) as a factor important to the feeling of empathy for cross-party targets. We think a more fully fleshed out, embodied target is important to the question of empathy, and in particular, how empathy is altered when the target is not only a political party outgroup member, but also a member of a minoritized group with a non-malleable identity. Hispanics targets were chosen for this study as members of the racial/ethnic outgroup since they are plausible members of either political party. We hypothesize that the addition of race/ethnicity as a descriptor of the target will reduce the empathy gap between Republicans and Democrats. The intersecting outgroup identities may cause Republicans to 1) feel more harmed by, and so 2) struggle to extend as much empathy to an explicitly Hispanic Democratic target. In the original study design, participants first answered multiple items about whether the opposing political party has caused them harm before being asked how much empathic concern they felt for the target. In our previous study, we counterbalanced this order, with half of the participants having empathy felt for the target measured first, as a better test of mediation by the causal mechanism of perceived harmfulness. Indeed, we found that having to answer questions about perceived harmfulness before felt empathy 1) increased ratings of the opposing party's harmfulness and 2) decreased empathic concern for members of the opposing party, providing further support for perceived harmfulness as mediator. We plan to repeat this counterbalanced order in this study to again serve as a more convincing test of mediation. We also plan to add a measure about the perceived harmfulness of the target's racial/ethnic group, to test for mediation along this ingroup/outgroup dimension.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Pickett and Baker, 2014, in Criminology
abstract_r: We selected the claim that the use of unilaterally positive items to measure crime attributions will lead to an underestimation of the size of the hydraulic relation between dispositional and situational attribution styles. Specifically, the association between dispositional and situational attribution styles should be negative when bidirectional sets of questions are administered to subjects. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “The findings reveal that using unidirectional sets of questions to measure these concepts likely results in…an underestimation of the magnitude of the negative relationships between attribution styles…” The claim was tested by using data from an experiment with a national sample (N = 826) of Internet panelists. Specifically, the authors estimate the multivariate relationship between attribution styles (Dispositional and Situational) using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analysis. The model specification can be gleaned from Table 4. The focal test result concerns the location of the estimated coefficient on the “Dispositional attributions" variable obtained from bidirectional group. This analysis yielded a statistically significant coefficient on the “Dispositional attributions" variable obtained from bidirectional group (b = -.17, RSE = .049, St. Coef. = -.196, p < .01 (two-tailed).

title_r: The impact of self-esteem manipulation through social exclusion on felt meaningfulness and the experience of meaning in life
abstract_r: Previous studies have shown that the satisfaction of basic psychological needs is associated with a greater sense of meaningfulness in work and everyday life contexts (Autin et al., 2022; Eakman, 2013; Martela et al., 2018). Conversely, need frustration is a predictor of negative psychological outcomes (Campbell et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2015). The aim of the present study is to investigate the effect of an acute frustration of self-esteem - one of the basic needs that has not previously been investigated in relation to meaning - on felt meaningfulness and the experience of meaning in life. Two studies found that participants report lower self-esteem (Zadro et al., 2004) and lower meaning in life (Stillman et al., 2009) following social exclusion. We aim to replicate and extend these findings by 1) employing two distinct measures of meaning (experience of meaning in life and perceived meaningfulness in ambiguous stimuli) and 2) showing that the loss of meaning following social exclusion is mediated by frustrated self-esteem. 3) In addition, we will investigate the influence of trait narcissism on self-esteem frustration. For this purpose, we will manipulate state self-esteem using a virtual ball-tossing game (Cyberball Game; Williams & Jarvis, 2006). In the game, participants are randomly allocated to an experimental group (socially excluded by the other players during the game) or to a control group (balanced condition). After playing the game, participants report perceived social exclusion during the game (manipulation check), their state self-esteem and mood. Felt meaningfulness is assessed after reading ambiguous sentences (Zen koans) and self-reports on meaning in life are collected using the Meaning in Life Measure (MILM; Hill et al., 2019). We expect that participants in the experimental group will report lower self-esteem, less meaning in life, and less felt meaningfulness compared to the control group. We hypothesize that self-esteem mediates the effect of social exclusion on measures of meaning. Additionally, we expect that higher trait narcissism will be positively associated with self-esteem frustration following social exclusion.

Study Title: Do Expectations and Perceptions of Personality Trait Change in College Students Match Reality?  

Authors: Andrew Rakhshani, Brent Donnellan, Richard Lucas, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman

Description: 
	This study aims to conceptually replicate two studies (Herbst, McCrae, Costa, Feaganes, & Siegler, 2000; Robins, Noftle, Trzesniewski, & Roberts, 2005) that compared perceived versus actual personality change and extend these works by also evaluating anticipatory personality change. We will conduct secondary analyses on a large, longitudinal dataset of a student cohort followed across four years of college. We intend to emulate the analyses described in each of the target studies and conduct additional analyses relating to anticipated personality change.
	Herbst and colleagues (2000) sought to determine whether self-reported perceived change in personality was associated with actual changes based on 6 to 9-year follow-up data of middle-aged adults. Participants completed the 240-item NEO-PI-R at baseline and again at follow-up. At follow-up participants were also asked to report on how they had changed since their intake using two measures of change. The first was a single item measure reflecting three perceived change groups (i.e., changed a good deal, changed little, or stayed pretty much the same). The second asked whether participants increased, decreased, or stayed the same on each of the Big 5 dimensions (e.g., Extraversion: “compared to how you were six years ago, how lively, cheerful, and sociable are you now?”). Analyses and results were presented as follows: 
(1) frequencies of perceived change groups (52% stayed the same, 39% changed a little, 9% changed a good deal); 
(2) chi-square test of perceived change groups by gender (men: 54% stayed the same, 38% changed a little, 8% changed a good deal; women: 48% stayed the same, 41% changed a little, 11% changed a good deal; slightly more women reported change 2(2, N = 2,241) = 7.7, p = .02);
(3) compared stability coefficients across perceived change groups by Big 5 factor (see table below); 
 
(4) compared profile stability coefficients across perceived change groups (see table above); 
(5) compared baseline and post (respectively) factor and facet (cannot replicate) scores across perceived change groups (specific effect sizes were not reported; Respondents who felt they had changed a good deal scored significantly higher in Neuroticism and Openness and lower on Agreeableness than the other two groups on both administrations); 
(6) frequencies of perceived factor-level change (see note in table below); 
 
(7) compared mean level change from baseline to follow-up by direction of perceived change (the factor level perceived change measure) using repeated measures ANOVAs with Scheffe post hoc tests (these effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared for Time by perceived change group interaction; see table above); 
(8) correlation of perceived change by domain and residual gain score (“the raw change score corrected for initial level”) for the same domain (All five correlations were positive and significant, ranging in magnitude of .10 for Agreeableness to .24 for Neuroticism; On average, perceptions of change accounted for less than 3% of the variance in measured change); and 
(9) percentage of discordance of perceived change group and actual change (Same group had significant declines in all but Agreeableness; More group increased only in Neuroticism and Agreeableness; Less group showed significant declines in all but A; 80% of the comparisons are discordant for the self-perceived Same group, 60% for the More group, 20% for the Less group).
	
Robins and colleagues (2005) sought to determine (1) the extent and in what ways young adults think their personality changes and (2) how much perceived change was associated with actual change. Their study included a third purpose involving a host of additional measures that our dataset does not include so everything to follow will reflect the two parts we can replicate. They followed a group of 295 young adults for six waves across four years of college. Participants completed the 60-item NEO-FFI during the first week of college and again at the end of the fourth year. At the end of the fourth year, participants were also asked to indicate how they had changed (1 = decreased to 5 = increased) since entering college using a single item for each Big 5 factor. To assess actual personality change, they regressed each year four factor score on the corresponding week one factor score and saved the standardized residuals. Relevant analyses were presented as follows: 
(10) frequencies of perceived change grouped by decreased, stayed the same, and increased for each Big 5 factor (Almost everyone (98%) believed that they had changed on at least one factor; see table below);

title_r: Understanding the visual constraints on lexical processing: New empirical and simulation results (Experiment 3)
abstract_r: It is well known that visual acuity is not uniform across the visual field. Acuity instead decreases precipitously from the center of vision. The region of maximum acuity, called the fovea, is comprised of the central 2º of the visual field, with a region of rapidly decreasing acuity called the parafovea extending an additional 5º of visual angle to either side of this. Although the photoreceptors required for perceiving fine detail are largely limited to these two regions of the visual field, it remains unclear precisely how the rapid drop off in visual acuity that results from the distribution of these photoreceptors affects our capacity to rapidly and accurately identify printed words. This project aims to investigate the physical constraints imposed by our visual system on reading by conducting a conceptual replication of a highly cited study by Rayner and Morrison (1981). The original study compared lexical-decision and naming performance at central fixation (0 degrees), or between 1 and 5 degrees to the left or right of central fixation. Participants were either instructed to maintain central fixation (no eye-movement condition) or move their eyes to the location of the stimulus (eye-movement condition). The proposed study improves on several features of the original study by (i) testing a much larger sample of participants; (ii) using a larger number of more highly controlled items that are not repeated during the experiment and that vary in both word length and frequency; (iii) ensuring participants maintain central fixation by tracking eye movements and terminating trials on which the participant moves their eyes. Previous experiments in this project measured lexical-decision performance for words and one-letter-different nonwords. This experiment tests naming performance for the same word stimuli at central fixation and at 1 and 2 degrees to both the left and right of fixation.

title_r: The "Go/No-Go" paradigm to assess spatial numerical associations - Experiment 2c
abstract_r: This study will use the "Go/No-go" paradigm to investigate spatial-numerical associations (SNAs) within UK adult participants. Eccher et al. (2025) used a computerised Go/No-go task to investigate SNA in a sample of Himba adults, Italian adults and Italian preschoolers. In each trial, participants were presented with a central fixation cross, followed by the first dot array (henceforth the “reference stimulus”) made up of 4, 12 or 36 dots. After a brief blank screen, participants then saw a second dot array (henceforth the “test stimulus”) displayed to either the left or right of the screen. In the increasing condition, participants were told to press the space bar when the test stimulus contained MORE dots than the reference stimulus. For example, when the reference stimulus contained 4 dots, the participant’s response would be recorded as correct only if the test stimulus contained 12 or 36 dots. If the reference stimulus was 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the test stimulus contained 36 dots. In the decreasing condition, participants were then instructed to only press the space bar when the test stimulus contained fewer dots than the reference stimulus. When the reference stimulus contained 36 dots, a participant's response would be recorded as correct when the test stimulus contained 12 or 4 dots. If the reference stimulus contained 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the target stimulus contained 4 dots. Both the increase and the decrease tasks started with 12 trials to familiarize the participants with the task (“training trials”), followed by 48 “experimental trials”, 30 of which were targets (i.e. trials that required a response) and 18 were distractors (i.e. trials that did not require a response). 50% of all trials were considered “SNA congruent”, whereby stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from left-to-right. The other 50% of trials were considered “SNA incongruent”, as the stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from right-to-left. For example, if a participant was completing the “increasing” condition and the test target stimulus contained 4 dots and the test stimulus contained 12 dots and presented on the right, this would be considered SNA congruent, as the target stimulus is always presented in the centre, and so the presentation of stimuli moves from left-to-right in order of magnitude. Conversely, in the “decreasing” condition, an SNA congruent trial may be one in which the target stimulus contains 36 dots, and the test stimulus contains 4 dots which is presented on the left. For further details of SNA congruent/incongruent conditions, see “Manipulated Variables"). We aim to replicate the original study’s findings, which demonstrated the potential presence of a spatial-numerical association. That is, participants will be faster and more accurate when responding to numerosities presented in a left-to-right direction, increasing in terms of magnitude, while participants’ responses will be slower and less accurate when those same numerosities are presented in a right-to-left order in terms of magnitude. In our replication, we will conduct the experiment online rather than in person; we will recruit adult participants in the UK; make a slight modification to the timing of the no-go trials, reducing the duration from three seconds (as in the original study) to 1.5 seconds; and we will double the number of trials. In the original study, there was a one-to-one correspondence between the total area taken up by the dot array stimuli and their numerical magnitude. That is, the 4-dot array will take up much less visual area than the 36-dot array. It may be that participants are making judgements based off total area of stimuli rather than extracting magnitude information. Therefore, in Experiment 2, we produced two novel types of dot array stimuli: “controlled” and “correlated” stimuli. The correlated stimuli are those which have a one-to-one correspondence between total area and numerosity. The controlled stimuli all share the same total area of dots, regardless of numerosity. We have also created five stimulus variations for each type of dot array to further prevent participants from relying on pattern recognition, thus creating a total of 30 stimuli. Crucially, trials are always matched in terms of controlled or correlated stimuli; for example, if a participant sees a controlled reference stimulus, then the test stimulus will also be controlled. Further information can be found in the “Manipulated Variables” section. For Experiment 2b, we wanted to further extend these findings to include an additional set of numerosities. In Eccher et al.’s (2025) original study, there were three numerosities used (4, 12, 36) which have a ratio of 3. As well as these stimuli, we created stimuli of 8, 16 and 32, this time with a ratio of 2, to investigate whether previously observed effects still hold for a new set of numerosities. As with stimulus type, the numerosity set will be consistent within trials, but the order of trials will be intermixed. In Experiment 2c, we replicate the procedure of Experiment 2b, but this time the numerosity set is a between-participants factor. Participants will be randomly allocated to one numerosity set for the entire duration of the experiment. This is to investigate whether the results of Experiment 2b can be explained by the intermixing of numerosity sets.

abstract_r: This is a conceptual replication of Henne et al. (2019). In this experiment, I will manipulate the causal structure (conjunctive|disjunctive) and the action type of the potential cause (action|inaction), and I will ask participants for their causal judgments. I will investigate whether there is an interaction between causal structure and the action type of the potential cause such that participants judge actions as more causal than inactions (the action effect) in conjunctive scenarios and they judge actions as less causal than inactions (the reverse-action effect) in disjunctive scenarios.

title_r: Replication of De Neys et al. (2013) at Thompson Rivers University
abstract_r: We are a group of Thompson Rivers University students and will be conducting a replication of the De Neys et al. (2013) study as part of the CREP project. Our team includes Sabrina Broad, Hayleigh Armstrong, Alexandra Melo, and Liam Campbell under the supervision of Eva Rubínová. We are seeking to replicate the study "Bats, balls, and substitution sensitivity: Cognitive misers are no happy fools" by Wim De Neys, Sandrine Rossi, and Olivier Houdé (2013). We are completing this direct replication with an online version of the study using Qualtrics. Participants will be recruited through Facebook. After participants provide consent with study participation and answer three demographic questions (age, gender, and language fluency), the survey will randomly assign participants into two groups. The first group will receive the standard version of the bat and ball problem, while the second group will receive the control version of the problem. After completing the math problems associated with each group, the participants will make confidence ratings associated with their responses (0%= Low confidence; 100%= High confidence). Finally, participants will answer a data quality question: "Finally, we would like to ask if you completed this study honestly. Do you think we should use your data?" We will exclude data from participants who answer "No" to this question. Participants will be debriefed at the end of the survey.

title_r: Preregistration: U.S. 2024 Election - Social Safety across Personal and Sociopolitical Relational Worlds
abstract_r: This project will use the federal election in the U.S. on November 5 2024 to examine how people sustain feelings of safety in social connection in the face of uncertainty about others’ motivations. The social safety system model (Murray et al., 2021) assumes that people exist within layers of interdependence, spanning close personal bonds (e.g., children, parents, and friends) and extended collective bonds (e.g., neighbors, health systems, and governments). It also assumes that people are highly motivated to feel safe (i.e., protected, cared for) in such social connections (Baumeister & Leary, 1995). Thus, being uncertain of the motivations of others in specific situations is threatening and motivates people to find an alternate source of safety. Research has revealed two safety-affirming defenses. Specifically, the experience of uncertainty in the personal relationships one shares with others—not being able to anticipate or explain the behavior of close intimates (e.g., romantic partners, children, friends)—motivates people to see the collective or sociopolitical relationships they share with others as especially trustworthy (e.g., government, political leaders). However, the experience of uncertainty in the collective or sociopolitical relationships one shares with others—not being able to anticipate or explain the behavior of one’s government, Prime Minister, or fellow citizens, for instance, motivates people to see the personal relationships they share with others, such as spouses, friends, and/or children, as especially trustworthy (Murray, Lamarche et al., 2021; Murray, Seery et al., 2021; Murray et al., 2023). The current research extends such theorizing to people’s experience of the highly contentious and uncertain federal election in the US. This project further tests the novel hypothesis that a person’s dis/advantage in life helps shape the likelihood that they will need and thus engage such safety-affirming defenses from pre- to post-election. People generally need to be more vigilant to how others might benefit/harm them when they are less advantaged or powerful than others, and thus, more dependent on them (Murray & Pascuzzi, 2024). Therefore, we expect experiences with relative disadvantage to heighten the safety-threat posed by not being able to anticipate or explain others’ behavior, more strongly engaging “safety-affirming” defenses. This project examines three markers of relative disadvantage as moderators of responses to uncertainty: (1) disadvantage in life circumstances (i.e., childhood instability, current socioeconomic status, racial minority status, financial worry), (2) disadvantage in political representation (e.g., one’s preferred party expecting to lose/losing the election), and (3) disadvantage in relationship circumstances (e.g., less trust in romantic partner, insecure attachment). To overview the study design, participants on Prolific will be invited to complete two short surveys, a pre-election survey administered one day in advance of the November 5th, 2024 general election and a post-election survey administered one day post-election. At the time of this writing, it is unclear whether the electoral college results will be known the day after the election (given legal efforts to mandate counting votes by hand in critical swing states). Therefore, depending on how events unfold, we may adjust the timing of the post-election survey (to a maximum of 5 days post-election) to better ensure knowledge of the Presidential outcome. This election study is designed as a conceptual replication and extension of our study of the July 2024 U.K. national election. However, differences in certainty about the outcome of the U.K. vs. U.S. election required adding/adjusting measures/planned composites for the U.S. sample. As one example, because it was clear that Labour would win the U.K. election, we could assume that participants would answer questions about the post-election future with a Labour government in mind. However, the lack of outcome certainty in the U.S. meant that we needed to ask questions about the future contingent on imagining both a Harris and a Trump presidency.

title_r: Do Norwegians still conform after 65 years?
abstract_r: The study we chose to replicate is Solomon Asch’s conformity experiment which was conducted in 1951. The purpose of the study was to investigate how opinions of others affect one’s own opinion, and how strong the social conformity urge can be. Asch’s original study used a group of seven to nine male college students assembled in a classroom for a psychological experiment in visual judgement. All but one of the subjects were confederates of the experimenter and were instructed to answer wrong in some of the trials for testing the real subject against social pressure. The subjects were informed that they would be comparing the length of lines. During the experiment, the subjects would be shown two different cards, one with a single vertical black line, and one with three vertical lines of different lengths. The subjects would be told to decide which of the three lines that matched the length of the card with a single line, in the order of their seating. The confederate subjects would be answering before the real subject. When the confederate subjects start answering against the obvious answer, Asch predict that the real subject would then feel insecure and conform to the answers of the group despite knowing the correct answer. The first statistical results were from a series in which a total of 123 subjects form three institutions of higher education participated. Two alternatives were open to the subject: he could either act independently repudiating the majority or repudiating the evidence of his own senses. Of the 123 participants, a considerable percentage yielded to the majority. Results typically used in majority of social psychology textbooks say that the responses on the critical trials were that 76 percent of participants conformed at least once to an incorrect answer by the majority (Smith & Haslam, 2017, p. 79). We have chosen to do a conceptual replication of Asch line judgement study but will be using similar elements like Milgram’s (1961) own replication study of Asch’s. We will, like Milgram, be using sound instead of lines and we are using Norwegians as our participants but are not including Frenchmen. We are only comparing the result data of the Norwegian participants in Milgram’s study. The Norwegians error rate was 62% in 1961. Asch’s line judgement study has inspired additional research on conformity and group behavior. It has given an insight on how, why, and when people conform and the effects of social pressure on behavior. Due to the original experiment not having strong external validity, since it was only white male American participants at roughly the same age, replications of this experiment could include a variety of participants, e.g., from different countries. This can give varying results and more knowledge about conformity and group pressure. A replication of this study will have few ethical issues, and as it is considered one of the most famous studies in psychology that had a huge impact on society, conducting replications of this would be advantageous. Based on the cultural development and the rise of individualism in the last decades, there is reason to believe that a replication of this experiment will not yield the same results (Myers et al., 2021, p. 279-280). Increased living standards and the globalization are two important variables that were absent during the previous testing, which may affect the potential social-sanctions and rewards that can correlate with conformity. By other words, there are new, missing and changed variables at this time. Therefore, we predict that people would be less likely to conform.

title_r: ITE-Social_Agreement
abstract_r: The current pre-registration is for a follow-up experiment of the previously pre-registered study (see https://osf.io/qk9v5). In the previous pre-registered study, we examined whether agreement with a social political opinion statement impacts the illusory truth effect (ITE) for these types of statements. To do so, we conducted a conceptual replication of the study by Riesthuis and Woods (exp 3; 2023) but made some minor changes (see https://osf.io/qk9v5). Specifically, 1) we only included social political opinion statements, 2) repeated and new statements were completely randomized, 3) power analyses were conducted to ascertain enough statistical power for equivalence and minimum-effect tests (Riesthuis, 2024), and 4) we added agreement ratings at the end of the experiment to examine its role in the ITE. The procedure of the experiment was the same as in Riesthuis and Woods (exp3; 2023). Specifically, in Part 1, participants viewed 30 random social political opinion statement and assigned categories. Then, participants engaged in a 5-minute distractor task. Afterwards, in Part 2, participants were asked to rate the truthfulness of 30 repeated and 30 new social political opinion statements. Last, in Part 3, participants were asked to indicate their political agreement with the social political opinion statements (i.e., agree, neutral, or disagree). Interestingly, the results showed equivalent subjective truthfulness ratings for social political opinion statements that were repeated and new. In other words, we found no evidence of an ITE for social political opinion statements. When only examining social political opinion statements that participants agreed with or were neutral about, we found evidence of equivalence meaning that repeated statements did not receive higher truth rating than new statements (90% CI fell completely within the equivalence bounds). The results concerning social political opinion statements that participants disagreed with were inconclusive (statistically significant effect but 90% CI included the smallest effect size of interest). This most likely due to the fact that participants more frequently agreed with or were neutral about the statements leading to lower statistical power for the analysis on disagreed statements. Considering the methodological improvements (e.g., more statistical power; equivalence tests; randomized repeated and new statements, etc.) of this replication study (vs exp 3 of Riesthuis & Woods, 2023) and the fact that the findings for the ITE for social political opinion statements in experiment 3 of Riesthuis and Woods (2023) were inconclusive (i.e., 90% CI included the SESOI; see Riesthuis, 2024), it seems that there may not be an ITE for social political opinion statements. However, it has been shown before that how information is encoded plays a crucial role in the ITE (Calvillo & Harris, 2022; Riesthuis & Woods, 2023). Hence, in the second experiment, we will examine whether indicating agreement with statements during encoding might lead to an ITE. Specifically, instead of assigning categories during encoding, participants will now rate their agreement with the statements during Part 1 and provide the first subjective truthfulness rating (i.e., timepoint 1). Hence, in Part 1 (i.e., timepoint 1) participants will read a social political opinion statement and decide if they politically speaking agree, disagree, or have a neutral opinion about the statement and also provide a truthfulness rating on a 7-point Likert scale. In Part 2 (i.e., timepoint 2), participants will only provide subjective truthfulness ratings for 60 social political opinion statements of which 30 were presented during Part 1. Hypotheses: 1) We do not expect an overall ITE for the social political opinion statements. That is, we expect the subjective truth ratings for social political opinion statements to be equivalent (given our smallest effect size of interest; SESOI) at timepoint 1 (truth ratings during encoding) and timepoint 2 (truth ratings during Part 2; within-item comparison; Dechêne et al., 2010). We also expect no ITE for social political opinion statements that were repeated versus new (truth ratings at timepoint 2; between-item comparison; Dechêne et al., 2010). 2) We also do not expect to find the ITE for social political opinion statements that participants agreed with. Specifically, we expect subjective truth ratings for social political opinion statements that participants agreed with to be equivalent at timepoint 1 (truth ratings during encoding) and timepoint 2 (truth ratings during Part 2). 3) We also do not expect to find the ITE for social political opinion statements that participants disagreed with. Specifically, we expect subjective truth ratings for social political opinion statements that participants disagreed with to be equivalent at timepoint 1 (truth ratings during encoding) and timepoint 2 (truth ratings during Part 2). 4) We also do not expect to find the ITE for social political opinion statements that participants were neutral about. Specifically, we expect subjective truth ratings for social political opinion statements that participants were neutral about to be equivalent at timepoint 1 (truth ratings during encoding) and timepoint 2 (truth ratings during Part 2). Methods Participants Participants will be recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk. Because the socio-political statements are specifically relevant for a population from the USA, one requirement is that participants have to be from the USA. Additional requirements were a HIT approval rate of 98% and more than 5000 HITs approved. Simulation based power analyses for a traditional null hypothesis significance two-tailed paired sample t-test (Riesthuis, 2024), for a Cohen’s dz = .29, and α = .05, indicated that we will need 200 participants to have .95 statistical power (see Rscript and Rmarkdown for power analyses). Using these parameters, we will also have .87 statistical power for minimum-effect testing. Lastly, using the same parameters, we also have .94 statistical power for equivalence testing (assuming the true raw mean difference is 0; .81 statistical power if we assume the true raw mean difference is .06). In line with previous research (Riesthuis & Woods, 2023; see https://osf.io/qk9v5), our SESOI was a .2 raw mean difference in subjective truth ratings on a 7-point Likert scale. We chose this SESOI because repeating information is a quite low-cost manipulation which can easily be repeated on social media platforms (e.g., retweets via X - formerly known as Twitter), meaning the effects can accumulate (Funder & Ozer, 2019). This is particularly relevant because previous research showed that multiple repetitions can increase the illusory truth effect (Hassan & Barber, 2021). Moreover, since we use ambiguous statements, these accumulations in subjective truth ratings can lead participants to assume the statements are true and we therefore deemed a raw mean difference of .2 as the SESOI. To calculate the standardized mean difference (Cohen’s dz), we used the standard deviations of (SD1 = 1.29, SD2 = 1.29) and correlation (r = .86) from the previous study (see https://osf.io/qk9v5). title_r: Do verbal rehearsal and visual imagery lead to differential memory traces in the left and right cerebral hemisphere (StratEffect)?
abstract_r: The study builds upon Alan Paivio’s observation that the instruction to use visual imagery while encoding words improves recollection of these words compared with a situation in which the words were only encoded by reading. Seamon & Gazzaniga (1973) postulate that these two “encoding strategies” rely on different processing systems located in different hemispheres. That is, a verbal processing system, which is specialized for speech and reading, may be seen to be primarily located in the left hemisphere, while a visual-spatial processing system, which deals with spatial relations of objects, is considered to be situated in the right hemisphere. Thus, the superiority of using visual imagery could be partially explained by utilizing right hemispheric visual-spatial processing in addition to the left hemispheric verbal processing. While these findings nicely illustrate the potential relevance of hemispheric specialisation for the understanding of cognitive phenomena like the dual-coding theory. The original study suffered from several shortcomings. Small sample size (N=6) and low number of trials per condition as well as technical limitations of the then available equipment, might be taken to question the reliability of the findings. Literature search yielded only two sources which indicated a replication of the original findings. Metzger & Antes (1976) replicate the findings (at least when using pictures a probe material, Experiment II), while also having small sample size and trial number. Bersted (1983) claims replication of the strategy effect (in a footnote) but the results are not presented in the citing article, and the original poster presentation/abstract is not available. At the same time, the literature search also did not reveal any failed replication attempts. Objective of the present study is to replicate the strategy effect in a large sample and using modern equipment.

abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: This registration preregisters our data collection and analysis plan for a replication of Eskine, Racinik, and Prinz (2011) at Tufts University (Spring, 2017). This plan was approved by the Collaborative Replication and Education Project team on Wed, Mar 8, 2017. Data collection, which has not yet begun, is slated to start as early as Fri, Mar 10, 2017. For full details, see the Wiki for this project, from which the following description of research questions and hypotheses was excerpted:

Research Questions

In this study, we will closely replicate an experiment reported by Eskine, Racinik, and Prinz (2011) . Eskine, Kacinik, and Prinz (2011) tested the hypothesis that moral judgments are influenced by our current emotional state. In their experiment, participants consumed a couple of swigs of a bitter, disgusting drink (Swedish Bitters), a sweet sugary drink (Minute Maid Berry Punch), or a neutral drink (water). Participants then evaluated the moral wrongness of a series of hypothetical scenarios. Results suggested that participants who drank the disgusting drink evaluated the behavior portrayed in the scenarios as significantly more morally wrong compared to participants who drank the sweet or neutral drinks. The authors further found some evidence to suggest that political orientation moderated this effect.

There are three reasons why this work is a great candidate for replication, especially in the context of a laboratory class this semester at Tufts University, PSY 42, Emotion Laboratory. First, the main objective of my emotion laboratory class is to teach students how to do research that examines the influence of emotion on behavior; the topic of this study perfectly fits the bill. Second, this study is one of several candidates for replication featured as part of the Collaborative Replication and Education Project (CREP) . CREP uses crowdsourcing to encourage replication by undergraduate researchers. It is a study that has been approved by IRBs and conducted by undergraduate researchers at a number of academic institutions, including Illinois Institute of Technology, Southern Oregon University, Wesleyan University, University of Minnesota, and others. Third, a replication that draws on a larger sample size will enable us to estimate the size of the effect with greater precision.

Hypotheses

This replication will test the same hypotheses examined by Eskine and colleagues (2011). They reported their hypotheses on page 296 as follows:

"If moral disgust really does stem from physical disgust, we hypothesized, then taste perception should affect moral processing such that a disgusting beverage should elicit greater moral disgust than a sweet beverage or a control beverage (water).

We hypothesized that if conservatives are indeed more sensitive to disgust, then the taste manipulation should affect their moral processing more strongly than the moral processing of liberals."

title_r: Replicating the Unconscious Working Memory Effect: A Multisite Preregistered Study.
abstract_r: Although in recent years some studies have found evidence suggesting that working memory (WM) may operate on unconscious perceptual contents, decisive demonstrations of the existence of unconscious WM are lacking. In the present Registered Report, we aim to replicate the first study on this topic by Soto et al. (2011), using a multisite sample from different laboratories, with a larger number of participants and trials than those typically used in previous studies. As a result, a highly-powered, open-access dataset will be available for researchers and future analyses. Furthermore, some minimal baseline requirements will be guaranteed for the experimental task (i.e., number of valid trials, motivation, and consistent labels for the perceptual awareness scale). We will critically test the hypotheses commonly proposed: above-chance performance in cue-present trials reported as unseen, a null correlation between performance and cue detection sensitivity, and a significantly above-chance intercept in the regression of performance on sensitivity. Crucially, the interpretation of all three results is based on the assumption that the measures are sufficiently reliable. Given the scarcity of reliability estimations in this literature, we will calculate these estimates for our measures.

title_r: Foodie Calls - A Preregistered Replication Study
abstract_r: When it comes to the question of who is going to pay on a first date, it is not always clear how the bill is shared. While the consensus is hard to reach in many societies, gender roles, which are greatly impacted by culture, play a huge role in determining the answer to this highly debated question. In societies where traditional gender roles and norms are clearly defined and exercised, it might be expected that it is usually men who pay the bill on a first date (Delucia, 1987; Jaramillo-Sierra &amp; Allen, 2013; Wu et al., 2021). In a study based on a US sample, Collisson and colleagues (2020) reported that some women, especially the ones with dark personality traits and traditional gender role beliefs are prone to abuse men in order to receive a free meal on a first date without feeling any actual romantic attraction. However, the impact of Dark Triad personality traits might be irrelevant in circumstances, if traditional gender roles are more explicitly pronounced in society because of the expected norms that suggest men should always pay. The aim of this study is to test the impact of the Dark Triad personality traits on the “foodie call” behavior, which refers to the situation “where a person, despite a lack of romantic attraction to a suitor, chooses to go on a date to get a free meal” (Collisson et al., 2020, p. 425). The study is designed as a pre-registered replication study. The materials are presented on the OSF website.

title_r: Modulation of visual contrast sensitivity with transcranial random noise stimulation
abstract_r: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) has been shown to significantly improve visual perception. These performance improvements manifested as both (i) after-effects of visual training combined with tRNS (Fertonani et al., 2011; Pirulli et al., 2013; Contemori et al., 2019; Herpich et al., 2019) and (ii) acute effects during tRNS (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; Ghin et al., 2018; van der Groen et al., 2018, 2019; Battaglini et al., 2019, 2020; Pavan et al., 2019). It has been postulated that the Stochastic resonance (SR) phenomenon underlie noise-induced signal enhancement in studies investigating the acute effect of tRNS on visual processing (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018, 2019; Battaglini et al., 2019, 2020; Pavan et al., 2019). SR describes the phenomenon that the response of nonlinear systems to weak, subthreshold signals can be enhanced by adding an optimal level of random noise (Moss et al., 2004; McDonnell and Abbott, 2009). One important feature indicative of the SR phenomenon is that noise benefits are a function of noise intensity and exhibit an inverted U-shape relationship. Thus, while the optimal level of noise benefits performance, excessive noise is detrimental (van der Groen and Wenderoth 2016; van der Groen et al. 2018; Pavan et al. 2019). Previous studies investigating the acute effect of tRNS on visual detection performance have shown that noise stimulation was particularly beneficial when the visual stimuli were presented with near-threshold intensity (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018; Battaglini et al., 2019). Currently, it is unknown whether signal enhancement via SR could be achieved separately within different neural substrates along the retino-cortical pathway. Inducing SR via tRNS offers a unique opportunity to investigate this question. Here we plan a series of three experiments which will be executed in three separate sessions. Experiment 1: TRNS over primary visual cortex (V1) has been shown previously to improve visual contrast detection (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016). Here we aim to replicate these results in a new cohort and to determine the optimal tRNS intensity for each individual participant. Experiment 2: Previous research has suggested that the retina and the optical nerve are highly susceptible to alternating currents (Schutter and Hortensius, 2010). Improvement in vision was reported after repetitive transorbital alternating current stimulation over the retina, in studies involving patients with optic neuropathy or after optic nerve lesions (Gall et al., 2010; Fedorov et al., 2011). The retina and the optic nerve are an interesting target because they can be reliably reached even with low transcranial electrical stimulation intensities, since the eyeball is an excellent conductor. Here we will test whether tRNS applied to the retina and the optic nerve improves visual contrast detection in accordance with the SR mechanism. We will apply different tRNS intensities to determine the optimal intensity for each individual participant. Experiment 3: It is currently unknown whether SR effects are additive when noise is applied to connected yet anatomically remote neural populations. Here we will investigate whether simultaneous application of tRNS to the retina and V1 causes additive effects.

title_r: What is the ideal time to provide corrective feedback? An approximate replication of Li, Zhu, & Ellis (2016)
abstract_r: This study is an approximate replication of Li, Zhu, and Ellis (2016) that examined the comparative effects of immediate and delayed corrective feedback on second language development. The purpose of this replication is to (1) examine the influence of feedback timing on vocational language learners and (2) verify the hypothesis that the advantage of immediate feedback over delayed feedback found by the original study is due to the practice opportunities available in immediate feedback. 175 first-year ESL learners at a vocational college will be divided into five groups including four experimental groups and one control group. The experimental groups will receive a two-hour treatment consisting of two dictogloss tasks and will receive immediate (during tasks), delayed (after both tasks), interim (between tasks), or no feedback on their wrong use of the English passive voice. It is hypothesized that immediate feedback will outperform interim feedback which in turn will show larger effects than delayed feedback.

title_r: Replicating Attribute Amnesia Effect in the Single-Stimulus Design
abstract_r: Attribute Amnesia refers to the phenomenon that subjects fail to report some features (e.g., colour) of a stimulus after they have been asked to repetitively report some other features (e.g., numeric parity) of the same stimulus (Chen & Wyble, 2015). This effect has shown strong replicability in the multi-stimuli design, in which there are normally one target among three distractors stimuli. Recently, Wang et al. (2021) furtherly showed the robustness of this effect when there was only one stimulus on the screen. As the main experiment of the current project will be conducted online, we aim to pre-register replication attempt of Experiment 1 of Wang et al. (2021) in the online-experiment setting. title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Imhoff et al. (2020; preprint), from PsyArXiv
abstract_r: We selected the claim that conspiracy theories that suggest that the coronavirus pandemic is a hoax are expected to primarily be related to refusal to engage in containment-related behavior (e.g., hygiene, physical distancing). This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “Whereas conspiracy beliefs describing the pandemic as a hoax were more strongly associated with reduced containment-related behavior, conspiracy beliefs about sinister forces purposefully creating the virus related to an increase in self-centered prepping behavior.” Containment-related behaviors was regressed on the ‘hoax’ conspiracy belief scale, and political orientation. This analysis yielded that believing that COVID-19 was a hoax was a strong negative predictor of containment-related behaviors like hand-washing and keeping physical distance, B=-0.647, SE=0.109, p<.001.

title_r: The Role of Working Memory in Scalar Implicature Comprehension in ADHD and Neurotypical Adults
abstract_r: This study investigates the real-time processing of sentences that can give rise to a phenomenon called “scalar implicature” in the psycholinguistics literature. A scalar implicature refers to when a sentence with a scalar term has both an implied and literal meaning. For instance, the scalar term ‘some’ implies “some and not all” but can also literally mean “some and possibly all”. Prior research indicates that the cognitive effort associated with producing the “some, and possibly all” interpretation is significantly less than the “some, but not all” interpretation. Several studies have demonstrated that accessing the latter interpretation requires more working memory resources (De Neys & Schaeken, 2007; Dieussaert et al., 2011; Marty et al., 2013; Antoniou et al., 2016; Cho, 2021). Independently of this, it has been observed that ADHD individuals have greater working memory deficits compared to neurotypical individuals (Kofler et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014). In this present study, we hope to build on previous findings suggesting that scalar implicatures require cognitive effort, by looking at how working memory load impacts implicature computation in a sentence verification task. We aim to compare the aforementioned groups (1. neurotypical adults and 2. adults with ADHD) to observe how working memory capacity differentially affects computation. This study will be an exact replication of De Neys & Schaeken’s (2007) with the addition of an ADHD group. We hypothesise that if working memory plays a role in scalar implicature computation, and if ADHD adults have a more limited working memory capacity compared to neurotypical adults, then the working memory load should affect their performance more than neurotypical adults’ performance. To our knowledge, the phenomenon of scalar implicature computation has not yet been studied in this population. This will not only build on our understanding of how diverse cognitive abilities affect scalar implicature computation, it will also allow us to understand how individuals with ADHD process language in real-time and how executive dysfunction, specifically working memory deficits, might impact pragmatic language comprehension more generally. While the research will not explicitly aid intervention, it will build on the growing literature. In the future, this might help open avenues for language intervention for this population, and enrich our understanding of the specific language difficulties that might need to be addressed. The overall aims of this study are to: 1. replicate the finding that working memory limitations impair the derivation of scalar implicatures 2. find out whether adults with ADHD, who have been demonstrated to have working memory deficits have different scalar implicature interpretation patterns compared to neurotypical adults.
