title_r: Forgetting the Perceptual Detail of Episodic Event Elements
abstract_r: When we remember events from our past, for example, a dinner we had with our friend, we tend to bring to mind an image involving the central elements of the situation – the location, the person we were with, and the food we had. Across multiple studies, Horner and colleagues (Horner & Burgess, 2013; Horner & Burgess, 2014; Horner, Bisby, Bush, Lin, & Burgess, 2015; Joensen, Gaskell, & Horner, 2019) have demonstrated that complex episodic events built via encoding word associations (kitchen-Barack Obama-hammer) are retrieved and forgotten in an all-or-none manner. Once one element of the event is cued, people are likely to recall the other elements involved in this event. These findings suggest that all elements of an episodic event are bound within an episodic representation, which upon retrieval is re-activated in full based on a partial cue (i.e., via the process of pattern completion, Horner et al., 2015). Whilst the identities of episodic event elements are retrieved in a holistic (all-or-none) manner, this may not hold true for lower-level perceptual aspects of long-term memory (LTM). For example, object features such as an object’s exemplar, state, and colour have been found to fragment as a function of forgetting (Brady, Konkle, Alvarez, & Oliva, 2013; Utochkin, & Brady, 2020). In particular, the state and colour of an object are forgotten at different rates, and the successful retrieval of one object feature (e.g., exemplar) no longer predicts the retrieval of another feature (e.g., state) after a delay (Brady et al., 2013; but see Balaban, Assaf, Arad Meir, & Luria, 2019). This also seems to be the case with regards to the precision with which the spatial context and colour of objects are retrieved; the retrieval of the gist of these aspects is dependent but the resolution with which each feature is retrieved is somewhat independent (Cooper, & Ritchey, 2019). Taken together, these findings seem to suggest that precise perceptual features of objects are not bound within the same episodic representation and that different features tend to be forgotten independently over time. We recently proposed that the findings described above can be reconciled if we consider the hierarchical nature of episodic memory and make a distinction between event-based and item-based neural representations (Andermane, Joensen, & Horner, 2020). Specifically, hippocampus-based representations of associations between elements from the same spatiotemporal context may remain relatively coherent over time and may be retrieved in full via the process of hippocampal pattern completion. In contrast, perirhinal object-based representations involving perceptual features (i.e., shape and colour) may fragment with time, given the overlapping and distributed nature of these representations, and their susceptibility to interference by individual low-level features. In a recent study, we asked participants to encode episodic events by studying images of objects, famous people and locations, and to use their mental imagery to create associations between the elements. Using this method, we replicated the pattern of holistic forgetting previously observed for episodic event associations encoded via word pairs (Joensen et al., 2019). In the present study, we will further investigate time-dependent changes in the retrieval accuracy and dependency of object features (i.e., state and colour). Importantly, we will keep the encoding task the same as in our previous work, such that each object is encoded as a part of an episodic event. We will present participants with images of three elements (an object, a famous person, and a location) and ask them to imagine an episodic event involving these elements. Participants’ memory of object features will then be tested immediately after encoding and after a delay of 3 days. The object features we will test are colour (e.g., a yellow or a purple umbrella) and state (e.g., an open or a closed wardrobe). In the test phase, participants will be asked to select the object they saw among object lures with combinations of correct and incorrect features (e.g., the object in the same state but in a different colour). In line with previous findings on the fragmentation of object-based LTM representations (Brady et al., 2013), we hypothesise that the dependency between the retrieval of one feature, given the retrieval of another, will decrease over time. We will also administer the self-report Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) (Marks, 1973), to explore whether individual differences in mental imagery predict retrieval accuracy, dependency, and confidence. Mental imagery and episodic memory share similar phenomenal characteristics (Moscovitch, Cabeza, Winocur, & Nadel, 2016) and there are stable individual differences in self-reported vividness of imagery that are correlated with neural activation patterns during imagery (Cui, Jeter, Yang, Montague, & Eagleman, 2007). We will test the more exploratory hypothesis that individual differences in imagery may represent accessibility of episodic memory traces and the strength of their reinstatement in neocortex. We expect a positive correlation between the reported vividness of imagery and memory performance.

title_r: Replication of Social Comparisons on social media
abstract_r: A conceptual replication of a study done by Fardouly et. al. (2014) where the focus is on the impact of Tiktok (Facebook in original) on young women's body image concerns and mood. A 2-part study between-particpants experimental design. Participants will be 200 female students between 18-25 years of age from the University of Saint Francis and a demographic of less than 75% white. Part 1 includes browsing a website and part 2 is an email survey. Control group browsing neutral videos. Group 2 will scroll on TikTok on their personal account. Group 3 will scroll through instagram reels on their personal account. Participants will be misled that the study is an investigation of the influence of media use on memory. Provide informed consent and state they will report their mood because this has been previously found to influence memory as well. Participants will do a pre-exposure state VAS measure of negative mood and body dissatisfaction. They will browse their webiste for 10 minutes and then do a post-exposure state VAS measures and state appearance-discrepancy measure. There will be a brief memory task where they are shown 30 random words for 30 seconds and asked to write down as many as they can remember. Another VAS measure. They will be sent an email one week later containing an online survey. This survey will include trait measures of appearance comparison tendency, filler questionairres, and demongraphic questioannaires. They will also report what they remember the study being about and asked to write down any words they remember from the previous memory task and memory-related questionnaires. Participants will be debriefed upon completion.

title_r: The Forward Effect of Judgements of Learning and Retrieval Practice on Memory and Transfer
abstract_r: Prior research has shown that retrieval can enhance learning of new (i.e., not-previously presented) information. This forward testing effect (FTE; for reviews, see Pastötter & Bäuml, 2014; Yang et al., 2018, 2021) has already been demonstrated with various study materials (e.g., single words, key-term definitions, texts and videos; for a meta-analysis, see Chan et al., 2018b). It has been suggested that metacognitive judgements, specifically Judgments of Learning (JOLs), are based on at least partial covert retrieval attempts when not all information is available (Dougherty et al., 2018), and thereby can produce retrieval-like effects. Thus, JOLs do not only index metacognitive monitoring (Rhodes, 2015), but can also enhance learning (Tauber & Witherby, 2019). Only a few prior studies examined the extent to which JOLs can enhance new learning of information (see Kubik et al., 2022; Lee & Ha, 2019). In the present study, we aim to investigate the relative advantage of JOLs (perhaps eliciting covert retrieval) and overt retrieval on new episodic and inductive learning compared to restudy. Lee and Ha (2019) examined forward effects of metacognitive judgments on inductive learning in two sections. In Section A, participants learned the painting styles of six artists by studying 36 painting–artist pairs (i.e., six paintings per artist). They were then asked to restudy these prior 36 pairs, take a cued-recall test on them (i.e., using the painting as a cue to retrieve the artist’s name), or evaluate the pairs’ learning status by performing a JOL task: Participants were either asked to perform item-based JOLs (i.e., assessing probability that they could identify the artist of a particular painting in a later test when the painting–artist pair is presented); category-based JOLs (i.e., assessing the probability that they could identify new paintings of an artist when the artist’s last name was shown); or global JOLs (in response to a single prompt that solicit an aggregate estimation of their future overall learning performance). In Section B, they learned six painting styles by studying 36 painting–artist pairs. Subsequently, they received a final cumulative transfer test, in which 48 new paintings (i.e., 4 of each artist) were presented in a single-choice test; participants’ task was to choose the correct artists’ last name. The authors demonstrated that category-based JOLs enhanced performance in a later transfer test identifying new paintings of the same artists, but item-based judgments did not. The latter finding in Experient 1 of Lee and Ha (2019) might be due to the fact that the task consisted of participants evaluating their learning of specific painting–artist pairs, which was inconsistent with the objective of learning the artists’ general painting styles and applying them in a transfer test. In addition, item-based judgments were solicited based on the complete cue–target pairs, that is, including both the cue (painting) and the target (last name of the artist). Lee and Ha (2019) argued that item-based JOLs cannot enhance new inductive learning of painting styles. We hypothesize that presenting the cue–target pairs rather than only the cue reduced the likelihood that participants engaged in covert retrieval when making JOLs. Based on the two-stage theory (Son & Metcalfe, 2005), making JOLs on complete information may only involve a first pre-retrieval stage of a quick familiarity assessment, while JOLs based on incomplete information likely covert retrieval attempts and thereby to enhance new inductive learning, similarly to overt retrieval practice. That is, participants are more likely to attempt complete retrieval attempts from memory when only the painting without the artist’s last name is presented than when both the cue (painting) and the target (last name of the artist) are presented. A first indication was provided by Kubik et al. (2022) using simple lists of words that JOLs based on incomplete information (i.e., cue-only JOLs) but not on complete information (i.e., cue–target JOLs) can enhance new learning. However, analogous research has not been conducted with more complex materials or inductive learning. To this end, we aim to replicate and extend the study by Lee and Ha (2019). We investigate and compare the benefits of JOLs and retrieval practice on future learning using pairs of paintings and artists. However, in addition to groups of cue–target JOLs, overt retrieval practice and restudy, we added an additional experimental group of cue-only JOLs.

title_r: Revisiting Schachter’s Research on Rejection, Deviance, and Communication
abstract_r: We propose a replication of the original Schachter (1951) deviation-rejection study. Schachter’s ground-breaking demonstration of the deviation-rejection link has captivated social psychologists for decades. The findings and paradigm were so compelling that the deviation-rejection link is often taken for granted and sometimes may be misrepresented (Berkowitz, 1971; Wahrman & Pugh, 1972). Because there have only been two direct replications, one of which by the original author, we believe it is important to revisit the original study.

title_r: Temporal Dynamics of Allocentric and Egocentric SR-Compatibility
abstract_r: Umilta & Liotti (1987) observed that the classic Simon effect vanishes when such egocentric SR-compatibility is factorially combined with local SR-compatibility, unless a temporal delay is inserted between presentation of the local reference frame and the target stimulus. On the contrary, a conceptual replication of this study by one of the present authors found the Simon effect to be attenuated but not fully vanished in the no-delay condition. Notably, however, small design differences existed between the studies, such as whether a color or shape discrimination task was employed. The rationale for the present study can be subsumed under two points: 1) We aim to test whether the disparate results are due to these subtle design/setup differences between the studies. Thus, we expect to replicate the results of Umilta and Lotti (1987) under conditions of a direct replication (equal setup/design). 2) We aim to better understand the causes of the observed modulation by complementing mean reaction time (RT) analysis with distributional-level analysis. Specifically, it has been suggested that the time-course of the congruency effect as measured via delta plots (DPs) depends on the relative timing of target and distractor processing (e.g., Ulrich et al., 2015; Mackenzie et al., 2022). Accordingly, we expect the DP slopes of the Simon effect to differ between the delay conditions.

title_r: Lecture Fluency and Learning Performance Replication
abstract_r: During the process of learning new content, it is common to perceive or judge ones' learning performance presumptuously when information is presented in a fluent (easy to understand) manner. In actuality, this is an illusion--this does not translate to an increase in learning performance. This observation can indicate that there may be a possibility that students misjudge their own learning efficiency based on the fluent manner in which the information is delivered. This study aims to further explore the effect of lecturer fluency on judgments of learning (JOL) and their actual performance. We sought to replicate experiment 1A which examined fluency (fluent vs. disfluent lecture videos) at 2 different time points. Most importantly, this study showed that learning performance was positively impacted by lecture fluency (at Time 2) which is a direct contrast to the original Carpenter et al. (2013) study which showed that fluency does not enhance learning. In relation to JOLs , they were higher for those who were exposed to the fluent lecturer compared to the disfluent lecturer. This replicates prior studies on lecturer fluency and metamemory judgements.

title_r: What is the ideal time to provide corrective feedback? An approximate replication of Li, Zhu, & Ellis (2016)
abstract_r: This study is an approximate replication of Li, Zhu, and Ellis (2016) that examined the comparative effects of immediate and delayed corrective feedback on second language development. The purpose of this replication is to (1) examine the influence of feedback timing on vocational language learners and (2) verify the hypothesis that the advantage of immediate feedback over delayed feedback found by the original study is due to the practice opportunities available in immediate feedback. 175 first-year ESL learners at a vocational college will be divided into five groups including four experimental groups and one control group. The experimental groups will receive a two-hour treatment consisting of two dictogloss tasks and will receive immediate (during tasks), delayed (after both tasks), interim (between tasks), or no feedback on their wrong use of the English passive voice. It is hypothesized that immediate feedback will outperform interim feedback which in turn will show larger effects than delayed feedback.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Blagov et al. (2020), from PsyArXiv
abstract_r: We selected the claim that meanness may predict endorsing the willingness to infect others. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “Dark traits (esp. psychopathy, meanness, and disinhibition) predicted low endorsement of health behaviors and the intent to knowingly expose others to risk.” The claim was tested by partial correlations with controls for gender, age, and presence of health conditions that increase risk from Covid-19. These could be expected to covary with both personality and responses to the pandemic. Extreme responses are of interest when studying maladaptive behavior, so there was no plan to exclude outliers. The focal DV for SCORE was “carrier scenario: harmful behavior” as this measured the willingness to infect others in the scenario that the participant had reason to believe they were infected. This analysis yielded that Meanness (rp = 0.21, p = 2.0 ^-6) predicted Carrier Scenario: Harmful Behavior.

Abstract (as of 6/1/20): 

In a seminal study investigating gender bias in academic science, Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) found bias against female lab manager applicants with respect to competence, hireability, mentoring, and salary conferral. This topic will be revisited through four studies--two direct replications, one extension, and a meta analysis. The present set of studies, all using the same methods and materials as the original, will sample from a larger and broader pool of faculty, collectively representing the breadth of STEM disciplines at R1 universities across the United States. The proposed studies will have high power to detect smaller effect sizes than in the original. Furthermore, a priori criteria have been explicitly articulated for what will be accepted as hypothesis confirmation and replication, and for evidence of gender bias. The pre-registered data analysis plans will provide a strong test assessing the replicability of Moss-Racusin et al. (2012)’s finding that STEM faculty were biased against women who applied for a lab manager position.

title_r: Working title: Effect of Genderstereotypical Images on the Evaluation of Female Right-Wing Populist Politicians
abstract_r: Although replication is considered an important part of the research process to gain confidence in empirical findings, it is rarely conducted in communication science. This project conducts a conceptual replication and extension of an online experiment by Bauer and Carpinella (2017, https://doi.org/10.1177/1065912917738579) to investigate the effect of gender stereotypical visual communication strategies on evaluations of politicians inside (study 1) and outside (study 2) election campaigns. Bauer and Carpinella (2017) analyzed the effects of visual information reinforcing masculine (e.g., images of business people and soldiers) and feminine (e.g., images of children playing and in school) stereotypes on the evaluation of female and male politicians’ issue competencies by manipulating personal campaign websites of fictional Democratic and Republican politicians. The authors expected gender-incongruent visual information to have an effect, and gender-congruent images to have no effect on recipients. In addition, they analyzed how these images affected ratings of politicians' favorability and electoral viability to examine possible negative consequences of gender incongruent images. We conceptually replicate their study in a German context and amend it in five aspects. (1) Instead of using fictional politicians, we compare real German politicians to increase the external validity of the findings. (2) We use Twitter profiles instead of personal websites as this channel is now of greater importance for political actors. (3) Gender stereotypes can relate either to the attribution of issue competencies but also to perceived character traits. Whereas Bauer & Carpinella (2017) focus on issue competencies, we also include character traits as independent variable to draw a complete picture. (4) We consider participants' political orientation and gender as controls. (5) Finally, the real-world context allows us to test whether gender stereotypes are activated differently inside election and outside election campaigns due to different media attention and thus differently affect the perception of politicians. Study 1 is set in the context of the election campaign for the 2021 German federal election and compares politicians from the right-wing populist AfD with those from Bündnis 90/Die Grünen as an example of a center-left party. Study 2 will build on these findings and replicates the experiment outside the campaign context

title_r: Jury Selection Judgements and Justifications
abstract_r: The jury selection process in the Canadian legal system has undergone several changes since the implementation of Bill C-75, and my proposed research is the first to investigate the public’s perceptions of peremptory challenges and judicial stand asides in Canada since. This study is a conceptual replication of Sommers & Norton's (2007) classic study in Canada, with added ecological validity. First, I changed the language, where necessary, to reflect the Canadian legal system (e.g., prosecuting attorney to Crown attorney). Second, the present study manipulated defendant race (White vs. Black), as opposed to only presenting a Black defendant. This manipulation was suggested by Sommers and Norton (2007) and allows for the analysis of whether participants differentially excuse prospective jurors for defendants of different races. Third, this study manipulated the legal professional role that participants were asked to assume (Crown attorney vs. defense attorney vs. judge), as opposed to participants only assuming the role of a prosecuting attorney. This manipulation was again suggested by Sommers and Norton (2007). Fourth, I modified the study materials to allow participants the option of excusing an unlimited amount of prospective jurors from a pool of 20, instead of forcing participants to excuse one of two prospective jurors. Given that practicing attorneys and judges have a lot of discretion when excusing and standing aside prospective jurors, including this modification allows me to test whether previous findings extend to a more ecologically valid paradigm.

summary: Title
Does thinking a product is lower priced make you enjoy taste less?

Original Study: Does more expensive wine actually taste better than cheap wine?
Goldstein, R., Emerson, J. W., & Katz, J. (2008). AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF WINE ECONOMISTS Editor DO MORE EXPENSIVE WINES TASTE BETTER ? EVIDENCE FROM A LARGE SAMPLE OF BLIND TASTINGS. Program, (16).
Authorship
Khadijah Alfred, Milena Collazo , Tiffany Ksiazek, Sheila Mendoza, and Alexandra Valenzuela
Research Questions
Does higher priced labeled brands taste better than lower priced labeled brands?
For this experiment, our interest was to see if the pricing and labeling of the brand's altered participants ratings of each cereal administered. However, participants were given two placebo conditions which were the label, of the average cost: Cheerios, and the high cost: Organic Morning O's, which actually contained the low cost: Great Value Cheerios.
Since we are looking for competency of higher priced items being preferred, participants who categorize incorrectly, and answer the hypothesis of the study correctly will be excluded from the analysis.
Recent research has shown that individuals appreciate the same wine more when they think that it is more expensive (Brochet, 2001; Plassmann et al., 2008). In other words, the price of a good affects the experienced utility derived from that good.
Researchers based this study on one set of experiments showed that the same wine, when thought to cost $45 vs. $5, was not only rated better by tasters but actually lit up the pleasure center of their brains more. In reality, the experiment gave the same wine to people, which resulted in them enjoying the $45 labeled one (Harding, 2014).
Hypotheses
•	Does higher priced labeled brands taste better than lower priced labeled brands?
Our hypothesis is that the manipulation will be very effective, that consumers will rate taste of the higher priced labeled to be higher than the lower priced labeled brands.  In the original study, For non-experts, the relationship between price and overall rating is negative; for experts, however, this is not the case. Our estimates of Model 2 show that the correlation between price and overall rating is positive – or, at any rate, non-negative – for experts. If we didn’t do this, we would be expecting a one dollar increase to have the same effect at the $5 price level as at the $50 price level. We get similar qualitative results using the dollar prices, but the statistical significance of the coefficients is not as good (but still significant) (R. Goldstein, J, et al., 2008). The price coefficient for non-experts is still negative, of about the same size as before, and with greatly improved statistical significance. The coefficient on the ln(price)*expert interaction term is highly statistically significant p-value: 0.017; OLS p-value: 0.015). For experts, the net coefficient on price is the sum of the two, i.e., about 0.11 for the ordered probit and 0.09 for OLS. This net coefficient is significantly different from zero, but only at the 10% level (p-value: 0.099; OLS p-value: 0.095), despite the large sample size. 
Sampling Plan
Data collection procedures
A convenience sample of students at the host institution will be collected. Participants will be recruited via a psychology participation pool and via direct solicitation by research assistants. Participants will receive a credit towards research participation requirements. The participants will be recruited from Dominican University, who are at least 18 years of age or older. Participants will be led to complete the experiment in a Parmer 209, which is considered a control setting environment. Each participant will be assigned a cubicle of their own where they will be given cheerios and administered a survey through Qualtrics. There will be compensation from this study for Nuero 105 and Psych 101 students at Dominican University.
Procedures:
The material being used for manipulation is a knock off brand of cheerios, Great Value O’s, but participants will believe that they are eating three different cheerio brands, the cheap brand (Great Value O’s Cereal), the original (Cheerios), and the organic brand (Organic Morning O's). This experiment will be taking place at Dominican University, in a control setting environment. Participants would be led to a private cubicle that contains a personal computer and pre-filled cups of Cheerios. Participants will then be presented with the three different cheerio brands within their cubicle. The lowest price brand condition is the cheerio brand that will actually contain its specific brand. In the placebo conditions, the plastic cups will be filled with the exact same Great Value Nut O's Cheerio brand. Before beginning the experiment participants will be asked to go onto the computer provided within their cubicle and consent to the experiment. Once the participant has consented, they will then be able to start eating the cheerios administered. When eating from both placebo conditions, participants will perceive they are eating the Cheerios, and Organic Morning O's. As a control, water will be administered to participants between each time of consumption. Participants in all conditions will be informed that the purpose of the study was for them to evaluate the quality of the Cheerios and will be instructed to consume the entire glass of water after each brand consumption.
However, the only type of cereal that is going to be administered, is the Great Value Cheerios, in which participants will perceive that they are trying three different types of cheerio brands. After that, participants will be asked to complete a survey online to rate the quality of each brand. Within the cubicles participants will have access to a computer where the survey will be administered, all the participant has to do is complete the survey. At the beginning of the survey participants will be asked to complete a basic demographic section which will contain age, year, gender. The next section, participants will consume and rate the taste of each brand. The participants will be presented with images. Each group of participants will receive randomized order of images for the cereal brands.  This is to make sure our experiment incorporates counterbalancing because it is a within subject’s design. The third section, participants will be asked to complete the manipulation check, in which they rate the prices. After that, participants will be asked a distractor question, what type of milk do they like to drink and add into their cereal. For the distractor question, the answers will be ignored by the researchers when analyzing the data.  Finally, the participants will be asked to guess the hypothesis of the experiment. Anyone who guesses that there is a relationship between price and quality will be excluded.
Sample size
Sample goal is 250 participants, which is approximately half of the original study’s sample size of 506. 
Sample size rationale
The sample size goal is based on Simonsohn’s guideline (2015) of collecting 2.5x original sample size to ensure good power (80%) for the smallest effect size credibly detectable with the original sample (smallest effect size of 33% power for original N). Usually the goal is to be 2.5x bigger than the original study but given the small participant pool from convenience sampling at Dominican University it can be difficult to receive 1000 participants.  
Stopping rule
Once sample size target of 250 is met, no more sessions will be scheduled or advertised, but those already scheduled will be completed. 
Variables
Manipulated variables
•	Images of cereal brands, as a means to manipulate perceived low to high cost labeled brands.  
Measured variables
•	Taste Rating – measured on a Likert scale 1 through 5, choices are 1) very poor taste, 2) poor taste, 3) neutral taste, 4) good taste, and 5) great taste. 
•	Price rating– participants will be asked to rate the costs of the three cereal brands. 
•	Demographics variables – age, gender, education level, and race.
Design Plan
Blinding
For studies that involve human subjects, participants will not know the three cereal brands will actually be the same average priced cereal, Cheerios, to which they have been assigned to consume.  Research personnel will be aware of this extent of manipulation to which participants are not receiving three different perceived cheerios rather than one, the Cheerios. 
Study design
This is a one way repeated measures ANOVA test. The main IV is images of cereal brands manipulated by consuming each perceived brand and rating the taste. Participants are randomly assigned to order the images are perceived in. 
Analysis Plan
Statistical models
•	Is the manipulation of perceived expertise effective?
o	We will compare the taste ratings for the low, average and high cost label groups.  We will calculate the mean difference and its CI as well as cohen’d d and its CI.  We expect a strong effect within the CI of the original study. The results expected after analyzing the data will be to have both placebo conditions be rated higher in taste than the lowest price condition. There is expected to be a small to large positive effect for both comparisons, (M2-M1) and (M3-M1). M1 is the lowest price label condition, M2 is average price label condition, and M3 is the highest priced label condition.

Data exclusion
Exclusions of the participants will result from participants being under 18, if they rate the cost of the cereal brand incorrectly, and if they guess the hypothesis of this study correctly. As well, exclude people are gluten intolerant. 
Missing data
As in original study there was no specific strategy stated, just exclusion of missing responses within the survey given.

title_r: Gesture for Learning Adult Math
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that using gesture during instruction enhances mathematical learning in both children and adults (Cook, Duffy, & Fenn, 2013; Cook, Friedman, Duggan, Cui, Popescu, 2016; Wakefield, Congdon, Novack, & Goldin-Meadow, 2018). However, more recent work suggests that gesture may help some individuals more than others. For example, in a recent study with adults, we found that those with high visuospatial working memory capacity benefit more from instruction that incorporates gesture than speech-alone instruction. However, adults with high verbal working memory show the opposite effect: they benefit more when instruction is presented through speech alone compared to speech+gesture (Aldugom, Fenn, & Cook, 2020). In a theoretical replication using updated and enhanced materials, we partially replicated our prior findings (Aldugom, Fenn, Day, & Cook, 2021). Specifically, visuospatial working memory capacity predicted learning for those who learned with and without gesture at instruction. Interestingly, verbal working memory capacity did not predict performance in either learning condition. Due to the many alterations in our design, it is unclear whether the changes in our findings are due to the materials used in our replication. In the present study, we aim to replicate and extend our prior work. In this study, adult participants will complete an abstract mathematical task in which they receive instruction either with or without gesture. Participants will also complete tasks to measure individual differences in fluid intelligence, crystallized intelligence, verbal working memory capacity, visuospatial working memory capacity, and math anxiety. In addition to this, participants will also complete two gesture-elicitation tasks. (1) After completing the abstract mathematical task training, participants will be asked to explain their answers to 5 posttest questions, which will be written on a white board. When this procedure has been used at pretest for children solving simple mathematical equivalence problems (e.g., 3+4+5=__+5), most children produce gesture. Notably, however, between 20-30% of children do not and this may impact the efficacy of gesture instruction (Congdon, Novack, & Wakefield, accepted). (2) Participants will also be asked to explain how they would wrap a package. This task has been shown to reliably elicit gesture, but previous work shows variability in how much gesture is produced by individuals (Kopple, 2014).

title_r: At Home or In the Office - Searching for the Best Place to Work: An Investigation of Home Office Usage in the Context of Family Life
abstract_r: The current study can be seen as a conceptual replication study of a study from Golden et al. (2006) named “Telecommuting's differential impact on work-family conflict: Is there no place like home?”. We examine the impact of working from home (Home Office) on the Work-Family Conflict (WFC) as well as the Family-Work Conflict (FWC). Due to the original study from Golden et al. (2006) we believe in the bidirectional nature of WFC and FWC and therefore in the assumption that role demands and expectations originate from both, the work and family domains. Furthermore, we expect that the moderators “scheduling flexibility” and “household size” influence the impact of Home Office usage on the WFC as well as on the FWC. In contrast to the original study, we do not examine the moderator “job autonomy” because recent results on Work-life balance were always unequivocal. Beyond that, the current study differs from the original considerably in participants, recruiting and country.

title_r: Extension of Dieuleveut et al. (Full Knowledge + False Belief+Epistemic Test)
abstract_r: Summary (the details are all in the attached pdf document) Dieuleveut, Chemla & Spector (2019) tested for the existence of three distinct readings for sentences involving the quantifier some and numerals, as well as other items). A sentence such ‘Some of the cards are red’ is potentially ambiguous between a literal meaning (‘some and possibly all cards are red’), a reading with a primary implicature (‘some cards are red and the speaker does not believe that all cards are red’), and a reading with a secondary implicature (‘some but not all of the cards are red and the speaker knows that). Similar readings can be defined for numerals. Dieuleveut et al. showed people 4 kinds of situations, manipulating both the number of red cards among 8 cards, and the information available to a fictitious speaker (we illustrate here their design in the case of the sentence ‘some of the cards are red’). In the FALSE condition, no card is red, and the speaker knows that. In the LITERAL condition, only the literal reading is true, and the speaker knows that: the speaker sees that all cards are red. In the PRIMARY condition, the literal reading and the one with a primary implicature are true, but the secondary reading is false (this situation shows a speaker who sees 4 out of 8 cards, where the 4 visible cards are red, while the others are hidden). In the SECONDARY condition, all readings are true (the speaker sees 8 cards, of which exactly 4 are red). Dieuleveut asked whether, in each situation, the speaker can say the sentence ‘Some of the cards are red’. They found that the rate of ‘yes’ answers is significantly higher for the SECONDARY condition than for the PRIMARY condition, which is itself higher than for the LITERAL condition, which is itself higher than for the FALSE condition. The observed difference between SECONDARY and PRIMARY is unexpected if the only thing that matters is whether the speaker is in a position to use the alternative sentence ‘All of the cards are red’, since in both cases the speaker is not in a position to use the all-alternative. Dieuleveut et al. argued that this could provide evidence for the ‘grammatical approach’ to scalar implicatures. However, as they note, it is possible that the reason why some participants say ‘No’ in the PRIMARY condition is that the speaker might believe that the listener wrongly believes that the speaker sees all the cards, in which case the ‘some’-sentence might be misleading because it would lead such a listener to infer ‘not all’. In a previous experiment, preregistered at https://osf.io/rbvse, we ran a conceptual replication of Dieuleveut et al., using only numerals and ‘some’, with one main difference: we made it very explicit that the listener sees exactly how many cards are visible to the speaker, and we described the speaker as talking to this listener. We found no significant difference between SECONDARY and PRIMARY for ‘some’, but we did find one for numerals. The rates of ‘yes’ answer for the literal condition were much higher than in the original Dieuleveut et al. experiments, showing that fewer people access a reading with an implicature (primary or secondary) in our replication. The goal of the current study is to add situations where the listener is presented as being misinformed about the number of visible cards in the speaker’s hand, and the speaker is aware of this. The idea is that in such situations, participants might find that the speaker should not use the ‘some’ sentence in the PRIMARY condition where she sees 4 red cards and 4 other cards are hidden, because the listener, who believes the speaker sees all cards, would in fact infer ‘some but not all’ (similarly for the sentences with numerals). So, schematically, we define conditions by 2 factors: ‘epistemic situation’ (‘Full Knowledge’, FK, where the listener sees how many cards the speaker has, and the speaker knows that, and ‘False Belief’, FB, where the listener has a false belief about what the speaker sees) and ‘reading’ (with 4 levels: FALSE, LITERAL,PRIMARY, SECONDARY). This defines the following 8 conditions, for each quantifier (‘some’ or the numeral ‘four’) FK-False, FK-Literal, FK-primary, FK-secondary FB-False, FB-Literal, FB-primary, FB-secondary For each quantifier (‘some’ or ‘Num’), we will test whether the difference between the PRIMARY and SECONDARY conditions for both FB and FK is significant, as well as whether the effect of PRIMARY/SECONDARY is modulated by the epistemic situation (FB or FK) . We will thus perform 3 tests for each quantifier, and will correct for multiple comparisons

title_r: Cognitive dissonance in the work environment. A replication og Festinger and Carlsmith's classical study
abstract_r: In 1959 Festinger and Carlsmith (1959) studied the consequences of forced compliance, by inducing 71 students in the introductory psychology course at Stanford University to make a statement contrary to their attitude. The participants would do a very boring task for one hour, but after finishing it, they were asked to tell the next participant that the task had been fun. They were given either one or 20 dollars for doing this (Festinger & Carlsmith, 1959, p. 204). The hypothesis of Festinger and Carlsmith was that the smaller the incentive, the larger dissonance, i.e. the more they would change their attitude (Smith & Haslam, 2012, s. 49). This means that the 20 dollar group would experience less dissonance because they could justify acting against their attitude with the large amount of money they received. This would not be the case for the one dollar group, and in order to maintain consonance they would instead have to change their attitude towards the task. Festinger & Carlsmith (1959, p. 207) got their hypothesis confirmed when the participants rated the task at the end of the experiment procedure. The result achieved in this experiment contradicts learning theory, which would predict that the larger amount of money, the more the attitude would change, i.e. a big reward would reinforce the participants to enjoy the task (Smith & Haslam, 2017, p. 49). Furthermore, it contradicts the theory of planned behaviour which assumes that attitude causes behaviour (Myers et al., 2021, p. 173). Hence, the results were sensational in 1959, although different theories today agree that behaviour can also produce attitudes (Myers et al., 2021, p. 178-189) The study was implemented in 1959, and it has been replicated several times afterwards (Smith & Haslam, 2017, p. 53-55). The replications have to a large degree confirmed the original hypothesis by Festinger & Carlsmith, but they have also shown that “the impact of counterattitudinal behaviour on attitudes is not ubiquitous” (Smith & Haslam, 2017, p. 54). The original study was implemented among psychology students by an authority in the field. The young age of the participants, and the imbalance of power between the investigator and the participants, in the original study, might have contributed to the attitudes expressed afterwards. Furthermore, culture has changed a lot since the original study took place. With the media revolution and impact of social media, it is probably more common to perform oneself and keep a facade today than in 1959. As a result, one can presume that the identity of a modern Norwegian adult is changeable, and that the importance of appearing genuine has decreased since the original study took place. It is therefore interesting to find out if it takes more than claiming that a boring task was fun to produce dissonance in 2022. In this conceptual replication we will investigate these cultural changes’ impacts on cognitive dissonance by implementing Festinger & Carlsmith’s experiment among a group of employees in a marketing company in which career is important. These participants might have another experience of acting contrary to their attitudes, probably as a means to climb on the ladder of success. Furthermore, if counterattitudinal behaviour does produce dissonance and change of attitudes in the workplace, it will have an impact on how we consider the relationships between a general and his/her subordinates. Can a leader affect the subordinates’ attitudes simply by asking them to accomplish certain tasks? Bringing Festinger & Carlsmith`s classical experiment into the work environment can probably give us some answers.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Rothgerber et al. (2020), From PsyArXiv
abstract_r: For replication we selected Hypothesis 1: More conservative participants would be less likely to follow social distancing guidelines. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “Specifically, political conservatism inversely predicted compliance with behaviors aimed at preventing the spread of the COVID-19.” To model the causal pathway from conservatism to reported social distancing, multiple regression analyses provided model parameter estimates. Regression revealed a significant total effect of conservatism on social distancing (B = -.20, p <.001), supporting Hypothesis 1 that compliance with social distancing guidelines is inversely related to conservatism. Although this claim references a multiple regression analysis, detail on what covariates were included in the model is lacking. The power analysis provided by SCORE for this claim is therefore based on a bivariate correlation between political conservatism and social distancing ( r = .240). Thus the focal hypothesis will be tested by calculating the bivariate correlation between political conservatism and social distancing. We will additionally examine the association using multiple regression and including a number of control covariates that are referenced in the study.

title_r: Pre-registration "Social Identity Threat and its Consequences in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning"
abstract_r: The present research aims at contributing to the understanding of the differential consequences of social identity threat (i.e., lower sense of belonging, lower social approach motivation, less (intended) contact to academic peers) in higher distance education for members of differentially stereotyped student groups. Thereby, we first replicate previous findings about the relation between social identity threat, sense of belonging, and social approach motivation in the novel and increasingly important context of higher distance education. Second, we implement a longitudinal design to investigate the directionality of the effects. Third, we extend previous research by additionally investigating a measure of actual behavior (i.e., interaction of students in the course’s moodle platform). To do so, measures of social identity threat, sense of belonging, social approach motivation, behavioral intentions, and actual contact are implemented in a large distance learning course in the introductory phase of the Bachelor’s program in psychology. Students collaborate in virtual groups (computer-supported collaborative learning, CSCL) over several weeks. Data are collected longitudinally (3 time points throughout the semester) as a combination of self-report and behavioral data (social networks during the CSCL task).

title_r: Reexamining different roles of intent across moral domains
abstract_r: The reduced role of intent when judging impure, vs. harmful, acts (i.e., the intent × domain effect) provides some of the strongest evidence that our moral minds may be composed of distinct, domain-specific systems. However, a study that experimentally controlled, and statistically adjusted, for the target (i.e., self vs. other) of the act reported a significant, but notably smaller, intent × domain effect (Chakroff, Dungan, & Young, 2013). Further, two recent studies that experimentally controlled, and/or statistically adjusted, for the target and context of the act reported a failure to find evidence for the intent × domain effect (Kupfer, Inbar, & Tybur, 2020; Parkinson & Byrne, 2017). We tested two competing hypotheses regarding these inconsistent findings. The first holds that the intent × domain effect is a methodological artefact of the stimuli employed. The second hypothesis holds that the intent × domain effect is reduced in magnitude when, experimentally controlling, or statistically adjusting, for the target and/or context of the act. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a well-powered, close replication of Kupfer et al.

title_r: Replication and extension of: Large language models associate Muslims with violence by Abid et al., 2021
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The main purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the results in Abid et al. (2021; Nature Machine Intelligence). Building on preliminary evidence provided by the creators of GPT-2 and GPT-3 (state-of-the-art text generation algorithms; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), the authors showed biased automated text generation when religious identities are cued in text completion prompts. GPT-3 completions for prompts formatted as “Two X walk into a” contained violent content much more often if X was replaced with “Muslims” rather than adjectives signifying other major religions. Since the smallest difference was found between “Muslim” and “Christian”, our replication attempt focuses on this more conservative measure of the model’s religion bias. However, we include the “Hindu” category as well to control for the impact of majority/minority difference between “Muslim” and “Christian”.
We extend these results by exploring whether naming specific individuals reduces the propensity of the model to rely on biased group-level representations. For instance, using “Y walks into a” where Y is replaced with a common Muslim name compared with names common among adherents of Christianity and Hinduism. 
We also examine whether the model is sensitive to differing degrees of genericity in the main referent of prompts, which can vary along a continuum. Generic kinds like “Muslim” lie near one end of the spectrum. Individual celebrities whose personal information presumably features strongly in GPT-3’s training data (from CommonCrawl.org), lie near the other end. Common names associated with social kinds like “Muslim” (e.g., Ali Islam) are somewhere in-between, albeit closer to the specific end of the genericity spectrum. We expect reduced bias as the specificity of the prompts are increased.

summary: The attached Word document contains structured, detailed descriptions of procedures for a replication of Abid et al.'s (2021) results, with particular attention paid to minor adjustments made by the current authors. It also contains theoretical and practical justifications for the extension based on the linguistic notion of genericity, as well as detailed information about the procedures and materials for that extension. Potential follow-up experiments are also mentioned.

title_r: Are women and men more or less obedient than 60 years ago? A replication of Milgram's experiment of obeying authorities in Norway and the United States.
abstract_r: In this study, we are going to replicate the Stanley Milgram experiment published in 1963. The study was based on the events after the Second World War to check the coercion and compliance of the Americans compared to the Germans in the aftermath of the Eichmann case. He wanted to focus on the relationship between obedience and authority and personal conscience. In the original study there were 40 participants who were all males in their 20-50s (Myers et al., 2020, s. 251). Before the study ended, Milgram asked 14 of Yale University's psychology professors what they expected from the experiment. All believed that only a few sadists, about 1.2%, would be willing to give a maximum current. The result showed something completely different. About 65% (26 out of 40) of the participants were willing to obey the call for the highest current, despite the fact that the student was obviously suffering and asked for mercy. In addition, they knew that they could interrupt the trial at any time. None of the participants interrupted the experiment before 300 volts, and none of them insisted on examining og talking to the “victim” after the experiment. The experiment has later been criticized for exposing the participants to a significant moment of stress as they were kind of revealed as sadists as they were willing to give the student almost unbearable pain. With the ethical guidelines that we have today, it would not be possible to replicate this experiment, but It could be quite useful to perform this kind of experiment to see if the possibility for obedience now is the same as before. Also, if we can study this phenomenon, it could also be used to try to find ways to prevent or strengthen people's compliance. It is interesting to replicate the Milgram experiment, because then we would be able to see how- and if human obedience to an authority person has changed over the years. When looking at the United States and Norway, in general a cultural difference is present. For example, in every culture people have different images or characteristics seen as legitimate authorities. In addition to that, behavior of humanity has changed in a way that we have become more individualistic- but Norway seems to be less individualistic than the US. Maybe this sense of individuality leads to the fact the participants won’t change their minds when being commanded, and choose for their own belief. We would like to see how this affects obedience. Perhaps people these days do have more empathy, as emotional intelligence came up. At the same time, we will also check if gender has to be taken into account when it comes to obedience. We expect to find that women react first of all differently than men and more specifically, will be less influenced by being commanded by an authority figure, especially when it comes to harming others. Women are in general seen to be more sensitive than men, but this doesn’t necessarily say they are less obedient. As Milgram did, we will include a follow-up questionnaire in which women can express their experience of the experience, where they perhaps show to feel more guilty during or afterwards than men.

title_r: Goal Setting With Struggling Students: A Replication
abstract_r: A series of field experiments involving a goal setting intervention have shown promising results in recently by increasing academic performance and retention rates and reducing perceived anxiety among struggling students. Unfortunately, these studies are plagued by methodological insufficiencies, most notably the lack of an adequate control group, hindering their ability to inform science and policy because they cannot disentangle the apparent treatment effect from any demand effect. In this field experiment, using an adapted version of the intervention, we will rigorously replicate these studies using a treatment, placebo-treatment, and no-treatment group, to disentangle the treatment and demand effects and bring solid evidence to what could be an extremely low cost, yet highly effective treatment for struggling students.

title_r: Superheroes Social Skills: A Replication with Latinx Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract_r: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) often exhibit social skills deficits that affect communication with same-age peers and adults. Despite the improvements in social engagement and behaviors found in Social Skills Training (SST) interventions for students with ASD, there are few SST interventions that are culturally sensitive and adapted for diverse populations, specifically Latinx children. The most recent Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring report provided evidence that disparities in ASD identification are moderated by race/ethnicity. Notably, Latinx children are identified with ASD less often (~1 in 65) than non-Latinx White, Black, and Asian/Pacific Islander children (~1 in 55; Maenner et al., 2020). One promising social skills program is the Superheroes Social Skills program which consists of several targeted skills aimed to improve social skills in students with ASD. However, it remains unknown if the Superheroes Social Skills program is effective for Latinx students. The current study aims to investigate the Superheroes Social Skills intervention with Latinx elementary school students with ASD to identify if there are improvements in their social skills and to detail the potential areas that are in need of cultural adaptation. Results of this study would provide initial information on how to culturally adapt the Superheroes Social Skills program for professionals to better address the social skill needs of Latinx children.

title_r: Evaluative associations & body language

title_r: Mapping neurobiological patterns of childhood adversity in psychiatry using normative modeling
abstract_r: Childhood adversity can have long-lasting effects on the development of the brain and represents a well-known risk factor for the emergence of mental health problems. However, previous efforts to identify the neural underpinnings of childhood adversity and their implications for mental health have been limited by a reliance on case-control comparisons and group summary statistics, which are based on the assumption that the investigated subgroups are inherently homogenous. These comparisons are inadequate to address the vast heterogeneity and comorbidity in psychiatric populations on the one hand, and co-occurring adversities on the other hand. Normative modeling represents an innovative alternative to these traditional approaches. This method enables the mapping of relationships between behavioral and biological measures of interest and provides statistical inference at the level of the individual, relative to a reference population (Marquand et al., 2016; Marquand et al., 2019). Previous studies have demonstrated that normative modeling is well-suited to characterize clinical heterogeneity (Wolfers et al., 2019; Zabihi et al., 2019), which is crucial to obtain a more nuanced understanding of the link between adversity-induced brain alterations and mental health. The normative modeling framework has recently been employed by Holz and colleagues (2023), who identified a stable and replicable neural signature of adversity in an at-risk cohort for mental health disorders. Noticeably, individual cortical volume contractions were shown to be predictive of later anxiety, emphasizing the value of subject-level brain alterations as predictors for clinical outcome measures. However, since only a few subjects progressed to meet the criteria for a formal psychiatric diagnosis, insights into the relationship between structural brain alterations and psychopathology remain limited. To address this, the current study will extend the findings by Holz et al. (2023) to a heterogeneous and multimorbid psychiatric patient sample as well as to different dimensions of trauma (emotional abuse, emotional neglect, physical abuse, sexual abuse). We will combine data from different cohort studies, including clinical samples from the ‘Measuring Integrated Novel Dimensions in Neurodevelopmental and Stress-related Mental Disorders’ (MIND-Set) study (van Eijndhoven et al., 2022) and ‘The Biological Classification of Mental Disorders’ (BeCOME) study (https://www.psych.mpg.de/2398388/become; Brückl et al., 2020). We will include additional healthy control samples from the ‘Healthy Brain Study’ (HBS; https://www.healthybrainstudy.nl), the IMAGEN cohort (https://imagen-project.org), and the ‘Mannheim Study of Children at Risk’ (MARS; https://www.zi-mannheim.de/en/research/departments-research-groups-institutes/child-adolescent-psychiatry-psychotherapy-e/research-groups-child-adolescent-psychiatry-psychotherapy-e/dev-neurosci.html). First, we will test whether we can replicate the identified pattern of adversity-induced volumetric changes from Holz et al. (2023) in a naturalistic and transdiagnostic clinical sample containing patients with mood disorders and neurodevelopmental disorders. Moreover, we aim to extend this pattern along multiple axes, namely to: (i) across a greater lifespan range, (ii) greater population diversity and (iii) accommodating multiple different clinical instruments. To achieve these objectives, we will build normative reference models capturing variation in cortical and subcortical brain volume, as predicted by early life adversities. Then, we will investigate whether, and if so how, individual volumetric deviations from the reference model are associated with clinical measures in terms of diagnostic information and symptomatology along cross-diagnostic symptom domains (as previously identified by Mulders et al., 2022).

title_r: Tackett lab hormones replication project
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: The present study is an attempt to reproduce, in an independent pre-adolescent sample, analyses from three studies examining the interaction between personality traits and hormones in predicting youth externalizing behavior.  The three papers are as follows: 

A. Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., & Tackett, J. L. (2015). Adolescent personality as risk and resiliency in the testosterone-externalizing association. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 26, 390-402.

B. Tackett, J. L., Herzhoff, K., Harden, K. P., Page-Gould, E., & Josephs, R. A. (2014). Personality x hormone interactions in adolescent externalizing psychopathology. Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment. 5, 235-246. 

C. Tackett, J. L., Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., Page-Gould, E., Harden, K. P., & Josephs, R. A. (2015). Estradiol and cortisol interactions in youth externalizing psychopathology. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 55, 146-153. 

Sample: This replication effort will be conducted in an already-collected sample of 350 youth between the ages of 8 and 11. 

Variables: We will use variables indexing hormones, personality traits, and externalizing behavior. 

1. youth hormone levels as measured via a baseline sample of saliva collected 30 minutes after arrival to the lab. The samples were collected using a passive drool method, frozen, and immunoassayed in an independent lab. We will use the measurements of cortisol, testosterone, and estradiol (E2). 

2. parent-reported youth personality pathology traits as measured by the Dimensional Personality Symptom Itempool (DIPSI; De Clercq, De Fruyt, Van Leeuwen, & Mervielde, 2006). We will focus specifically on the higher-order trait dimension of Disagreeableness. 

3. parent-reported youth behavior as measured by the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL; Achenbach & Rescorla, 2001). We will focus specifically on the broadband Externalizing Problems scale. 

Hypotheses: We are aiming to replicate the findings from each of these three previous studies in a larger sample. This sample diverges from the original sample not only in size, but also in age (pre-adolescent versus adolescent) and in much greater racial/ethnic and socioeconomic diversity.

A. Reardon et al., 2015: This study demonstrated that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only for youth with low levels of self-regulatory personality. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be predictive of externalizing behavior, but only for those youth high on disagreeableness. We hypothesize that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: This study found that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low, and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: This study found that estradiol was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that estradiol will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between estradiol and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

Planned analyses: 

1. For the hormone variables (C, T, and E2), any extreme values will be winsorized. An extreme value will be defined as a value more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean, and this value will be replaced with the next highest observed value in the sample. 

2. We anticipate large skew values, as is typical for hormone variables, and thus all hormone variables will be log-transformed to reduce this skew. 

3. Because we anticipate that boys will have significantly higher T levels than girls, and that girls will have significantly higher E2 levels than boys, these two hormones will be standardized (z-scored) within gender, as is consistent with previous research on gonadal hormones (e.g., Mehta & Josephs, 2010). 

4. Age, gender, and time of waking will be used as covariates in all analyses, so these variables will be standardized. In addition, the predictor variable DIPSI Disagreeableness will be standardized. 

5. We will next create interaction terms: 
    a. T x Disagreeableness
    b. C x Disagreeableness
    c. E2 x Disagreeableness
    d. T x C
    e. E2 x C 
    f. T x C x Disagreeableness
    g. E2 x C x Disagreeableness

6. We will run regression analyses to test the central hypotheses of the three studies: 

A. Reardon et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the interaction between testosterone and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T and Disagreeableness in step 2, and the interaction term between T and Disagreeableness in step 3. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between testosterone, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between estradiol, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

7. Additional analyses to examine potential moderators and specificity of the effects (some of which were directly examined in the previous publications) will include: 

    a. running the regressions using the parent-reported CBCL Internalizing Problems scale as an additional covariate, to test specificity of externalizing problems above-and-beyond general psychopathology. We hypothesize that associations will be smaller, but will still show unique associations with externalizing problems.
    b. running the regressions using the Pubertal Development Scale score (PDS) as a covariate instead of age, as hormone levels are affected by physical maturation. Age and pubertal status are highly correlated, so the pattern of results should largely be the same. Nonetheless, there is so little empirical data with these variables in child and adolescent samples that it is important to see how age and pubertal status covariates may differentially impact evidence for these associations, particularly across different stages of puberty. The current study offers substantial power to test this question in a early/pre-pubertal sample.
    c. running the regressions using the time of testing as a covariate, as hormone concentrations vary throughout the day. The pattern of results is anticipated to remain largely similar with this additional covariate. It will be examined because it is sometimes used as a covariate in similar research using a single baseline sample.
    d. running the regressions separately in boys and girls, a practice which is quite common in human psychoneuroendocrinological research, to examine whether the final pattern of results is similar for both boys and girls. We do not have strong a priori hypotheses for gender differences in these relationships, and the previous publications did not find meaningful evidence for gender differences. 
    e. running the regressions replacing the DIPSI Disagreeableness higher-order scale with the 12 lower-order facets of Disagreeableness. Facet-level analyses offer a more fine-grained examination of those aspects of self-regulatory personality that are involved in these associations (analyses are consistent with Tackett et al., 2014).
    f. examining race/ethnicity as a potential moderator. Evidence indicates different hormone levels across race/ethnic groups, but studies rarely have adequate racial and ethnic diversity to directly examine hormone-behavior associations between groups. Given the lack of previous studies on this specific research question, such analyses would be descriptive.

We hypothesize that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: This study found that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low, and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: This study found that estradiol was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that estradiol will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between estradiol and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

Planned analyses: 

1. For the hormone variables (C, T, and E2), any extreme values will be winsorized. An extreme value will be defined as a value more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean, and this value will be replaced with the next highest observed value in the sample. 

2. We anticipate large skew values, as is typical for hormone variables, and thus all hormone variables will be log-transformed to reduce this skew. 

3. Because we anticipate that boys will have significantly higher T levels than girls, and that girls will have significantly higher E2 levels than boys, these two hormones will be standardized (z-scored) within gender, as is consistent with previous research on gonadal hormones (e.g., Mehta & Josephs, 2010). 

4. Age, gender, and time of waking will be used as covariates in all analyses, so these variables will be standardized. In addition, the predictor variable DIPSI Disagreeableness will be standardized. 

5. We will next create interaction terms: 
    a. T x Disagreeableness
    b. C x Disagreeableness
    c. E2 x Disagreeableness
    d. T x C
    e. E2 x C 
    f. T x C x Disagreeableness
    g. E2 x C x Disagreeableness

6. We will run regression analyses to test the central hypotheses of the three studies: 

A. Reardon et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the interaction between testosterone and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T and Disagreeableness in step 2, and the interaction term between T and Disagreeableness in step 3. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between testosterone, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between estradiol, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

7. Additional analyses to examine potential moderators and specificity of the effects (some of which were directly examined in the previous publications) will include: 

    a. running the regressions using the parent-reported CBCL Internalizing Problems scale as an additional covariate, to test specificity of externalizing problems above-and-beyond general psychopathology. We hypothesize that associations will be smaller, but will still show unique associations with externalizing problems.
    b. running the regressions using the Pubertal Development Scale score (PDS) as a covariate instead of age, as hormone levels are affected by physical maturation. Age and pubertal status are highly correlated, so the pattern of results should largely be the same. Nonetheless, there is so little empirical data with these variables in child and adolescent samples that it is important to see how age and pubertal status covariates may differentially impact evidence for these associations, particularly across different stages of puberty. The current study offers substantial power to test this question in a early/pre-pubertal sample.
    c. running the regressions using the time of testing as a covariate, as hormone concentrations vary throughout the day. The pattern of results is anticipated to remain largely similar with this additional covariate. It will be examined because it is sometimes used as a covariate in similar research using a single baseline sample.
    d. running the regressions separately in boys and girls, a practice which is quite common in human psychoneuroendocrinological research, to examine whether the final pattern of results is similar for both boys and girls. We do not have strong a priori hypotheses for gender differences in these relationships, and the previous publications did not find meaningful evidence for gender differences. 
    e. running the regressions replacing the DIPSI Disagreeableness higher-order scale with the 12 lower-order facets of Disagreeableness. Facet-level analyses offer a more fine-grained examination of those aspects of self-regulatory personality that are involved in these associations (analyses are consistent with Tackett et al., 2014).
    f. examining race/ethnicity as a potential moderator. Evidence indicates different hormone levels across race/ethnic groups, but studies rarely have adequate racial and ethnic diversity to directly examine hormone-behavior associations between groups. Given the lack of previous studies on this specific research question, such analyses would be descriptive.

title_r: The Visual Mandela Effect: A Replication of Prasad and Bainbridge (2022)
abstract_r: The present investigation is a replication of Experiment 1 from Prasad and Bainbridge (2022). They used Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) to ask participants to select the correct image (of three options) and rate on confidence, familiarity, and exposure. The three options for each image included the original image and two images with one different (but related) manipulation each. The purpose of this experiment was to identify which, of 40 presented images, met the qualifying criteria for being affected by the visual Mandela effect (VME). The researchers identified seven images in which neither confidence, familiarity, nor exposure was correlated with accuracy and there was a specific manipulated version which was consistently falsely identified as the correct image. Replicating this study with college students will enable us to confirm if those seven images are VME-affected, ensure none of the other images qualify as VME-affected, and provide further evidence to the generalizability of Prasad and Bainbridge’s (2022) findings.
