title_r: Middle School Students’ Use of Text Sources in a Scenario-Based, Argumentative Writing Task
abstract_r: Overview We will conduct a conceptual replication of a study reported by Crossley et al. (2021) to examine how middle school students’ argumentative writing performance is predicted by their source integration. We will administer to students a digital, scenario-based assessment about a scientific topic that requires them to individually produce argumentative essays. Then, using a cross-sectional design, we will examine how holistic writing quality (dependent variable) is predicted by measures of (a) essay length, (b) essay and source overlap, and (c) plagiarism. We will also examine whether there are differences in holistic writing quality, essay and source overlap, and plagiarism as a function of disability status. Background and Rationale Facility with selecting, evaluating, and integrating information from digital and print sources is a central component of college- and career-readiness in English language arts (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013; National Governors Association & Council of Chief State School Officers, 2010; National Research Council, 2013), science (Britt et al., 2014; Goldman et al., 2016; National Research Council, 2013), social studies (Goldman et al., 2016; National Council for the Social Studies, 2013; van Drie & van Boxtel, 2008), and mathematics (Weber, 2018). Beginning in sixth grade, for instance, students are expected to “[g]ather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources; assess the creditability of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and providing basic bibliographic information from sources” (CCSS.W.6.8) (National Governors Association & Council of Chief State School Officers, 2010). Such skills are particularly important when crafting written arguments (Ferretti et al., 2023). For example, students are expected to “[s]upport their [written] claim(s) with clear reasons and relevant evidence, using creditable sources…” (CCSS.W.6.1A) (National Governors Association & Council of Chief State School Officers, 2010). Unfortunately, much research has shown that children, adolescents, and adults often struggle with searching for sources, evaluating their relevance and trustworthiness, and integrating their contents (Anmarkrud et al., 2022; Bråten et al., 2018; Britt & Aglinskas, 2002; Goldman et al., 2012; Many, 1996; Segev-Miller, 2007; Strømsø et al., 2013). Source use performance can vary considerably, though, depending on the context and task being performed (Afflerbach & Cho, 2009; Rouet et al., 2017; Wiley & Voss, 1999), features of the source(s) (Kim & Millis, 2006; Kurby et al., 2005; Saux et al., 2017), and a wide array of individual differences factors (Anmarkrud et al., 2022; Nelson & King, 2022). Argumentative reasoning is also critical for college- and career-readiness (National Governors Association & Council of Chief State School Officers, 2010; National Research Council, 2012). Indeed, argumentative reasoning tasks, often in the form of writing, are a ubiquitous feature of middle, secondary, and higher education (Ferretti & Lewis, 2019; Fischer et al., 2018). Moreover, learning in language arts, science, and social studies is often measured, at least in part, through argumentative writing tasks (Ferretti & Graham, 2019). Although such tasks can reveal important insights into the breadth and depth of students’ understanding of a topic, it is resource intensive to score and provide feedback on students’ writing (Wolf Nelson, 2014). Accordingly, there has been great interest in developing automatic scoring methods (Shermis & Wilson, 2024). A wide array of commercial and open source automated essay evaluation tools have been developed (Shermis & Wilson, 2024). These tools can capture information about specific aspects of writing (e.g., length, cohesion) as well as overall, holistic quality (Ramineni & Deane, 2017). In this study, we will use open source natural language processing tools to capture measures essay and source overlap and plagiarism in middle-school students’ argumentative writing (Crossley et al., 2016). We will then use regularization and cross-validation methods to examine how these measures predict students’ holistic writing performance.

title_r: The Effect of Animacy on Structural Priming: A Replication of Bock, Loebell and Morey (1992)
abstract_r: Bock et al. (1992) found that the binding of animacy features onto grammatical roles is susceptible to priming in sentence production. Moreover, this effect did not interact with structural priming. This finding supports an account according to which syntactic representations are insensitive to the consistency of animacy-to-structure mapping This account has contributed greatly to the development of syntactic processing theories in language production. However, this study has never been directly replicated and the few related studies showed mixed results. A meta-analysis of these studies failed to replicate the findings of Bock et al.(1992). Therefore, we will conduct a well-powered replication (n=500) that follows the original study as closely as possible. We predict an effect of structural priming and an animacy priming effect, which would replicate Bock et al.’s findings. In addition, if syntactic representations are indeed independent of semantic information about animacy, we expect to replicate Bock et al.’s (1992) observed null interaction between structural priming and animacy binding; if not, there should be a significant interaction.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Lai & Poletiek (2011) in Cognition
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Lai et al (2011) is: The claim that when participants in Experiment 1 were exposed to the set of same strings, generated by an AnBn grammar G, the ordering of the exemplars affected learning: in the ‘starting small’ (SS) condition, syllable strings were presented progressively according to their level of embedding, while in the random condition, exactly the same set was presented randomly, and the SS group outperformed the random group. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “In [an] artificial grammar experiment…learning was observed only when the training set was staged.” The claim was tested using a t-test on mean d-prime values (calculated from forced-choice responses to items at each stage of training as either grammatical or ungrammatical) of participants in the ‘starting small’ vs random condition, yielding that, overall, the SS group, d prime = 1.51 (73% correct), highly outperformed the random group, d prime = .08 (52% correct), t (26) = 3.94, p = .001.

title_r: Interpersonal Factors Associated with Self-harm Among Callers to the Massachusetts Problem Gambling Helpline
abstract_r: A recent study (Gray & Edson, 2025) assessed the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide (Joiner, 2005) among individuals with past-year gambling experience. This study found that feelings of perceived burdensomenss mediate the relationship between problem gambling and suicide ideation, especially at higher levels of thwarted belongingness. Debt stress was also found to mediate the relationship between problem gambling and perceived burdensomeness. The findings of this study suggest that the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide is a relevant framework for explaining elevated levels of suicidality among individuals experiencing gambling problems. While the findings of this initial study are insightful, conceptual replication is greatly needed among a more targeted sample of individuals experiencing problems with gambling. This study will apply the base methodology of Gray and Edson (2025) to a sample of callers to the Massachusetts Problem Gambling Helpline. We will also extend their methodology to assess new potential moderators (e.g., Financially Focused Self-concept) and conduct an exploratory analysis focused on gamblers whose financial or social difficulties from gambling at least partially prompted their Helpline call.

title_r: replication of Yin et al., 2021
abstract_r: In this study we aim to replicate one of the key findings from the paper by Yin et al. (2021, https://doi.org/10.1177/1359105319869977). This replication is part of the overarching project “Replication of Findings in Neuroimaging – MDD” (ReFiNe-MDD, https://osf.io/n86q9/) using data from various cohorts. The project aims to a) estimate the percentage of replicable findings in the area of brain structural gray matter correlates related to variables relevant for depression, b) identify study characteristics associated with replicability of neuroimaging findings, and c) deduct methodological guidelines to foster replicability of findings in this area of research. Therefore, a minimum of 60 single replications will be conducted. In this replication study, we will examine the association between depressive symptoms, sleep quality, and gray matter volume (GMV) in the insula among young adults. The original study by Yin and colleagues (2021) found that the GMV of the right insula mediates the relationship between depressive symptoms and sleep quality. Existing literature highlights that poor sleep quality is a common issue among young adults (Buboltz Jr. et al., 2009; Krističević et al., 2018). A substantial number of young adults also report experiencing depressive symptoms (Qin et al., 2018; Shorey et al., 2022). There is evidence supporting a strong link between these depressive symptoms and poor sleep quality (O’Callaghan et al., 2021). The insula appears to be an important neural structure involved in both, depressive symptoms and sleep quality. Studies have shown that major depressive disorder is associated with reduced GMV in the insula (Ancelin et al., 2019; Stratmann et al., 2014). Lower GMV in this region has also been linked to poorer sleep quality (Sung et al., 2020). These findings point toward a potential mediating role of the insula's GMV in the relationship between depressive symptoms and sleep quality.

title_r: Stage 1 registered report for replication of Experiment 1 and 2 of “Axe the tax: Taxes are disliked more than equivalent costs” (Sussman & Olivola, 2011)
abstract_r: Stage 1: Sussman and Olivola (2011) reported that people in the US show a stronger preference to avoid tax-related costs than to avoid tax-unrelated monetary costs of the same size and coined the term Tax Aversion to describe the phenomenon. The original Experiment 1 and 2 results indicated that people are willing to incur increased timely costs to receive a discount when it refers to taxes (e.g., “axe-the-tax discount”) than when it just refers to a regular discount (e.g., “customer rewards”). Their paper has received considerable attention and is often cited in tax behavior research when referring to citizens’ general aversion to taxes. We propose close replications of Experiments 1 and 2 in two high-powered studies in the US (N = 600 and N = 700, respectively). Because the original study was conducted in a country that relies on a sales tax system, where consumption taxes are very salient, we additionally propose conducting both replication studies in the UK to test whether the effect also applies to a value added tax system (again N = 600 and N = 700, respectively). The replication studies will test whether Tax Aversion is a stable phenomenon in the US and whether the effect extends to a consumption tax system where payments do not represent an out-of-pocket cost.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from van Dijck et al. (2009), from Cognition
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Van Dijck et al (2009) is the Experiment 1 finding that during parity judgment that the SNARC-effect (spatial-numeric association of response codes) remained under spatial load, but this difference did not remain under a verbal load condition, supporting the hypothesis that verbally mediated spatial representations can be the critical determinants of the SNARC-effect. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “The SNARC-effect disappeared under verbal load in parity judgment and under spatial load in magnitude comparison.” In a 2 (load present or absent) x 2 (memory load task, spatial or verbal between subjects) design, participants’ reaction times to identify numbers as odd/even with their left or right hand were converted to dRT (median RT right response–median RT left response) for each number separately. Per subject, dRTs were entered in a regression analysis with magnitude as predictor. The weight of the magnitude predictor expresses the size of the SNARC-effect (spatial-numeric association of response codes). These regression weights were entered in a repeated measure ANOVA with Condition (baseline or load) as within-subject variable and Memory-modality (spatial or verbal) as between-subject variable. Any potential influence of differences in RT between the baseline and load condition was ruled out by introducing this difference (overall RT load–overall RT baseline) as a covariate. This analysis yielded a significant Condition X Memory-modality interaction [F(1,37) = 4.56, p < .04].

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Zakharova et al. (2014), From Comparative Political Studies
abstract_r: Attempted replication of the following claim from Zakharova & Warwick (2014): Correcting for the propensity for respondents to overestimate the policy distance of opposite-side parties, most systems show a double role for bilateralism: Not only is there a valence penalty for opposite-side parties, but there is also a tendency for distance to count more heavily against these parties. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Indeed, with DIF corrected, most surveys reveal tendencies not only for opposite-side parties to be given lower valence scores in general, but also for policy distance to be counted more heavily against them." The model advanced in the study has three main components: the valence judgment an individual makes of a party, which is the explanandum, plus two potential causal factors, the left–right ideological or policy distance between the individual and the party being evaluated and an indicator of whether or not the individual is on the opposite side of the left–right spectrum from that party (“opposite side”). To assess whether the impact of distance on valence judgments is different for opposite-side parties, the authors also include the interaction between the opposite-side indicator and policy distance. In Table 2, the authors present analyses previously reported with one key difference: Party and individual positions are those generated by the A-M [Aldrich–McKelvey] rescaling. The specific election selected to provide evidence is Australia 2007 (top row of Table 2), and the focal term is ‘Objective distance × Opposite side’ (see Table 2 for details). In Table 2, the interaction term is significantly negative in fully 19 of the regressions. In 14 of these, moreover, it coexists with a significant negative effect for the opposite-side variable. This means that bilateralism plays a double role in these cases: Parties located on the other side of center from the respondent tend to receive a net valence penalty, and they also tend to experience a more rapid decline in their valence assessments with increasing distance (from ‘Australia 2007’ row of Table 2, ‘Objective distance × Opposite side’ term: Coefficient = −0.125; SE = 0.017; p < .001 [two-tailed]).

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Flesia et al. (2020), from PsyArXiv
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Flesia et al. (2020) is that higher income is associated with lower levels of perceived stress. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Being female, having low income and living with other people were associated with higher levels of stress." Multiple regression analysis was run including sociodemographic variables. The PSS-10 (Perceived Social Stress) score was set as the dependent variable, while gender, age, education, monthly income, number of family members, and student status were entered as covariates. Monthly income was found to contribute to the level of perceived stress. From Table 1, unstandardized coefficient = -0.463, p = 5.403 e^-4.

title_r: Exploring the Effects of Satisfaction on Unethical Behaviour Intentions: An Extension of Jones and Kavanagh (1996)
abstract_r: The current study represents an extension of Jones and Kavanagh’s (1996) vignette study, exploring the effect of situational and personal factors on unethical work behaviour. Adding to this prior study and it's recent direct and conceptual replication (Evans et al., 2024), this study focuses on the different types of work experience/satisfaction indicators, differentiating between work environment, salary, appreciation and general perceptions of satisfaction. Participants will be randomly allocated to different vignettes upon which these factors vary, before being assessed on their intent to behave unethically. The current study will therefore provide the basis for a more rigorous understanding of the role of satisfaction, and it's many constituent components, in predicting intentions to behave unethically at work.

title_r: A replication of the attribution effect of contracts and victims in government blame evasion
abstract_r: In the field of public administration and policy, outsourcing services have become a common strategy in modern government operations. As society develops, governments delegate some public service functions to third-party institutions, aiming to improve efficiency, reduce costs, or leverage professional resources. In China's context, the regulatory system for outsourcing public services is in a stage of continuous improvement and development. On one hand, relevant laws and regulations are gradually being established to standardize the process and responsibility allocation of outsourcing services; on the other hand, public concern over the quality and safety of public services is increasing. Once an accident or incident occurs, determining the responsibilities of the government, outsourcing providers, and other relevant parties becomes a critical issue that needs to be addressed urgently. The transportation of hazardous chemicals, as a public service with high risk and professional requirements, involves numerous complex issues related to management, supervision, and responsibility definition. Moreover, the community correctional offender, community moral model, and ordinary citizen have different identities and role constructions within the social structure. In the context of outsourced hazardous chemical transportation, their rights protection and differences in social perception may lead to varying public attitudes and tendencies towards responsibility attribution. This repeated experiment is based on the aforementioned background, altering the type of public service and the identity of victims in the original experiment, to explore how outsourcing form and victim identity attributes influence perceptions of responsibility attribution and principles of equal protection in the Chinese context. It aims to provide theoretical support and practical references for further improving policies and management mechanisms for outsourced public services. This study aims to delve into whether public services are outsourced and how the identity attributes of victims influence attitudes toward liability attribution in hazardous chemical transportation accidents. It also seeks to analyze the relationship between these factors and the definition of responsibility and outsourcing decisions in public management policies. The study will test whether, after the transformation of public service nature, the phenomenon of liability attribution contradicting social identity theory as predicted in the original research still exists. This will provide empirical evidence and theoretical support for optimizing service outsourcing policies, risk prevention, and the construction of liability systems in China's public management field, thereby enhancing the management efficiency and social benefits of public service outsourcing and promoting the adaptive development and improvement of public management policies in local contexts.

title_r: Can infants extract low transitional probability words from natural language input?
abstract_r: There is substantial evidence suggesting that infants as young as 8 months of age can use statistical information between syllables to segment speech (Karaman & Hay, 2018; Pelucchi et al., 2009a, 2009b; Saffran et al., 1996). However, the majority of research has only tested infants’ ability to segment words with perfect or near-perfect between syllable co-occurrence statistics (i.e., transitional probabilities ~ 1.0). Much less is known about how infants extract and represent syllable sequences with lower transitional probability (TP). In the current study, we seek to replicate and extend previous findings by having infants take part in a statistical learning task and examine their ability to extract both high-transitional probability (HTP; TP=1.0) and low-transitional probability (LTP; TP=0.3) words from a naturally produced Italian corpus.

title_r: Comparing Visual Perspective and Belief Reasoning in Autism Spectrum Conditions
abstract_r: The following study expands on our previous work investigating the relationship between Visual Perspective Taking (VPT) and Belief Reasoning (BR) using a novel combined paradigm in the general population (Experiment 1: https://osf.io/efp87; Experiment 2: https://osf.io/v87hp; Experiment 3: https://osf.io/cbjfa). The relationship between VPT, especially level-2 (VPT-2), and BR has been long postulated. Both of these processes allow humans to relate to one another by creating a shared reality on which effective communication can be based. However, previously, the fields of VPT (-2) and BR have been investigated mostly independently using separate tasks and, so far, their relationship was only explored using correlations between separate task outcomes (e.g., Hamilton, Brindley & Frith, 2009). Both have been argued to be part human mentalizing abilities, that is, the capacity to represent others’ mental, emotional, and experiential states. The conceptual similarity between VPT-2 and BR is corroborated by a number of observations regarding similarities in age of development, relationship to social skills and to autistic characteristics (e.g., for review, Hamilton et al., 2009). Based on these conceptual and empirical similarities, VPT-2 and BR have even be proposed to draw on common processing resources, yet without a strong empirical foundation beyond correlations. It was therefore essential to characterise more precisely the relationship between VPT-2 and BR and our previous OSF-preregistered study, comprising three experiments (Experiment 1: https://osf.io/efp87; Experiment 2: https://osf.io/v87hp; Experiment 3: https://osf.io/cbjfa), was aimed at addressing this knowledge gap. In short, we observed and replicated the novel effect that processing another’s true belief about the visual world is slower and more error prone than processing their perspective (despite requiring identical responses in our novel paradigm), thus, suggesting that while VPT-2 and BR might indeed be closely related, processing another’s belief appears to require additional resources. The following investigation will expand on our previous work by comparing VPT and BR in those with Autism Spectrum Conditions (ASCs). Visual Perspective Taking (level 2) VPT-2 is the ability to predict the visual experience of another agent from their unique point of view (Michelon & Zacks, 2006). The current investigation will focus on VPT-2, which refers to an understanding that an object that is viewed simultaneously by the self and another (from different viewpoints) will create different visual experiences as their viewing circumstances differ (Flavell et al., 1981). To successfully complete VPT-2 tasks, one must deliberately inhibit one’s current egocentric view of the object, and then mentally transform/rotate the self into the other’s viewpoint (Zacks & Michelon, 2005; Kessler & Thomson, 2010). It has been demonstrated by Kessler and colleagues (Kessler & Rutherford, 2010; Kessler & Thomson, 2010; Kessler et al., 2014) that this process of mental self-rotation involves substantial parts of the body schema and can therefore be likened to a simulation of a body rotation. This process is only required when the angular disparity between the self and the other is large enough to prevent a simple extrapolation of the egocentric perspective, which is the case when the angular disparity approaches or exceeds 90 degrees. In the current project, angular disparity between participant and avatar will therefore be varied between 0 and 90 degrees. Belief Reasoning BR and false-BR in particular is perhaps the most common Mentalizing index (Quesque & Rossetti, 2020), and requires the ability to impute mental states of others and oneself (Wimmer & Perner, 1983). To successfully complete false-belief tasks, a participant must decouple another’s false-belief from their own egocentric reality and simultaneously hold their own belief and the other’s opposing belief in mind (Baron-Cohen, Leslie & Frith, 1985). On the other hand, if the other holds a true belief, this decoupling process is not required to the same extend as the beliefs are not contradictory. This is reflected in shorter reaction times in true-belief conditions, relative to false-belief conditions (Back & Apperly, 2010). False beliefs are typically created by changing the location of an object without the other person knowing (e.g. while they are away), but false beliefs can also be elicited by changing the content or identity of an object (see Hogrefe, Wimmer & Perner, 1986). In the current project, false beliefs will be established by changing the identity of the target object; that is, the target object hidden under a bucket will be swapped for another without the protagonist knowing. Accordingly, the protagonist will maintain a true belief, if the target object is not swapped. Autism Spectrum Conditions ASCs, also referred to as Autism Spectrum Disorders (Bargiela, Steward and Mandy, 2016) and includes Asperger’s Syndrome, atypical autism and Pervasive Developmental Disorder (Baron-Cohen et al., 2009). ASCs represent a specific cognitive style, which is characterised by differences in how beliefs are processed. ASCs have been repeatedly linked with specific mentalizing difficulties and with hampered BR in particular (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985, Frith, 2001, Happe, 1995). Domain-general ASC accounts, e.g. Decoupling (Frith et al., 1991; Leslie, 1987) and Simulation theories (Langdon & Coltheart, 2001) of Mentalizing, agree that VPT-2 should also be challenging for ASCs because both require decoupling or simulation. Evidence indeed suggests that VPT-2 is also affected in ASC (Pearson, Ropar, Hamilton, 2013), but it remains unclear, if to the same extend as BR or not. Alternatively, domain-specific or modular accounts, e.g. Eye Direction Detector (EDD; Baron-Cohen, 1995), suggest that EDD is responsible for both VPT levels and an additional Theory of Mind module is required for BR. Understanding whether VPT-2 is similarly or less impaired in ASCs as BR will not only help us distinguish between modular and broad theories of ASC and ‘Mentalizing’, but it will also shed light on mentalizing abilities more generally and whether a domain-general account or a modular account would be mechanistically more appropriate to distinguish between different mentalizing processes. The current investigation VPT-2 and BR will be compared in a population of adults with and without ASCs using our combined VPT2-BR paradigm. The second iteration of our paradigm used in Comparing Visual Perspective Taking and Belief Reasoning, Experiment 2: Comparing self and other (https://osf.io/v87hp) will also be used here. The main advantage of this iteration of the paradigm is that it can capture potential memory contributions to BR judgements. All three of our previous iterations revealed greater processing demands (RTs and/or ERs) associated with BR relative to VPT. Iteration 2 allows us to assess whether the additional processing demands associated with BR are more likely to be due to memory or social processes. Previously we found that the additional processing is unlikely to be due to memory processes, however this may differ in ASCs.

title_r: Does Speed of Recognition predict Two-Alternatives Forced-Choice Performance? Replicating and Extending Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018)
abstract_r: Does the speed of single-word recognition errors predict performance in subsequent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) trials that include the error item? Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018) found effects of this kind in two experiments and account for them in terms of a continuous memory-strength signal guiding recognition decisions. In the 2AFC task, Starns et al. (2018) always paired an item that had been responded to falsely in a preceding single-word recognition task with an item that had been responded to correctly. Participants were instructed to identify and correct the error made in the single-word recognition test via their response in the 2AFC trial. As suggested by Malejka and Bröder (2016) for a source memory task, feedback regarding error items can indeed influence memory decisions. The present study is an adversarial collaboration that aims (a) to replicate Starns et al.’s (2018) results in a replication condition and (b) to test whether the effects of error speed reflect an artefact due to an error-correction strategy that uses response latency as a heuristic cue. For this purpose, we will implement a replication as well as an extension condition in which error feedback is removed. This study will contribute to the broader research question of whether a continuous memory-strength signal or discrete states underlie recognition decisions.

title_r: Investigating the effect of relived autobiographical pain on cognitive inhibition
abstract_r: Research indicates that increased pain decreases key cognitive processes needed for everyday life (e.g., cognitive inhibition). The more pain a participant reports experiencing, the slower they are to inhibit a natural response. Chen et al. (2008) used this decrease as an objective pain measure, finding that participants’ RTs were significantly slower after reliving greater levels of pain from recalled autobiographical memories of painful experiences. Reading their report, however, Chen et al. (2008) used a reduced cognitive inhibition Stroop task (16 items), thus lacking the sensitivity to potentially elicit cognitive inhibition (which the task measures). They also only analysed participants’ response RT, generally, rather than their cognitive inhibition ability, specifically. Thus, whilst they correctly reported that increased pain can decrease response RTs, we feel they could have gone further and investigated whether increased pain also dulls inhibition RTs, too. This study is, therefore, looking to replicate their original finding, and then extend that finding to investigate whether the reduction in RTs extend to cognitive inhibition, too. We intend to use a longer, more sensitive Stroop task to do this. This will not only strengthen Chen et al.’s conclusion, should we replicate their response RT result, but also allow us to investigate our primary aim regarding the impact of pain on cognitive inhibition. Further, this study will look to investigate whether cognitive Stroop task performance is a valid, objective measure pain by analysing the relationship between participants’ self-reported pain levels and their subsequent cognitive task performance.

title_r: How self-construal influences the consequences of social comparison (CCREP3)
abstract_r: Does self-construal have an influence on the consequences of social comparison (as in Gardner et al., 2002)? Gardner et al. (2002, study 1) found that interdependent self-construal is a factor that influences the consequences of social comparison on self-evaluation. Participants were primed with interdependent or independent self-construal and then asked to compare themselves to a friend and a stranger, in a self-relevant and a self-irrelevant task. As a measurement for the influence of social-comparison participants guessed if the stranger and the friend got the answers in a knowledge task correct. In the self-relevant task men projected a better performance for strangers than their friends, when primed with the independent self-construal. When primed with the interdependent self-construal men projected in both tasks a better performance for the friend compared to the stranger. For women there was no significant three-way interaction (prime, self-relevance, relationship). We will conceptually replicate this finding with a few adaptations. In the present study, participants perform a self-relevant task after being asked which performance facet is more important (speed / accuracy). Further, the participants are asked what category they define as in-group (gender, employment, location) to represent the comparison between friend and stranger in the original study. Furthermore, Gardner et al. (2002) explained the gender differences, with men and women having a different chronic self-construal. We will not merely assume gender differences in chronic self-construal but measure it directly and look at its influences. The present research question is if self-construal (chronic) influences the consequences of social comparison on self-evaluation (as in Gardner et al. 2002).

title_r: The effect of majority-minority shift and status threat on Whites' support for voting restrictions
abstract_r: This project has several purposes. First is to extend work on the effects of majority-minority demographic shift reminders on Whites' perceived anti-White discrimination, political conservatism, and prejudice against ethnic minority groups (e.g., Craig & Richeson, 2014; 2017) to their support for restrictions to voting rights. This is in response to current efforts by some Republican state legislatures to restrict voting rights. Such evidence would imply racial motives behind these legislative initiatives. The second purpose is to more directly replicate some of those previous findings on those particular outcome variables mentioned above. This is in response to several unpublished failed close replications by our lab. The third is to examine the meaning of past findings that these demographic shift reminders increase Whites' status threat. Based on pilot data, we consider whether the status threat measure typically used by Craig & Richeson is psychologically meaningful, or instead simply a manipulation check. Given that this measure has frequently been treated as a mediator of the effects of demographic shift reminders on sociopolitical outcomes, it is important to determine whether this measure captures whether participants actually demonstrate a perceived threat to their group's status, or if they are simply affirming the manipulation.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Calzo et al. (2013), in Health Psychology
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Calzo et al. (2013) is that that, controlling for weight status and pubertal development, sexual minority males would report higher levels of desire for toned/defined muscles and concerns with weight and shape than heterosexual males; the higher levels of desire for toned/defined muscles is the portion of this hypothesis selected for the SCORE program [note that pubertal development was dropped from the analyses in the results reported here]. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: “...gay and bisexual participants reported greater desire for toned muscles than completely and mostly heterosexual males...” Drawing on data from the Growing Up Today Study (GUTS), the authors test the claim with longitudinal regression using generalized estimating equations (GEE) in SAS, accounting for the correlation of repeated measures within the individual and clustering by siblings within the same family. The dependent variable in the model selected for the SCORE program (Table 2, column 2) is desire for toned/defined muscles, and the sample includes observations from ages 14–25. The predictor of interest is a term for gay/bisexual, and the reference category is completely heterosexual. The model adjusts for geographic region and weight status effects (see column 2, Table 2 for details about the model specification). Gay and bisexual participants reported significantly greater desire for toned and defined muscles than completely heterosexual participants (beta = .39, 95% C.I. = .21, .57).

title_r: Effects of conceptual size on long-term memory for physical size
abstract_r: This study follows up on the OSF project "Do object retinal size and conceptual size interact in long-term memory? Using preferred physical sizes." The results of that study replicated findings from our previous work, showing a main effect of physical size (better memory for physically large than small objects) as well as a main effect of conceptual size (better memory for conceptually small than large objects). However, despite using preferred physical sizes (in accord with the preferred sizes found by Konkle & Oliva, 2011), no interaction was observed between physical and conceptual size. The present study aims to replicate the basic finding that physical size is better represented and remembered when it coincides with conceptual size. Using manipulations such as drawing, imagining, and preferential viewing, Konkel and Oliva (2011) found that objects are represented and remembered in a consistent visual size that is proportional to the logarithm of their conceptual (real-world) size. Here, we aim to replicate this finding using a long-term memory paradigm similar to our previous experiments, in which both physical and conceptual size are manipulated. However, rather than testing memory only for object identity (i.e., “WHICH OBJECT did you see”), we will additionally test memory for an object’s physical size (i.e., “IN WHICH SIZE did you see this object”). Stimuli will appear in small or large physical sizes during encoding, and participants will subsequently be tested both on their identity and their encoded size using a four-alternative forced choice (4-AFC) test involving two items (target, foil) appearing in the two potential sizes (small, large). Experimental parameters will largely follow our previous study (see OSF: Do object retinal size and conceptual size interact in long-term memory? Using preferred physical sizes), with a few changes detailed below.

title_r: The impact of anti-elitism attitudes on the relationship between analytic thinking and conspiracy beliefs across five European countries
abstract_r: In this study, we will replicate and extend the findings of Mehl et al. (2024) by examining the association between conspiracy beliefs, populist attitudes, and analytic thinking across five European countries: Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary, Poland, and Germany. By employing different operationalizations of key variables, we seek to determine the robustness of the original findings in diverse populations. Specifically, we will investigate whether the association between analytic thinking and conspiracy beliefs is moderated by populist attitudes, specifically anti-elitism. Additionally, we will explore potential country-level variations in these relationships. If the original findings do not replicate in all countries, we will conduct further analyses to identify additional factors, such as institutional trust, voting behavior, and political satisfaction, that may influence the relationship between conspiracy beliefs, populist attitudes, and analytic thinking. One of the effects they attempted to reproduce was Van Lange et al.'s study on Social Value Orientation (SVO) and Family Size. title_r: Finding the Repressors’ True Emotions: Identifying Repressive Coping Style via an Implicit Measure of Emotional States
abstract_r: Repressive copers are defined as people who self-report themselves as having low anxiety, while simultaneously displaying conflicting unconscious signs of having high anxiety (Weinberger et al., 1979). To conceptualize this in simpler terms, repressive copers are people who tend to avoid negative/ threatening information automatically (Myers, 2000, 2010; Myers, et al., 2007). The interesting component of repressive copers is that they describe themselves as experiencing lower levels of anxiety, yet when measured through an emotional arousal assessments repressive copers are found to experience higher levels of anxiety. There are important implications of repressive copers when discussing the validity of research relating to self-reported anxiety or neuroticism; namely, the measurements used were unable to accurately determine the emotional state of these repressive copers (Eysenck, 2000). The expected percentage of repressive copers in a given population varies depending on multiple factors (Myers, 2010). In a non-clinical and relatively young population the average number of individuals, who would be categorized as repressive copers, is between 10-20 percent (Myers, 2010, 2008; Myers & Reynolds, 2000; Myers & Vetere, 1997). This percentage significantly increases as the population ages and/ or encounters various medical issues (Myers, 2010, 2008; Myers & Reynolds, 2000; Myers & Vetere, 1997). The existence of this specific population has drastic implications in every study that employs some form of explicit emotional measure. Essentially, there is always a not insignificant portion of a sample whose results were not valid under the employed measurement. Due to the potential problems repressive copers may pose for those utilizing explicit emotions scale more work needs to be done with this population. This study aims to do that through two main components. The first is a conceptual replication of Weinberger et al. (1979) study, which reported a large response time differences in repressors when facing a internal threatening emotion, such as anxiety. We hope to replicate those response time findings using updated stimuli. This will further support the need to account for repressive copers in sampling. Additionally, we are using an Implicit measure of emotion to see if it is able to measure repressors' emotions more in line with what the response time differences suggest (such as heightened states of anxiety). This way we will be able to measure repressive coper's emotions more discretely than physiological methods allow.

title_r: Implicit and explicit tax aversion and its behavioral outcomes: study 2 – preregistration plan
abstract_r: Tax aversion is quite a novel phenomenon in the field of fiscal psychology. The term ‘tax aversion’ refers to an individual propensity in escaping taxes more pronounced than the equal tendency in avoiding any other sort of payments. The current proposal aims to investigate tax aversion employing both implicit and explicit attitudinal measures to determine the presence and the extent of the phenomenon in the Italian context. The current study is part of a comprehensive research project composed by three independent studies. Each study aims to measure both implicit and explicit attitudes towards taxes, by employing the Implicit Association Test, a close replication of experiments 1 and 2 of Sussman and Olivola (2011), and two different validated scales measuring explicit attitude (Tax Compliance Inventory TAX-I (Kirchler, Wahl, 2010); Perceived Fiscal Sacrifice Scale (Ferrari, Randisi, 2013).

title_r: Facets of Loneliness, Mental Health, and Social Media Use: Fine-grained Associations in a Sample of Young Adults in Japan
abstract_r: Loneliness is a common health concern that has gained increasing relevance during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Before the pandemic, 9% of Japanese adults reported feeling lonely, while 41.1% of the Japanese population was categorized as being lonely during the pandemic (DiJulio et al., 2018; Stickley & Ueda, 2022). Loneliness is a subjective negative feeling of insufficient social connection with others (Perlman & Peplau, 1981) and can be categorized into social and emotional loneliness (Weiss, 1973). Social loneliness refers to the absence of community and social networks, while emotional loneliness captures the absence of attachment and close relationships. These types of loneliness are related differently to mental health symptoms. In a network analytic study, Wolters and colleagues (2023) examined the comprehensive associations between social and emotional loneliness, social isolation, depression, general anxiety, and social anxiety. The findings unveiled that social loneliness was associated with social isolation, while emotional loneliness was connected to social anxiety and depression in a sample of Dutch students (Wolters et al., 2023). To build on these findings, the current study seeks to investigate the comprehensive association of loneliness and loneliness-related variables in three parts. First, we will replicate the network model from Wolters et al. (2023) in a sample of young adults in Japan (aged 18-29 years). Second, we will extend the replication model by including loneliness-related variables, such as social media use and social avoidance. Previous studies have reported an association between social media use and loneliness. The evolutionary theory of loneliness hypothesizes that loneliness triggers avoidance in social situations (Cacioppo & Cacioppo, 2018; Wu et al., 2024). Third, we will examine the longitudinal associations between loneliness and loneliness-related variables using a panel network approach.

title_r: Information Transfer of Solutions to a Novel Problem (the “Rubik’s Twist Task”) Within and Between Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults. How Accurately do Chains of Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults Predict Their Performance on a Novel Problem-Solving Task (the “Rubik’s Twist Task”), and Does This Differ Depending on Whether They Complete the Task With Someone of a Matched or Mis-Matched Neurotype?
abstract_r: Brief Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (henceforth “autism”) is characterised by impairments in social communication and interaction (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). This currently prevailing deficit-model of autism assumes differences in communication between autistic and non-autistic people are solely a result of autistic shortcomings (Milton, 2012). However, recent research examining non-autistic to autistic, and autistic to autistic, social interaction has begun to challenge this, suggesting that social and communication difficulties experienced by autistic people may be the result of a mismatch between autistic and non-autistic communication styles. For example, autistic communication may be more direct and literal - a style potentially deemed rude by non-autistic people but favoured by autistic (Sasson et al., 2017; Crompton, Hallett et al., 2020). This may lead to autistic people feeling more comfortable and relaxed around other autistic people (Crompton, Ropar et al., 2020; Crompton, Hallett et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021; Granieri et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2021) and thus preferring to spend time with them (DeBrabander et al., 2019; Morrison et al., 2020). Conversely, when autistic people interact with non-autistic people their behaviours, social judgements, and resulting misunderstandings can exacerbate autistic social difficulties (Milton, 2012; DeBrabander et al., 2019; Botha & Frost, 2020). Direct evidence of intact communication efficacy between autistic partners, and selective breakdowns in communication between autistic and non-autistic partners, was published by Crompton, Ropar et al. (2020, henceforth “Crompton et al., 2020”). A cultural learning paradigm (known as a “diffusion chain”; Flynn & Whiten, 2008) was utilised to measure the transmission of information within “chains” of eight people where (a) all participants were autistic (b) all participants were non-autistic, and (c) participants alternated between autistic and non-autistic. The authors found that autistic people transferred information to and from other autistic people as effectively as non-autistic people transferred information with non-autistic people. However, information sharing broke down – that is, significantly less information was transferred – in the mixed chain which alternated between autistic and non-autistic people. Crompton et al. (2020) did have some limitations in that it included a relatively modest sample (N=72) and recruited from a single geographical location. The authors therefore performed an extensive replication, including a substantially larger sample and recruitment from three independent sites. The study we propose in this pre-registration utilises data from this replication study. Crompton et al. (2020) tasked participants with retelling a fictional story, thus the information to be remembered and transmitted was language based and in a specific format. Consequently, to assess whether the effect was generalisable to a less verbal task, the replication study included a “Rubiks Twist” task. It is this task we propose to analyse in this pre-registration. The task will be described in more detail below, but in essence it used the same diffusion chain paradigm but instead of retelling a story, participants were asked to create a dog shape from a 3D puzzle toy known as a Rubik’s Twist. Chains consisted of six participants and the first participant watched a video of an experimenter successfully creating a dog shape from this toy. The Rubik’s Twist consisted of 24 prism-shaped wedges that could be twisted or turned to create a wide range of shapes and thus this new task was inherently more visual in nature and likely drew on a different range of cognitive abilities. Note, although the task did not necessarily require the transmission of verbal information to obtain the task goal, it was not a completely non-verbal task and the use of verbal communication (e.g., information about how to perform certain actions) is likely to have aided performance. In addition to replicating the original study, the authors extended it by exploring whether being informed of the diagnostic status of one’s interaction partner affects information transfer. In Crompton et al. (2020), participants were informed of the diagnostic status of their partner prior to commencing an interaction. However, in real-world interactions many autistic adults choose not to disclose their diagnosis to avoid bias and discrimination (Jones et al., 2021) and emerging evidence suggests that awareness of an autism diagnosis influences how autistic people are perceived by non-autistic, but not other autistic people (DeBrabander et al., 2019; Sasson & Morrison, 2019). A diagnostic-informing manipulation was therefore added to explore whether such patterns have downstream effects on communication and information sharing. Our first aim is to examine the effect of matched and mismatched neurotype on information transfer in this less verbal task. Information transferred is referred to as “Objective Performance” and consists of a score to represent how closely the dog shape a participant produces matches that of the dog shape shown to the first participant via video. We predict a replication of the original (Crompton et al., 2020) finding showing that information transfer degrades most rapidly in chains of mixed interactions, compared with chains of single-neurotype interactions. However, it is possible that the different cognitive requirements presented by our new task – namely, a decrease in verbal and language skills and an increase in visuospatial (Carroll, 1993; Frick et al., 2013) – could act to diminish some of the communication difficulties/potential anxieties faced by the mixed pairs, making the task more resilient to mismatches in communication style. Moreover, the requirement to draw on different cognitive capacities could disproportionally increase performance in one group. Secondly, we will extend our analyses from objective performance to examine participants’ subjective performance which will enable us to answer questions on accuracy of self-assessment in autistic and non-autistic people. Self-assessment refers to an ability to accurately gauge one’s level of task performance and is considered an aspect of metacognition (DeBrabander et al., 2021). Under- or over-assessing one’s abilities can have a detrimental influence, not only on current task performance, but also broader functional outcomes (Bowie et al., 2007; Harvey & Pinkham, 2015). Moreover, reduced self-assessment accuracy has even been shown to predict functional outcomes better than objective performance (Gould et al., 2015; Silberstein et al., 2018). The literature relating this area to autism is sparse – studies on autism and metacognition often focus on assessment of one’s own mental state (Bird & Cook, 2013) or memory (Grainger et al., 2014) rather than performance. A recent study (DeBrabander et al., 2021) looked at self-assessment and performance on specific general and social cognitive tasks, finding evidence that autistic adults may show lower self-assessment accuracy than non-autistic adults on social cognitive tasks. However, this study looked at self-assessment in an individual capacity, but accurate self-assessment may also be important for changing one’s behaviour - and thus outcomes - in “real time” during interactions e.g., assessment of performance in an interview or meeting, or during a collaborative task. These data provide a unique opportunity to examine self-assessment accuracy in autistic and non-autistic people and how this may have been affected by interacting with someone of the same or a different neurotype. Thirdly, we will examine whether being in an informed or uninformed diffusion chain (i.e. knowing the diagnostic status of one’s interaction partner) affects objective and subjective performance. As discussed above, disclosing an autism diagnosis influences how autistic people are perceived by non-autistic people, and may therefore have a downstream effect on communication (Sasson & Morrison, 2019; DeBrabander et al., 2019; Thompson-Hodgetts et al., 2020) and information sharing.

title_r: The effect of transcranial direct current stimulation on the interplay between executive control, behavioral variability and mind wandering: A registered report
abstract_r: Mind wandering (MW) is a pervasive mental phenomenon that describes our tendency to lose focus during prolonged situations that require sustained attention. It has been hypothesized that mind wandering is tightly linked to (the loss of) executive control. The dorso-lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is one of the core regions that has been consistently linked to executive functioning and is hence highly likely to be related to maintaining sustained attention and avoiding mind wandering. Therefore, a range of brain-stimulation studies attempted to non-invasively modulate mind-wandering propensity using transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) of the DLPFC. Initially, several studies reporting successful modulation of mind-wandering propensity using traditional non-focal, low-intensity tDCS over the DLPFC provided an optimistic outlook (Axelrod, Rees, Lavidor, & Bar, 2015; Kajimura, Kochiyama, Nakai, Abe, & Nomura, 2016; Kajimura & Nomura, 2015). However, since then several studies have failed to replicate this effect (e.g., Coulborn et al., 2020), including a large-scale, pre-registered direct replication study (Boayue et al., 2019) suggesting that the initial positive results that were based on very low sample-sizes might have been a statistical fluke (but see (Axelrod, Zhu, & Qiu, 2018; Csifcsak et al., 2019). More recently, however, a study implementing a novel experimental paradigm and an improved high-definition tDCS (HD-tDCS) stimulation protocol showed promising results in reducing the amount of mind wandering during the experimental task (Boayue et al., 2020). However, these initial results were not pre-registered before the study was conducted and hence give only preliminary evidence. In the current study, we aim to replicate the effect found by Boayue et al. (2020) using a pre-registered study design. In addition, we want to gain a further understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying the effect by recording electroencephalogram (EEG) and pupillometric data before, during and after brain-stimulation. Boayue et al., (2020) found that HD-tDCS over the left DLPFC during the FT-RSGT task could decrease the propensity of mind wandering. The study implements a random finger-tapping task, where the participants are encouraged to maximise the randomness of left-right finger-tapping sequences. In addition, subjects are regularly queried about their attentional state using thought-probes. In our study, two experimental groups – one receiving sham and one receiving real stimulation – will be tested with this task in three sessions: One baseline session before start of the stimulation, one online-stimulation session while the stimulation device is active and an offline post-stimulation session. The stimulation protocol will be the same 4x1 HD-tDCS protocol over the DLPFC as in our previous study (Boayue et al., 2020). Our equipment allows both the stimulation of brain areas and recording the EEG from the same electrodes during baseline and offline periods.

title_r: Illusory truth effect of fake business news
abstract_r: In this conceptual replication study, we would like to replicate and extend the illusory truth effect of political fake news found by Pennycook et al. (2018) to the marketing field. Our study will test whether repeated exposure to business-related fake news increases the accuracy evaluation of those fake news. We will also test if this effect holds across different types of fake news warnings. For exploratory purposes, the moderating role of illusory pattern-perception, anti-big business attitudes and attention to the news will be also tested.

title_r: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Multiple Representations in Equation-Solving Problems - An Eye Tracking Study
abstract_r: Multiple external representations (MERs) play an important role in the learning field of mathematics. Whereas the CTML and the ITPC model assume that the heterogeneous combination of symbolic and analogous representations fosters learning, the Design, Functions and Tasks framework implicates that learning benefits depend on the specific functions of MERs. The current paper will be a conceptual replication study of one of the few studies comparing single representations, heterogeneous and homogeneous MERs in the context of mathematics learning. In a balanced incomplete block design, the participants will be provided single representations (graphic, text, or formula) or a heterogeneous (e.g., text + graphic) or homogeneous (text + formula) combination of these to solve linear system of equations problems. Gaze behavior, task performance, and time on task will be recorded. On the basis of previous research, learning with MERs is expected to be superior to learning with single representations. Moreover, heterogeneous representations are expected to be superior to homogeneous ones. The relationship between MERs and performance is assumed to be (serially) mediated by cognitive load and number of transitions. Additionally, text is expected to be fixated more often and longer than formula or graphic.

title_r: Foveal vision contribution to peripheral object recognition
abstract_r: In this study we use a procedure introduced by Fan et al. (2016). Participants are presented with visual stimuli in the periphery. They have to identify whether the stimulus matched a learned object. At fixation a mask is presented. The main variable is the delay between stimulus onset and mask onset. A feedback signal specific to the foveal cortex has been proposed. The evidence comes from neuroimaging studies showing that when observers are presented with an object in the periphery, object category information can be decoded from the foveal retinotopic cortex (Williams et al., 2008) and that performance is affected by transcranial magnetic stimulation applied to the foveal cortex (Chambers et al., 2013). In addition to the neuroimaging studies, psychophysical experiments have manipulated the information presented in central and peripheral vision. The results show that processing of a visual object in the periphery is modulated by masking information at the fovea (Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2016; Yu & Shim, 2016). These psychophysical studies therefore support the feedback hypothesis. In the paradigm used by Fan et al. (2016) observers performed a task on peripheral stimuli, and noise was presented in fovea at different stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). Observers maintained fixation on a central mark, and fixation behaviour was monitored thanks to an eye-tracker. Importantly, the noise caused impairment only for SOA of 250-ms, and only for tasks that required processing of object shape. The study also included fMRI data showing shape representation in the foveal cortex. Fan et al. report several control experiments. In one of these a shape has to be memorised by the participant and the task is to detect whether the stimulus in the periphery matched the one in memory. This peripheral stimulus was presented only in the upper right field, while the noise was again in the foveal region. The stimuli were 3D rendered abstract shapes, known in the literature as spikies (de Beeck et al. 2006). Our Experiment is a conceptual replication of the control experiment reported in Fan et al. (2016). Because this experiment was only a control we were unable to locate all details of the methods. We have, however, kept as close as possible to the original design. In particular we will use a match to memory task, we will use the same class of stimuli (spikies) as Fan et al., and an increased power. The mask will also be similar and include a dynamic set of random dots changing over time. The SOA levels will be as in Fan et al.: 50, 150, 250, 350 and 450 mse plus the no-noise baseline condition.

title_r: Harnessing Simulated Experience to Help People Make Better Investment Decisions (Validity Test)
abstract_r: In order to make satisfactory investment decisions, investors must know and understand the risks that they face. An investor's comprehension of risk can differ considerably depending on how that risk is learned or communicated. Finance professionals typically communicate risks using descriptions, for instance, in the form of financial reports, mutual fund brochures, insurance brochures, investor education programs, and market research. These documents report risks using summary of historical returns and their respective probabilities. However, investors could also acquire knowledge about financial risks in other ways, that is, by observing the development of stock prices or through their own investment experience. For instance, day-traders decide to purchase a stock by simply observing prior stock movements, or, individual investors increase their subscription to IPO auctions subsequent to previous successful experience (e.g., Kaustia & Knupfer, 2008). The literature documents that the manner in which knowledge about risks is acquired or communicated, has a dramatic influence on investor's understanding of risk and their willingness to accept it. For example, our previous work shows experimentally that people who learn about a stock market crash from experience are more likely to stay out of the market than people who learn from descriptions (i.e., the "depression babies" effect), even when wealth effects are kept equivalent (Lejarraga, Woike, & Hertwig, 2016). Recent studies have shown that, in general, people not only seem to be persuaded more by their experience than from described sources of information, but also may arrive at more accurate subjective assessments of a given risk, even if experience is simulated. For example, Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013) and Bradbury, Hens and Zeisberger (2014) show that simulations of the stock market, which are closer to the notion of witnessing than experiencing through action, help investors understand risk accurately, and lead them to invest more in the stock market than investors that learn from described sources. On the other hand, Lejarraga and Gonzalez (2011) show that exhaustive descriptive information is often neglected when the subjects have the chance to also experience the information by sampling. That is, people who have experience and descriptions, make choices as if descriptions were omitted. Consistent with this observation, Barron, Leider, and Stack (2007) show that people are more likely to ignore a described warning if they have already experienced a series of safe outcomes, but they are more likely to be persuaded by the warning if they have no previous experience. These studies converge in that people tend to overweight the information they gain from experience over that which is provided in a descriptive form, which can lead to more accurate risk assessments, as long as the experiences made are representative of the environment. Our studies attempt to extend previous research in two ways. First, we seek to conduct a conceptual replication of the study of Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013). This involves exposing participants in an investment task to four different risk communication interventions and observing how the interventions affect participants’ risk taking behaviour, factual knowledge about the encountered decision environmnet, and subjective assessments of confidence and satisfaction. Second, we will extend the study of Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013) by manipulating whether or not people have had prior experiences with the decision environment, when exposed to the risk communication intervention. Specifically, one group of people will build up experience with the decision environment by making a series of decisions with feedback prior to being exposed to the risk communication intervention, while the other group, akin to Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013), will be given the risk communication intervention straight away. Using this setup, we will be able to provide a better estimate of how effective the four risk interventions are in informing people about financial risks in situations involving no prior experiences and explore how and whether prior experiences impact the effectiveness of the four interventions. In this particular study, we will compare the behavior using the description tool with the risk tool, the latter with improved instructions.

title_r: Role of awareness for durability of DR bindings/learnt DR pairings
abstract_r: The study is a conceptual replication of Experiment 1 (Frings, Moeller & Horner, 2015, Acta Psychologica). In a training block consisting of five blocks a 20 trials (equaling a total of 100 trials), participants classify objects as larger/smaller than a shoebox. Objects are presented in duplicated fashion on screen (flanking a fixation marker). Irrelevant stimuli (distractors, letters, symbols or digits) are used as fixation marker. Each marker is presented once per block. Furthermore, across each block, each marker is consistently paired with the same response (left/right key press). After a brief filler task (1:30 Min), a test phase follows, consisting of one block (40 trials). In the test phase, the task is slightly changed, as participants classify objects as bigger/smaller than a waste bin. The crucial manipulation concerns compatibility of distractors to assigned responses in the test block, as 50% are presented in trials that require a response that is compatible with the paired D-R assignment in the preceding training blocks, whereas the remaining 50% of distractors are presented with incompatible responses. It is expected that performance is better (i.e., faster, more accurate) for compatible DR responses, compared with incompatible DR responses in the test block. In addition to this, memory for DR pairings is assessed to explore whether compatibility effects in the test blocks resulted from explicit awareness of DR pairings during training. All participants receive an awareness test for each distractor that assesses memory for the response that was most often required for each distractor. However, timing of the awareness measure was manipulated: As the test block effectively no longer has any contingent DR pairings, which might extinguish or reduce awareness for learned DR pairings, half of the participants are probed for awareness before the test block, the remaining participants are probed for awareness after the test block. The timing of the memory test (before/after test block) is also considered as a moderator.

title_r: Investigating the Role of Gaze Cues on the Communication-Induced Memory Bias
abstract_r: Investigating the role of gaze cues on the communication-induced memory bias. In this conceptual replication study, we use a screen-based violation of expectation (VOE) paradigm to investigate whether 9-month-old infants process different information about novel objects when an object is introduced in a communicative referential versus non-communicative referential context (Yoon, Johnson, & Csibra et al., 2008; Okumura, Kobayashi, & Itakura, 2016; but see Silverstein, Gliga, Westermann, & Parise, 2018). In 12 test trial videos, an object will be shown together with one adult (action phase). We will manipulate the communicative context depicted in the videos such that the adult either looks at object after looking in the direction of the infant (communicative context) or the actor looks at the object individually without addressing the infant at all (non-communicative). After each video, the scene will be occluded before it reveals one of three different outcomes: the object infants had just seen in the action phase (no change, baseline), the object they had just seen but at a novel position (location change), or a new object (identity change). By manipulating both the communicative context and features of the object in the subsequent outcome phase, we aim to conceptually replicate the previous finding that observed communicative context may bias infants to encode surface features which support learning about object kinds (i.e., object identity) over spatial-temporal information (i.e., object location). In contrast to previous studies examining this effect, we will use a study setup and data processing procedure that will allow us to implicitly extract infants’ looking time response by using eye tracking technology instead of manually coding infants’ looking behavior.

title_r: Beneficial and adverse consequences of aggression: Replication
abstract_r: Aggression is argued to have addictive properties (see Golden et al., 2017). Retaliatory aggression is often reinforcing as indicated by heightened activity in brain regions associated with reward processing (Brune et al., 2013; Chester & DeWall, 2016). Provoked individuals reap hedonistic rewards when retaliating (e.g., Chester & DeWall, 2017; de Quervain et al., 2004). Moreover, revenge-related feelings of pleasure, satisfaction, and gratification motivate some individuals to compulsively seek revenge (Dyduch-Hazar et al., 2022). Engagement in behavior despite adverse consequences is one of the features of addictive behavior (e.g., Potenza, 2008). Thus, the question arises: would individuals still retaliate if retaliating brings them adverse consequences? This research aims to address this issue.

title_r: Fork of Wealth and Happiness: Replication of Diener, E., Ng, W., Harter, J., & Arora, R. (2010) at University of Vienna.
abstract_r: General Information This project is part of the Direct+Plus CREP replication (https://osf.io/px0sw/) of a study by Diener et al. (2010). The 27 students will perform the replication study as a part of a seminar at the Department of Occupational, Economic and Social Psychology, led by Andre Julian Hartmann and Martin Müller (both graduate students) at the University of Vienna (Austria). Materials All materials are developed together with the students during the seminar and will be added to the project before starting data collection. In addition to the items of the original study, items for further research questions will be added as a direct+ replication. We also participate in the Direct+Plus project by Jordan Wagge containing two questions that deal with financial security. Procedure All students are using the same survey, advertising materials, and OSF page since this is an online study. Every student will sample N = 10 (total targeted sample: N = 270) students living in Vienna within their social circle. Original Abstract The Gallup World Poll, the first representative sample of planet Earth, was used to explore the reasons why happiness is associated with higher income, including the meeting of basic needs, fulfillment of psychological needs, increasing satisfaction with one's standard of living, and public goods. Across the globe, the association of log income with subjective well-being was linear but convex with raw income, indicating the declining marginal effects of income on subjective well-being. Income was a moderately strong predictor of life evaluation but a much weaker predictor of positive and negative feelings. Possessing luxury conveniences and satisfaction with standard of living were also strong predictors of life evaluation. Although the meeting of basic and psychological needs mediated the effects of income on life evaluation to some degree, the strongest mediation was provided by standard of living and ownership of conveniences. In contrast, feelings were most associated with the fulfillment of psychological needs: learning, autonomy, using one's skills, respect, and the ability to count on others in an emergency. Thus, two separate types of prosperity—economic and social psychological—best predict different types of well-being. Student Researchers Siepmann Florian

title_r: Subjectivity in gradable adjectives: Does your age influence what counts as old?
abstract_r: The meaning of gradable adjectives like tall, heavy, and old is vague. While they are concerned with quantifiable properties of instances (height, weight, age), there is no agreed upon boundary between short and tall, light and heavy, or young and old. As a result, speakers can disagree as to whether someone is old or not without committing an error (a phenomenon known as faultless disagreement). This project, conducted as a bachelor thesis at Erasmus University Rotterdam, is concerned with the question of how speakers determine the boundary between positive and negative instances of vague adjectives. For tall and heavy, Verheyen, Dewil, and Égré (2018) have shown that people tend to use themselves as a yardstick when ascribing these adjectives to human figures of varied measurements: subjects’ height and weight requirements for applying tall and heavy were found to be positively correlated with their personal measurements. This project constitutes a conceptual replication of Verheyen et al.’s findings to establish whether people use their own age as a yard stick to determine whether faces of various ages are old or not. title_r: Representative bureaucracy and perceived legitimacy in crisis situations: Experimental replication in Chinese context
abstract_r: The impact of gender representation on perceived legitimacy has been widely validated in the United States, South Korea, South Asia, and other regions (Baniamin&Jamil, 2023; Pyo, 2023). This study attempts to replicate Riccucci et al., 2014's research through experiments to explore whether symbolic representativeness is established in China. Specifically, the first part of the study changed policy areas, the second part adjusted the measurement of gender representation and controlled for sequential effects, and the third part explored whether gender representation remains effective in crisis situations. Therefore, we designed a 6 (three gender ratios and two occurrence orders) × 2 (high/low Performance) × 2 (Normal/Crisis) Investigation Experiment based on the original experiment.

title_r: Exploring the Effect of Social Distance on Medium Preferences in Interpersonal Communication: A Replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope (2013, Experiment 2)
abstract_r: The present research aims to replicate Amit, Wakslak and Trope (2013, Experiment 2) study which investigated the effect of social (psychological) distance on participants' medium preference for interpersonal communication. Their results showed that participants preferred invitations dominated by pictures for ‘close’ guests and dominated by words for ‘distant’ guests. These findings support construal level theory - which states that people use more abstract representations when mentalizing targets that are more psychologically distant. The present study will conduct a close and extended replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope (2013, Experiment 2) to assess the results reproducibility.
