title_r: Modulation of visual contrast sensitivity with transcranial random noise stimulation
abstract_r: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) has been shown to significantly improve visual perception. These performance improvements manifested as both (i) after-effects of visual training combined with tRNS (Fertonani et al., 2011; Pirulli et al., 2013; Contemori et al., 2019; Herpich et al., 2019) and (ii) acute effects during tRNS (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; Ghin et al., 2018; van der Groen et al., 2018, 2019; Battaglini et al., 2019, 2020; Pavan et al., 2019). It has been postulated that the Stochastic resonance (SR) phenomenon underlie noise-induced signal enhancement in studies investigating the acute effect of tRNS on visual processing (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018, 2019; Battaglini et al., 2019, 2020; Pavan et al., 2019). SR describes the phenomenon that the response of nonlinear systems to weak, subthreshold signals can be enhanced by adding an optimal level of random noise (Moss et al., 2004; McDonnell and Abbott, 2009). One important feature indicative of the SR phenomenon is that noise benefits are a function of noise intensity and exhibit an inverted U-shape relationship. Thus, while the optimal level of noise benefits performance, excessive noise is detrimental (van der Groen and Wenderoth 2016; van der Groen et al. 2018; Pavan et al. 2019). Previous studies investigating the acute effect of tRNS on visual detection performance have shown that noise stimulation was particularly beneficial when the visual stimuli were presented with near-threshold intensity (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018; Battaglini et al., 2019). Currently, it is unknown whether signal enhancement via SR could be achieved separately within different neural substrates along the retino-cortical pathway. Inducing SR via tRNS offers a unique opportunity to investigate this question. Here we plan a series of three experiments which will be executed in three separate sessions. Experiment 1: TRNS over primary visual cortex (V1) has been shown previously to improve visual contrast detection (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016). Here we aim to replicate these results in a new cohort and to determine the optimal tRNS intensity for each individual participant. Experiment 2: Previous research has suggested that the retina and the optical nerve are highly susceptible to alternating currents (Schutter and Hortensius, 2010). Improvement in vision was reported after repetitive transorbital alternating current stimulation over the retina, in studies involving patients with optic neuropathy or after optic nerve lesions (Gall et al., 2010; Fedorov et al., 2011). The retina and the optic nerve are an interesting target because they can be reliably reached even with low transcranial electrical stimulation intensities since the eyeball is an excellent conductor. Here we will test whether tRNS applied to the retina and the optic nerve improves visual contrast detection in accordance with the SR mechanism. We will apply different tRNS intensities to determine the optimal intensity for each individual participant. Experiment 3: It is currently unknown whether SR effects are additive when noise is applied to connected yet anatomically remote neural populations. Here we will investigate whether simultaneous application of tRNS to the retina and V1 causes additive effects.

title_r: Online experiment comparing GPs’ antibiotic prescribing decisions to a clinical prediction rule
abstract_r: Background: The validated “STARWAVe” clinical prediction rule uses seven factors to guide risk assessment and antimicrobial stewardship in children with cough (short illness duration, temperature, age, recession, wheeze, asthma, vomiting). Recently, we manipulated these factors in clinical vignettes to determine their influence on General Practitioners (GPs’) risk assessments and antibiotic prescribing decisions. Relative to STARWAVe, GPs used three factors appropriately (age, wheeze, vomiting) and one inappropriately (short illness duration). The remaining three factors were not investigated (temperature, recession, asthma). Aim: To assess the influence of all seven STARWAVe factors on GPs’ risk assessments and prescribing decisions. We expect to replicate our previous findings; we have no hypotheses concerning the three factors that were not investigated. We will also vary the method of obtaining risk estimates, to explore its effect on GPs’ responses. Finally, we will test whether parental concern for the child’s wellbeing might increase risk estimates and/or prescribing odds. Design and setting: Experiment comprising clinical vignettes administered to 180 UK GPs online. Method: GPs will be randomly assigned to view 32 (of 64) vignettes depicting children with cough. Vignettes will comprise the seven STARWAVe factors, varied in a fractional factorial design. Per vignette, GPs will estimate risk of deterioration in one of two ways (randomly assigned) and indicate whether they would prescribe antibiotics. Finally, GPs will see an additional vignette, suggesting that “the parent is quite concerned”. Using mixed-effects regression, we will measure the influence of STARWAVe factors, risk elicitation method, and parental concern on GPs' estimates and decisions.

title_r: Inter-trial interval and Negative Priming in the Manual Stroop task
abstract_r: There is debate as to whether negative priming (NP) occurs in the manual version of the Stroop task. Mills et al. (2019) made the point that previous studies showing such an effect were confounded; the NP condition was compared against trials that would necessarily produce particularly short RTs (e.g., trial and/or target repeats). Mills et al. then provided empirical support for this. We have however undertaken two pre-registered studies controlling for the issue Mills et al. highlighted but still showed a manual NP effect. The intended experiment will examine whether the reason they failed to show manual NP was because they used a relatively long inter-trial interval (ITI; i.e., 1116 ms) compared to the one we employed (i.e., 500 ms). We will replicate our basic procedure under two conditions; a long (1116 ms) and short (500 ms) ITI. The ITI account predicts that NP will occur in the short but not long ITI conditions. In other words, a significant interaction between the Stroop condition and ITI (as outlined more specifically below).

title_r: Does cognitive flexibility influence mind-wandering frequency? An empirical test of the switching perspective of mind-wandering
abstract_r: According to the switching perspective of mind-wandering (Wong et al., 2023), mind-wandering is a form of task-switching and is associated with cognitive flexibility. Previous correlational studies have tested this assumption, showing that individuals who report a greater tendency to mind-wander in questionnaires also demonstrate more flexible task-switching performance (e.g., more voluntary task switching). However, no study investigated the causal influence of cognitive flexibility on mind-wandering frequency at an intraindividual level. The present study aims to determine if cognitive flexibility influences the frequency of mind-wandering episodes. To achieve this, we replicate a study on cognitive flexibility and stability (Geddert & Egner, 2022) using the cued task-switching paradigm and include mind-wandering probes to measure the frequency of mind-wandering episodes. To manipulate cognitive flexibility and stability, we vary the proportion of task-switch (vs. repeat) trials and the proportion of congruent (vs. incongruent) trials, assuming that a high proportion of switch trials increase cognitive flexibility whereas a high proportion of incongruent trials increase cognitive stability. In addition to replicating previous findings, we expect to observe a tendency toward more mind-wandering episodes in instances of high cognitive flexibility. title_r: The Influence of Others' Actions on Perspective Taking (Verbal Responses) (1)
abstract_r: The present experiment is a follow-up study of our previous experiment that investigated how observation of others’ actions affects perspective taking (the link to the preregistration of the previous experiment is https://osf.io/qyf94). The current experiment will use a different method for registering participants’ responses. We will measure the reaction times and accuracy rates of participants’ verbal responses. In the previous study, participants responded by pressing keys on the keyboard presented in two different layouts. The response time analyses showed significant spatial key compatibility effects that made it harder to analyze the effects of action observation in perspective taking. Therefore, we aim to investigate this effect without the variance in the data that comes from using key responses that have spatial mapping. In addition, some researchers note that the pattern of increased reaction times with the increased angular disparity between the participant and the model in perspective taking tasks could be resulting from different spatial key compatibility effects (May & Wendt, 2013). Therefore, it is important to see if this pattern in the data could be also reliably found when not using a response method that has any spatial compatibility with stimuli. Kessler and Rutherford (2010) have shown that the increase of reaction times with angular disparity is persistent when using verbal responses. We aim to replicate these findings.

title_r: Perceptual Load and distractor type: Distractor Time Exposure
abstract_r: In our past study (Manini et al, 2021), we tested two attentional capture theories, which are based on opposite results even if using similar tasks. With the hypothesis that these differences may be caused by different types of distractor (i.e., inside vs. outside the attentional focus), we conjointly tested the perceptual load theory (Forster & Lavie, 2008b) and the attentional dwelling hypothesis (Gaspelin et al., 2016). Results were partially in line with our hypothesis that larger/reduced interference would be observed under high than low perceptual load for inside/outside distractors. However, even if we always found substantial differences in the attentional capture depending on the type of distractor used and on the perceptual load, we replicated the typical pattern predicted by the perceptual load theory only when using the original paradigm used by Foster and Lavie (2008b) (like In our last registered experiment: https://osf.io/hztn5), but not when using a different paradigm as the one in Manini et al. (2021). For this reason, we are conducting an experimental series based on the abovementioned experiment, to understand which variables are critical for observing or not the pattern predicted by the perceptual load theory, i.e., reduced distraction effect under high perceptual load for outside distractors. We conducted a second experiment (https://osf.io/sqv8k) in which we used this same paradigm, but manipulating between participants the stimuli time exposure: 100ms like in the original paradigm (Forster & Lavie, 2008b) and 200ms as the one used in Manini et al. (2021). After ruling out the possibility that stimuli time exposure was a relevant variable involved in the results, we conducted a third experiment (https://osf.io/uektd) to understand whether the way by which perceptual load is manipulated - between vs within blocks – represents an important modulating factor. This variable was presented separately between different blocks (as in the original experiments by Forster and colleagues) or within the same blocks (as in Manini et al., 2021). However, we found similar results independently of this manipulation. Because it seems that both variables alone (stimuli time exposure and perceptual load order presentation) do not explain the discrepancies between the original Forster and Lavies’ and Manini and colleagues’ study, we decided to run another experiment in which we will use both variables like in Manini et al. (2021), but manipulating the distractor time exposure. That is, while we will maintain constant the stimuli time exposure (200 ms) and the load presentation (mixed within blocks) like in our previous study, we will also manipulate between blocks the time exposure of the distractor: it will disappear after 200 ms together with the search array (similar to Manini et al., 2021), or will remain displayed until response (like many experiments of Forster and colleagues). Regarding the relevant distractor, the only relevant modifications that were made in relation to the previous experiments are changing the valid/invalid proportion.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.

title_r: Examining the effects of police killings in the United States on attitudes of Black Londoners: A reproduction and replication
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that high-profile incidents of police misconduct can reduce trust and confidence in the police among the wider public (Kochel, 2019; Nägel & Lutter, 2021; Reny & Newman, 2021). However, the effects of these ‘vicarious’ experiences can be heterogeneous and even null depending on the institutional and societal context, sub-population, and specific circumstances of the event. There is relatively little research on to what extent incidents of police violence in one country resonate across the globe, influencing individual attitudes towards local police. The study ‘Phantom Pains’ in the British Journal of Political Science aimed to address this research gap by assessing the impact of the death of Eric Garner in the United States on Londoner’s attitudes towards the London Metropolitan Police in the United Kingdom (Laniyonu, 2021). His study takes advantage of the overlap between fieldwork conducted for the Metropolitan Police Attitudinal Survey and the event, utilizing the interview date as an instrumental variable to assign respondents to treatment (post-event) or control (pre-event). This type of quasi-experimental design, known as unexpected event during survey design [UESD], assumes that because the event is ‘unexpected’ assignment to treatment and control is as-good-as-random, conditional on a set of assumptions. Laniyonu (2021) analysed treatment effects using regression discontinuity design [RDD], and found that Black Londoners had significantly lower support for the Metropolitan Police following the death of Eric Garner. White and South Asian respondents showed little to no change following the event. However, recent research on UESD has highlighted a number of potential issues embedded in the design that can threaten internal validity and the robustness of results. These issues include the extent to which all key assumptions related to ignorability and excludability are addressed, evaluating robustness across methodological choices and model specifications, and checking for heteroskedasticity due to highly unbalanced groups. Analyzing robustness across models is particularly important as there can be many potential analytical choices or “forking paths” available when executing empirical research. For example, in relation to UESD, researchers may opt for different methodological designs (e.g. regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences or straightforward before/after comparisons), select or compute the optimal bandwidth(s), and calculate different standard errors. In addition, as Laniyonu (2021) rightly states, the generalizability of UESD studies is often limited due to the focus on a single case and context. The current study aims to reproduce and replicate the effect of Eric Garner’s death in New York City on attitudes towards the police in London. As a first step, using the data and statistical code provided by Laniyonu (2021), we aim to reproduce the results presented in the paper. Here we will also evaluate the robustness and reliability of results by assessing the ignorability and excludability assumptions, as well as alternative design strategies and specifications, as recommended in the UESD literature (Muñoz et al., 2020; Nägel & Nivette, 2022). In doing so, we plan to implement the full range of ‘good-practice-recommendations’ discussed in the literature, thus providing a comprehensive and rigorous understanding of the hypothesized effect. In the second step we aim to conduct a replication of another high-profile event (i.e. the death of George Floyd in 2020) on attitudes towards the police using the same data from the Metropolitan Police Attitudinal Survey in London. This pre-registration focuses specifically on outlining the hypotheses, research design, and analyses planned for the George Floyd replication.

title_r: Harnessing Simulated Experience to Help People Make Better Investment Decisions
abstract_r: In order to make satisfactory investment decisions, investors must know and understand the risks that they face. An investor's comprehension of risk can differ considerably depending on how that risk is learned or communicated. Finance professionals typically communicate risks using descriptions, for instance, in the form of financial reports, mutual fund brochures, insurance brochures, investor education programs, and market research. These documents report risks using summary of historical returns and their respective probabilities. However, investors could also acquire knowledge about financial risks in other ways, that is, by observing the development of stock prices or through their own investment experience. For instance, day-traders decide to purchase a stock by simply observing prior stock movements, or, individual investors increase their subscription to IPO auctions subsequent to previous successful experience (e.g., Kaustia & Knupfer, 2008). The literature documents that the manner in which knowledge about risks is acquired or communicated, has a dramatic influence on investor's understanding of risk and their willingness to accept it. For example, our previous work shows experimentally that people who learn about a stock market crash from experience are more likely to stay out of the market than people who learn from descriptions (i.e., the "depression babies" effect), even when wealth effects are kept equivalent (Lejarraga, Woike, & Hertwig, 2016). Recent studies have shown that, in general, people not only seem to be persuaded more by their experience than from described sources of information, but also may arrive at more accurate subjective assessments of a given risk, even if experience is simulated. For example, Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013) and Bradbury, Hens and Zeisberger (2014) show that simulations of the stock market, which are closer to the notion of witnessing than experiencing through action, help investors understand risk accurately, and lead them to invest more in the stock market than investors that learn from described sources. On the other hand, Lejarraga and Gonzalez (2011) show that exhaustive descriptive information is often neglected when the subjects have the chance to also experience the information by sampling. That is, people who have experience and descriptions, make choices as if descriptions were omitted. Consistent with this observation, Barron, Leider, and Stack (2007) show that people are more likely to ignore a described warning if they have already experienced a series of safe outcomes, but they are more likely to be persuaded by the warning if they have no previous experience. These studies converge in that people tend to overweight the information they gain from experience over that which is provided in a descriptive form, which can lead to more accurate risk assessments, as long as the experiences made are representative of the environment. Our studies attempt to extend previous research in two ways. First, we seek to conduct a conceptual replication of the study of Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013). This involves exposing participants in an investment task to four different risk communication interventions and observing how the interventions affect participants’ risk taking behaviour, factual knowledge about the encountered decision environmnet, and subjective assessments of confidence and satisfaction. Second, we will extend the study of Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013) by manipulating whether or not people have had prior experiences with the decision environment, when exposed to the risk communication intervention. Specifically, one group of people will build up experience with the decision environment by making a series of decisions with feedback prior to being exposed to the risk communication intervention, while the other group, akin to Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013), will be given the risk communication intervention straight away. Using this setup, we will be able to provide a better estimate of how effective the four risk interventions are in informing people about financial risks in situations involving no prior experiences and explore how and whether prior experiences impact the effectiveness of the four interventions. We expect to replicate Kaufmann et al’s findings that experienced-based simulations are superior to description or graphic-based formats and hope to observe that these differences are all the more pronounced when the risk communications interventions are met with prior experience.

title_r: (Study 4) The Effects of Visual Embellishments on Comprehension and Memorability of Charts
abstract_r: Many researchers and design experts condemn the use of chart junk or visual embellishments, attributing it to creating distraction and hindrance in comprehensibility of charts. In contrast, some experts encourage the use of chart junk as a way to achieve better engagement, approachability, and memorability. This controversy about chartjunk or visual embellishment raises questions about its benefits, role in visualization, and conditions under which it is appropriate to use. Despite numerous studies trying to address this controversy throughout decades, chartjunk still remains a contentious topic in the visualization community. Therefore, to address the discrepancies in previous works and to shed further light on the issue, our project aims to replicate and build upon the canonical work by Bateman et. al. (2010) where they investigated the effects of visual embellishments on comprehensibility, memorability, and preference of charts. Three previous replication studies of the Bateman et. al. study were performed by 3 groups of graduate student researchers (including the authors of the current work), and several issues regarding the study design, delivery, and methodology were identified through group discussions and reflections. Our current evaluation plan is designed to address the issues identified in the previous iterations. Therefore, the objective of our evaluation project is to investigate the effects of visual embellishments on interpretability, memorability, and preference of charts. We plan to achieve this by conducting a remote study mimicking the original study by Bateman et. al, 2010.

title_r: Replication of the Emotional Path to Action at BYU-Idaho Winter 2021
abstract_r: The Emotional Path to Action is a study conducted by German researchers, Pfattheicher, Nockur, Böhm, Sassenrath, and Petersen that determines if empathy can promote behaviors that lead to social distancing and wearing face masks. The replication contains a few alterations, although the purpose of this study is to manipulate the same variables as the original and examine their effects. We want to gain an understanding of empathy leading towards prosocial behaviors; not only towards the pandemic, but also towards the spread of other communicable diseases. The original study contains a sample of approximately 1,500 participants, whereas the replication performed constraints a much smaller sample of around 200 participants. The participants were separated into three conditions (empathy, information, and control) at random. All conditions act as an independent variables to the dependent variable of whether or not participants feel empathy, thus compelling them towards social distancing and wearing a face mask. Information-only condition: Text provided, a CDC statement on the benefits of wearing a face mask and social distancing. Empathy condition: Text provided, a personal account of a woman who had contracted the COVID-19 virus in addition to her already present auto-immune disease. This text was originally in German and has been translated to English. Control condition: No additional text was provided. We are using two questionnaires that provide questions about one’s willingness to adhere to COVID-19 regulations. One of the questionnaires will be a control while the other will include vignettes which are designed to elicit an empathic response. The questionnaire is administered through email and will be scored using a five-point likert scale.

title_r: Directed forgetting in WM of deeply processes items: Impact of post-cue duration
abstract_r: Working memory (short WM) is the system responsible for holding mental representations temporarily available for later use in thought or action (Oberauer et al., 2018). Because WM has a severely limited capacity, WM content needs to be constantly updated to focus on current, relevant information. Supporting seamless updating, WM is remarkably efficient in getting rid of outdated information from WM as evident in robust directed forgetting effects in WM: In a recent study from our lab (Dames & Oberauer, in press), participants were instructed to remember a list of up to six sequentially presented words. After the offset of each word, a memory cue indicated whether this word should be remembered or could be forgotten. On a small subset of trials, we probed one of the to-be-forgotten (TBF) words – on all other trials, only to-be-remembered (TBR) words were tested. We found that memory performance for TBF words was much poorer than for TBR words (directed-forgetting effect). Forgetting in WM was accompanied by facilitation effects for the remaining, still relevant TBR words in WM. Together, consistently poor recognition performance for TBF words and facilitation of TBR words demonstrated that intent had a strong impact on WM maintenance. In this study, we concluded that a combination of two processes causes directed forgetting in WM: One process reduces memory strength of earlier memory representations as a function of subsequently encoded events. Another process rapidly encodes or boosts memory strength only when the person intends to remember that information. In a previous experiment, we manipulated the time between the offset of the memory cue and the onset of the next word (cue-stimulus-interval, CSI). We observed that binding memory for both TBR and TBF items increased over CSI (same slope, no interaction). These findings are in line with the notion that both TBR and TBF items are initially encoded into WM with some weak level of strength and then TBR items are boosted by, for instance, particularly attending these items (attentional boost), explaining the observed difference in memory performance between TBR and TBF items. Our observation that both TBR and TBF items increase to a similar degree over CSIs is in line with the assumption that the initial encoding of TBR and TBF item into WM depletes a limited WM resource (e.g., Popov & Reder, 2020). According to this theory, larger CSIs would give the resource time to replenish benefitting the encoding of new items. In the present study, we want to replicate these findings and further extent this line of research by testing whether we can observe directed-forgetting effects for deeply processed items. Potentially, by deeply processing all items, they are encoded into WM in such a way that makes it harder to subsequently remove them as previously observed in a study (Oberauer, 2018). In the present experiment, we will use a similar design as in the previous experiments but additionally instruct participants to categorize the displayed words into referring to either a concrete vs. abstract entity. That is, during item presentation, participants are asked to categorize the words into concrete (e.g., bottle) or abstract (e.g., love) words. Immediately after they categorized an item, we will present the memory cue. We will assess participants’ item and binding memory in form of a two-step test: First, we will test participants’ item memory by presenting one randomly selected old word and a completely new word in the center of the screen. Using their computer mouse, participants’ first task will be to select the word that was previously presented in that trial. Next, to measure participants’ binding memory, we will ask participants to select the frame the old word was previously presented in by clicking on it.

title_r: The Work for Environmental Protection Task: A strict Replication with a New Zealand Student Sample
abstract_r: We are interested in validating an online task which can be used to measure an individual’s intention to act or hypothetical actions, in comparison to their actual behaviour. This study will investigate how willing individuals are to incur a behavioural cost (time, effort, money etc) to produce environmental benefits through their work on an online number identification task. The Work for Environmental Protection Task (WEPT) allows participants to exert voluntary extra efforts to complete a number identification task in exchange for donations to a nominated non-profit environmental organization. In running this study, we aim to better understand the relationship between behavioural costs and pro-environmental behaviours, as well as the relationship between pro-environmental behaviours and self-reported measures of environmental concern/effort. This research will strictly replicate Lange and Dewitte (2022), though will be conducted with a New Zealand student population. Our research questions are: 1) Will participants complete fewer WEPT pages as behavioural costs increase? 2) Will participants complete more WEPT pages as environmental impact (increasing donation amount) increases? 3) Will the number of completed WEPT pages be positively related to a self-report measure of the propensity to show pro-environmental behaviour in everyday life? 4) Will the donation size that a participant generates for the environmental organization be positively related to a participant's self-report measure of environmental concern and bio-spheric value orientation?

title_r: Comparing two approaches to assessing human habit formation
abstract_r: Practice often renders behavior habitual. Two specific approaches, appealing to the longstanding idea of habit as a reflex-like stimulus-response association (Du, Krakauer, and Haith 2022; James 1890), have been used in human experiments to assess whether habits have been established through practice. Both approaches require participants first to practice a visuomotor association between a set of stimuli and associated responses before changing the required association. Under the Remapping approach, required responses are switched between a subset of stimuli. If the originally learned association is habitual, participants would persist in making the original responses rather than the revised one (Grol et al. 2006; Hardwick et al. 2019; Hélie, Waldschmidt, and Ashby 2010). Under the Withholding approach, some stimuli no longer require any response at all. If the originally learned association is habitual, participants would persist in generating responses to the revised stimuli, rather than withholding responses (Delorme et al. 2016; Watson and de Wit 2018; de Wit et al. 2018). According to the stimulus–response association framework, both approaches should similarly reveal the formation of habit and the practice effect on habit formation. However, existing findings using these two approaches are inconsistent. In our recent study (Du and Haith 2023), we directly compared the Remapping and Withholding approaches while matching the various aspects of the experimental protocols. Through experimental results and computational models, we demonstrated that the formation of habit differed between the Remapping and Withholding approaches; habit was observed after ~1000 trials of practice under the Remapping group, but not in the Withholding group. We suggest that the Remapping and Withholding approaches to assessing habit in fact target distinct forms of habits associated with different components of action control: response preparation and response initiation, respectively. However, one alternative explanation for our results is that the Remapping task is more difficult to perform than the Withholding task. In particular, when assessing habit formation, we remapped four (out of eight) stimuli to new responses in the Remapping group. Therefore, participants needed to remember the four revised stimuli and the four new responses they were now associated with. By contrast, in the Withholding group, participants needed only to remember the four revised stimuli and one new response (i.e., to not make a key press). This difference in difficulty may account for the difference in habit formation observed across conditions. The goal of this pre-registered study is to test this explanation. To do so, we will replicate our previous study with one major manipulation which allows us to match the difficulties between the Remapping and Withholding groups.

title_r: Automatic categorization of letters as consonants and vowels: Evidence from letter matching
abstract_r: Studies in visual word recognition showed that consonant and vowel letters are processed differently during reading (e.g., Chetail & Content, 2012, 2013; Chetail, Drabs, & Content, 2014; Duñabeitia & Carreiras, 2011; Lupker, Perea, & Davis, 2008; New & Nazzi, 2014), thus suggesting that the reading system categorizes letters as consonants and vowels. However, none of the previous studies has reported direct evidence that letters are automatically categorized into consonants or vowels to our knowledge, whereas this assumption is frequently implicitly taken for granted by researchers. We tested this hypothesis several times in the lab in the last years (e.g., Drabs, Chetail, & Content, 2013a, 2013b, 2014). In each study, we used the matching task on letter pairs. Participants performed a nominal identity task in which they had to respond ‘same’ when two letters had the same name whatever the case (e.g., A-a, E-E). They also performed a categorical identity task in which they had to respond ‘same’ when the two letters belonged to the same category (e.g., AA, Aa, A-e, G-N). The task order was counterbalanced between participants. Critically, in the nominal identity task, negative trials included letter pairs that belonged to the same letter category (e.g., EA, oE, BF, Cd) or not (e.g., AF, Eb). Based on previous demonstrations of interference of nominal identity on physical matching (Posner & Mitchell, 1967), we predicted an interference of categorical identity on nominal matching if letter categorization as consonants or vowels is automatic. It should be more difficult to decide that two letters are different in terms of nominal identity if they belong to the same category. In three experiments, we found that the expected effect was significant only when the categorical identity task was performed before the nominal identity task (magnitude of the effect: ~36 ms). In the reverse order, there was a systematic trend in the same direction (~10 ms), but it was statistically reliable in none of three experiments. Moreover, we observed that the categorical interference effect was different according of the case of letters, with a larger effect for case different pairs (e.g., Ae vs. Ac) than for case identical pairs (e.g., AE vs. AC or ae vs. ac). We conducted Bayesian analyses, but the Bayes Factor fell in the non-decidable zone (BF ~ 1). One possibility is thus that there is a real effect, but that its magnitude is relatively small (of the order of 5-15 msec). In order to gain reliable evidence for H1 or H0 with sufficient statistical power, we decided to replicate the nominal identity task (i.e., without the categorical identity task before) with 500 participants (by mean of crowdsourcing via Amazon Mechanical Turk services) and we pre-registered the study on OSF.

title_r: Automatic categorization of letters as consonants and vowels: Evidence from letter matching
abstract_r: Studies in visual word recognition showed that consonant and vowel letters are processed differently during reading (e.g., Chetail & Content, 2012, 2013; Chetail, Drabs, & Content, 2014; Duñabeitia & Carreiras, 2011; Lupker, Perea, & Davis, 2008; New & Nazzi, 2014), thus suggesting that the reading system categorizes letters as consonants and vowels. However, none of the previous studies has reported direct evidence that letters are automatically categorized into consonants or vowels to our knowledge, whereas this assumption is frequently implicitly taken for granted by researchers. We tested this hypothesis several times in the lab in the last years (e.g., Drabs, Chetail, & Content, 2013a, 2013b, 2014). In each study, we used the matching task on letter pairs. Participants performed a nominal identity task in which they had to respond ‘same’ when two letters had the same name whatever the case (e.g., A-a, E-E). They also performed a categorical identity task in which they had to respond ‘same’ when the two letters belonged to the same category (e.g., AA, Aa, A-e, G-N). The task order was counterbalanced between participants. Critically, in the nominal identity task, negative trials included letter pairs that belonged to the same letter category (e.g., EA, oE, BF, Cd) or not (e.g., AF, Eb). Based on previous demonstrations of interference of nominal identity on physical matching (Posner & Mitchell, 1967), we predicted an interference of categorical identity on nominal matching if letter categorization as consonants or vowels is automatic. It should be more difficult to decide that two letters are different in terms of nominal identity if they belong to the same category. In three experiments, we found that the expected effect was significant only when the categorical identity task was performed before the nominal identity task (magnitude of the effect: ~36 ms). In the reverse order, there was a systematic trend in the same direction (~10 ms), but it was statistically reliable in none of three experiments. Moreover, we observed that the categorical interference effect was different according of the case of letters, with a larger effect for case different pairs (e.g., Ae vs. Ac) than for case identical pairs (e.g., AE vs. AC or ae vs. ac). We conducted Bayesian analyses, but the Bayes Factor fell in the non-decidable zone (BF ~ 1). One possibility is thus that there is a real effect, but that its magnitude is relatively small (of the order of 5-15 msec). In order to gain reliable evidence for H1 or H0 with sufficient statistical power, we decided to replicate the nominal identity task (i.e., without the categorical identity task before) with 500 participants (by mean of crowdsourcing via Amazon Mechanical Turk services) and we pre-registered the study on OSF.

title_r: Replication of Asymmetric Hedonic Contrast: Pain is More Contrast Dependent than Pleasure, BYU-Idaho 2021
abstract_r: The members of the team are Jennifer Sepulveda, Juan Ortiz, Joshua Riding, and Heather Whittle, working under Dr. Brady Wiggins at Brigham Young University - Idaho. This project is a replication of study 2a from Asymmetric Hedonic Contrast: Pain Is More Contrast Dependent Than Pleasure by Voichek and Novemsky (2021). The original study tested the strength of hedonic contrast in the presence of different reference points. Authors created a fictional situation to test how individuals interpreted information under different circumstances. Participants took a survey in which they were randomly assigned to read about Hospital A that was considering testing an experimental drug that would either increase or decrease the mortality rate by 50% (the high reference point) or 5% (the low reference point.) Participants were then asked to make a recommendation for Hospital B where an experimental drug would increase or decrease the mortality rate by 10%. The hypothesis of the original authors was that a high reference point would increase the likelihood of recommending a risky drug. Their results showed that the participants who were in the high reference point group were more likely to recommend the hospital try the drug than those in the low reference point group. The current study is a replication of what Voicheck and Novemsky did in this study. Our replication will use participants from general psychology classes at Brigham Young University- Idaho. The pool of participants is one difference between our replication and the original study. We do not foresee any concerns with this difference. Another difference between the studies is the software used for analyzing the data. The original study used R and replication uses JASP.

title_r: Neglect of task-relevant body-related action effects
abstract_r: In the sense of ideomotor theories, actions are controlled by the anticipation of their environment- and body-related effects (e.g., Hommel, 2013; Pfister, 2019). For some actions (e.g., when using a tool with a lever), these effects are not compatible. While there is some evidence that the interference posed by spatially incompatible action effects can be overcome by downregulating body-related effect codes, as reflect by reduced tactile sensitivity in the effector (Liesner & Kunde, 2020), we could not replicate this finding. When asked to judge whether they did or did not perceive a tactile stimulation on the effector, participants performed worse shortly before and during movements compared to a rest condition, but the (in-)compatibility of the effects produced by the movement did not affect performance substantially. We argue that the spatial nature of the incompatibility in the main task (moving a target on the display to the left/right by moving the hand to the right/left) induced a neglect of spatial effect codes related to the agent's body, but not (or to a weaker extent) a neglect of intensity-related effect codes, as tested in the previous experiment. The current study aims to test the hypothesis that the neglect of body-related action effects that are in one dimension (e.g., spatial) incompatible with environment-related action effects is limited to effect codes related to this dimension. Participants will move a digital tool (i.e., a cursor) to the right or left by moving their hand with the computer mouse in either the same (compatible) or the other direction (incompatible). Shortly before or after movement initiation, they will receive a weak, but perceivable tactile stimulation on either a left or a right location on their active hand and will be asked to judge the location.

title_r: Psychopathology and ruminating, savoring, and sharing in the daily lives of adolescents during the Corona pandemic
abstract_r: Adolescence compared to childhood and adulthood, is characterized by more intense positive and negative emotions (Verma, & Larson, 1999; Silk, Steinberg, & Morris, 2003), more dynamic emotional states (Somerville, Jones, & Casey, 2010), and greater sensitivity to social and emotional stimuli (Spear, 2009; Bailen, Green, & Thompsom, 2019). In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic radically changed the already emotionally rich lives of adolescents worldwide, presenting them with unprecedented challenges for their emotional wellbeing. To navigate the landscape of fluctuating emotions and to adapt to daily life under the extraordinary circumstances introduced by the pandemic, adolescents need emotion regulation. At present, few studies have investigated emotion regulation processes in daily life during pandemics or how these processes are related to psychopathology and contextual factors such as intensity of daily positive and negative events. In the current study, we will investigate rumination, savoring, and sharing in the daily life of adolescents during the social distancing measures put in place in Belgium due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Specifically, we will assess if current psychopathology and event intensity are associated with rumination and sharing in response to negative daily events, and with savoring and sharing in response to daily positive events. To do so, we will use data from an extra measurement within the ongoing SIGMA study (Kirtley et al., 2021; Achterhof et al., 2021), conducted with 173 adolescents from the SIGMA cohort in Flanders (Belgium). Data were collected between 04.05.2020 and 10.05.2020, during the first COVID-19 related lockdown in Belgium. In this extra measure within the SIGMA study, psychopathology was assessed via a self-report questionnaire as a part of a large battery of self-report questionnaires, filled in online at home. Intensity of daily positive and negative events, rumination, sharing, and savoring were measured during a six-day ESM (Experience Sampling Method) period as a part of a momentary ESM survey delivered to the participants 10 times per day. As we have also recently conducted a daily life study with data collected before the pandemic where the same variables were assessed in daily life with similar methodology and the same emotion regulation items, we consider the current study a conceptual replication (i.e., re-testing the same hypotheses again with a different sample, study design, time-period, or measurement method) of previous research (Hiekkaranta et al., 2021). Replication studies are rare in the field of emotion regulation and we are not currently aware of any daily life replication study in this area. Replication studies, though rarely conducted, are vital in testing both the robustness and universality of effects observed in previous studies. Therefore, given the nature of the current conceptual replication study, we derived hypotheses from the results of the study that we aim to replicate.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Ku and Zaroff (2014) in the Journal of Environmental Psychology
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Study 1 of Ku and Zaroff (2014) is: Higher I/E participants [intrinsic relative to extrinsic values scores] show higher willingness to pay to protect the environment. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "In both 169 university students (M = 21.11, SD = 1.10) and 347 adults (M = 31.65, SD = 14.48) of Chinese ethnicity, the higher endorsement of intrinsic relative to extrinsic values was indeed related to a higher willingness to pay to protect the environment (Studies 1 and 2)...". The claim is tested by comparing the mean WTP (willingness to pay) score in the relative intrinsic group and the relative extrinsic group. As a whole, the hypothesis was supported as the relative intrinsic group obtained a mean score of 4.01 (SD = .71) on the WTP (willingness to pay), which was significantly higher than the relative extrinsic group's mean score of 3.30 (SD = .59), t(79) = 4.87, p < .001, r = .48. Note: There is an error in the published results-- the above standard deviations had been switched. None of the other results of this analysis changed. These are the correct results: As a whole, the hypothesis was supported as the relative intrinsic group obtained a mean score of 4.01 (SD = .59) on the WTP (willingness to pay), which was significantly higher than the relative extrinsic group's mean score of 3.30 (SD = .71), t(79) = 4.87, p < .001, r = .48.

title_r: Transgressor and Bystander Reactions to Counterspeech on Twitter
abstract_r: This study aims, among other things, to replicate and extend the findings by Munger (2017). The prior study dealt with counterspeech against the disparaging use of the word "nigger" (henceforth called “n-word”) on social media platform Twitter. If the counter-speaker was a user who was perceived as white and had many followers, there was a substantial reduction in further use of the n-word by the addressee of the counter-speech (henceforth called transgressor) under certain circumstances. We aim to replicate the findings that counterspeech from a high-status ingroup member substantially reduces the subsequent use of the n-word compared to no counterspeech. Moreover, a re-analysis that we conducted of the data provided by Munger (https://github.com/kmunger/Replication-Materials-for-Tweetment-Effects-on-the-Tweeted) indicated that prior use of the n-word moderated the association between counterspeech by low-status accounts and subsequent use of the n-word. Prior use of the n-word was more positively associated with subsequent use of the n-word if a low-status account engaged in counterspeech than if no-one intervened. We investigate if this previously un-reported reactance effect can be replicated. Finally, we examine how bystanders react to the intervention by looking at how many "favorites" the respective comments receive and how many comments are subsequently written within the same conversation for or against the counterspeech comment.

title_r: Shimojo et. al Replication
abstract_r: “Mere exposure” has long been studied as an effect that informs social preference. Gaze is an important part of perceptual exposure, and is especially important in social contexts where eye contact is meant to communicate interest. Our study will attempt to replicate Shimojo et al.’s (2003) paper, which aimed to further examine the part that orienting behavior plays in informing preferential choice decisions. They also sought to find whether gaze informs preferential choice, gaze just follows once a choice is made, or they both reinforce each other. Their original study ran experiments that had one group of participants look at faces and decide which one was more attractive. The faces were put in pairs based on how similar they were in attractiveness (as rated, on a scale from 1 to 7, by a different group of participants); those with similar attractiveness (differences in ratings being less than or equal to 0.25) were paired together. A third (control) group had to decide which face, using the same pairings, was more round. The original investigation found that gaze was biased more towards the ultimately chosen face when participants had to choose which face was more attractive versus which face was more round. Our investigation will attempt to replicate these results by re-running the latter two studies using computer cameras to track eye movements. In this way, another important question that our replication seeks to answer is whether computer cameras can be used to effectively track eye movements for the purpose of psychological experiments.

title_r: The effect of selective spatial attention on the development of secondary hyperalgesia: a replication study
abstract_r: Cognitive factors, such as attention, play an important role in the modulation of pain and in the development of pain chronicity. We attempt to replicate one such effect found in a previous study conducted by Filbrich et al., 2020, which shows how the experimental induction of central sensitization, a key factor in the development of secondary hyperalgesia, can indeed be modulated by selective spatial attention. Secondary hyperalgesia occurs after tissue injury. It refers to a condition of increased sensitivity to mechanical stimuli within the injured area and the surrounding skin. It is hypothesized that the intense and sustained activation of peripheral nociceptors enhances the responsiveness of the neurons in the central nervous system. This causes the phenomenon known as central sensitization which is considered to play a key role in the development of chronic pain. As in Filbrich (2020), we will manipulate the impact of selective spatial attention by asking healthy volunteers to selectively focus their attention on target stimuli applied on one of the two forearms while we apply high frequency stimulation on both forearms. To assess the effect of the manipulation, we will measure perceived intensity to mechanical pinprick stimuli on both arms at three different moments: at T0, before applying high-frequency stimulation (HFS), at T1, immediately after having applied HFS in combination with the selective attention task, and finally at T2, 20 minutes after the whole procedure. Moreover, at T2, we will estimate the extent of the area of secondary hyperalgesia on both arms by applying mechanical pinprick stimulation along two axes: (1) medial-later, and (2) proximal-distal. title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Welzel & Deutsch (2012), From the British Journal of Political Science
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Welzel & Deutsch (2012) is that more prevalent emancipative values elevate an entire society’s protest level. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Focusing on ‘emancipative values’, two ecological effects are shown: (1) the prevalence of emancipative values lifts people’s protest above the level that their own emancipative values suggest (elevator effect); (2) the prevalence of these values enhances the impact of people’s own emancipative values on protest (amplifier effect)." The claim is tested with the random intercepts, random slopes Combined Model in Table 1. The dependent variable, Non-Violent Protest, is a 0-1.0 index indicating a person’s tendency to protest, with a priority for remembered over imagined protest. It is regressed on societal-level variables, individual-level variables, and their interaction, as specified in the model. The variable of interest for testing the claim is the term for a society’s ‘emancipative climate,’ measured by a society’s respondents’ average on the emancipative values index (see the Combined Model in Table 1 for details on the specification). The combined model in Table 1 shows that the findings of the separate models hold under mutual controls. Societal-level values show an elevator effect (unstandardized coefficient on societal level-values term [SL-Values (‘Emancipative Climate’)] = 0.54, T-value = 4.6, p < 0.010).

title_r: Motivated empathy intervention
abstract_r: Description Understanding empathy as a motivated process is common within psychology today (Zaki, 2014; Cameron et al, 2022). In essence, we tend to empathize more when we have underlying motives to do so. One underlying motive that has been suggested to increase empathy is the social desirability and normativity of empathy (Zaki, 2014; Schumann et al, 2014; Weisz & Zaki, 2017). Empathy’s normativity as underlying motivation to empathize was explicitly tested by Weisz and colleagues (2021) and showed significant effects on several outcome measures. Another motive that has been suggested to increase empathy is to simply inform people that empathy is not fixed and unaffectable, but rather motivated and affectable in several ways. Several studies have demonstrated that presenting empathy as being malleable rather than fixed leads to increased empathic behavior (Schumman et al, 2014; Weisz et al, 2021; Hasson et al, 2022). Recently, Weisz and colleagues and Hasson and colleagues explicitly tested motivation-based interventions on empathic behavior, with mixed results. Weisz and colleagues did not find any difference between their conditions for empathy with outgroup members. Neither did they find any condition-based differences between empathy-related ratings of outgroup members on several items (Weisz et al, 2021). They speculate that their interventions, designed to bolster empathic approach behavior, did not affect typical avoidance behavior, such as avoiding empathizing with outgroup members. However, they point out that their experiment was not designed to characterize underlying intervention mechanisms. Interestingly, Hasson and colleagues tested a kind of malleability intervention, telling people that empathy is not limited but unlimited. That lead to more outgroup empathy towards outgroup members measured on several empathy-related items (Hasson et al, 2022). They even suggest a mechanism for the increase in empathy toward outgroup members: when people no longer believe that empathy is limited but unlimited, they think that they have empathy to spare for outgroup members; whereas when people believe that empathy is limited, they save their empathy for their ingroup members (ibid). Their approach can hence be understood as decreasing avoidance behavior, given that people avoided empathizing with outgroup members due to their belief that empathy is a limited resource best saved for ingroup members. Study 1 In a first study, we will reuse the two interventions Hasson and colleagues used in their second study. We will also create two additional interventions. The first one is based on informing people that we can regulate our empathy, without telling them it is unlimited. The second one is based on informing people about the socially desirable effects of empathy and how it is valued in many communities. A fifth condition will be used as control and be about risky financial investments, not empathy. We will test our interventions online, using Prolific, in a potential outgroup context. Participants will be presented with stimuli consisting of a story about a man, Tyrone in one version and John in the second version and make several empathy-related ratings regarding how they felt about the man while reading the story. Participants will also be offered to make real financial donations to the YMCA, which is an organization the man in the story attends to receive help with basic needs. Prolific registers participants’ ethnicity and in the experiment, we will ask explicitly about how they perceived the ethnicity of the man in the story. By matching participants on ethnicity and expected perceived ethnicity of the man in the story, we will try to create an outgroup measure, where e.g. black participants read about John (more likely to be perceived as white). In effect, we test four motivation-based interventions’ effects on empathy to see if we can replicate previous results obtained by Hasson and colleagues and test how well their interventions perform compared to our novel interventions based on an understanding of motivated empathy.

title_r: Fork of Wealth and Happiness: Replication of Diener, E., Ng, W., Harter, J., & Arora, R. (2010) at University of Vienna.
abstract_r: General Information This fork is part of the Direct+Plus CREP replication (https://osf.io/px0sw/) of a study by Diener et al. (2010). Every student manages a fork of the official replication OSF page as a part of a seminar at the Department of Occupational, Economic and Social Psychology, led by Andre Julian Hartmann and Martin Müller (both graduate students) at the University of Vienna (Austria). Materials All materials are developed together with the students during the seminar and will be added to the project before starting data collection. In addition to the items of the original study, items for further research questions will be added as a direct+ replication. We also participate in the Direct+Plus project by Jordan Wagge containing two questions that deal with financial security. Procedure All students are using the same survey, advertising materials, and OSF page since this is an online study. Every student will sample N = 10 (total targeted sample: N = 270) students living in Vienna within their social circle. Original Abstract The Gallup World Poll, the first representative sample of planet Earth, was used to explore the reasons why happiness is associated with higher income, including the meeting of basic needs, fulfillment of psychological needs, increasing satisfaction with one's standard of living, and public goods. Across the globe, the association of log income with subjective well-being was linear but convex with raw income, indicating the declining marginal effects of income on subjective well-being. Income was a moderately strong predictor of life evaluation but a much weaker predictor of positive and negative feelings. Possessing luxury conveniences and satisfaction with standard of living were also strong predictors of life evaluation. Although the meeting of basic and psychological needs mediated the effects of income on life evaluation to some degree, the strongest mediation was provided by standard of living and ownership of conveniences. In contrast, feelings were most associated with the fulfillment of psychological needs: learning, autonomy, using one's skills, respect, and the ability to count on others in an emergency. Thus, two separate types of prosperity—economic and social psychological—best predict different types of well-being.

title_r: GW4 21-22: Devaluation effects in food-specific response inhibition training: An independent conceptual replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Food-specific inhibitory control training (F-ICT) is a behavioural intervention in which participants learn to associate certain food-types with the inhibition of behaviour. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of such training in reducing food evaluations (e.g., Chen et al., 2016; Chen, Veling, de Vries, et al., 2018; Veling et al., 2013a), changing food choices (e.g., Veling et al., 2013b; Veling, Chen, et al., 2017), decreasing food intake (e.g., Lawrence, Verbruggen, et al., 2015; also see Allom et al., 2016) and even promoting weight loss (Lawrence, O’Sullivan, et al., 2015; Nederkoorn et al., 2010; Veling et al., 2014; see Jones et al., 2016 for a meta-analysis). This has led some researchers to suggest that F-ICT may be a cost-effective intervention with clinical utility (Carbine & Larson, 2019; Jones et al., 2016, 2018). 

One explanation for the effectiveness of F-ICT on health-related outcomes is provided by the Behaviour Stimulus Interaction (BSI) theory (Chen et al., 2016; Veling et al., 2008; Veling, Lawrence, et al., 2017), which proposes that during training food stimuli are devalued to reduce the response conflict caused by the need to inhibit motor responses towards (highly) appetitive items and thus facilitate task performance. In a series of six experiments using the Go/No-Go Task, Chen et al. (2016) examined the effect of of food-specific response inhibition training on stimulus devaluation by pairing appetitive stimuli with cues to respond (go stimuli) or with cues to not respond (no-go cues or the absence of cues). Providing evidence of stimulus devaluation, findings indicated that attractiveness ratings of no-go foods reduced after training whilst ratings of go-foods increased. This effect was then replicated in two preregistered experiments (Chen, Veling, Dijksterhuis, et al., 2018) and across obese and normal-weight individuals (Chen, Veling, de Vries, et al., 2018), showing consistently that no-go foods were rated as less attractive post-training compared to go-foods and untrained foods. 

The aim of the current study is to conceptually replicate the devaluation effect found by Chen et al. (2016) for food attractiveness ratings in a high-powered and representative sample, as well as exploring potential moderators of these effects.

title_r: The role of speech register in foreign word learning
abstract_r: In comparison to speech directed to adults (adult-directed speech; ADS), infant-directed speech (IDS) has altered acoustic-prosodic characteristics, such as a slower speech rate, a higher fundamental frequency, greater pitch variation, vowel hyperarticulation, and longer pauses, as well as structural characteristics, such as repetition and simplified sentences (Fernald, 1992; Gleitman, Newport, & Gleitman, 1984; Kuhl et al., 1997). Young infants can successfully segment (Thiessen, Hill, & Saffran, 2005) and learn words (Ma, Golinkoff, Houston, & Hirsh-Pasek, 2011) presented in IDS at younger ages than ADS, suggesting that these modifications may facilitate infants’ acquisition of their first language. Adult language learners also receive modified speech input. Foreigner-directed speech (FDS), which is characterized by hyperarticulated vowels, is hypothesized to have a didactic origin similar to that of vowel hyperarticulation in IDS (Uther, Knoll, & Burnham, 2007). Yet, the facilitatory role of speech modifications in foreign language processing has received little attention. One such study did investigate the facilitatory role of IDS in adult ab initio learners. Golinkoff and Alioto (1995), found that English-speakers are able to learn new names for objects when those names were presented in IDS but not ADS, suggesting that speech modifications also aid foreign language learners. In the current study, we will first replicate the original study of Alioto and Golinkoff with German-speaking adults and extend these results to investigate whether FDS has a similar impact on word-learning in a foreign language as IDS.

title_r: Self Regulation Ontology Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Previously (Eisenberg et al., 2019), our lab leveraged exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on the dependent variables (n=193 DVs) extracted from 522 individuals’ performances on a large range of tasks (n=37 tasks, n=129 DVs) and self-report surveys (n=22 surveys, n=64 DVs) broadly related to the psychological construct of ‘Self Regulation’. While 12 factors were recovered from the survey DVs, only 5 factors were recovered from task-derived DVs. of the 5 task factors, 3 (speeded information processing, caution, and perception/response) were strongly related to DVs that were parameters of drift diffusion modeling (DDM): drift rate, threshold, and non-decision time, respectively. This may indicate that DDM captures fundamental dimensions of cognition. Alternative, this could suggest that examining the data through the lens of DDM conceals otherwise fundamental cognitive factors that are central to other taxonomies in the literature (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000), like shifting, updating, and inhibition. 
	To investigate these possibilities, we plan to perform EFA and the subsequent analyses of Eisenberg et al. (2019) on the original data, replacing the DDM parameters with reaction time, accuracy, and within-subject reaction time standard deviation. We propose two competing hypothesis classes.  First, the factors recovered could be similar in number and occupy a similar factor space and axes as the original factors. For example, we could again find a 5-factor solution, but dependent variables that previously loaded on speeded information processing, caution, and perception/response may now load onto RT variance, accuracy, and mean reaction time, respectively. Within this class, a more specific outcome would be that these new factors provide worse fits to the data than the original factors. This would indicate that the additional assumptions of the DDM combined with the original modeling parameters produce dependent variables which better reflect the underlying psychological factor space. Alternatively, the new factors could better fit the data compared to the old factors, indicating that the additional assumptions of DDM distort the data in some way, and would encourage further investigation. 
	Second, the new factor solution may be fundamentally different in factor number and factor space/axes. For example, the original 5-factor solution may give way to a higher-dimensional solution in which dependent variables map onto more traditional psychological constructs like attention, working memory, shifting, inhibition, etc.  Alternatively, we may recover a set of factors more obscure that do not map cleanly onto the original factor solution or existing taxonomies of cognitive processes (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000). 
	The first class of hypotheses would provide evidence that the Eisenberg et al. (2019) ontology is robust to the presence or absence of the DDM modeling and transformation of the raw reaction and accuracy data. Alternatively, the second class of hypotheses would suggest that the ontology (Eisenberg et al., 2019) is more idiosyncratic to analytical decisions like whether to analyze the data through the lens of the DDM.

title_r: Approach-motivated positive affect reduces breadth of attention: replication of Domachowska et al. (2016)
abstract_r: Emotions and moods not only influence the contents of cognitive processes (e.g., which stimuli we attend to), but they also modulate how information is processed (e.g., how narrow or wide the focus of attention is, for review see Bolte & Goschke, 2010; Goschke & Bolte, 2014). More specifically, there is evidence that positive affect is associated with a broadened focus of attention and a bias towards global or holistic aspects of stimuli, whereas negative affect is associated with a constricted focus of attention and promotes the processing of local details (see Fredrickson, 2013; Friedman & Förster, 2010, for reviews). This is a replication of a study conducted by Irena Domachowska. She used the task of Gable and Harmon-Jones [Gable, P. A., & Harmon- Jones, E. (2008). Approach-Motivated Positive Affect Reduces Breadth of Attention. Psychological Science, 19(5), 476–482]. In this influential paper, the authors demonstrated positive affect high in approach motivation to reduce the breadth of attention. The present replication study includes a direct replication of Experiment 2 from the original paper by Irena Domachowska (2016) using the same affective and control stimuli and comparing positive affect high in approach motivation, positive affect low in approach motivation and neutral affect within one experiment.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Fox (2009), From the Journal of Labor Economics
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Fox (2009) is that firm-size wage gaps increase with job responsibility. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "I present the fact that wage gaps due to firm size increase with job responsibility." Firm-size wage gaps by job responsibility are estimated in the U.S. using the U.S. SIPP data. The author uses the three-digit occupation codes to formulate four examples of firm-size wage gaps between occupations, in which titles suggest one group of occupations may be supervising another group – the focal example used as evidence for the SCORE program is white-collar versus blue-collar workers. The author estimates a series of regressions that compare workers at large firms to workers at small firms within the same industry, where size in measured in three intervals for both firm size and establishment size: 1-24, 25-100, or more than 100. Each model regresses the log of hourly wages on indicators for the interactions of size intervals and job responsibility, an indicator for coverage by a collective bargaining agreement, an indicator for location in a metropolitan area, and industry indicators. Standard errors are corrected for heteroskedasticity across worker panels and an AR(1) term in worker-specific disturbances. The base estimation sample is all male, full-time employees in the private sector. The regression selected as evidence for the SCORE program compares the blue-collar wage gap between firms sized 1-24 and firms sized 100+ with the white-collage wage gap across the same two firm sizes. For firm size, a formal statistical test that the 100+ versus 1–24 size wage gaps are the same for blue- (wage gap = .181, SE = .007) and white-collar workers (wage gap = .236, SE = .008) is rejected with a p-value less than .001.

title_r: Does Motor Coordination Increase Obedience to Authority?
abstract_r: Psychological research seeks to understand the dynamics of obedience to authority by unraveling the factors that shape individuals' willingness to comply with the demands of authority figures (e.g., Götz et al., 2023; for a recent review, see Kaposi, 2022). One factor that decreased obedience in the original Milgram obedience studies was spatial proximity to the victim and/or spatial distance from the experimenter (Milgram, 1974). However, the latter manipulation arguably also prevented participants from coordinating their actions with the experimenter. Furthermore, motor coordination with others (Milgram, 1974) and motor synchronization with the experimenter prior to the critical immoral task (Wiltermuth, 2012) have been shown to increase obedience. Consequently, the coordination between the participant and others in form of a joint effort (or the lack thereof; Sebanz et al., 2006) may play a role in facilitating compliance (vs. defiance) above and beyond physical distance to the victim (or proximity to the experimenter). After all, joint action theorizing (Fernández‐Castro & Pacherie, 2023) and research (Michael et al., 2016) suggest that high levels of coordination strengthen commitment to the joint effort due to increased interdependence and the resulting mutual expectations (and/or social pressures) between co-actors (see also Tomasello, 2019). Based on the idea that obedience is best understood as an asymmetric joint action (Götz et al., 2023; Götz et al., in prep.), the present research seeks to elucidate the potentially facilitative role of coordination - and/or the detrimental role of its absence – for compliance with the experimenter’s demands in a novel distance-to-the-lab setting (i.e., distance from the victim and distance from the experimenter). In a first experiment, we replicated the findings of the ‘object-destruction’ experiments (Götz et al., 2023) in a remote setup. In the original research, participants were demanded/told (cf. Martens et al., 2007) vs. asked (including a reminder of their freedom of choice) to destroy bugs (among other objects) by grinding them in a manipulated electric coffee grinder (between-participants design). In fact, no bug was harmed. In the remote setup, the two conditions were identical to the previous experiment but participant and experimenter met via Zoom video-telephony, with the participant at home and the experimenter and all materials (e.g., the ‘destruction machine’, the live bugs for the crucial destruction task, coffee beans for the control destruction task) in the laboratory. The destruction machine was connected to the experimenter’s computer in the lab via a programmable USB power socket. Thus, the participant could start the destruction machine directly by pressing the “Z” key on his/her keyboard using Zoom’s remote-control feature, which mirrors the participant’s keyboard on that of the experimenter’s computer in the lab. Participants were first instructed to destroy seven coffee beans before being presented with the bug-destruction task. After each destruction task, participants self-reported their current affective state (arousal, pleasure, and dominance) on SAM scales (Bradley & Lang, 1994), as well as feelings of responsibility and agency. Consistent with findings from other obedience research manipulating the distance from the victim (Milgram, 1974), the levels of obedience were increased relative to the original laboratory experiments. Self-reported levels of affect, agency, and responsibility were similar to those in the original experiments (see Götz et al., 2023), suggesting no mediating role of participants’ conflict experience. However, participants’ increased levels of obedience are inconsistent with previous findings that had shown that distance from the experimenter increases defiance. One explanation for this surprising aspect of Experiment 1 might be a primacy of distance from the victim over distance from the experimenter. In the present research, though, we pursue an alternative explanation, arguing that in Experiment 1, distance from the experimenter was confounded with a high degree of (motor) coordination between participant and experimenter. After all, the remote setting required the experimenter to play a more active role than in the original, laboratory-based experiments by Götz et al. (2023). Specifically, the experimenter, rather than the participant, poured the bugs through a funnel into the manipulated coffee grinder and signaled the participant to start the machine by nodding. Thus, participants had to coordinate with the experimenter in order to perform the assigned tasks, which further strengthened the joint action character of the setting (Sebanz et al., 2006; descriptively more so in the demand condition; cf. the agency and responsibility results of Experiment 1). In the present research, we aim to directly test the influence of motor coordination between participant and experimenter on participants' (dis)obedience in the remote setup (introduced in Experiment 1) above and beyond the distance to the lab. To this end, one group of participants will directly replicate the high-coordination demand condition from Experiment 1. In the low-coordination demand group, however, the participants will not only control the destruction machine by pressing a key on their keyboards, but also a second machine that is used to first pour the destruction objects into the manipulated coffee grinder. Specifically, participants will be instructed to pour the beans and/or bugs into the destruction machine by pressing keys 1-7 on their keyboards before destroying them by pressing the “Z” key. To avoid any coordination, participants will not see the experimenter during the destruction tasks. Please note that during the destruction tasks (beans, bugs), the camera must be switched from the built-in laptop camera to an additional external camera. This allows us to limit the experimenter’s non-visibility in the low-coordination condition to the destruction tasks. However, the experimenter will be present in both conditions and will be able to respond immediately to participants’ questions. All other measures (e.g., self-reported affective state, feelings of agency, and feelings of responsibility) will be identical to Experiment 1 (including video recordings and ratings).
