title_r: Does high talker variability improve the learning of non-native phoneme contrasts? A replication
abstract_r: Acquiring non-native speech contrasts can be difficult. A seminal study by Logan, Lively and Pisoni (1991) established the effectiveness of phonetic training for improving non-native speech perception: Japanese learners of English were trained to perceive /r/-/l/ using minimal pairs over 15 training sessions. A pre/post-test design established learning and generalisation. In a follow up study, Lively, Logan and Pisoni (1993) presented further evidence which suggested that talker variability in training stimuli was crucial in leading to greater generalisation. These findings have been very influential and “high variability phonetic training” is now a standard methodology in the field. However, while the general benefit of phonetic training is well replicated, the evidence for an advantage of high over lower variability training remains mixed. We propose a large-scale replication of the original studies using updated statistical analyses to confirm whether learners generalise more after phonetic training using multiple talkers over a single talker.

title_r: Reasoning cognitive conflict and political ideology: ideological belief bias and reasoning processes
abstract_r: Belief bias in reasoning occurs when individuals are more likely to accept conclusions consistent with their belief than inconsistent conclusions, regardless of their validity. Recent evidence suggests that this bias also appears in relation to the political orientation of individuals (Calvillo et al., 2020). In this study, we will examine whether the political ideology of French individuals biases their reasoning in syllogisms with politics-related content (conceptual replication). We will first measure the political orientation of the participants. Then, in a second step, we will manipulate belief bias through 8 syllogisms with political content (ideological belief bias) and 4 with non-political content (belief bias).

title_r: Global measures of foreign accent in L2 European Portuguese
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that native speakers can accurately detect notes of foreign accents in short sentences (Hansen et al., 2017; Huensch & Nagle, 2021). The present study aims to investigate how L1 European Portuguese speakers rate a variety of TL (target-like) and NTL (non-target-like) L2 utterances based on a variation in vowel nasality and vowel quality for accentedness, comprehensibility, and intelligibility. We replicated the method by Munro and Derwing (1995a) and Huensch and Nagle (2021). The only difference is that we included sentences with a varied degree of nasality and vowel quality, with no additional morphosyntactic errors, focusing on the productions of L1 Ukrainian speakers of L2 European Portuguese on intermediate and advanced proficiency levels. The speech samples were elicited through an extemporaneous elicitation task adapted from Saito et al. (2016). 60 L1 European Portuguese listeners will transcribe (intelligibility) and rate the utterances on a 100-point slider scale (accentedness and comprehensibility) (Huensch & Nagle, 2021). The current study is a follow-up of the two previous studies preregistered on OSF.

title_r: Artificial Intelligence in Psychological Practice: Perspectives and preferences of mental health practitioners on the use of AI in clinical practice.
abstract_r: This is a quantitative, cross-sectional investigation, that conceptually replicates Aktan, Turhan, and Dolu's (2022) research on attitudes and perspectives toward artificial intelligence (AI) in psychotherapy. This conceptual replication is primarily guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which posits that perceived usefulness and ease of use determine an individual's behavioral intention to use technology. It is further complemented by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), a more comprehensive model explaining user intentions and usage behavior by integrating elements from eight previous technology acceptance models. Moreover, the author will make use descriptive and correlational designs, which will be conducted online using convenience or snowball sampling to recruit approximately 200 participants. These participants will consist exclusively of mental health clinicians currently practicing or actively involved in the field, specifically licensed psychologists, clinical counselors, and psychiatrists. The primary purpose of this study is to investigate the current attitudes and perceptions of psychology practitioners regarding the utility and integration of AI in their clinical practice, including the specific perceived benefits and barriers/concerns they identify. This focused approach aims to explore the generalizability of the original findings within a more specific professional context and offer insights into how enhancing awareness of psychotherapy's effectiveness and building trust in AI tools might increase the acceptance of AI-based psychotherapy (Aktan et al., 2022).

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2011), from the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2011) is the Experiment 1 claim that participants who were asked to estimate the upper bound of a distribution (e.g. taxi cab numbers at a taxi company) made predictions that reflected the effects of multiple observations in a way consistent with Bayesian inference and with a “density” heuristic, but not with other existing heuristics that the authors consider. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “The results indicate that people integrate prior knowledge and observed data in a way that is consistent with our Bayesian model, ruling out some simple heuristics for predicting the future.” The claim was tested in part with Experiment 1, which manipulated the number of observations that participants had available to make a judgement. For the focal test selected for the SCORE project, participants were told the serial number of a taxicab (as well as being given the information that all cabs are given a unique number between 1 and the total number of cabs in the company) and asked to guess the number of cabs in the company, after seeing the number of one, three, or 10 taxis. Critically, the first taxi had the highest number; subsequent taxis had lower numbers. After excluding participants who gave implausible predictions (i.e. the company owning less than 103 taxis, indicating a misunderstanding of instructions) and responses more than 3 standard deviations from the mean, responses were trans-formed to t / t_past, where t is the raw score and t_past is the largest example and submitted to a one-way within-subjects analysis of variance (ANOVA). This analysis yielded that participants in the ‘taxicab’ scenario gave estimates of the total number of taxis that were sensitive to the number of observations they had seen, F(2, 44) = 9.57, MSE = 3.69, p < .001.

title_r: Perceptual load and distractor type: Mixed Load Blocks
abstract_r: In our past studies (Manini et al, 2021, https://osf.io/sqv8k and https://osf.io/hztn5); we tested two attentional capture theories, which observe opposite results even if using similar tasks. With the hypothesis that these differences may be caused by different type of distractors (i.e., inside vs. outside the attentional focus), we conjointly tested the perceptual load theory (Forster & Lavie, 2008b) and the attentional dwelling hypothesis (Gaspelin et al., 2016). Results were partially in line with our hypothesis. However, even if we found substantial differences in the attentional capture depending on the type of distractor used and on the perceptual load, we could replicate the typical pattern predicted by the perceptual load theory only when using the original paradigm used by this theory (like In our last registered experiment: https://osf.io/hztn5). For this reason, we are conducting an experimental series based on the abovementioned experiment, to understand which variables are involved in results discrepancy. We conducted a second experiment (https://osf.io/sqv8k) in which we used this same paradigm, but manipulating between participants the stimuli time exposure: 100ms like our past study and 200ms as the one used in Manini et al. (2021). After ruling out the possibility of the stimuli time exposure being a relevant variable involved in the results, we will conduct a third experiment in which we will manipulate the perceptual load presentation. This variable will be presented separately between different blocks (as in the original experiments by Forster and colleagues) or within the same blocks (as in Manini et al., 2021).

title_r: Close Replication of Muñoz, De Los Reyes: The dark triad and honesty rules in romantic relationships
abstract_r:

Close Replication of Muñoz, De Los Reyes: The dark triad and honesty rules in romantic relationships

item29: 1.	Verbal description of the effect I am trying to replicate (optional)  The study “The dark triad and honesty rules in romantic relationships” by Muñoz and De Los Reyes (2021) examined the connection between the three traits of the dark triad (i.e., Psychopathy, Machiavellianism and Narcissism) and honesty rule endorsement in romantic relationships, defined as obligatory rules and discretionary rules. Obligatory rules consist of strict standards for honest communication, while discretionary rules provide the flexibility to determine when deception is appropriate. We are trying to replicate the following hypotheses:  1.	High Psychopathy positively predicts discretionary rule endorsement.  2.	High Psychopathy negatively predicts obligatory rule endorsement.  3.	High Machiavellianism positively predicts discretionary rule endorsement. 4.	Narcissism shows no effects on either honesty rule endorsement.   2.	It is important to replicate this effect because (optional)  With the replication crisis in mind, it is important to strengthen the confidence in the reliability of the reported effects, so that this replication study should promote the confidence in the postulated relationships between the dark triad traits and honesty rule endorsement (Brandt, 2014).  Further, in the original study, 98.05% of the participants were Hispanics and most of the participants were female. Thus, this replication study which will be conducted with a German sample and a more balanced gender ratio will help to answer the question concerning the generalizability of the findings of the original study to other contexts.   3.	The effect size of the effect I am trying to replicate is (optional)  1.	The effect size of the effect between psychopathy and discretionary rule endorsement is r = .26.  2.	The effect size of the effect between psychopathy and obligatory rule endorsement is r = -.10. This effect is mentioned as significant in the text but not in the attached bivariate correlation matrix.  3.	The effect size of the effect between Machiavellianism and discretionary rule endorsement is r = .28.  4.	The confidence interval of the original effect is (optional)  Not specified   5.	The sample size of the original effect is (optional)  Two different sample sizes are reported in the paper. According to the text, the sample size is N = 257, but according to the bivariate correlation matrix, the sample size is N = 258.    6.	Where was the original study conducted? (e.g., lab, in the field, online) (optional)  The original study was conducted online.   7.	What country/region was the original study conducted in? (optional)  The researchers are from University of Texas, but it is not clear in the text where the study was conducted in.  8.	What kind of sample did the original study use? (e.g. student, Mturk, representative) (optional)  The original sample consisted of n = 221 females, n = 35 males, n = 1 or 2 other (see Point 5). 95.33% of the participants were between 18 and 29 years old and 98.05% self-identified as Hispanic. No further information were given.  9.	Was the original study conducted with paper-and-pencil surveys, on a computer, or something else? (optional)  The original study was conducted on a computer.    Designing the Replication Study  10.	Are the original materials for the study available from the author? (optional)  -	No  11.	I know that assumptions (e.g., about the meaning of the stimuli) in the original study will also hold in my replication because (optional)  We will use validated and empirically tested questionnaires. For the assessment of the Dark Triad character traits, we will use the Short Dark Triad (SD3; Jones & Paulhus, 2014) which includes 9 items each for Machiavellianism, Narcissism and Psychopathy. It was already translated to German so we will use the translated version (Malesza et al., 2017). The other questionnaire we will use is a measure of honesty rules endorsement in relationships which includes 21 obligatory rule statements and 22 discretionary rule statements (Roggensack & Sillars, 2014). This questionnaire is written in English, so we will translate it to German. The translations will be checked by an English native speaker. By that we will make sure that the original meaning will not be distorted. For both questionnaires we will use a 5-point Likert-type scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree). We will also ask for participants age, culture and gender to rule out any impact on the effect.  12.	Location of the experimenter during data collection (optional)  Not applicable   13.	Experimenter knowledge of participant experimental condition (optional)  Not applicable   14.	Experimenter knowledge of overall hypotheses (optional)  All experimenters know about all hypotheses.   15.	My target sample size is (optional)  Our target sample size is N = 256, but we will collect N = 270 participants because of possible exclusions.  16.	The rationale for my sample size is (optional)  An a priori power analysis for correlation was conducted, assuming an effect size of r = .26 (which was smallest significant effect reported in the original study), setting Type I error rate at  = .05 and power at 99%.    Documenting Differences between the Original and Replication Study  17.	The similarities/differences in the instruction are (optional)  -	Different  18.	The similarities/differences in the measures are (optional)  -	Close   19.	The similarities/differences in the stimuli are (optional)  Not applicable   20.	The similarities/differences in the location (e.g., lab vs. online; alone vs. in groups) are (optional)  -	Exact  21.	The similarities/differences in remuneration are (optional)  The remuneration is not given in the paper. There will be no remuneration in our replication.   22.	The similarities/differences between participant populations are (optional)  -	Close   23.	What differences between the original study and your study might be expected to influence the size and/or direction of the effect? (optional)  Because we do not have the original materials there might be differences in the instruction text of the study and as already mentioned (see Point 11), we will self-translate the English questionnaire for honesty rules endorsement in relationships to German.   24.	I have taken the following steps to test whether the differences listed in the previous question will influence the outcome of my replication attempt (optional)  The translations will be checked by an English native speaker. By that we will make sure that the original meaning will not be distorted (see Point 11).  Analysis and Replication Evaluation  25.	My exclusion criteria are (e.g., handling outliers, removing participants from analysis) (optional)  We will exclude participants who don’t give their consent to participate and those who are younger than 18 years. If participants answer one of the attention check questions incorrectly, participants will be excluded afterwards.   26.	My analysis plan is (justify differences from the original) (optional)  First we will calculate descriptive statistics for all relevant variables (i.e, Machiavellianism, Psychopathy, Narcissism, obligatory rule endorsement and discretionary rule endorsement). Then, we will calculate an intercorrelation matrix for all relevant variables. Lastly, we will conduct two regression analyses with each trait of the dark triad as the predictor for obligatory rule endorsement and discretionary rule endorsement as dependent variables.   27.	A successful replication is defined as (optional)  We interpret our replication as success if the standard significance criterion (p < .05) is fulfilled and if the effect is in the same direction as the original effect (OSF, 2015).  28. title_r: Children’s alphabet knowledge profiles and prediction of reading and spelling outcomes
abstract_r: Alphabet knowledge, as measured during early childhood, is an important indicator of later reading success and difficulties (National Early Literacy Panel, 2008; Piasta et al., 2012). Although most children eventually master letter names and letter sounds, developmental patterns in children’s alphabet learning may matter for later outcomes (Heilmann et al., 2018; Piasta, Logan, Farley, et al., 2022; Torppa et al., 2006). For example, some children may have initially lower levels of alphabet knowledge in the fall of preschool, perhaps due to limited learning opportunities to that point, yet readily learn letter names and sounds across the preschool year. Other children with initially lower levels of alphabet knowledge may not make much progress, which may signal difficulties with orthographic or phonological processing. As such, both levels and learning of alphabet knowledge may be important to consider. In the current study, we conceptually replicate and extend emerging work examining profiles of young children’s alphabet learning and associations with later outcomes. First, we use a large sample of preschool children who are and are not identified as at-risk for later reading difficulties and apply a person-centered approach to determine whether we are able to replicate prior profiles of alphabet knowledge and learning. The person-centered approach allows for consideration of measures of both initial level and gain in alphabet knowledge, such that we can consider levels and learning, and overcomes statistical limitations inherent to measures on which mastery is expected. Previous studies have identified profiles that comprised (a) children who had initially high alphabet knowledge and little gain due to ceiling effects/mastery, (b) children who had lower alphabet knowledge initially but exhibited substantial learning over time, and (c) children who had lower alphabet knowledge initially and minimal learning over time (Piasta, Logan, Farley, et al., 2022; Torppa et al., 2006). Second, we extend prior work by closely examining the profiles of alphabet learning exhibited by children identified as at-risk for reading difficulties and determining whether profile membership predicts their word identification, word attack, and spelling skills 1.5 years later. Torppa et al. (2006) found that letter name knowledge profiles predicted Grade 1 reading skills, and Piasta, Logan, Farley, et al. (2022) found that letter name and letter sound profiles predicted literacy skills at kindergarten entry, even when profiles did not differ substantially in initial alphabet knowledge levels. We specifically test three hypotheses derived from this available literature. In addition to furthering understanding of alphabet development, findings have research and practice implications for early literacy assessment, progress monitoring, and risk identification.

title_r: "The Impact of Victim Photographs on Mock Jurors’ Emotions and Verdicts” (Study 3)
abstract_r: In two previous studies, we have examined the impact of viewing photographs of a victim of violence before she was hurt on mock jurors’ moral emotional responses to learning about the harm and on their case judgments. In the second study, we also investigated whether seeing the contrast of pre-harm and post-harm photographs influenced judgments above and beyond seeing either pre- or post-harm photographs alone. In both studies, we found no effect of seeing pre-harm photographs alone (compared to no photographs) on conviction rates. In Study 2, we replicated previous research in that seeing post-harm photographs (compared to no photographs) increased conviction rates through disgust. Specifically, participants who saw gruesome post-harm photographs, compared to no photographs, reported more disgust and in turn were more likely to vote guilty. We also found support for our contrast hypothesis in Study 2. When participants saw the combination of pre- and post-harm photographs, compared to post-harm photographs alone, they reported more anger and sympathy, which in turn increased convictions. In this study, we will expand this line of research by examining whether the race of the victim (Black, Latina, or White) influences the effect of seeing both pre- and post-harm photographs on mock juror judgments.

title_r: Replicating the unconscious working memory effect: A multisite Registered Report.
abstract_r: Although in recent years some studies have found evidence suggesting that working memory (WM) may operate on unconscious perceptual contents, decisive demonstrations of the existence of unconscious WM are lacking. In the present Registered Report, we aim to replicate the first study on this topic by Soto et al. (2011), using a multisite sample from different laboratories, with a larger number of participants and trials than those typically used in previous studies. As a result, a highly-powered, open-access dataset will be available for researchers and future analyses. Furthermore, some minimal baseline requirements will be guaranteed for the experimental task (i.e., number of valid trials, motivation, and consistent labels for the perceptual awareness scale). We will critically test the hypotheses commonly proposed: above-chance performance in cue-present trials reported as unseen, a null correlation between performance and cue detection sensitivity, and a significantly above-chance intercept in the regression of performance on sensitivity. Crucially, the interpretation of all three results is based on the assumption that the measures are sufficiently reliable. Given the scarcity of reliability estimations in this literature, we will calculate these estimates for our measures.

title_r: Introducing a visual component to the bystander effect. Revisiting the seizure experiment.
abstract_r: In 1968 Darley and Latané invited 72 New York University undergraduate psychology students to participate in what they believed would be a discussion concerning problems that students might face in a high pressure, urban environment. Each round would include one participant, who was placed alone in an individual room, only given a pair of headphones and a microphone. Participants were given the impression that they would be discussing with other participants who were seemingly also placed in individual rooms. They were told that they would be anonymous and that the researchers would not listen in on the discussion itself, but rather do their measurements through a questionnaire later on. The participants were made to believe that the experimenter would not interfere during the discussion. The discussion was organized so that each participant spoke for two minutes, whilst the other “participant’s” microphones were turned off. After everyone had spoken, “participants” would in turn comment on what had been said and then the whole session would end with a free discussion. All contributions apart from the participant’s own were all recordings. This allowed the researchers to vary in the number of people the participant believed to be present, as well as keeping the content of the discussion constant for each round. For each round the “victim” spoke first, telling the others in a convincing manner that he was prone to getting seizures, particularly in pressing situations. The real participant was the last to speak. The commenting part followed, where the seizure prone first “participant” made a few calm comments, before starting to experience medical difficulties, expressing audible distress, and then collapsing. Only silence followed. The researchers measured the percentage of participants who left the room to notify the experimenter about the problem, which was the measurement of whether they helped or not, as well as how long it took them if they did. They found that both these measures varied as a function of the number of other people participants believed to be present. The less people, the more likely they were to intervene and the faster they would do so. The internal validity of the original study is high. Participants were put in random group sizes; they varied in the order that the standardized voices were played; reactions and debrief conversations indicated clearly that participants perceived the emergency as real. However, the external validity (ability to generalize the cause-effect findings) needs to be reviewed. Firstly, the interpersonal relationship between the participant and the victim is clinical in nature. Not being able to build any degree of rapport with the victim is arguably too distanced from potential real-life settings. Even a short interpersonal gaze could tilt the decision in favour of helping. Secondly, the sample was too narrow in terms of age, gender, education and socio-economic status. Our conceptual replication will be addressing these two points through the use of different methods and a more diversified sample pool. The experiment itself we will test the notion of seeing versus not seeing the victim in a bystander setting. We expect to find the bystander effect to still be in effect as in the original study, but to a lesser degree on account of the participant being able to see the victim. This means more participants will help and they will wait less before doing so. Having a more diversified pool is not expected to have much effect on the results but it could give the study a higher external validity.

title_r: Distractor-resilient visual search: The effect of explicit instruction about spatial probabilistic information
abstract_r: This is a pre-registration of an experiment designed to examine the effects of explicit instruction on spatial information of frequent distractor locations in visual search. Wang and Theeuwes (2018, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance) demonstrated that when a distractor singleton repeatedly appears at a high-probability location, participants can learn to suppress that location through statistical learning, thereby minimizing the detrimental impact of the distractor on search performance. Building on this finding, the present study investigates whether providing prior information about the likely location of distractors modulates this type of suppression. We previously conducted a direct replication of the original paradigm, which confirmed the robustness of the effect (Experiment 1; not pre-registered). In Experiment 2, we employ a similar paradigm but introduce an additional condition in which participants are explicitly informed about the high-probability distractor location. This allows us to examine whether such explicit knowledge facilitates or interferes with suppression based on statistical learning.

abstract_r: Student researchers: Ava Bogan, Andrew Felsted, Brevin J. Robertson, Alexander Osorio Faculty advisor: Bradford J. Wiggins, Brigham Young University-Idaho Replication of People Endorse Harsher Policies in Principle Than in Practice- Study #2 Eitan D. Rude and Franklin Shaddy 2024 Here is the link to the original studies OSF page: https://osf.io/69rjm/ We will be conducting a replication of the authors study number 2 looked at how peoples judgements about errors in policy change depending on whether they are thinking about preventing errors before they happen or fixing errors after they've happened, and whether the policy involves punishments or rewards. The authors wanted to know do people think certain errors are worse than others depending on the situations. The study had 917 U.S. adults from the Amazon Mechanical turk platform. The design of the study was a 2x2x3 structure with the policy types being punishment vs reward, the framing being either prevent or fix, and then there was 3 scenarios participants were given. the 3 scenarios were the employee pay scenario, car insurance scenario, and the water use taxes scenario. The key findings were that for punishment policies people preferred to prevent false negatives or in other words they wanted to make sure guilty people didn't get away with something. Then for reward policies it was the opposite. People preferred to prevent false positives or stop those undeserved rewards, but then they wanted to fix false negatives or in other words people that didn't get their reward should be compensated.These patterns were consistent throughout all three scenarios. People seem to be more concerned with helping people harmed by mistakes after the fact, rather than stopping errors ahead of time. At Brigham Young University we are conducting a replication of this study. There are some key differences in our replication compared to the original study. The original study hosted the survey on the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform but we will be using qualtrics to distribute the scenarios to students, we will still be using the 2x2x3 setup. They are both administered online though. Also we wont be able to obtain as many participants as the original. Our population will consist of college aged religious students which is a key difference in our demographics compared to the original study. This could possibly be a confounding variable. Our survey being distributed will have its data collection ending Data collection will be closed on Monday June 30th 2025 at 11:59 P.M. mountain time zone. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "We found that health workers reported higher risk perception, level of worry, and knowledge as related to COVID-19 infection compared to general population". As main analysis, we [study authors] computed hierarchical logistic regression on the dichotomic responses reported overall our participants about preoccupations, opinions, and behaviors relatively to their experience with the new coronavirus. This analysis allowed us to estimate the odds to obtain a positive response to a particular question given a set of parameters. The stronger predictor of risk perception was the group: healthcare workers showed about 2.5 times the odds of other participants to perceive themselves at risk of infection. From Table 3, odds ratio = 2.72, p < 0.01.

title_r: Confirming category-specific retrospective and prospective memory enhancement induced by reward
abstract_r: Past studies have shown that memory enhancement occurs retrospectively and prospectively for conceptually related stimuli that were conditioned with reward and punishment. In a series of preceding studies in our lab (currently unpublished), we originally intended to investigate whether such category-specific adaptive memory effects can be extended to more complicated learning and encoding paradigms. We aimed to replicate the effect with item memory of images as well as words in a context where there is associative learning of words and images. Our studies however resulted in a lack of conclusive evidence for retrospective and prospective memory enhancement for word and image items through category-based generalisation. In an attempt to shed light on the underlying effect, we attempt now to closely replicate the original study by [Patil et al. 2017] using only image stimuli. In contrast to the original laboratory-based experiments, we will use online experiments and extend the original study to include a condition which investigates prospective memory effects that have not been previously explored in the reward paradigm.

title_r: Logical representation priming between verbs
abstract_r: Feiman and Snedeker (2016; Experiment 3) observed that logical representations can be primed between verbs. In a Dutch replication of this experiment, however, we failed to replicate this result. In order to further test the robustness of the effect of logical representation priming between verbs, we conducted a power analysis and observed that both Feiman and Snedeker's original experiment as well as our replication experiment were underpowered. Therefore, we shall conduct a well-powered near-replication of Feiman and Snedeker's experiment, which will elucidate the question of whether logical representations specify verb meaning.

title_r: Novelty Preferences and Toddler's Memory Decisions
abstract_r: A vast amount of research has been conducted to establish that infants and toddlers can form and retain memories and to understand the factors that underlie age-related improvements in memory. However, little research has focused on how decision processes influence memory performance. As toddlers begin to develop more language skills, adults increasingly ask them to utilize their memory and with this preregistration we wish to investigate how toddlers use their memories in service of a current goal. A previous study in our lab has shown that during a visual paired comparison paradigm, toddlers will choose the new image over the previously familiarized item due to their tendency to look at new images (novelty preferences). This tendency is reduced and their memory decisions are aided by a brief 5% change in the size of the old image, which results in a perceived brief flicker of that image. This suggests that disengaging the toddler’s gaze towards the new item may support memory decisions. With this preregistered study, we wish to accomplish two goals. 1. We wish to replicate these findings in a new sample of toddlers. 2. We wish to extend these findings and examine whether a flicker elsewhere on the screen (and not on the target) will suffice to disengage the toddlers’ attention and aid their memory decisions. Alternative hypotheses can be advanced depending on whether attention directed to the target is necessary to observe a benefit to decision making, or whether instead disengaging attention away from the novel stimulus suffices.

title_r: Do Infants Expect Lower Status Agents to Conform to Higher Status Agents?
abstract_r: Previous studies have found that 10 to 13-month-old infants are able to use the relative size of two agents (Thomsen et al., 2011), and 6 to 12-month-old infants are able to use the relative numerical size of agents’ groups (Pun et al., 2016) to infer the status of each character, in relation to the other. Infants expect agents who are larger in physical size, and/or belong to larger groups, to be of higher status than smaller agents, or those who belong to numerically smaller groups, and, in both situations, expect lower status agents to yield to their higher status counterparts in right-of-way contests. Moreover, 21-31 month-old toddlers display a preference for dominant agents who win right-of-way contests (Thomas et al., 2016), except when the dominant characters “win” through the use of force, as this appears to generate preferences for the character who yielded (Thomas et al., 2018). Overall, infants and toddlers appear to use the relative size of agents, or the group size of those agents, to infer who is more likely to be of higher status. Infants use this understanding to generate predictions regarding which character should yield to the other, and young toddlers appear to make nuanced judgements regarding which character they prefer, based on both status and how such status is acquired. This study seeks to build on this previous research in two ways. First, we seek to replicate and extend the findings that infants use the relative size of agents to infer their status, in relation to the other, and then use their relative status to generate expectations regarding who is more likely to yield to the other (i.e. yielding condition). We will also examine whether infants expect lower status agents to conform to the actions of higher status agents (i.e. conformity condition). If, as we expect, infants expect size to be representative of status, and use this to generate expectations regarding which of two characters should be more likely to yield to the other, then they should be surprised when the larger character yields access to a desired object or opportunity to the smaller character (hypothesis 1). Also, if infants are able to use size of agents to infer status, and expect lower status characters to conform to the behavior of higher status characters, then they should be surprised when the larger character conforms to the behavior of the smaller character (hypothesis 2). Our study would extend previous evidence for size-based dominance in competitive or zero-sum contexts to a novel situation. It may also provide evidence for an additional dominance-based inference in infancy: that infants expect lower status characters to conform to the actions of higher status characters.

title_r: Confirmatory analyses testing longitudinal stability of learning rates, exploratory behavior, and action precision in substance use disorders over a 1-year period
abstract_r: We aim to replicate the results of a previous longitudinal study [1] in which we used computational modelling in conjunction with behavior on a decision-making (three-armed bandit) task within a transdiagnostic sample of individuals with substance use disorders (SUDs) as well as healthy comparisons (HCs). There we found evidence of significant learning rate differences between HCs and SUDs that were stable from baseline to 1-year follow up. Moreover, we found exploratory evidence that baseline differences in multiple model parameters (most notably learning rates from negative outcomes) predicted symptom changes over time, primarily in stimulant users. An “action precision” parameter reflecting value-sensitivity in choice also appeared to change over time in a manner that tracked symptom improvement. In the present study, we will use an analogous analytic approach to our previous study to test the hypothesis that these same results will be found in a new sample of participants. These participants will be drawn from the confirmatory subsample of the Tulsa 1000 dataset [2] that was specifically set aside for replicating prior results found in the exploratory subsample of this dataset.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Andrew (2014), from Social Forces
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Andrew (2014) is that primary-grade retention has lasting effects on educational attainments well after a student is initially retained: Retaining a child in early primary school reduces his or her odds of high school completion. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "I find consistent evidence of a causal effect of early primary school grade retention on high school completion." Table 7 displays estimated grade-retention effects from both the covariate adjustment models with matched samples. The dependent variable is “High school completion.” The selected test result can be found in Table 7 under the heading “NELS88 propensity”. In a covariate adjustment model including all matching covariates, early primary-grade retention reduces the odds of high school completion by about 75 percent in the matched NELS88 sample (log odds ratio = -1.40, SE = .25, OR = .144, p = .05 or less).

title_r: Untitled Replication of Side-to-side differences in lower extremity biomechanics during multi-directional jump landing in volleyball athletes
abstract_r: This research study is a replication study that will contribute to a large-scale international replication project in sports and exercise science whose overall aim is: To produce high level systematic and transparent replication trials of experimental trials published within the last five years in top tier sports and exercise science journals using a randomized, unbiased selection method. Large scale replication projects have been undertaken by, among others, the Open Science Collaboration in the form of the Reproducibility Project in Psychology and the Many Labs Project (Klein et al., 2014; Open Science Collaboration, 2015). These projects ignited the debate on the replication crisis in social science due to their difficulty in replicating selected effects and the variability in results. One goal of replication is to bolster our collective confidence in the veracity of novel claims by providing diagnostic evidence about those claims (Nosek et al., 2015; Nosek and Errington, 2020) when the original and replication study are similar in all “theoretically relevant dimensions” such as study design, methods, and materials (Earp, 2020, p. 120). Given the interdisciplinary nature of the sports science field and the overlap with the psychological sciences, there is reason to believe the sports science field faces similar replication issues (Caldwell et al., 2020). The replicability of sports science research has yet to be examined despite the identification of concerns within the field (Halperin et al., 2018; Heneghan et al., 2012; Knudson, 2017). As a result, the overall goal of this project is to sample a range of topics in an unbiased manner across the field of sports science for an initial estimation of the replicability of those findings. This is the first natural step in the assessment of replicability of the field, therefore, the project will attempt to replicate numerous effects once rather than multiple replications of a specific effect or theory. As it is essential to run multiple independent experiments to determine if findings in sports science have a consistent and accurate pattern, and are strongly supported (Earp and Trafimow, 2015), the proposed study is one of many studies to be replicated. The objective of this specific proposed study is to replicate (i.e. repeat) the work of Komsak Sinsurin, Sarun Srisangboriboon, and Roongtiwa Vachalathiti published in the Europen Journal of Sports Sciences in 2017 titled “Side-to-side differences in lower extremity biomechanics during multi-directional jump landing in volleyball athletes”. title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Ishida et al. (2010), from Social Science and Medicine
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Ishida et al. (2010) is that intimate partner violence (IPV) victimization is significantly associated with Paraguayan women’s poor mental health status, as measured by the risk of common mental disorders (CMD) and suicidal ideation. The association of IPV victimization with the risk of CMD is the portion of this finding selected for the SCORE program. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "The results from multivariate logistic regression models demonstrate that controlling for women’s socioeconomic and marital status and history of childhood abuse and their male partners’ unemployment and alcohol consumption, IPV is independently associated with an increased risk for common mental disorders (CMD) and suicidal ideation measured by the Self Reporting Questionnaire (SRQ-20)." Evidence for the finding is found in Table 5, which presents the results of three multivariable logistic regression models of each measure of mental health status. The outcome measure in the analysis selected for the SCORE program is CMD risk, and the independent variable/treatment selected is emotional violence within the previous 12 months (current) (see CMD risk Model 3 in Table 5 for details). The introduction of other key covariates only slightly decreases the odds ratios, and most of them remain statistically significant in Model 3, suggesting that a large portion of the association between IPV and CMD risk is independent of these covariates (odds ratio for IPV-Last 12 months-Emotional = 1.58, 95% confidence interval = 1.35, 1.86, p < 0.001). We aim to replicate this finding using similar, nationally-representative data from Nicaragua that was collected around the same time frame.

title_r: An updated systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of protein intakes effects upon lean soft tissue mass, muscle, strength, and function in healthy adults
abstract_r: Pre-registration (PROSPERO Template) REVIEW TITLE AND BASIC DETAILS Review title An updated systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of protein intakes effects upon lean soft tissue mass, muscle, strength, and function in healthy adults Review Rationale In a recent systematic review and meta-analysis Nunes et al. (2022) examined the dose-response effects of protein intake upon lean soft tissue mass, muscle, strength, and function. However, whilst they examined both categorical protein intake (‘<1.2 g/kg/day’, ‘1.2–1.59 g/kg/day’ and ‘≥1.6 g/kg/day’) as well as continuous (as g/kg/day) the latter utilised only linear functional forms which imply a constant slope of proteins effect across varied intakes. It may be the case that some kind of non-linear functional form may better describe the dose-response relationship. For example, in earlier work Morton et al. (2018) used a piecewise linear model and estimated a so-called “breakpoint” where a plateau in protein intakes effects might occur. Tagawa et al. (2021; 2022) have also reported possible non-linear functional forms where they utilised piecewise splines. However, both approaches are somewhat limited in specifically forcing a single “breakpoint”. Instead, more flexible modelling strategies using extensions of generalised additive models to meta-analytic scenarios may allow for clearer determination of the dose-response function based on existing studies data. Further, the use of singular models renders dose-response estimates conditional on that particular model. Whilst the models previously explored may have plausibility, at least over the range of data available, these previous analyses have also not made any attempts at comparing functional forms implied by different models. However, even comparing amongst different candidate models with regards to the relative evidence for and against different functional forms as being the underlying data generating process has limitations. Any predictions are conditional on the candidate model selected and selection process. Indeed, when fitting models to data, even when all are plausible candidates, there is uncertainty in the possible models that could be fit and the selection process. However, with Bayesian approaches to modelling it is simple to combine, in a weighted fashion determined by their relative evidence, estimates from all models examined and directly incorporate this uncertainty (Hinne et al., 2020). Adopting a Bayesian approach for evidence synthesis also allows the incorporation of prior information that might be relevant to inference. For example, we also have precise estimates of the effects of resistance exercise without additional protein intervention from previous meta-analyses (e.g., Steele et al., 2023). Most previous protein intake intervention studies have examined resistance exercise as a concomitant intervention. As such we can also utilise these estimates, in addition to those from non-resistance exercise control groups, to set informative priors for the expected effect sizes at habitual protein intakes (i.e., without an intervention to increase protein intake). Thus, we sought to revisit the studies that were included in the review of Nunes et al. (2022), in addition to updating searches since the date of their last search to include any newer studies. We will replicate and extend the systematic searches conducted previously. Previous meta-analyses examining the effects of protein intake upon the outcomes noted have typically not pre-registered a smallest effect size of interest range to draw conclusions regarding the meaningfulness of the effects identified. Here we set the smallest effect size of interest to interpret the slopes of the dose response function for increases reflecting the typical intervention in terms of increasing protein intake above habitual levels. This would enable both current recommendations to be updated if necessary and also generate a functional form enabling more precise theoretical predictions of effects that future studies might offer severe tests of i.e., predicted magnitudes of condition by time interaction effects for comparing different doses of protein in a randomised trial. Review objectives To explore the dose-response relationships between manipulation of protein intake and both lean soft tissue mass, muscle, strength, and function in healthy adults. Keywords Protein, Lean soft tissue mass, Muscle, Strength, Physical Function, Dose-response, Resistance training ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA Inclusion Condition or domain being studied We will examine studies including healthy adults and which manipulated protein intake experimentally (i.e., randomised controlled trials) with or without inclusion of a concomitant resistance exercise intervention. Lean soft tissue mass, muscle, strength, and function were the primary focus. Population Adult participants (healthy) aged 18 years or older. Intervention(s) or exposure(s) Additional protein ingestion with or without the addition of resistance exercise (increasing protein ingestion as the primary intervention using nutritional supplements or diet at any dose or level). Comparator(s) or control(s) Placebo or no intervention (control). Outcomes Lean soft tissue mass (or a closely related measure i.e., fat-free mass; Heymsfield et al., 2024), direct measures of muscle mass/size (both whole muscle and muscle fiber), muscle strength and performance in tests of physical function. Context Any setting. Study Design Parallel group randomised trials. Exclusion Studies including participants with decreased mobility, frailty, obesity, or any chronic or infectious diseases were not included. Also, interventions were carefully screened for the presence of any potential active ingredient that might impact lean soft tissue mass gain other than protein (i.e. creatine, phosphatidic acid, omega-3 fatty acids, anabolic steroids, and beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate [HMB]) or if they were intended to cause weight loss (e.g., energy restriction). If a particular study testing potential active supplements had intervention groups fitting our inclusion criteria, the study was included and assessed to extract the respective arm based data of protein and control/placebo interventions only. No restrictions were imposed regarding additional protein dose or the duration of the intervention protocol SIMILAR REVIEWS Check for similar records already in PROSPERO or OSF No similar review records were identified at time of search when we began planning this project (15th May 2025) SEARCHING AND SCREENING We will replicate the search strategy used in the previous review of Nunes et al. (2022). The previous strategy including results can be seen here: (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/action/downloadSupplement?doi=10.1002%2Fjcsm.12922&file=jcsm12922-sup-0005-Search_strategies_.pdf). Study design Exclusively Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs) utilising parallel group designs. Search language restrictions English Search date restrictions Searches will be limited to September 2020 onwards as we are updating the existing review of Nunes et al. Studies will be initially screened by title and abstract, and subsequently by full text if they met the relevant inclusion criteria. We will also extract contrast data between timepoints where reported. Studies will be reviewed and screened for the study design, protein supplementation or increased protein prescription intervention, subject characteristics, placebo/control information, body composition, resistance training protocols, and strength or physical testing outcomes. title_r: What affects DMN activity during task switch?
abstract_r: Default Mode Network (DMN) activity, measured with fMRI, typically increases during internally directed thought and decreases during external tasks. However, Crittenden et al. (2015) and Smith et al. (2018) found increased DMN activity during demanding external task-switches between different cognitive domains, compared to within-domain switches and task repeats. In our previous experiment, we aimed to replicate this effect in a similar paradigm and test if DMN switch activity reflects increased representation of broader context. In Core DMN, we found significant activity for all task switches (versus task repeats), and stronger activity for switches between rest and task. Although scene context was decodable, there was no evidence that this differed by switch type. Surprisingly, we did not see greater DMN activity at between-domain versus within-domain switches. This may depend on overall task-set complexity, because we used two domains and four task types whereas the previous studies used three domains and six task types. We hypothesize that the disappearance of the domain-dependent task-switch effect in DMN is due to the decrease of number of domains in the paradigm. We aim to investigate this in a follow-up study contrasting DMN activity during task-switch trials when the tasks are drawn from either two or four domains. Furthermore, in the same paradigm we plan to compare DMN activity for task-switches between domains belonging to different cognitive chunks formed through learning and practice. We hypothesize that DMN activity will be greater for between-chunk than within-chunk switches. To assess whether effects might be due to changes in task expectancy for different numbers of domains, half of the experiment will use the same task expectancy as previous experiments, where the trials are balanced by switch type and globally by task, while including all task transitions; the other half of the experiment will restrict the possible task transitions to create an even task expectancy regardless of switch type and number of domains.

title_r: Spatial-Arithmetic Associations in Vertical Dimensions
abstract_r: Previous studies have found a relationship between arithmetic processing and spatial associations. Specifically, numbers are usually mapped from left to right (Mental Number Line and SNARC effect), and addition and subtraction tend to cause shifts in horizontal attention (for example, addition often shifts attention rightward, while subtraction shifts attention leftward). Most previous research has focused on the left-right relationship, but there has been little research on the vertical dimension. The left-right association is thought to be influenced largely by cultural practices, such as reading and writing direction. In contrast, up-down associations may stem more from early sensorimotor experiences, such as infants observing objects being stacked upwards. Therefore, some researchers believe that arithmetic processing may have even stronger associations with vertical spatial attention. However, previous findings have been inconsistent, possibly due to cultural differences or differences in experimental methods. In Experiment 1, we replicated Liu et al. (2017)'s study and added eye movement measures to their design. The results showed that neither reaction times nor the overall average fixation positions revealed significant differences. However, a time-series analysis of gaze positions indicated a significant difference during specific time windows—between the presentation of the operator and the appearance of the next number. This result suggests that vertical spatial-numerical associations may occur transiently but systematically during certain phases of the calculation process. The absence of an overall effect may be due to the relatively short duration of these vertical spatial-numerical associations. Additionally, the lack of such an effect in Liu et al. (2017) might be attributed to the late presentation of spatial targets, by which time the attentional shift may have already diminished. In Experiment 2, we will present target stimuli at any stage of the calculation process. This approach will allow us to determine whether reaction times are also affected, thereby testing the robustness of the effect.

title_r: Revisiting Schachter’s Research on Rejection, Deviance, and Communication
abstract_r: We propose a replication of the original Schachter (1951) deviation-rejection study. Schachter’s ground-breaking demonstration of the deviation-rejection link has captivated social psychologists for decades. The findings and paradigm were so compelling that the deviation-rejection link is often taken for granted and sometimes may be misrepresented (Berkowitz, 1971; Wahrman & Pugh, 1972). Because there have only been two direct replications, one of which by the original author, we believe it is important to revisit the original study.

title_r: Replication of “When He Doesn’t Mean You: Gender-Exclusive Language as Ostracism”
abstract_r: Stout and Dasgupta (2011) found in three studies that exposure to generic masculine or what they termed “gender-exclusive language” led women to feel ostracized. The purpose of this work is to conduct a high-powered replication of this effect, using the methods of their Study 1.

title_r: Measuring grit in learning Spanish
abstract_r: Learning a language takes grit. A study recently came out in the journal Language Teaching Research, in which the authors (Teimouri, Plonsky, & Tabandeh, 2020) gave language learners (of English as a second language) a 20-item grit survey. At Michigan State University, we plan to give MSU Spanish language learners the same survey which we obtained from the original study's authors (this is a replication study) to see if MSU students have grit in the same way. The survey in this study will also be presented as "now" (during COVID-19) and "then" (pre-COVID-19), asking students to reflect on their learning from last year in the fall. Thus, our hope is to see how COVID-19 may be affecting Spanish language learners' grit—how grit is dynamic and may change due to environmental or contextual changes. This study will be conducted in different Spanish language courses at Michigan State University. The responses will then be used as a tool for research on Spanish grit, comparing the results of this study with the results of the prior (original) 2020 study by Teimouri and colleagues.

title_r: „Individual differences in need for cognition and decision making in the Iowa Gambling Task - a Replication”
abstract_r: Within the frame of our seminar (M4: Experimentelles Arbeiten), we would like to replicate the study “Individual differences in need for cognition and decision making in the Iowa Gambling Task” by Jason L. Harman. The study was published in 2011 in the journal Personality and Individual Differences. It includes two experiments of which we would like to replicate the first one. The main research question was whether individuals low in Need for Cognition (NFC) (a personality variable operationalized with a questionnaire of how subjects would rate their requirement and ability of difficult cognitive thinking) process gains and losses differently than those high in NFC. Our sample will consist of 90 psychology students who are not familiar with the study. Our replication of the study will take no longer than 20 minutes. We are curious to find out if we can replicate the results of the original experiment. Using the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT), a decision making paradigm, we will simulate a real world situation in which decision making is dependent on multiple factors such as risk, uncertainty, learning from experience, rewards and punishments. We will assess NFC with the 16-item short version of the German NFC scale (Bless et al., 1994) to categorize the participants into two different groups: NFC high and NFC low.

title_r: Replication of "Big number, big body: Jersey numbers alter body size perception" by Shams et al. 2023
abstract_r: This study measures whether or not the quantitative size of football jersey numbers affects subject perception of the football player’s physical size. This measurement of perception is not done using real images of football players in jerseys, but rather cartoon icons. After correcting for confounds in experiment 2, the original study found a significant effect between jersey number and perceived size (larger jersey number makes subjects think the players are bigger). The skin/clothing color of the players, as well as the physical/visual size of the displayed numbers are all controlled, so we believe we are replicating some effect relating to the conceptual size of the numerals; however, the scales used for subject judgment were displayed AFTER the stimulus was shown, leading to questions on whether the effect on perceived size is in fact perception from memory, on online (live, in the moment) perception. Thus in our replication, we are creating another condition where the scale used to evaluate size is shown simultaneously with the stimuli. If jersey number affects online perception, we believe the result will replicate with this new condition; however, if the presence of number in fact alters memory rather than perception, only the original study version will replicate.

title_r: Crossmodal transposed word serial processing
abstract_r: Evidence has supported the idea that readers lexically process words serially (one at a time), but evidence by Mirault et al. (2018) has demonstrated a transposed word effect. This effect is where readers have difficulty deciding that sentences such as “do love you me? “are ungrammatical, in which the transposition of two adjacent words (i.e., love you) would form a grammatical sentence, compared to sentences in which the transposition of two words does not result in grammaticality (e.g. the cat white was slowly). This has been taken as evidence for the parallel lexical processing of multiple words simultaneously. Evidence has also shown that the transposed word effect can be attributed to a combination of noisy bottom-up word position coding and top-down syntactic constraints. This effect can be interpreted within serial, as opposed to parallel, reading models. The present study will examine the transposed word effect by varying modality input and type of processing for which each of the two transposed words will be presented. However, we aim to replicate the previous findings in students and assess this with different input modalities (auditory and crossmodal) and different processing strategies (visual transposed word parallel, crossmodal transposed word serial and crossmodal transposed word parallel). In this experiment, we manipulate sequence type and experiment. Thus, we expected that the transposed word effect in the crossmodal transposed word serial processing should be replicated (such that transposed words are responded to more slowly and are more error prone than control words). The main focus is on accuracy. Huang and Staub (2021) argued that the integration of word n+1 may begin before the integration of word n is complete, which may allow the transposed word effect to occur. As a result, the findings we observed may be more likely to ensue, as there is a higher likelihood that word n would be completed when the integration of word n+1 began when all words were presented and heard, the transposed word effect should be smaller or not present in crossmodal serial relative to visual transposed word serial and parallel processing and auditory transposed word tasks.

title_r: Relationships between greenspace exposure, street activity, and crime across US cities
abstract_r: Natural environments can have wide ranging effects on behavior and cognition, specifically criminal behavior. Here we investigated how urban tree canopy, park visits, and local street activity relate to crime levels in various US cities. Previous work using 2017 cell phone mobility data found that local street activity and park visits in Chicago and New York were negatively associated with both violent and non-violent crime. Tree canopy was negatively associated with crime in Chicago only, while the regression coefficient was also negative but not significant in NYC. Visits to other amenities, such as museums, were not associated with crime. Using a new source of cell phone mobility data which covers the United States for 2018-present, we plan to replicate the analyses in other US cities. This will determine whether the previous findings generalize more broadly to cities across the US.

title_r: Evaluating the Effects of Visual Embellishments and Context on Comprehension, Recall and Preference of Charts
abstract_r: Many researchers and design experts condemn the use of chart junk or visual embellishments, attributing it to creating distraction and hindrance in comprehensibility of charts. In contrast, some experts encourage the use of chart junk as a way to achieve better engagement, approachability, and memorability. This controversy about chartjunk or visual embellishment raises questions about its benefits, role in visualization, and conditions under which it is appropriate to use. Despite numerous studies trying to address this controversy throughout decades, chartjunk still remains a contentious topic in the visualization community. Therefore, to address the discrepancies in previous works and to shed further light on the issue, our project aims to replicate and build upon the canonical work by Bateman et. al. (2010) where they investigated the effects of visual embellishments on comprehensibility and memorability. Three previous replication studies of the Bateman et. al. study were performed by 3 groups of graduate student researchers (including the authors of the current work), and several issues regarding the study design, delivery and methodology were identified through group discussions and reflections. Our current evaluation plan is designed to address the issues identified in the previous iteration and also aims to build upon the original study by introducing the factor of context. Therefore, the objective of our evaluation project is to investigate the effects of visual embellishments on interpretability, memorability and preference of charts with and without the presence of context and to characterize common pitfalls and setbacks in replication studies in general. We plan to achieve this by conducting two remote studies - one that uses the charts out of context mimicking the original study by Bateman et. al, and one where the charts are embedded in parts of their original article. In both of the studies, participants will be shown 4 visually embellished and plain charts each, with or without context, and will be required to answer a few questions regarding them. Both studies will have a second part that will test the participants’ memorability of the charts using mixed methods of interviews and questionnaires. Using the responses of the participants for both parts of both the studies, we will conduct our analysis to probe into the effects of visual embellishments on interpretability, preference of charts, and recall ability. Finally, a comparison of the two studies (with and without context) will provide us with insights on the effect of context on the three mentioned factors.

title_r: List-Strength Effect in Recognition Memory: Display Time
abstract_r: Ratcliff et al. (1990), Experiment 1, our replication and an extension, found an inverted list-strength effect: a bigger effect of stimulus-duration in pure lists than in mixed lists. Our current theoretical explanation (our hypothesis) of the inversion depends critically on the assumption that participants encode, but then disregard shallow stimulus features following pure-long lists only. This experiment tests whether the effect depends on the display time of the stimulus or the amount of study time. One group is a replication group, where stimuli are displayed for the entire duration, 500 ms or 2000 ms, varying both study time and display time. The second group will display all stimuli for 500 ms and for the long duration, the remaining 1500 ms will display a blank screen. This equates display time while varying study time. title_r: The effect of darkness on cheating in a non-visual task
abstract_r: A previous study showed that darkness could increase cheating by creating a sense of “illusory anonymity” that let individuals expect that they would be difficult to be perceived by others (Zhong et al., 2010). We have successfully replicated the phenomena reported by Zhong et al. (2010) in an early study (https://osf.io/nkjq5). However, our findings about the participants’ perceived anonymity did not support their explanation. According to our results, we propose another hypothesis here. The outcome of the task in the dark environment could present a kind of “ambiguity”. It means that it is difficult for participants (and also experimenters) to visually confirm the results because the illumination conditions are too dark. In this situation, do participants tend to believe that the outcome is in their favor and then report it without a closer check of the true outcome? Therefore, we try to use this experiment to test a new hypothesis on the mechanism of darkness increasing cheating.

title_r: Social learning in a spatially correlated multi- armed bandit
abstract_r: There has been considerable research effort into understanding how social information is used by humans, including computational models of this integration process, such as Decision Biasing or Value Shaping. However, previous studies have generally investigated social information use when the observer and demonstrator were doing the exact same task with the exact same goal. Yet, learning from others who may have different goals or preferences is common in everyday life. Using the socially correlated bandit, we have previously found that our Social Generalization model most accurately predicts human behaviour when rewards are correlated, but not identical (Witt et al., 2023). Here, we aim to replicate this finding, and additionally investigate how social learning affects exploration behaviour compared to individual learning settings.

title_r: Psychometric Reliability of ERN and Pe Across Flanker, Stroop, and Go/No-Go Tasks: A Direct and Conceptual Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The purpose of this study is to replicate and extend work on the psychometric reliability of cognitive control event-related potentials (ERPs) as a function of increasing trials across three different tasks (Meyer et al., 2013, Psychophysiology). Our primary aim is a direct replication of Meyer et al. (2013) to determine the number of trials needed for adequate psychometric internal consistency (.70) of the error-related negativity (ERN) recorded during flanker, Stroop, and Go/no-go tasks using classical test theory estimates (i.e., coefficient alpha). Our second aim is to extend these findings by conducting a conceptual replication examining generalizability theory estimates of internal consistency (i.e., dependability) of ERN, correct-response negativity (CRN), post-error positivity (Pe), post-correct positivity (Pc), and their difference scores (ERN, Pe; error minus correct) as a function of the number of trials across the three tasks. We will use post-estimation contrasts to identify task differences in dependability and ICC estimates as function of the number of trials recoded.

title_r: Understanding the visual constraints on lexical processing: New empirical and simulation results (Experiment 2)
abstract_r: It is well known that visual acuity is not uniform across the visual field. Acuity instead decreases precipitously from the center of vision. The region of maximum acuity, called the fovea, is comprised of the central 2º of the visual field, with a region of rapidly decreasing acuity called the parafovea extending an additional 5º of visual angle to either side of this. Although the photoreceptors required for perceiving fine detail are largely limited to these two regions of the visual field, it remains unclear precisely how the rapid drop off in visual acuity that results from the distribution of these photoreceptors affects our capacity to rapidly and accurately identify printed words. This project aims to investigate the physical constraints imposed by our visual system on reading by conducting a conceptual replication of a highly cited study by Rayner and Morrison (1981). The original study compared lexical-decision and naming performance at central fixation (0 degrees), or between 1 and 5 degrees to the left or right of central fixation. Participants were either instructed to maintain central fixation (no eye-movement condition) or move their eyes to the location of the stimulus (eye-movement condition). The proposed study improves on several features of the original study by (i) testing a much larger sample of participants; (ii) using a larger number of more highly controlled items that are not repeated during the experiment and that vary in both word length and frequency; (iii) ensuring participants maintain central fixation by tracking eye movements and terminating trials on which the participant moves their eyes. A previous experiment in this project measured word identification in both the left and right visual fields. This experiment tests a wider range of eccentricities (0-5 degrees) in the right visual field—the direction of reading in English.

title_r: Extreme weather, climate change, climate action and uncertainty distress: A replication study using network analysis.
abstract_r: Both extreme weather and climate change have been linked to distress and at times mental health problems. Pro-environmental actions have often been related to higher distress. The uncertainty distress model (Freeston et al., 2020) proposes that in real-world situations, perceptions of threat and uncertainty contribute to distress. Freeston, Sermin-Read, et al. (2023) recruited a community sample (N = 327) who completed an online survey. Network analysis was used to analyse the relationships between the variables. Exposure to extreme weather, perceptions of climate change, climate change distress and pro-environmental action were measured along with symptoms of adjustment disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, and uncertainty intolerance and behaviours. They reported there was variable exposure to extreme weather, but greater exposure was associated with more severe post-traumatic symptoms. Pro-environmental action was associated with greater severity of adjustment disorder symptoms. The perception that climate change was happening now was linked positively to pro-environmental action and negatively to perceptions of uncertainty about whether climate change was happening. The results replicated several findings from the emerging climate change distress literature and are consistent with some predictions of the uncertainty distress model, but not others. Aim: The main aim of the current study is to conduct a replication using network analysis with 1) improved measurement in some areas (see above and in measures section), 2) a larger and more diverse sample (see recruitment methods). The network analysis will follow the previous analysis as much as possible to facilitate comparison. Methods: The study will essentially replicate the previous study with the following modifications: inclusion of heatwaves; expand the type, timescale and impact of warnings; differentiated assessment of disruption; fuller range of emotional responses; shortened/improved versions of other measures. A larger sample will be sought, recruited to increase not only the diversity and representativeness of the sample, but also the geographical distribution and so the range of experiences of extreme weather. Results: Descriptive analyses of the participants, the experiences of extreme weather, and network analysis will be reported, based on the previous study.

title_r: AMENDED PREREG. Moment-to-moment changes in “feeling moved” and how it relates to alexithymia and affect consciousness
abstract_r: NOTE: This is an amended version of the prereg. submitted for this OSF-project on September 24, 2020. The data collection for this study is taking place in three rounds. After the first round of data collection, we obtained unrealistically high intra-individual correlations between certain variables (i.e. cross-correlations between time series) that are implausibly (or even impossibly) high and indicate that participants did not engage in the task in the way that we tried to instruct them to and/or had technical difficulties. As a remedy for this issue, we decided to submit this amended prereg. where we have changed the exclusion criteria to exclude the most extreme outliers. The changes from the original prereg are all found within the sections "exclusion criteria" and "existing data". According to the kama muta theory, emotional reactions that people often describe as “feeling moved” are typically instances of a distinct emotion that, within the theory, is called kama muta. The theory states that kama muta is elicited by the appraisal of a sudden intensification of a communal sharing relationship, positively valenced, and involves physiological sensations including goosebumps and a sense of warmth in the chest. Schubert et al. (2016) tested these statements by measuring participants’ moment-by-moment self-reported reactions to videos that are typically described as “very moving”. The current study is a conceptual replication and extension of Schubert et al. (2016). To address limitations of the between subject-measurements in the original study, we will measure correlations between time series of various reactions and experiences within subjects. We will also test kama muta theory against the theory that “feeling moved” when perceiving acts of outstanding morality is a distinct emotion labelled “elevation” (Haidt, 2003) and the view that “feeling moved” involves an interplay of positive and negative emotions (Menninghaus et al., 2015, 2017). Finally we will test whether measures of one’s ability to grasp one’s own emotions can explain why people differ in the degree to which they report feeling moved when exposed to stimuli considered to be “very moving”.
