title_r: How does temporal framing of climate change influence the acceptance of mitigation policies?
abstract_r: Previous Research has shown, that people's environmental attitudes are influenced by differences in temporal focus of environmental comparison messaging and that temporal focus is moderating the relation between political affiliation and environmental attitudes. Especially, in a study by Baldwin & Lammers (2016) conservatives tended to be more positively affected by past- compared to future-focused environmental comparisons. A replication study by Kim et al. (2021) could not replicate the substantial positive impact of past-focussed environmental comparisons for conservatives, but could found future-focused environmental messages to be relatively more agreeable to liberals. In another replication study by Stanley et al. (2021) a moderation of temporal focus was found for a US sample but not for a UK sample. In sum, previous research has to our knowledge so far been carried out mostly in the US and only in english speaking countries. Thus, in our study we will study potential effects of temporal framing on a German sample, focussing on the support for high impact climate change mitigation policy measures as a dependent variable. We will do so in a an online study with an experimental between subject design. References: Baldwin, M., & Lammers, J. (2016). title_r: How self-talk influence social stress: the role of self-distance
abstract_r: This study is a conceptual replication of Study 2 from "How self-talk influences social stress: the role of self-distance." The research aims to examine how the use of first-person versus non-first-person language during self-reflection affects emotional regulation under social stress. The study adopts a single-factor, repeated-measures design. Participants (college students with no history of mental illness, balanced gender ratio) will complete a social stress task (Trier Social Stress Task, TSST) under two conditions: First-person condition: Participants reflect on their emotions using first-person pronouns (e.g., "I"). Non-first-person condition: Participants reflect using non-first-person pronouns (e.g., "he/she" or their own name). Participants' anxiety levels will be measured at three stages using the Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS): baseline (T1), post-manipulation (T2), and post-task (T3). Behavioral performance during a public speaking task will be evaluated by independent raters. The hypothesis predicts that participants in the non-first-person condition will experience lower anxiety and perform better in the social stress task compared to those in the first-person condition. This study extends the original research by expanding the participant pool to include both male and female students, and adapting the stress task to a public speaking scenario, enhancing ecological validity. Additionally, written reflections will be used to manipulate self-distance, allowing for more precise analysis through linguistic patterns. The findings aim to validate the cross-cultural applicability of self-distance strategies, offering insights into the effects of self-talk on emotional regulation in diverse cultural and gender contexts.

title_r: Study 1: Depressive symptoms and autobiographical specificity early in the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract_r: Overgeneral autobiographical thinking - including lower specificity of past and future events - is commonly observed in a range of psychopathologies, including depressive disorders (Dalgleish et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2007; Addis et al., 2016), both during episodes and in remission (e.g., Watkins & Teasdale, 2001), as well as subclinically (e.g., dysphoria; MacLeod & Cropley, 1995). The psychological consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic, such as increased threat, isolation, and uncertainty, all have the potential to influence both mood and future thinking, which prompted us to include measures of depressive symptoms and autobiographical specificity in our larger online project - Thinking Beyond COVID-19 (osf.io/zfs98). Although data collection in this 2-year longitudinal project is still ongoing (to be completed in May 2022), in this “sub-study” we plan to analyze data from the first two surveys (S0 and S1) collected early in the pandemic (May 2020). Although we have some knowledge of existing data via data cleaning and processing, as well as other analyses (as described in detail in this pre-registration), this plan is being pre-registered prior to linking depression data with autobiographical specificity data, and thus before any study-specific statistical analyses are conducted. The first objective of this sub-study is to investigate whether severity of current depressive symptoms, and/or a history of depression, is associated with reduced autobiographical specificity as measured using two tasks (Sentence Completion Task, Event Description Task) and two specificity scoring protocols (Autobiographical Thought Specificity and Autobiographical Interview scoring). We also examine whether the effect of depression on specificity is stronger for future relative to past autobiographical thinking, and whether effects at the detail level can be decoupled from effects at the event level. The second objective is to the valence, content and phenomenology of autobiographical responses in depression. To this end, we examine word counts (e.g., related to valence and specific content) using Linguistic Inquiry Word Count, as well as subjective ratings. Finally, because autobiographical responses are collected online, this study also provides an opportunity for conceptual replication of effects reported in previous in-person studies.

title_r: Contralateral delay activity as a marker of visual working memory capacity: a multi-site registered replication
abstract_r: Visual working memory (VWM) is a temporary storage system capable of retaining information that can be accessed and manipulated by higher cognitive processes, thereby facilitating a wide range of cognitive functions. Electroencephalography (EEG) is used to understand the neural correlates of VWM with high temporal precision, and one commonly used EEG measure is an event-related potential called the contralateral delay activity (CDA). In a landmark study by Vogel and Machizawa (2004), the authors found that the CDA amplitude increases with the number of items stored in VWM and plateaus around three to four items, which is thought to represent the typical adult working memory capacity. Critically, this study also showed that the increase in CDA amplitude between two-item and four-item arrays correlated with individual subjects’ VWM performance. Although these results have been supported by subsequent studies, a recent study suggested that the number of subjects used in experiments investigating the CDA may not be sufficient to detect differences in set size and to provide a reliable account of the relationship between behaviorally measured VWM capacity and the CDA amplitude. To address this, the current study, as part of the #EEGManyLabs project, aims to conduct a multi-site replication of Vogel and Machizawa's (2004) seminal study on a large sample of participants, with a pre-registered analysis plan. Through this, our goal is to contribute to deepening our understanding of the neural correlates of visual working memory.

title_r: Associations between Temporal Discounting and Clinically Relevant Personality Traits
abstract_r: Within intertemporal choice tasks, people tend to devalue a future reward relative to a sooner reward as a function of delay until receipt, a phenomenon known as temporal discounting (Frederick et al., 2002). Previous large-scale studies have shown that the tendency to discount future rewards more strongly is related to personality variables in the general population such as impulsivity or extraversion (see Keidel et al., 2021, for a review). Also, higher rates of temporal discounting have been found in different clinical populations (e.g., in ADHD, eating disorders, etc.), suggesting that temporal discounting might be an important transdiagnostic marker of mental disorders (Amlung et al., 2019). Given the continuum assumption of psychopathology which postulates that mental disorders are at the extreme of dimensions of clinically relevant traits (Krueger et al., 2018; Krueger & Markon, 2006), it can be assumed that there is also a link between these traits and temporal discounting in the general population. Therefore, the primary aim of this project is to examine whether individual differences in personality traits that take an extreme form in clinical samples can also account for individual differences in temporal discounting in the general population. Additionally, we aim to replicate the date/delay effect in intertemporal choice (LeBoeuf, 2006; Read et al., 2005). title_r: Associations between Temporal Discounting and Clinically Relevant Personality Traits
abstract_r: Within intertemporal choice tasks, people tend to devalue a future reward relative to a sooner reward as a function of delay until receipt, a phenomenon known as temporal discounting (Frederick et al., 2002). Previous large-scale studies have shown that the tendency to discount future rewards more strongly is related to personality variables in the general population such as impulsivity or extraversion (see Keidel et al., 2021, for a review). Also, higher rates of temporal discounting have been found in different clinical populations (e.g., in ADHD, eating disorders, etc.), suggesting that temporal discounting might be an important transdiagnostic marker of mental disorders (Amlung et al., 2019). Given the continuum assumption of psychopathology which postulates that mental disorders are at the extreme of dimensions of clinically relevant traits (Krueger et al., 2018; Krueger & Markon, 2006), it can be assumed that there is also a link between these traits and temporal discounting in the general population. Therefore, the primary aim of this project is to examine whether individual differences in personality traits that take an extreme form in clinical samples can also account for individual differences in temporal discounting in the general population. Additionally, we aim to replicate the date/delay effect in intertemporal choice (LeBoeuf, 2006; Read et al., 2005). The date/delay effect is a framing effect revealing that the tendency to discount future rewards is less pronounced when time until reception of rewards is framed as dates compared to delays (e.g., days). As a previous study has shown that the date framing reduces temporal discounting in a clinical group particularly strongly (i.e., substance abusers; Klapproth, 2012), we wish to examine whether the date framing reduces temporal discounting specifically in people with higher scores in clinically relevant traits. Accordingly, in this project, we aim to investigate three main questions: 1. To what extent are different clinically relevant traits in the general population associated with temporal discounting? 2. Does the date/delay effect replicate? 3. Is the magnitude of the date/delay effect in intertemporal choice associated with clinically relevant traits? In other words: Does a date framing (as compared to delay framing) reduce temporal discounting more strongly in participants who show higher scores on specific clinically relevant traits?

title_r: Blind Implantation Put to the Test - Replication of "A New Method to Implant False Autobiographical Memories"
abstract_r: In 2022 Otgaar et al. developed a paradigm, which is used to implant false autobiographical memories of childhood events using an online study. In previous studies concerning false memories, extensive interviews were used to the same effect. Thus, this new method, called “blind implantation”, is not only much more cost efficient than the previous ones but, according to the authors, shows the same success rate as well. The online study was conducted on two occasions. In the first survey the participants were asked to indicate if and how often they had experienced various events during their childhood. During the second survey, they were shown only 5 events and were told that they previously indicated having experienced all of them, even though they hadn’t. One of the events, the critical event, had not been experienced by the participants, according to their own answers. One group of participants was told they had experienced the critical event once while the other group was told they had indicated having experienced the event multiple times. Participants were then asked to rate (1) the strength of their belief in the event happening to them and (2) the strength of their specific recollection of the event on one item each. Otgaar et al (2022) differentiate these two components of memories as one can belief something happened, without having concrete memories of the event, like for example in the event of being born. Each variable was measured on an 8-point Likert-Scale with scores higher than 5 indicating the presence of a false belief and/or memory, according to the authors. Participants were then asked to complete an imagination task. They were told the task would help them recover any memories. After completion they were asked to rate (1) the strength of their belief and (2) the strength of their recollections again. Finally, they were asked to provide any further information in an open text box if they could. The paradigm was tested on 99 participants from Belgium and Romania and the authors showed that dependant on the group they were assigned to between 9% and 30% of participants indicated either (1) a false strong belief about a specific event, (2) a false strong memory about the specific event, or (3) both. The present study does not aim to be a direct replication, but rather to test the proposed paradigm and to assess if it is indeed possible to produce false memories and false beliefs with this method. To achieve this the following changes to the original study were made: 1. The present study will be conducted solely in German and use a bigger sample than the original study. We aim for 300 participants in accordance with the a-priori Power Analysis reported under point 13 and 14 on page 10f.. 2. There will only be one experimental group instead of two. This experimental group will assess the “single event” option. The other group will be a control group that will not receive the suggestion of having indicated that they experienced the critical event. 3. The present study will also use more than one critical event. It is important that these events are comparable concerning their plausibility, their emotional valence, and their emotional intensity. This increases generalizability and aims to limit the number of participants that must be excluded, which was a big problem in the original study. A preliminary study will assess the plausibility, emotional valence, and emotional intensity of different events so that three comparable critical events can be chosen for the main study. With these changes we would like to attain enough information to answer the question: Does blind implantation, as proposed by Otgaar et al. (2022), really work?

title_r: Facilitating Effects of Linguistic Labels in Concept Formation
abstract_r: In this study we aim for a conceptual replication of the second experiment by Lupyan et al. (2007) with changes concerning the stimulus set and the experimental procedure. In this regard, we want to investigate whether the categorization performance is influenced by written linguistic terms, so called labels, even if those are entirely redundant, thus possessing no semantic meaning. Furthermore, we aim to investigate the influence of nonverbal labels on category formation. For this reason, participants will be divided into three subgroups (verbal label group, nonverbal label group, no-label group). All groups will be tasked with correctly assigning fish images to the two underlying categories throughout the entire experiment. title_r: Do human infants understand simple arithmetic?: A (virtual) replication
abstract_r: The violation-of-expectation task provides a conceptual replication of Wynn’s (1992) infant arithmetic experiments. In the original study, 5-month-old infants were shown an event where a toy on stage was covered by a small screen, then a second toy was brought in from the side of the stage and placed behind the screen (essentially 1 + 1). During the expected outcome trials, the screen was lowered to reveal two objects and looking time to this outcome was measured. During the unexpected outcome trials, the screen was lowered to reveal a single object. The results showed infants look significantly longer at the unexpected compared to the expected outcome. A separate group of infants saw a subtraction event (2 - 1 = either 1 or 2) and again infants looked significantly longer at the unexpected outcome. We chose this study because it is one of the most cited and replicated studies for infant object knowledge (Baillargeon, 1994; Bremner, et al., 2017; Chiang & Wynn, 2000; Cohen & Marks, 2002; Huntley-Fenner, Carey, & Salimando, 2002; Koechlin, 1997; Simon, Hespos & Rochat, 1995; Uller, Carey, Huntley-Fenner, & Klatt, 1999; Wakeley, Rivera, & Langer, 2000; Wynn & Chiang, 1998). The successful replications have used 3-dimensional live displays and 2-dimensional screen displays. In addition, there is converging evidence from a variety of dependent measures including looking time, eye tracking, and ERP. We hypothesize that the phenomenon should replicate in a virtual setting using a platform like Zoom and early data support this prediction. However, if online administration does affect infants’ ability to detect the violation, this study will help delineate the factors that influence performance.

title_r: Children's Understanding of Others' Perspectives
abstract_r: Previous research indicates that young children often struggle to understand how others’ visual experiences can be different from their own. In a classic study, Masangkay et al. (1974) found that in a verbal task, children can identify whether others can see an object earlier in development than they can identify others’ visual experiences of objects (e.g., as upright vs. upside-down). Recent research has found complementary evidence in toddlers: that 14- to 15-month-old infants can reason about an agent’s actions on an object in terms of the agent’s visual access to the object but not the agent’s visual experience of the object (e.g., as upright vs. upside-down; Woo et al., 2024). Does young children’s difficulty to understand others’ visual experiences reflect a genuine limit to early mental state reasoning? Here, we identify a limitation of past research: that it has largely taken place in minimally social contexts, involving a single agent whose mind participants may not be motivated to represent. Perspective-taking may be more important when children are engaged in social interaction with someone (e.g., trying to show someone else a picture). Perspective-taking is a key aspect of teaching. In the present experiment, we put 3- to 4-year-old children in the role of the teacher, and we asked them to show a picture or a book to another person (either an experimenter or the child’s own caregiver) who faced them. Would children consider the visual experience of their social partner, or would they prioritize their own perspective? In addition to this task, we sought to replicate past findings by Masangkay et al. (1974) that children struggle to answer questions about others’ visual experiences that differ from their own.

title_r: Masterthesis in vivo BrainVol - IQ
abstract_r: The association of brain size and intelligence has been subject to research for a long time (e.g. Rushton & Ankney, 2007). Recent meta-analyses (McDaniel, 2005; Pietschnig et al., 2015; Gignac & Bates, 2017) estimated small to moderate (Pearson) correlations between in vivo brain volume and intelligence. The estimates differ substantial in size. Depending on the used inclusion criteria and meta-analytical methods, the estimates range from r = .24 (Pietschnig et al., 2015) up to r = .39 (Gignac & Bates, 2017). The investigations of possible moderators have also yielded different results. Whereas McDaniel (2005) identified sex and age to be significant moderators, Pietschnig et al. (2015) concluded the opposite. Some moderators have been examined only by one research team and, considering the differences above, need conceptual replication. Ethnicity as a possible moderator has been discussed thoroughly in the literature (e.g. Rushton & Ankney, 2007), but never has been included in a meta-analysis due to lack of data (McDaniel, 2005). Analyses regarding the presence of dissemination bias reached different conclusions as well. Considering these inconsistencies and open questions, this planned study seeks to achieve several goals: (1) Give an additional reasonable estimate of the association of in vivo brain volume and intelligence based on updated data and alternative analysis procedures. (2) Investigate the impact of researcher´s data and analysis decisions (or broadly termed researcher´s degrees of freedom) on the summary effect estimates. (3) Replicate moderator analyses conclusions that were reached unanimously or only have been conducted once (non-clinical vs. patients, correlation of applied intelligence measurement with g). (4) Investigate contradictory conclusions about certain moderators (age, sex). (5) Investigate a potential moderator never analyzed in a meta-analysis on the subject before (ethnicity). (6) Provide information about the extent of bias in the updated data and investigate, why Pietschnig el al. (2015) and Gignac and Bates (2017) reached different conclusions. This will include a replication of a decline effect (Schooler, 2011; Pietschnig et al. 2019) found by Pietschnig et al. (2015). (7) Discuss conclusions about a reasonable effect size estimate range of in vivo brain volume and intelligence. Discuss utility, usability and cost-effectiveness of used methods. In order to achieve these goals, the largest meta-analysis on the subject (Pietschnig et al., 2015) will be updated, expanded, and conducted with additional specification choices. Several sensitivity analyses will be conducted in reference to data and analyses decisions made by the previous meta-analysts. Subsequently all these possible specifications will be included in multiverse, specification curve, and combinatorial analyses (Voracek et al., 2019), to examine inconsistencies regarding the synthesized general effects. Moderators will be investigated with subgroup analyses and meta-regression approaches. A Bayesian meta-analysis will conclude this planned study, exploring the use of non-frequentist methods for the investigation of the association of in vivo brain volume and intelligence.

title_r: Hotel towels re-explored: why descriptive and reciprocity norms are (not) influential
abstract_r: We are conducting an extended conceptual replication of Goldstein et al. (2007; 2008). Goldstein et al., 2008 is an influential study, cited 3568 times (Google scholar: 22/10/19), showing that appealing to social norms is more influential than appealing to the environment when aiming to persuade hotel guests to reuse their towels (i.e., act more sustainable during their visit). Results have been replicated, showing both consistent (e.g., Mair & Bergin-Seers, 2010; Reese et al., 2014; Schultz et al., 2008) and conflicting results (Bohner & Schlüter, 2014). In synthesizing these findings, a Bayesian meta-analysis confirmed that social norms are indeed more effective overall than environmental appeals (Scheibehenne et al., 2016).

Here, we attempt a conceptual replication of these findings in an online experiment. title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Bateson (2012), from American Political Science Review
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Bateson (2012) is that individuals who report recent crime victimization will be more politically active and engaged than their peers. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Analysis of survey data from five continents shows that individuals who report recent crime victimization participate in politics more than comparable nonvictims." The claim is tested with data from four regional barometer surveys using nine separate dependent variables. The author finds supportive evidence in every combination of survey and dependent variable; for the SCORE program, the community action dependent variable (frequency of solving problems in community or neighborhood) using the LAPOP/AmericasBarometer 2010 data is used. The dependent variable is regressed on reported crime victimization (coded 1 if the respondent said he or she was the victim of any crime in the past 12 months, and coded as 0 if the respondent said that he or she did not experience any crimes in the past 12 months), along with respondent’s sex, age in years, age squared, socioeconomic status, education, and urbanization. The model includes country fixed effects, with robust standard errors clustered by municipality. The coefficient on victimization is positive and statistically significant (coefficient = 0.0334, robust SE = 0.00317, p < 0.001) [Table 4, first column, top row].

title_r: Gender stereotypes about intellectual ability in Japanese children
abstract_r: There are common stereotypes associated with high-level intellectual ability, where men are more intelligent and smarter than women. A previous study reported that gender stereotypes about intellectual ability emerges during early childhood (Bian, Leslie, and Cimpian, 2017). Specifically, US-American 6-year-old girls, but not 5-year-old girls, were less likely than boys to indicate that their own gender were smart when presented with photo stimulus (e.g., female pictures). Rather, they attributed “nice” to their own gender. However, it is still unknown whether such stereotypes develop through similar routes in other populations. The present study examines development of gender stereotypes in Japanese society, in which gender gaps in adults regarding various activities has been shown with the highest degree among wealthy countries. Arecent report (2019) of the World Economic Forum has shown the large gender gaps in Japanese society (ranked 121st out of the 153 countries; US-America was placed 53rd) regarding the general gender-balance of four categories of economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. The large gender gaps in Japanese society has also been shown in intellectual activities, such as science engagement. Holman et al (2018) analyzed the PubMed and arXiv databases and estimated the gender of 36 million authors from >100 countries publishing in >6000 journals, covering most disciplines of Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics, and Medicine from 2002. The study found that the gender gaps appear likely to persist for generations, and varied greatly across countries, with Japan having the lowest percentage (20.4%) of women authors (estimation of 2016). The present study examines whether stereotypes associated with high-level intellectual ability are observed in Japan. Specifically, in Study 1, children will be presented with a female/male photo or a girls/boys photo stimuli, and asked to indicate which persons are smart/nice. Moreover, the second aim of Study 1 is to examine how children begin to have such stereotypes. There are huge individual differences in Japanese parental beliefs about sex roles (e.g., Sakaguchi & Hashimoto, 2009). Given that, we examine whether parental beliefs about sex roles can be related to their children’s gender stereotypes associated with high-level intellectual ability. In Study 1, rich perceptual cues (faces and clothings) may induce children’s gender stereotypes. Thus, in Study 2, we aim to replicate the finding in Study 1 and assess whether simpler stimuli with poor perceptual cues can induce the stereotypes using stick figures instead of photo stimulus.

title_r: Replication of The Bipolarity of Affect and Depressive Symptoms with Extensions to Fear of Positive Evaluation
abstract_r: Aim: We aim to replicate and extend Dejonckheere et al. (2018) who investigated how depressive symptoms are associated with the within-person correlation between positive affect (PA) and negative affect (NA). For some individuals, PA and NA can co-exist at the same time as part of a rich and nuanced emotional state. For others, PA and NA exhibit bipolarity, such that one is much less common when the other is present (tending to be mutually exclusive). The original study by Dejonckheere et al. (2018) found that higher depression was associated with higher bipolarity. In the current study, we introduce two key extensions: - Theoretical Extension: Depressed persons high in Fear of Positive Evaluation (FPE) tend to suppress or dampen PA and experience NA even in response to positive situations, suggesting greater affective co-activation or emotional blending. Hence, we explore whether FPE— a construct related to depression and affective regulation — is associated with lower affective bipolarity. - Statistical Extension: We will test two multiple regression models with a three-way interaction term in each model. Our predictors will include (1) mean PA, (2) mean NA, (3) correlation of PA and NA, (4) mean PA x mean NA, (5) mean PA x correlation of PA and NA, (6) mean NA x correlation of PA and NA, and (7) mean PA x mean NA x correlation of PA and NA, to account for ambivalence which would be for those with high PA and high NA presentations.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Bezu et al. (2012) in World Development.
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Bezu et al. (2012) is as follows: The regression results show that growth in consumption expenditures increases with the household’s ex ante share of nonfarm income. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "We find that: (1) households’ consumption expenditure growth is positively correlated with the initial share of nonfarm income..." The authors regress the change in the logarithm of expenditure per adult equivalent on initial share of nonfarm income and a range of control variables. To allow for the potentially nonlinear relation the authors include a third order polynomial in the nonfarm share. The authors report and discuss here only the random effects estimation results. Results are in Table 6. The term selected is the linear term of ‘Share of income from RNFE [rural nonfarm employment] in total expenditure’ (see Table 6 for details). As shown in Table 6, there is a positive correlation between the share of income from RNFE and expenditure growth. The coefficients on the linear (‘Share of income from RNFE in total expenditure’: Coefficient = 0.591; Robust std. err = 0.128; significant at the 1% level) and squared terms are positive and significant and the coefficient on cubic term negative and also significant, yielding a highly nonlinear relationship.

title_r: HSE - A replication of an experiment "On the Interaction of Theory and Data in Concept Learning"
abstract_r: Project Description: This project aims to replicate the seminal experiment from Murphy and Allopenna's (1994) study "On the Interaction of Theory and Data in Concept Learning," which investigates how theoretical knowledge influences the learning and categorization of concepts. The original study demonstrated that people do not merely rely on observable data to form categories but also use prior theoretical knowledge to guide their learning, interpretation, and generalization of concepts. In this replication, the objective is to validate the original findings by examining the interplay between theory-driven expectations and data-driven evidence during the process of concept acquisition. Participants will be presented with a series of learning tasks where they are required to categorize stimuli based on given rules or theories and the observable features of the stimuli. The experiment will manipulate the alignment or conflict between theoretical information and presented data to observe how participants integrate these sources of information when forming concepts. The replication will utilize a similar experimental design, employing PsychoPy and Pavlovia for data collection. This approach ensures methodological rigor while allowing for efficient, web-based participant recruitment and testing. By successfully replicating this study, the project will enhance the understanding of how humans learn and apply concepts, particularly in situations where theoretical expectations and empirical data interact.

title_r: Is olfactory loss a sensitive symptomatic predictor of COVID-19? A preregistered, crowdsourced study
abstract_r: Chemosensory loss has taken on a new meaning for people worldwide as loss of smell (and taste, as well as chemesthesis) has become a prominent symptom of COVID-19, now recognized by health authorities including the CDC. As part of an international effort to better understand this chemosensory connection to COVID-19, the GCCR questionnaire is currently implemented in 32 languages and targets people who have or recently have had an upper respiratory infection (e.g., common cold, influenza, suspected or confirmed COVID-19). The initial analyses of a subset of these data (up to April 18th) confirm substantial loss of smell, taste and moderate chemesthesis loss (e.g., the burn of chili peppers, the cooling of menthol, tingle of carbonation) in individuals with COVID-19; notably, this loss was independent of nasal obstruction. The results (Parma et al., 2020) showed largely overlapping patterns of chemosensory impairment in people with COVID-19 confirmed by laboratory tests versus those diagnosed by symptoms alone (e.g., a clinical assessment by a medical professional). After exploration of the second data tranche of the GCCR dataset up to May 14th (henceforth, May dataset), as detailed in our previous preregistration (https://osf.io/ek8jq/), we discovered that after standard cleaning procedures, we had failed to reach the minimal number of participants (N =480) per group that we had declared previously. We therefore waited additional time to reach and surpass the N = 480 threshold, while we explored the available database. With this new pre-registration, we are reporting our planned analyses of the dataset that will be downloaded on July 3rd (henceforth, July dataset) and that is hence not yet available. This new preregistration aligns with our previous one (https://osf.io/ek8jq/), therefore preserving the main goals of the study. Here, we also refine our hypotheses based on the knowledge gained during initial exploration of the May 14th dataset. Below are the major edits that we have introduced and that we intend to apply to the July dataset: Criteria to determine the C19+ and C19- groups (section 17): based on current analyses, we replicate the previously published drop in smell and taste ratings during vs. before the illness in COVID-19 (Parma et al., 2020). However, we observed small but significant differences in chemosensory ratings between the clinically assessed and the lab tested COVID-19 group. In this new preregistration, we therefore follow a more conservative approach and propose to limit analysis to the comparison of participants who reported to have received a lab test for the C19+ vs. C19- analysis. Characterization of multiple diagnostic groups based on smell ratings, as smell change is the assumed most predictive symptom differentiating COVID-19 from other respiratory illnesses: COVID-19 clinical assessment, COVID-19 positive (C19+) lab tested, COVID-19 negative (C19-) lab tested, Unknown (not diagnosed/tested, yet with symptoms). Inclusion of a new goal: exploration and prediction of post C19+ smell loss recovery. In summary, these are goals being pre-registered for investigation in the July dataset . We will determine if we can replicate the previously published results on smell, taste, chemesthesis and nasal obstruction change during COVID-19 versus before COVID-19 (Parma et al., 2020) in participants reporting clinically assessed and lab tested COVID-19 based on data collected since the first data snapshot GCCR001 collected in April 2020. We will compare chemosensory and nasal obstruction changes of the C19+ with participants reporting to have received a negative COVID-19 lab test (C19-). We will determine if a pattern of chemosensory changes, other symptoms, and/or demographics can be identified that discriminate C19+ vs. C19- We will determine if a pattern of chemosensory changes, other symptoms, and/or demographics can be identified that discriminate those with C19+ who recover from smell loss vs. those who do not within the timeframe of the survey completion.

title_r: Can Imagined Contact Really Be Delivered Through the Web? Preregistered Tests of Web-Delivered Imagined Contact
abstract_r: The purpose of this research is to test whether the positive effects of imagined contact remain when the contact scenario is delivered through the web. Previous research has determined that direct intergroup contact (real-life contact) significantly reduces prejudice towards a variety of outgroups (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006). A meta-analysis by Pettigrew and Tropp (2006) presents empirical evidence suggesting that direct intergroup contact, when structured according to pre-established conditions set forth by Allport (1954), can significantly reduce prejudice for a vast array of groups. The positive effects of imagined contact scenarios have been documented by Husnu and Crisp (2010). However, the imagined contact study conducted by Husnu and Crisp was done in a controlled laboratory setting (2010). The present study will test the effect of web-delivered imagined contact. In order to do this, the current research will compare the effectiveness of 4 different imagined contact scenarios. The first scenario will be a non-elaborated control and will be an exact replication of the scenario used in experiment 4 of West et al., 2011. The second scenario will be a non-elaborated treatment and is also an exact replication of the experimental condition scenario used in study 4 of West et al., 2011. The third scenario will be an elaborated control adapted from experiment 4 of West et al. (2011) and modified with information from Hodson et al. (2015). The last scenario will be an elaborated treatment adapted from experiment 4 of West et al. (2011) and modified with information from Hodson et al. (2015). The elaborated conditions have been added in order to test whether the extent of elaboration in a web-delivered setting amplifies the effects of imagined contact. As in the West et al. (2011) study, the current research will examine the effects of imagined contact on schizophrenic individuals using attitudes and intergroup anxiety measures. A previous study conducted by Dr. Nicol and OCdt Bordeleau showed that elaborated imagined contact delivered through the web did not reduce intergroup anxiety towards American-Muslims. The present study will limit the comparability problem associated with the previous study by replicating quasi-exactly study 4 of West et al. (2011). By doing so, the results of the current study will be more easily compared to the results obtained by West et al. (2011). The present study will be able to highlight whether or not the method of delivery (web) leads to significant improvement in attitudes and/or a reduction in intergroup anxiety.

title_r: A Pre-registered Falsification Test of the Decision by Sampling Model and Rank-order Effect
abstract_r: Many social scienctists have assumed that people’s preferences can be described by stable and coherent “utility” functions. This notion of stable utility functions has been challenged by cognitive psychologists who suggest that preferences are malleable and constructed in the moment, but neither camp has explained how the perceived utilities themselves arise. One influential attempt to do so is the Decision by Sampling (DbS) model which suggests that a quantity’s subjective value is its rank-order in a momentarily activated memory sample. DbS thus implies that manipulating the recently experienced stimulus distribution should change people’s valuations, for example from the typically assumed concave shape of the utility function to a convex shape. However, recent studies have pointed out methodological errors in the evidence previously thought to support this prediction (and thus DbS). In this pre-registered study, we replicate the previous paradigm but correct the methodological errors to test if such a “rank-order” manipulation does change valuations. We derive qualitative predictions from DbS to verify that our conditions yield distinct predictions. Confirming the predicted effect would vindicate DbS and suggests that the phenomenon is not an artefact of methodological limitations of the previous studies.

title_r: Examining the mechanisms underlying action slips: A competition between goal-directed processes
abstract_r: In this study we aim to investigate the mechanism underlying action slips, sometimes also referred to as habitual errors. Hardwick et al. (2019) showed that action slips occur if an overtrained response-outcome contingency is reversed and people are asked to respond under time pressure. The authors explain this effect with a stimulus-driven process, claiming that people do not process any contingency information under time pressure. In the current study, we seek to test an alternative explanation. We propose that the old, overtrained contingency is likely to be retrieved and thus to gain control over behavior under time pressure. The first aim is to provide a conceptual replication of the effect by Hardwick et al. (2019) that overtraining of a response-outcome contingency leads to action slips under time pressure. The second aim is to test whether action slips occur because participants rely on old response-outcome contingencies. To show this, we developed an additional task in which participants have to report response-outcome contingencies under time pressure. We predict that overtraining results in participants retrieving old response-outcome contingencies under time pressure. This would suggest that action slips can occur as the result of errors in the retrieval of contingency information, rather than a separate process that does not involve contingency processing.

abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Roberts et al. (2010) is that Spanish-speaking ELLs [English language learners] begin school with lower general literacy levels than native English speakers and Asian-language speaking ELLs and continue to lag behind in general reading ability through the elementary school years (Hypothesis 1); the comparison of Spanish-speaking ELLs and Asian-language speaking ELLs in the continuation of the lag is the portion selected. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Additionally, Spanish ELLs had statistically significantly less growth over time than did Asian ELLs, with differences being most notable on reading evaluation–related tasks." To address the first two predictions, the authors estimated a series of latent growth models of reading achievement for native-English-speaking students and for the ELL subgroups of interest. To estimate the effect of primary language on reading achievement, the authors estimated a three-group model for Spanish-language-speaking ELLs, Asian-language-speaking ELLs, and native-English-language-speaking groups. The result selected is the mean slope difference between the Spanish-language-speaking minority students and the Asian-language-speaking group (see Table 2 for details). Spanish-language-speaking minority students differed from the Asian-language-speaking group on all parameters in the table. Mean slope difference (the selected parameter) was about 5.0 (p < .01) for comparison of Asian-language speakers (from Table 2, slope estimate/SE: Spanish = 30.18/1.19; Asian = 35.18/0.83).

title_r: Preschooler's sensitivity to higher-order relations "symmetry" and "monotonocity"
abstract_r: In this study, we are interested in whether or not young children (4 and 5-years of age) are sensitive to higher-order relational mappings. The study is an online conceptual replication of Kotovsky & Gentner, 1996 where it was shown that 4-year-olds succeeded at easier relational mappings (where a single dimension varies in identical ways across the target and the match) , but failed at harder mappings (where the the target dimension varies in one way (e.g., getting monotonically bigger) and the match in the inverse way (e.g., monotonically smaller).

title_r: Eye-tracking investigation of infants' social evaluation of helpers and hinderers
abstract_r: The current project seeks to contribute to the continued investigation of preverbal infants' social evaluation of prosocial and antisocial characters. In a series of related studies, we created high-definition, pre-recorded versions of the Hill puppet show (e.g., Hamlin, Wynn, & Bloom, 2007; Hamlin, 2015). The initial motivation was to create a high quality, shareable, and standardized set of stimuli to facilitate both independent replication attempts as well as large-scale collaborative projects such as ManyBabies4. The initial line of studies sought to conceptually replicate Hamlin (2015) by testing infants virtually over the video conferencing tool Zoom, and found mixed results. A marginally significant age effect also emerged, where 9- to 12-month-olds, but not 6- to 8-month-olds, showed a visual preference for the Helper over the Hinderer. That said, it remains unclear whether these mixed findings are due to (a) Methodological difference, i.e. Zoom versus in-person testing, (b) Differences between the new stimuli and older stimuli, or (c) Other factors. Thus, the current project has two primary objectives: (1) To follow up on the mixed findings obtained by the series of Zoom studies, and (2) To conceptually replicate Hamlin (2015) using the new set of higher quality video stimuli. Though similar, these two objectives are evaluated separately as the Zoom studies utilized a preferential looking measure, whereas Hamlin (2015) utilized a manual forced choice measure. The current project also has a secondary objective: To follow up on the relationship between goal understanding and social preference found in Tan & Hamlin (2022). There exist numerous methodological differences between the current project and Tan & Hamlin (2022), such as the different age range, choice of stimuli (animated hill show versus recorded live puppet show), and stimuli blocking design (8 familiarization trials + 1 test trial in the current project; 6 x 2 blocks of familiarization trials + 2 test trials in Tan & Hamlin, 2022). Therefore, the current project should not be taken as a replication attempt; instead, we seek to follow up on the suggestive findings by conducting the same analyses. This project closely follows a long line of work using the Hill paradigm (e.g., Hamlin, Wynn, & Bloom, 2007); a pre-recorded puppet show will be used (e.g., Hamlin, 2015), as opposed to an animated version of the show (e.g., Tan & Hamlin, 2022). There are three primary motivations for this design choice. First, the current project, as well as a line of virtual studies that used the same stimuli (separately pre-registered), seek to conceptually replicate the Hamlin (2015) findings, with additional analyses being informed by Tan & Hamlin (2022). Thus, instead of using animation, we recreated the video recordings of puppet shows so that the stimuli across all studies were maximally similar. We opted to recreate high quality recordings because the virtual format (i.e. Zoom) inevitably results in a drop in video quality. Anticipating, and to compensate for this loss, we refilmed the puppet show using high resolution cameras. The two remaining motivating factors informed our decision to opt for video recordings instead of live performed puppet shows. Firstly, the consistency of having pre-recorded puppet shows (as opposed to live performed puppet shows) allows us to fully utilize the rich data output from the eye-tracker because we can synchronize timing across every trial. In other words, it allows us to split the stimuli into clear phases and compare both across trials within the same infant, as well as across each infant. Secondly, the eye-tracker available at our facility is incompatible with live shows. 9- to 12-month-old infants will watch videos in which a protagonist character attempts but fails to climb up a steep hill. After several attempts, a second character will enter the scene and either help the protagonist by pushing it up the hill (the Helper) or hinder the protagonist by pushing it down (the Hinderer). After several trials, infants' preference for the helper versus the hinderer will be assessed via two measures: A single preferential looking trial, as well as a manual forced-choice paradigm (see Measured variables and Analysis plan for details).

title_r: Replication of Side-to-side differences in lower extremity biomechanics during multi-directional jump landing in volleyball athletes
abstract_r: This research study is a replication study that will contribute to a large-scale international replication project in sports and exercise science whose overall aim is: To produce high level systematic and transparent replication trials of experimental trials published within the last five years in top tier sports and exercise science journals using a randomized, unbiased selection method. Large scale replication projects have been undertaken by, among others, the Open Science Collaboration in the form of the Reproducibility Project in Psychology and the Many Labs Project (Klein et al., 2014; Open Science Collaboration, 2015). These projects ignited the debate on the replication crisis in social science due to their difficulty in replicating selected effects and the variability in results. One goal of replication is to bolster our collective confidence in the veracity of novel claims by providing diagnostic evidence about those claims (Nosek et al., 2015; Nosek and Errington, 2020) when the original and replication study are similar in all “theoretically relevant dimensions” such as study design, methods, and materials (Earp, 2020, p. 120). Given the interdisciplinary nature of the sports science field and the overlap with the psychological sciences, there is reason to believe the sports science field faces similar replication issues (Caldwell et al., 2020). The replicability of sports science research has yet to be examined despite the identification of concerns within the field (Halperin et al., 2018; Heneghan et al., 2012; Knudson, 2017). As a result, the overall goal of this project is to sample a range of topics in an unbiased manner across the field of sports science for an initial estimation of the replicability of those findings. This is the first natural step in the assessment of replicability of the field, therefore, the project will attempt to replicate numerous effects once rather than multiple replications of a specific effect or theory. As it is essential to run multiple independent experiments to determine if findings in sports science have a consistent and accurate pattern, and are strongly supported (Earp and Trafimow, 2015), the proposed study is one of many studies to be replicated. The objective of this specific proposed study is to replicate (i.e. repeat) the work of Komsak Sinsurin, Sarun Srisangboriboon, and Roongtiwa Vachalathiti published in the Europen Journal of Sports Sciences in 2017 titled “Side-to-side differences in lower extremity biomechanics during multi-directional jump landing in volleyball athletes”. title_r: Unknown vocabulary density and reading comprehension: Replicating Hu & Nation 2000
abstract_r: Hu and Nation’s (2000) study, which stipulated that second language (L2) readers need to be familiar with 98% of lexical items for adequate text comprehension, has become highly influential in L2 vocabulary research and pedagogy. This research has since been the foundation for numerous lexical coverage studies (e.g. Nation, 2006; Schmitt, 2010). However, the 98% critical threshold figure is based on findings from a research project in which a regression analysis was conducted with 66 university students in New Zealand. The present study replicates Hu and Nation’s research in a context different from a typical Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) context with a sample of 105 Sri Lankan adult L2 learners in a non-academic context. They will each take two different Vocabulary Levels Tests and read one of five versions of two reading texts at different levels of density of unknown words, before answering comprehension questions.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Denson & Chang (2009), from American Educational Research Journal
abstract_r: Students benefit from being enrolled on a campus where other students are more engaged with various forms of diversity, irrespective of their own level of engagement; in particular, the peer group average measure of curricular diversity has a significant positive effect on a student’s general academic skills. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Not only do students benefit from engaging with racial diversity through related knowledge acquisition or cross-racial interaction but also from being enrolled on a campus where other students are more engaged with those forms of diversity, irrespective of their own level of engagement." This claim was tested by constructing an index for general academic skills (confirmed by a factor analysis of the self-report outcome items) as the dependent variable, and, among other predictors, creating a measure of curricular diversity (a composite of three items on the survey that asked the students if they had taken an ethnic studies course, attended a racial-cultural awareness workshop, or participated in an ethnic-racial student organization since entering college.) The focal model (Model 7) includes predictors at both the student and institution level, including both student and institution average levels of curricular diversity and cross-racial interaction; the full specification of this model can be seen in Equation 4. The focal predictor is the effect of institutional curricular diversity on individual students’ general academic skill. In Model 7 (the final model), the student body’s average level of curricular diversity engagement (gamma _05 coefficient = .31, t = 3.84, p < 0.001) had a significant positive effect on general academic skills.

title_r: Frequency attenuation in the masked priming paradigm: a large-scale online study
abstract_r: The research on visual word recognition of the past 20 years has rested on the well-accepted assumption that the masked priming technique (i) taps onto lexical access rather than episodic memory, since masked repetition priming effects may be elicited for words (but not for non-words); but (ii) it operates before lexical access is complete, since low-frequency and high-frequency words elicit numerically and statistically similar priming effects. Both these two pieces of information seem to be corroborated by a number of studies on the topic: from the seminal paper by Forster and Davis 1984, to more recent ones (e.g., Nievas 2010). However, a small subset of studies have actually reported a significant interaction effect between repetition priming and frequency, with the low-frequency words eliciting repetition priming effects around the double the size of the repetition priming effects elicited by high-frequency words (Bodner & Masson 2001, Kinoshita 2006, Norris & Kinoshita 2008). This literature, however, suffers from two main problems. First, all previous studies on the frequency attenuation effect base their materials on Francis & Kučera 1967’s frequency database, which has been argued to report unreliable frequency estimates, in addition to being outdated for the present times (Brysbaert & New 2009). Second, all these studies suffer from a not-negligible lack of power, as also sadly common in cognitive sciences (Brysbaert & Stevens 2019). For this reason, we want to run a replication study testing the potential interactive effects of repetition priming and word frequency, while tackling both methodological issues just described. We first ran a first online experiment (Experiment 1) primarily to test whether a novel online stimulus presentation online program, Labvanced, is actually able to elicit the visual masked repetition priming response on a sample larger than any reported in the literature (N=299). Our results showed that masked repetition priming may be successfully elicited on the online platform Labvanced. Experiment 1 was also useful to assess the typical range of standard deviation across conditions and paired correlations in online experiments, so to run a more precise power analysis to base further follow-up experiments on. Experiment 2 was therefore designed to tackle the issue of frequency attenuation effects in the masked priming response by capitalizing on modern technologies to recruit online a sample size large enough to potentially detect even small effect sizes which would have little probability of detection otherwise.

title_r: Effects of prior beliefs on the causal illusions - Study 1: Replication of Vicente et al. (2023)
abstract_r: Vicente et al. (2023) showed that people who hold positive beliefs in pseudoscience tend to develop illusory causal connections for both conventional and alternative medicine. On the other hand, those who have negative beliefs in pseudoscience tend to form illusory causal connections for traditional medicine, but they are less likely to do so for alternative medicine. This current study continues to explore how prior beliefs in pseudoscience influence our judgments about the causality in both conventional and alternative medical treatments. Importantly, we are using a different group of participants compared to the earlier study.

title_r: Replication of Stellar, Gordon, Anderson, Piff, McNeil, & Keltner (2018; Study 3)
abstract_r: We are completing a direct replication of Awe and Humility (Stellar, et. al) as part of a group project for our Research Methods in Social Psychology course at McGill University. In the initial study they hypothesized, “We predicted that compared with a neutral control condition, momentary experiences of awe will lead to a more balanced disclosure of one’s personal strengths and weakness” which we also will be aiming to falsify with our additional question predicting that there will be a negative relationship between high levels of trait narcissism and behaviourally measured state humility levels after exposure to awe-inducing stimuli as compared to non-narcissistic trait possessing individuals. Replication Overview: The experimental manipulation of awe will be induced by using a standardized video induction. Participants’ state humility is assessed by a behavioral measure: the number of strengths and weaknesses listed, as well as the ratio between the two. Replication Methods The replication methods used in this study are identical to the methods used in the original Stellar et al. study. The participants are randomly assigned by the Qualtrics computer program to one of two conditions where they will watch a video that is two minutes in length. Control: a nonemotional video intended to elicit only feelings of relaxation and calmness in participants. Experimental: a perspective from Earth zooming out into the cosmos, should elicit awe in participants. After the video, participants will write for two minutes about their strengths and weaknesses, starting with their strengths. They are instructed to imagine that they would discuss these strengths and weaknesses with someone they just met. There will be a visible timer counting down from two minutes to zero while they write. Participants are then asked to rank the extent to which they feel happiness, fear, awe, wonder, and amazement from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much). After the data is collected, two coders who are blind to participant conditions will read through the responses and count the number of strengths and weaknesses as well as the balance. Additional Hypothesis Methods: We are conducting a direct replication, so there will be no deviations from the original study. The only addition to the original study will be the NPI and follow-up analysis. The materials relevant to our additional question will only be presented to participants after they have completed the measures from the direct replication. Participants will complete steps one to three from the original research methods. Afterwards, they will complete a narcissistic personality inventory (NPI) After the data is collected, two coders who are blind to participant conditions will read through the responses and count the number of strengths and weaknesses as well as the balance. The data will be sorted into narcissistic and non-narcissistic categories based on their scores on the NPI for both treatment and control groups. Analysis: For the direct replication portion of the study, we will directly follow the analysis outlined in the Stellar paper where they first removed participants that met the criteria for exclusion. They log transformed each of their dependent variables (number of strengths, number of weaknesses) which were both positively skewed, they calculated the balance between the two and then log transformed that data as well to meet the assumptions of normality. After, they conducted independent samples t-tests to compare the balance of disclosing strengths vs weaknesses between awe and neutral conditions. They then conducted a multiple regression analysis with awe and happiness as independent variables that predict humility, controlling for condition (awe and control). Analysis of our Additional Research Question: Data Transformation: We will follow the same procedure as performed in initial study by Stellar, first seeing if any participants meet criteria for exclusion and then we will perform a log transformation on each of our DVs, if our data is positively skewed to ensure the assumption of normality is met. For our balance we will be calculating the difference between number of strengths and weaknesses and then likely log transforming those values. This ensures our data is normally distributed in order to conduct our multivariant analysis of variance (MANOVA). Key Effects: We will be conducting a two-way MANOVA to examine 2 factors: Awe Treatment Control Narcissism Narcissistic Non-Narcissistic We will be studying the effects these factors have on our three dependent variables quantifying our state humility: Number of Strengths Number of Weaknesses The Difference between the number of Strengths and Weaknesses We chose to do a two-way MANOVA rather than multiple two-way ANOVAs to control for familywise error rate that we would encounter in conducting multiple two-way ANOVAs. We will be testing for a main effect of inducing awe, main effect of narcissism, and an interaction effect between inducing awe and narcissism across all dependent variables simultaneously. If our hypothesis is correct, the interaction effect will be significant, this would suggest the impact of awe on humility is impacted by levels of trait narcissism. If the two-way MANOVA indicates significant main effects or interactions we will follow up with univariate ANOVAs for each DV (number of strengths, number of weaknesses, and balance). This will help clarify which specific variables contributed to the multivariate effect. If the interaction is significant in our MANOVA or univariate ANOVAs we will conduct simple main effects analyses for both factors to explore how one factor affects the DVs at each level of the other factor. In the cases where the univariate ANOVAs show significant main effects or interactions, we will perform post-hoc tests to make pairwise comparisons between levels and determine which specific groups differ from each other. We will use Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference (HSD) test to control for multiple comparisons, minimizing the risk of Type I error. Since we’re analyzing both the simple main effects and conducting post-hoc tests, we will report effect sizes using partial eta squared to provide insight into the magnitude of the effects. title_r: Expectations effects in search termination
abstract_r: In two previous studies we used the timing of decisions about absence in a detection task to investigate implicit beliefs about facilitating effects of expectation on perception. We used a paradigm where expected events are detected more readily than unexpected events: subjects are faster to detect letters when surrounded by other letters that make it into a meaningful word. We replicated this effect of context on the timing of decisions about presence, but found that context did not significantly modulate the efficiency of decisions about target absence. This finding is consistent with the absence of metacognitive representation of the facilitating effects of expectations on perception. Here, we test the generalizability of this finding to a different task (visual search) and type of expectation (stimulus familiarity). We utilize the established finding that searches are easier when the target is unfamiliar and the distractors are familiar compared to the opposite setting (Wang, Cavanagh, & Green, 1994), and use the timing of decisions about absence to ask whether subjects can metacognitively represent this fact, and whether they can use this knowledge to make efficient decisions about target absence. By examining the timing of decisions about target absence in the very first trials of the task (Mazor & Fleming, 2022), we distill stimulus-specific search termination mechanisms from generic criterion-adjustment heuristics (Chun & Wolfe, 1996).

title_r: Brohmer et al. IRSP Submission
abstract_r: One topic that repeatedly sparks debates in politics and the society is “gender-neutral language”. For instance, in languages such as German, French, or Hindi, plural forms of job occupations and societal roles are often in a generic-masculine form instead of a gender-neutral form. Although meant as “generic”, this generic-masculine form excludes women from everyday language and might even entail the cognitive effect that listeners and readers will less likely think of women. Several studies have demonstrated this and related cognitive effects in the past. Due to the societal relevance of gender-neutral language, we propose a direct replication and extension of a classic German study by Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun (2001, Experiment 2; https://doi.org/10.1177/0261927X01020004004) in a multi-lab setting.

title_r: (2022) MORI Online Enlightenment
abstract_r: In the MORI paradigm, a pair of participants watch an event and then later discuss the event before answering individual memory questions about that event. Unbeknownst to participants, they see slightly different versions of the event. The objective here is to create a situation in which during discussion, participants introduce misinformation to one another. Experimenters can then assess co-witness conformity–the degree to which a partner’s memory reports influence the participant’s own memory reports. Across a number of experiments, a robust co-witness conformity effect has been observed (i.e., lower final memory questionnaire accuracy for details where a partner introduced incorrect information). In two previous pilot experiments, we validated an online version of the MORI paradigm (in student and Prolific samples). We replicated co-witness conformity effects in both samples, suggesting that a virtual online version of the procedure is viable. A recent experiment (Cadavid & Luna, 2020) found that the co-witness conformity effect was reduced with an enlightenment warning (Blank, 1999), where participants were told about the different video versions and the experiment purpose before completing a final memory test. However, another experiment did not find a reduction (although they used a warning that did not explicitly mention that participants witnessed slightly different events; Fernandes et al. (2020)). Thus, it is not entirely clear whether enlightenment-based warnings are able to reduce/eliminate the co-witness conformity effect. The aim of this experiment is to replicate Cadavid & Luna (2020) in our version of the MORI paradigm, which uses video/audio chat (Cadavid & Luna used only text chat).

title_r: Verb Bias Effects When Interpreting Syntactically Ambiguous Sentences: A replication of Ryskin et al. (2016)
abstract_r: This experiment is replicating Ryskin et al. (2016) which tested the presence of verb bias effects in a computer-based study in a lab setting. In the sentence, “touch the bunny with the shoe”, “with the shoe” is most likely demonstrating an instrument with which to “touch” the bunny. This is an instrument-biased verb while “choose the frog with the feather” demonstrates a modifier-biased verb: “with the feather” indicates which frog to choose. We are replicating a study that proposes these biases are relied on when interpreting syntactically ambiguous sentences. Participants will hear an instruction with modifier-biased, instrument-biased, or equibiased verbs while an ambiguous display is presented and then make an interpretation. Eye tracking, mouse movements, and clicking behavior will be observed to test the presence of biases.

title_r: Memory suggestibility and high confidence errors in younger and older adults: A replication
abstract_r: This project is a replication of Dodson and Krueger (2006). We will use the same key materials (video and memory questionnaires) as the original authors, but our data will be collected online instead of in the lab, and we will use a different distraction memory task. We seek to address one key research question: Are older adults more likely to commit high confidence false memory errors, compared to younger adults? To answer this question, we will focus on replicating a specific subset of the key analyses from the original study(see below), with an increased sample size, and using both frequentist and Bayesian statistics. Similar to the original study, we include participants from three different groups. (1) Younger and (2) Older adults, who complete the test in one session, and (3) Younger adults who are invited to complete the source memory test after a two day delay (i.e., the Young-delay group), seeking to match overall memory performance levels with that of the older adults.

title_r: Main study
abstract_r: Does concern for others or sympathy lead to vicarious optimism for others (i.e., being optimistic about the chances of negative life events happening to another person)? As a conceptual replication study, the present work examines for the first time influencing factors and basic mechanisms of vicarious optimism, a new social psychological finding in the field of optimism research. In contrast to the original study by Kappes and colleagues (2018), the present study focusses on concern and sympathy for another person as determining factors of vicarious optimism. We not only manipulate but measure sympathy for a target and concern for a target, target conceptualized as a person representative for a social group. Consequently, the unique predictive value of both factors on the optimistic learning bias can be determined. Thus, we are focusing on a more precise analysis of the effect. Furthermore, instead of sympathetic vs. non- sympathetic (two categories) we use a continuous measure for a more fine-grained analyses of the effect. To learn which factor drives the effect would also advance the theory.

title_r: Examining the mechanisms underlying action slips: A competition between goal-directed processes
abstract_r: In this study we aim to investigate the mechanism underlying action slips, sometimes also referred to as habitual errors. Hardwick et al. (2019) showed that action slips occur if an overtrained response-outcome contingency is reversed and people are asked to respond under time pressure. The authors explain this effect with a stimulus-driven process, claiming that people do not process any contingency information under time pressure. In the current study, we seek to test an alternative explanation. We propose that the old, overtrained contingency is likely to be retrieved and thus to gain control over behavior under time pressure. The first aim is to provide a conceptual replication of the effect by Hardwick et al. (2019) that overtraining of a response-outcome contingency leads to action slips under time pressure. The second aim is to test whether action slips occur because participants rely on old response-outcome contingencies. To show this, we developed an additional task in which participants have to report response-outcome contingencies under time pressure. We predict that overtraining results in participants retrieving old response-outcome contingencies under time pressure. This would suggest that action slips can occur as the result of errors in the retrieval of contingency information, rather than a separate process that does not involve contingency processing.

title_r: Replicating the factor structure of the IDLaS-NL battery in adulthood
abstract_r: The IDLaS-NL battery contains 31 tasks of linguistic and non-linguistic skill.
