summary: Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication

Kathryn V. Walter & Daniel Conroy-Beam

Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara 

Date pre-registered on the Open Science Framework: April 17, 2018
This document was fixed in its current form prior to data analysis, all later amendments will be visible.

Date Made Public: April 17, 2021

Correspondence regarding this pre-registration should be addressed to Kathryn V. Walter, Email: kathryn.walter@psych.ucsb.edu, or using the comment function on the Open Science Framework. 
Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.
Control variables. We will include a series of four control variables.  These control variables will be GDP per capita (CIA World Factbook), latitude (CIA World Factbook), most common religion (CIA World Factbook), and world region (based on Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006). 
Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). Finally, this approach lets us conduct all analyses within the same modeling framework, allowing clearer interpretation of the results.
 	For all cross-cultural comparisons, we will report both a base model with no controls and models that attempt to approximate relevant controls used in the original papers (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). Each of these control models will include a standard set of control variables: latitude, GDP per capita, world region, and most common religion. These variables were chosen because they were each used in the papers we are replicating. 
 All data analysis will be conducted in R. All data and script will be made available at the time of publication.  
Sex Differences in Mate Preferences
To assess sex differences in mate preferences across cultures, we will fit five multilevel models, one for each preference (kindness, intelligence, health, good financial prospects, physical attractiveness). In these models the preference variable will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. Mate preference variables will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Actual Partner Age
We will fit one multilevel model to assess sex differences in actual partner age across cultures. In this model the difference between self and partner age will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Multivariate Effect Size
We will use the five preference variables to calculate the Mahalanobis distance (D) between males and females within each country. We will additionally calculate D separately for putatively sex-differentiated preferences (good financial prospects and physical attractiveness) and those not expected to be as strongly sex differentiated (intelligence, kindness, health). We will use bootstrapping to estimate 95% confidence intervals around these D values for each country. Finally, we will use a Monte Carlo cross-validated logistic regression to assess the ability of preferences to predict participant sex. Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each fold of this cross-validation will leave out 10% of the data for testing. The relevant outcome variable will be the percentage of participant sexes accurately predicted by the model in the testing set. This process will be repeated for 10,000 iterations to provide an estimate of predictive accuracy and estimated confidence intervals around this accuracy. 
Pathogen Prevalence
We will test for the effect of pathogen prevalence on ideal mate preferences in a series of multi-level models predicting preferences from nation-level pathogen prevalence indices. We will fit three multilevel models for each of the five mate preference variables. Each model will use the relevant ideal mate preference as the outcome variable and predict this variable using one of three pathogen prevalence indices. The first will be the index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad and Buss (1993). The second index will be the years of life lost by communicable diseases variable used by Debruine et al. (2010). The third pathogen prevalence index will be a new index created by combining two variables from publicly available databases: years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015). To create the third index using these variables, we will standardize and average the two variables for each country. We will check the validity of this new index by computing its correlation with the other two indices; however, we will use the index in analyses regardless of its relationship to others. 
Gender Equality 
To examine the effect of nation-level gender equality on sex differences in mate preferences, we will fit a series of multilevel models predicting ideal mate preferences from sex and nation-level gender quality. Each model will have one of the five ideal preference variables as an outcome variable. These models will use the interaction of participant sex and a gender equality variable as the predictor, along with all relevant main effects. The gender equality variables used will be the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999); the updated GDI; the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI); and the Gender Inequality Index (GII), as well as a composite variable created through principal components analysis (PCA) using the updated GDI, GGGI, and GII. We will enter these three variables into a PCA and extract the first principle component. Scores on this principle component will be used as each country’s gender equality score. We will check the validity of this composite measure of gender equality by calculating its correlation with the other measures of gender equality; however, we will use this principle component regardless of its relationship to the other indices.

Correspondence regarding this pre-registration should be addressed to Kathryn V. Walter, Email: kathryn.walter@psych.ucsb.edu, or using the comment function on the Open Science Framework. 
Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.
Control variables. We will include a series of four control variables.  These control variables will be GDP per capita (CIA World Factbook), latitude (CIA World Factbook), most common religion (CIA World Factbook), and world region (based on Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006). 
Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). Finally, this approach lets us conduct all analyses within the same modeling framework, allowing clearer interpretation of the results.
 	For all cross-cultural comparisons, we will report both a base model with no controls and models that attempt to approximate relevant controls used in the original papers (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). Each of these control models will include a standard set of control variables: latitude, GDP per capita, world region, and most common religion. These variables were chosen because they were each used in the papers we are replicating. 
 All data analysis will be conducted in R. All data and script will be made available at the time of publication.  
Sex Differences in Mate Preferences
To assess sex differences in mate preferences across cultures, we will fit five multilevel models, one for each preference (kindness, intelligence, health, good financial prospects, physical attractiveness). In these models the preference variable will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. Mate preference variables will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Actual Partner Age
We will fit one multilevel model to assess sex differences in actual partner age across cultures. In this model the difference between self and partner age will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Multivariate Effect Size
We will use the five preference variables to calculate the Mahalanobis distance (D) between males and females within each country. We will additionally calculate D separately for putatively sex-differentiated preferences (good financial prospects and physical attractiveness) and those not expected to be as strongly sex differentiated (intelligence, kindness, health). We will use bootstrapping to estimate 95% confidence intervals around these D values for each country. Finally, we will use a Monte Carlo cross-validated logistic regression to assess the ability of preferences to predict participant sex. Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each fold of this cross-validation will leave out 10% of the data for testing. The relevant outcome variable will be the percentage of participant sexes accurately predicted by the model in the testing set. This process will be repeated for 10,000 iterations to provide an estimate of predictive accuracy and estimated confidence intervals around this accuracy. 
Pathogen Prevalence
We will test for the effect of pathogen prevalence on ideal mate preferences in a series of multi-level models predicting preferences from nation-level pathogen prevalence indices. We will fit three multilevel models for each of the five mate preference variables. Each model will use the relevant ideal mate preference as the outcome variable and predict this variable using one of three pathogen prevalence indices. The first will be the index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad and Buss (1993). The second index will be the years of life lost by communicable diseases variable used by Debruine et al. (2010). The third pathogen prevalence index will be a new index created by combining two variables from publicly available databases: years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015). To create the third index using these variables, we will standardize and average the two variables for each country. We will check the validity of this new index by computing its correlation with the other two indices; however, we will use the index in analyses regardless of its relationship to others. 
Gender Equality 
To examine the effect of nation-level gender equality on sex differences in mate preferences, we will fit a series of multilevel models predicting ideal mate preferences from sex and nation-level gender quality. Each model will have one of the five ideal preference variables as an outcome variable. These models will use the interaction of participant sex and a gender equality variable as the predictor, along with all relevant main effects. The gender equality variables used will be the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999); the updated GDI; the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI); and the Gender Inequality Index (GII), as well as a composite variable created through principal components analysis (PCA) using the updated GDI, GGGI, and GII. We will enter these three variables into a PCA and extract the first principle component. Scores on this principle component will be used as each country’s gender equality score. We will check the validity of this composite measure of gender equality by calculating its correlation with the other measures of gender equality; however, we will use this principle component regardless of its relationship to the other indices.

Correspondence regarding this pre-registration should be addressed to Kathryn V. Walter, Email: kathryn.walter@psych.ucsb.edu, or using the comment function on the Open Science Framework. 
Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.
Control variables. We will include a series of four control variables.  These control variables will be GDP per capita (CIA World Factbook), latitude (CIA World Factbook), most common religion (CIA World Factbook), and world region (based on Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006). 
Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). Finally, this approach lets us conduct all analyses within the same modeling framework, allowing clearer interpretation of the results.
 	For all cross-cultural comparisons, we will report both a base model with no controls and models that attempt to approximate relevant controls used in the original papers (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). Each of these control models will include a standard set of control variables: latitude, GDP per capita, world region, and most common religion. These variables were chosen because they were each used in the papers we are replicating. 
 All data analysis will be conducted in R. All data and script will be made available at the time of publication.  
Sex Differences in Mate Preferences
To assess sex differences in mate preferences across cultures, we will fit five multilevel models, one for each preference (kindness, intelligence, health, good financial prospects, physical attractiveness). In these models the preference variable will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. Mate preference variables will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Actual Partner Age
We will fit one multilevel model to assess sex differences in actual partner age across cultures. In this model the difference between self and partner age will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Multivariate Effect Size
We will use the five preference variables to calculate the Mahalanobis distance (D) between males and females within each country. We will additionally calculate D separately for putatively sex-differentiated preferences (good financial prospects and physical attractiveness) and those not expected to be as strongly sex differentiated (intelligence, kindness, health). We will use bootstrapping to estimate 95% confidence intervals around these D values for each country. Finally, we will use a Monte Carlo cross-validated logistic regression to assess the ability of preferences to predict participant sex. Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each fold of this cross-validation will leave out 10% of the data for testing. The relevant outcome variable will be the percentage of participant sexes accurately predicted by the model in the testing set. This process will be repeated for 10,000 iterations to provide an estimate of predictive accuracy and estimated confidence intervals around this accuracy. 
Pathogen Prevalence
We will test for the effect of pathogen prevalence on ideal mate preferences in a series of multi-level models predicting preferences from nation-level pathogen prevalence indices. We will fit three multilevel models for each of the five mate preference variables. Each model will use the relevant ideal mate preference as the outcome variable and predict this variable using one of three pathogen prevalence indices. The first will be the index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad and Buss (1993). The second index will be the years of life lost by communicable diseases variable used by Debruine et al. (2010). The third pathogen prevalence index will be a new index created by combining two variables from publicly available databases: years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015). To create the third index using these variables, we will standardize and average the two variables for each country. We will check the validity of this new index by computing its correlation with the other two indices; however, we will use the index in analyses regardless of its relationship to others. 
Gender Equality 
To examine the effect of nation-level gender equality on sex differences in mate preferences, we will fit a series of multilevel models predicting ideal mate preferences from sex and nation-level gender quality. Each model will have one of the five ideal preference variables as an outcome variable. These models will use the interaction of participant sex and a gender equality variable as the predictor, along with all relevant main effects. The gender equality variables used will be the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999); the updated GDI; the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI); and the Gender Inequality Index (GII), as well as a composite variable created through principal components analysis (PCA) using the updated GDI, GGGI, and GII. We will enter these three variables into a PCA and extract the first principle component. Scores on this principle component will be used as each country’s gender equality score. We will check the validity of this composite measure of gender equality by calculating its correlation with the other measures of gender equality; however, we will use this principle component regardless of its relationship to the other indices.

summary: Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication

Kathryn V. Walter & Daniel Conroy-Beam

Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara 

Date pre-registered on the Open Science Framework: April 17, 2018
This document was fixed in its current form prior to data analysis, all later amendments will be visible.

Date Made Public: April 17, 2021

Correspondence regarding this pre-registration should be addressed to Kathryn V. Walter, Email: kathryn.walter@psych.ucsb.edu, or using the comment function on the Open Science Framework. 
Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.
Control variables. We will include a series of four control variables.  These control variables will be GDP per capita (CIA World Factbook), latitude (CIA World Factbook), most common religion (CIA World Factbook), and world region (based on Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006). 
Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). Finally, this approach lets us conduct all analyses within the same modeling framework, allowing clearer interpretation of the results.
 	For all cross-cultural comparisons, we will report both a base model with no controls and models that attempt to approximate relevant controls used in the original papers (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). Each of these control models will include a standard set of control variables: latitude, GDP per capita, world region, and most common religion. These variables were chosen because they were each used in the papers we are replicating. 
 All data analysis will be conducted in R. All data and script will be made available at the time of publication.  
Sex Differences in Mate Preferences
To assess sex differences in mate preferences across cultures, we will fit five multilevel models, one for each preference (kindness, intelligence, health, good financial prospects, physical attractiveness). In these models the preference variable will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. Mate preference variables will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Actual Partner Age
We will fit one multilevel model to assess sex differences in actual partner age across cultures. In this model the difference between self and partner age will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Multivariate Effect Size
We will use the five preference variables to calculate the Mahalanobis distance (D) between males and females within each country. We will additionally calculate D separately for putatively sex-differentiated preferences (good financial prospects and physical attractiveness) and those not expected to be as strongly sex differentiated (intelligence, kindness, health). We will use bootstrapping to estimate 95% confidence intervals around these D values for each country. Finally, we will use a Monte Carlo cross-validated logistic regression to assess the ability of preferences to predict participant sex. Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each fold of this cross-validation will leave out 10% of the data for testing. The relevant outcome variable will be the percentage of participant sexes accurately predicted by the model in the testing set. This process will be repeated for 10,000 iterations to provide an estimate of predictive accuracy and estimated confidence intervals around this accuracy. 
Pathogen Prevalence
We will test for the effect of pathogen prevalence on ideal mate preferences in a series of multi-level models predicting preferences from nation-level pathogen prevalence indices. We will fit three multilevel models for each of the five mate preference variables. Each model will use the relevant ideal mate preference as the outcome variable and predict this variable using one of three pathogen prevalence indices. The first will be the index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad and Buss (1993). The second index will be the years of life lost by communicable diseases variable used by Debruine et al. (2010). The third pathogen prevalence index will be a new index created by combining two variables from publicly available databases: years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015). To create the third index using these variables, we will standardize and average the two variables for each country. We will check the validity of this new index by computing its correlation with the other two indices; however, we will use the index in analyses regardless of its relationship to others. 
Gender Equality 
To examine the effect of nation-level gender equality on sex differences in mate preferences, we will fit a series of multilevel models predicting ideal mate preferences from sex and nation-level gender quality. Each model will have one of the five ideal preference variables as an outcome variable. These models will use the interaction of participant sex and a gender equality variable as the predictor, along with all relevant main effects. The gender equality variables used will be the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999); the updated GDI; the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI); and the Gender Inequality Index (GII), as well as a composite variable created through principal components analysis (PCA) using the updated GDI, GGGI, and GII. We will enter these three variables into a PCA and extract the first principle component. Scores on this principle component will be used as each country’s gender equality score. We will check the validity of this composite measure of gender equality by calculating its correlation with the other measures of gender equality; however, we will use this principle component regardless of its relationship to the other indices.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Case & Paxson (2011) in Demography.
abstract_r: The claim selected from Case & Paxson (2011) is that the quality of maternal and child health care has deteriorated in regions with high recent HIV prevalence relative to regions with low recent HIV prevalence. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Regions of countries that have light AIDS burdens have witnessed small or no declines in health care, using the measures noted above, while those regions shouldering the heaviest burdens have seen the largest erosion in non-HIV-related health services for pregnant women and children." The authors test the selected claim using multiple waves of Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) for 14 sub-Saharan African countries. The authors examine antenatal care, birth deliveries, and rates of immunization for children born between 1988 and 2005. The test of the claim is based on an OLS regression of the receipt of antenatal care on the focal independent variable - HIV Prevalence in Year of Birth. The analysis also controls for year-of-birth fixed effects and mother and child characteristics, incluhding the mother’s education in years, the mother’s age at the birth in years, the child’s age in months, an indicator for the child’s sex, and an indicator of whether the family lived in an urban area. The focal test result concerns the location of the estimated coefficient in the “HIV Prevalence in Year of Birth” term found in Table 3 under the heading “Had Antenatal Care”. When the authors include country-region fixed effects so that identification comes from change in HIV prevalence within a region over time, they find that higher HIV prevalence is associated with a significantly lower probability of reporting antenatal care, b = -1.734, SE[corrected for clustering at the region level] = .331.

title_r: Wealth and Happiness: Replication of Diener, E., Ng, W., Harter, J., & Arora, R. (2010) at University of Vienna.
abstract_r: This project is part of the Direct+Plus CREP replication (https://osf.io/px0sw/) of a study by Diener et al. (2010). As a part of a seminar at the Department of Occupational, Economic and Social Psychology, led by Andre Julian Hartmann and Martin Müller (both graduate students) at the University of Vienna (Austria), 27 students will perform the replication. In addition to the direct replication, we include two blocks of items not included in the original study (Direct+ replication). In Block 4, we add two questions that deal with financial security from the Direct+Plus project by Jordan Wagge. In Block 5, we include three questions concerning spending behavior. Including these additional items was motivated by a literature search were each student group presented a paper of their interest and developed a research question and hypotheses. A review about spending behavior from Aknin et al. (2018) was selected. The authors propose a research shift away from household income towards everyday spending decisions and show that individuals can use their disposable income to increase their happiness by investing in experiential (rather than material) purchases and prosocial spending. Regarding the direct replication, we will follow Diener et al. and: (1) test the relationship between income and different types of well-being (life evaluations, positive emotions, and negative emotions); (2) look at physical and psychological needs as potential mediators of this relationship; and (3) examine whether the relationship between income and well-being varies across groups (limited by the student sample). In the original study, it was also tested whether happiness is higher in wealthy nations than poorer nations. Because as a single CREP replication we do not have the resources to replicate the Gallup World poll in full, we can only make deductions based on our local sample. Although, a meta-analysis of all participating labs replications might also investigate this question. Regarding the direct plus (concepual) replication, we expect experiential purchases (compared to material purchases) and prosocial spending behavior (i.e., donating money to charity organizations, spending to help others) to positively effect subjective well being.

title_r: Will They Get Along? Infants’ Expectations about Third Party Social Relationships Based on Language: An online replication of Liberman et al. 2017
abstract_r: This study did not yield significant results because infants were looking at ceiling. We conducted a couple of pilot versions to find the optimal looking time window after this study. We will now pre-register a second version of this study with a looking time window that is not at ceiling. While research has shed light on infants’ ability to recognize and even prefer their native language at a remarkably young age, little research has studied whether infants use language as an indicator of social groups. The present study will be replicating a 2017 study “Preverbal Infants Infer Third-Party Social Relationships Based on Language” by Liberman, Woodward, and Kinzler. While the 2017 study was conducted in-person in a laboratory setting with video stimuli projected on a large screen, this study will be conducted online on the Lookit website (lookit.mit.edu). Another noteworthy difference is that the 2017 study involved infant-controlled test trials (i.e., test trials ended if infants looked away for longer than 2s or 30s has elapsed), while this study will not (i.e., test trials will be presented the same length regardless infant looking). This study will test whether the same patterns and findings from the 2017 study will be replicated in an online paradigm despite these differences.

title_r: Closing the attentional window - Exp 4
abstract_r: Our second experiment, was a more direct replication of their study using the original materials used by Sana and Carpenter (2023). This led to a successful replication of their findings. They proposed that when participants are pretested this opens a attentional window that increases attention on all material until the answers are found. When the pretested material is at the beginning there is no, or reduced, benefit to non-pretested information. In contrast, when it is at the end of the lesson the material before the pretested information is attended to more closely which in turn benefits memory after a short delay. The third experiment manipulated the presentation of the text to "close" the attentional window, reducing any broader benefit of pretesting. To do this, we found the clause relating to each pretested item and make the text bold, reducing the need to search for the information. In this experiment, we bolded the non-pretesed information and kept everything else the same. Participants will study one long expository text about Yellowstone national park. This text was used previously in Sana and Carpenter (2023). Participants will will: 1) Answer 10 short questions before reading the text (No feedback) 2) Read the text (Pretested information bolded) (8 minutes) 3) Answer 5 short questions as a distractor task (5 minutes, no feedback) For example, “Names as many breeds of dog as you can” for one minute 4) Answer 20 multiple-choice questions (10 pretested, 10 non-pretested, no feedback) We suspect that the entire experiment will take 30 minutes, to complete this process. We use very similar material and questions and aimed to follow their procedure as closely as possible.

title_r: Citizens' blame/praise of politicians for service failure/success
abstract_r: This project conducts a set of replications and extensions of the survey experiment study of James et al. (2016) which estimated the effects of information cues summarizing service delivery arrangements on citizens’ blame of English local government politicians for poor street maintenance. A mixed experimental design will be conducted to support 3 layers of studies: (1) We will conduct a direct replication of the original study using the same cues in England, and generalize it to Hong Kong and South Korea by tailoring the survey instruments into local languages. This study aims to test whether the theory (that contracting reduces the blame of politicians) holds across the three regions. We will also extend the study by adding a new outcome variable examining “responsibility”. (2) We will extend the original study to cover a full publicness framework and explore the effects of information cues indicating different levels (i.e., high vs. low) of political and economic control in service delivery arrangements on citizens’ blame of local politicians for poor street maintenance. This study will be conducted comparatively in England, Hong Kong, and South Korea. (3) We will extend previous experimental designs to the context of public service success and test the theory of negativity bias, which suggests that citizens’ blame of politicians for public service failure is higher than citizens’ praise of politicians for public service success, irrespective of the cues about service delivery arrangements across the three regions.

title_r: ReaderBank 2024 - Imagination Quiz Online Replication
abstract_r: Subsequent to an initial pilot study, we aim to run this replication study to investigate the cognitive processes of imagination within fiction readers. Using an online survey consisting of a novel 'Imagination Quiz', we will determine whether findings from an initial pilot study on reading and imagination in a specific reading population (attendees at a large international book festival) replicate within the general population (from casual to keen readers). In this study, we will explore the underlying factor structure of imagination as it relates to fiction reading, and to confirm previous findings that suggested a three-factor model comprising 'People Models,' 'Voice & Language,' and 'Space & Vision.' Additionally, we seek to examine how individuals' reader profiles correlate with these factors. We plan to explore the relationships between individuals' engagement with different dimensions of imagination and their propensity for vivid visual imagery and thought suppression. This will provide insights into how different readers experience and represent narrative content, and help identify the potential cognitive mechanisms that underlie these experiences.

title_r: Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication
abstract_r: This pre-registration should be considered alongside the pre-registration entitled “Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication and Extension” (Kredlow, M. A. (2021, March 5). Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication and Extension. Retrieved from osf.io/4b2ea) as the groups in this study comprise 4 of the 12 groups in that larger study. In this experiment, we will attempt to replicate findings from Hupbach et al. 2007 (Experiment 1) by conducting an online version of their study. The current study will occur online and involve 3 sessions spaced ~48 hours apart (Monday, Wednesday, Friday). At Session 1, participants will learn 18 objects. At Session 2, following memory reactivation (or without reactivation) participants will learn 18 new objects. At Session 3, participants will be asked to recall the objects they learned at Session 1. A detailed description of the experiment is provided below: Session 1: Participants watch a video of the experimenter providing instructions for the experiment. Participants are asked to learn a list of 18 objects. To facilitate learning, they name the objects one by one, as each object emerges from a virtual blue basket. After participants name all 18 objects individually, there is a 30 second delay during which they solve a series of basic arithmetic questions. Then, participants are asked to recall the objects that they learned. They complete this process 4 more times. Session 2: Approximately 48 hours after Session 1, participants complete Session 2. Participants assigned to memory reactivation are shown an image of the blue basket from Session 1 and are asked whether they remember it. They are also asked a multiple choice question about the task that they completed at Session 1. They also see an instructional video of the same experimenter from Session 1 and the online study formatting (background color, layout, text font) is the same as Session 1. Participants who do not receive reactivation are given instructions by a different experimenter and the online study formatting (background color, layout, text font) is different than it was at Session 1. All participants are then asked to learn a new list of objects (different from the list they learned at Session 1). All 18 new objects are presented on one page. Participants are given up to 3 minutes to name the objects followed by 30 seconds to study the objects and try to remember them. After naming and studying the 18 objects, there is a 30 second delay during which participants solve a series of basic arithmetic questions. Then, participants are asked to recall the objects that they learned. They complete this process 4 more times. Session 3: Approximately 48 hours after Session 2, participants complete Session 3. Participants watch an instructional video given by the experimenter from Session 1. The online study formatting (background color, layout, text font) is the same as in Session 1. Then, participants are asked to recall as many objects as possible from Session 1 and are given unlimited time to do so. Once participants have recalled as many objects as possible, there is a 30 second delay during which participants solve a series of basic arithmetic questions. This process is repeated 4 more times. title_r: Approach/Avoidance training in the gender domain: the role of self-associations
abstract_r: Previous literature suggests that approach training modifies attitudes and the self-concept via self-associations vis-à-vis approached stimuli. By self-association, we mean here a mental connection between a certain category of stimuli and the self so that the individual integrates this category of stimuli into the self. In a seminal study, Kawakami and colleagues (2008) showed that repeatedly moving a joystick toward pictures of mathematics (i.e., approach) leads individuals to associate themselves more with mathematics in a subsequent Implicit Association Test (IAT) as compared to moving a joystick away from pictures of mathematics (i.e., avoidance). These results have been recently replicated by Batailler and colleagues (2021) with a different approach-avoidance training (i.e., using the Visual Approach Avoidance by the Self Task, VAAST, Rougier et al., 2018). Approach-avoidance training (AAT) effects on self-associations were also obtained with social categories. Indeed, non-Black participants trained to approach Black people associated themselves more to Black people in an implicit association task than those trained to avoid Black people (Phills et al., 2011). Phills and collaborators also showed that, at the level of the brain (iP300 wave linked to categorization), approach training alters the categorization process. P300 amplitudes decrease when stimuli are psychologically similar on a dimension relevant for the task. That is what we observed here, so black people were categorized as significantly less different from themselves in training conditions when approaching black people. Here, from a cumulative science perspective, we seek to replicate and extend this effect on another social group: the group of women. Similar to Phills et al. (2011), who tested the AAT effect on the association of non-black people with black people, we chose to test this effect of association with women on men only. If the effect is replicated, future research should verify whether this self-association effect favored with women following an AAT is also found in women.

title_r: Too complex for Simon? The influence of stimulus complexity on the Simon effect: A replication of Hommel(1994)
abstract_r: This study investigates the influence of stimulus complexity onto the Simon effect. The Simon effect describes the correspondence between irrelevant stimulus location and response location (e.g. Hommel (1993)), meaning a spatially compatible response to a stimulus is faster than a spatially incompatible response even if stimulus position is irrelevant. According to Hommel (1993) the Simon effect is reduced when relevant and irrelevant stimulus features are temporally separated. This is called the temporal overlap account. Hommel(1993) demonstrated this effect across various experimental manipulations, including stimulus onset delay, stimulus eccentricity, and stimulus quality. In a subsequent study, Hommel (1994) extended this line of research by focussing on the role of stimulus complexity. There are two conditions differing in complexity. The simple condition involves the discrimination of colour stimuli (blue vs. yellow) within a reference frame. The moderately complex condition requires participants to distinguish between shape stimuli, specifically a square and a rectangle, also within a reference frame. According to Hommel (1994), the Simon effect decreases as task complexity increases. To further investigate this claim, we introduce a third, more complex form condition, in which participants respond to a five-pointed star and a six-pointed star. In contrary to Hommel (1994) we investigate not only the global Simon effect, but also the local Simon effect. Hommel (1994) and Umiltà and Liotti (1987) only mention „the Simon effect“, while we suggest that there are two different types of Simon effects as shown by Baess and Bermeitinger (2025). The global Simon effect arises when the spatial compatibility is determined by the absolute position of the stimulus on the screen (e.g., left vs. right side of a monitor). The local Simon effect emerges when spatial compatibility is defined within a localized frame of reference. The Stimuli appear either on the left or right of the monitor and always either within the left or right frame. Umiltà and Liotti (1987) observed only a local Simon effect in their delay condition, which led to the emergence of the debate between the Attentional Zooming Theory and the Temporal Overlap Theory. The Attentional Zooming Theory postulates that attention can shift between spatial locations, affecting response times in the Simon effect, based on target congruence. Hommel (1994) adopted the experimental layout used by Umiltà and Liotti (1987), but manipulated the difficulty of the relevant feature (color vs. shape). The aim of our study is to replicate the results of Hommel (1994). In line with Hommel (1994) we investigate the following hypothesis: We expect to find a global Simon effect in the colour condition and no global Simon effect in the form condition. Additionally, we expect to find no global Simon effect in the complex form condition. Reference: Hommel, B. (1994). Effects of irrelevant spatial S-R compatibility depend on stimulus complexity. title_r: GCCR002: Value of quantifying smell, taste, and chemesthesis changes in the differential diagnosis of COVID19 vs other respiratory illnesses: a multi-national study
abstract_r: Chemosensory loss has taken on a new meaning for people worldwide as loss of smell (and taste, as well as chemesthesis) has become a prominent symptom of COVID-19, now recognized by health authorities including the CDC. As part of an international effort to better understand this chemosensory connection to COVID-19, a questionnaire was implemented in 29 languages for people who have had an upper respiratory infection (e.g., common cold, influenza, suspected or confirmed COVID-19). The initial analyses of a subset of these data confirm substantial loss of smell, taste and chemesthesis (e.g., the burn of chili peppers, the cooling of menthol, tingle of carbonation) in individuals with COVID-19; notably, this loss was independent of nasal obstruction. The results had minimal differences between people with COVID-19 confirmed by laboratory tests versus those diagnosed by symptoms alone (e.g., a clinical assessment by a medical professional). In the current study, which builds on these initial findings, our aims are three-fold. We will determine if we can replicate the previous results on smell, taste, chemesthesis and nasal obstruction change during COVID-19 versus before COVID-19 (Parma et al., under review) in participants reporting COVID-19 based on data collected since the initial data snapshot. We will compare chemosensory and nasal obstruction changes of the COVID-19 group with participants reporting other respiratory illnesses (non-COVID respiratory illness or nCRI group) using the data of the supersample (all data since study initiation). We will determine if a pattern of chemosensory changes, other symptoms, and/or demographics can be identified that discriminate COVID-19 from nCRI. Authors of this project: Global Consortium for Chemosensory Research (GCCR) following the GCCR002 collaboration agreement.

title_r: Closing the attentional window - exp 1
abstract_r: This first experiment is a conceptual replication of Sana and Carpenter (2023) experiment one. They found that when material at the end of the lesson was tested there was larger benefit to non-pretested material and less of a benefit to pretested material, in comparison to when pretested questions were at the beginning. They proposed that when participants are pretested this opens a attentional window that increases attention on all material until the answers are found. When the pretested material is at the beginning there is no, or reduced, benefit to non-pretested information. In contrast, when it is at the end of the lesson the material before the pretested information is attended to more closely which in turn benefits memory after a short delay. Participants will study two texts, one about Yellowstone national park the other on the planet Saturn. These texts have been used previously by my collaborator Dr Pan and in Sana and Carpenter (2023). For each text they will: 1) Answer 10 short questions before reading the text (No feedback) 2) Read the text (8 minutes) 3) Answer 5 short questions as a distractor task (5 minutes, no feedback) For example, “Names as many breeds of dog as you can” for one minute 4) Answer 20 multiple-choice questions (10 pretested, 10 non-pretested, no feedback) We suspect that the entire experiment will take 45 minutes to one hour, to complete this process twice, once for each test. We use very similar material and questions and aimed to follow their procedure as closely as possible. If we are able to successfully replicate the main effect of pretesting and interaction then we plan to follow up with a subsequent experiment in order to test the boundaries of the attentional window hypothesis.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Fitzgerald et al. (2018), from Social Forces
abstract_r: The claim selected from Fitzgerald et al. (2018) is that working time is positively associated with higher state-level carbon emissions. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Our findings suggest that over the 2007–2013 period, state-level carbon emissions and average working hours have a strong, positive relationship, which holds across a variety of model estimation techniques and net of various political, economic, and demographic drivers of emissions." The authors estimate Prais-Winsten models with panel corrected standard errors (PCSEs) for the fixed effects models. They estimate two-way fixed effects models by including both state-specific and year-specific intercepts. They also correct for first-order auto-correlation (i.e., AR(1) correction) within panels and treat that AR(1) process as common to all panels. The specification of the model containing the selected test result can be gleaned from Table 4, Model 1: Scale(FE). The selected test involves the location of the estimated coefficient in the “Working hours” term. In model 1 (Table 4), the authors find that the scale effect of working hours on carbon emissions is positive and significant. Specifically, in model 1, they find that, over time, a 1 percent increase in average working hours per worker is associated with a 0.668 per-cent increase in emissions, holding all else constant (b = .668, SE = .179, p < .001).

title_r: The effect of negative valence on false memory formation in the DRM paradigm: A Paradigmatic Replication
abstract_r: The Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM; Roediger & McDermott, 1995) task is a prominent paradigm that examines whether and how false memories can arise. In this task, participants learn lists of words semantically associated with a non-presented critical lure. Subsequently, individuals’ memory is tested in the form of a recall or recognition test. Research shows a robust false memory effect – individuals tend to recall or recognize the non-studied critical words that were not present in the lists. However, when applying these findings to legal or clinical contexts, the DRM has been criticized for not capturing the (negative) emotional nature of such real-life memories. As a result, several lines of research have aimed to integrate the emotional component of memories within the DRM, for example, by employing negatively valenced word lists (vs neutral lists). Based on the fuzzy trace theory (Bookbinder & Brainerd, 2016; Reyna & Brainerd, 1995), negative information (vs neutral) may facilitate false memory formation by enhancing gist processing. Empirical evidence on the directionality of the effect is not fully clear-cut, specifically, the results on the recall test vary. Therefore, to get a more precise estimate of the DRM effect using negative content (vs neutral), we decided to conduct a paradigmatic replication of the effect.

title_r: Harnessing Simulated Experience to Help People Make Better Investment Decisions
abstract_r: In order to make satisfactory investment decisions, investors must know and understand the risks that they face. An investor's comprehension of risk can differ considerably depending on how that risk is learned or communicated. Finance professionals typically communicate risks using descriptions, for instance, in the form of financial reports, mutual fund brochures, insurance brochures, investor education programs, and market research. These documents report risks using summary of historical returns and their respective probabilities. However, investors could also acquire knowledge about financial risks in other ways, that is, by observing the development of stock prices or through their own investment experience. For instance, day-traders decide to purchase a stock by simply observing prior stock movements, or, individual investors increase their subscription to IPO auctions subsequent to previous successful experience (e.g., Kaustia & Knupfer, 2008). The literature documents that the manner in which knowledge about risks is acquired or communicated, has a dramatic influence on investor's understanding of risk and their willingness to accept it. For example, our previous work shows experimentally that people who learn about a stock market crash from experience are more likely to stay out of the market than people who learn from descriptions (i.e., the "depression babies" effect), even when wealth effects are kept equivalent (Lejarraga, Woike, & Hertwig, 2016). Recent studies have shown that, in general, people not only seem to be persuaded more by their experience than from described sources of information, but also may arrive at more accurate subjective assessments of a given risk, even if experience is simulated. For example, Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013) and Bradbury, Hens and Zeisberger (2014) show that simulations of the stock market, which are closer to the notion of witnessing than experiencing through action, help investors understand risk accurately, and lead them to invest more in the stock market than investors that learn from described sources. On the other hand, Lejarraga and Gonzalez (2011) show that exhaustive descriptive information is often neglected when the subjects have the chance to also experience the information by sampling. That is, people who have experience and descriptions, make choices as if descriptions were omitted. Consistent with this observation, Barron, Leider, and Stack (2007) show that people are more likely to ignore a described warning if they have already experienced a series of safe outcomes, but they are more likely to be persuaded by the warning if they have no previous experience. These studies converge in that people tend to overweight the information they gain from experience over that which is provided in a descriptive form, which can lead to more accurate risk assessments, as long as the experiences made are representative of the environment. Our studies attempt to extend previous research in two ways. First, we seek to conduct a conceptual replication of the study of Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013). This involves exposing participants in an investment task to four different risk communication interventions and observing how the interventions affect participants’ risk taking behaviour, factual knowledge about the encountered decision environmnet, and subjective assessments of confidence and satisfaction. Second, we will extend the study of Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013) by manipulating whether or not people have had prior experiences with the decision environment, when exposed to the risk communication intervention. Specifically, one group of people will build up experience with the decision environment by making a series of decisions with feedback prior to being exposed to the risk communication intervention, while the other group, akin to Kaufmann, Weber and Haisley (2013), will be given the risk communication intervention straight away. Using this setup, we will be able to provide a better estimate of how effective the four risk interventions are in informing people about financial risks in situations involving no prior experiences and explore how and whether prior experiences impact the effectiveness of the four interventions.

title_r: Replication of Eyewitness Accounts of Females and males (Powers, Andriks, & Loftus, 1979)
abstract_r: The proposed replication study will aim to explicate gender differences in the accuracy of eyewitness memory in the light of new suggested methodological and analytical rigour. The university students will be the participants. The basic aim is to carry out a study based on new suggestions that prescribe for the pre-determination of sample size based on power analysis and effect size. As per the current publication standards, the detailed biographic features will be included to make the findings more useful for the future replications, meta-analysis and generalization. In place of Washington Pre-College Test (1975) to measure the intelligence of the participants, the proposed study will use the Raven Progressive Matrices Test (John & Raven, 2003), a culture-free measure of Intelligence. Other reasons for using this measure are unavailability, inappropriateness for Indian sample and cultural issues. To screen out the participants on sex-stereotypes, an adapted version of Sex-Role Inventory (Broverman et al., 1972) or any other more relevant to the cognitive performance (eyewitness memory in this case.) will be used. The study will use filler activities slightly different from the original study. In place of slides, we will use two video-clips as witness materials. There is a slight difference in the analytic plan of the data. In place of only t-test, we plan to use a 2x2 ANOVA. There is no mention of age and other demographic details in the original study. In the proposed study, we will choose randomly male and female participants with the age ranging between 20 years to 25 years. We have applied for the Ethics Committee to the University where this study is proposed to be conducted. We will also collect informed consent from the participants.

title_r: Influence of label on categorization
abstract_r: The study is a conceptual replication of Lupyan et al. (2007) and it's about the investigation if redundant labels affect category formation. The aim of this experiment is to find out whether written linguistic terms, called labels, have an influence on categorisation performance, even if they are redundant. For this purpose, the participants will be divided into two groups, a label group and a no-label group. Both groups will be presented fish belonging to two categories (approach and avoid fish) and will have to learn and decide which category the fish belong to. In a training phase, both groups will receive auditory feedback after making their decision. The label group also receives written labels for the categories in the training phase. In a subsequent test phase it will be checked whether the categories have been learned and formed, in addition any feedback will be omitted. It is expected that labels will facilitate the learning and formation of categories.
