title_r: Yet another replication: Effects of Cognitive Load on Pragmatic vs. Logical Interpretations
abstract_r: In the preregistered experiment titled 'Another replication: Effects of Cognitive Load on Pragmatic vs. Logical Interpretations' we failed to replicate the previous findings of a negative relationship between cognitive load and the rate at which speakers compute implicatures (e.g. De Neys & Schaeken, 2007, Marty et al. 2013). This experiment is yet another attempt to replicate this result. The only factor that was changed in the current experiment is one aspect of the picture presentation: While in all previous experiments, the time of presentation for the picture was fixed, we now let subjects submit their sentence ratings ad libitum. This means that in contrast to previous experiments, subjects can control how much time they spent on processing the picture (given the sentence). Such a presentation is closer to the way stimuli were presented in the previous experiments we are attempting to replicate. It is worth noting, however, that the hypotheses underlying these previous studies do not predict that this variation should influence the results; nor does the interpretation of these results offered in the literature predict this influence.

title_r: Replication of Putting GPT's Creativity to the (Alternative Uses) Test
abstract_r: In this study, we examine whether we can replicate the findings of Stevenson and colleagues (2022), where the creative ability of GPT-3 was compared to human creativity on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) - one of the most widely used verbal creativity tests – to establish the current state of AI's ability to come up with original and useful ideas. However, developments in this field are rapid and plenty – making the original study possibly already outdated. Moreover, as the authors mentioned, the comparison was not quite fair, as there was a difference in language (Dutch responses translated to English for humans and English responses for GPT-3) and there were differences in the instructions for GPT-3 and humans, where standard instructions were used for humans and optimized instructions for GPT-3. With this study, we want to replicate the findings of Stevenson et al. (2022) with minimal task differences for human participants and GPT runs, we will use the newest GPT engine (GPT-3.5-turbo), and we want to use a larger sample size. We will use the same scoring methods as in the previous study, as well as new ones to improve upon the flexibility measure, a measure that is often confounded with fluency. Also, in order to assess the response sets as a whole instead of assessing each response individually we will include snapshot creativity (Silvia et al., 2009). With this study, we not only want to compare GPT's and people's creative abilities, but also gain insight into the creative process of both and bring to light any similarities and differences between them.

title_r: Moment-to-moment changes in “feeling moved” and how it relates to alexithymia and affect consciousness
abstract_r: According to the kama muta theory, emotional reactions that people often describe as “feeling moved” are typically instances of a distinct emotion that, within the theory, is called kama muta. The theory states that kama muta is elicited by the appraisal of a sudden intensification of a communal sharing relationship, positively valenced, and involves physiological sensations including goosebumps and a sense of warmth in the chest. Schubert et al. (2016) tested these statements by measuring participants’ moment-by-moment self-reported reactions to videos that are typically described as “very moving”. The current study is a conceptual replication and extension of Schubert et al. (2016). To address limitations of the between subject-measurements in the original study, we will measure correlations between time series of various reactions and experiences within subjects. We will also test kama muta theory against the theory that “feeling moved” when perceiving acts of outstanding morality is a distinct emotion labelled “elevation” (Haidt, 2003) and the view that “feeling moved” involves an interplay of positive and negative emotions (Menninghaus et al., 2015, 2017). Finally we will test whether measures of one’s ability to grasp one’s own emotions can explain why people differ in the degree to which they report feeling moved when exposed to stimuli considered to be “very moving”.

title_r: Resource Scarcity Priming and Face Perception: A Replication of Study 1 of Rodeheffer et al. (2012) in Japan
abstract_r: Research in multiple domains in the social sciences has shown that people narrow the range of their in-groups when resources are scarce. Recent psychological research has shown that resource scarcity also affects face perception. For example, in their first experiment, Rodeheffer et al. (2012) showed that White participants who viewed a slideshow depicting resource scarcity were more likely to judge biracial faces (created by averaging one White and one Black face) as Black than those who viewed a slideshow depicting resource abundance. This finding has theoretical and social impacts because it suggests that in-group narrowing due to resource scarcity can occur "unconsciously" in the "perception" stage, before attitudes and behaviors. However, almost all research showing resource scarcity's effect on face perception uses WEIRD samples. In addition, the replicability of the finding is a matter of debate. Therefore, in this study, we will conduct a replication study of Study 1 of Rodeheffer et al. (2012) in Japan. Because we will use the Japanese sample, the "in-group" is East Asian in this study. We will use South Asians as the "out-group" in this study (see our article for detailed reasons). This study will provide insights into the generalizability and replicability of the resource scarcity priming effect on face perception.

title_r: Children's Understanding of Aspectuality and False Belief– A Cross-Cultural, Multi-Method Approach
abstract_r: In this study, we aim to tackle two ongoing crises in developmental science on the replicability and generalizability of empirical research. That is, we will conceptually replicate a study by Rakoczy et al. (2015) showing that the development of false belief (FB) understanding (assessed by the classic change-of-location false belief task) around age 4 occurs in tandem with children’s aspectuality (Asp) understanding (assessed by a novel aspectuality change-of-location false belief task). By aspectuality understanding, we mean the understanding that other people’s beliefs/representations are aspectual, i.e., representing objects/situations always and necessarily under some aspect of description only. The original study draws conclusions from data from 3-6-year-old children from an urban German community. To test whether the developmental link between Asp and FB generalizes beyond Minority World communities, we will also run the study among children from two indigenous small-scale, rural communities: the Hai||om and the Khwe of Namibia. Given methodological issues in cross-cultural replication research (Syed & Kathawalla, 2022), the second focus of the study will be on comparing FB and Asp within two distinct task formats: first, we will test children in a pretense-heavy task format as they are typically applied and validated in Minority World contexts (see Rakoczy et al., 2015). For example, children are asked to predict the beliefs not of real-world agents but representations thereof (i.e., toy figurines) as these figurines engage with depictions of real-world objects. Since such task formats rely on children’s exposure to pretense and abstract reasoning, such protocols may introduce additional difficulties to children growing up without such cultural emphases (i.e., the rural Namibian children involved in this research). Thus, we intend to compare a pretense-heavy task format with a more interactive format in which the child is directly involved in the task while confronted with real-world objects and agents.

title_r: Replication of Boroditsky and Ramscar (2002), Study 2
abstract_r: Background People can think of time as moving toward themselves or moving away from themselves. These perceptions of time are categorized as the Ego-moving Perspective, where you think of yourself as moving forward through time, and the Time-moving Perspective, where you think of time as coming toward you (Boroditsky & Ramscar, 2002). It has been shown that adoption of these perspectives on time is influenced by our experiences acting in the world. Boroditsky & Ramscar’s (2002) demonstrate that moving through space in the world affects one’s perspective on time. Here, we focus on their Study 2. In this study, experimenters approached individuals in different places of a lunch line (i.e., 1st quarter of the line, 2nd quarter, etc.). They asked the individuals an ambiguous temporal question: “Next Wednesday’s meeting has been moved forward two days. What day is the meeting now that it has been rescheduled?” The question of interest is whether participants would indicate that the meeting was on Monday or Friday, and whether the participants’ location in the line would predict the odds of responding Monday or Friday. Boroditsky and Ramscar (2002) found that participants’ position in the line (indicating how much spatial motion they experienced moving through the line) affected their time perspective. Those further along in the line were more likely to think of themselves moving through time and therefore were more likely to respond that the meeting was now on Friday. Boroditsky and Ramscar’s (2002) study was one of the first experimental demonstrations of naturalistic spatial experience influencing the perception of time published in the cognitive science literature. To our knowledge, there has been no effort to replicate Boroditsky and Ramscar’s (2002) Study 2. The current pre-registered project represents an effort to replicate the original study as a means of assessing the generality of the effect. Research Questions and Predictions Our primary research question is as follows: Can we replicate the results of Boroditsky and Ramscar’s (2002) Study 2, where they observed that experiencing movement through a line affected participants’ perspective on time as demonstrated in their responses to the Monday/Friday question? Few studies have looked at the movement-space-time relationship in naturalistic settings and the more naturalistic studies such as Boroditsky and Ramscars’ (2002) Study 2 have not to our knowledge been replicated. A successful replication would provide further confidence that the space-time relationship can be observed to affect people’s behavior outside the lab, and that the effect generalizes across participant populations and locations. We predict that we will be able to successfully replicate Boroditsky and Ramscar’s (2002) results, demonstrating that participants who have moved through line for a longer time will be more likely to view themselves as moving through time, and will therefore be more likely to answer "Friday" to the question that is asked. Method Participants. Boroditsky and Ramscar’s (2002) original study had 70 participants. We will aim to collect data from 100 participants, or as many participants as we can get within the time constraints of our semester. Procedure. Experimenters will work in teams. One experimenter will monitor the targeted line and the other will approach individuals in the line for participation in the study. The experimenters will target a participant who arrived in line, and will start a timer to determine how long they have been waiting in the line at the point when they are approached to participate in the study (This is the “actual time” variable). The experimenters will either approach the prospective participant right after identifying them (so that they have not been waiting in line very long; first third of the line), or wait until they have reached the middle of the line (second third of line) or the front of the line (final third of the line). The experimenter will approach the prospective participant and indicate that we are doing a psychology experiment that involves answering two questions. If they consent to participate, we will ask the critical question: Next Wednesday’s meeting has been moved forward two days. What day is the meeting now that it has been rescheduled? Once the participant answers, the experimenter will ask them how long they have been waiting in line (this is the “estimated time” variable). After getting the response, the experimenter will thank the participant for their time. Data Analysis The primary dependent variable in our task is the binary coding of participants’ responses (0 = Monday, 1 = Friday). We will analyze this variable using logistic regression. In the regression model, we will predict the odds of a “Friday” response from the participants based on the participants’ position in the line (coded as a continuous variable: first third = 1, second third = 2, final third = 3), their estimated time in line (responses in minutes, as specified in the Method section), and their actual time in line (responses in minutes, as specified in the Method section). Boroditsky and Ramscar (2002) found that position in line and estimated time in line predicted the odds of a “Friday” response when analyzed alone, but that estimated time in line was the only significant predictor when both variables were included in their analysis. On this basis, we predict that our logistic regression should show that estimated time in line is a significant predictor of “Friday” responses and that position in line is not a significant predictor when both variables are present in the analysis. Our analysis will also allow us to assess whether estimated time in line is a significant predictor of “Friday” responses when the participants’ actual time in line is also included in the analysis. We do not have strong predictions about which of these two measures of the participants’ duration in line will be a significant predictor of “Friday” responses, though we expect that one (or both) should predict the participants’ responses. Such a finding would be considered a replication of Boroditsky and Ramscar’s (2002) finding that movement through a line affects the way that participants think about time.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Karraker & DeLamater (2013), From the Journal of Marriage and Family
abstract_r: The claim selected from Karraker & DeLamater (2013) is that, among married men and women, remarriage is associated with a lower odds of sexual inactivity. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Characteristics such as marital happiness, premarital cohabitation, and remarriage are also associated with levels of inactivity or activity." The claim is tested using survey data collected from married adults ages 57 to 85. title_r: Exploring the development of racial biases
abstract_r: Our study intends to follow up on the Perszyk et al., 2019 study that assessed 30 4- to 5-year-olds’ implicit and explicit responses to other children that varied systematically in both race (White and Black) and gender (male and female). Study 2 found that children responded less positively to Black neutral faces than White neutral faces. Importantly though, the sample size of the study was small and participants were predominantly White children from a majority White middle-class US community. Thus, in the present study we aim to replicate the findings, but with a larger and more diverse sample in order to extend the generalizability of these findings, and more specifically examine the extent to which the findings from the original study which was done with only White children also extend to children of color.

title_r: Levels of Processing Effects on Memory for Color-Object Associations
abstract_r: To investigate whether the levels of processing framework also applies to basic perceptual features in visual associative memory, we replicate and extend a study by Ovalle-Fresa et al. (2021) in an online setting. Specifically, we replicate Experiment 3, where participants encoded the colors of objects for later recall. Participants encoded the object-color associations either under deep or shallow encoding conditions. Depending on the levels of processing condition, participants either indicated whether the object was pleasant for them or whether there was a straight line in the object. The pleasantness judgement represents the deep encoding condition and the line judgement represents the shallow encoding condition. Here we expect to replicate the result of better associative memory for the deep encoding condition compared to the shallow encoding condition. Because several other alternative explanations are possible for this finding, we further extended the study by manipulating the levels of processing through different encoding instructions. Specifically, in the deep encoding condition participants were asked to compare the real size of the object to the size of a displayed reference object (i.e., a shoebox) in real life. In the shallow condition, participants were asked to compare the actual size of a displayed object (i.e., shoebox) on the screen. If the levels of processing framework applies to basic perceptual features in visual associative memory, we should find a similar pattern: better memory for deep encoding condition compared to the shallow encoding condition. Such a pattern would support the conclusion that the reason for the difference in memory performance in the original experiment lies in levels of processing differences and rules out possible alternative explanations for the memory benefit in the pleasantness judgment condition (e.g., relevance of color or the self, or a broader attentional focus in the pleasantness judgment).

title_r: Implicit and explicit tax aversion and its behavioral outcomes: study 1 – preregistration plan
abstract_r: Tax aversion is quite a novel phenomenon in the field of fiscal psychology. The term ‘tax aversion’ refers to an individual propensity in escaping taxes more pronounced than the equal tendency in avoiding any other sort of payments. The current proposal aims at investigating tax aversion employing both implicit and explicit attitudinal measures to determine the presence and the extent of the phenomenon in the Italian context. The current study is part of a comprehensive research project composed by three independent studies. Each study aims to measure both implicit and explicit attitudes towards taxes, by employing the Implicit Association Test, a close replication of experiments 1 and 2 of Sussman and Olivola (2011), and two different validated scales measuring explicit attitude (Tax Compliance Inventory TAX-I (Kirchler, Wahl, 2010); Perceived Fiscal Sacrifice Scale (Ferrari, Randisi, 2013).

title_r: Curiosity as a function of retrieval failures in younger and older adults
abstract_r: Curiosity is the desire to seek information. Multiple different theories are used to explain what kinds of information trigger curiosity. One of the models with the most support is the "Region of Proximal Learning" model of curiosity (Metcalfe et al., 2020). According to this model, people are more curious about "almost known" items. That is, if you have no knowledge about the topic, you won't be curious. Similarly, if you are certain of the answer, your curiosity levels will be low. However, if you are on the verge of knowing the information, your curiosity will peak (Metcalfe et al., 2017). Thus, in the context of new learning, an inverted U-shaped function relates curiosity and perceived success in learning. In the current work, we are addressing whether a similar relationship between curiosity and retrieval of known information is apparent. Specifically, in the context of retrieval from the knowledge base, retrieval failures might elicit different levels of curiosity. Previous work examined the relationship between four phenomenological experiences of retrieval failure and curiosity. As expected, curiosity varied as a function of the type of retrieval failure, with answers close to the accessibility threshold resulting in higher curiosity in younger adults (Lee et al., manuscript in preparation). Here, we extend this work to an older population. Curiosity is associated with improved memory (McGillivray et al., 2015) and with a multitude of benefits for healthy aging (Sakaki et al., 2018). Therefore, studying curiosity in aging is of extreme importance. Studies on the effect of aging on curiosity have yielded mixed results. It is thought that curiosity declines in aging (Sakaki et al., 2018). Nonetheless, it seems like the difference is not necessarily on curiosity levels in general, but on the kinds of information that trigger curiosity. Individuals are more likely to seek information to which they attribute the most value, and these preferences differ between younger and older adults (Swirsky & Spaniol, 2024). Previous studies using general knowledge questions found no age-related differences in levels of curiosity but showed that uncertainty is only associated with curiosity in younger adults (Camp et al., 1985). As such, it is possible that older adults would not show the same trends predicted as younger adults. In this study, younger and older adults will be presented with 100 general knowledge questions. They will be given the option to give the answer, or indicate the kind of retrieval failure they are undergoing (It’s on the tip of my tongue, It’s in there somewhere, I used to know but forgot, and I never knew). Participants will then be asked to rate their curiosity on a 7-point Likert Scale. Finally, participants will be asked to answer the same questions on a final multiple-choice memory test. With this study, we hope to replicate the findings that curiosity increases for "almost known" items using the four phenomenological experiences of retrieval failure. We also hope to establish how aging affects curiosity, specifically, if aging changes the relationship between curiosity and the distance from the threshold of accessibility.

title_r: Registered Report [Stage 1]: Can Agentic Black Women Get Ahead? An Experiment Revisited
abstract_r: Livingston et al. (2012) found that Black women were buffered against gender backlash; whether Black women were dominant or supportive towards an employee did not affect people’s perceptions of them as leaders in an organization. In contrast, White women incurred a status penalty for being dominant. Twelve years later, no direct replication has been published, and related research reached different conclusions: that Black women experience the most gender backlash for being dominant (as a politician) or that race does not affect gender backlash (for expressing anger). Given the seemingly contradictory results and limitations of previous research (e.g. no preregistration and small sample size), the relationship between race and gender backlash warrants reexamination. In this registered report, we conduct a high-powered, direct replication and extension of the primary findings in Livingston et al.

abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Buchner et al. (2009) is that source memory is better for faces encountered in a cheating context than for faces associated with a context of trustworthiness. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "In contrast, source memory for faces associated with a history of cheating (i.e., memory for the cheating context in which the face was encountered) was consistently better than source memory for other types of faces". This claim is tested by the within-subject independent variables being behavioral history (cheating, irrelevant, trustworthy) and the DV of interest being the change in the source memory model parameter d when the model is constrained with the null hypothesis (dCheat = dTrust, or the probability of recognizing a cheater’s face = the probability of recognizing a trusted face), measured with the goodness of fit statistic G squared and tested by calculating a chi squared goodness-of-fit statistic, which resulted in dCheat (the probability of recognizing a cheater's face) = dTrust (probability of recognizing a trusted face), delta G squared (1) = 9.07, using a chi squared goodness-of-fit test, p< 0.01.

title_r: Religion & the Dictator Game Online Study
abstract_r: Does religion promote prosocial behaviour? Despite numerous publications that seem to answer this question affirmatively, divergent results from recent meta-analyses and pre-registered replication efforts suggest the issue is not yet settled. Additional uncertainty lingers around whether (a) the effects of religious cognition on prosocial behaviour obtain through implicit cognitive processes, explicit cognitive processes, or both; and (b) whether religious cognition increases generosity only among people disinclined to share with anonymous strangers. Here we propose two experiments designed to address these concerns. In Experiment 1 we will seek to replicate Shariff and Norenzayan’s demonstration of the effects of implicit religious priming on Dictator Game offers to anonymous strangers; unlike Shariff and Norenzayan, however, we will use an online environment where anonymity is virtually assured. In Experiment 2, we will introduce a “taking” option to allow greater expression of baseline selfishness. In both experiments, we will seek to activate religious cognition implicitly and explicitly. Finally, we will use multiple methods to meta-analyse all available experiments that test the effect of religious priming on Dictator Game transfers. Our results will provide new insight into an important interdisciplinary issue, and guidance on how best to activate religious cognition in the laboratory.

title_r: The influence of anchor biases on flexible social preference comparisons.
abstract_r: Self preferences oftentimes overly inform how people make inferences about others. Yet, it remains unclear whether this sort of social anchoring and adjustment away from self preferences persists when comparing different individuals to wider society. One intriguing possibility is that self anchor biases distort reference frame transformations even when comparing individuals’ social preferences to the world at large. We developed a task that examines whether self-anchoring biases influence the comparison of strangers’ preferences to different individuals and groups. In our experiment, participants give a social preference rating for themselves, as well as individuals and groups that can be either similar or dissimilar to the participant. Subsequently, participants infer a stranger’s preferences learned relative to one of two previously rated individuals, and decide how the stranger’s preferences relate to the similar or dissimilar group. We aim to replicate an observation in previous work of self anchoring and adjustment biases towards similar individuals and extend this finding to similar groups. Consequently, we anticipate that self-anchor biases will distort transformation of social preferences when assimilating a stranger's preferences into a more global ‘allocentric’ reference frame.

title_r: Receptivity to Instructional Feedback: Replication and Examination of its Links to Motivation and Cognitive Ability in Secondary School
abstract_r: Feedback models assume individual differences in student’s willingness or readiness to accept feedback (Lipnevich et al., 2016; see Panadero & Lipnevich, 2021 for an overview of models). Receptivity to instructional feedback (RIF; Lipnevich et al., 2021) may be a prerequisite for feedback to be effective and thus explain the heterogeneous findings in feedback research (Wisniewski et al., 2020). RIF comprises of four components: Experiential Attitudes, Instrumental Attitudes, Cognitive Engagement, and Behavioural Engagement (Lipnevich et al., 2021). This study aims to examine RIF's links to related students characteristics, namely to personality traits, motivation and cognitive ability, which all have been identified to play a vital role in the feedback process. Moreover, this study aims to link RIF to academic achievement. Specifically this study addresses the following research questions: 1. Does the German version of the RIF scale show a four-factor structure? 2. Is there a global receptivity factor, next to the four-factors proposed by Lipnevich et al. (2021)? 3. Does the RIF instrument measure equally across gender? 4. Are RIF components (Experiential Attitudes, Instrumental Attitudes, Cognitive Engagement, and Behavioural Engagement) related to Big-Five personality factors (Openness, Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism)? 5. Are RIF components (Experiential Attitudes, Instrumental Attitudes, Cognitive Engagement, and Behavioural Engagement) related to motivation? 6. Are RIF components (Experiential Attitudes, Instrumental Attitudes, Cognitive Engagement, and Behavioural Engagement) related to cognitive ability? 7. Are RIF components (Experiential Attitudes, Instrumental Attitudes, Cognitive Engagement, and Behavioural Engagement) related to achievement in school?

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Alves et al. (2018), from Psychological Science
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Alves et al (2018​, Experiment 1)​ is that because a novel group is associated with and evaluated on the basis of their unique attributes, participants prefer the first of two ‘alien’ groups when unique traits are negative and shared attributes are positive, but the reverse is true when the unique attributes are positive and shared attributes are negative. This reflects the following from the papers abstract: “Participants preferred the first group over the novel group as long as the groups’ unique attributes were negative.” The claim was tested using a chi-squared test comparing participants’ choice for either the first or second of two ‘alien’ groups, across two conditions where the alien tribes displayed either three shared positive and three unique negative traits or three shared negative and three unique positive traits. When shared traits were positive and unique traits were negative, most participants preferred the first tribe over the second tribe (first: n = 68; second: n = 36). In contrast, when shared traits were negative and unique traits were positive, most participants preferred the second tribe over the first tribe (first: n = 44; second: n = 62), chi squared(1, N = 210) = 12.02, p < .001; φ = −.24

abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This registration serves as an amendment to the focal hypothesis in the previously registered replication of a research claim from Trémolière et al. (2012), from Cognition. The original registration can be found here: https://osf.io/a7gd2.

summary: This registration serves as an amendment to our original preregistration (available here: https://osf.io/a7gd2). We have updated the SCORE focal hypothesis (H*) to more precisely define the pattern of findings expected for a replication.

The original H* was defined as: "a significant interaction between the mortality salience condition (death vs. pain, between subjects) and the scenario type (harm-conflict vs. harm control, within subjects), where the pattern of this interaction is such that people in the death condition are less likely to give utilitarian responses to the harm-conflict scenarios."

The pattern of findings expected for a replication have been more precisely defined as the following: "We expect that people in the death condition give less utilitarian response than people in the pain condition on the harm-conflict dilemmas, whereas we expect that there will be no (or significantly smaller) effect of death/pain condition on harm-control dilemmas."

We have collected about 2/3 of our intended final sample at the point of this amendment. We have reached our first stopping point (230 participants), where we found no significant interaction. Since this point, we collected 100 more participants, but have not yet computed the statistical test, nor did we look at the group level averages in any way.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Yoo et al. (2017), from Psychological Science
abstract_r: The claim selected from Yoo et al. (2017) is that in representative population samples from the United States and Japan, the linkage between positive affect and blood lipids differs: positive affect is positively associated with healthy lipid profiles in the United States, whereas this association is absent in Japan. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “As predicted, positive affect was associated with healthier lipid profiles for Americans but not for Japanese.” HDL-C (high-density lipoprotein cholesterol) was log-transformed and regressed on positive affect (centered at the mean within cultures), culture (coded as a binary variable; U.S. = .5, Japan = −.5), and the interaction between culture and affect. The final model also included negative affect and demographic and health status variables including age, gender, years of education, chronic health conditions, and use of cholesterol medication. This analysis yielded a significant interaction between positive affect and culture for HDL-C (high-density lipoprotein cholesterol), b = 0.022, 95% confidence interval (CI) = [0.001, 0.045], partial eta squared = .03, t(1372) = 2.00, p = .046.

title_r: Study 1: Conceptual Replication of Children’s Preferences for Shared-Language Speakers
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Background.
This is a conceptual replication of the study conducted with 5-year-old children described in Kinzler et al. (2007). The original study showed 8 monolingual English-speaking children, two children speaking: one spoke in French and one in English. They found that participants preferred to have the child who spoke the same language as them (English) as their friend.

The purpose of this study is to conceptually replicate these findings with a different type of stimuli that we plan to use in a subsequent study with a different research question. Here, children will observe puppets speaking, instead of human children. We will ask if children prefer speakers of their shared language, even when the speakers are puppets.

Logic and Hypotheses.
Question: Will 4-to-5-year-old, monolingual English-speaking children choose English-speaking puppets as their friends?
Hypothesis: We expect that 4-to-5-year-old children will choose the English-speaking puppet to be their friend, in line with Kinzler et al.’s (2007) results.
Interpretation: If this is the case, we will interpret this as evidence that children prefer puppets who speak their language.
Alternative: If children choose both puppets equally often or choose the non-shared language puppet it would suggest they do not interpret the language spoken by puppets the same way as humans.

summary: Background.
This is a conceptual replication of the study conducted with 5-year-old children described in Kinzler et al. (2007). The original study showed 8 monolingual English-speaking children, two children speaking: one spoke in French and one in English. They found that participants preferred to have the child who spoke the same language as them (English) as their friend.

The purpose of this study is to conceptually replicate these findings with a different type of stimuli that we plan to use in a subsequent study with a different research question. Here, children will observe puppets speaking, instead of human children. We will ask if children prefer speakers of their shared language, even when the speakers are puppets.

Logic and Hypotheses.
Question: Will 4-to-5-year-old, monolingual English-speaking children choose English-speaking puppets as their friends?
Hypothesis: We expect that 4-to-5-year-old children will choose the English-speaking puppet to be their friend, in line with Kinzler et al.’s (2007) results.
Interpretation: If this is the case, we will interpret this as evidence that children prefer puppets who speak their language.
Alternative: If children choose both puppets equally often or choose the non-shared language puppet it would suggest they do not interpret the language spoken by puppets the same way as humans.

Sample Plan.
We will test at least 25 children, or until we reach a Bayes Factor of 10 for our alternative hypothesis, with a maximum of 50 children (refer to analyses below).  Participants will be monolingual English-speaking children (i.e., children exposed to English 90-100% of the time) based in the United States.

Participants.
Participants will be children of 4 and 5 years of age (i.e., 48 months and 0 days to and 71 months and 15 days) of age from the United States, expanding on the age found in previous literature to show a language-based social preference (Kinzler et al., 2007).

Design.
This study will take place via synchronous recorded online video-chat sessions to increase the accessibility of our research. Here, we measure children’s social preference for puppets who either share their language or do not share their language. The study will follow a within-subjects design, which means each participant will be shown two pairs of puppets.

Procedure.
Each child will be shown videos of two sets of puppets speaking towards the camera. In each set one of the puppets will speak the same language as the participant, (English) and one of the puppets will speak a different language (French or Hindi).

After each trial’s familiarization video, children will be played an audio clip of each puppet over a screenshot of the two puppets facing the camera. They will be asked “Which puppet sounded like this?” as an attention check to ensure they can accurately link the puppets with their respective shared and non-shared languages.

Then, accompanied by the same screenshot of the two puppets side-by-side, children will be asked the following questions: “Whom would you like to have as your friend?” and “Why is that?” (Kinzler et al., 2007).

Dependent Variables.
The primary dependent measure will be a 0-1 binary response of “shared” or “non-shared”. This refers to whether children select the puppet that spoke in English (shared language) or the puppet that spoke in Hindi or French (non-shared language) in response to the question, “Whom would you like to have as your friend?”.

Primary analysis.
To analyze the data, we will run one-sample one-sided Bayesian binomial tests for children’s responses in JASP (JASP Team, 2024), which compares the likelihood of the data given the null hypothesis that children will be at chance in choosing the puppets who share their language or not to the alternative hypothesis that children will choose the puppet who shares their language more than half of the time. We will look at the data as a whole (across both conditions) and within each condition.

Secondary Analyses.
Children’s Explanations: Exploratory qualitative analysis on the open-ended “Why?” question where children explain their choice.

In secondary analyses, we will compare across conditions (Hindi versus French). We will use a mixed effects model to test for effects of condition using the package brms: Outcome ~ Condition + (1 | Participant). Where, “Outcome” refers to whether participants chose the shared-language puppet, and “Condition” refers to the order of the puppets sets (English-French or English-Hindi first) and position and color of the shared-language puppet.

We will also test for order effects by running a model with Outcome ~ Condition*Order + (1 | Participant), where order is whether the Hindi or French condition came first, though we will likely be underpowered to find an interaction.
Decisions about whether a participant and/or participant test trial is excluded will be determined before their data are analyzed.

Exclusion Criteria.
Participant test trials will be marked as missing based on the following criteria:
Experimenter error (e.g., the experimenter goes off script); Not choosing one puppet or saying “I don’t know”; Giving two responses and not confirming a single answer on the binary measure; Parental or outside interference: (i.e., an individual tells the participant what response to say to the experimenter); Participants who are not between the ages of 4 years 0 months 0 days and 5 years 11 months 15 days; Children who fail the attention check questions after 2 repetitions.

Participants will be excluded and replaced if they meet any of the above criteria, either determined live at the time of the study or when reviewed after the experiment. 

Pilot data.
We initially ran a between-subjects pilot for this study. Nine out of 11 participants in this version chose the English-speaking puppet.

Next, we collected within-subjects (n=5) and found that 7 out of 10 choices were made in favor of the English-speaking puppet.

The current pilot data are trending towards the expected outcome, that monolingual English-speaking children will prefer the English-speaking puppet as their friend.

References.
Kinzler, K. D., Dupoux, E., & Spelke, E. S. (2007). native language of social cognition. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 104(30), 12577–12580. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0705345104

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Böhnke & Link (2017), from European Sociological Review
abstract_r: The claim selected from Böhnke & Link (2017) is that, as a consequence of poverty, people reduce the frequency of gathering together with others and downsize visits with/from friends, acquaintances, or neighbours, which confirms the accumulation hypothesis; the finding for frequency of gathering together is the portion selected. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Our results support central findings from cross-sectional studies with a longitudinal research design: contacts frequencies and the resource potential of a network decline; however, contacts to family members and the number of close friends remain unaffected." To identify the effects of poverty on social relationships, the authors regress the described dummy variable poverty status on the different measures of social relationships using a fixed-effects approach. Although four of the five dependent variables are ordinal, and one is a count variable (close friends), the authors show the linear regression models’ results and compare the coefficients between the different models. Figure 2a and b shows selected coefficients of the multiple fixed-effects regressions. The full regression tables can be found in the appendix. The selected dependent variable is ‘get together,’ and the selected comparison is ‘poor vs. not poor’ (see Figure 2 and ‘Get-together’ model in Table A2 for details). The fixed-effects model shows that the frequency of gathering together with other people is reduced in reaction to poverty. This effect is statistically significant at the minimum on a 95 per cent level, but it is small (-0.0291 (get together) on a four-point scale) (from ‘Get-together’ model in Table A2, ‘Poor’ term: estimate = -0.0291; SE clustered on person level = 0.0091; P < 0.01 [two-tailed test]).

title_r: A replication of an experiment "On the Interaction of Theory and Data in Concept Learning"
abstract_r: Project Description: This project aims to replicate the seminal experiment from Murphy and Allopenna's (1994) study "On the Interaction of Theory and Data in Concept Learning," which investigates how theoretical knowledge influences the learning and categorization of concepts. The original study demonstrated that people do not merely rely on observable data to form categories but also use prior theoretical knowledge to guide their learning, interpretation, and generalization of concepts. In this replication, the objective is to validate the original findings by examining the interplay between theory-driven expectations and data-driven evidence during the process of concept acquisition. Participants will be presented with a series of learning tasks where they are required to categorize stimuli based on given rules or theories and the observable features of the stimuli. The experiment will manipulate the alignment or conflict between theoretical information and presented data to observe how participants integrate these sources of information when forming concepts. The replication will utilize a similar experimental design, employing PsychoPy and Pavlovia for data collection. This approach ensures methodological rigor while allowing for efficient, web-based participant recruitment and testing. By successfully replicating this study, the project will enhance the understanding of how humans learn and apply concepts, particularly in situations where theoretical expectations and empirical data interact.

title_r: Another Replication: Effects of Cognitive Load on Pragmatic vs. Logical Interpretations
abstract_r: In the preregistered experiment titled 'Replication: Effects of Cognitive Load on Pragmatic vs. Logical Interpretations' we failed to replicate the previous findings of a negative relationship between cognitive load and the rate at which speakers compute implicatures (e.g. De Neys & Schaeken, 2007, Marty et al. 2013). This experiment is another attempt to replicate this result. The only difference between this experiment and our previous attempt is that in this experiment we are presenting the context picture against which our target sentences are judged in one frame, while previously the elements of the picture were presented in a sequence of 6 frames. Such a presentation is closer to the way stimuli were presented in the previous experiments we are attempting to replicate. It is worth noting, however, that the hypotheses underlying these previous studies do not predict that this variation in picture presentation should influence the results; nor does the interpretation of these results offered in the literature predict this influence.

title_r: Implicit and explicit tax aversion and its behavioral outcomes: study 3 – preregistration plan
abstract_r: Tax aversion is quite a novel phenomenon in the field of fiscal psychology. The term ‘tax aversion’ refers to an individual propensity in escaping taxes more pronounced than the equal tendency in avoiding any other sort of payments. The current proposal aims to investigate tax aversion employing both implicit and explicit attitudinal measures to determine the presence and the extent of the phenomenon in the Italian context. The current study is part of a comprehensive research project composed by three independent studies. Each study aims to measure both implicit and explicit attitudes towards taxes, by employing the Implicit Association Test, a close replication of experiments 1 and 2 of Sussman and Olivola (2011), and two different validated scales measuring explicit attitude (Tax Compliance Inventory TAX-I (Kirchler, Wahl, 2010); Perceived Fiscal Sacrifice Scale (Ferrari, Randisi, 2013).

title_r: Do price endings still communicate value and quality? Analysing image effects in a scenario-based approach.
abstract_r: The effects of price endings have been investigated for decades (e.g., Bader and Weinland,1932), but the results are still inconsistent. The intention of our study is to examine the existence of image effects of price endings, as extensively elaborated by Schindler (1991) and to determine their strength. Within the broad field of image effects we are particu-larly interested in the subcategories quality image and price image. Some study results indicate that 9-ending prices convey the feeling of good value for money (Schindler, 1991; Naipaul & Parsa, 2001; Schindler & Kibarian, 2001; Schindler, 2006) but the impression of poor quality (Schindler, 1991; Schindler & Kibarian, 2001), while 0-ending prices give the impression of good quality (Schindler, 1991; Naipaul & Parsa, 2001), but appear more expensive (Schindler, 1991). We will specifically investigate the image effects of 9-ending prices, that fall just below a round price and 0-ending prices. Our study is strongly orientated towards the methods used by Naipaul and Parsa (2001) and can be seen as conceptual replication. We will present a scenario to the participants that will cause the necessity of purchasing a new bicycle and either requests a decision based on value for money or product quality. Then we will show two exem-plary online shops that differ in their price endings to evaluate whether the given scenario has an influence on the preference for a certain price ending. Moreover, we will exploratively analyze situational und personal influences.

title_r: Effects of goal-oriented unconscious thinking on logical problem solving.
abstract_r: When making decisions and judgments, we employ deliberate logical thinking or intuition. Many dual-process models assume that analytical Type 2 operates at a conscious level, while intuitive Type 1 functions subconsciously (Evans & Stanovich, 2013). In contrast, unconscious thinking in the Unconscious Thought Theory (UTT; Dijksterhuis and Nordgren, 2006; Dijksterhuis and Strick, 2016) possesses both Type 1 and Type 2 properties, deviating from established dual-process models. UTT suggests that unconscious thinking operates beyond consciousness while being goal-directed over time. In other words, UTT's unconscious thinking might not align with the dual-process model's processing style. It exhibits distinct attributes at the unconscious level, encompassing aspects of careful and analytical processing. While there are partial similarities with Type 2 of the dual-process theory, operating at a conscious level, notable differences also exist. Regarding UTT's goal-oriented thinking, a study by Garrison & Handley (2017) illustrated that engaging in goal-oriented unconscious thinking improves logical reasoning performance compared to not doing so. In the realm of conscious and unconscious thinking, as per dual-process theory, relying more on conscious thinking (deliberation) generally yields better performance than primarily depending on unconscious thinking (intuition). The present study will be a conceptual replication of the original task used in the previous study (Garrison & Handley, 2017) on improving performance on logical reasoning tasks.

title_r: The effect of Working Memory Encoding on Subsequent Long-Term Memory Representations: Sequential Presentation
abstract_r: We are exploring wheter Working Memory (WM) encoding enhance the subsequent Long-Term Memory (LTM) representations, using sequential presentation. This study is a close replication of Forsberg, A., Guitard, D., & Cowan, N. (2020). Working memory limits severely constrain long-term retention. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 1-11, but uses sequential (instead of simultaneous) presentation in the working memory task. First, participants will study a total of 288 unique memory items in a WM task, at varying set sizes. Each item will be presented by itself (i.e., sequential presentation), for 250 ms followed by a blank interval of 250 ms, and then the next item. After all items in a set have been presented, there will be a 2000 ms delay. Each participant will complete 88 WM trials (48 trials at set size 2, 24 trials at set size 4, 16 trials at set size 6). Hence, participants will see a total of 96 items at each set size (set size 2, 48 trials x 2 items; set size 4, 24 trials x 4 items, set size 6, 16 trials x 6 items). The order of trials and items will be randomized for each participant. Next, participants will complete a brief distraction task (60 seconds). During this task, participants will verify mathematical equations of the form a×b+c=d, where a, b, and c were integers from 1 to 9 and d was equal to a×b +c or differed from that expression by ±1. The integers for a, b, and c will be drawn randomly with replacement from the integers 1 to 9, inclusive. The results of the equations d will have a 50% chance of being correct. Participants click respond by clicking “Correct” “Incorrect” on the screen. Memory will be measured in the WM tasks, and then again in the LTM task. In the WM task, participants will respond to a central probe item, by clicking on one of the following options on the screen: : I'm sure I saw it’, ‘I think I saw it’, ‘I guess I saw it’, ‘I guess I didn't see it’, ‘I don't think I saw it’, or ‘I'm sure I didn't see it’ In the LTM task, participants will respond to each probe item clicking on one of the following options on the screen: ‘I'm sure I saw it’, ‘I think I saw it’, ‘I guess I saw it’, ‘I guess I didn't see it’, ‘I don't think I saw it’, or ‘I'm sure I didn't see it’. Items which were probed in the WM task will not be probed in the LTM task. Each participant will respond to a total of 272 items in the LTM test (136 new items, 36 items from set size 2, 40 items from set size 4, and 60 items from set size 6).

title_r: Does the corollary discharge provide the sensory content of inner speech? A preregistered direct replication and extension of Scott (2013)
abstract_r: The mental production of speech or "inner speech" is a remarkable and foundational ability in humans, involved in many daily activities such as reading, writing, remembering, or planning. Inner speech is generally accompanied by a subjective multisensory (mainly auditory) experience. However, the cognitive processes leading to these sensory percepts remain poorly known. One prominent perspective is that the sensory content of inner speech would correspond to the predicted sensory consequences of inhibited speech acts. Scott (2013) provided experimental evidence suggesting that inner speech indeed involves the mental simulation of speech acts, as evidenced by sensory attenuation of the concomitant perception of external speech sounds. However, Scott (2013) assessed silent speech, but not inner speech, which in contrast to silent speech, does not involve visible articulatory movements. The present work aims to replicate and extend the study of Scott (2013) to assess whether inner speech attenuates the perception of concomitant external speech sounds.

title_r: Hotels re-explored: experience and influence of normative appeals
abstract_r: We are conducting an extended conceptual replication of Goldstein et al. (2007; 2008). Goldstein et al., 2008 is an influential study, cited 3568 times (Google scholar: 22/10/19), showing that appealing to social norms is more influential than appealing to the environment when aiming to persuade hotel guests to reuse their towels (i.e., act more sustainable during their visit). Results have been replicated, showing both consistent (e.g., Mair &amp; Bergin-Seers, 2010; Reese et al., 2014; Schultz et al., 2008) and conflicting results (Bohner &amp; Schlüter, 2014). In synthesizing these findings, a Bayesian meta-analysis confirmed that social norms are indeed more effective overall than environmental appeals (Scheibehenne et al., 2016).

title_r: Replication of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.

title_r: Accelerated CREP - RRR: Turri, Buckwalter, &amp; Blouw (2015)
abstract_r: According to the Justified True Belief (JTB) account of knowledge, a person’s ability to know something is defined by having a belief that is both justified and true (i.e., knowledge is justified true belief). However, this account fails to consider the role of luck. In 1963, Gettier argued that JTB is insufficient because it does not account for certain situations, called Gettier cases, wherein a person is justified for believing something true but only because of luck. It is unclear whether lay people’s intuitions about knowledge lead them to agree with Gettier, such that lay people believe that individuals in these cases lack knowledge (referred to as Gettier intuitions). We attempt to provide a robust estimate of the Gettier intuition effect size by replicating Turri and colleagues’ (2015) Experiment 1. The Collaborative Replications and Education Project (CREP) selected this study for replication based on its undergraduate appeal, feasibility, and pedagogical value. However, in light of some inconsistent results, suboptimal designs, and inconsistent evidence for cultural variation (e.g., Machery et al., 2015; Nagel, et al., 2013; Seyedsayamdost et al., 2015; Starman &amp; Friedman, 2012; Weinberg et al., 2001), the improved methodology of Turri et al. (2015) make it an important study to replicate cross-culturally. Therefore, we propose a multisite collaborative preregistered replication of Turri and colleague's (2015) Experiment 1 (35 labs from 14 countries across 4 continents signed up at time of submission; expected minimum N = 1,500). Results of this study are expected to provide a clearer picture of the Gettier intuition effect size, lay people’s theory and practice of knowledge, and potentially cross-cultural similarities and differences. title_r: Do Weapon Primes Increase Aggression?
abstract_r: Berkowitz and LePage (1967) provided the first evidence that merely exposing participants to guns increases their aggression (i.e., the weapons effect). A recent meta-analysis revealed that this weapon priming increased aggressive behavior, cognitions, and appraisals. Yet, the effect on aggressive behavior was small (d = .21) and potentially inflated by multiple sources of bias. We therefore propose to conduct a high-powered, pre-registered conceptual replication and extension of the weapons effect. We adapted a recently validated, within-subject behavior-priming paradigm to test this effect. On each trial, participants will be shown a picture of a gun or a chair, and aggression will be measured through participantsâ decisions to steal raffle tickets from an ostensible opponent. Two hundred and sixty-one participants from three different locations varying in gun-ownership rates (Wyoming, U.S., Pennsylvania, U.S., and New South Wales, Australia) will complete this task. If the weapons effect is robust, we expect to replicate it in this task. Furthermore, this study will allow us to examine the potential moderating effects of gun ownership, gun usage, participant gender, trait aggression, and cultures/locations with varying gun ownership. Our study will provide a statistically powerful opportunity to conceptually replicate and extend an effect with important societal implications.

title_r: Assessment of research quality, scholarly productivity and citation impact of UK academic psychologists and clustering of UK universities into groupings: A replication and extension study.
abstract_r: It is no question that higher education institutions in the United Kingdom (UK) excel in research, development and innovation. Such productivity in the education sector massively contributes to economic growth, with the government investing billions of dollars each year to actively encourage research excellence (Hewitt-Dundas, 2012). A study by Mazzucchelli et al., (2019) examined the impact of research productivity of Australian academic psychologists and tried to understand how an increase in research productivity at universities forms the basis for judgments concerning various matters. They observed that academics in various university groupings (like the Group of Eight) and academic levels (professor, lecturer) differed in terms of lifetime citation, number of publications and h-index. These differences can have a two-fold impact - on an institutional level, these can influence rankings of universities, funding and prestige. On an individual academic’s level, research productivity informs decisions about job selection, career progression and research grant applications. The aim of this study is to understand if these findings replicate in the context of the United Kingdom by observing research patterns across various university groupings that exist in the United Kingdom (e.g. Russell group, Million Plus, GuildHE etc). In addition, this study will extend its research question by focusing its attention on the Russell group universities and examine their claim of “Research Excellence” by verifying if these universities appear together in a cluster when applying the statistical method of cluster analysis. Furthermore, we will compare the university grouping and academic levels in terms of their average publication quality (as operationalised by the SJR metric). We expect Russell Group universities and more senior academics to perform significantly better in this measure of quality. We may also run further exploratory analysis to understand the effects of other factors like gender on research performance on a global scale and compare pairs of university groupings to understand this phenomenon in depth. What does research productivity mean to us? Mazzucchelli et al., (2018) used an academic’s lifetime papers published, lifetime citations and h-index as quantitative indicators of research productivity. Building on the assumption that a high number of papers published does not necessarily mean that those papers are also of high standards, this study will go beyond by trying to assess the quality of their research productivity. A high-quality journal does not publish any and every paper. The highly selective nature of such journals makes them prioritize the quality of research as a prime factor before approving it for publication. The SJR developed by Scopus is a widely used proxy for research quality. The current study will attempt to assess the quality aspect of research productivity by comparing the average SJRs of papers published by academics at different seniority levels in different university groupings.

title_r: Can fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS) be used to detect congruency effects?
abstract_r: Presenting a visual stimulus at a set frequency elicits a steady state visual evoked response in the human encephalography at the exact frequency of stimulation. If a second, oddball, stimulus is presented at set periodic intervals a secondary frequency band is observed at the rate of oddball presentation, thus indicating oddball detection. This fast periodic oddball paradigm (FPOP) has traditionally been applied to show humans detection of faces amongst non-face stimuli (Rossion, 2014). Recently Lochy, Van Belle &amp; Rossion (2015) have used the FPOP to indicate human detection of words amongst pseudowords, thus suggesting fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS) may be sensitive to detection of word like stimuli. The current project aims to see if this detection extends beyond word form to the semantic level through utilising Stroop like stimuli and using incongruent targets as oddballs. ******Planned Design***** Experimental conditions and theoretical hypotheses: We intend to use four conditions. 1. Colour words embedded in pseudo-words (all written in black ink). From this we hope to replicate Lochy et al (2015) and find detection of words amongst pseudo-words. We would therefore predict separate frequency modulations evident at the frequency of stimulus presentation (6Hz) and oddball, colour word, presentation (2Hz). 2. Colour words embedded in pseudo-words (all written in colour ink, colour words always incongruent). From this we hope see if adding colour removes or alters the effect. This is an exploratory comparison with a two tailed hypothesis. If colour does not influence the effect we expect to find separate frequency modulations evident at the frequency of stimulus presentation (6Hz) and oddball, colour word, presentation (2Hz), just as in condition 1. If colour does influence the effect we expect that we would not find two modulation frequencies. 3. Colour words embedded in pseudo-words (all written in colour ink, colour words are always congruent). From this we hope see if congruency might influence oddball detection. This is an exploratory comparison . If congruency enhances the effect predicted in condition 1 (i.e. separate frequency modulations evident at the frequency of stimulus presentation (6Hz) and oddball, colour word, presentation (2Hz)), we would expect to find the same effect but with increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The null hypothesis to this would be that we would see the same effects within the frequency spectra (i.e. separate frequency modulations evident at the frequency of stimulus presentation (6Hz) and oddball, colour word, presentation (2Hz)) but the SNR would not be enhanced relative to condition 1. 4. Congruent colour words embedded within incongruent colour words. From this we hope see if participants can detect congruency differences. This is an exploratory comparison . If the detection of words extends beyond basic form processing, to the semantic level, we would predict that participants would detect congruent oddballs embedded within incongruent colour-words. Thus, we would expect the same pattern of results predicted in condition 1 (i.e. separate frequency modulations evident at the frequency of stimulus presentation (6Hz) and oddball, colour word, presentation (2Hz)). The null hypothesis would be that we did not see separate frequency modulation for oddballs thus, congruent oddballs would not be detected and we would see a single modulation at 6Hz. The stimuli to be used in these conditions can be viewed using the Example_conditions_Script.py in the attached files this can be run using the free downloadable software Psychopy (Peirce 2007;2009). Independent variable: Our independent variables will be colour and congruency. Dependant variable: Our dependant variable will be the frequency modulation of EEG spectra. Sample size: n=30 This study is to be run in conjunction with "Validating the Emotiv EPOC EEG system for studying unimodal and cross-modal Stroop effects" (see linked component) for that reason the sample size will be the same. Previous studies have used much smaller sample sizes due to the high SNR allowed by the FPVS method (eg. Lochey et al. n=10). For this reason a sample size of 30 is judged to be sufficient to detect any effect.

title_r: The Experiences of Dating Couples: Replication of Murray et al (2002), Study 3
abstract_r: The purpose of this research project is to closely replicate a study originally published by Dr. Sandra Murray and her colleagues in 2002. Murray et al. (2002) found that individuals scoring lower (vs. higher) on self-esteem were more sensitive to perceived rejection from their romantic partner and reacted to this perceived threat by feeling less positive about their romantic partner, diminished closeness in their relationship, and heightened self-doubt. Moreover, the original researchers found that, in reality, the partners of lower and higher self-esteem persons reported similar levels of forgiveness, satisfaction, and other relationship outcomes, meaning that the increased defensiveness felt by lower self-esteem persons when they perceived rejection was unwarranted. This research has important implications for how people approach their relationships and negotiate conflict. Replicating the original study, we will use a paper-and-pencil task to lead half of the experimental participants (1/4 of the total participants) to believe that their partner perceives a large number of faults in them (the other half of participants will not be led to believe this). abstract_r: This study aims to replicate De Neys original study of participant’s substitution bias through two math questions in varying order, and then asking the participants to rate their confidence in their answers. The problems are presented to participants after the De Ney’s et al. protocol, and are counterbalanced (half participants will receive two item question first then one item, and the other half will receive one item then two item). Each condition will be comprised of 25 students, so approximately 100 students in the study total. These problems are presented with a rating of confidence question. The survey will be given online via Qualtrics for easier access as well as face-to-face in classrooms. We hypothesize students will rate their confidence higher when the substitution is absent when compared to the substitution being present. We also hypothesize with multiple choice options, the accuracy in answers will be improved and confidence will be highest. \n

title_r: Replication and Extension of Functional Family Therapy-Gangs: Randomized Controlled Trial of Gang-Involved Youth on Pre-Trial and Probation Supervision in the Denver Area
abstract_r: This proposal focuses on Functional Family Therapy-Gangs (FFT-G), which is an extension of a therapeutic intervention targeting youth presenting problem behaviors—Functional Family Therapy (FFT)—that is designed to help troubled youth and their families overcome delinquency, substance abuse, and violence. In 2009, Drs. Thornberry and Gottfredson led an advisory group of leading prevention scientists and gang researchers in selecting FFT to adapt to address the severity of risk factors observed with gang populations, as a large body of research highlights the importance of household dynamics for youth gang members. The associated manual and trainings became known as FFT-G. A subsequent RCT of FFT-G with a sample of adjudicated youth in Philadelphia revealed reductions in recidivism over an 18-month period (Gottfredson et al., 2018) , . This study will replicate the study design and outcomes from Thornberry and Gottfredson’s evaluation by implementing FFT-G in the Denver area. We will target juveniles on pre-trial and probation supervision who are embedded in gangs, which is distinguishable from the Philadelphia evaluation, as 15% of their sample had ever been a member of a gang and only half maintained high gang risk. The FFT-G model is designed to serve the dual function of gang prevention and intervention. Thornberry and Gottfredson’s important work focused on the former; ours will focus on the latter. We will use official records in conjunction with youth and parent reports to compare outcomes 18 months after youth were assigned at random to FFT-G or treatment-as-usual (TAU) conditions.

title_r: A systematic replication of the worst performance rule
abstract_r: The worst performance rule (WPR) states that when reaction times are ranked from fastest to slowest and then correlated with intelligence test scores, the slowest reaction times predict participants' intelligence better than the mean or best reaction times. Previous research suggests that the size of the WPR effect may be moderated by the difficulty or g-loading of RT tasks. Because there is substantial variation in sample size, sample characteristics and trial numbers across the different studies, we aim to replicate the WPR in a large, heterogenous sample using a variety of RT task. Our main aim is to replicate that the size of the WPR effect varies systematically with the difficulty or g-loading of tasks.

title_r: A systematic replication of the worst performance rule
abstract_r: The worst performance rule (WPR) states that when reaction times are ranked from fastest to slowest and then correlated with intelligence test scores, the slowest reaction times predict participants' intelligence better than the mean or best reaction times. Previous research suggests that the size of the WPR effect may be moderated by the difficulty or g-loading of RT tasks. Because there is substantial variation in sample size, sample characteristics and trial numbers across the different studies, we aim to replicate the WPR in a large, heterogenous sample using a variety of RT task. Our main aim is to replicate that the size of the WPR effect varies systematically with the difficulty or g-loading of tasks.

title_r: Are affective factors related to individual differences in facial expression recognition?
abstract_r: Evidence that affective factors (e.g., anxiety, depression, affect) are significantly related to individual differences in emotion recognition is mixed. Palermo et al. (2018 Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance) reported that individuals who scored lower in anxiety performed significantly better on two measures of facial-expression recognition (emotion-matching and emotion-labeling tasks), but not a third measure (the Multimodal Emotion Recognition Test). By contrast, facial-expression recognition was not significantly correlated with measures of depression, positive or negative affect, empathy, or autistic-like traits. Because the range of affective factors considered in this study and its use of multiple expression-recognition tasks mean that it is a relatively comprehensive investigation of the role of affective factors in facial expression recognition, we carried out a direct replication. In common with Palermo et al. (2018), scores on the DASS anxiety subscale negatively predicted performance on the emotion recognition tasks across multiple analyses, although these correlations were only consistently significant for performance on the emotion-labeling task. However, and by contrast with Palermo et al. (2018), other affective factors (e.g., those related to empathy) often also significantly predicted emotion-recognition performance. Collectively, these results support the proposal that affective factors predict individual differences in emotion recognition, but that these correlations are not necessarily specific to measures of general anxiety, such as the DASS anxiety subscale.
