title_r: European farmers’ risk attitudes – A cross-country replication of Bocquého et al. (2014)
abstract_r:
European farmers’ risk attitudes – A cross-country replication of Bocquého et al. (2014) Background: Risk and uncertainty are at the core of many questions in agricultural economics, and agricultural economists have been interested in estimating farmers’ risk attitudes for several decades (e.g., Binswanger, 1980; Iyver et al., 2020). In particular, risk attitudes are an important modeling input, and they are of broad interest to policy makers and insurance companies. There is a large diversity of approaches to study farmers’ risk attitudes, and this literature is scattered, with few studies systematically investigating differences across countries and farming systems (Iyer et al., 2020). One popular method to study risk attitudes are incentivized gambles and lotteries based on multiple price lists (e.g., Holt and Laury, 2002). These lotteries have been widely applied to investigate farmers’ risk attitudes (see Iyer et al., 2020 for a recent overview of studies). One of the most widely cited studies in this area is that of Bocquého et al. (2014). This study uses the multiple price lists developed by Tanaka et al. (2010) to investigate whether Expected Utility Theory (EUT) or Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) better describes farmers’ attitudes towards risk and uncertainty in a sample of French farmers. The authors use structural models to estimate EUT and CPT parameters. They also estimate models that adjust for socio-demographic heterogeneity. They find that farmers are risk-averse in the gain domain under EUT and exhibit loss aversion and overweighting of small probabilities under CPT. This replication proposal focuses on exploring the robustness and boundaries of the estimates of Bocquého et al. (2014). The replication will entail two exercises. First, we have obtained the original data and code from the authors and we will replicate the analysis. This allows us to establish a coherent econometric benchmark to compare the original model results with those obtained by us. Second, we will apply a similar protocol in several European countries and for different farming systems (see list below). Our replication focuses on the same question as the original study: Are farmers’ risk attitudes better described by EUT or by CPT? We also strive to showcase best practices for cross-country data collection in future replication efforts in experimental agricultural economics by embracing open science practices (i.e., follow a pre-registration with power calculations, open data, and open methods). Method: Our replication will reproduce the same experimental design (focused on the risk task, while the original study also had a longer survey including also an ambiguity and time tasks) but will deviate in some aspects. These deviations are needed, partly for feasibility considerations, but also because we strive to test a simpler protocol capable of yielding results of equivalent quality and robustness. First, the original study investigated 107 farmers from 64 towns in the French Bourgogne region in a 2-hour face-to-face interview. Our data collection will take place online. Second, the sample will be more diverse, both in terms of origin and farm type. While French farmers will also be interviewed in the replication (from both South and North West of France), we will also rely on a mix of convenience and random samples of farmers from other European regions across a wide range of farming systems. We want to achieve a comparable statistical power as the original study (assuming the same effect sizes) at country level, i.e., there should be 107 farmers or more for most countries. In total, we expect a substantially larger pooled sample. We will discuss deviations from the original estimates (if any) against the background of amendments in the protocol and the cultural/economic contexts. Third, while every farmer received a payment in the original study, we will incentivize a certain proportion of farmers with a cash payment or a close equivalent (e.g., vouchers for a popular online shopping outlet in the respective country). Fourth, the exchange rate in the experiment will be known to our participants a priori, because the original procedure with an envelope that contains the exchange rate – only revealed after the lotteries – is difficult to mimic online. The analysis will report the results of the same structural models as the original study (without covariates) and to explore the impact of (other) covariates. Due to the different contexts, we will define a set of covariates that overlap for our various cases in the original study (most notably age and gender). Similar to the original study, we will employ a series of robustness tests to understand how other reference points than zero might drive results for CPT estimates. The authors started to develop a joint survey instrument in Qualtrics in English. Once the English master version is approved by the different country teams, they will be responsible for translation and data collection processes. Additional remarks: We are very confident that we will have collected data from at least three countries/cases of the list below before fall 2021 (and others might also join). The exact samples to be covered are still uncertain. As a result, we want to bring to your attention that there might be a change in co-authors. All authors of this concept note have been in contact by email, and the coordination team at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences has organized a joint meeting in December 2020. title_r: The impact of self-esteem manipulation through social exclusion on felt meaningfulness and the experience of meaning in life
abstract_r: Previous studies have shown that the satisfaction of basic psychological needs is associated with a greater sense of meaningfulness in work and everyday life contexts (Autin et al., 2022; Eakman, 2013; Martela et al., 2018). Conversely, need frustration is a predictor of negative psychological outcomes (Campbell et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2015). The aim of the present study is to investigate the effect of an acute frustration of self-esteem - one of the basic needs that has not previously been investigated in relation to meaning - on felt meaningfulness and the experience of meaning in life. Two studies found that participants report lower self-esteem (Zadro et al., 2004) and lower meaning in life (Stillman et al., 2009) following social exclusion. We aim to replicate and extend these findings by 1) employing two distinct measures of meaning (experience of meaning in life and perceived meaningfulness in ambiguous stimuli) and 2) showing that the loss of meaning following social exclusion is mediated by frustrated self-esteem. 3) In addition, we will investigate the influence of trait narcissism on self-esteem frustration. For this purpose, we will manipulate state self-esteem using a virtual ball-tossing game (Cyberball Game; Williams & Jarvis, 2006). title_r: Study 1 (Direct Replication)
abstract_r:
**CREP Project: #20-43** 
 
**PROTOCOL TITLE:**   
Evaluation of Meat Consumption 
 
**PRINCIPAL INVESTIGATOR (PI):**   
*Name:* Heather Urry   
*Department:* Psychology 
 
**Purpose of the study:** 
 
This study is a direct replication of one experiment from research conducted by Sparkman and Walton (2017) that investigated dynamic and static norms in relation to meat consumption. Our study aims to determine whether dynamic norms lead to a greater desire to change one’s eating habits than static norms.  
 
**Background / Literature Review / Rationale for the study:** 
 
In the original study by Sparkman and Walton (2017), the researchers found that participants were more interested in reducing their meat consumption if they first learned that norms for reducing meat consumption have been increasing over the past 5 years. This was compared to a condition in which there was no implied change; the norm was presented as static.  
 
We are replicating this study because the topic is of general interest and importance. In addition, this study is among those available for undergraduate student groups to replicate with faculty mentorship as part of the Collaborative Replications and Education Project.  
 
**Participant Population:** 
 
We will study adult participants currently in the United States who are at least 18 years old, each of whom may participate in the study just once. (Vegan/vegetarian participants will be excluded from analyses but not from participating in the study.) 
 
**Research Locations and Sample Size:** 
 
*Research Locations* 
 
This research will be administered online via a Qualtrics survey. Participants will complete it in a location of their choosing that offers a computer with internet access. 
 
*Sample Size* 
 
We seek to recruit at least 122 participants, the same number of participants studied by the original authors. A sample of 122 participants – 61 in each of two norm conditions – will give us 80% power to detect medium standardized effects of Cohen’s *d* = 0.51 or larger for the difference in self-reported interest between the dynamic and static conditions.   
 
The original authors reported an effect size of Cohen’s *d* = 0.41. Ideally we’d have enough participants to detect an effect of that size with adequate power in this study. This would require 94 participants per group for a total of 188 participants.   
 
Even better, we should have enough participants to detect an effect that’s so small that the original authors would have been unlikely to detect it. To that end, Simonsohn (2015) suggests specifying in one’s power analysis an effect size the original authors could have detected with only 33% power.  In this case, with 118 participants included in the key analysis, the original authors had 33% power to detect an effect size of Cohen’s *d* = 0.28.  To have 80% power to detect an effect size of *d* = 0.28 or larger, we would need to collect data from 201 participants per group for a total of 402 participants.  
 
Our maximum N will be 3,000.  
 
**Procedures Involved:** 
 
We are conducting a between-subjects experiment in which we will manipulate type of norm (dynamic, static). Participants will complete this research online via a Qualtrics survey. We anticipate that each participant will take 5-10 minutes to complete the study. The study will unfold over the course of the Fall 2020 semester.  
 
The survey will start by assessing the GeoIP location of potential respondents. For people whose GeoIP location suggests they are not currently in the United States, the survey will explain our eligibility criteria and then take the respondent to a message noting their ineligibility. Otherwise, the survey will proceed to the informed consent form. 
 
After providing informed consent, participants will respond to a Captcha verification item to prevent bot responses to the online survey. They will also provide answers to three eligibility items (age at least 18 years, have not participated before, and currently in the United States) to prevent participation by people who are ineligible. Participants who are ineligible or decline to answer will then see a message explaining that they are ineligible.  
 
Participants who are eligible will then read instructions related to their randomly-assigned norm condition. In the static-norm condition, participants will read: 
 
    Recent research has shown that 30% of Americans make an effort to limit their meat consumption. That means that 3 in 10 people eat less meat than they otherwise would.  
 
In the dynamic-norm condition, participants will read: 
 
    Recent research has shown that, in the last 5 years, 30% of Americans have now started to make an effort to limit their meat consumption. That means that, in recent years, 3 in 10 people have changed their behavior and begun to eat less meat than they otherwise would. 
 
After reading the statement, each participant will respond to the following items: 
 
1.	How interested are you in eating less meat? (1 = not at all, 4 = somewhat, 7 = extremely). 
2.	Most people eat breakfast, lunch and dinner everyday. That means they eat 21 meals in a typical week. For those that make an effort to eat less meat, how many times do you think they eat a meal without meat in a week? 
3.	What percentage of people do you think make an effort to limit their meat consumption? 
4.	Which best describes your political ideology? (1 = very liberal, 7 = very conservative) 
5.	What word or phrase best describes your gender?  
6.	Are you vegetarian or vegan? 
7.	What is your current age in years? 
8.	What word or phrase best describes your race and/or ethnicity? 
9.	Did you participate to earn SONA credit or for a chance to enter a drawing? (SONA credit, Drawing, Neither; I'm volunteering) 
 
Finally, participants will see the debriefing form and an item in which they will have the option to exclude their data from the final data set, if they wish.  
 
Some items will require a response from participants; they will always have a “decline to answer” option so they are not compelled to provide information they do not wish to share. 
 
Participants who say they took part for compensation in the form of entering a drawing will, upon clicking the survey submission button, be redirected to a new contact information survey in which they can provide their name and email address if they wish to be entered into a drawing to receive $50 as compensation. Participants who say they took part for compensation in the form of SONA credit will receive 0.5 credits in the SONA credit system. 
 
Some pages in the survey will be set to measure the time participants spend on them for exploratory analyses.   
 
**Confirmatory Analyses:** 
 
We will exclude from analyses participants who identify as vegetarian/vegan, participants who decline to include their responses in the final data set after debriefing, participants who select the "decline to answer" option for key variables in each analysis, and participants who do not complete the survey through to the debriefing form and thus do not have the opportunity to withdraw their data. 
 
After applying these exclusions, we will repeat the same analyses reported by Sparkman and Walton (2017) as follows:  
 
1.	A t-test to see if type of norm (dynamic, static) affects self-reported interest in reducing meat consumption.  
2.	A multiple regression to see if type of norm affects self-reported interest in reducing meat consumption when accounting for variation explained by gender and political orientation.  
3.	Two additional t-tests to see if type of norm (dynamic, static) affects estimates of the percentage of people who limit their meat consumption and the number of meatless meals per week eaten by people who say they limited their meat consumption. 
 
We will also report descriptive statistics and standardized effect sizes as reported by the original authors. 
 
In addition, we anticipate that there may be outlying observations or responses suggesting a lack of good-faith participation (e.g., based on open-ended information or extremely fast completion times). We may repeat our confirmatory analyses without these observations to see if conclusions change. 
 
**Known Deviations** 
 
1. We are recruiting participants in the United States, probably most of whom will be students at Tufts and/or people in the Boston area of Massachusetts. The original researchers recruited participants using Amazon's Mechanical Turk. 
2. We will offer participants the opportunity to enter a drawing for USD 50 dollars or to earn credit in partial fulfillment of course requirements as incentives to participate. In the original study, participants on Mechanical Turk received USD 25 cents. 
3. For our replication, the survey will include eligibility items (Captcha verification, age at least 18 years, have not participated before, and currently in the United States) before participants complete the survey items that address confirmatory hypotheses. 
 
**Incomplete Disclosure or Deception:** 
 
In the consent form, we tell participants that we are not disclosing all information about the nature and purpose of the study and that, at the end of the study, they’ll receive a full explanation. Specifically, we do not disclose our specific focus on whether dynamic versus static norms influence interest in reducing meat consumption, or that we’re measuring how much time they spend on various pages of the survey and other variables of interest, as described above. This incomplete disclosure is necessary because full participant knowledge could impact their responses and compromise our results. We do not believe this incomplete disclosure violates the rights or welfare of participants because a) we correctly inform potential participants in the consent form that we’re conducting a study to evaluate meat consumption, b) we correctly inform participants about the general procedures of the study, namely that they’ll be completing a survey and demographic items, and c) we will fully debrief participants afterwards, including providing them the opportunity to decline to include their responses in the final data set.  
 
**Recruitment Methods:** 
 
We will recruit a convenience sample of participants. Study personnel will recruit people they know by word of mouth in person or via email, or by posting an invitation to participate on social media such as Facebook, Twitter, or other websites, including the Psychology Department’s SONA paid system website. The materials note that we’re recruiting adults ages 18 years and up who are currently in the United States and have not participated in this research previously. We will also recruit participants via the Psychology Department’s SONA credit participant pool. Participants will earn 0.5 credits in partial fulfillment of departmental course requirements. 
 
**Consent Process:**  
 
Participants will provide informed consent by reading the consent form online and then clicking a button in the Qualtrics survey.  
 
To ensure participant understanding of the study and its procedures, participants will have as much time as they would like to consider their participation. Should they have questions, the consent form will provide contact information for the PI. Participation will be dependent upon consent; participants will not be able to continue to the survey unless they have consented to participate. 
 
To minimize the possibility of coercion or undue influence, the consent form will make it clear that participation is voluntary and that potential participants may choose not to participate without penalty; similarly, the consent form will make it clear that participants may withdraw their participation without penalty too. In addition, researchers will not use unduly influential or coercive language in recruitment materials. 
 
 
**Compensation:**   
 
Some participants will have the opportunity to enter a drawing for $50. Participants who opt in and provide a valid email address in the contact information survey will be eligible. The drawing will take place after data collection is complete, likely on or near Wednesday, December 9, 2020. We will choose at least one winner. Compensation will be issued via Venmo or PayPal.  
 
Other participants will have the opportunity to earn 0.5 credits in partial fulfillment of course requirements via the Psychology Department’s SONA credit participant pool. 
 
The level of compensation is expected to be adequate to incentivize participation without being unduly influential. Participants who submit a survey but indicate they wish to exclude their data from analyses will still be eligible for compensation. 
 
There are no costs to participants. 
 
**Potential Benefits to Participants:**  
 
There are no direct benefits to participants beyond the educational experience of participating and the knowledge that they are contributing to our understanding of human psychology. 
 
**Risks to Participants:** 
 
The risks to participants are minimal. Procedures are largely limited to responding to survey questions about meat consumption and providing demographic information. These are common everyday experiences. For participants taking part in exchange for entering a drawing as compensation, there is also a slight risk of a breach of confidentiality because we are collecting identifiers (names, email addresses) from the participants who wish to enter the compensation drawing. However, the data we are collecting would not be considered sensitive by reasonable standards, thus the severity of a breach, in the unlikely event one were to occur, would be quite low in magnitude. See Data Management and Confidentiality, section, for the steps we will take to mitigate this risk.  
 
**Withdrawal of Participants:** 
 
We will not withdraw participants from the research without their consent.  
 
If participants withdraw by indicating they would like us to exclude their data from the final data set, we will delete their responses when the data are downloaded from Qualtrics, prior to analysis or sharing in a public web repository. We will not be able to delete responses from any participants who may contact the PI after-the-fact because survey data files will not enable us to identify their specific responses. 
 
**Data Management and Confidentiality:** 
 
All information will be collected via Qualtrics surveys that are housed in the PI’s password-protected account. The data collection survey will only house participant data without personal identifiers; the contact information survey will only house participant identifiers (name, email address) without data.  
 
To mitigate the risk of a breach of confidentiality, we will not maintain a link between identifiers and data. In addition, only individuals who have been approved as study personnel under this protocol will be given collaborative access to the surveys through their Tufts password-protected Qualtrics account on an as-needed basis. 
 
Once data collection is complete, the PI will download the data and contact information from the two surveys and store them on a password-protected Tufts computer. After verifying that the data are deidentified, she will make the data available in a public web repository for access by other researchers, including the student researchers in her PSY 32 course. The data will, thus, be stored indefinitely.  
 
As soon as the PI has completed the compensation drawing process, she will delete the contact information from the computer and from Qualtrics to further mitigate risk of a breach of confidentiality. 
 
**Provisions to Protect the Privacy and Confidentiality of Participants and the Research Data:** 
 
Participants will complete this study on a computer with internet access at a time and location of their choosing. We are not asking them to provide sensitive, personal information. Survey items are innocuous questions about meat consumption and demographics, but participants are free to decline to answer as they wish. In addition, our data management plan, as articulated above, is designed to minimize the risk of a breach of confidentiality. As such, participant privacy is well-protected.  
  
 
**Data Sharing:** 
 
The deidentified data will be shared in a public web repository (e.g., Open Science Framework, github, or other) for access by anyone with an internet connection indefinitely. Other researchers may use the data to contribute to a meta-analysis of direct replications of the original study by Sparkman and Walton (2017), and some may download the data to see if they can reproduce our results or generate novel insights in new analyses.

title_r: A Replication Study-Postoperative Complications in Bariatric Surgery using Age and BMI Stratification: A Stusy using ACS-NSQIP data (2014)
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate the findings of Sanni et al.'s (2014) research on postoperative complications in bariatric surgery patients. The original research utilized age and BMI stratification and data from the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS NSQIP) to identify the relationship between these variables and postoperative complications. The findings of the original study revealed significant associations between age, BMI, and postoperative complications. The replication plan aims to confirm these associations and identify the factors that lead to postoperative complications in patients undergoing bariatric surgery. The replication study proposes a comprehensive plan consisting of three types of analyses: pure replication, measurement and estimation analysis (MEA), and theory of change analysis (TCA). These analyses are designed to validate and expand on the discoveries of the original study. The pure replication phase is a critical step in the replication process, aiming to reproduce the original analyses accurately. This phase involves performing the statistical tests used in the original study to confirm the significant risk factors identified in the original study. Overall, the pure replication phase ensures the accuracy of the research findings. Conducting MEA (Measurement and Estimation Analysis) is crucial for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the findings. Employing alternative methods such as nonparametric tests will provide a more comprehensive analysis and help validate the results obtained in the pure replication phase. It is important to ensure that the conclusions drawn from the original study are robust and can be replicated using different statistical techniques. The concluding step, TCA (Theory of Change Analysis), will broaden the scope of the original study by examining the correlation between wound complications and diabetes status (YES/NO) among patients undergoing bariatric surgery. This analysis will employ Chi-Square tests and logistic regression 3 models to assess the association between diabetes and wound complications among patients undergoing bariatric surgery while accounting for variables including age and BMI. Through replicating the original study's findings and employing alternative analytical approaches, this research aims to enhance understanding of the determinants influencing postoperative complications among individuals undergoing bariatric surgery. Furthermore, by exploring novel inquiries concerning wound complications in patients with diabetes, this study aspires to inform the establishment of evidence driven protocols for bariatric surgery selection criteria, thereby fostering advancements in patient care and outcomes.

title_r: Unethical Behaviour in the Workplace: A Direct and Conceptual Replication of Jones &amp; Kavanagh (1996)
abstract_r:
Welcome to the project page for a new collaborative project exploring unethical workplace behaviour!  
 
@[youtube](https://youtu.be/eUv6hr0Lp7k) 
 
 
 
We're currently looking for groups of individuals to support data collection for two projects - a direct and conceptual replication of Jones and Kavanagh (1996). This is a fun study looking at individual and situational factors, and would be perfect for a BSc or MSc dissertation student-supervisor dyad! 
 
We're looking to identify data collection teams that, in exchange for authorship of the Stage 2 Registered Report, can... 
 
 - Create a data-collection team (1-3 people) with at least 1 student (any level; including undergraduate, postgraduate and doctorate)  
 - Collect ethical approval from your institution (unless you do not require approval or can be covered by pre-existing approval) 
 - Collect a minimum of 100 participants before the end of July 2023 
 
 
____ 
You can sign up to one or both of the following: 
 
**Direct Replication:** You must be able to recruit UK-based psychology- and/or management-based students from any year of their Undergraduate or Postgraduate study for a brief 15-minute questionnaire. 
 
**Conceptual Replication:** You must be able to recruit participants from the US and/or UK who are employed. This study requires participants to complete a 15-minute questionnaire and a 5-minute follow-up questionnaire 7-28 days later. 
___ 
 
. 
 
. 
 
 
___ 
 
If you'd like to be involved, we've outlined all the key steps required to sign up and start data collection in a handy document. 
 
**Instructions and Sign-up:** https://osf.io/9yfbg/ 
 
____ 
 
For more information, contact project lead Dr Thomas Rhys Evans on thomas.evans@greenwich.ac.uk or @ThomasRhysEvans

title_r: A Multi-Site Collaboration of Hostile Priming Effects-In-Principle Acceptance version
abstract_r: In 1979, Srull and Wyer reported a study where a brief exposure to hostile stimuli caused participants to subsequently rate an individual as being more hostile. Srull and Wyer (1979) went on to be one of the most influential studies in social cognition: It has been cited in over 1,000 academic publications, the “Donald” vignette has been used in dozens of subsequent studies, and the results served as a foundation for subsequent priming studies that extended priming effects beyond the domain of social judgments (e.g., e.g., Bargh, Chen, &amp; Burrows, 1996; Dijksterhuis &amp; van Knippenberg, 1998). However, a Registered Replication Report (RRR; McCarthy et al., 2018) that contained 26 independent samples and several thousand participants did not find the predicted effect and cast doubt on whether the methods reported by Srull and Wyer would reliably produce a hostile priming effect. However, the RRR deviated from the original methods in a few ways and some criticisms of the methods were raised after the publication of the RRR. The current proposed study is intended to address these criticisms and provide a critical test of whether Srull and Wyer-esque methods can reliably produce a hostile priming effect. The current study will involve several labs who each collect an independent sample of data. Each lab will conduct a close replication of Srull and Wyer (1979) and each lab will pretest stimuli so they can conduct a conceptual replication of Srull and Wyer (1979) using stimuli that are developed specifically for their locally-available participants. Collectively, this study will test the replicability of Srull and Wyer-esque methods to produce a hostile priming effect.

title_r: Replication of the Hindsight Bias and extension on the role of depressive symptoms
abstract_r: Replicability and reproducibility are essential for scientific credibility, promoted through open science practices. Mental health research often deals with variable and time-changing characteristics, making it challenging to implement these practices, especially in studies of social behavior and cognition. These studies must be investigated through replication-extension models to promote theoretical expansion and generalization. The seminal research by Fischhoff (1975) on hindsight bias is highly relevant, whereas evidence suggests interactions with depressive symptoms. However, few studies have explored such interaction and there are no replications with a Brazilian population. This project aims to conduct a replication of Experiment 2 of the Fischhoff study (1975) in hindsight bias in a Brazilian sample, including an extension to the original research to broaden its scope of clinical relevance in depressive symptoms. This will be a cross-sectional study conducted through a self-completed electronic form on the Qualtrics XM platform in a sample of 240 Brazilians over 18 years. The original material will be adapted to our population through cultural adaptation. Depressive symptoms will be evaluated through the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Bank v1.0 (PT-BR version). Following the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines, the study will be pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) platform and the Data Management Plan Tool (DMP Tool) was used for data management. Statistical analysis (comparison between groups and mediation) will be conducted using the R software.

title_r: Religion &amp; the Dictator Game Online Study
abstract_r: Does religion promote prosocial behaviour? Despite numerous publications that seem to answer this question affirmatively, divergent results from recent meta-analyses and pre-registered replication efforts suggest the issue is not yet settled. Additional uncertainty lingers around whether (a) the effects of religious cognition on prosocial behaviour obtain through implicit cognitive processes, explicit cognitive processes, or both; and (b) whether religious cognition increases generosity only among people disinclined to share with anonymous strangers. Here we propose two experiments designed to address these concerns. In Experiment 1 we will seek to replicate Shariff and Norenzayan’s demonstration of the effects of implicit religious priming on Dictator Game offers to anonymous strangers; unlike Shariff and Norenzayan, however, we will use an online environment where anonymity is virtually assured. In Experiment 2, we will introduce a “taking” option to allow greater expression of baseline selfishness. In both experiments, we will seek to activate religious cognition implicitly and explicitly. Finally, we will use multiple methods to meta-analyse all available experiments that test the effect of religious priming on Dictator Game transfers. Our results will provide new insight into an important interdisciplinary issue, and guidance on how best to activate religious cognition in the laboratory.

title_r: Registered Report: The transcriptional network for mesenchymal transformation of brain tumours
abstract_r: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of 50 papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012. This Registered Report describes the proposed replication plan of key experiments from “The transcriptional network for mesenchymal transformation of brain tumours” by Carro et al. (2010), published in Nature in 2010. The key experiments included in this replication focus on testing the contribution of two “master regulator” transcription factors (C/EBPβ and STAT3) toward synergistically initiating the mesenchymal transformation of gliomas. During this replication attempt, CEBPB and STAT3 expression will be ablated in a human glioma cell line with the resulting changes in mesenchymal markers measured, as shown in Figure S8A. Tumor cells treated with shRNAs targeting both CEBPB and STAT3 will be injected into immunocompromised mice, and the resulting effects in tumor severity and mesenchymal signature will be assessed, as shown in Figures 5A and 5B. The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is a collaboration between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange and the results of the replications will be published in eLife.

title_r: Investigating the Role of Gaze Cues on the Communication-Induced Memory Bias
abstract_r: In this conceptual replication study, we used a screen-based violation of expectation (VOE) paradigm to investigate whether 9-month-old infants process different information about novel objects when an object is introduced in a communicative referential versus non-communicative referential context (Yoon, Johnson, & Csibra et al., 2008; Okumura, Kobayashi, & Itakura, 2016; but see Silverstein, Gliga, Westermann, & Parise, 2018). In 12 test trial videos, an object was shown together with one adult (action phase). We manipulated the communicative context depicted in the videos such that the adult either looked at the object after looking in the direction of the infant (communicative context) or the actor looked at the object individually without addressing the infant at all (non-communicative). After each video, the scene was occluded before it revealed one of three different outcomes: the object infants had just seen in the action phase (no change, baseline), the object they had just seen but at a novel position (location change), or a new object (identity change). By manipulating both the communicative context and features of the object in the subsequent outcome phase, we aimed to conceptually replicate the previous finding that observed communicative context may bias infants to encode surface features which support learning about object kinds (i.e., object identity) over spatial-temporal information (i.e., object location). In contrast to previous studies examining this effect, we used a study setup and data processing procedure allowing us to automatically extract infants’ looking response using eye tracking technology instead of manually coding infants’ looking behavior. Note: In the overall study (published in Open Mind: https://doi.org/10.1162/opmi_a_00114) we refer to this project as “Experiment 1”. This OSF project is directly linked to the OSF project "Investigating the Communication-Induced Memory Bias in the Context of Third-Party Social Interactions" (https://osf.io/mp9td/).

abstract_r: Nestler, Blank and Egloff (2010) provided evidence for a separate components view of the hindsight bias by demonstrating theoretically predicted dissociations between the hindsight components memory distortion, inevitability impression, and foreseeability impression. In this project (conducted in the context of the bachelor thesis of Ricarda Theobald), we aim to replicate the results of the third study reported in Nestler et al. (2010). This experiment focused on the dissociation between inevitability and foreseeability impressions by investigating their susceptibility to causal reasoning processes and metacognitive feelings of surprise in a hypothetical hindsight bias design. In the replication study, we will use the same videos and nearly identical questionnaires to investigate the research questions. Furthermore, it is aimed to assess more than twice the participants compared to the original study. 12/07/2017: We have started with the acquisition of the participants one week ago.

title_r: Can Imagined Contact Really Be Delivered Through the Web? Preregistered Tests of Web-Delivered Imagined Contact
abstract_r: The purpose of this research is to test whether the positive effects of imagined contact remain when the contact scenario is delivered through the web. Previous research has determined that direct intergroup contact (real-life contact) significantly reduces prejudice towards a variety of outgroups (Pettigrew &amp; Tropp, 2006). A meta-analysis by Pettigrew and Tropp (2006) presents empirical evidence suggesting that direct intergroup contact, when structured according to pre-established conditions set forth by Allport (1954), can significantly reduce prejudice for a vast array of groups. The positive effects of imagined contact scenarios have been documented by Husnu and Crisp (2010). However, the imagined contact study conducted by Husnu and Crisp was done in a controlled laboratory setting (2010). The present study will test the effect of web-delivered imagined contact. In order to do this, the current research will compare the effectiveness of 4 different imagined contact scenarios. The first scenario will be a non-elaborated control and will be an exact replication of the scenario used in experiment 4 of West et al., 2011. The second scenario will be a non-elaborated treatment and is also an exact replication of the experimental condition scenario used in study 4 of West et al., 2011. The third scenario will be an elaborated control adapted from experiment 4 of West et al. (2011) and modified with information from Hodson et al. (2015). The last scenario will be an elaborated treatment adapted from experiment 4 of West et al. (2011) and modified with information from Hodson et al. (2015). The elaborated conditions have been added in order to test whether the extent of elaboration in a web-delivered setting amplifies the effects of imagined contact. As in the West et al. (2011) study, the current research will examine the effects of imagined contact on schizophrenic individuals using attitudes and intergroup anxiety measures. A previous study conducted by Dr. Nicol and OCdt Bordeleau showed that elaborated imagined contact delivered through the web did not reduce intergroup anxiety towards American-Muslims. The present study will limit the comparability problem associated with the previous study by replicating quasi-exactly study 4 of West et al. (2011). By doing so, the results of the current study will be more easily compared to the results obtained by West et al. (2011). The present study will be able to highlight whether or not the method of delivery (web) leads to significant improvement in attitudes and/or a reduction in intergroup anxiety.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.

title_r: ZfP Protocol: suffering and understanding in punishment
abstract_r: ABSTRACT. When people exact retribution on moral offenders, what psychological goals are our punishments designed to realize? This study represents a conceptual replication and extension of recent research on two proximate drivers of retribution: evidence that the perpetrator suffered , and evidence that he understood why he is being punished. Using a contrastive vignette method, we will present U.S. adults with vignettes about a fictitious high-seriousness (robbery) and low seriousness (theft) crime. In a between subjects design, we will independently vary perpetrator suffering (present vs. absent) and perpetrator understanding (present vs. absent), as well as the participant’s perspective (personal vs. impersonal). Following Gollwitzter and Denzler (2009), we will estimate punishment goal-fulfillment by measuring sentencing recommendations and punishment satisfaction ratings before and after exposure to the manipulations. We hypothesize that goal fulfillment will be greatest following combined evidence of suffering and understanding.

title_r: Are affective factors related to individual differences in facial expression recognition?
abstract_r: Evidence that affective factors (e.g., anxiety, depression, affect) are significantly related to individual differences in emotion recognition is mixed. Palermo et al. (2018 Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance) reported that individuals who scored lower in anxiety performed significantly better on two measures of facial-expression recognition (emotion-matching and emotion-labeling tasks), but not a third measure (the Multimodal Emotion Recognition Test). By contrast, facial-expression recognition was not significantly correlated with measures of depression, positive or negative affect, empathy, or autistic-like traits. Because the range of affective factors considered in this study and its use of multiple expression-recognition tasks mean that it is a relatively comprehensive investigation of the role of affective factors in facial expression recognition, we carried out a direct replication. In common with Palermo et al. (2018), scores on the DASS anxiety subscale negatively predicted performance on the emotion recognition tasks across multiple analyses, although these correlations were only consistently significant for performance on the emotion-labeling task. However, and by contrast with Palermo et al. (2018), other affective factors (e.g., those related to empathy) often also significantly predicted emotion-recognition performance. Collectively, these results support the proposal that affective factors predict individual differences in emotion recognition, but that these correlations are not necessarily specific to measures of general anxiety, such as the DASS anxiety subscale.

title_r: Effects of Concordant and Discordant Interpersonal Motives within Idiographic Motive Networks.
abstract_r: In this project, we assess idiographic networks of interpersonal motives using the Experience-Sampling method (ESM; Csikszentmihalyi and Larson, 1987). The interpersonal aspects of behavior and experience play an important role within clinical psychology and psychotherapy (Hopwood et al., 2013; Kernberg, 1988; Kiesler, 1983). It is assumed that interpersonal motives orchestrate interpersonal experience and behavior (Hopwood et al., 2021; Horowitz et al., 2006). With regard to psychopathology, interpersonal aspects play a major role in personality disorders, but also accompany disorders such as depression and social phobia (Cain et al., 2010; Caspar et al., 2005; Conroy et al., 2009; Grosse Holtforth et al., 2006). Consistency theory (Grawe, 1998) states two major sources of inconsistency, incongruence and discordance. Incongruence as opposed to congruence describes the feedback that experiences are dissatisfying to the underlying motives. When motivational tendencies inhibit each other, which means that satisfaction or realization of one motive is accompanied by incongruence of other motives, it is called discordance (Grawe, 2004). Motives can also promote each other (concordance) or be independent of each other. The planned study focuses on recording the temporal course of activation and (dis-)satisfaction of interpersonal motives in daily life. On that basis, idiosyncratic motive networks are formed. In such a person-specific motive network, the motives can promote each other, impair each other, or be independent of each other. There are so-called approach motives that are supposed to satisfy basic psychological needs by realizing appetitive experiences. Avoidance motives protect these needs from being violated by avoiding aversive experiences (Elliot et al., 2006; Grosse Holtforth, 2008). In a published study with a similar design, idiosyncratic networks of the seven most important individual approach motives were calculated and linked to subclinical depressive symptoms (Lüdtke et al., 2025). Concordance was associated with fewer depressive symptoms. Discordance was linked to more depressive symptoms, but only according to bootstrapping analyses and when discarding individuals without any subclinical depressive symptom or discordant relation in the motive network. The study has demonstrated the feasibility of the assessment method as a promising diagnostic tool. In the current project, we aim to replicate and extend the mentioned study while addressing its limitations. The goal is to assess idiographic networks of the five most important individual approach and the three most important individual avoidance motives and link network characteristics such as concordance and discordance to measures of psychological well-being, subclinical psychopathology, interpersonal problems, as well as affect.

title_r: Public Servants: Stereotypes, attitudes, reputation, and stigmata
abstract_r: In this study, we will do a direct replication of Willems (2020), and we will add an elaboration. We collect data in in Denmark, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Austria, and Germany. We use the exact same type of association question as in Willems (2020). Willems, J. 2020, Public servant stereotypes: It is not (at) all about being lazy, greedy, and corrupt. Public Administration. 98(4): 807-823. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/padm.12686 In addition to replication, we will have five additions to Willems (2020). First, we will perform a cross-country comparison. The data will be collected in five countries. These countries are Austria (AT), Germany (DE), Denmark (DK), The Netherlands (NL), New Zealand (NZ). Second, as some professions in some languages have different words for the female and the male form, we will test both forms (e.g., in German: Police officer, male: Polizist; female: Polizistin). As a result, we will also test (as an independent variable) the difference between the female and the male wording of professions (if relevant in a particular language). Third, we will include more professions, compared to Willems (2020). The professions we will test are: Public servant, (with variations in some languages for ‘Public sector employee’, and ‘Government official’), Politician, Mayor, Tax officer, Police officer, Firefighter, Nurse, Teacher, Professor, Lawyer, Salesperson, Banker, Social entrepreneur, and Volunteer. Fourth, for the German language (samples in Germany (DE) and Austria (AT)), we include two additional different wordings for public servant (three wordings for public servant in total), as there are different types of public sector workers: the additional wordings are Beamter (male)/Beamtin (female) and Öffentlich Angestellter (male)/Öffentlich Angestellte (female) in German. In English, they can be translated to public sector employee and government official. Similarly in Dutch, we add three denominations for public servant: "Ambtenaar", "Werknemer in de publieke sector", "Overheidsambtenaar"; for Danish we use: “Offentlig ansat” and “Embedsmand”. Fifth, we will analyze the subsamples’ stereotypical associations that clearly relate to personal traits. For example in Willems (2020) all words associations were included. For example, for banker, words such as ‘money’ and ‘smart’ were associated. Given the theoretical relevance of specific personal traits in stereotype research, we will conduct an additional analysis with only the associations that are traits.

title_r: Confirmation bias: Snyder & Swann (1978) 40 years later
abstract_r: Building on the seminal work of Snyder and Swann (1978), the aim of the present study is to provide new evidence for the hypothesis-confirming bias. In Snyder and Swann’s article (Study 2, 1978), participants had to investigate if another participant was extraverted or introverted. For that purpose, participants were paired and each was assigned either the role of “interviewer” or the role of “target”. Half of the interviewer-participants were instructed to assess to what extent the target was extraverted and the other half were instructed to assess to what extend the target was introverted. After receiving the instructions, they had to select a limited number of questions to ask to the target out of a large set of questions biased either in favor of extraversion or in favor of introversion (plus unrelated questions). The authors showed that interviewer-participants appear to have formulated confirmatory hypothesis-testing strategies (i.e. they selected extraverted questions when they were instructed to investigate whether the target was extraverted and similarly for introversion). In a series of several studies, we tried to extend this effect to the evaluation of a target. An initial study was conducted to replicate and extend Snyder and Swann (1978) effects on confirmatory hypothesis-testing with a few differences: a) all participants were assigned the interviewer role and the target was fictitious and b) participants received feedback (ambiguous on the dimensions of extraversion/introversion) regardless of their experimental condition. Also, participants had to evaluate the target on the bases of a short description of a so-called other participant. In this initial study, we replicated the effect of hypothesis confirmation in the "choice of questions" task. However, on the evaluation of the target, the results were unexpected. Participants in the extravert condition judged the target as more introverted than participants in the introvert condition (Study 1). These results were replicated in one other study for the choice of questions (Study 2) and in two other studies for the evaluation of the target (Studies 2 and 3). A possible explanation could be in terms of the strategy implemented by the participants. Individuals would tend to adopt similarity strategies (i.e., seek information consistent with the standard; Mussweiler, 2003). However, depending on the specific motivation, they could put in place strategies to find differences. In the case of our study, the participants were able to perceive that the instructions were biased either in the direction of introversion or in the direction of extroversion. The participants may therefore have wanted to correct this bias by focusing on the search for difference and not similarity. In the case where the participants received strong expectations (for example, with statistical information, Study 2), they may have been motivated to validate this hypothesis and therefore look for the similarities. It is also possible that the mismatch between the target of comparison and the stimulus led participants to focus on dissimilarities (Herr et al., 1983; Mussweiler, 2003). Indeed, the description of an introvert and an extravert presented to participants is stereotypical and can be considered as an extreme standard of comparison whereas the target to be evaluated has rather ambiguous characteristics. When extreme standards of comparison are made salient and the stimulus to be evaluated is ambiguous, there may be an insufficient match between the two resulting in contrast effects (Herr et al., 1983). If participants did indeed adopt a difference-seeking strategy, this could explain why they rated the target as more extraverted when they were instructed to test the introversion hypothesis, and vice versa. To test this possibility, we will conduct another study similar to the initial study. As in Study 1, participants will be randomly instructed to determine whether the target is introverted (vs. extraverted). The only difference is that for half of participants we will be primed to focus on similarities and the other half to focus on differences. The second part of the experiment will remain unchanged. For the first task, we expect participants to show confirmatory hypothesis-testing strategies regardless of primed focus (high vs. low). However, in the second task, we expect different outcomes. The hypothesis is that participants primed to focus on similarities will form impressions consistent with the experimental condition (i.e. the target should be seen as introvert in the introvert condition and extravert in the extravert condition). On the other hand, we expect participants primed to focus on differences to form impressions opposed to their experimental condition, replicating results of Study 1.

title_r: CODy - Compassion for Others in Dyads
abstract_r: We are conducting a conceptual replication study of a recent study at Heidelberg University (Schültke et al., 2024). The aim of the study is to examine the effects of dyadic compassion meditation on heart rate variability (HRV), affect, and social closeness in couples, to expand the evidence base for the use of partner meditation in couples therapy and in non-clinical contexts. The sample consists of non-clinical couples. After random assignment to one of three groups, following the induction of negative emotions the couples will either engage in compassion meditation together (dyadic group) or separately in different rooms (individiual group), or they will watch a video (control group). Heart rate data will be collected using EEG, along with demographic information and data on heart rate control variables, relationship quality, closeness, mindfulness, compassion, meditation experience, interoceptive awareness, emotion regulation, and affect. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the University of Mannheim. We expect HRV to decrease when negative emotions are induced. Additionally, we expect the affect to worsen. Following the start of the meditation/video viewing, we expect HRV, affect and social closeness to increase more strongly in the experimental groups than in the control group. Furthermore, we expect these factors to increase more strongly in the dyadic group than in the individual group. Reference Schültke, L., Warth, M., Alpers, G. W., Ditzen, B., & Aguilar-Raab, C. title_r: Examining the Modulating Effects of Reinforcement Learning and Explicit Instructions on Cognitive Stability and Flexibility
abstract_r: Context-sensitive adaptations of cognitive stability and flexibility, two key functions of cognitive control, are a prerequisite for goal-directed behavior (Dreisbach & Fröber, 2019; Dreisbach & Wenke, 2011; Egner, 2023; Goschke, 2003). Cognitive stability and flexibility are assumed to be associated with complementary benefits and costs in performance (Dreisbach & Fröber, 2019; Goschke, 2013; but see e.g., Egner, 2023). The flexibility to switch between tasks is traded off against the cost of distractibility (Dreisbach et al., 2005; Tharp & Pickering, 2011), while a stable task focus comes at the concurrent cost of rigidity (Hefer & Dreisbach, 2017). In the planned study, we aim to investigate potential modulators of these cognitive control states. Being able to reliably modulate or induce meta-control processes that promote stability and flexibility is not only of theoretical relevance but may potentially enable us to predict, reduce, or even optimize the costs of control configurations in various contexts. Various studies have demonstrated a modulating influence of reward on mobilization of cognitive control as well as on the mode of cognitive control (Dreisbach & Fischer, 2012; Dreisbach & Fröber, 2019; Goschke & Bolte, 2014). Extending previous research on reward effects, some studies have further demonstrated that not only specific behaviors but also higher-order control processes can be modulated via reinforcement learning by linking reward to varying abstract control demands. For example, disproportionally reinforcing task switches compared to repetitions led to more voluntary switching behavior and smaller interference from response-incongruent trials (Braem, 2017). Making reward more contingent on incongruent than congruent trials led to reduced congruency effects (Held et al., 2024). Reinforcement learning thus operates on the level of abstract meta-control processes, modulating future control states. Building on these findings, in the planned study, we will investigate whether selectively rewarding cognitively stable or flexible behavior increases goal shielding or shifting respectively. Control states are suggested to be subject to deliberate meta-control strategies. It has been shown that individuals adjust their level of cognitive flexibility based on information about to-be-expected control demands (Liu & Yeung, 2020). Previous studies have further reported instructed adjustments in participants’ degree of parallel processing (Lehle et al., 2009; Lehle & Hübner, 2009). Similarly, we observed corresponding adaptations in participants’ cognitive flexibility in terms of altered task-switch costs when we explicitly instructed them to switch flexibly between tasks compared to when we instructed them to shield their current task against distractions (Bartossek et al., 2024; unpublished manuscript). Because evidence for instruction-based adjustments of meta-control strategies is scarce, another aim of the present study is to replicate our previous findings and test if cognitive control modes can be regulated strategically in a top-down manner. Furthermore, a current debate revolves around the mechanisms underlying stability and flexibility. While control-dilemma theory suggests a stability-flexibility tradeoff (Dreisbach & Fröber, 2019; Goschke, 2003, 2013; Goschke & Bolte, 2014), recent studies suggest that stability and flexibility can be independently regulated (Geddert & Egner, 2022; Bejjani et al., 2022; Egner, 2023; Nack & Yu-Chin, 2023; Geddert & Egner, 2024). The present study thus additionally aims to test the hypothesis of an antagonistic relationship between cognitive stability and flexibility. To these ends, we will conduct two online task-switching experiments. In Experiment (Exp.) 1, we will selectively reward participants for either stable or flexible behavior throughout experimental blocks. Thereby, we aim to investigate whether abstract control states can be induced via reinforcement learning. In Exp. 2, we will present strategy instructions targeted at promoting either increased cognitive stability or flexibility. By testing whether these explicit instructions will induce corresponding strategic adjustments of control states, we aim to replicate our previous finding of volitional control regulations. Additionally, fluctuations in cognitive stability and flexibility might arise independently of the manipulations in Exp. 1 and 2 at individual subject levels. As stability and flexibility are hypothesized to involve a tradeoff (Dreisbach & Fröber, 2019; Goschke, 2003, 2013; Goschke & Bolte, 2014), we will test if individual adjustments in cognitive stability between conditions negatively correlate with concurrent changes in cognitive flexibility in both experiments.

title_r: Observer-rated environmental sensitivity and its characterization at genetic, physiological, and behavioral level
abstract_r: The main aim of the current study is to characterize heightened environmental sensitivity at behavioral, physiological, and genetic level in a large sample of three-year-old children. We have three subgoals. The first is to test and replicate the psychometric properties of a recently developed behavioral rating system of environmental sensitivity in children: the Highly Sensitive Child-Rating system (HSC-RS; Lionetti et al., 2019). In a previous study (Lionetti et al., 2019), first evidence was found for a psychometric reliable and valid measure of environmental sensitivity. However, in Lionetti et al. (2019) only a subsample of the total sample (n = 292) were included (not all data were coded yet). Therefore, in the current study we will test whether we can replicate the factor structure, distribution, and reliability in the full sample (n = 537). The following aspects are new and have not been tested before in regards to observed sensitivity. Secondly, we will investigate whether we can identify different sensitivity groups based on the continuous observed sensitivity score. Previous studies in children (Pluess et al., 2018) and adults (Lionetti et al., 2018) using self-reported sensitivity, found evidence for a three group solution with around 30% of individuals falling into the high sensitivity group (i.e., orchids), 40% into the medium sensitivity group (i.e., tulips), and 30% falling into the low sensitivity group (i.e., dandelions). Third, we aim to characterize observed heightened sensitivity in young children (i.e., age 3) in terms of extensively investigated markers of environmental sensitivity at multiple levels of analysis (i.e., behavioral, physiological, and genetic level).

title_r: Effectiveness and Efficiency of Instruction vs Feedback-Based Multimedia Learning Activities
abstract_r: A previous study identified the distinct effect of multimedia feedback on conditional probability problem-solving performance (Gök et al., 2025). The study detected distinct effects for including multimedia in initial instruction versus feedback. More specifically, multimedia materials in the initial instruction led students to perceive the problems as less difficult and spontaneously draw more diagrams relative to only text in the initial instruction, while multimedia materials in feedback resulted in improved accuracy on a posttest compared to only text in the feedback. However, it remains unclear (1) whether instruction and feedback-based learning activities are equally effective in this context and (2) whether combining instruction and feedback is necessary compared to only including feedback-based learning activities, given that previous study under a similar context questioned the necessity of the initial instruction stage (Asher et al., 2025). The current study will address these questions in the context of multimedia learning of conditional probability problem solving with a refined design of three conditions. One only receives instruction-based activities (instruction-only condition), one only receives feedback-based activities (feedback-only condition), and one last condition receives both instruction and feedback-based activities (instruction+feedback condition). We will compare the learning outcomes of these conditions, and since different types of learning activities may not be equally time-demanding, we will also calculate and compare the efficiency of learning of these conditions. Finally, we will also replicate and extend the metacognitive measure of our previous study. Students will rate how difficult and how helpful each learning activity. These measures will help us determine students’ metacognitive awareness of how much they learn from feedback.

title_r: An empirical generalization and extension of “Talk and types? The effect of digital interfaces on citizens’ satisfaction with standardized public services”
abstract_r: This is an empirical replication of Prokop and Tepe’s (2022) “Talk and types? The effect of digital interfaces on citizens’ satisfaction with standardized public services”. Prokop and Tepe (2022, 427) “found that replacing face-to-face communication with a digital interface has no effect on citizens’ satisfaction, nor does it mitigate the effect of psychological costs, service failure, and recovery”. We replicate this study in Shenzhen PR China. Shenzhen is a leading smart city with many hi-tech firms. Citizens in Shenzhen, compared to the average Chinese citizens, are younger, better educated and more accepting and familiar with the use of digital technology. We use a different population to test the same research questions and hypotheses. We alter the original hypotheses given the findings in the original study and the context in which we test these hypotheses: H1: Satisfaction in public service encounters with digital interfaces is similar to face-to-face encounters. The original experiment found that the type of service had no direct effect on citizens’ satisfaction. Shenzhen is the first city in China to carry out reform and opening up, and its economy has developed rapidly. The local government has led many reforms in public services, such as social security and public housing, to establish a service-oriented government. As a result, we expect there are no significant differences in satisfaction across different service types (ID card, certificate of no criminal conviction, and recordation receipt for public rental housing which is similar to the 3 service types in original study). In the replication study, we add minimum living guarantee (dibao) card as a higher degree of stigmatization in China. That’s because our search of existing stigmatization studies in Chinese academic journals focuses on grassroots cadres (Ren et.al 2024) and government departments such as urban management (Xie and Tian 2013), and also some studies explore the stigmatization of minimum living guarantee card which is one of the basic public services in China (Chen and Yue 2023). But for the stigmatization effect of minimum living guarantee is also mixed in China. Therefore, the difference in stigmatization would be small and relatively weak. H2: Applying for potentially stigmatizing public services harms citizens' satisfaction, but the effect is relatively weak. Due to differences in political systems and cultures, citizens in Shenzhen have higher trust in government. This would reduce the impact of service failures and recovery on satisfaction, and, therefore, we maintain the original hypotheses by expecting the size effects to be lower than in the original experiment: H3a: Service failure has a negative effect on citizens' satisfaction. H3b: Explaining and apologizing for service failure increases satisfaction compared to service failure without explanation and apology.

abstract_r: This study extends our initial investigation conducted in the Netherlands by examining the perceived similarity structure of 22 positive emotions in four additional countries: the United States, Italy, South Africa, and Chile. title_r: What is real? Can people distinguish between human and AI voices?
abstract_r: The purpose of this research is to replicate the study done by Barrington, Cooper, and Farid (2025), with focus on the naturalness task which answers the question of how accurately participants can distinguish human voices from AI-generated voices. Unlike the original research, we will not replicate the identity task of the experiment in which participants assessed whether two voices belonged to the same or two different people. Our study applies a within-subjects design where each participant classifies both real and AI clips, presented randomly, with an equal chance of hearing either. As AI and voice-cloning technology specifically have developed rapidly over recent years, creating new risks in security, media, and private communication, it is important to investigate whether people can detect artificially generated voices from natural ones. We want to replicate the original study with a younger sample of participants to see if the results in the younger populations differ. Based on the findings of the original study, we expect that participants' accuracy for distinguishing between human voices from AI-generated clips will be above random guessing (i.e. 50%), with higher accuracy for real over artificial voices.

title_r: Brain Network Lateralization in Autism: A Replication and Expansion of Peterson et al. (2024)
abstract_r: As integral characteristics for neurotypical development, the developmental timeline for the degree and direction of lateralization may act as indicators for neurodevelopmental disruptions. For example, differences in the functional organization of language may contribute directly to language impairment (Stefanatos & Baron, 2011). Autism spectrum disorder has been linked to differences in lateralization, including reduced lateralization during language development (Eyler et al., 2012; Herbert et al., 2002; Herringshaw et al., 2016; Kleinhans et al., 2008; Knaus et al., 2008, 2010). Work by Jouravlev et al. (2020) identified differences in lateralization in autism specific to language regions of the brain. However, a more recent study by Peterson et al. (2024) examined lateralization differences across eight functional networks and identified decreased lateralization in autism for three networks: language, salience/ventral attention-A, and control-B. Furthermore, it was found that language delay stratified language lateralization, with group differences in language lateralization occurring between autistic males with language delay and neurotypical individuals. However, the sample employed in Peterson et al. (2024) was limited in size and only included autistic males, so it is unknown whether these results can generalize to autistic females. The aim of the present replication is to examine the findings reported in Peterson et al. (2024) within a larger sample, as well as perform several exploratory analyses.

abstract_r: We are replicating key findings from Cipollina and Sanchez (2025) - “It’s best not to discuss or see sexual orientation: An examination of sexuality blindfolding". We predict a successful replication; specifically: we predict that Discussion Avoidance will be negatively correlated with i) heterosexual privilege awareness, ii) LGBQ equity support, and iii) LGBQ allyship while being positively associated with iv) LGBQ discomfort and v) racial colorblindness. We predict that for Category Evasion will have null zero-order correlations (or small, but significant effects, i.e., r less than or equal to |0.10) with those same outcomes, magnitudes which were considered null in the original study. However, when Category Evasion is entered in as a predictor along with Discussion Avoidance, we believe we will replicate significant predictive betas for both dimensions of SSB. For Category Evasion, we believe it will positively predict: i) privilege awareness, ii) equity support, and iii) allyship; while negatively predicting iv) LGBTQ discomfort and v) racial colorblindness. title_r: Conceptual replication of Dignath et al., 2022, experiment 3 - particular focus on emotional Stroop task (E.g., Soutscheck and Schubert, 2013) 'Do self-related primes influence the processing of conflicts in the emotional domain?'
abstract_r: Previous research has shown (e.g., Dignath et al., 2022) that Congruency Effects (CE) in a gender Stroop task are significantly reduced when self-related primes are used compared neutral primes in a control condition. The significant interaction of the factors ‘congruency’ and ‘prime’, indicated reduced CEs in experimental blocks with self-referential information compared to control blocks. Here, we ask whether this phenomenon can be replicated also in the emotional domain. We will closely replicate experiment 3 of Dignath et al. (2022), but instead of a gender task, emotional Stroop task will be employed (modelled after Soutscheck & Schubert, 2013), in which participants must classify facial expressions as positive or negative, while ignoring clearly positive or negative valenced words. In line with the study of Dignath et al. (2022), the main question of this experiment is how self-referential primes modulate CEs. Going beyond previous research, we ask whether similar effects can be generalized to the emotional domain. We consider two possible accounts. The attentional bias account assumes that CEs should be increased in the self-referential condition, because self-referential primes draw attention towards the task-irrelevant dimension and hence should enhance CEs. Specifically, for emotional stimuli, it has been suggested that attention is not only quicker engaged by emotional stimuli, but also impairs attentional disengagement. In contrast, the priming of control account holds that CEs in the self-referential condition should be reduced, because self-relevance boosts cognitive control over task-irrelevant response tendencies. Indeed, it has been suggested that the inextricable link between control and self-referential information is particularly strong for emotional material.

title_r: Effects of Spatial Attention on Visuocortical Processing: A Multi-Laboratory Replication of Clark & Hillyard (1996)
abstract_r: Whether selective attention alters initial sensory processing or instead only operates at higher cortical stages (often referred to as early vs. late selection) is a foundational question in cognitive neuroscience. Investigating the influence of covert visual selective attention, Clark and Hillyard (1996) found that directed attention modulated the amplitude of several early components (P1 and N1) of the visual event-related potential (ERP) derived from the ongoing electroencephalogram (EEG). However, attended and non-attended visual stimuli did not produce statistically different amplitudes in the C1 or P2 components. Dipole source estimation of the neural locus of these ERPs indicated that the C1 originated in primary (striate) visual cortex (V1), while the later components primarily arose from extrastriate visuocortical areas. Together, these results led to the conclusion that sustained spatial attention enhances the sensory gain of early visual processing in V1 via feedback projections from the extrastriate visual cortex where the P1 and N1 are generated. Despite the influential nature of this original work in EEG and cognitive neuroscience more broadly, recent research has reignited the debate on which stage of the visual processing hierarchy is influenced by attention. As part of the #EEGManyLabs project (Pavlov et al., 2021), we will be revisiting this issue by conducting a multi-site, high-powered direct replication of Clark and Hillyard (1996).
