title_r: Do different types of conflict interact?: An evaluation of Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) - Experiment 4
abstract_r: In distractor-interference tasks (e.g., Stroop, Simon, flanker), participants are slower and more error-prone in incongruent trials – where a distractor cues a different response than the target – than in congruent trials – where a distractor cues the same response as the target. This difference in performance, known as the congruency effect, arguably reflects greater response conflict in incongruent trials – which cue two opposing responses – than in congruent trials – which cue only one response. Although all distractor-interference tasks involve response conflict, the literature distinguishes between different types - or sources - of conflict that can occur in different tasks (Kornblum, 1990). Tasks such as flanker and Stroop involve stimulus-stimulus type conflict wherein the distractor and target convey semantically incongruent information. For example, in a color-based flanker task, the color of a central target square may be red, while the color of flanking distractor squares is green. On the other hand, the Simon task involves stimulus-response type conflict wherein the stimulus location is incongruent with the location of the correct response. For example, a Simon stimulus may appear on the left side of the screen but require a response with the right hand. Here, the distractor (stimulus location) is incongruent with the response (right-hand keypress) not with the identity of another stimulus. The distinction between different types of conflict suggests that people may process one type of conflict (e.g., stimulus-stimulus conflict) independently of another type of conflict (e.g., stimulus-response conflict). This is a core premise of conflict-specific accounts of cognitive control (Kornblum, 1990; Egner, 2008), which argue that control processes adapt to different forms of conflict independently of each other. In order to assess whether two distractors engender different types of conflict (e.g., stimulus-stimulus conflict and stimulus-response conflict), Egner (2008) proposed using hybrid distractor-interference tasks. For example, one could combine the Stroop and Simon tasks into a hybrid Stroop-Simon task. Here, on every trial, one would make a left or right response to identify the ink color of a Stroop color word stimulus presented on the left or right side of the screen. Egner (2008) argued that if Stroop and Simon distractors engender different types of conflict (i.e., stimulus-stimulus and stimulus-response conflict, respectively), which the brain processes independently, then the Stroop and Simon effects should sum additively. On the other hand, if Stroop and Simon distractors engender the same type of conflict, which the brain processes in a dependent fashion, then the Stroop and Simon effects should interact. However, two findings complicate the logic of Egner’s (2008) approach to identifying different domains of conflict, making it difficult to assess evidence for the conflict-specific account of cognitive control. First, within-trial interactions between the congruency of one distractor (e.g., Stroop) and the congruency of another distractor (e.g., Simon) may depend on the presence of a large congruency effect (Rey-Mermet, 2020). Second, a reactivation aversion effect (RAE) – in which one must execute a previously abandoned response – can produce interactions between two congruency effects regardless of whether the associated distractors engender the same or different types of conflict (Schlaghecken and Maylor, 2020). We elaborate on each of these findings below. First, Rey-Mermet (2020) found that within-trial interactions between the congruency effects of two distractors depend on the presence of a large congruency effect. In particular, Rey Mermet (2020) found – in a hybrid Stroop-flanker task – that interactions between Stroop and Flanker congruency are largest when the Stroop effect is large. Rey-Mermet (2020), therefore, concluded that observing a large congruency effect is a necessary condition for observing within-trial interactions of the sort that Egner (2008) describes. Weissman et al. (2020) observed similar results in a hybrid Stroop-Simon task. Here, the interaction between the Stroop and Simon effects was also greater when the Stroop effect was relatively large vs relatively small. With this in mind, it is unclear whether within-trial interactions between different congruency effects index dependent forms of conflict, or merely the presence of large congruency effects. Second, and crucial for the present study, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) found that a RAE – in which one must execute a previously abandoned response – can produce within-trial interactions between congruency effects in a hybrid prime-Simon task. In each trial of this task, participants first saw a prime arrow stimulus at the center of the screen. Next, they saw a probe arrow Simon stimulus. Participants were required to identify the direction of the probe arrow. The direction of the prime arrow could point in either the same (prime-compatible trials) or different (prime-incompatible trials) direction as the probe arrow, producing a prime compatibility effect. In addition, the location of the probe arrow could be the same (probe-congruent trials) or different (probe-incongruent trials) as the required response location, producing a probe congruency (i.e., Simon) effect. Critically, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) note that a RAE is possible only in prime-compatible, probe-incongruent trials. This is because the prime first cues one response (e.g., left), the probe location then cues the opposite response (e.g., right) and finally, the probe direction requires making the response originally cued by the prime (e.g, left). Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) argue that this response switching (e.g., left, then right, then left) creates confusion at a metacognitive level that lengthens response time selectively in prime-compatible, probe-incongruent trials. This possibility is problematic for Egner’s (2008) method because a RAE will produce an interaction between prime compatibility and probe (i.e., Simon) congruency by increasing RT in prime-compatible, probe-incongruent trials. Consistent with this possibility, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) found an interaction suggesting a RAE in their prime-Simon task. Therefore, it appears that a RAE can explain interactions between two congruency effects without any recourse to a dependency between two distractors that engender the same type of conflict. Nonetheless, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) suggest that a modified version of Egner’s (2008) method may still distinguish whether two distractors engender the same or different types of conflict. In particular, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) suggest that one can avoid the influence of the RAE in their task by evaluating how the probe congruency (i.e., Simon) effect differs between prime-neutral and prime-incompatible trials (rather than between prime-compatible and prime-incompatible trials). Indeed, since the RAE only influences RT in trials with congruent primes, the RAE cannot influence the probe congruency (i.e., Simon) effect in prime-neutral or prime-incompatible trials. Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020), therefore, suggest that Egner’s (2008) logic can be reapplied to interactions between prime compatibility and probe congruency when one restricts the former factor to neutral and incompatible primes. Interestingly, Schlaghecken and Maylor (2020) found evidence (Experiment 1, horizontal trials) that the probe congruency (i.e., Simon) effect did not differ between prime-neutral and prime-incompatible trials (i.e., they did not find an interaction). This finding is consistent with the idea that prime compatibility and probe (i.e., Simon) congruency effects reflect two different types of conflict (i.e. stimulus-stimulus and stimulus-response respectively), which the cognitive system processes independently of each other (Kornblum, 1990). title_r: CREP #25-43: Registration of Study 1 from Muenks et al. (2020)
abstract_r: As part of the Collaborative Replications and Education Project, we aim to conduct a replication of Study 1 from Muenks et al. (2020): “Does My Professor Think My Ability Can Change? Students’ Perceptions of Their STEM Professors’ Mindset Beliefs Predict Their Psychological Vulnerability, Engagement, and Performance in Class.” The original study had focused on professor mindset and student psychological vulnerability within the context of STEM courses. Participants watched a video of a professor going over course expectations and rated their anticipated belonging, evaluative concerns, course engagement, course interest, and anticipated course performance. Replicating Study 1 from Muenks et al. (2020) as part of the Collaborative Replications and Education Project could help us improve our understanding of how professor mindsets may influence student outcomes in STEM courses across cultures and languages. One element we added was a condition in which participants were told the clip was from the first day of an Introduction to Astronomy course rather than a Calculus I course. Previous research shows that 25% of four-year college students have moderate to high math anxiety (Jones, 2001, as cited in Beilock & Willingham, 2014). As such, we selected the Introduction to Astronomy course to see whether similar results could be found for STEM courses in which math is not a salient feature. One other difference is that our sample will consist of college students enrolled in at least one psychology course on our campus rather than drawing from an online research platform. We expect to replicate results from the original study and find that students in the fixed mindset condition would demonstrate more evaluative concerns, less anticipated course engagement, less anticipated course interest, and lower anticipated course performance relative to the control group and the growth mindset group. To analyze our data we plan on running correlations between variables and running analyses of covariance (ANCOVAs; with race, gender, and personal mindset beliefs entered as covariates), following the original study, in order to test for replication of results. Also following the original, we will run mediation analyses with professor mindset as the predictor, psychological vulnerability as the mediator, and course engagement, interest, anticipated course performance, and dropout intentions as possible outcome variables (each of which will be a separate analysis).

title_r: Testing the confounding role of response biases in OC presence/absence asymmetries
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that individuals with high OC tendencies, as well as those with clinical OCD, struggle to make inferences about absence in a visual search paradigm (Toffolo et al., 2013, 2014; 2016). This difficulty was reflected in an association between OC tendencies and search times only in target-absent trials, but not in target-present trials (this selective association will be termed “absence–presence asymmetries”). However, a recent large-scale online study failed to conceptually and directly replicate this finding (Sarna et al., 2024). The authors suggested several OC-related explanations for this discrepancy; however, recent empirical work (Sarna et al., 2025; Zorowitz et al., 2023) highlighting the systemic confounding influence of response biases may offer a surface-level explanation for the inconsistency between the original findings and the failed replication. In the present experiment, we aim to test whether OC-related absence–presence asymmetries may have been masked by uncontrolled inattentive responding. To this end, we directly replicate the design of Toffolo et al. (2013) while incorporating rigorous controls for inattentive responding and acquiescence.

title_r: Replication of Muenks et al. (2020) at McGill University
abstract_r: Project #25-47 This is a replication study of Muenks et al. (2020)’s paper ‘Does My Professor Think My Ability Can Change? Students’ Perceptions of Their STEM Professors’ Mindset Beliefs Predict Their Psychological Vulnerability, Engagement, and Performance in Class’. We are a team of psychology undergraduates at McGill University conducting this replication study for the course PSYC351: Research Methods and Laboratory in Social Psychology. Lead contributors: Seol Han, Alina Hu, Maria Kiremitci, Alice Liu, Sofia Moreno, Suruchi Mungrati Acknowledgements: Dr. Eric Hehman and Travis Lim from McGill University In Study 1 of Muenks et al. (2020), faculty mindset beliefs were experimentally manipulated and students were exposed to STEM professors who endorsed either fixed or growth mindset beliefs. The proposed hypothesis was that students experience more psychological vulnerability when exposed to a STEM professor who endorses more fixed mindset beliefs, compared to when they have no information about the STEM professor’s mindset beliefs. Furthermore, greater anticipated psychological vulnerability would predict lower anticipated course engagement, interest and performance. In our replication, we aim to follow the same protocol by recruiting a target sample size of 100 participants from McGill university’s psychology participant pool through the SONA management system. In addition to the original study’s research questions, our goal is to understand the relationship between individual cultural orientation (collectivism vs. individualism) and the effects of a professor’s mindset of intelligence (growth vs. fixed vs. control) on students’ academic engagement, interest, and anticipated performance after a brief video exposure. We propose measuring individual cultural orientation because the professor-mindset manipulation is an authority-delivered social norm cue, and cultural orientation reliably moderates norm uptake. Students higher in collectivism should align more with the professor’s displayed mindset (greater boosts after growth; larger decrements after fixed) due to greater authority/norm sensitivity, whereas students higher in individualism may show weaker effects or reactance to fixed messages. Thus, cultural orientation should qualify—and help explain variance in—the main CREP effects on academic engagement, interest, and anticipated performance. We predict significant Mindset × Cultural Orientation interactions, with the growth–fixed gap largest among more collectivistic students. To address our additional hypothesis, participants’ cultural orientation will be assessed with the Cultural Orientation Scale (Triandis & Gelfland, 1998), which uses Likert-type questions to quantify the extent to which individuals endorse collectivistic versus individualistic values.

title_r: Replication of Pennycook, Cannon, & Rand (2018; Study 2) at McGill University
abstract_r: The project involves a direct replication of Study 2 from Pennycook et al. (2018), which examines how familiarity and motivated reasoning impact participants’ ability to differentiate between real and fake news headlines. We will recruit approximately 100 undergraduate students drawn from the SONA participant pool at McGill University. The replication methods used in this study are identical to the methods used in the original Pennycook et al. study 2, there will be no deviations. The purpose of the replication is to investigate if the original hypothesis and results are upheld when replicated. We expect the outcomes will be consistent with the results from the original study. In addition to the replication, we are going to investigate if individuals with higher scores on the gullibility scale are more susceptible to believing fake news headlines. We will score participants on gullibility levels and explore the relationship between these scores and susceptibility to believing the fake news headlines from the initial task. The only change to the original study will be an additional measure of gullibility using a self-report questionnaire developed by Teunisse, A. K. et al. (2020). The materials relevant to our additional question will only be presented to participants after they have completed the measures from the direct replication. The purpose of this additional hypothesis is to explore the relationship between individual gullibility levels and susceptibility to believing fake news. We hypothesize that participants who are more accurate at differentiating real and fake news headlines will score lower on the gullibility self report scale.

title_r: Causal Evidence for Representation-Specific Recruitment for Motion Direction Using TMS
abstract_r: Participants were asked to maintain the motion direction of an RDK while performing a same/different discrimination task on two additional RDK motion directions. There are two discrimination conditions, where the stimulus being maintained in memory is either in between (middle) or to one side (side) of the discrimination stimuli in the feature space (Teng and Kravitz, 2019). We expect to replicate previous results, where the middle condition reduces the perceived difference between the two motion directions, resulting in a higher discrimination threshold, and the side condition results in a greater perceived difference and lower thresholds. We also expect the discrimination stimuli will introduce systematic biases in the continuous recall of the maintained information, with higher accuracy in the middle than the side condition. Critically, in this experiment we expect that TMS to Area MT+ during the ISI between encoding and discrimination will destabilize the VWM representation, causing the interference between VWM and perception to decrease. The difference between the middle and side conditions should therefore decrease for both discrimination and recall.

title_r: Investigating the impact of semantic category and task instructions on conceptual cueing
abstract_r: Conceptual cueing effect refers to behavioural findings showing that encountering certain concepts selectively biases attention toward spatial locations that are congruent with the words’ semantic meanings (Chatterjee, 2001). For instance, words like ‘HEAVEN’ or ‘JOY’ direct gaze upward, whereas ‘BASEMENT’ and ‘BITTERNESS’ orient attention downward. This effect is potentially useful in investigating how abstract mental concepts are associated with concrete perceptual features, and how people utilise these mental concepts to guide visual attention. Existing literature disputed over whether conceptual cueing effect is elicited automatically or depends on explicit processing of cues’ semantic meanings. Earlier investigations have generally assumed that conceptual cueing occurs automatically without needing to instruct participants to explicitly process the semantic-space mapping (Meier & Robinson, 2004). Meanwhile, later reports only observed conceptual cueing with explicit task instructions(Shaki & Fischer, 2023). A more recent meta-analysis noted that raising cue valences’ task relevance would increase effect size of conceptual cueing, but is not necessary to observe this effect (Pohl & Miklashevsky, 2025). These discrepant findings hint toward a lack of understanding of cognitive mechanisms and contributing factors in which conceptual cueing effect originates from. In a previous replication attempt, we employed a paradigm used in a previous study using emotional words as cues (Gozli et al., 2013). As shown in Figure 1a, this paradigm first displays a cue word at the screen centre, then asks participants to identify the geometric shape of a target that appears either above or below the cue. Participants are asked to only respond to emotional words (with furniture words as catch words), but they do not need to explicitly consider the valence of the cues. Using this task, we did not observe conclusive evidence for the conceptual cueing effect. Previous studies have shown that some semantic categories only produce conceptual cueing effect when task instructions ask participants to explicitly process the semantics of the cue words (e.g. when participants only react to words with particular meanings; de la Vega et al., 2012; Shaki & Fischer, 2023). For other categories however, for instance words that refer to direction (e.g. ‘UP’ and ‘DOWN’) conceptual cueing occurs both in implicit and explicit instructions (Gibson & Sztybel, 2014). So we hypothesized that the negative finding in our replication of Gozli et al, 2013, could be due to the cue words not being explicitly processed. In fact, it is not known if emotional words need to be explicitly processed in terms of their valence to produce conceptual cueing. Hence with the current experiment, we seek to answer this question and compare the results between emotional cues and words referring to spatial directions, that more consistently produce strong conceptual cueing (Shaki & Fischer, 2023). Through this investigation, we aim to specify the factors that are pre-requisites of conceptual cueing effect. To this end, we will adapt the original paradigm to assess whether semantic categories of cues and explicit evaluation of cue valence impact on participants’ reaction time and accuracy (Gozli et al., 2013). In a three-way within-subject factorial design, we will compare the effects of emotion words (e.g. ‘JOY’ and ‘SAD’) against direction words (e.g. ‘UP’ and ‘DOWN’) on participants’ task performance in congruent and incongruent conditions. Furthermore, we will manipulate participants’ levels of semantic processing of cues with different task instructions: in implicit semantic processing condition, participants will be asked to respond when the cue word describes a specified category (emotion or direction), and to withhold response when the word describes furniture (i.e. catch trials). In explicit semantic processing condition, participants will be asked to respond only if the cue belongs to a specified category and in addition has a specific meaning (e.g. positive emotion or upward direction). Examples of different task instructions are depicted in Figure 1c. Furthermore, participants will complete two self-report inventories, Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS) and Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21) at the end of experiment. We will use these scores to assess participants’ sensitivity to positive and negative emotions and how they influence participants’ reaction toward emotion cue words (Langvik & Borgen Austad, 2019; Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995). Figure 1 (uploaded as S01E02Paradigm.png). schematic examples of a) trial procedure, b) on-screen stimuli display in current experiment, and c) elements of two experiment blocks. Each block starts with 6 practice trials, followed by 60 experiment trials, resulting in a total of 528 trials and 24 total repetitions for each cue word.

title_r: The effect of “you guys” (versus “you all”) on women’s perceptions of ostracism
abstract_r: Stout and Dasgupta (2011) found that, when women were exposed to language that included only male referents (e.g., “he,” “guys”), they felt more ostracized/less belonging than when exposed to gender-inclusive (e.g., “he or she”) language. We recently conducted a high-powered and pre-registered replication of Stout and Dasgupta’s Study 1. In that now completed replication attempt, we observed the same findings as Stout and Dasgupta: women in the gender-exclusive condition found the language more sexist, reported more anticipated job-based ostracism, and less job-based motivation and identification than those in the gender-inclusive condition. In the Stout and Dasgupta (2011) work, they examined gender-exclusive language in an employment context, as the gender-exclusive language was embedded in the description of a company/job. The purpose of this pre-registered study is to examine if gender-exclusive (versus gender-inclusive) language prompts women to anticipate more ostracism in an educational context. Moreover, in Stout and Dasgupta (2011), gender-exclusive language was created by using only male pronouns (he, his, him) and the term “guys.” In modern contexts, using male pronouns like “he” as a generic stand-in for people of all gender identities is increasingly rare and likely seen as socially unacceptable. However, using “guys” as a generic stand-in for people of all gender identities is still rather ubiquitous and may be seen either as a socially acceptable form of gender-exclusive language or perhaps not even recognized as gender-exclusive. In this work, we will present women with an alleged transcript of a professor’s opening remarks on the first day of the semester. This professor’s remarks will include the phrase “you guys” (in the gender-exclusive condition) or the phrase “you all” (in the gender-inclusive condition). We will investigate whether “you guys” (versus “you all”) is perceived as exclusionary by women.

title_r: Hawaii Perceivers Replication
abstract_r: This study attempts to replicate the key finding reported in Pauker et al. (2018) that perceivers' ability to categorize multiracial faces as multiracial depends on geographic contexts. In line with the original Pauker et al. (2018) study, participants will be sampled from Hawaii and outside of Hawaii (specifically Southern California) and multiracial categorization data for these two samples will be compared. In addition to this primary test, we will also test three additional hypotheses that were explored by Pauker et al. (2018), though to be clear, we view these tests as secondary to the primary goal of the current replication attempt. First, we will explore whether the composition of the multiracial faces corresponds with differences in categorizations as multiracial, and second, we will test whether racial composition interacts with sample location. Finally, we will test whether contact with multiracial people mediates the relationship between region and multiracial categorizations. In attempting to replicate these focal effects, we will also test for potential differences in hypodescent.

title_r: The "Go/No-Go" paradigm to assess spatial numerical associations - Experiment 6
abstract_r: This study will use the "Go/No-go" paradigm to investigate spatial-numerical associations (SNAs) within UK adult participants. Eccher et al. (2025) used a computerised Go/No-go task to investigate SNA in a sample of Himba adults, Italian adults and Italian preschoolers. In each trial, participants were presented with a central fixation cross, followed by the first dot array (henceforth the “reference stimulus”) made up of 4, 12 or 36 dots. After a brief blank screen, participants then saw a second dot array (henceforth the “test stimulus”) displayed to either the left or right of the screen. In the increasing condition, participants were told to press the space bar when the test stimulus contained MORE dots than the reference stimulus. For example, when the reference stimulus contained 4 dots, the participant’s response would be recorded as correct only if the test stimulus contained 12 or 36 dots. If the reference stimulus was 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the test stimulus contained 36 dots. In the decreasing condition, participants were then instructed to only press the space bar when the test stimulus contained fewer dots than the reference stimulus. When the reference stimulus contained 36 dots, a participant's response would be recorded as correct when the test stimulus contained 12 or 4 dots. If the reference stimulus contained 12 dots, a response would only be correct if the target stimulus contained 4 dots. Both the increase and the decrease tasks started with 12 trials to familiarize the participants with the task (“training trials”), followed by 48 “experimental trials”, 30 of which were targets (i.e. trials that required a response) and 18 were distractors (i.e. trials that did not require a response). 50% of all trials were considered “SNA congruent”, whereby stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from left-to-right. The other 50% of trials were considered “SNA incongruent”, as the stimuli were presented as increasing in magnitude from right-to-left. For example, if a participant was completing the “increasing” condition and the test target stimulus contained 4 dots and the test stimulus contained 12 dots and presented on the right, this would be considered SNA congruent, as the target stimulus is always presented in the centre, and so the presentation of stimuli moves from left-to-right in order of magnitude. Conversely, in the “decreasing” condition, an SNA congruent trial may be one in which the target stimulus contains 36 dots, and the test stimulus contains 4 dots which is presented on the left. For further details of SNA congruent/incongruent conditions, see “Manipulated Variables"). We aim to replicate the original study’s findings, which demonstrated the potential presence of a spatial-numerical association. That is, participants will be faster and more accurate when responding to numerosities presented in a left-to-right direction, increasing in terms of magnitude, while participants’ responses will be slower and less accurate when those same numerosities are presented in a right-to-left order in terms of magnitude. In our replication, we will conduct the experiment online rather than in person; we will recruit adult participants in the UK; make a slight modification to the timing of the no-go trials, reducing the duration from three seconds (as in the original study) to 1.5 seconds; and we will double the number of trials. In the original study, there was a one-to-one correspondence between the total area taken up by the dot array stimuli and their numerical magnitude. That is, the 4-dot array will take up much less visual area than the 36-dot array. It may be that participants are making judgements based off total area of stimuli rather than extracting magnitude information. Therefore, in Experiment 2, we produced two novel types of dot array stimuli: “controlled” and “correlated” stimuli. The correlated stimuli are those which have a one-to-one correspondence between total area and numerosity. The controlled stimuli all share the same total area of dots, regardless of numerosity. We have also created five stimulus variations for each type of dot array to further prevent participants from relying on pattern recognition, thus creating a total of 30 stimuli. Crucially, trials are always matched in terms of controlled or correlated stimuli; for example, if a participant sees a controlled reference stimulus, then the test stimulus will also be controlled. Further information can be found in the “Manipulated Variables” section. In Experiment 5 (previously called 2b), we wanted to further extend these findings to include an additional set of numerosities. In Eccher et al.’s (2025) original study, there were three numerosities used (4, 12, 36) which have a ratio of 3. As well as these stimuli, we created stimuli of 8, 16 and 32, this time with a ratio of 2, to investigate whether previously observed effects still hold for a new set of numerosities. Unlike in Experiment 4 (previously called 2a), the numerosity set will be a between-participants factor, to ensure that the intermixing of sets does not confound whether an SNA effect is observed. In Experiment 5, we found no SNA effects, unlike in Experiments 2 and 4. Moreover, when combining the results from Experiments 2 and 5, the SNA effect observed in Experiment 2 disappeared. As such, we are conducting Experiment 6 using the same procedure as in Experiment 6, except the sample size is tripled compared to Eccher et al.’s (2025) original sample. This will more robustly demonstrate whether an SNA is truly present using this task.

title_r: Emotional inertia in daily life: A dynamic structural equation modelling analysis of the role of emotion regulation strategy use
abstract_r: Emotional inertia refers to experiencing affective states that are particularly resistant to change. Negative affect inertia is linked to markers of maladjustment and is thus assumed to reflect a form of poor emotional regulation. Recent research using ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data has suggested that emotion regulation strategy use may partially mediate emotional inertia, with certain strategies, such as rumination being associated with the maintenance of a negative affective states. The present study builds on this by providing a replication attempt to examine the mediating effects of rumination, suppression, and reappraisal (Bagnara et al., 2024) as well as an extension to additionally examine the role of acceptance in negative affect inertia.

title_r: Van Peppen et al. (2018) Replication Project
abstract_r: The present study examines how learning through self-explanations enhance critical thinking skills. By replicating Van Peppen et al. (2018), we aim to find study strategies educators can use (i.e. self explanations) to promote critical thinking among college students. Students will be assessed on their baseline critical thinking skills, and receive instructional guidance. Participants will either receive self-explanations or no self-explanations afterward. The study will then measure whether their critical thinking skills have improved through the posttest. We predict that students who receive the self-explanation condition will have higher critical thinking skills compared to those who did not receive the self-explanation intervention. The original study examines these effects in the classroom, but the replication study will be conducted online.

title_r: Replication of Visual sense of number vs. sense of magnitude in humans and machines
abstract_r: This project is a replication attempt of the human experiment in "Visual sense of number vs. sense of magnitude in humans and machines" (Testolin et al., 2020). The original research found that human adults's numerosity discrimination accuracy is primarily driven by the numerosity dimension, rather than other continuous features such as spacing or dot size, supporting the hypothesis that animals are endowed with a number sense, as opposed to estimating numerosity from continuous magnitudes. In addition, non-numerical magnitudes, though not the primary perceptual attribute in numerical representation, still modulate humans' performance. I aim to test the replicability of this finding by implementing the same paradigm in a new group of participants.

title_r: Human Bayesian Mentalizing
abstract_r: Mentalizing, or theory of mind (ToM), typically refers to individuals’ ability to infer others’ mental states—such as beliefs, intentions, and desires—based on their past choices and the evidence they received. Mentalizing by predicting and interpreting others’ behavior and mind is crucial for social interaction, which contributes to the development of social cognition and the formation of social networks. Despite its importance, the mechanisms by which we learn about others in dynamically changing and uncertain environments remain poorly understood. Of particular interest to us is the dynamics through which individuals navigate interactions with agents of varying mentalizing capacities. Do individuals behave differently when interacting with opponents with more or less sophisticated ToM? This is the research question we are starting to address in this project. A promising way to think about ToM is as a so-called Bayesian inference process. One particularly useful computational model, the k- ToM model [1], uses Bayesian inference to describe how we form beliefs about others’ beliefs. It describes ToM as a recursive process, where k is the depth of recursion that describes the number of layers of belief an agent can represent ("I think you think I think..." etc.). These k-ToM agents can be 0-ToM (no mentalising), 1-ToM (simple mentalising), or 2-ToM (sophisticated mentalising). In a previous study [1], it was demonstrated that 1-ToM and 2-ToM models can explain participants’ internal states in terms of inferring their opponents’ minds, and that participants exhibited different behavioral performance when playing against different k-ToM agents. However, there are several limitations in this previous study: 1. The study concluded that participants’ learning rules were opponent-independent based on group-level model comparisons, but it did not include a direct validation procedure (e.g., trial-by-trial or individual-level analyses) to test whether participants might switch strategies when facing opponents of varying ToM sophistication. 2. The original article does not provide full raw data, which limits independent verification and replication. Therefore, we aim to replicate the experiment in social-frame from [1], focusing specifically on mentalizing across opponents of varying k-ToM sophistication. Using pre-existing libraries [2], we can create computer agents that perform this recursive Bayesian inference with different k levels when playing simple two-choice, two-player games (e.g. hide-and-seek where there are only 2 places you can hide). Then, these can be artificial agents for human participants to play against. To address our research question, participants will play a series of hide and seek games against k-ToM artificial agents. The opponent will switch over the course of the experiment. We will look at how participants performance (accuracy) changes along with different opponents and chasing their trial-by-trial k-ToM level with [2]. REFERENCES [1] Devaine et al. title_r: Emotional Words, Cognitive Control and its Effects on Post-Error Slowing
abstract_r: A bachelor's thesis as part of research investigating the influence of emotions on the Post-Error Slowing effect (PES). Specifically, based on a conceptual replication of Experiment 1 by Landman and van Steenbergen (2020), the effect of phasic arousal and valence on cognitive control is explored by examining the effect of emotional versus neutral words embedded in a four-color flanker task. Previous results show that emotions influence cognitive control, with research mostly focused on adaptive control following correctly answered incongruent trials. Here, we are interested in a related, but different effect: the slow down after an error. We expect that this post-error slowing (PES) is modulated by emotional words.

title_r: Pre-Registration of a Replication of an original Study by Jon Roozenbeek & Sander van der Linden et al. “Fake news game confers psychological resistance against online misinformation”
abstract_r: A close replication attempt will be conducted of Jon Roozenbeek & Sander van der Linden 2019 “Fake news game confers psychological resistance against online misinformation” Roozenbeek, J., & van der Linden, S. (2019) in the context of a Master thesis. We will test if active inoculation through exposure to common manipulation techniques in the “Bad News Game” can confer cognitive immunity against manipulative Fake-News. By exposing the general techniques that underlie many (political) persuasion attempts, following the authors’ original assumption, we assume that broad-scale attitudinal resistance should be present. It is also hypothesized that people will rate each of the test items (but not the control items) as less reliable after playing the game and therefore displaying a cognitive inoculation effect.

title_r: Reassessing Cannabis’ Cognitive Effects in Mice: Replication of Okon et al. (2015)
abstract_r: The present study is a conceptual replication and extension of Okon et al. (2015), who examined the effects of long-term Cannabis sativa administration on visuospatial learning in CD1 mice. The original study reported that cannabis-treated mice showed impaired learning and memory in the Morris Water Maze task. As cannabinoid research has advanced significantly over the past decade, there is a need to reassess these conclusions using more rigorous and contemporary research practices. The purpose of this replication is to re-evaluate these effects using a larger and more diverse sample, an expanded set of dose treatments, and three age groups (young, middle-aged, and old) to assess whether THC produces dose and age-dependent changes in cognitive performance. We expect low-dose THC (0.3–1 mg/kg) to preserve or improve cognitive performance, particularly in older mice, while higher doses (10–20 mg/kg) are expected to impair learning across all ages.

title_r: The Big 5, Self-Compassion, Psychological-Well-Being
abstract_r: This research project is a conceptual replication of Hicks and Yuktis 2018 study "The Big Five, Type A Personality, and Psychological Well-Being", which examined whether type A personality predicted psychological well-being beyond the Big Five personality traits. Because Type A was not a significant predictor in the original study, we replaced it with self-compassion. This decision was based on a literature search on which factors predict psychological well-being. For reasons of convenience and time we also do not include social desirability as a control variable. Our study aims to examine the relationships between Psychological Well-Being (PWB), self-compassion, and the Big Five personality traits, in order to better understand how stable characteristics like personality and modifiable emotional resources like self compassion influence psychological well being. The study is motivated by the idea that personality traits, particularly neuroticism, extraversion, conscientiousness and openness to experience have been consistently linked to significant well-being outcomes. However, personality does not fully predict who thrives psychologically. Self-compassion has emerged as an important predictor of positive mental health, and may serve as a mediating or moderating mechanism that helps explain why some individuals experience higher well-being despite having less favorable personality profiles. The purpose of this project, therefore, is to analyze whether self-compassion contributes significantly to psychological well-being after accounting for personality traits, and whether it functions as a psychological buffer in individuals with personality tendencies associated with lower well-being. The expected outcomes of the project include: Confirming known associations between the Big Five traits and psychological well-being, particularly the negative association with neuroticism and the positive associations with extraversion and conscientiousness. Demonstrating that self-compassion is positively related to PWB, above and beyond personality traits.

title_r: Are affective factors related to individual differences in facial expression recognition?
abstract_r: Evidence that affective factors (e.g., anxiety, depression, affect) are significantly related to individual differences in emotion recognition is mixed. Palermo et al. (2018 Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance) reported that individuals who scored lower in anxiety performed significantly better on two measures of facial-expression recognition (emotion-matching and emotion-labeling tasks), but not a third measure (the Multimodal Emotion Recognition Test). By contrast, facial-expression recognition was not significantly correlated with measures of depression, positive or negative affect, empathy, or autistic-like traits. Because the range of affective factors considered in this study and its use of multiple expression-recognition tasks mean that it is a relatively comprehensive investigation of the role of affective factors in facial expression recognition, we carried out a direct replication. In common with Palermo et al. (2018), scores on the DASS anxiety subscale negatively predicted performance on the emotion recognition tasks across multiple analyses, although these correlations were only consistently significant for performance on the emotion-labeling task. However, and by contrast with Palermo et al. (2018), other affective factors (e.g., those related to empathy) often also significantly predicted emotion-recognition performance. Collectively, these results support the proposal that affective factors predict individual differences in emotion recognition, but that these correlations are not necessarily specific to measures of general anxiety, such as the DASS anxiety subscale.

title_r: Feeling capable and valued - A preregistered (replication-with-extension) of Bacq & Alt (2018)
abstract_r: This study is a preregistered replication-with-extension of Bacq and Alt (2018), who examined how empathy influences social entrepreneurial (SE) intentions via two mechanisms: SE self-efficacy (agentic pathway) and social worth (communal pathway). Their original two-wave study with SE students showed that empathic concern and perspective-taking strengthened SE self-efficacy and social worth, which in turn enhanced SE intentions. We replicate this core model using the same constructs and theoretical framework to ensure comparability, with three key modifications. First, the study employs a single-wave survey design rather than the original two-wave structure to improve feasibility and reduce participant attrition; procedural and statistical remedies (e.g., anonymity and marker-variable checks) will mitigate potential common-method bias. Second, the measure of social worth has been adapted to allow broader applicability beyond project-based SE courses. The original wording (“the people I helped”) was course-specific, so the revised items assess the general sense of being valued, appreciated, and trusted by others for one’s contributions, aligning with the conceptual definition of social worth as feeling needed, cared about, and valued by others. Third, the empathy scales for perspective-taking and empathic concern are measured on 7-point scales instead of the original 5-point scales to harmonize all predictor constructs, increase response granularity, and enhance comparability. Our extension also introduces a broader student sample that includes both SE-course students and non-SE students. This design addresses potential selection bias inherent in studying only SE students, who may already be predisposed toward social impact careers. By including non-SE students, the study tests whether the proposed mechanisms operate consistently across both groups. If the mechanisms are correct, they should explain variation in SE intentions across groups, not just high levels among SE students. The outcomes will contribute to (social) entrepreneurship research by (a) reinforcing confidence in prior findings, (b) addressing potential selection bias in SE education research, and (c) clarifying the extent to which empathy-driven mechanisms explain differences in SE intentions across student populations.

title_r: Testing the Effects of Multiple Stigmas on Discrimination in the German Housing Market in political right and political liberal voting cities - a conceptual replication of Mazziotta, Zehr and Rohmann
abstract_r: Die Population umfasst private Vermieter*innen in sechs ausgewählten deutschen Städten, die basierend auf AfD-Wähleranteil bei der Europawahl 2024 klassifiziert werden. Die Städte Bielefeld (10,6%), Braunschweig (8,6%) und Aachen (10,8%) repräsentieren Regionen mit einem “niedrigen” AfD-Wähleranteil, während Chemnitz (28,2%), Magdeburg (22,0%) und Gelsenkirchen (27,7%) Regionen mit einen “hohen” AfD-Wähleranteil darstellen. Die Rekrutierung erfolgt indirekt durch das gezielte Senden standardisierter E-Mail- Anfragen über die Plattform Immoscout24 an private Vermieter*innen, die Immobilienanzeigen in den genannten Städten online geschaltet haben. Listings werden basierend auf vorher festgelegten Einschlusskriterien ausgewählt. title_r: Behavioral Observations Reduce the Probability of Injury: A replication
abstract_r: Behavioral Observations Reduce the Probability of Injury: A replication AUTHORS: Lizzie Smith, Charlie Wills, Ethan Fountain, Elizabeth Arnold, Madalyn Stephens, Drew Sipe, Shawn Bergman, & Tim Ludwig Introduction Occupational safety is a highly effective area for applying behavior analysis in the workplace (Ludwig & Laske, 2022). Behavioral safety programs are designed to reduce workplace injuries by observing employee behavior and identifying potentially risky behaviors. These programs often include behavioral observations, where employees use a checklist to identify unsafe behaviors and provide quick, helpful feedback. Past research has consistently shown that these programs can lower injury rates over time (Ludwig & Laske, 2023). This study will use a statistical model to determine whether behavioral observations made during the past week influence the probability of incidents happening over the next seven days. Methods Safety data from a southern oil refinery company (2022–2024) will be analyzed to replicate findings from a chemical manufacturing plant (2017 - 2019). A rolling sum time-series logistic regression analysis will test whether the number of observations or hazards reported over the past seven days influenced the likelihood of an incident occurring in the subsequent seven-days. In the replication, the control variables included day of the week, actual week, number of responses marked safe/unsafe/NA, questions responded to, people per day, hours worked per day, and employee count. In the new analysis, these variables serve as predictors rather than controls. Analysis We will apply a rolling sum time series logistic regression model to capture 14‑day safety trends. This model should not only allow us to replicate previous findings but to test the time lag for all predictors. Our hypothesis is that increased safety observations reduce incident likelihood within seven days. Previous findings from a chemical manufacturing plant (2017–2019) showed each additional observation lowered incident odds by 23% in Manufacturing and 17% in Maintenance over three days, preventing an estimated four and 16 incidents annually. Replicating and extending these results will strengthen validity and enhance predictive power. Implications The replication of our findings will strengthen evidence that increased safety observations reduce injury probability. With greater dataset granularity, we expect higher statistical power and improved validity of our methodology as a practical tool for reducing workplace injuries. This replication will serve as a foundation for developing a predictive model capable of estimating daily injury probability and assessing the sustained impact of safety observations. As digital monitoring and AI tools advance, our study highlights the critical role human-generated safety observations continue to play in reducing workplace incidents. References Ludwig, T. title_r: Vocabulary learning at first exposure: Replication of Gullberg, Roberts & Dimroth (2012) and Shoemaker & Rast (2013)
abstract_r: This article puts forward several proposals for replicating two well-known FIRST EXPOSURE studies dealing with the earliest stages of adult second language acquisition. Both of them enquire into the word-level knowledge that complete beginners are able to extract from minimal input when exposed to a new lan-guage for the first time. They also focus on several input variables that may enhance learning from minimal input. However, the first, by Gullberg et al. (2012), uses audiovisual input in Dutch learners of Chinese to assess word recognition and word meaning after watching a short video; while the second, by Shoemaker and Rast (2013), uses oral input with French learners of Polish to measure word recognition before and after 6.5 hours of intensive classroom exposure. Close and approximate replications of these studies can help to re-evaluate and generalise the findings, as well as contributing additional relevant data to the field.

title_r: Exact replication of Kozłowska et al. (2023) The Napoleon complex, revisited: Those high on the Dark Triad traits are dissatisfied with their height and are short
abstract_r: The dark triad is a personality taxonomy that, unlike the Big Five, focuses primarily on negative social personality traits: Psychopathy, Narcissism, and Machiavellianism. It has attracted much attention over the past 20 years after Paulhurst et al. coined the term in 2002, and research on the correlation between Dark Triad traits and other factors has increased drastically. One such example is the correlation of the Dark Triad traits with height dissatisfaction and with physical height itself. Kozłowska et al. recently published these results (2023) and concluded that the theory of the so-called "Napoleon complex" seems to be correct. Briefly summarized, the "Napoleon complex" is the idea that smaller men are at a disadvantage and compensate for this through negative behavior. In their results, Kozłowska et al. found that there was a significant negative correlation between Dark Triad traits and height in men. They also found that those scoring high on Dark Triad traits are more dissatisfied with their own height. This is interesting because it is one of the first studies to examine the relationship between Dark Triad traits and attitudes towards height, as well as physical height. Other studies of height in psychology often show no, or a positive, correlation. Therefore, it is of interest to conduct an exact replication study to verify or reject these findings in order to strengthen the current evidence base and thus lay the groundwork for further research on this topic. This study is an exact replication study of a cross-sectional study. By using an online questionnaire and replicating the statistical analysis, we hope to answer the research questions of the original study: 1. are characteristics of the dark triad associated with the desire to be taller, 2. are characteristics of the dark triad associated with shorter height, and 3. are the correlations stronger in men than in women. For this purpose, we will recruit 616 participants through the study platform 'Prolific' to answer the following questionnaires and baseline information anonymously: 1. Dark Triad Dirty Dozen Questionnaire. 2. Height Dissatisfaction Subscale of the Male Body Attitudes Scale. 3. Demographic data. We will analyze the hypotheses using the same statistical methods as in the original study, i.e., Pearson correlation coefficient, Fischer Z-transformation, Steiger's Z-test, and multiple linear regressions.

title_r: Replication of Side-to-side differences in lower extremity biomechanics during multi-directional jump landing in volleyball athletes
abstract_r: This research study is a replication study that will contribute to a large-scale international replication project in sports and exercise science whose overall aim is: To produce high level systematic and transparent replication trials of experimental trials published within the last five years in top tier sports and exercise science journals using a randomized, unbiased selection method. Large scale replication projects have been undertaken by, among others, the Open Science Collaboration in the form of the Reproducibility Project in Psychology and the Many Labs Project (Klein et al., 2014; Open Science Collaboration, 2015). These projects ignited the debate on the replication crisis in social science due to their difficulty in replicating selected effects and the variability in results. One goal of replication is to bolster our collective confidence in the veracity of novel claims by providing diagnostic evidence about those claims (Nosek et al., 2015; Nosek and Errington, 2020) when the original and replication study are similar in all “theoretically relevant dimensions” such as study design, methods, and materials (Earp, 2020, p. 120). Given the interdisciplinary nature of the sports science field and the overlap with the psychological sciences, there is reason to believe the sports science field faces similar replication issues (Caldwell et al., 2020). The replicability of sports science research has yet to be examined despite the identification of concerns within the field (Halperin et al., 2018; Heneghan et al., 2012; Knudson, 2017). As a result, the overall goal of this project is to sample a range of topics in an unbiased manner across the field of sports science for an initial estimation of the replicability of those findings. This is the first natural step in the assessment of replicability of the field, therefore, the project will attempt to replicate numerous effects once rather than multiple replications of a specific effect or theory. As it is essential to run multiple independent experiments to determine if findings in sports science have a consistent and accurate pattern, and are strongly supported (Earp and Trafimow, 2015), the proposed study is one of many studies to be replicated. The objective of this specific proposed study is to replicate (i.e. repeat) the work of Komsak Sinsurin, Sarun Srisangboriboon, and Roongtiwa Vachalathiti published in the Europen Journal of Sports Sciences in 2017 titled “Side-to-side differences in lower extremity biomechanics during multi-directional jump landing in volleyball athletes”. title_r: Replication Study of Infants’ Visual Cortical Connectivity and Later Autism
abstract_r: Backgrounds and Research Questions In an earlier study (Hardiansyah et al., 2025), we found that functional connectivity within 5-month-old infants’ visual cortex (VC) during viewing of social and non-social stimuli were predictive of their autism symptoms in toddlerhood. Specifically, we reported that connectivity between V1 and extrastriate area in theta band during non-social stimulus processing and in gamma band during social stimulus processing to be strong predictors (R2 > 50%) of later autism. Considering the potential importance of these findings in terms of identifying early markers of autism here we seek to replicate the results with an independent group of infants to provide further evidence in support of our earlier conclusions (Hardiansyah et al., 2025). Therefore, using data from the BASIS Network (https://www.basisnetwork.org) in the U.K., comprising eighty one 5-month-old infants representing both elevated autism likelihood and typical development groups, we plan to apply the same functional connectivity analyses (detailed in “Methods & Analysis” section) as used in our previous paper to address the following research questions: Hypothesis #1: Infants’ theta functional connectivity between V1 and extrastriate area during non-social stimulus processing is positively linked to their later autistic symptoms at 36 months. Hypothesis #2: Infants’ gamma functional connectivity between V1 and extrastriate area during social stimulus processing is positively linked to their later autistic symptoms at 36 months. In addition, we will assess whether the putative associations are moderated by familial likelihood status.

title_r: Effectiveness and Efficiency of Instruction vs Feedback-Based Multimedia Learning Activities
abstract_r: A previous study identified the distinct effect of multimedia feedback on conditional probability problem-solving performance (Gök et al., 2025). The study detected distinct effects for including multimedia in initial instruction versus feedback. More specifically, multimedia materials in the initial instruction led students to perceive the problems as less difficult and spontaneously draw more diagrams relative to only text in the initial instruction, while multimedia materials in feedback resulted in improved accuracy on a posttest compared to only text in the feedback. However, it remains unclear (1) whether instruction and feedback-based learning activities are equally effective in this context and (2) whether combining instruction and feedback is necessary compared to only including feedback-based learning activities, given that previous study under a similar context questioned the necessity of the initial instruction stage (Asher et al., 2025). The current study will address these questions in the context of multimedia learning of conditional probability problem solving with a refined design of three conditions. One only receives instruction-based activities (instruction-only condition), one only receives feedback-based activities (feedback-only condition), and one last condition receives both instruction and feedback-based activities (instruction+feedback condition). We will compare the learning outcomes of these conditions, and since different types of learning activities may not be equally time-demanding, we will also calculate and compare the efficiency of learning of these conditions. Finally, we will also replicate and extend the metacognitive measure of our previous study. Students will rate how difficult and how helpful each learning activity. These measures will help us determine students’ metacognitive awareness of how much they learn from feedback.

title_r: Testing for prediction-error driven compensatory contagion effects following action observation
abstract_r: Watching biased performance can elicit imitative contagion and compensation biases depending on instructions (Ikegami et al., 2018). Across two experiments participants watched an actor systematically throw or reach towards the corner of a target array. When participants were told that the actor was aiming to various locations and only correct attempts were shown, subsequent attempts were biased towards the observed performance, replicating imitative motor contagion effects (Heyes, 2011). In contrast, when participants were told that the actor was aiming to the target centre, subsequent performance was biased away from the now perceived error towards the opposite diagonal of the grid in a compensatory fashion. Prediction errors, that is differences between actual and expected performance, drive updates to an individual’s own “internal model” of the observed action (Ikegami & Ganesh, 2017) and are thought to underlie such observation-induced compensatory effects. We will perform a conceptual replication of the Ikegami and colleagues (2018) studies, testing for both compensatory and imitative contagion effects in a golf putting task, using a repeated measures’ (rather than between-participants’) design. A repeated measures design will allow us to test how the perception of errors versus perceived correct action outcomes changes observation-induced biases in a person’s putting, providing a more stringent test of the effects of action observation on an observer’s short-term performance. We are using a golf putting task because we have previously shown compensatory biases from observed errors when dyads practiced golf putting together (Scott et al., in review). Experienced golfers will watch videos of an actor putting to a target grid. The actor’s putting location and instructions about their aiming location will vary across four blocked conditions. In a 2 Actor putting location (same or different to observer) X 2 Error condition (correct or error) orthogonal design, we will show videos of an actor putting to the centre (same as the observer) or corner (different to the observer) of the grid and will covary the instructions about the actor’s goal location to indicate if the actor’s putts were correct or errorful (Fig. 1). In this design, the ‘different’ conditions (i.e., watch corner) replicate the groups tested by Ikegami et al. (2018) and the ‘correct, different/corner’ and ‘error, different/corner’ conditions are designed to elicit imitative contagion and compensatory contagion effects respectively. In the new “same” conditions (i.e., watch centre), a prediction error should still be generated when the actor erroneously putts to the centre when instructions state that the actor is aiming to the corner, thus resulting in compensatory biases (Ikegami et al., 2018). Alternatively, compensatory biases might be suppressed in this ‘error, corner/different’ condition because the actor’s aiming location is different to the participant’s and because the observed centre ‘errors’ are the same as the participants putting goal (putt to centre). The ‘watch centre, predict centre’ condition serves somewhat as a control condition where no biases are expected. Participants will putt to and watch an actor putt to a 9 square grid made up of 30cm x 30cm squares marked on a custom 245cm x 550cm putting surface (Camry Golf Greens). Participants will aim to a target located in the middle of the centre square, located 205 cm from the golf ball’s start position. On physical execution trials, participants will wear visual occlusion goggles that will block vision at the moment of putter-ball contact and will wear noise cancelling headphones, occluding all outcome feedback. The removal of outcome feedback replicates conditions used by Ikegami et al (2018), preventing outcome-feedback based adaptation, as a result of seeing errors in their own putting. Participants will first complete a brief familiarization where they will perform 5 putts to the target grid with and without feedback followed by a pre-test where they will perform 5 putts with and without feedback. The four experimental conditions will be completed in a blocked design. In each condition, five execution (t = 10) and four observation (t = 20) mini-blocks will be repeated in an interleaved order. In execution mini-blocks participants will putt to the centre of the grid without feedback. In observation mini-blocks, the actor’s putting location and instructions will vary based on the experimental condition. Participants will verbally report the outcome grid number after each observation trial to keep attention focused on the task. After each experimental condition, participants will complete a washout block putting to the centre target with full visual feedback, in order to facilitate return to baseline performance. Participants will complete a minimum of 10 washout trials and will continue to putt until they are within 1 standard deviation of the pretest mean constant error (maximum = 25 trials).

title_r: Facets of Loneliness, Mental Health, and Social Media Use: Fine-grained Associations in a Sample of Young Adults in Japan
abstract_r: Loneliness is a common health concern that has gained increasing relevance during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Before the pandemic, 9% of Japanese adults reported feeling lonely, while 41.1% of the Japanese population was categorized as being lonely during the pandemic (DiJulio et al., 2018; Stickley & Ueda, 2022). Loneliness is a subjective negative feeling of insufficient social connection with others (Perlman & Peplau, 1981) and can be categorized into social and emotional loneliness (Weiss, 1973). Social loneliness refers to the absence of community and social networks, while emotional loneliness captures the absence of attachment and close relationships. These types of loneliness are related differently to mental health symptoms. In a network analytic study, Wolters and colleagues (2023) examined the comprehensive associations between social and emotional loneliness, social isolation, depression, general anxiety, and social anxiety. The findings unveiled that social loneliness was associated with social isolation, while emotional loneliness was connected to social anxiety and depression in a sample of Dutch students (Wolters et al., 2023). To build on these findings, the current study seeks to investigate the comprehensive association of loneliness and loneliness-related variables in three parts. First, we will replicate the network model from Wolters et al. (2023) in a sample of young adults in Japan (aged 18-29 years). Second, we will extend the replication model by including loneliness-related variables, such as social media use and social avoidance. Previous studies have reported an association between social media use and loneliness. The evolutionary theory of loneliness hypothesizes that loneliness triggers avoidance in social situations (Cacioppo & Cacioppo, 2018; Wu et al., 2024). Third, we will examine the longitudinal associations between loneliness and loneliness-related variables using a panel network approach.

title_r: Prevalence-induced Concept Change in the Judgement of Male Bodies: A Replication and Extension of Devine et al. (2024)
abstract_r: The following study aims to replicate H1b from Devine et al. (2023). Here, the authors found that men were sensitive to prevalence-induced concept changes (PICC) when judging whether male bodies varying in muscularity were muscular or not, but not when judging whether male bodies varying in body fat were overweight or not. Furthermore, they found that men were overall faster in judging whether a body is muscular compared to judging whether a body is overweight. Taken together, these results lead the authors to suspect that men might have an attentional bias towards idealized male bodies, which manifests in faster and more selective extraction of muscle-related body information. Thus, Devine et al. show that PICC may not represent a general perceptual effect, but rather could be moderated by the specific stimulus category. Our main goal of the current study is to replicate the effect found that the strength of PICC in the judgment of male bodies depends on the specific stimulus category (weight-related, muscle-related). Furthermore, we intend to replicate the difference in response times between the judgments of these stimulus categories. The study design will be adjusted to control for possible confounding factors such as the order of the presented stimulus category. In addition, the stimulus material (computer-generated male bodies) will be adapted in order to achieve better comparability between the stimulus categories. Furthermore, we will examine whether the degree of body dissatisfaction (BD) related to different body characteristics (weight-related, muscle-related) influences whether participants judge muscle-related bodies faster than weight-related bodies, or vice versa. Recent studies suggest that attentional biases toward body-related stimuli specifically affect men with higher BD rather than the general population, and that the impact might differ depending on whether men experience more muscle-related or weight-related BD (Joseph et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2018; Porras-Garcia et al., 2020; Talbot & Saleme, 2022; Kirby et al., 2023). Therefore, BD will be measured separately for both stimulus categories (weight-related, muscle-related) (Ralph-Nearman & Filik, 2018).

title_r: A replication and extension of “Task difficulty modulates the disrupting effects of oral respiration on visual search performance” (Yoshimura et al. 2019)
abstract_r: The relationship between breathing and cognition is gaining increasing interest, with nasal breathing linked to greater neurophysiological synchrony compared to oral breathing. This synchrony could impact cognitive functions like attention and memory. Yoshimura et al. (2019) examined whether respiratory pathway (oral vs. nasal) affects visual search performance. In their second experiment, oral breathing combined with reduced target discriminability led to increased reaction time (RT) intercepts compared to nasal breathing, but only in the most difficult search condition. In this pre-registered report, we aim to replicate their RT effects and provide a more sensitive test of respiration effects by examining search efficiency across a wider range of difficulties. Using a within-subjects design, participants will complete a visual search task under oral and nasal breathing conditions, with target-distractor orientation differences ranging from 2° to 6°. This will show whether oral breathing speeds RT under difficult conditions (replicating Yoshimura et al.) and reduces search slopes (extending their findings). By examining both intercept and slope effects, we seek to determine whether oral breathing disrupts pre-search or post-search processing and/or impairs search efficiency. This research contributes to understanding how breathing pathway influences attentional processing during visual search tasks.

title_r: Repetition of the Mere Exposure Effect: Sensory Variance's Limiting Function
abstract_r: One of the most well-known and often quoted discoveries in the field of social psychology is the mere exposure effect. This effect, which was first described by Zajonc in 1968, asserts that a person's like of a stimuli increases with exposure. According to Zajonc, organisms typically gravitate toward familiar things and steer clear of unknown ones, and familiarity is a basic mechanism in deciding preferences. Repetition regularly raises liking scores for a variety of neutral stimuli, including geometric forms, pictures, and meaningless words, according to classic research. Over the years, this discovery has been repeated and validated in a number of domains, including as political opinions, consumer behavior, interpersonal attractiveness, and perceptual fluency. The mere exposure effect may not, however, apply to all situations or stimuli. The emotional valence of the stimulus (positive, neutral, or negative emotional content) can be a significant border condition for this effect, according to recent research. According to certain research, the mere exposure effect is very potent when exposed to neutral or slightly positive stimuli, while it diminishes or vanishes completely when exposed to negative stimuli. For instance, Harmon-Jones and Allen (2001) discovered that liking scores for unpleasant images did not rise with the number of repetitions. Similarly, Monahan, Murphy, and Zajonc (2000) demonstrated that repetition only enhanced liking for neutral or positive stimuli, even when they were offered unintentionally; this effect was not observed for negative stimuli. These results imply that avoidance reactions may be triggered by emotionally unpleasant stimuli, therefore familiarity's "fluency" effect may not be enough to boost liking. This circumstance draws attention to a significant gap in the literature: Even though the mere exposure effect is a fairly potent phenomenon, it is unclear under what circumstances this effect either disappears or becomes weaker. Specifically, whether emotional valence is a limiting variable is unclear. By systematically altering emotional valence and retesting the traditional mere exposure effect, this work seeks to close this gap. This method will make it easier for us to comprehend how repetition-based familiarity affects assessments and identify the kinds of stimuli where this effect shouldn't be anticipated. Participants in the study's replication phase will be shown a series of neutral images; some will be shown just once, while others will be shown several times (e.g., five times). Repeated neutral images are expected to obtain increased like scores based on the classic finding. Images having negative emotional content will be used in the study's boundary condition section. It is anticipated that the mere exposure effect will either not be seen or be significantly weaker in negative valence stimuli based on earlier findings in the literature. There are two main ways that this study will add to the body of literature. First, it will enable the use of digital presentation techniques to retest a well-known social psychology finding in a modern sample. When evaluating the consistency of traditional psychological effects in modern settings and with various participant groups, replication studies are crucial. Second, the inclusion of emotional valence as a moderating variable will contribute to theoretical discussions about the relationships between familiarity and emotion and offer a more thorough knowledge of the conditions under which the mere exposure effect functions. If the results validate the hypotheses, they will demonstrate that familiarity only boosts liking for neutral stimuli, whereas emotional content inhibits the familiarity effect for negative stimuli. This finding will contradict the current literature and may indicate that repetition-based liking increases may be independent of emotional valence if, in contrast to predictions, the mere exposure effect is also seen with negative stimuli. By precisely outlining the study's hypotheses, procedures, variables, and analysis strategy prior to data collection, this preregistration seeks to promote a more transparent and trustworthy research process. This will avoid any bias that can result from formulating hypotheses after the fact or from being flexible in the research process.

title_r: Decision-making biases varying as a function of font personality
abstract_r: The framing effect demonstrates a proven cognitive bias which shows that people change their risk preferences when they view identical options through gain or loss perspectives (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981). People tend to avoid risks when options are presented with positive frames (e.g. saving lives) but they become more risk-taking when options are presented with negative frames. The framing effect has been studied in different fields but researchers have not fully understood how text visual elements affect its boundaries. Research on "type psychology" shows that font personality creates substantial effects which influence how readers understand text content and their judgments about information credibility and depth (Childers & Jass, 2002; Oppenheimer, 2006). The research does not show how organizations use their current decision-making systems to handle different levels of formal and informal communication. The research investigates this study conducts a conceptual replication of the Asian Disease Problem from Tversky and Kahneman (1981) by introducing Font Personality as a new variable. The research shows that formal fonts will not change the standard framing effect because these fonts align with the professional tone of medical information. The research shows that using casual fonts in presentations leads to worse risk assessment because these fonts make risks appear less dangerous and minimize the effect of framing effects. The study examines visual environment impacts on logical choice processes through a 2x2 between-subjects design which evaluates two independent variables: Frame (Gain vs. Loss) and Font Type (Formal vs. Informal).
