title_r: Replication of the Stroop Effect With a Task-Difficulty Boundary Condition
abstract_r: The Stroop effect is one of the most robust and frequently replicated findings in cognitive psychology. First described by J. R. Stroop of defined by (1935), the impact shown by the colour matched the color of the word corresponding word (e.g., printed in blue ink “Red“ for the word) is making a mistake when naming the ink color and more reliable observation refers to individuals react more slowly (e.g., "red" for the word)." printed in red ink). This phenomenon demonstrates the automaticity of reading: because reading is a highly practiced and automatic process, it interferes with the task of naming the ink color, which is a more controlled process."" For this reason, the Stroop task has been widely used as a measure of selective attention, response inhibition and executive functions. Decades of research have established the Stroop effect as a central measure in cognitive psychology, with replication across different populations, age groups, modalities and task variants. Studies consistently show that incongruent trials result in longer reaction times and lower accuracy than congruent trials. This suggests the cognitive conflict that occurs when automatic and controlled processes compete. Despite the robustness of the basic Stroop effect, researchers have noted that the magnitude of the effect varies depending on contextual and task-related factors. For example, stimulus presentation rate, task instructions, cognitive load, and individual differences such as working memory capacity can influence the size of the Stroop effect. One variable that may play a particularly important role in modulating the Stroop effect is overall task difficulty. When a task is easy, individuals may have sufficient attentional resources to suppress the automatic tendency to read the word. However, when the task becomes more challenging - for example, by presenting the stimuli more quickly or by shortening the response time - cognitive control resources may be strained. Under these conditions, the interference created by the incongruent stimuli may increase, leading to a larger Stroop effect. Some studies have suggested that higher difficulty increases interference, but the evidence is not entirely consistent. Different paradigms operationalize “difficulty” in different ways, and few studies have systematically compared easy and difficult versions of the Stroop task in the same participants. This discrepancy represents a significant gap in the literature and highlights the need for a pre-recorded review of task difficulty as a boundary condition for the Stroop effect. This study aims to fill this gap by creating a previously recorded replication of the Stroop effect, varying the task difficulty within the subjects. Participants will complete two versions of the Stroop task: an easy condition in which stimuli are presented at a slower pace and with a longer response window, and a difficult condition in which stimuli are presented at a faster pace and require a faster response. In both conditions, participants will encounter congruent and incongruent trials. This design allows us to examine not only the classic Stroop effect, but also whether the magnitude of the distractor effect changes as overall task demands increase. The current study provides transparency in hypotheses, methods, and planned analyses by using a previously recorded design. The first aim of the study is to replicate the finding that incongruent trials lead to slower reaction times than congruent trials. The second goal is to test the hypothesis that task difficulty reduces the strength of the Stroop effect; therefore, conflict will be greater in the difficult condition (reaction time difference between incongruent and congruent trials) than in the easy condition. Since pre-registration reduces the flexibility in analytical decisions and prevents the creation of hypotheses later, this study was designed to provide precise and reliable evidence about the robustness of the Stroop effect and boundary conditions. In general, this pre-registered research contributes to the literature by explaining how cognitive control processes function under different task demands. Understanding the conditions in which automated processes more often hinder controlled responses can deepen our understanding of the mechanisms of attention and inform broader theories of cognitive control.

title_r: Moral Conviction's Resistance to Majority Pressure Under Threat and Social Support Conditions
abstract_r: Social conformity, the phenomenon where individuals change their behavior, attitudes, or beliefs to fit the expectations of a group or society, often occurs unconsciously or involuntarily, even in situations that conflict with their own views, rather than through direct coercion. According to Carla Capuano and Peggy Chekroun's (2024) article, "A Systematic Review of Research on Conformity," the phenomenon of conformity was first proposed by Asch in the 1950s using a visual perception task method he developed to measure conformity. While Asch's conformity paradigm remains valid, alternative methods have been developed that are more economical and adaptable to different populations due to limitations such as requiring a large number of physical participants. Research shows that conformity can be observed in both children and adults, with limited effects on age and gender, although some studies (though inconsistent results) suggest that girls may exhibit higher conformity than boys. When cultural factors are examined, it has been observed that conformity is generally higher in collectivist cultures; however, most studies superficially assess cultural influences, failing to adequately investigate other dimensions (norm tightness, hierarchy, cultural complexity). The influence of personality traits (the Big Five) on conformity is limited and context-dependent; for example it has been noted that a high level of stability can increase normative conformity. Conformity motivations are explained by two main processes: normative influence (seeking social acceptance) and informational influence (seeking truth). Research shows that individuals are more prone to conforming to social norms and more resistant to moral norms. Majority characteristics, group belonging, and emotional expression are strong external factors shaping conformity. It has been noted that individuals conform more to in-group members and groups they feel familiar with or close to. Neurocognitive findings have revealed that the posterior medial frontal cortex, ventral striatum, and dorsal medial prefrontal cortex are activated during conformity in relation to error signals, cognitive dissonance, and motivation processes. Although similar behaviors have been observed in animal studies, direct comparisons with human conformity are limited. In general, social conformity can be seen among numerous age, gender, culture, and personality groups. Technological advancements, online environments, and artificial intelligence are adding new dimensions to social conformity research (Capuano, Chekroun, 2024). In their study, Nicholas P. Aramovich, Brad L. Lytle, and Linda J. Skitka (2012) tested whether moral conviction rigidity influenced resistance to conformity, examining whether participants changed their opinions publicly and privately in environments with and without social support. Overall, participants reduced their opposition to torture under the influence of the majority; 80% slightly changed their opinion in front of the group, and the majority influence persisted in the private report. However, participants with strong moral conviction demonstrated resistance to the majority both in public and privately, regardless of the presence of social support (Aramovich, Lytle, Skitka, 2012). This study aims to conceptually replicate Aramovich, Lytle, and Skitka's (2012) findings on moral conviction and resistance to majority influence, and also to examine how the perceived threat context shapes this relationship. It includes an experimental extension that tests whether the protective role of moral conviction against majority pressure weakens under threat cues that reinforce safety-based, fear- and anxiety-inducing factors. In this context, while the experimental design generally retains its form from the original study, adjustments have been made to allow the testing of the variable to be measured. Although the study was conducted in a laboratory setting, measuring the role of threat manipulation can theoretically examine the validity of moral conviction and resistance to majority pressure, not only in the laboratory context but also in contexts where high authoritarianism or widespread societal threat perceptions are created and prevail. This could increase the potential of the conceptual replication to test the limits of social conformity in different cultural and political contexts.

title_r: Replication of the Framing Effect With Number Skill as a Boundary Condition
abstract_r: The framing effect is finding in psychology about how people make decisions. It shows that people often choose differently depending on how the information is worded, even when the outcomes are actually the same. The study is the “Asian disease problem” from Tversky and Kahneman (1981). In this scenario, people are told that a disease will kill 600 people. The options in the gain frame explain how many people will be saved. Loss frame explains how many people will die. People’s choices change a lot. In the gain frame, most people choose the safe option. In the loss frame, most prefer the risky option. A change in wording creates a strong effect in behavior. Many studies have repeated this effect, so it is considered very reliable. However, not everyone shows the framing effect in the same way. Some people show a big difference between gain and loss frames. Some almost respond the same in both versions. This can say that personal differences have an impact. Understanding this is important for real-life decisions too. One personal factor studied in this area is numeracy. It means how comfortable and skilled someone is with numbers. Numeracy includes understanding percentages, reading probabilities, and noticing the logic behind a problem. People with higher numeracy are better at dealing with number. For example, they often interpret medical risks or financial information more accurately. Peters and colleagues (2006) showed that highly numerate people give more consistent answers to numerical problems and are less distracted by irrelevant details. This is related to the framing effect. In the original framing tasks, the two conditions are mathematically same. The only difference is the wording. Some researchers think that people with high numeracy may be better at understnading that both frames tell the same outcome. However, results across studies do not same. Some studies show that numeracy reduces framing effects. For example, Peters et al. (2006) found that high-numeracy individuals focused more on the actual numbers and were less influenced by the frame. But other research does not support this. Bruine de Bruin et al. (2007) said that people make decisions in different ways. Numeracy is only one part of this. Sometimes people with higher numeracy do not make better or more stable choices in tasks like framing. Their findings showed that the influence of numeracy was not certain. Because of this, there is still a gap. We do not know for sure whether numeracy always reduces the framing effect. This study aims to contribute by replicating the classic framing effect and testing whether numeracy changes the behaviour. Like in the orijinal study, participants will be randomly assigned to either the gain-frame or loss-frame condition. After making their choice, they will complete a numeracy scale that measures their number skill. Based on their scores, participants will be divided into low-numeracy and high-numeracy groups. This division creates two clear groups. The dependent variable will be a 1–7 rating of their decision (risky or safety). This design creates a 2 × 2; frame groups (gain vs. loss) and numeracy groups (low vs. high). This allows us to test both the framing effect and the interaction between framing and numeracy. This study is important for two main reasons. First, it contributes to open science by preregistering a direct replication of a Framing Effect. Second, it helps clarify whether numeracy changes how people are affacted by framing. If numeracy moderates the effect, this can suggest that numerical skills help people resist decision-making biases. If we do not find moderation, it may mean that the framing effect is strong across different numeracy levels. Other factors may explain the personal differences we see in framing responses. Each result can help us better understand how people make decisions.

title_r: Replication of the Stroop Effect with Cognitive Load as a Boundary Condition
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate the classic Stroop effect (Stroop, 1935) and examine whether cognitive load moderates attentional interference during a color-naming task. Participants will complete congruent and incongruent Stroop trials under low and high cognitive load conditions. It is predicted that reaction times will be slower and accuracy lower in incongruent trials, with greater Stroop interference under high cognitive load. The study will clarify how working memory resources influence attentional control, contributing to cognitive psychology research on executive functions. Keywords: Stroop Effect, Cognitive Load, Attention, Executive Function, Replication

title_r: Replication of Savani & Wadhwa (2024): Choice Mindset and Anchoring Bias: Cognitive Load as a Boundary Condition
abstract_r: Literature Review and Motivation: Anchoring bias refers to people becoming overly attached to given initial values (such as the seller's initial offer) and failing to move far enough away from that value in subsequent evaluations. From the classic work of Tversky & Kahneman to the present day, anchoring has been repeatedly observed in both artificial laboratories and realistic bargaining scenarios. One of the fundamental explanations for anchoring is that people are unable to adequately utilize the cognitive regulation systems necessary to move away from their starting points. "Choice mindset" is an important concept added to the anchoring literature in recent years. This concept suggests that simply reminding individuals that they "can choose" changes their cognitive and perceptual processing styles. Savani & Wadhwa (2024), in line with this perspective, showed that when participants in bargaining scenarios were shown a simple reminder sentence ("You can choose any amount…"), people made counteroffers that were further away from the seller's initial offer. According to the authors, this effect arises through a cognitive mechanism that prompts individuals to consider more alternative values. In other words, the results suggest that even very small interventions (nudges) can actually reduce strong cognitive biases like anchoring. Gap in the Literature: While the effect of choice mindset on anchoring gives us some insight, research related to this effect is still very limited. In particular, the gap regarding the conditions under which this effect emerges and disappears persists in the literature. Savani & Wadhwa (2024) showed preliminary findings indicating that choice mindset emerges depending on cognitive resources and that the effect of choice nudge diminishes under high cognitive load. However, the study result was tested in only one context and within one study. Furthermore, independent preregistered replications are not available. Therefore, it is unclear how robust, generalizable, or repeatable the interaction between choice mindset and cognitive load is. Additionally, existing studies in the literature mostly use within-subject or mixed designs, but whether this effect can be systematically replicated in the general process using purely between-subject designs has not been systematically tested. Based on this, we can say that the uncertainty regarding how strong or weak the "cognitive load" moderator will be in a simpler experimental setting constitutes a research gap. This study aims to clarify the literature and present a systematic replication framework conducted by students. Present study: In this study, the finding suggested by Savani & Wadhwa (2024), "choice reminder reduces anchoring," is planned to be independently tested and conceptually replicated as pre-registered within a simplified design. Participants will be shown a single bargaining scenario, and each participant will be assigned to only one condition. The study design will be conducted as between-subjects and includes two factors. First, the presentation of the choice reminder (present vs absent), and second, cognitive load (high vs low). Thus, four experimental groups will be created. Participants will see a fixed value ($150) as the quoted price and enter a counteroffer. In the choice condition, the sentence "You can choose to offer any amount that you want. It's your choice!" will be displayed below the quoted price. In the control condition, this sentence will not be displayed. Participants in the high cognitive load condition will be given a simultaneous logo counting task, while those in the low load condition will not have this task. This approach provides a clear and analytical explanation of the extent to which the anchoring-reducing effect of the choice mindset depends on cognitive resources. The fundamental expectation is that the choice reminder will move the counteroffer away from the anchor, and that this effect will weaken or disappear completely under high cognitive load. In this pre-registration, hypotheses, study design, measurements, sampling plan, and analysis strategy are presented transparently before the data collection phase. Ultimately, the aim is to systematically test the lack of a "cognitive-load boundary condition" in the literature.

title_r: Replication of ‘Promoting Conservation Behaviors by Leveraging Optimistic and Pessimistic Messages and Emotions’ in a European Context
abstract_r: This study investigates whether optimistic and pessimistic conservation messages influence emotional responses and conservation-related intentions. The original study by Martell & Rodewald (2024) found a small but significant effect of pessimistic messages on donation intent, but no clear effects on pro-conservation behaviors or political action intentions. We replicate this design in a European context using updated stimuli based on European biodiversity trends. Participants will be randomly assigned to pessimistic, optimistic, combined, or control conditions and will report emotional responses and intentions to donate, engage in conservation behaviors, and participate in political actions. Our goal is to assess whether both the observed and non-observed effects generalize to a European sample.

title_r: A cross-sectional network analysis of social camouflaging, safety behaviours, autistic traits and social anxiety symptoms in young people.
abstract_r: Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition characterised by social communication differences, repetitive behaviours, specific interests, and/or sensory behaviours, that begins early in life (Lord et al., 2020). Co-occurring mental health conditions have been frequently reported in autistic individuals, with up to 70% of people with autism diagnosed with at least one, and almost 50% diagnosed with multiple co-occurring mental health conditions (Lai et al., 2019). Anxiety disorders are particularly prevalent, especially in adolescents (Hollocks et al., 2022). Social anxiety disorder (SAD) especially has high co-occurrence rates in autistic children and adolescents, with numbers ranging from 29% to 57% (Bellini, 2006; Hollocks et al., 2022; Kuusikko et al., 2008; Simonoff et al., 2008). SAD is a condition characterised by a persistent fear of being humiliated or scrutinised by others (American Psychiatric Association 2013). Individuals with social anxiety often fear that they will say or do something that they believe will be humiliating or embarrassing. The high co-occurrence rates may be attributable to autism-specific characteristics that act as risk factors for the development for social anxiety, such as social anhedonia, intolerance of uncertainty, poor emotion regulation, and poor general social skills (as well as autism-specific social behavioural differences) (Lei et al., 2025). Social behavioural difficulties and poor social skills may be a risk factor especially of note for autistic individuals, as their social experiences influence their cognitions around social situations, leading to the formation of assumptions regarding social acceptance and social impressions (Lei et al., 2025). Adolescence also has been found to be developmentally significant in social anxiety, with onset tending to be during this period of life (Solmi et al., 2022; Miers et al., 2014). This may be related to the increased social demands of adolescence (La Greca & Ranta, 2015), but also factors such as the increased risk-taking and sensitivity to social evaluation (Crone & Dahl, 2012) and the social and environmental changes (such as going to college) (Cleary et al., 2011) typical of adolescence. Social anxiety in adolescence has also been linked to considerable impairment through adulthood (Leigh & Clark, 2018). A key maintenance factor perpetuating social anxiety is the use of safety behaviours (Clark & Wells, 1995). Safety behaviours are strategies used in response to social-evaluative threat in social situations (Wong & Rapee, 2016), intended to manage or avert a perceived threat and increase the person’s sense of safety (Salkovskis, 1991). These can be subdivided into two main categories: ‘impression management’, in which individuals with social anxiety self-monitor and adjust their behaviour in order to come across as ‘normal’ to a social peer; and ‘avoidance’, in which individuals with social anxiety avoid social contact to reduce the chances of embarrassment – such as by speaking less or staying on the edges of social groups (Evans et al., 2021). As highlighted in the Clark & Wells (1995) model, the use of safety behaviours reinforces and perpetuates social anxiety cognitions and symptoms, as it prevents disconfirmation of overly-negative beliefs and extinction of fear (Wells et al., 1995). Previous work has also found that the Clark and Wells’ model of social anxiety is suitable for adolescents and autistic individuals when taking into account adolescent- and autism-specific risk factors (Leigh & Clark (2018), Lei et al (2025)). Similarities have been observed between social camouflaging and safety behaviours, with both associated with higher rates of social anxiety symptoms. Social camouflaging behaviours are learned behaviours used by autistic individuals to reduce the appearance of their autistic traits in a social situation (Hull et al., 2019). These can be subdivided into three categories: ‘assimilation’, where an autistic individual attempts to act in ways that ‘fit in’ with others in the social situation; ‘masking’, where an autistic individual attempts to hide autistic traits or seem non-autistic; and ‘compensation’, where an autistic individual attempts to compensate for social difficulties (Hull et al., 2019). Social camouflaging behaviours have been theorised to be a strategy for hiding or managing autistic traits. More recently, it has been considered as a method of transactional impression management (IM) used by autistic individuals in order to navigate social and professional situations and their challenges (Ai et al., 2022) – impression management is a social behaviour distinct from the safety behaviour, aiming to regulate information and steers others’ perceptions of the self, fostering an idealised public self-image within an interaction (Goffman, 1959). Increased social demands in adolescence have also been linked to the establishment of masking behaviours in autistic individuals, to reduce negative social responses (Hull et al, 2017). However, while social camouflaging behaviours may serve a social function, they have also been linked with worse mental health outcomes and increased burnout (Pyszkowska et al., 2024). Lei et al. (2024) examined the associations between camouflaging, autistic traits and social anxiety, and between safety behaviours, autistic traits and social anxiety in a sample of autistic and non-autistic adolescents with social anxiety. They found a strong correlation between self-report measures of camouflaging behaviour factors (as taken from the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire subscales) and safety behaviours (as taken from the Adolescent Social Behaviours Questionnaire subscales), and social anxiety cognitions (as taken from the Adolescent Social Cognitions Questionnaire subscales). Factor analysis indicated significant construct overlap between safety behaviour and social camouflaging items, loading onto four factors of ‘self-focused attention’, ‘social avoidance’, ‘assimilation’, and ‘mental rehearsal’, suggesting they are interlinked. Furthermore, masking and safety behaviours were found to be significantly associated with symptom severity of social anxiety rather than autism traits, particularly with masking from camouflaging and IM and avoidance from safety behaviours. This suggests that safety behaviours and masking behaviours are connected, both to each other and to a theorised common basis in social anxiety. In this project, we aim to investigate the relationships between social camouflaging behaviours, safety behaviours, social anxiety symptoms, and autistic traits in young people through network analyses. The network approach to psychopathology suggests that mental disorders are best understood as a network of interacting symptoms and symptom clusters, generated by a pattern of direct connections between symptoms – a pattern which reflects the connectivity of symptoms and the co-occurrence of symptom groups (Borsboom, 2017). Thus, by understanding and investigating disorders as a network, it offers the potential to intervene on the disorder system by targeting the link between symptoms to change the network structure; we can also better understand the structure of a disorder or the connections between symptoms by taking a network approach. Network approaches are exploratory, allowing us to consider the relationships between symptoms without necessarily requiring a prior theory or hypothesis. Connections between variables (in this case, symptoms or behaviours) can be represented, given the presence of other variables. This provides a useful basis for the formation of further theories, as well as exhibiting the connections between the variables. Through network analyses, we can replicate and expand upon previous findings, defining more specific connections, leading to a better understanding of symptom pathways. This project extends the work of Lei et al. (2024), which found a significant overlap between social camouflaging and safety behaviours, as well as a correlation between both behaviours and social anxiety symptoms. It is further informed by Pyszkowska (2024), who undertook a network analysis investigating associations between social camouflaging behaviours, social anxiety, and autistic traits, as well as autistic burnout, in a group of adults with autism, social anxiety, or both. title_r: The Effects of Memory Suppression on Recall Delay in the Think/No-Think task
abstract_r: The effects of memory suppression on later recall in the Think/No-Think (TNT; Anderson & Green, 2001) task is usually assessed with the difference in total recall score between No-Think and baseline (not manipulated) words, referred to as suppression-induced forgetting (SIF). However, this binary recall score may be too insensitive to detect the effects of memory suppression. The time it takes to recall the memory may be a more sensitive measure. Some previous studies using modified versions of the TNT task suggest that previously suppressed words are indeed recalled more slowly than baseline words or words that were retrieved (Haghighi et al., 2020; Nishiyama & Saito, 2021: Study 2). These studies, however, used modified versions of the TNT task. Here, we attempt to replicate the effects of memory suppression on recall delay using a standard TNT task with word pairs, in a larger sample (planned N = 80, compared to N = 20 and N = 45, respectively) and with a preregistered analysis plan. Further, we will assess recall delay for emotionally negative words, besides neutral words. We hypothesize that the recall of No-Think words will be slower than recall of baseline words. As an exploratory variable, we include memory suppression strategy, namely thought avoidance and thought substitution, in a randomized between-subjects design.

title_r: Replication of Hsieh et al. (2022): Colour Information and Facial Age Estimation
abstract_r: We replicate the psychological study "Colour information biases facial age estimation and reduces inter-observer variability", by Hsieh et al., we expect to come to the same conclusions as in the paper (all the experiments, which we replicate as faithfully as possible, to give the same results as in the paper) This project is a direct replication of Experiments 1 and 2 from the study 'Colour information biases facial age estimation and reduces inter-observer variability' by Hsieh et al. (2022). The purpose of this study is to investigate the role of holistic chromatic information in facial age perception. Specifically, we aim to determine if the presence of color information (versus greyscale) and the manipulation of red-green contrast bias perceived age or affect the consistency of age judgments between observers. We will recruit 40 participants for an in-person, controlled lab experiment using a within-subjects design. Stimuli will consist of 200 face images from the Chicago Face Database (CFD), manipulated using the CIE Lab color space to ensure perceptual accuracy. The experiment consists of two tasks: 1. Colour vs. Greyscale: Comparing age ratings for original colour images against greyscale images (created by setting CIE Lab a* and b* channels to zero) to test the effect of color presence on inter-observer variability. 2. Red-Green Contrast: Comparing age ratings for images with increased vs. decreased red-green contrast (created by scaling the CIE Lab a* channel) to test for systematic bias in age perception. We hypothesize that (1) inter-observer variability will be significantly lower in the Colour condition compared to the Greyscale condition, and (2) faces with increased red-green contrast will be rated as significantly younger than faces with decreased contrast. Additionally, we will perform an exploratory analysis to test if these effects differ by stimulus ethnicity.

title_r: Replication of Ballinger & Crocker (2020) Study 4
abstract_r: This research project is a direct replication of Study 4 from Ballinger and Crocker's (2020) "Understanding Whites' Perceptions of Multicultural Policies: A (Non)Zero-Sum Framework?", adapted for the United Kingdom context. The original US study challenged prevailing assumptions by demonstrating that White Americans do not necessarily perceive multicultural diversity policies—which explicitly value racial and ethnic differences—as threatening to their identity, contrary to the "exclusion hypothesis" that suggests majority groups feel excluded by such policies. The primary purpose is to test whether this "nonzero-sum" finding generalises to the UK, where different historical contexts, public discourse around multiculturalism, and demographic patterns may influence how White employees perceive diversity policies. This replication is theoretically important because it tests whether the nonzero-sum perception of multiculturalism reflects a broader phenomenon in Western democracies or is specific to the contemporary American context. We will replicate the original 2 (Diversity Policy: colorblind vs. multicultural) × 2 (Status Threat: threat vs. control) factorial design with UK employees (target N = 860). Participants will read about a fictional company's diversity policy and report anticipated social identity threat across four indicators: bias expectations, belonging, negative affect, and performance expectations. Our pre-registered analysis plan includes: (1) direct replication using the original weak priors to enable direct comparison; (2) confirmatory testing with theory-informed directional priors to provide a more rigorous test; and (3) equivalence testing to determine whether any effects are practically meaningful (|d| < 0.20). We will use sequential Bayesian analysis with pre-specified stopping rules (BF₀₁ ≥ 10 or ≤ 0.1) to ensure efficient data collection. Expected outcomes include either: (a) replicating the null effect, suggesting majority groups' nonzero-sum perceptions of multiculturalism generalise across Western contexts; or (b) finding increased identity threat, indicating important cultural moderators. Both outcomes would significantly advance our theoretical understanding of when and why diversity initiatives may or may not trigger majority group backlash, with practical implications for implementing inclusive organisational policies. Preliminary disclosures: - Due to timing constraints, data collection started before the submission of this pre-registration. At present, ~130 responses have been collected but we have not viewed any of them. - Generative AI (Gemini 2.5 and Claude 4 Opus) was used to draft the registration; all details were reviewed and edited by the first author.

title_r: The Preference for Simple Explanations and Interventions in the Pursuit of Efficiency: Study 3 – A pre-registered replication of Sehl et al. (2024).
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

People often find bullet points easier to understand than prose and generally prefer simpler explanations over complex ones. This preference reflects Occam’s razor—the idea that unnecessary assumptions should be avoided—and is considered an “explanatory virtue.” Some argue that simple explanations are more likely to be true, though probability alone may not fully explain the phenomenon (Vrantsidis & Lombrozo, 2022).

Sehl et al. (2024) propose that the preference for simplicity reflects a broader tendency to favor efficiency in goal-directed activities. Explanation is one such activity: understanding an outcome is more efficient when fewer causes or assumptions are invoked. From this “efficiency” perspective, the preference for simplicity should appear not only in explanatory judgments (why an outcome occurred) but also in process judgments (how an outcome could be achieved). The theory further predicts that statistical information about reliability or generality of causes (e.g., base rates, likelihoods) can reduce or even reverse the simplicity preference. Seven preregistered experiments supported these predictions.

Because prior participants were mostly from the United States (via CloudResearch and Prolific), questions remain about the universality of these findings. The present study replicates Experiments 1, 2, and 7 of Sehl et al. (2024), testing the claim that preferences for simpler explanations reflect pursuit of efficiency. By using Japanese participants, we examine cross-cultural generality, extend the theory’s applicability, and contribute to comparative research on cultural variation in cognition.

This study (Study 3 of the project) focuses on replicating Sehl et al.’s Study 7. Their findings indicated that when a complex cause was more probable, the preference for the simple explanation diminished, particularly in process judgments.

In Study 7 of the previous work, participants more often chose the simple cause in explanatory than in process judgments. They also showed stronger preference for the simple cause when likelihoods were 80% vs. 65% than when they were 90% vs. 65%. Although the interaction was not statistically significant, a single-sample test revealed that only in the process-judgment condition with 90% vs. 65% likelihoods was the complex cause chosen significantly more often.

Judgments overall were shaped more by perceived probability of success (that an explanation was true or a process would succeed) than by ease of comprehension or number of factors. Probability information had greater weight in process judgments, whereas number of factors mattered more in explanatory choices.

title_r: The Preference for Simple Explanations and Interventions in the Pursuit of Efficiency: Study 1 and 2 – A pre-registered replication of Sehl et al. (2024).
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

People often find information presented in bullet points easier to understand than lengthy prose, and in general prefer simpler explanations over more complex ones. This preference aligns with the principle of Occam’s razor, which holds that unnecessary assumptions should not be introduced, and has been regarded as one of the “explanatory virtues” used to evaluate the quality of explanations. Some have argued that simple explanations are more likely to be true than complex ones. However, it has also been suggested that probability alone cannot fully account for this phenomenon (Vrantsidis & Lombrozo, 2022).

Sehl et al. (2024) propose a novel theory that the preference for simplicity is not unique to explanation itself, but rather stems from a broader tendency to favor efficient means of achieving goals. Providing an explanation is a goal-directed activity aimed at understanding the causes of an outcome, and from this perspective, explanations with fewer causes and assumptions can be seen as more efficient. According to this “doing things efficiently” account, the preference for simpler causes should manifest not only when judging why an outcome occurred (explanatory judgments), but also when evaluating how an outcome could be achieved (process judgments). Moreover, the theory predicts that when statistical information about the reliability or generality of causes (e.g., base rates or likelihood of effect occurrence) is provided, the preference for simplicity may weaken or even reverse. Sehl et al. support these predictions with evidence from seven preregistered experiments.

However, participants in prior studies were recruited primarily from the United States (via CloudResearch and Prolific), leaving open questions about the universality of these findings. The present study attempts to replicate Experiments 1, 2, and 7 of Sehl et al. (2024), focusing on the claim that preferences for simpler explanations result from the pursuit of efficiency. By conducting this replication with Japanese participants, we aim to test the cross-cultural generality of the findings, broaden the scope of the theory’s applicability, and contribute to comparative research on potential cultural differences in cognitive processes.

In this study, we will try to replicate Sehl et al. (2024)’s Study 1 and 2.

title_r: Replicating the coherence illusion on numerosity perception using a sequential two-alternative forced choice task
abstract_r: The Approximate Number System (ANS) is believed to play a crucial role in facilitating the representation of visual numbers and is thought to establish a basis for symbolic mathematics. Exploring the systematic influences of visual features on our perception of numerosity can offer insights into the mechanisms through which ANS representations are generated from visual input. Prior work using a numerosity comparison task has shown that decreasing visual coherence of orientation and color reduces perceived numerosity (DeWind, Bonner, & Brannon, 2020; Qu, DeWind, & Brannon, 2022). One possibility is that visual coherence influences the allocation of numerosity-related attention between the two arrays and that the coherence illusion would not extend to judgments that do not involve simultaneous comparison. In the current experiment, we test whether we can replicate the color coherence effect using a two-interval forced choice task where reference and test patches are presented in succession.

title_r: Implicit ambivalence elicited by novel persons image primes (evaluative priming and gender priming tasks)
abstract_r: Past work has found evidence that novel person image primes trigger bivalent implicit evaluations (i.e., facilitate the classification of positive targets and the classification of negative targets in the evaluative priming task). In the current study, we want to rule out the potential alternative explanation that novel person images simply facilitate classification of any target classification task. To do so, we will have participants complete two tasks: an evaluative priming task and a gender priming task. The evaluative priming task is similar to the one used in previous work where a novel person’s image (or a neutral object that serves as a baseline) is presented as a prime and participants categorize subsequently presented positive and negative word targets in terms of valence (i.e., as positive or negative). In the gender priming task, the target words are male- or female-related words (e.g., guy, sir, man, gal, lady, woman) and participants are asked to categorize them in terms of gender (i.e., as male or female). We expect to replicate previous research findings that in the evaluative priming task novel person image primes trigger bivalent implicit evaluations, facilitating the classification of both positive and negative targets. But we expect that in the gender priming task, novel person image primes will show a congruency effect such that novel person image primes facilitate categorization of gender congruent targets, as compared to gender incongruent targets.

title_r: Caballero 2021 Replication Project
abstract_r: This project is a direct replication of Study 2 from Caballero et al. (2021), which examined whether experiencing economic scarcity leads individuals to adopt a more concrete (lower-level) construal style compared to those in conditions of economic sufficiency. The study uses the Bimboola economic-scarcity manipulation, assigning participants to imagine living in either a highly resource-constrained economic group or a financially comfortable group. Construal level is assessed using the Behavioral Identification Form (BIF; Vallacher & Wegner, 1989), administered both before and after the economic manipulation to capture within-person changes in abstraction. The purpose of the replication is to evaluate whether the original finding, namely a significant interaction between time (pre–post) and economic condition (scarcity vs. nonscarcity), can be reproduced in a U.S.-based online sample recruited through Prolific. According to the original study, participants assigned to economic scarcity showed a decrease in abstract construal after the manipulation, whereas participants assigned to nonscarcity showed an increase. No baseline differences in construal level were observed prior to the manipulation. The planned replication follows the original procedure as closely as possible: participants complete 12 BIF items at baseline, complete the Bimboola assignment with stimuli adapted for online presentation, and then complete another 12 BIF items. Manipulation checks assessing perceived poverty and wealth of one’s assigned group are also included, mirroring the original study to confirm that the scarcity induction functions as intended. The primary analysis will test the Time × Condition interaction on BIF scores using a mixed ANOVA with one between-subjects factor (scarcity vs nonscarcity) and one within-subjects factor (pre vs post). This is the identical model reported in Caballero et al. (2021). Simple effects will be examined only if the interaction is significant. Participants will be excluded if they fail an attention check. I will recruit 72 participants and will apply preregistered exclusions to that sample. The expected outcome is a successful replication of the original interaction, with scarcity reducing abstraction and nonscarcity increasing it. The project also serves as part of a replication-based training assignment, and results will be used to assess the robustness of the original effect and contribute to broader evidence on whether brief scarcity primes reliably influence cognitive construal. Findings will be reported according to preregistered analyses and shared openly through this OSF project.

title_r: When Does Social Exclusion Reduce Stereotyping? A Chatroom-Based Replication of Individuation Effects in Impression Formation
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate the core finding of Claypool et al. (2014) that social exclusion reduces reliance on stereotypes and promotes individuated impression formation. Based on Social Monitoring System Theory, the original research suggests that experiences of exclusion heighten motivation for social reconnection, leading individuals to process social targets more deeply rather than relying on category-based judgments. To address limitations of prior paradigms that relied on recall tasks or human–computer interaction, the present study adopts a chatroom interaction paradigm to induce social exclusion in a more ecologically valid interpersonal context. Participants will be randomly assigned to a social exclusion, social inclusion, or control condition and will engage in an online group discussion with trained confederates. Following the manipulation, participants will complete measures assessing basic psychological needs and emotional states, and then perform an impression formation task adapted for the Chinese cultural context. They will evaluate occupational targets described with mildly counter-stereotypical behaviors on stereotype-related and irrelevant traits. We hypothesize that socially excluded participants will show lower stereotype-consistent trait ratings than included or control participants. This study tests the robustness and generalizability of the social exclusion–individuation effect using a real-time social interaction paradigm in a non-Western context.

title_r: Correlates of spoken language and broader communication skills in a large heterogenous cohort of minimally verbal school-age children
abstract_r: This pre-registration will evaluate data from the first wave of the project "Elucidating mechanisms of language growth in minimally verbal children", a longitudinal observational study following the communicative progress of minimally verbal 4-12 year olds with autism and/or intellectual disability in the UK. The project aims to collect 3 subsequent waves of data (at one year intervals) and thus also investigate related longitudinal questions. We will pre-register detailed analytic plans relating to later data collection at future points, using a modular approach, however we also outline the key research questions now, to maximise transparency. See section “Longitudinal Research Questions” below for further details. Data collected at Time 1 will address four key research questions: RQ1: What is the relative contribution of speech skills to concurrent expressive spoken language level? Emerging evidence suggests speech-motor planning difficulties may present an additional barrier to communication for some neurodivergent individuals (over and above differences in social motivation, joint attention or sensory processing), known as the “apraxia hypothesis”. This theory challenges the prevailing “speech attunement hypothesis”, which posits that socio-cognitive skills remain the key driver of individual differences in language development, even in minimally verbal children. This research question seeks to examine correlates of expressive spoken language in minimally verbal children, to test these competing hypotheses. The sample will have a limited range of expressive language skills initially, due to the study inclusion criteria. We aim to replicate previous studies that found concurrent speech skills explain much of this variation in minimally verbal children (H1) (Chenausky et al., 2019, Saul & Norbury, 2020). We also aim to test whether the positive relationship between speech skills and expressive spoken language (if replicated) holds whilst controlling for two other potential sources of variance: the child’s receptive language and their communicative competence (H2). Communicative competence encompasses social motivation, pragmatic ability and sophistication of verbal and non-verbal communication skills. Models for H1 and H2 will be presented on an unadjusted basis and also after controlling for variables expected to also contribute to individual differences in expressive spoken language, such as sex, socio-economic status, non-social autism symptoms, loss of skills (regression) and adaptive skills. Age is not predicted to be an important covariate, given the atypical developmental profile of the group studied. RQ2: Does communicative competence predict wellbeing of minimally verbal children and their carers? Parents of autistic children report elevated levels of parenting stress and depressive symptoms relative to parents of typical children (Cohrs & Leslie, 2017; Hayes & Watson, 2013). This may be due to both shared genetic risk factors, and heightened stress associated with parenting a child with additional needs. We will test the hypothesis that a major contributing factor to parent wellbeing is the child’s ability to effectively communicate their needs (via non-verbal cues, words, signs or other means, as indexed by communicative competence). We also anticipate that increased communicative competence will be associated with higher child wellbeing. There are currently no appropriate self-report measures of wellbeing for minimally verbal primary aged children. We will therefore use a novel proxy measure: parent-reported child wellbeing based on external indices of happiness and unhappiness (Dillon & Carr, 2007). Increased parent and child wellbeing inadequately capture the more global impact of having a child with complex communication needs on family life, so we will also take a third measure of parents’ satisfaction with family life, as measured by two subscales of a bespoke questionnaire co-produced with autism community members (Autism Family Experience Questionnaire, AFEQ, Leadbitter et al., 2018). We hypothesise that all three wellbeing measures will be significantly positively correlated with each other (H3a), and that the child’s communicative competence will predict all three wellbeing measures (H3b), and we will test this with adjusted and unadjusted models (using the same covariates as for H1 and H2). RQ3: Do motor abilities predict speech skills in minimally verbal children? Early motor skills predict concurrent and later language abilities, in typical development and autism (Leonard & Hill, 2014, Mody et al., 2017, Wu et al., 2021). Early motor skills and their trajectories predict autism symptoms and language abilities in siblings with elevated likelihood of an autism diagnosis (LeBarton & Landa, 2019, Patterson et al., 2021). The link between motor skills and language may be partly mediated by speech skills, and this relationship has rarely been studied in minimally verbal school aged children (Butler & Tager-Flusberg, 2022). We aim to characterise the motor skills of children in this study and examine their relationship with speech skills. We hypothesise that two distinct latent factors will emerge: one pertaining to oral motor skills and the other to fine and gross motor skills (which we have labelled general motor skills, H4a). We hypothesise that both constructs will predict concurrent speech skills (H4b). RQ4: Which subgroups of minimally verbal children emerge from a data driven cluster analysis of communication-related measures? Finally, we will use a data driven approach to replicate and extend previous cluster analyses and latent profile analyses of minimally verbal children’s communication abilities, to validate previously observed constellations of strengths and challenges (Belmont et al, 2013, Broome et al, 2022, Maes et al, 2022, Reetzke et al., 2022). Broome et al. (2022) identified three clusters of children (those with generally low language/speech abilities, those with generally high language/speech abilities, and a third group who had high receptive language skills but poor speech and expressive language). Replicated evidence of this third cluster (H5) would support existence of a disconnect between social abilities and vocal output in a subgroup of minimally verbal children. We aim to use all the communication-related measures gathered in this study in an agglomerative hierarchical cluster analysis, and then report descriptive statistics on the resulting clusters relating to non-social autism symptoms, motor skills, adaptive skills and demographic measures.

title_r: Replication Study: Feeling capable and valued
abstract_r: This study is a preregistered replication-with-extension of Bacq and Alt (2018), who examined how empathy influences social entrepreneurial (SE) intentions via two mechanisms: SE self-efficacy (agentic pathway) and social worth (communal pathway). Their original two-wave study with SE students showed that empathic concern and perspective-taking strengthened SE self-efficacy and social worth, which in turn enhanced SE intentions. We replicate this core model using the same constructs and theoretical framework to ensure comparability, with three key modifications. First, the study employs a single-wave survey design rather than the original two-wave structure to improve feasibility and reduce participant attrition; procedural and statistical remedies (e.g., anonymity and marker-variable checks) will mitigate potential common-method bias. Second, the measure of social worth has been adapted to allow broader applicability beyond project-based SE courses. The original wording (“the people I helped”) was course-specific, so the revised items assess the general sense of being valued, appreciated, and trusted by others for one’s contributions, aligning with the conceptual definition of social worth as feeling needed, cared about, and valued by others. Third, the empathy scales for perspective-taking and empathic concern are measured on 7-point scales instead of the original 5-point scales to harmonize all predictor constructs, increase response granularity, and enhance comparability. Our extension also introduces a broader student sample that includes both SE-course students and non-SE students. This design addresses potential selection bias inherent in studying only SE students, who may already be predisposed toward social impact careers. By including non-SE students, the study tests whether the proposed mechanisms operate consistently across both groups. If the mechanisms are correct, they should explain variation in SE intentions across groups, not just high levels among SE students. The outcomes will contribute to (social) entrepreneurship research by (a) reinforcing confidence in prior findings, (b) addressing potential selection bias in SE education research, and (c) clarifying the extent to which empathy-driven mechanisms explain differences in SE intentions across student populations.

title_r: Strengthening Democracy with interventions: A conceptual replication of a megastudy in the Netherlands
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Voelkel et al. 2024 published an intervention tournament aimed at testing interventions to reduce affective polarization, support for undemocratic practices and support for political violence in the United States. We will conduct a conceptual replication of this intervention tournament in the Netherlands. We will include five interventions from Voelkel et al. 2024, and, where necessary, adapt them to the different national context. We will also include three existing interventions that are already in use in the Netherlands, but to our knowledge, have not been evaluated. We also developed five new interventions that will be tested in the study. We adapted the dependent variables of the study to the national context while also refining their operationalization to improve instrument quality. We will test our interventions using a random sample of 22,500 Dutch citizens from the general adult population in the winter of 2026.

title_r: Memory for Degraded Speech
abstract_r: The present study will provide a conceptual replication of Rabbitt (1966), investigating the impact of speech in noise on subsequent recognition memory performance. Unlike Rabbitt, we will employ a within-participant design and use both words and sentences as stimuli, allowing us to manipulate the contextual richness of speech. We will also examine the impact of two levels of multi-talker babble noise, with an easier (+7 dB) and a more challenging (+1 dB) SNR condition, alongside a clear speech control condition. Between encoding and recognition portions, participants will complete Raven's Advanced Progressive matrices, primarily as a distractor task, but also as a measure of fluid intelligence.

title_r: Sense of agency and recognition memory: A replication of Hon and Yeo (2021)
abstract_r: Hon and Yeo (2021) demonstrated that word recognition (i.e., “hit” responses) is facilitated when words are presented within a moving box whose motion is triggered by a participant’s voluntary keypress. We will conduct a replication study to examine the reproducibility of the findings from their Experiment 2, which employed essentially the same methodology as Experiment 1 and yielded comparable results, but was implemented with improved experimental control. In their Experiment 2, a box moved upward or downward either in a direction corresponding to, or opposite from, the participant’s action (an upward or downward keypress), with either a minimal (100 ms) or longer (900 ms) temporal delay. After the box reached its destination, a word was presented inside the box. This “action” task was followed by a surprise recognition test for the words. Temporal and spatial congruency were manipulated to modulate the sense of agency over the visual feedback. Under conditions of spatial congruency and minimal delay, both the rated sense of agency and recognition performance (i.e., hit rate) were higher than in conditions with incongruent and/or delayed feedback, suggesting that an enhanced sense of agency may improve recognition memory. Our previous study (Tsuji & Imaizumi, 2022) failed to show any improvement in recognition memory for word stimuli (i.e., feedback of voluntary action) as a result of action–feedback congruence, although the rated sense of agency was successfully manipulated. However, our experimental task and design were not sufficiently comparable to Experiment 2 of Hon and Yeo (2021). Therefore, the present study aims to conduct a more direct replication of their findings using more closely matched experimental procedures.

title_r: Breathing Route Does Not Affect Visual Search: A Pre-Registered Replication and Extension
abstract_r: The relationship between breathing and cognition is gaining increasing interest, with nasal breathing linked to greater neurophysiological synchrony compared to oral breathing. This synchrony could impact cognitive functions like attention and memory. Yoshimura et al. (2019) examined whether respiratory pathway (oral vs. nasal) affects visual search performance. In their second experiment, oral breathing combined with reduced target discriminability led to increased reaction time (RT) intercepts compared to nasal breathing, but only in the most difficult search condition. In this pre-registered report, we aim to replicate their RT effects and provide a more sensitive test of respiration effects by examining search efficiency across a wider range of difficulties. Using a within-subjects design, participants will complete a visual search task under oral and nasal breathing conditions, with target-distractor orientation differences ranging from 2° to 6°. This will show whether oral breathing speeds RT under difficult conditions (replicating Yoshimura et al.) and reduces search slopes (extending their findings). By examining both intercept and slope effects, we seek to determine whether oral breathing disrupts pre-search or post-search processing and/or impairs search efficiency. This research contributes to understanding how breathing pathway influences attentional processing during visual search tasks.

title_r: Wakeful rest benefits for intentionally encoded material.
abstract_r: Our previous work has shown that word recall is enhanced when learning is surrounded by wakeful rest as opposed to an effortful task. In Experiment 1 (Raza et al., 2025 - https://doi.org/10.1177/17470218251346156), using intentional encoding, rest was found to benefit memory both proactively and retroactively. In Experiment 2 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/H79B2), using incidental encoding, rest was found to benefit memory proactively but not retroactively. In Experiment 1, participants reported an overall greater tendency to deliberately rehearse words during the retention interval, and these rehearsal ratings differed between groups. Whereas, in Experiment 2, rehearsal was less likely overall (due to the memory test being unexpected) and rehearsers were removed from the analysis (because we were interested in the effects of rest in the absence of rehearsal). The difference in results regarding the retroactive rest effect between Experiments 1 and 2 could either be due to this difference in word rehearsal or the difference in encoding strategy. The aim of this Experiment is to disentangle these potential explanations, by investigating the effect of peri-encoding wakeful rest for intentionally encoded material that is not rehearsed. Taken with the results of our previous Experiments, if this Experiment finds a retroactive benefit of rest, this would challenge the rehearsal-based explanation for this effect and suggest that encoding intentionality is an important boundary condition for this effect. This finding would not be inconsistent with Consolidation theory, which might claim that only intentionally encoded material may benefit from rest because selective consolidation processes occur for salient or future-relevant information, at least in this type of paradigm. Taken with our previous results, if this Experiment does not find a retroactive benefit of rest, this would support the rehearsal hypothesis, suggesting that the effect only appeared in Experiment 1, and perhaps elsewhere in the literature, due to uncontrolled rehearsal of learned materials. This would challenge current instantiations of Consolidation theory. We hope to replicate the proactive benefit of rest in this Experiment, as this was observed in both Experiment 1 and 2 already.

title_r: A Replication Study of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation-Induced Heart-Brain Coupling
abstract_r: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is a prominent stimulation target for the treatment of Major Depressive disorder (MDD) with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). The therapeutic effect of DLPFC stimulation likely stems from the DLPFC–subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) connectivity. A recent study suggested that there is an overlap of the hubs in the depression network, including the DLPFC, sgACC, and vagus nerve (VN), with the heart-brain axis, and that stimulation of these hubs consequently leads to heart rate (HR) decelerations. A specific 10 Hz Dash rTMS protocol (‘neuro-cardiac guided rTMS version 2.0’, NGC-2.0 rTMS) has been proposed to induce coupling of TMS and HR changes (heart-brain coupling; HBC). This research encompasses two studies aimed at exploring the effects of NGC-TMS targeting the DLPFC. In the Study-1, we will replicate and corroborate previous findings with a larger cohort of twenty healthy young participants. These participants will undergo NGC-TMS sessions targeting the DLPFC, supplemented by sham TMS, across three sessions. Following these findings, the Study-2 will examine the robustness of HBC by assessing various stimulation intensities by targeting the most effective target identified in the Study-1.

title_r: Partial replication of: Deception consequences and the influence of moral narratives
abstract_r: In this study we aim to replicate, in a higher-powered study, part of our previous pre-registered study (https://osf.io/wfcn5). The part we will replicate is related to the suggestive evidence from the previous study according to which, contrary to our hypothesis, (negative) narratives in support of lying increase (rather than decrease) truth-telling rates in a situation where the consequences of lying have a relatively high impact on a third party. We will examine the robustness of this result by running an experiment based on the same game where a person is faced with a decision that involves a tradeoff between being honest and maximising own material payoff that comes at a relatively high cost for another person (setting that was referred to as the HIGH impact setting in the previous study). We will compare a baseline treatment where participants can decide whether to lie or not without receiving any social information, with a treatment where, before making their decision they are presented with other participants’ negative narratives promoting dishonesty. In our previous study, positive narratives proved to have a large and significantly positive effect on honesty. For completeness, we will also run the treatment where participants are presented with other participants’ positive narratives promoting honesty and further test the robustness of the previous results.

title_r: Computational Mechanisms of Attribute Translations
abstract_r: This research project aims at replicating and extending previous findings regarding the behavioral, attentional, and cognitive effects of the behavior intervention technique attribute translations (Mertens et al., 2020; Oberbauer et al., 2025). Participants will complete a hypothetical consumer choice task on two sessions where they will be asked to choose between washing machine appliances. In session one, participants will receive information about the price, consumption, and popularity of the appliances. In session two, participants will be randomly assigned to one of several groups and either receive the same information as on session one (control) or receive attribute translations (either in addition to or instead of consumption information). We expect to replicate behavioral, attentional, and cognitive effects described in Oberbauer et al. (2025) for groups that receive attribute translations in addition to the original attribute and explore whether these effects differ when the attribute translation replaces the original attribute.

title_r: Investigating Hybrid Search with Eye-Tracking: A Replication of Drew, Boettcher, and Wolfe (2017)
abstract_r: This is a replication of Drew, T., Boettcher, S. E., & Wolfe, J. M. (2017). One visual search, many memory searches: An eye-tracking investigation of hybrid search. Journal of Vision, 17(11), 5-5. This study investigates how three factors affect performance of visual search: (1) memory set size: the number of targets the participant must memorize and then search for; (2) visual set size: the number of distractors (not memorized) and targets on the screen; and (3) target presence. By measuring response times and eye-movement patterns, the study tests the hypothesis that observers make a single search through the visual image in a hybrid search. A hybrid search occurs when an observer is searching for one of a number of possible targets that they hold in memory. We plan to run the same analyses as Drew et al. regarding behavioral results, eye-tracking results, and FVF analysis.

title_r: Replication of Pennycook et al. (2018) at The University of Alabama
abstract_r: We are a group of undergraduate students completing this replication as a project in Dr. Alexa Tullett's Flexa Lab. Original Abstract The 2016 U.S. presidential election brought considerable attention to the phenomenon of “fake news”: entirely fabricated and often partisan content that is presented as factual. Here we demonstrate one mechanism that contributes to the believability of fake news: fluency via prior exposure. Using actual fake-news headlines presented as they were seen on Facebook, we show that even a single exposure increases subsequent perceptions of accuracy, both within the same session and after a week. Moreover, this “illusory truth effect” for fake-news headlines occurs despite a low level of overall believability and even when the stories are labeled as contested by fact checkers or are inconsistent with the reader’s political ideology. These results suggest that social media platforms help to incubate belief in blatantly false news stories and that tagging such stories as disputed is not an effective solution to this problem. It is interesting, however, that we also found that prior exposure does not impact entirely implausible statements (e.g., “The earth is a perfect square”). These observations indicate that although extreme implausibility is a boundary condition of the illusory truth effect, only a small degree of potential plausibility is sufficient for repetition to increase perceived accuracy. As a consequence, the scope and impact of repetition on beliefs is greater than has been previously assumed. Replication Objectives In this study, we aim to replicate an existing study, which examined whether repeated exposure to fake news headlines and stories influences participants to have more belief in them. This study also aims to add to the literature on the illusory truth effect. Based on the conclusions of the original study, we hypothesize that a) repetition of extremely implausible fake news stories will not increase the belief that participants have in their truth, b) repetition of plausible false and true news headlines will increase participant belief in their accuracy, and c) warning participants that the headlines they are seeing may be false will decrease perceived accuracy of both true and false headlines.

title_r: Exploring ostracism and rejection with different agents in a virtual restaurant (text + image modality)
abstract_r: • Restaurants are a good example where robots can be used to counteract skill shortages. However, processes of social inclusion and exclusion are yet not well-explored in human-robot teams. Previous vignette studies (Arlinghaus et al., 2025, 2026) figured out that social exclusion by human coworkers might be more harmful than social exclusion by robot coworkers. We aim to replicate this finding in different modalities (text, text + image, video, VR). All studies deal with restaurant workplaces where participants face social inclusion, ostracism, or rejection by human coworkers, humanoid robot coworkers, or mechanic robot coworkers. Throughout all studies, we explore the effects of social inclusion and exclusion on perception, need fulfillment, and attribution processes. In this particular study, we let people read texts with images. The images stem from the VR environment.

title_r: A Replication Study of "Business as Plan B: Institutional foundations of gender inequality in entrepreneurship across 24 industrialized countries."
abstract_r: This study conducts a hybrid replication of Thébaud's (2015) investigation of institutional foundations of gender inequality in entrepreneurship across 24 industrialized countries. We combine exact replication—by designing our own survey instrument following the original methodology—with constructive replication by extending the sample to include non-industrialized countries. This extension tests the generalizability of Thébaud's institutional explanations beyond industrialized contexts and addresses a significant scope limitation in the original work. While the original study analyzed Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) data from 2001-2008, our contemporary data collection necessarily reflects current conditions, which allows us to assess whether the institutional mechanisms identified by Thébaud remain operative in today's entrepreneurial landscape. Our custom survey design reduces measurement error and provides better control over data quality compared to secondary data sources. We document all methodological differences from the original study, conduct power analyses to ensure adequate statistical confidence, and perform cross-country adjustments to address potential threats to validity arising from sample heterogeneity between industrialized and non-industrialized settings. This replication adds scientific value by simultaneously testing the robustness and temporal stability of influential findings while examining boundary conditions and alternative mechanisms in diverse economic contexts.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from from Kappes et al (2012), from Journal of Experimental Social Psychology
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Kappes et al (2012) is: We selected the claim that mental contrasting (versus control conditions) affects the strength of associations between the obstacle of reality and instrumental behavior (hereafter referred to as obstacle-behavior associations) (Statement 2), which reflects "mental contrasting paired with low expectations of success leads to weak associations between obstacles of reality and behavior instrumental to overcome these obstacles" (Statement 1), as found in the paper's abstract. The claim is tested by comparing obstacle-behavior associations between mental contracting conditions (contrasting or irrelevant content) using hierarchical regression analysis (Statement 3), which resulted in, when in expectations of success were low, participants in the mental contrasting condition showed weaker obstacle-behavior association effects than those in the irrelevant content control condition, t(90) = 2.45, p = 0.02 (Statement 4). In addition to the claim selected by SCORE, this study plans to test the main findings of the original paper. The replication team believes that the main finding of interest is that mental contrasting (versus control conditions) interacts with expectations of success to affect the strength of associations between the obstacle of reality and instrumental behavior. The claim is tested by using hierarchical regression analysis with conditions (dummy-coded) and success expectations (continuous, 1-7 scale), and testing for two interactions (one with each dummy-variable). From the original paper: “adding the interaction terms significantly improved the model, R2change=9%, Fchange(2,90)= 3.97, p= .02.” This study will replicate all effects found within the hierarchical regression model conducted for the main analysis as reported in the original paper. These include that in “the mental contrasting condition expectations predicted strong obstacle–behavior associations (indicated by faster reaction times), ꞵ=−.44, t(90)=2.36, p=.02. Expectations did neither predict obstacle–behavior associations in the reverse contrasting condition, ꞵ=.14, t(90)=.97, p=.33, nor in the irrelevant content control condition, ꞵ=.18, t(90)=1.12, p=.23.” Planned follow-up contrasts of the effects of each condition at low and high expectations of success will be conducted. From the paper’s abstract: “mental contrasting paired with high expectations of success creates strong associations between obstacles of reality and behavior instrumental to overcome these obstacles” while "mental contrasting paired with low expectations of success leads to weak associations between obstacles of reality and behavior instrumental to overcome these obstacles.” The analysis in the original paper found when “expectations of success were high (expectations=7), participants in the mental contrasting condition showed stronger obstacle–behavior associations than participants in the reverse contrasting condition, t(90)=2.46, p=.02, and participants in the irrelevant content control condition, t(90)=2.58, p=.01. Yet when expectations of success were low (expectations=1), participants in the mental contrasting conditions showed weaker obstacle-behavior association effects than those in the reverse contrasting condition, t(90) = 2.32, p = .02.” Lastly, this study will also test the effect of condition on the health goal and on obstacles activating behaviour generally. Therefore, the effect “of condition on expectancy-dependent associative strength between obstacles of reality and instrumental behaviors for the health concern (the non-elaborated concern)” will be tested in the same way as the above set of analyses. The analysis in the original paper found that adding “the interaction terms did not improve the model, Fchange(2,90)=.008, p=.99, and there was neither a main effect for expectations, t(90)=.88, p=.38, nor an interaction effect between expectations and condition, ts>.16, psb.90.” In the original paper, the effect of mental contrasting on trials with an interpersonal obstacle prime and health behaviour target found that adding “the interaction terms did not significantly improve the model, Fchange(2,90)=.34, p=.71, and there was neither a main effect for expectations, t(90)=.23, p=.82, nor an interaction effect between expectations and condition, ts>.78, psb.42.”

abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Weidmann & Callen (2013) is that the relationship between (in)security and election fraud should be in the form of an inverted U-shape. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "It predicts (i) that the relationship between violence and fraud follows an inverted U-shape and (ii) that loyalty networks of both incumbent and challenger react differently to the security situation on the ground. The claim is tested with the logit models presented in Table 2. The dependent variable is a binary measure of fraud, calculated by grouping polling stations by district and applying the Beber–Scacco last-digit test to the total vote count. The dependent variable takes the value of 1 if this test is significant at the 5 percent level for a particular district. The authors measure violence as the number of attacks per capita against the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF). In Model 1 (the model selected as evidence for the SCORE program), it is included in both linear and squared form. In conjunction with a positive and significant coefficient for the linear term,the claim is tested with the coefficient on the squared term (see Model 1 for specification details). Model 1 confirms Hypothesis 1, since the linear term of the violence measure receives a positive and significant coefficient, and the squared term a negative one (coefficient on Violence (election, squared) term = -13.748, SE clustered at the regional command level = 4.720, p< 0.01).
