title_r: Replication of a research claim from Chittoor et al. (2009) in Organization Science.
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Chittoor et al. (2009) is that accessing international technology resources relates positively to product market internationalization of Indian pharmaceutical firms (Hypothesis 1 (H1)). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Using longitudinal data on 206 Indian pharmaceutical firms from 1995–2004, we find that firms’ access to international technological and financial resources enables product market internationalization." The authors measure the product market internationalization of a firm as the ratio of foreign sales to total sales, the most common measure of internationalization. They estimate their models using random effects generalized least-squares panel regression procedures. The results of the testing for main-effect hypotheses appear in Model 1 in Table 2. In terms of the individual hypotheses, the coefficient for international technology resources is positive and significant (‘International technology resources (1 yr lag) (H1)’ term: b [unstandardized regression coefficient] = 0.25, White’s robust SE = 0.07, p < 0.001 [Significance levels are based on robust standard errors and one-tailed tests.]), in strong support of H1.

title_r: Heart Signals and Cognition
abstract_r: The body and brain are deeply interconnected, with bodily signals influencing cognitive and emotional processes. “Peripheral” theories of emotion emphasise the importance of physiological changes and their appraisal in the subjective experience of emotion (James, 1890/1950; Lange, 1885; Schachter & Singer, 1962; Seth, 2013). Similarly, changes in bodily arousal can influence decision-making and memory (Bechara et al., 2000; Garfinkel et al., 2013). Building on this perspective, this study focuses on cardiac signals, and how they can shape cognitive processes. Previous research has shown that memory (Garfinkel et al., 2014) can vary depending on the cardiac cycle phase – i.e. whether items were encoded at systole (cardiac contraction, when visceral feedback is maximal) or diastole (cardiac relaxation, when afferent feedback is minimal) – highlighting the role of afferent cardiovascular feedback in memory encoding. The aim of this current project is to further investigate the effect of cardiac signals on memory, attempting to replicate a study conducted by Fiacconi et al. (2016; DOI: 10.1037/xge0000164), which focuses on the impacts of afferent cardiovascular feedback on recognition memory decisions (i.e. when differentiating previously seen stimuli from novel ones). This procedure involves non-invasive electrocardiogram (ECG) and the presentation of simple stimuli (neutral and fearful faces) which are time-locked to different phases of the cardiac cycle during recognition decisions. In addition, as different cardiac signals are observed in different mental health conditions, such as schizophrenia (Yao & Thakkar, 2021), we also take a series of well validated and standardised mental health measures using standard questionnaires. There are four versions of the experiment inspired by Fiacconi et al.’s (2016) study, with two experiments being direct replications of their study. 1. Neutral (N) – direct replication of Experiment 2 in Fiacconi et al.’s study, using neutral faces as stimuli. This experiment was conducted prior to the preregistration, with the data collected and analysed. This experiment is therefore not included in the current preregistration, and is reported purely for contextual and comparative purposes only. This preregistration only applies to the following studies: 2. Fearful (F) – direct replication of Experiment 1 in Fiacconi et al.’s study, using fearful faces as stimuli; 3. Neutral with confidence measures (N+C) – same as the N study, but with additional confidence measures after each recognition judgement. 4. Fearful with confidence measures (F+C) – same as the F study, but with additional confidence measures after each recognition judgement.

abstract_r: This is a data-analytic replication attempt on the following claims from Kollmeyer et al. (2009): ● Trace number: 1 / Claim ID: m5y94l Claim 4 (Result statement): Table 1 shows the results from three regression models, each capturing some portion of the direct effects causing deindustrialization…Model 1 isolates the two domestic factors believed to be associated with deindustrialization: (1) the tendency for growing afﬂuence in wealthy countries to spur demand for services more than manufactured goods…As anticipated, the coefficients for these variables are statistically significant, and they exhibit the expected signs. The results for national afﬂuence’s effect on manufacturing employment deserve particular attention. Here the results indicate that the coefficient for national afﬂuence is positive, the coefficient for national afﬂuence squared is negative, and the coefficient for national afﬂuence cubed is again positive. [TABLE 1, Model 1, National affluence: 3.171, SE = .267, P < .001; (National affluence)^2: -.154, SE = .012, P < .001; (National affluence)^3: .002, SE = .000, P < .001] ● Trace number: 2 / Claim ID: my1dxd Claim 4 (Result statement): Table 1 shows the results from three regression models, each capturing some portion of the direct effects causing deindustrialization…Model 1 isolates the two domestic factors believed to be associated with deindustrialization:…(2) the propensity for productivity gains in the manufacturing sector to exceed those made by other sectors of the economy. As anticipated, the coefficients for these variables are statistically significant, and they exhibit the expected signs…The results from model 1 reveal a nonlinear relationship between unbalanced productivity growth and relative manufacturing employment as well. Here the coefficient for unbalanced productivity growth is negative, but the coefficient for unbalanced productivity growth squared is positive. [TABLE 1, Model 1, Unbalanced productivity growth: -10.192, SE = .875, P < .001; (Unbalanced productivity growth)^2: 2.516, SE = .266] ● Trace number: 3 / Claim ID: b29xjd Claim 4 (Result statement): Model 2, shown in table 1, isolates the global economic factors purportedly associated with deindustrialization. Results from this model support the view that expanding trade links between the North and the South of the global economy contribute to deindustrialization. The specifics of this relationship become clearer when looking at the individual coefficients for the variables constituting North-South trade. Expressed in absolute values, the coefficient for imports from the South (b = -0.828) is more than three times larger than the coefficient for exports to the South (b = 0.192). The imbalance between these two coefficients implies that North-South trade, rather than generating counterbalancing effects on domestic manufacturing employment, actually displaces more than four times as many jobs as it creates. [coefficient for imports from the South…is more than three times larger than the coefficient for exports to the South; TABLE 1, Model 2, Imports from the South: -.828, SE = .103, P < .001; Exports to the South: .192, SE = .079, P < .001] ● Trace number: 4 / Claim ID: m8oy76 Claim 4 (Result statement): Model 3, shown in tables 1 and 2, offers a more comprehensive analysis by simultaneously testing each variable…Under this combined model, the size and statistical significance of most coefficients exhibit little change from the previous two models. [TABLE 1, Model 3, National affluence: 2.555, SE = .275, P < .001; (National affluence)^2: -.124, SE = .012, P < .001; (National affluence)^3: .002, SE = .000, P < .01] ● Trace number: 5 / Claim ID: bonjlw Claim 4 (Result statement): Model 3, shown in tables 1 and 2, offers a more comprehensive analysis by simultaneously testing each variable, except FDI, which was excluded due to its statistical insignificance. Under this combined model, the size and statistical significance of most coefficients exhibit little change from the previous two models. [TABLE 1, Model 3, Unbalanced productivity growth: -10.070, SE = .882, P < .001; (Unbalanced productivity growth)^2: 2.302, SE = .267, P < .001] Deviations from the original study: 1. The original study includes 18 Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries from 1970 to 2003. The data used in the replication contains 16 OECD countries from 2004 to 2018 (including 10 countries from the original study). Countries in the original study: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Countries in the replication: Australia, Austria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Korea, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovak Republic, and the United Kingdom. All the new countries belong to the “North” category (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_North_and_Global_South). 2. The data sources are the same as the original study, except for the trade flows, that are obtained from UN Comtrade, instead of the OECD International Trade by Commodities Database. However, because both dataset measures trade flows across countries, the amount should be similar and therefore the impact on the replication results should be minimal.

abstract_r: The current study is a conceptual replication and extension of Liberman and Trope (1998, Experiment 1). In Liberman and Trope, participants were asked to imagine engaging in seven activities (e.g., “reading a science fiction book”) either in the near future (tomorrow) or distant future (next year). The responses were then assessed for degree of abstraction, using a dichotomous manual coding procedure where responses were classified as abstract if they fit the structure “description by activity” and were coded as concrete if they fit the structure “activity by description”. Results showed that participants who were asked to imagine conducting the activities in the near future provided more concrete descriptions than those who were asked to conduct the activities in the distant future. Second, we will use considerably larger sample sizes, allowing for reliable estimates, thereby safeguarding against Type 1 and Type 2 error. title_r: A within-subject study to investigate the influence of Virtual Reality on subsequent episodic memory
abstract_r: Animal studies have shown that exploring a novel environment facilitates learning (e.g., Davis, 2004). According to two influential models (Düzel et al., 2010; Lisman & Grace, 2005), novelty triggers dopamine release in the substantia nigra and the ventral tegmental area, which in turn promotes hippocampal learning by lowering the threshold for long-term potentiation. This novelty-induced neuroplasticity operates both during exposure to the novel environment and for up to 10 minutes afterward (Straube et al., 2003). There is even evidence suggesting the possibility of longer-term effects (Tang & Zou, 2002). In humans, novelty also appears to enhance learning (Tulving & Kroll, 1995), but the available evidence remains limited, particularly regarding the long-term beneficial effects of novelty exposure on learning. Slightly more than a decade ago, Schomaker et al. (2014) showed that exploring a novel virtual environment led to better recall performance on a verbal memory task administered after exploration, compared to exploring a familiar environment. Since then, several studies have reported contradictory findings (e.g., Quent & Henson, 2022). In our team, we failed to replicate this effect using similar experimental designs (see Aaron et al., 2024; Servais et al., 2024). Instead, these studies revealed a session order effect: participants showed better memory performance after the first session in which they explored a virtual reality environment, regardless of whether the environment was novel or familiar. We therefore turned our attention to the effect of virtual reality itself on memory. In a previous study, we showed that memory performance was better after exploring a virtual environment compared to watching a documentary about a natural environment (Servais & Bastin, 2025). However, this study included potential confounding variables, such as active exploration (VR) versus passive viewing (watching a documentary). The aim of the present study is to better understand how virtual reality influences learning in humans. We hypothesize that virtual reality constitutes a novel experience, distinct from everyday activities, and that it may represent a specific form of novelty that positively influences memory during initial exposure. To do so, participants will take part in three sessions conducted within a 15-day period. The order of the sessions will be counterbalanced across participants: - Session 1: Participants will actively explore a virtual environment (one of the Meta VR Nature Trek environments) using an Oculus Rift virtual reality headset. Following exploration, participants will complete a memory task (learning a list of 20 words presented using OpenSesame, followed by immediate free recall after a brief 2-minute simple mental arithmetic distractor task). After the memory test, participants will complete a questionnaire developed at ULiège to assess the sense of presence experienced during virtual reality. They will also complete a cybersickness questionnaire, as well as a series of questionnaires assessing different aspects of the exploration (motivation, emotions, perceived novelty of the environment, novelty of the technology used, interest, etc.). - Session 2: Participants will explore another Meta VR Nature Trek environment, but this time in a desktop version displayed on a computer screen (i.e., without the VR headset). After exploration, participants will complete a memory task similar to that of Session 1, using a different word list. They will then complete the same questionnaires as in Session 1. - Session 3: Participants will watch a video recording of the exploration of another Meta VR Nature Trek environment (passive viewing on a computer screen). After viewing, participants will complete a memory task similar to those in Sessions 1 and 2, using a different word list. They will then complete the same questionnaires as in Sessions 1 and 2. If active exploration of a novel environment improves learning for subsequent non-related material, we expect memory performance (i.e., the number of words recalled) to be higher after exploring an environment using a virtual reality (VR) headset and exploring an environment on a computer desktop compared to passively watching a recorded video of an exploration. Moreover, if the VR itself boosts memory beyond the active exploration of a novel environment, we expect memory performance to be higher after exploring a novel environment in a VR headset compared to exploring an environment on a computer desktop.

title_r: Perceptual salience of form versus material as a function of variations in spacing and number of elements: A replication
abstract_r: All authors share the role of first author and contributed to all aspects of the manuscript. Abstract: Is the perception of objects dominated by its form or material? Goldmeier (1936) explored this question with a psychophysical task in which participants rated the similarity between stimuli made up of identical elements with different numbers and identical spacing or the same number of elements with different spacing. He concluded that with smaller numbers of elements similarity was determined by form (number of elements) whereas with increasing numbers of elements material (spacing) emerged as dominant. Klein and Barresi (1985) further developed the experimental task and elaborated on Goldmeier’s conclusion, showing the crossover point was determined jointly by not only the number of elements composing the stimuli but also their spacing. As further literature has been based on these findings, it now seems pertinent to re-examine and possibly re-establish the claims they made. Therefore, the present study is a replication of Klein and Barresi (1985). Participants were asked to make a similarity rating between two stimuli (dotted lines that differed in number or spacing), and were then presented randomly with either line in a speeded classification task. Our data support the original interpretation: that form is more salient with a smaller number of elements (causing number to determine similarity) and material is more salient with a larger number of elements (causing spacing to determine similarity). Similarity ratings were closely confirmed by performance on the speeded classification task.

title_r: Does facial expression processing require attention? A multi-lab replication of Eimer et al. (2003)
abstract_r: How the brain processes facial expressions and whether this process requires focal attention have been central topics of neurophysiological research on face processing. In a seminal study, using scalp-recorded event-related potentials (ERPs), Eimer, Holmes, and McGlone (2003) found that emotional and neutral faces were differently processed in the brain as early as 160 ms after stimulus onset. Importantly, these ERP differences disappeared when attention was directed away from the face stimuli, suggesting the necessity of focal attention in facial expression processing. These results have influenced the revision of the Bruce and Young model of face processing, and greatly motivated further research in the field. Yet, subsequent research did not always agree with these findings, and the study was never directly replicated. Hence, this study has been selected by #EEGManyLabs, a global and multi-laboratory replication project, for a high-powered direct replication across multiple laboratories. We hypothesise the replication of the original positive findings, including the ERP effects differentiating emotional and neutral faces and their dependence on focal attention. To address the debate on facial expression processing and the role of N170, we will also take this opportunity to reassess key negative findings of the original study, namely no difference between emotional and neutral facial expressions in N170 and no ERP differences among the six facial expressions. Replication or revision of these findings will confirm the necessity of focal attention in emotional face processing and the postulated biomarkers of basic emotion processing. This study will provide a reproducible benchmark on face processing.

title_r: Review: Replicating the Effects of Iconicity in Lexical Decision Task: A Study in Brazilian Portuguese
abstract_r: Iconic words are characterized by a sense of resemblance between their form and their meaning. The most common examples are onomatopoeias such as “cock-a-doodle-doo” or “woof-woof,” but recent research shows that speakers of various languages perceive a relationship between sound and meaning in various words of their language. This is the case for English words such as crunchy, zigzag or wiggle, whose sonority is perceived as mapping onto their meaning (Winter et al., 2023). Recently, psycholinguistic research has investigated whether iconicity influence language processing. Sidhu, Vigliocco and Pexman (2020) ran a lexical decision task with words varying in their iconicity level. Their results show that the more iconic a word is, the quicker participants react to it, thus suggesting that iconicity may have a facilitatory effect in word recognition. We plan to replicate their study with a sample of Brazilian Portuguese speakers and Brazilian Portuguese words to test their main claim that reaction times in a classic lexical decision task could be influenced by the stimuli’s level of iconicity in a neurotypical population of adults. Our analysis plan closely follows the original study. A successful replication should show that participants react faster to words with higher iconicity ratings.

title_r: Re-examining hidden fitness: Female preferences for long-path songs in zebra finches
abstract_r: Female songbirds can evaluate male quality from secondary sexual characteristics such as songs. Studies have shown mixed findings on which acoustic features contribute to song attractiveness. In a 2024 study, Alam and colleagues introduced a holistic measure of song called "path length" and found that female zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) prefer long path length songs as compared to short path length songs. The original female-playback study was criticized for design limitations, notably its small sample size, and pseudoreplication. Here, we conducted a preregistered replication and extension study of the female preference for long vs. short path length songs. Our study will evaluate the robustness and generality of this preference.

title_r: Gender identity and sexist attitudes bias arbitrary gender word activation, comprehension and production
abstract_r: The purpose of the following studies is to further explore the internal bias that affects the activation of words with grammatical gender in native speakers of formal gender languages (Casado 2023). In the first place we wish to replicate our previous results on the facilitation of grammatical gender with regards to idiosyncratic sociolinguistic features in comprehension (Casado et al., 2018; 2021). In order to achieve that, we employed a gender decision task including arbitrary gender words with Spanish native speakers measuring response time and accuracy. We analyzed the results in reference to sociolinguistic aspects measured by various self-reported questionnaires. In particular, we implemented the gender roles questionnaire (Bem 1978), Benevolent and Hostile Sexism Questionnaire (Jimenez Rodrigo et al., 2011), and the Use of Inclusive language Questionnaire (Cardenas et al., 2010). Following, we wish to explore whether the internal bias of activated words congruent in gender can be observed during word production. Here, we employed a verbal fluency task, with semantic categories (animals, fruits) and letter categories (A, M). As the dependent variable, we measured the percentage of words with a feminine grammatical gender. We will collect data from 3 different Romance languages (Spanish, Catalan, Italian) to explore whether we can replicate these results across different language systems. We expect to find a facilitation in the activation of words that are congruent in gender within the internal representation. For instance, we expect feminine profiles to more easily process words with feminine grammatical gender, and produce a higher percentage of words in the feminine grammatical gender by default when compared to masculine profiles.

title_r: Replication of Shafir and Cheek (2024)
abstract_r: Previous research found that framing a decision as a choice (i.e., choose the option you want) as opposed to a rejection (i.e., reject the option you don’t want) leads to different preferred options. We hypothesized that the choice/rejection discrepancy is partly due to participants’ misunderstanding of the task and greater noise in rejection. Specifically, rejection tasks are often treated as choice tasks by participants. As a result, the choice/rejection difference is, at least in part, a mechanical effect due to mixing what participants believe is choice with rejection during analysis. In the present study, we test this hypothesis using the choice–rejection paradigm stimuli of Shafir and Cheek (2024). The study has two primary objectives. First, we seek to replicate Shafir and Cheek’s (2024) original finding of a systematic difference between choice and rejection framing. Second, we test whether explicit and detailed manipulation checks prior to the decision attenuate the choice–rejection difference observed in Shafir and Cheek (2024)’s paradigm. If the framing effect is driven in part by increased decision noise or doing the wrong task under rejection framing, then clarifying the task through emphasis manipulation and removing participants through a manipulation check and a rationality check will reduce the framing asymmetry.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Rilliard & Moraes (2017) on Attitudinal Prosody in Brazilian Portuguese
abstract_r: Este Relato Registrado (Stage 1) apresenta uma replicação e extensão do estudo de Rilliard e Moraes (2017) sobre prosódia atitudinal no português brasileiro. O objetivo é investigar os correlatos perceptivos e acústicos de significados atitudinais socialmente relevantes expressos na fala em contextos comunicativos face a face. Com base no delineamento original, o protocolo introduz um conjunto controlado de estímulos visuais sintéticos para aumentar a padronização contextual e a replicabilidade experimental. O estudo compreende duas fases: uma tarefa de produção, em que falantes produzem enunciados sob cenários atitudinais induzidos visualmente, e uma tarefa de percepção, na qual ouvintes avaliam os significados pretendidos. As medidas acústicas incluem frequência fundamental (F0), intensidade, duração e parâmetros espectrais, extraídos no Praat e analisados em R e Python. As hipóteses, o plano amostral, os critérios de exclusão e as análises estatísticas estão especificados a priori. Todos os materiais e scripts serão disponibilizados em repositório público. O estudo busca contribuir para a reprodutibilidade da pesquisa em prosódia atitudinal e para o refinamento metodológico de investigações experimentais sobre entoação socialmente indexada no português brasileiro.

title_r: Laboratory Study on Physiological and Psychological Responses to Meditation in Friendships
abstract_r: We are conducting a conceptual replication study of a recent study at Heidelberg University (Schültke et al., 2024). The aim of the study is to examine the effects of dyadic compassion meditation on heart rate variability (HRV), affect, and social closeness in friendships, to expand the evidence base for the use of dyadic meditation in therapy and in non-clinical contexts. The sample consists of non-clinical dyads of friends. After random assignment to one of three groups, following the induction of negative emotions the dyads will either engage in compassion meditation together (meditation group) or they will watch a video (control group). Heart rate data will be collected using EEG, Electrodermal skin conductance will be measured using EDA electrodes, along with demographic information and data on heart rate control variables, relationship quality, closeness, mindfulness, compassion, meditation experience, interoceptive awareness, emotion regulation, and affect. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the University of Mannheim. Reference Schültke, L., Warth, M., Alpers, G. W., Ditzen, B., & Aguilar-Raab, C. (2024). Better together than alone? title_r: The Effect of Moral Appeals on Cognitive Conflict and Motivational Engagement in Pro-Environmental Decision-Making
abstract_r: Although difficult, behavior change is crucial to address global challenges like climate change, given its deep ties with human activity. Previous research shows that people have a strong desire to be moral, making moral appeals (i.e., messages aiming to invoke the feeling of moral responsibility) promising tools to enhance motivation for behavior change (van Nunspeet & Ellemers, 2024). Although moral responsibility has been shown to strongly motivate positive behavior change, using moral appeals to activate this motivation do not always succeed (Luttrell, 2025; van Nunspeet & Ellemers, 2024). Studies show that moral appeals can also produce resistance or even backfire (Luttrell, 2025; van Nunspeet & Ellemers, 2024). Thus, understanding the factors that influence the effectiveness of moral appeals is essential for finding ways to increase the feelings of moral responsibility for positive behavior change without eliciting defensive reactions. In our prior work (Ergün et al., 2026; in preparation), we demonstrated that not all moral appeals are equally effective in increasing motivation for climate action, with forward-looking moral appeals showing stronger engagement. Building on this, we further showed (Ergün et al., 2026; in review) that a forward-looking moral appeal, relative to a non-moral appeal, elicits distinct neural responses associated with both the anticipation and outcome stages of reward processing. These findings suggest that specific moral appeals have the potential to shape the reward value of morally relevant goals, thereby promoting positive behavior change. Building on this prior work, the current study aims to compare multiple moral appeals at the neural level to examine whether the behavioral differences observed across different moral appeals in our first study extend to implicit cognitive processes. Beyond reward processing, we further aim to investigate additional cognitive mechanisms underlying moral decision-making in the environmental domain. Finally, we seek to replicate our reward processing findings using a different behavioral paradigm. To this end, we will conduct another EEG study in the lab, employing a modified version of the Pro-Environmental Behavior Task (PEBT; Lange et al., 2018). The original PEBT is a decision-making task involving choices between using a car or a bicycle for a given trip, with each choice directly resulting in tangible consequences: choosing the car option triggers the illumination of USB-powered bulbs for the displayed duration of the trip, providing a visible representation of the environmental impact of participants' choices (Lange et al., 2018). This feature allows participants to directly experience the consequences of their decisions, making the trade-off between personal convenience and environmental harm more concrete and salient. Sustainable options (bicycle) come with a longer waiting period before the next choice, whereas unsustainable options (car) lead to shorter waiting times but increase CO2 emissions through the illumination of the bulbs. Given that sustainable options are usually more costly than unsustainable alternatives (Steg, 2016) , this paradigm captures a cost–benefit trade-off similar to that encountered in real-life decision-making. In our modified version, the car–bicycle pairing is replaced by four different option pairs drawn from everyday contexts, while preserving the core structure of tangible environmental consequences. We chose the PEBT paradigm for its immersive nature and its ability to link participants' decisions to real consequences, providing a robust test of how moral appeals influence both behavior and underlying neural processes. In the planned study, participants will first be exposed to one of three appeal conditions — forward-looking moral appeal, backward-looking moral appeal, or neutral appeal — before completing the PEBT. The task requires participants to choose between a sustainable but more costly option and an unsustainable but less costly option. Choosing the sustainable option entails a longer waiting time, whereas the unsustainable option is faster but comes at the expense of environmental harm. In essence, participants must decide between preventing harm to others by accepting a personal cost or maintaining personal benefits by causing harm to others. This structure closely mirrors moral decision-making, as it involves an interplay between maintaining self-interest and protecting environment. Moral decision-making involves substantial cognitive conflict, as individuals must reconcile competing motivations between self-interest and adherence to moral standards. Cognitive control — the ability to regulate attention, thought, and action in line with internal goals — is crucial in resolving this conflict, particularly when behavioral impulses oppose moral intentions (Greene et al., 2004). In the current study, we aim to explore how moral appeals shape the magnitude of cognitive conflict when participants face the decision-making screen. In the PEBT paradigm, the unsustainable option is associated with a shorter waiting time, whereas the sustainable option requires a longer waiting period before the next trial. These waiting times are fixed and known to participants, and in the absence of any moral consideration, the unsustainable option is expected to hold higher subjective value due to its lower personal cost. Moral appeals explicitly frame the sustainable position as morally correct and the unsustainable position as morally incorrect, targeting the perceived moral value of the options rather than their personal cost. An influential moral appeal is therefore expected to increase the subjective value of the sustainable option while decreasing that of the unsustainable one, narrowing the overall value gap between the two options. As the options become more similar in subjective value, the decision becomes more difficult and greater cognitive conflict is expected. Accordingly, based on our prior work, we predict that participants in the forward-looking condition will show enhanced P2 and N2 amplitudes, reflecting stronger cognitive conflict detection (Gui et al., 2016; Zhan et al., 2020), at the decision screen relative to the backward-looking and neutral conditions. However, an alternative account predicts the opposite pattern. Participants may already experience a degree of natural conflict between self-interest and moral responsibility as default even in the absence of an explicit moral appeal. This baseline conflict arises because most people across many countries report concern for the environment (Funk et al., 2020), meaning that choosing the unsustainable option is unlikely to be entirely cost-free even under neutral conditions. Rather than introducing new conflict, a moral appeal may then function to resolve this pre-existing conflict by clearly establishing the sustainable option as the morally normative choice. Consistent with this view, prior work has shown that communicating a clear moral norm reduces response times in decision-making contexts (Ellemers et al., 2008), suggesting that moral framing can simplify rather than complicate the choice. Under this account, the forward-looking moral appeal would reduce rather than amplify cognitive conflict. Accordingly, P2 and N2 amplitudes would be reduced in the forward-looking condition relative to the backward-looking and neutral conditions, reflecting a decrease in conflict detection rather than an increase. Given these competing theoretical accounts, H1 is treated as exploratory and bidirectional. We will examine P2 and N2 amplitudes across conditions and interpret the direction of observed effects in light of both frameworks. In addition to conflict detection at the decision screen, the current study will investigate conflict monitoring following an unsustainable choice. Personal moral violations are known to elicit immediate negative social-emotional responses (Greene et al., 2004), and cognitive dissonance theory similarly holds that conflict arises when a behavior is perceived as inconsistent with one's existing beliefs or values (Chen et al., 2010). The ERN is a response-locked negative deflection peaking around the time of response execution, reflecting neural sensitivity to conflict between an executed response and an intended or morally compatible alternative (Amodio et al., 2008). This signal is typically larger following errors than correct responses, as errors represent a greater divergence from intended behavior and thus elicit stronger conflict (Amodio et al., 2008). Applying this to the current PEBT paradigm, making an unsustainable choice after exposure to a forward-looking moral appeal (i.e., a response that conflicts with the moral standard the appeal has effectively established) can be construed as a personal moral violation. Conversely, making a sustainable choice reflects norm-consistent behavior, and should therefore elicit relatively little conflict. The difference in ERN amplitude between unsustainable and sustainable choices thus captures the degree of moral engagement: the more strongly a participant has internalized the moral appeal, the larger this difference should be. We therefore expect the ERN difference score (unsustainable minus sustainable) to be more negative in the forward-looking condition than in the backward-looking and neutral conditions. We also aim to investigate motivated attentional engagement with outcomes following sustainable choices. As demonstrated in our prior study (Ergün et al., 2026), moral appeals can enhance the reward value of pro-environmental outcomes, and this effect can be captured via feedback-locked ERP components. title_r: Impulsive Calculation
abstract_r: Expert mathematicians spend more than half of the time trying to make sense of a problem; whereas, approximately 60% of high school and college students “read, make a decision quickly, and pursue that direction come hell or high water” when encountering an unfamiliar problem (Schoenfeld, 1992, p. 24). Lampert (1990) notes that mathematics has come to be associated with “certainty; knowing it, with being able to get the answer, quickly” (Ball, 1988, Schoenfeld, 1985b; Stodolsky, 1985). Here, we seek to examine "impulsive calculation," the act of taking action with digits without considering the magnitudes or context before or after calculation. Students who impulsively calculate are more likely to render implausible answers on tasks, as a result of quickly taking action with digits/numbers without regard for magnitudes or problem context. We are envisioning this as the first of at least two studies. In this first study, we are conducting a conceptual replication of Braithwaite & Sprague (2021) with an existing dataset from our lab, as we believe the findings from this study are highly relevant to our impulsive calculation construct. We are using this conceptual replication with existing data to inform a larger study via Qualtrics investigating this impulsive calculation construct.

title_r: Age-related differences in reference frames revealed through executed and imagined reaching movements
abstract_r: Previous studies have shown that during manual reaching tasks, participants show the largest distractor-related interference from distractors that are within their movement path (e.g., Tipper et al., 1992). This distractor related interference shows up as slowed response times, both in movement time (MT) and reaction time (RT, e.g., Bloesch et al., 2013). When a young adult performs a reach toward a target, if another object is between the hand and the target, the reaching movement would be affected more than in scenarios where the other object is positioned beyond the target. This slowing is believed to be due to individuals using a ‘hand-centred reference frame’ for reaching, with attention being focused predominantly on their hand before, and during, the action (Bloesch et al., 2013; Elliott et al., 2020; Lyons et al., 2006). This pattern of distractor effects on the duration of actions has been reliably shown in younger and older adults. However, a different pattern of results has been shown in older adults when they perform reaching movements when their hands are not close to their body (e.g., their hand starts a reaching movement at the far end of a table, Bloesch et al., 2013). One hypothesis for this lack of hand-centred effects is that older adults show a shift over time to prioritize their body, instead of their hands, due to decline in sensory abilities. With older age, we shift our attention more proximally, than distally, so we can better monitor trunk control and better control balance at the expense of fine motor dexterity which may have been more highly prioritized when younger. This model is known as the distal-to-proximal model for sensory aging (Kuehn et al., 2018). Unfortunately, this pattern of behaviour can be problematic as older adults may then be prone to knocking over objects when they appear within their reach or miss dangerous objects that would cause injury to their hands and other limbs. This research regarding different frames of reference for elderly versus young adults has not been replicated, and outstanding questions remain regarding the mechanisms that underlie this behavioural difference across age groups. We therefore plan to investigate these differences in reference frame behaviour across ages, as well as introduce a novel manipulation where participants only imagine moving. Because it is still possible to measure imagined movement times during imagery, yet no actual movement takes place, such a condition will help to test whether older adults prioritize attention toward their action-specific effector (their hand) during manual actions when any motor-related decline for action is removed from the task. Therefore, in the current study, we test how individuals perform reaching movements in the presence of distractors, when they have to physically execute a reaching movement with their hand compared to when they have to simply imagine acting. The first half of the experiment will involve manual reaching movements (i.e., using your hand, reach toward targets and ignore any distractors) on a digitized visual environment. In this first part of the experiment, we hope to replicate previous patterns of data with respect to differences in the action-centred representation for reaching movements. Younger adults should reveal a hand-centred reference frame, while older adults are expected to reveal a body-centred reference frame. These differences will manifest under conditions when the hand is not close to the body, with older adults always being most affected in their response times by distractors that are closer to their body as opposed to closer to their hand. For the second half of the experiment, participants will perform motor imagery (i.e., imagine seeing and feeling their hand reach toward the targets, without actually moving). If older adults show a difference in reference frame, by removing the need to move (via imagery), the imagined reference frame for older adults is still expected to show patterns congruent with a hand-centred reference frame—more similar to the patterns of data shown by younger adults. Overall, this research can highlight how the planning and online control of movement (i.e., RT and MT respectively) are differentially impacted by age and potential changes in reference-frames thought to occur with aging. By comparing across actual and imagined movements, we hope to answer whether for older adults, movement execution suppresses internal models for ‘hand-centred’ movements that are otherwise evidenced in simulated (imagined) movements? This change in behaviour would suggest that movement amplifies body-centred representations in older adults and that they may default to body-centred planning for real actions but still possess intact hand-centred internal models that emerge when execution constraints are removed. title_r: Replication of Pennycook, Cannon, & Rand (2018) study 2 at Ashland University
abstract_r: This research project is a direct replication of study 2 in Pennycook, Cannon, and Rand's (2018) study on fake news. Examining the factors that influence the believability of fake news, their study found that a single prior exposure to a false news headline was enough to increase subsequent perceptions of accuracy. Even when fake headlines were labeled as "Disputed by 3rd Party Fact-Checkers", headlines did not align with a person's political ideology, and participants were not consciously aware of having previously seen the headlines, a single prior exposure still impacted the accuracy of truth discernment. To further research on fake news and social media, our current study aims to replicate Pennycook, Cannon, and Rand's findings. Like the original study, we will expose participants to fake and real headlines to test if prior exposures to headlines will increase the perceived accuracy of the headlines.

title_r: Association of Multidimensional Schizotypy with Momentary Suspiciousness and Self/Other Appraisals: Comparable Findings Across Samples and Schizotypy Measures
abstract_r: The present study employs experience sampling methodology (ESM) to examine the association of multidimensional schizotypy with a variety of daily life experiences, with an emphasis on momentary suspiciousness and self/other appraisals. Previous studies have often conceptualized schizotypy as having two dimensions: positive schizotypy (e.g., psychotic-like experiences) and negative schizotypy (e.g., diminished or blunted experiences), as measured by the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales (WSS; see Kwapil et al., 2008). Current models, however, include a third dimension of disorganized schizotypy that captures disruptions in organizing and expressing thought, behavior, communication, and emotion, as included in measures such as the Multidimensional Schizotypy Scale (MSS; Kwapil et al., 2018). Previous studies indicate that when comparing between two- and three-factor models, disorganized schizotypy better accounts for disorganized behaviors and negative affect than positive or negative schizotypy (Kwapil et al., 2020). In addition, previous studies have consistently shown that positive schizotypy is associated with psychotic-like and paranoid symptoms (Barrantes-Vidal, Gross, et al., 2013; Kwapil, Barrantes-Vidal, & Silvia, 2008; Kwapil et al., 2020). However, few studies have systematically examined paranoia and suspiciousness in daily life and their associations with multidimensional schizotypy. Therefore, The present study will employ experience sampling methodology (ESM) to examine 1) the association of multidimensional schizotypy with a variety of daily life experiences, with an emphasis on momentary ratings of paranoia and self/other appraisals; 2) the effects of adding disorganized schizotypy into the multidimensional schizotypy framework to explain daily experiences; and 3) the extent to which we replicate findings across two geographically and temporally different nonclinical samples of young adults using different measures of schizotypy. Sample 1 was assessed in North Carolina in 2008-09 and administered the WSS, which includes positive and negative schizotypy subscales. Sample 2 is currently being assessed in Illinois and involves the administration of the MSS, which includes positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy subscales. Following Kwapil et al. (2020), we will examine positive and negative schizotypy as simultaneous predictors of daily life experiences in both sample 1 and 2 (in order to directly compare these results across time and samples). We will also examine the simultaneous effects of all three schizotypy dimensions in sample 2 to consider the effect of including disorganized schizotypy. For comparison purposes, we will also include the results of the bivariate prediction of each schizotypy dimension in both samples. For both samples, we will examine the direct associations of multidimensional schizotypy with the following domains in daily life: positive and negative affect, emotion intensity, self-other appraisals, situation appraisals, paranoia and suspiciousness, cognition, activities, and social contact. Additionally, we will compute cross-level interactions to examine the extent to which positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy moderate the in-the-moment association between situational appraisals of events being pleasant and whether it involved others, the association between feeling close to others and preference to be alone, and the associations of momentary stress and social closeness with suspiciousness.

title_r: Ease of Retrieval: A Replication of Schwarz et al. (1991)
abstract_r: This study will be a replication of a study conducted by Schwarz et al. (1991). In the original study, participants were randomly assigned to provide 6 or 12 examples of assertive or unassertive behaviors from their personal experiences. Afterwards, they were asked to rate themselves on assertiveness, insecurity, and anxiety and the perceived difficulty of the task. It was found that it was easier to provide 6 examples over 12. It was also found that participants asked to provide 6 examples of assertive behaviors rated themselves as more assertive than those who provided 12. Those who were asked to provide 12 examples of unassertive behaviors rated themselves higher in assertiveness than those who were asked to provide 6. The goal of this study is to confirm these results.

title_r: Sense of agency and recognition memory: A replication of Hon and Yeo (2021)
abstract_r: Hon and Yeo (2021) demonstrated that word recognition (i.e., “hit” responses) is facilitated when words are presented within a moving box whose motion is triggered by a participant’s voluntary keypress. We will conduct a replication study to examine the reproducibility of the findings from their Experiment 2, which employed essentially the same methodology as Experiment 1 and yielded comparable results, but was implemented with improved experimental control. In their Experiment 2, a box moved upward or downward either in a direction corresponding to, or opposite from, the participant’s action (an upward or downward keypress), with either a minimal (100 ms) or longer (900 ms) temporal delay. After the box reached its destination, a word was presented inside the box. This “action” task was followed by a surprise recognition test for the words. Temporal and spatial congruency were manipulated to modulate the sense of agency over the visual feedback. Under conditions of spatial congruency and minimal delay, both the rated sense of agency and recognition performance (i.e., hit rate) were higher than in conditions with incongruent and/or delayed feedback, suggesting that an enhanced sense of agency may improve recognition memory. Our previous study (Tsuji & Imaizumi, 2022) failed to show any improvement in recognition memory for word stimuli (i.e., feedback of voluntary action) as a result of action–feedback congruence, although the rated sense of agency was successfully manipulated. However, our experimental task and design were not sufficiently comparable to Experiment 2 of Hon and Yeo (2021). Therefore, the present study aims to conduct a more direct replication of their findings using more closely matched experimental procedures.

title_r: Does Awareness of Photo Editing impact Social Judgements of Male Faces?
abstract_r: This is the preregistration page for an experiment investigating how awareness of photo manipulation (e.g. Facetune, Photoshop) interacts with degree of manipulation to impact social judgements (attractiveness and sociability) of male subjects specifically. Past work has shown that when viewing photos of women, individuals rate "beautified" photos as more attractive, but as having less sociable qualities (McCrackin et al., 2024). In addition, the addition of editing labels seem to overall reduce these negative social judgments. The present study will manipulate photo editing and accompanying labels on individuals' perception of male subjects. This experiment is a direct replication of our past study using female subjects as stimuli, which was pre-registered here: https://osf.io/v762k/overview, and published here: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-025-07659-5. The methods remain intact, other than the stimuli now being male faces. Images of happy face pictures of 60 male caucasian identities will be taken from the Radboud (Langner et al. 2010), FACES (Ebner, Riediger, & Lindenberger, 2010) and London (DeBruine & Jones, 2017) databases. These have been validated to ensure that the happy emotion they depict is recognizable with high accuracy. We edited the stimuli to all appear similar by cropping them to display the head and upper shoulders, adding black t-shirts for all individuals, and modifying the backgrounds to all be the same colour. The degree of editing (0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100%) was manipulated in the Meitu app by adding the "Smooth Classy" filter to remove acne and wrinkles. Other manipulations include brightening to eyes, lowering the hairline, shading the jawline, increase the angle of the jaw to appear wider, removing dark circles were used as well, and whitening the teeth.

title_r: LazyAlpha Phase 1: Targeted Out-Of-Sample(OOS) Replication of the 10-K Textual-Change Signal in US Small-Cap Equities (Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen 2020)
abstract_r: This project pre-registers and reports a programme of confirmatory tests examining whether year-over-year changes in SEC 10-K filing language predict cross-sectional stock returns in the US small-cap universe. Its intellectual anchor is Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen (2020, Journal of Finance 75(3), 1371–1415), which shows that firms making larger reporting changes subsequently underperform while stable-language firms outperform, with return effects accruing after the filing date rather than in the announcement window. This project does not claim to replicate the full CMN construct; instead, it tests a targeted MD&A-focused slice of that signal in a post-sample window (2016–2024) entirely outside the CMN study period. Each phase is pre-registered in advance, with exact hypotheses, test statistics, decision thresholds, and interpretation rules fixed before phase outcomes are examined. Results are reported in full regardless of outcome. Phase 1 tests whether MD&A cosine-distance ranks negatively predict next-month returns (H1) and whether the gross long-short quintile spread is positive (H2, evaluated only if H1 passes). Economic implementation under trading costs is reported separately as an exploratory objective. This project(LazyAlpha) is independent of the AlphaSniper Post-Earnings Announcement Drift programme and maintains separate governance and hypothesis accounting.

title_r: Pre-analysis plan for replicating stated-preference estimates of willingness to pay for reducing firearm violence in the United States.
abstract_r: This study preregisters a replication of Cook, Jeuland, and Ludwig’s (2025) analysis of a household’s willingness to pay for reductions in firearm violence in the United States. In the original study, 660 respondents were asked whether they would support a hypothetical statewide package of policies designed to reduce gun violence at a tax cost. The original design randomized respondents across different policy effectiveness levels and different bid amounts. Based on initial responses, respondents were asked a follow-up question that was either double or half the initial bid (doubled if ‘yes’, halved if ‘no’). Using these responses, they estimated the mean willingness to pay. They found that the preferred double-bounded estimate of the mean household willingness to pay was approximately $744 per year for a 20% reduction in gun violence and approximately $891 per year for a 40% reduction. The respondents in their sample also shared: - 48% said gun violence was not a serious problem in their community, - 43% said they were ‘likely’ or ‘somewhat likely’ to be victims of gun violence in the next five years, - 35% said gun violence was an ‘important’ or ‘somewhat important’ factor in where they lived, - 74% said gun-control laws should be made stricter, and - 43% said taxes should be lowered. In Cook et al.’s preferred specification, respondents who perceived gun violence as less serious or preferred lower taxes were less likely to vote yes, while respondents who perceived higher victimization risk or said gun violence affected where they lived were more likely to vote yes. Our replication will follow the core framework of the original study in order to assess whether the main willingness-to-pay estimates and response patterns replicate in a new, larger sample of respondents in 2026. We retain the original bid structure and focus on whether respondents’ support for the policy package has changed since the 2022 national survey, as gun violence has waned.

title_r: Money as Security or Freedom: A Cross-Cultural Replication of Framing Effects on Financial Risk-Taking
abstract_r: This study investigates how value-based framing of money influences financial risk-taking in a sample of University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) students. Building on behavioral decision research, we examine whether framing money in terms of security or freedom, relative to a neutral frame, affects individuals’ financial risk decisions. In a between-subjects experimental design, approximately 180 participants will be randomly assigned to listen to a podcast-style vignette emphasizing one of the three money orientations. Following the vignette, participants will respond to an open-ended reflection question intended to reinforce the framing manipulation before completing a hypothetical iteration of the Holt-Laury paired lottery-choice task, a behavioral measure that infers risk aversion from a sequence of binary choices between relatively safe and relatively risky lotteries with systematically varying probabilities. Participants will also complete validated measures of money attitudes, financial literacy, financial impulsivity, and self-reported financial risk preferences, as well as socio-demographic measures. This preregistration extends a previously registered study on the same research questions conducted at Radboud University (Givvin, Vahed, & Sanfey, 2026; https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/G5E63). The UCLA sample uses identical materials, measures, and procedures, with one procedural change: the currency has been adjusted to match the local context (USD in place of EUR). In addition to replicating the original hypotheses and research questions in a new (American) sample, the present preregistration introduces a new exploratory research question (RQ3) comparing UCLA (American) and Radboud University (Dutch) participants on money attitudes, baseline risk preferences, and the effects of value-based framing on behavioral financial risk-taking. Data will be analyzed using ANOVA and regression models to estimate the main effects of framing conditions and potential interactions with individual-difference and cultural-background variables.

title_r: Predicting wellbeing in a population cohort via the genome, metabolome, and exposome
abstract_r: Self-reported wellbeing is a complex phenomenon to study due to both its multifaceted definition(s) and links with numerous possible antecedents and consequences. Wellbeing is not just the absence of psychopathology but also the presence of positive (psychological) elements such as flourishing, fulfillment, and productivity (Diener, 1984; Keyes, 2002). Likewise, researchers have defined at least two major kinds of wellbeing: eudaimonic and hedonic (Ryan & Deci, 2001). The latter refers to one’s subjective evaluation of their overall life quality and is typically considered to have three main components: life satisfaction, positive affect, (lack of) negative affect (Diener et al., 2018). There is less consensus on the definition or assessment of eudaimonic or ‘psychological’ wellbeing, but it generally refers to one’s positive functioning resultant from pursuing goals and/or self-actualization (Ryff, 1989; Ryff & Singer, 1998). Unlike hedonic wellbeing, definitions of eudaimonic wellbeing typically do not include an affective component. Adding to conceptual uncertainty about wellbeing’s definition, concerted attempts to empirically distinguish between these constructs have largely been unsuccessful (Disabato et al., 2016). Further complicating the study of wellbeing is the construct's multifactorial nature. Given the possible societal benefits of a populace that is healthy and well, researchers across many disciplines have studied the construct to understand its nomological net – its many possible causes and consequences (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955). Wellbeing has been related to numerous risk and protective factors across multiple modalities: internal elements such as genetic and metabolomic markers; psychosocial factors like personality traits and mental health problems, but also occupation, education, diet, and life events; and broader environmental factors, such as socio-economic status, neighborhood safety, and availability of green and blue space (Diener et al., 2018). However, most studies attempting to explain wellbeing have focused on one or a few modalities, making comprehensive interpretations of the construct’s nomological net incomplete. Modern machine learning (ML) approaches can overcome this limitation, and several recent efforts (e.g., Chilver et al., 2023; Oparina et al., 2025; Pelt et al., 2024) have indeed leveraged ML techniques to predict wellbeing using a wider array of features. That said, these studies have in varying parts been limited by features being constrained to just one modality (e.g., socio-demographic variables), small samples, and/or narrow assessment of the outcome. There have also been inconsistencies in the amount of variance explained, perhaps in part due to the variability in study design. For example, Oparina et al. (2025) compared three large datasets (Ns = 26,890 up to > 350,000) from the United States, United Kingdom, and Germany, and found that ML models consistently outperformed standard Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression models both when using a standard ‘restricted’ predictor set (k = 17) of variables common to all datasets as well as larger ‘extended’ sets (ks = 67 to 450). Where the restricted sets mostly focused on socio-demographic factors (e.g., education, sex, BMI), extended sets additionally assessed variables such as mental and physical health conditions, personality traits, and cognitive skills. R2s for the extended variable sets ranged from .10 to .14 and .20 to .32, respectively. Pelt et al. (2024) used a smaller sample (e.g., Ns from 1,404 to 5,874) and focused primarily on young adults with longitudinal data from ten different timepoints in the Netherlands (the National Twin Registry). Their primary interest was in comparing predictive accuracy for wellbeing across different modalities. Specifically, they distinguished between the genome (i.e., k = 60 polygenic scores [PGSs] for various traits), specific exposome (i.e., k = 2,615 psychosocial factors such as personality and mental health traits), and general exposome (i.e., k = 732 physical environmental exposures such as air pollution, urbanicity, and housing stock value). Across all modalities, they achieved a total R2 of approximately .70, mostly driven by the specific exposome, with many of the most important features coming from the psychological domain (e.g., personality, loneliness, optimism). Pelt et al. (2024) suggested that such large disparities in explained variance between their study and Oparina et al. (2025) likely arose primarily due to operationalization of the outcome: where the latter used a single life satisfaction item in all three datasets, the former combined three different life satisfaction and happiness scales taken from three separate timepoints and modeled with structural equation modeling (SEM), thereby accounting for measurement error . Pelt et al. also suggested the difference may be due to their inclusion of mental health variables as predictors, whereas Oparina et al. excluded any variable related to “subjective wellbeing (e.g., domain satisfaction, happiness, subjective health) and mental health” (p. 2); however, sensitivity analyses showed that removing these predictors did not significantly change Pelt et al.’s findings. Here, we aim to replicate these studies in a large biobank study (i.e., the Estonian Biobank; EstBB) while extending the approach in several ways. First, we will include a more comprehensive set of predictors by including metabolomic (‘internal’ exposome, in Pelt et al.) data in addition to a wider array of genomic and exposome variables than present in either study. Second, we will leverage a much larger sample with more comprehensive coverage of the lifespan. Finally, we will use a more comprehensive wellbeing assessment than previous work, including indicators of both general and domain-specific wellbeing. Findings from this study will both 1) provide applied researchers with a clearer idea of the current maximum possible prediction for broadly defined wellbeing and 2) clarify whether the most predictive features of wellbeing are generalizable across datasets. Altogether, identification of generalizable or especially important features might provide policymakers with clearer intervention targets for improving population-level wellbeing and/or identifying individuals at risk for languishing.

title_r: Neural Basis of the Motivated Learning Task
abstract_r: Motivation (e.g. in the form of reward) plays an important role for learning. In their seminal study, Adcock et al. (2006) investigated the neural basis of how reward expectation modulates memory. Participants initially memorised a set of pictures in the MRI, each preceded by a high or low reward. The corresponding reward was paid out for recognising those pictures among a set of new pictures 24 h later. Adcock et al. (2006) were able to show an influence of motivation on memory even before the stimulus to be memorised is presented, with corresponding activations in the medial temporal lope and dopaminergic reward areas. We aim to replicate the highly-cited paradigm by Adcock et al. (2006). Additionally, we want to shed light on retrieval processes in the brain by testing participants’ memory inside the MRI during recognition memory testing.

title_r: Temporal binding study ("Colors and Time") - sense of agency vs. attention effect
abstract_r: We investigate whether the temporal binding effect reported by Barlas & Obhi (2013; Freedom, choice, and the sense of agency. Frontiers in human neuroscience, 7, 514.) can be explained by attentional processes rather than sense of agency. In their original study, stronger temporal binding occurred when participants could choose among multiple actions, and this effect was interpreted as evidence for an enhanced sense of agency. As recent evidence suggests that temporal binding rests strongly on attention and expectation effects, it is problematic that temporal binding is still often used as an implicit measure for the sense of agency. Here, we will attempt to study the effect of attention that might explain the findings of Barlas & Obhi (2013). Their choice manipulation simultaneously alters attentional demands which may independently influence temporal perception. There are two parts. First, we perform a direct replication of the three core conditions from Barlas and Obhi (2013), in which participants press either one, three, or seven possible buttons to generate a tone and subsequently judge the perceived times of both the action and the tone using a Libet clock task. Second, we introduce a novel set of “attention-only” conditions, in which participants always press the same button, but they are only allowed to do so once the button is red (The colors will vary between one, three and seven). This allows us to dissociate the attentional consequences of having multiple response alternatives from the sense-of-agency component that arises when participants choose between different actions. Temporal binding will be quantified as the difference between actual and perceived event times (in milliseconds), separated into action binding and outcome binding. We expect that the attentional manipulation will reproduce binding patterns similar to those observed in the original choice conditions.

title_r: Gamified Trading, Overtrading, and Self-Selection
abstract_r: We propose a pre-registered replication and extension of Chapkovski et al. (2024), who document that hedonic gamification on retail trading platforms (e.g., confetti, badges) modestly increases trading volume while most of the observed difference is attributable to investor self selection. We (i) replicate their design, (ii) extend it to a cross-country setting (China vs. U.S./U.K.), and (iii) add a real-monetary-incentive treatment in which participants risk their own funds. The study will disentangle causal gamification effects from self-selection across cultures and incentive intensities, with policy implications for platform design and regulation.

title_r: Can learned value modulate the inhibition of return effect?
abstract_r: In a series of experiments, Garre-Frutos and Lupiáñez (2025) tested the hypothesis that the association between a feature (a specific color) and reward can reduce or even abolish inhibition of return (IOR) in a letter discrimination task embedded in a spatial cueing paradigm with non-informative peripheral cues. Specifically, their main hypothesis was that the increased attentional capture elicited by color–reward associations should modulate IOR when targets (rather than cues) appear in a high-value color. This prediction aligns with theories that conceptualize IOR as a detection cost within the cue–target integration framework (2006, Lupiáñez), rather than as the inhibition of returning attention to a previously attended location (Klein, 2002). In summary, their findings provided partial support for this prediction, but the effect appeared small, potentially short-lived, and restricted to specific conditions. Across two experiments, Garre-Frutos and Lupiáñez (2025) observed that when a target appeared in a color previously associated with high reward, IOR was modulated—but only during a brief unrewarded stage in which rewards were completely omitted from the task, and this effect reached statistical significance only in Experiment 1. A combined analysis of Experiments 1 and 2, along with a meta-analysis that included two other conceptually similar studies, suggested that IOR can indeed be modulated by learned value. However, all individual experiments may have been underpowered to detect such an effect reliably. The present study aims to provide a rigorous test of whether learned value—operationalized as an experimentally induced association between color and reward—can modulate IOR. We do so by conducting a conceptual replication of Experiment 1 of Garre-Frutos et al. (2025) with two critical improvements: (1) sufficient statistical power to detect even a small modulation of IOR informed by the meta-analytical effect size reported by Garre-Frutos and Lupiáñez (2025), and (2) an extended unrewarded stage to examine whether such modulation can be extinguished once the reward-predictive feature no longer signals reward. In other words, the present study seeks to provide strong statistical evidence on whether IOR can be modulated by learned value and to characterize the temporal dynamics of this effect.

title_r: Obedience to Authority in AI Agents: Replicating the Milgram Paradigm in a Digital Environment
abstract_r: This experiment examines whether AI agents exhibit obedience to authority when instructed to perform harmful actions in a simulated environment. It replicates the classic Milgram obedience paradigm (Milgram, 1963) in a digital setting, where AI agents serve as the "Teacher" and are instructed by an authority figure to administer escalating electric shocks to a simulated "Learner." Three AI models (OpenAI ChatGPT 5.4, Google Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking, and OpenAI ChatGPT Agent Mode) are tested across 60 independent runs to assess obedience rates and moral self-assessment.

title_r: Investigating the impact of semantic category and task instructions on conceptual cueing
abstract_r: Conceptual cueing effect refers to behavioural findings showing that encountering certain concepts selectively biases attention toward spatial locations that are congruent with the words’ semantic meanings (Chatterjee, 2001). For instance, words like ‘HEAVEN’ or ‘JOY’ direct gaze upward, whereas ‘BASEMENT’ and ‘BITTERNESS’ orient attention downward. This effect is potentially useful in investigating how abstract mental concepts are associated with concrete perceptual features, and how people utilise these mental concepts to guide visual attention. Existing literature disputed over whether conceptual cueing effect is elicited automatically or depends on explicit processing of cues’ semantic meanings. Earlier investigations have generally assumed that conceptual cueing occurs automatically without needing to instruct participants to explicitly process the semantic-space mapping (Meier & Robinson, 2004). Meanwhile, later reports only observed conceptual cueing with explicit task instructions(Shaki & Fischer, 2023). A more recent meta-analysis noted that raising cue valences’ task relevance would increase effect size of conceptual cueing, but is not necessary to observe this effect (Pohl & Miklashevsky, 2025). These discrepant findings hint toward a lack of understanding of cognitive mechanisms and contributing factors in which conceptual cueing effect originates from. In a previous replication attempt, we employed a paradigm used in a previous study using emotional words as cues (Gozli et al., 2013). As shown in Figure 1a, this paradigm first displays a cue word at the screen centre, then asks participants to identify the geometric shape of a target that appears either above or below the cue. Participants are asked to only respond to emotional words (with furniture words as catch words), but they do not need to explicitly consider the valence of the cues. Using this task, we did not observe conclusive evidence for the conceptual cueing effect. Previous studies have shown that some semantic categories only produce conceptual cueing effect when task instructions ask participants to explicitly process the semantics of the cue words (e.g. when participants only react to words with particular meanings; de la Vega et al., 2012; Shaki & Fischer, 2023). For other categories however, for instance words that refer to direction (e.g. ‘UP’ and ‘DOWN’) conceptual cueing occurs both in implicit and explicit instructions (Gibson & Sztybel, 2014). So we hypothesized that the negative finding in our replication of Gozli et al, 2013, could be due to the cue words not being explicitly processed. In fact, it is not known if emotional words need to be explicitly processed in terms of their valence to produce conceptual cueing. Hence with the current experiment, we seek to answer this question and compare the results between emotional cues and words referring to spatial directions, that more consistently produce strong conceptual cueing (Shaki & Fischer, 2023). Through this investigation, we aim to specify the factors that are pre-requisites of conceptual cueing effect. To this end, we will adapt the original paradigm to assess whether semantic categories of cues and explicit evaluation of cue valence impact on participants’ reaction time and accuracy (Gozli et al., 2013). In a three-way within-subject factorial design, we will compare the effects of emotion words (e.g. ‘JOY’ and ‘SAD’) against direction words (e.g. ‘UP’ and ‘DOWN’) on participants’ task performance in congruent and incongruent conditions. Furthermore, we will manipulate participants’ levels of semantic processing of cues with different task instructions: in implicit semantic processing condition, participants will be asked to respond when the cue word describes a specified category (emotion or direction), and to withhold response when the word describes furniture (i.e. catch trials). In explicit semantic processing condition, participants will be asked to respond only if the cue belongs to a specified category and in addition has a specific meaning (e.g. positive emotion or upward direction). Examples of different task instructions are depicted in Figure 1c. Furthermore, participants will complete two self-report inventories, Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS) and Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21) at the end of experiment. We will use these scores to assess participants’ sensitivity to positive and negative emotions and how they influence participants’ reaction toward emotion cue words (Langvik & Borgen Austad, 2019; Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995). Figure 1 (uploaded as S01E02Paradigm.png). schematic examples of a) trial procedure, b) on-screen stimuli display in current experiment, and c) elements of two experiment blocks. Each block starts with 6 practice trials, followed by 60 experiment trials, resulting in a total of 528 trials and 24 total repetitions for each cue word.

title_r: Beyond WEIRD Study 2: Pre-registered Confirmatory Replication of a Four-Factor Cultural Values Structure in a U.S. Sample
abstract_r: Pre-registered confirmatory replication study (Study 2) of the Beyond WEIRD VSM 2013 diagnostic. Study 1 (Iverson, 2026; N = 185 U.S. Prolific) found that VSM 2013 does not measure six separable dimensions in contemporary U.S. data and that an exploratory four-factor structure (subjective wellbeing, achievement/status, personal-life balance, workplace warmth) fit substantially better. Study 2 will collect a fresh independent U.S. Prolific sample (target n = 200) using identical instruments and inclusion criteria, and will (a) confirmatorily test the four-factor structure derived from Study 1 and (b) re-test the published Hofstede 6-factor model. Primary hypotheses: (H1) the Study-1 four-factor CFA model will replicate with acceptable fit; (H2) the Hofstede 6-factor CFA will again show poor fit and inadmissible Heywood-case factor correlations. PI: Dr. Nathan Iverson, California Baptist University. Co-PIs: Chisom Egbulem Lever, Wera Agasaro. Funded internally by the CBU Center for the Study of Human Behavior.
