title_r: Effort Matters Part 4: Replication of Janiszewski and Uy (2008) – Precision of the Anchor Influences the Amount of Adjustment
abstract_r: This project is a direct replication and extension of Janiszewski and Uy (2008), which demonstrated that the precision of a numerical anchor influences the magnitude of adjustment in judgment and estimation tasks. Specifically, precise numerical anchors (e.g., 4,988) were found to produce smaller adjustments than rounded anchors (e.g., 5,000), suggesting that anchor precision shapes the granularity of mental representations during estimation. The present study aims to replicate this anchor precision effect while examining whether participant effort influences the strength and reliability of the observed effect. Although concerns regarding the replication crisis in psychology have primarily focused on methodological and statistical explanations such as low power, publication bias, and analytic flexibility, comparatively little attention has been paid to the validity of participant performance. This project investigates whether variability in participant effort may contribute to attenuated effect sizes and inconsistent replication outcomes. Approximately 43 undergraduate participants will complete a series of numerical estimation scenarios under varying anchor precision conditions (rounded, precise-under, and precise-over) and motivational framing conditions (intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and control). Following the estimation task, participants will complete a battery of established performance validity measures, including the Dot Counting Test, Reliable Digit Span, and Trial 1 of the Test of Memory Malingering (TOMM), in order to assess participant effort and data validity. The primary objective of the study is to determine whether the original anchor precision effect replicates and whether the effect is moderated by participant effort and motivational context. It is expected that precise anchors will produce smaller adjustments than rounded anchors, consistent with the original findings. It is also expected that this effect will be stronger and more reliable among participants demonstrating valid performance and under conditions designed to promote higher effort. More broadly, this project aims to contribute to ongoing discussions regarding reproducibility in psychological science by examining participant effort as a measurable and theoretically meaningful determinant of observed experimental effects.

title_r: Unfinished Tasks and Rumination: A Replication Study on the Mediating Role of Competence Need Satisfaction and the Moderating Effects of Proactive Work Behavior and Leisure Crafting
abstract_r: Work-related rumination (WRR) defines a state of perseverative cognitive activation in which work continues to occupy the employee's mind during off-job hours (Querstret & Cropley, 2012). Research distinguishes between three components: problem pondering, detachment, and affective rumination. Among these, only affective rumination has a negative valence, while problem pondering is positive and detachment is neutral. A growing body of literature indicates that unfinished tasks link most strongly to affective rumination (Wendsche et al., 2026), with recent research suggesting that competence need satisfaction mediates the relationship and proactive work behavior moderates it (Weigelt et al., 2019). To extend prior work, this study will examine leisure crafting, contributing to the understanding of potential moderators under which the relationship between unfinished tasks and affective rumination holds, thereby providing opportunities for intervention research.

title_r: On the Influence of Attention-Directing Cues on the Simon Effect: A Replication of Hommel´s (1993) Experiment 6
abstract_r: Simon (1969) showed that people process the location of a stimulus even when it is actually irrelevant for solving the task. For example, if a blue stimulus is shown on the right side and requires a right response (i.e. congruent trial), reaction times are shorter and less error-prone than for incongruent trials. This difference between compatible and incompatible trials became known as the Simon effect. The effect is considered robust and has been replicated in many different experimental designs. However, it remains unclear what exactly causes the processing of the irrelevant information. In particular, two theoretical explanatory approaches have emerged in research: the attentional-shift hypothesis and the referential-coding hypothesis. The attentional- shift hypothesis posits that the spatial code in a Simon task arises from a shift in attention (Stoffer, 1991). According to this hypothesis, the appearance of a stimulus automatically triggers a shift in attention towards its position, whereby the stimulus is encoded as “left” or “right” depending on the direction of this shift. The referential coding hypothesis, on the other hand, explains the effect through relational coding processes. According to this approach, the spatial position of a stimulus is encoded relative to a frame of reference, such as an object (Hommel, 1993). Stoffer (1991) is among the proponents of the attentional-shift hypothesis and assumes different attentional subprocesses underlying the Simon effect. He tested this prediction by differentiating between two different precues, namely a large box precue or two small precues. In line with his assumption, he found a reliable Simon effect only for the small box display, but not for the large box display and saw this as confirmation of the attentional-shift hypothesis. According to Stoffer, a larger rectangle in which a target was to appear later should not lead to an attentional shift, whereas two adjacent squares, in one of which a target subsequently appears, should cause a shift in attention. From the perspectives of the referential coding hypothesis, the differentiation between the various types of attention would be irrelevant, as it does not argue on the basis of the aspect of attention. Hommel (1993) questioned the explanation provided by Stoffer (1991), conducted six experiments and varied them slightly to test specific assumptions. The first three experiments of Hommel (1993) used the stimulus display with the large box (as done in Stoffer, 1991), but displayed it centrally. Experiment 4 to 6 tested further assumed attentional influences by including spatial cues before target presentation. The spatial cues could be valid, neutral and invalid. If attention mechanisms influence the Simon effect, then the validity of the cue should modulate the Simon effects. However, this was not found in any experiment. The present study aims at replicating Experiment 6 from Hommel (1993). The original study used only 14 participants for a complex design involving several factors, which is the reason for the current direct replication. This experiment focused specifically on “zooming-out” attention and manipulating the attention with preceding cues in the form of an asterisk. In some cases, the cue was on the same side as the target (valid cue). In some cases, it was on the opposite side (invalid cue). The logic behind the attentional-shift theory would be that a Simon effect occurs only when attention shifts, i.e., only in invalid trials or when the cue is centrally located. Conversely, an attentional shift occurs with invalid cues, which should result in a Simon effect. According to the referential coding theory, the Simon effect is not dependent on attention, and therefore not dependent on guidance by the cue; a Simon effect should be found here in all cue conditions. This is also what Hommel (1991) found as a result. We will adhere strictly to the design and procedure of Experiment 6, merely increasing the number of participants and testing Hommel´s (1993) findings. Hommel, B. (1993). title_r: An investigation of preschoolers’ phonological training in its context
abstract_r: Does the intervention FonoMix (Löwenbrand et al., 2011) affect preschoolers' phonological awareness (PA) by its own account, or is it the result of differences in implementation of the intervention or secondary factors (spontaneous PA activities) arising from the introduction of the intervention in a preschool? When preliterate children are trained in PA, effects are observed on literacy up to grade four (Byrne and Fielding-Barnsley, 1991; Lundberg, 1994). However, previous studies do not investigate how the intervention generates its effect. We will discuss how the context, i.e., implementation, secondary effects, and/or the context such as the early childhood center, the teachers in the room, and the group of children, modulate or mediate the effect of an intervention andthus explain both between-group and within-group variances in an intervention effect. Teachers are observered during FonoMix sessions focusing on implementation of the intervention. Children are observed during two days focusing on spontaneous PA-activities. The study have undergone ethical vetting. Caregivers give informed consentand children give continuous consent during observations. We expect to replicate positive effects of PA-interventions on literacy (e.g., Fälth et al., 2020) as measured with LegiLexi. In addition find effects of the contextand the secondary factors according to our observational protocols indicating frequencies of spontaneous PA-activities. We extend previous theoretical studies (Matta et al., 2023), and study observations of activities and interplay between teachers and children during a PA-intervention to reveal the underlying mechanisms of theinterventions. Results could change how we develop new generations of interventions not specific to PA.

title_r: Action error and observation-based contagions in pointing movements: Testing kinematic prediction errors (Study 2)
abstract_r: The following study registration is a second study to follow up on a pattern of null results from Study 1 (pre-registration: https://osf.io/ptsbv). The rationale and predictions for this new study are similar to Study 1, and as such, the background information is repeated here. There are methodological differences in this new study and the rationale for these differences is detailed in the final paragraphs of the introduction. Watching the actions of others can elicit unintentional performance biases, with the direction depending on the instructions accompanying the demonstration (Ikegami et al., 2018). Watching presumed “correct”, yet different actions (such as someone putting to a different target), can cause performance biases in the same direction as the watched action (Gray & Beilock, 2011; Ikegami et al., 2018; Kilner et al., 2003; Peters et al., in review). These imitative contagions can occur both from watching another person’s body kinematics (e.g., Takeuchi et al., 2018) and also just by seeing the outcomes of their action, such as the flight of a ball or its landing position (e.g., Gray & Beilock, 2011). Unintentional imitation is thought to occur as a result of shared representations for action and observation of action (e.g., Prinz, 1997; Shin et al. 2010). The representation generated from watching a different action is thought to interfere with the representation used for action planning on subsequent execution (Brass & Heyes, 2005; Heyes, 2010, 2011). A different type of action observation contagion has been identified in response to seeing presumed errors. In the case when an actor is thought to be aiming to one target, but misses, subsequent performance of the observer has been shown to be biased away from the observed error (Ikegami et al., 2018; Ronchi et al., 2018). This “compensatory contagion” (Ikegami et al., 2018) is thought to be prediction error dependent. The difference between the expected and actual performance of the actor creates a prediction error, which is thought to drive updates to the observer’s action planning processes for their own actions (Ikegami et al., 2019; Ikegami & Ganesh, 2017). However, prediction and task errors are always confounded and therefore it is possible that the “prediction” itself is not a necessary component of the bias. Just seeing an errorful action (i.e., target miss) may be sufficient to drive compensations in execution following the observed error. In the absence of a prediction error, watching a “miss” might induce a more cognitive strategy to avoid making the same mistake. To replicate and extend these effects, we tested experienced golfers watching both “on-target” and errorful putts of an actor (pre-registration available at https://osf.io/p629c). Across four blocked conditions, we covaried the location of the actor’s putts on a nine-square target grid (centre, corner) and the instructions about the actor’s intended aiming location to manipulate the presence of an error. We expected to replicate imitative effects for the observer’s putting to a centre target after observing presumed target "hits" to the corners. We expected to find compensatory effects after observing presumed "misses" toward the corners. In our new condition, where the observer saw presumed “misses” to the centre target, we also expected compensatory biases in subsequent putting to the centre target, even though there was now no discrepancy between the representations generated through observation and action. In terms of our actual results, predicted imitative biases were present after watching the actor “correctly” putt to the corner, but not when those same corner putts were perceived as errors. Watching “misses” to both corner and centre squares did not lead to imitative biases as predicted, but contrary to our predictions, neither did it lead to compensatory biases (Peters et al., in review). There are several explanations as to why we did not show compensatory biases from error observation in our previous experiment. One explanation might be due to task differences between our task (golf putting) and the aiming and throwing tasks where compensatory biases have previously been shown (Ikegami et al., 2018; Ronchi et al., 2011). There is evidence that expert observers are attuned to the kinematic features of the actions of others and that action outcomes can be anticipated from body kinematics (for reviews see Torricelli et al., 2023; Müller & Abernethy, 2012). In past work (Ikegami et al., 2018; Ronchi et al., 2011), the actor’s kinematics may have divulged more information about the upcoming target error, making kinematic prediction errors (i.e., differences between the expected and observed kinematics) more salient and ultimately driving compensation biases. This saliency may be due to either the increased forces (and hence arm swing) needed to throw a baseball and/or the direct aiming (without an implement) to targets, both different to golf putting. In golf putting, the adjustments to the swing of the club between targets of different distances is subtle therefore, kinematic prediction errors would be suppressed. There is evidence that these kinematic prediction errors are important in driving compensatory biases from error observation (Ikegami et al., 2014; Saito et al., 2024). When kinematic prediction errors were suppressed by removing the goal belief about the actor’s aiming location (negating a prediction), interference from observation on action was reduced (Ikegami et al., 2014). However, in this manipulation, task error (i.e., success or failure) was also suppressed along with kinematic errors and therefore the role of kinematic prediction errors is still somewhat unclear. There is evidence that movement outcomes, either ball flight or ball landing position, without observation of action kinematics, are sufficient to drive imitative biases (Gray & Beilock, 2011). Biases from observed outcomes are thought to be driven by strong relationships (e.g., Catmur & Heyes, 2019; Heyes, 2011) or perhaps a shared common code (e.g., Prinz, 1997; Shin et al., 2010) for actions and their effects. Conversely, Ikegami and Ganesh (2014; 2017) suggest that seeing the actor’s kinematics is a necessary source of information to drive prediction errors and biases as a result of error observation. This suggestion was based on a study where kinematic prediction errors and outcome prediction errors were isolated and shown independently when two groups of skilled participants watched the same videos of a novice throwing to a dart board (Ikegami & Ganesh, 2014). The videos were spatially occluded to show the movement kinematics but not the dart flight or outcome, and participants predicted where the dart would land. To suppress outcome prediction errors and show only kinematic prediction errors, participants were told that the actor was aiming to a centre target and were shown the body kinematics associated with target “misses”. After predicting the throw’s outcome, no outcome feedback was provided. To suppress and isolate kinematic prediction errors, a second group was told that the actor was aiming to various targets and only correct attempts were shown, such that there would be no prediction about what the actor’s kinematics should look like. After making the prediction about the throw’s landing position, participants received outcome feedback about where the dart landed to elicit an outcome prediction error. Only kinematic prediction errors impacted the observer’s subsequent performance (and self-error estimations). However, limiting the interpretation of these results, task-related errors (i.e., “hit” or “miss”) were not controlled across the two groups. Kinematic prediction errors were always associated with “misses” while outcome prediction errors were always associated with “hits”. To address concerns from previous studies, with respect to the task and the salience of the kinematic prediction errors, we conducted a replication (Study 1; https://osf.io/ptsbv) of the hand-to-target aiming study by Ikegami et al (2018, Experiment 2). In this Ikegami et al study, there were imitative and compensatory biases after watching others. Our replication therefore, also involved target-directed reaching on a touchscreen computer. We expected that kinematic prediction errors would be more salient than those observed in golf putting, due to the direct relationship between hand movements and target success. Aiming movements were also expected to be less variable than putting, affording more power to see the small, expected effects, if present. Different to Ikegami et al (2018), we also manipulated the type of information shown in the videos to show the whole movement (i.e., kinematics and outcomes, replicating Ikegami et al.), or only target outcomes. Through this manipulation we were able to test if kinematic prediction errors were necessary to drive any potential compensatory biases independently from trials which are seen as outcome ‘hits’ (correct) or ‘misses’ (errors). Contrary to predictions, there was no evidence of imitative biases after watching hits, nor was there evidence of compensation after watching errors, regardless of whether participants watched the actor’s kinematics or outcomes (all ps > .76). Despite replicating the task and instructions given by Ikegami and colleagues in Study 1, one potential reason as to why we did not show the same effects was that our targets were displayed on a smaller screen, which may have masked kinematic prediction errors in the videos and subsequently observation-induced biases. Therefore in this new Study 2, we will again replicate the design and methods of Ikegami et al (2018), but with greater spacing between the targets, hence resulting in more salient kinematic differences between target hits and misses. title_r: Algorithm Reliance: A Cross-Country Replication with Neuro Evidence
abstract_r: We propose a pre-registered replication and extension of Snyder et al. (2025) to investigate the behavioral and cognitive drivers of algorithm reliance. Beyond the original queueing system framework, this study introduces a cross-country dimension by comparing an advanced economy (the original U.S. sample) with an emerging market (China). This comparison allows us to test whether the significant global disparities in AI trust and acceptance moderate the "learning by using" process and the eventual adoption of algorithmic advice. Furthermore, we extend the original behavioral findings with neurophysiological evidence using eye-tracking technology. By identifying physiological indicators of the shift from deliberate, "slow" consultation to "fast" defaulting, we aim to map how workers manage limited cognitive resources, as conceptualized by Boyacı et al. (2024), under varying levels of system load. Our results seek to provide a more nuanced, culturally sensitive, and cognitively grounded understanding of human-algorithm collaboration in modern service environments.

title_r: Replication of Leung, Paolacci, and Puntoni (2018, Study 5): Consumption Motives and Resistance to Product Automation, with a German University Student Sample
abstract_r: This project is a replication of Study 5 ("Biking Motives") from Leung, Paolacci, and Puntoni (2018), Man Versus Machine: Resisting Automation in Identity-Based Consumer Behavior, published in the Journal of Marketing Research, 55(6), 818–831. The original Study 5 tested whether participants whose consumption motive frames a product as identity-relevant are less likely to opt into an automated feature for that product than participants whose motive frames the product as utilitarian. In the original study (N = 200, U.S. residents recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk), participants in the identity-motive condition (a bike for weekend cycling excursions that allow them to "enjoy the cycling activities and enhance your skills as a cyclist") chose a free battery-assisted pedaling feature significantly less often than participants in the non-identity-motive condition (a bike for commuting to work, "to facilitate your commute"; 57% vs. 80%, χ²(1) = 12.94, p < .001). We replicate the original two-cell between-subjects design with a target sample of approximately 100 German university students recruited via convenience sampling. Our primary statistical test is a Pearson chi-square test of independence examining whether choice differs by experimental condition (df = 1, two-tailed, α = .05). In line with the original study, we do not apply Yates’ continuity correction. As a robustness check, we additionally estimate a logistic regression model predicting choice from experimental condition. The expected outcome is a directional replication of the original effect, with potential attenuation due to (a) the deliberately smaller sample size (N = 100 vs. the original N = 200 (b) the cultural shift from U.S. MTurkers to German university students (Germany has a strong utilitarian biking culture and high e-bike adoption rates), and (c) the convenience-sampling approach. Full materials, data, and analysis code will be made publicly available upon project completion.

title_r: Comparing healthy foods vs. "healthy" and unhealthy UPFs
abstract_r: Previous research in our laboratory (e.g., Pineño, Albano, & Vadillo, 2026; Pineño & DeStefano, 2026) has shown that: (1) healthy foods are implicitly preferred based on tastiness, (2) junk foods are implicitly preferred based on desirability, and (3) junk foods are explicitly preferred based on tastiness when compared to unprocessed foods, but not when compared to cooked foods (e.g., Mediterranean and Asian dishes). The present series of studies seeks to clarify the role of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) in these effects by disentangling the concepts of *junk food* and *ultra-processed food*. In our previous research, the foods classified as junk foods were also UPFs, which led us to use the terms *junk food* and *UPF* interchangeably. However, not all UPFs are necessarily junk foods. Although many UPFs are high in fat, sugar, and salt (HFSS), others are designed to provide nutritional benefits through the addition of protein, fiber, vitamins, minerals, or other nutrients. Furthermore, UPFs often have practical advantages such as extended shelf life, convenience, affordability, and accessibility, particularly in areas with limited access to fresh foods. The present research examines whether the implicit and explicit preferences observed in our previous studies are driven by ultra-processing itself or by the rewarding characteristics typically associated with HFSS foods. To address this question, we compare unprocessed foods with two distinct categories of UPFs: (1) HFSS-UPFs (i.e., the category previously referred to as junk foods), and (2) healthier UPFs characterized by lower levels of fat, sugar, and salt and lower caloric density. If desirability-based preferences reflect the incentive salience or addictive potential associated with highly rewarding foods, then such preferences should be strongest for HFSS-UPFs and attenuated or absent for healthier UPFs. In contrast, if ultra-processing itself drives these effects, then both categories of UPFs should elicit similar patterns of preference. ### Hypothesis 1: Unprocessed Foods vs. HFSS-UPFs This comparison serves as a conceptual replication of our previous findings. **H1a.** Participants will show an implicit preference for unprocessed foods based on tastiness. **H1b.** Participants will show an implicit preference for HFSS-UPFs based on desirability. **H1c.** Participants will show an explicit preference for HFSS-UPFs based on tastiness. ### Hypothesis 2: Unprocessed Foods vs. Healthier UPFs This comparison tests whether ultra-processing alone is sufficient to produce the desirability-based preference previously observed for HFSS-UPFs. **H2a.** Participants will show an implicit preference for unprocessed foods based on tastiness. **H2b.** The implicit desirability preference observed for HFSS-UPFs will be significantly reduced when the comparison category consists of healthier UPFs. Consequently, participants will show either a weaker implicit preference for healthier UPFs based on desirability or no reliable desirability-based preference for either category. **H2c.** Participants will show an explicit preference for unprocessed foods based on tastiness, or at minimum a substantial attenuation of the explicit tastiness advantage previously observed for HFSS-UPFs. ### Hypothesis 3: Healthier UPFs vs. HFSS-UPFs This comparison provides the most direct test of whether the observed preferences are driven by the rewarding characteristics of foods rather than by ultra-processing per se. **H3a.** Participants will show an implicit preference for HFSS-UPFs based on tastiness. **H3b.** Participants will show an implicit preference for HFSS-UPFs based on desirability. **H3c.** Participants will show an explicit preference for HFSS-UPFs based on tastiness. Collectively, these studies test the prediction that desirability-based preferences track the rewarding properties of foods, particularly those associated with HFSS-UPFs, rather than the mere presence of ultra-processing. If supported, the findings would suggest that the implicit desirability effect previously observed in our research reflects the incentive salience of highly rewarding foods and may therefore provide insight into the mechanisms underlying the addictive potential of certain UPFs.

title_r: How visual and body-related action goals shape the arrow-based Simon effect
abstract_r: Most of the time, we perform actions with the goal of producing perceptual changes in our environment. Some models of action control, inspired by ideomotor theory, assume that our actions are indeed represented via those intended effects (e.g., Hommel et al., 2001). Sometimes, however, we aim to affect the state of our body itself, regardless of the consequences of our action in the environment, e.g., when stretching to relieve tensions in our muscles. Indeed, there is evidence that actions can be represented via such body-related effects as well (for a review, see Pfister, 2019). This distinction becomes especially intriguing when agents perform actions where both codes of those two effects - body-related and environment-related - are incompatible within a relevant feature. Imagine, for instance, turning a computer mouse 180 degrees - a visible cursor movement to the right will then be accompanied by the proprioceptive and tactile experience that comes with moving the arm to the left. Now, the action could be represented by two distinctly different spatial codes - a right code for the effect on the screen, and a left code for the effects related to the body. Most evidence suggests that the visual action effect is usually dominant (Kunde et al., 2007; Janczyk et al., 2015; for a review, see Sutter et al., 2013). However, this dominance has been found to be eliminated if agents act with the explicit goal to move the body (Hommel, 1993; Sabek et al., 2024). The present study serves as a conceptual replication of these findings in an online setting: Participants move an arrow on a screen to either the right or left in response to the arrow's color. Crucially, the direction of the arrow is irrelevant - only the color determines the correct response. In one condition, arrow movements to the right [/left] will be produced by mouse movements to the right [/left]. Here, the irrelevant stimulus feature (i.e., the arrow's direction) can therefore either be compatible with both effect types (e.g., arrow points right and the color prompts an arrow movement to the right that is produced by a mouse movement to the right), or incompatible with both (e.g., arrow points right, but the color prompts an arrow movement to the left that is produced by a mouse movement to the left). This will likely produce a Simon effect, with shorter response times in trials where the irrelevant stimulus feature is compatible as compared to incompatible with both kinds of effects. In a second condition, arrow movements to the right [/left] will be produced by mouse movements to the left [/right]. Here, the irrelevant stimulus feature (i.e., the arrow's direction) will therefore always be compatible with one effect, but incompatible with the other (e.g., arrow points right, but the color prompts an arrow movement to the left that is produced by a mouse movement to the right). Crucially, we will compare two groups of participants across these two conditions: One will be instructed in a manner that establishes an environment-related action goal (e.g., if the arrow is blue, move it to the left side of the screen), while the other will be instructed to pursue a body-related goal (e.g., if the arrow is blue, move the mouse to the right). While this should not affect the Simon effect in the condition where body- and environment-related effects are compatible, it has been shown to produce opposite RT patterns in the condition where both are incompatible (Hommel, 1993). Specifically, we expect that performance in the visual-goal condition will benefit when the arrow points in the same direction as the visual effect about to be perceived, while performance in the body-goal condition will benefit when the arrow points in the same direction as the body-related effects about to be perceived.

title_r: Acceleration Perception With Location Reproduction Replication
abstract_r: In previous studies (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3MW9S), we have found an expectation effect of gravity on reported acceleration perception such that downward moving stimuli are reported as less accelerating than upward moving stimuli — a repulsion from the expectation that objects normally accelerate toward the ground. This experiment aims to further understand the relative perceptual and decisional contributions to the effect. We therefore employ a paradigm where perception is measured via reproduction of perceived locations, rather than decisions about the acceleration profile. In this way, expectations about acceleration can be observed through participant reproduction of a location as opposed to decisions about the acceleration itself. Post hoc analysis of a pilot study (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BV3N2) revealed evidence for a repulsion in this reproduction paradigm and a follow up study (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/6TRCX) found a marginal effect of the pre-registered analysis. To determine whether there really is a reliable repulsion, we want to replicate the study with a larger sample size and add an additional analysis approach. Full details in the Preregistration document attached.
